Title: Latin America's Challenges in an Era of Secular Stagnation
text: Latin America's Challenges in an Era of Secular Stagnation1 1 Lecture presented at the Peterson Institute for International Finance, October 7th 2016. Pablo Garc92a-Silva Member of the Board - Central Bank of Chile Many thanks to the Peterson Institute for the opportunity to give this lecture on the state of Latin Americaabs macro economy, as well as its place in our shifting global environment. The opportunity is doubly appreciated as it allows me to cast a view a bit over the immediate horizon and beyond the day to day concerns of monetary policy. Important as these are, we oftentimes end up focused only on the short term conjuncture, unable to think through over the short term. We can hence miss the chance to look at the broader challenges we face in Latin America. Today I want to focus on the economic growth and adjustment challenge Latin America faces. Indeed, the pace of economic growth in Latin America has been below disappointing in recent years. Not since the episodes of the severe sovereign, financial and exchange rate crisis of early in this century we have witnessed such an underperforming of growth, compared to the world as a whole, and compared to both to advanced and emerging economies. Figure 1 d0 Comparative growth performance It could be argued that the openness of LAC economies has determined its growth performance over time. Given that international trade has remained muted, then maybe there lies the explanation for the weak growth in LAC? The answer is no. Admittedly global trade shows now a marked deceleration compared with the nineties, but it has remained stable following up overall global economic growth since the beginning of the decade. Thus, underperformance by LAC is still apparent once contrasted with the ups and downs of global trade. Forming up a view regarding the short term vs long term nature of this growth slump is particularly challenging is the current characteristics of the global growth process, usually dubbed secular stagnation, where d2[economies] suffer from an imbalance resulting from an increasing propensity to save and a decreasing propensity to invest. The result is that excessive saving acts as a drag on demand, reducing growth and inflation, and the imbalance between savings and investment pulls down real interest ratesd3.2 2 Summers, L. (2016), d2The Age of Secular Stagnation: What It Is and What to Do About Itd3, Foreign Affairs, February. It is hard to argue that some of these aspects might be at play once one looks at the revisions in expected growth and investment across different regions. Across the globe we have seen material downgrades in both variables since early last year, a pattern that can actually be traced to even earlier. It is noteworthy that although the contraction in expected investment growth is widely shared across economies, Latin America boasts the largest cumulative decline in expected GDP growth for 2016. (Figure 2) Figure 2 d0 Expected 2016 Growth and Investment revisions since January 2015 Source: Consensus Forecast. Commodity exporters include Australia, Canada and New Zealand. As a response to low trend and actual growth, low growth of real incomes, high savings relative to investment, and low or even negative inflation, neutral interest rates have been estimated to have declined. Recent studies show that the level of the neutral real interest rate has actually fallen systematically around the world, and may even indicate real neutral monetary policy rates that are negative. This has been one of the reasons used to justify the need for ultra loose monetary policy stances in mayor advanced economies. (Figure 3) Figure 3 d0 Real neutral interest rate in advanced economies Source: K. Holston, T. Laubach and J.C Williams (2016), d2Measuring the Natural Rate of Interest: International Trends and Determinants,d3 August. The implications of a persistent secular stagnation, with the resulting ultra-loose monetary stimulus in the advanced economies, needs to be seriously taken into account for Latin Americad5s prospects. This is either is a risk scenario with a high likelihood of occurrence, or it is actually the current reasonable baseline. Either way, we need to ponder what the implications of secular stagnation can be for growth in Latin America going forward. From this vantage I will elaborate three main themes in my presentation. Firstly, I will discuss how the ultra loose monetary policies in Advanced Economies have changed or distorted the standard international monetary transmission mechanism, and will contrast the current situation with the immediate aftermath of the Great Financial Crisis. I believe this change has bearings on the nature of the cross border spillovers from monetary policies to Latin America. Secondly, secular stagnation has implications for medium term growth. It will be useful to recap what the views are regarding the drivers of growth for Latin America, and how secular stagnation can affect them. Thirdly, I will conclude by discussing to what extent we have the appropriate policy levers and policy space in Latin America to manage the implications of these policies in the short term, as well as what challenges we face in the medium run to achieve higher and sustainable rates of economic growth. The implications of extraordinary monetary measures in advanced economies A useful starting point is a simplified version of the mechanism of monetary policy transmissions and international spillovers.3 A common approach is to visualize domestic the monetary policy stance (current and expected) affects expected inflation by way of two main channels: the credit and expenditure channel and the exchange rate channel. A monetary expansion results in increased inflation through both channels, as it encourages credit generation, provides incentives to anticipate consumption and investment decisions, boosts employment, while at the same time depreciating on impact the value of the currency, as shown in the diagram below. 3 A more detailed version of the transmission mechanisms as seen at the Central Bank of Chile can be found in d2Central Bank of Chile: Monetary Policy in an Inflation Targeting Frameworkd3 (2007), box No. 5. Figure 4 d0 Mechanisms of monetary policy transmission It is straightforward to add an international dimension to this view, driven by the spillovers of monetary policy in the rest of the world. International monetary conditions will affect cross border portfolio and direct investment flows, through bank and non-bank intermediaries, and will as well have an impact in currency valuations (amongst other asset prices). In a simplified way, his will impact domestic inflation through similar channels as domestic monetary policy: on the one hand cross-border flows change local borrowing and lending conditions, which have an effect on the aggregate real economy, whilst exchange rate movements impact the domestic prices of imported goods. How does this play out in terms of the implications for domestic monetary policy? Letd5s take as an example a monetary easing in the United States to deal with a debilitated US economy. This will encourage lending and risk taking, will depreciate the dollar against other currencies in the world and will push up commodity prices. Across the world economies see their currencies strengthen and experience capital flowing in. Since the domestic dynamics are not necessarily those of the US, it may be expected that monetary policy will become tighter to avoid an inflationary surge. Such a tighter policy is in turn consistent with the appreciating currencies vis-88-vis the US Dollar. Over time, to the extent that lax monetary policy in the US succeeds in boosting growth and raising expected inflation, interest rate increases, strengthening the dollar in the world and reversing the previous process. Thus, as the US economy strengthens, the other economies are confronted with depreciating exchange rates pressures and capital outflows, pushing them into a weakening cycle that is addressed with a looser monetary policy. Thus, some degree of monetary policy autonomy is achieved from this exchange rate flexibility, easing the process of adjustment insofar it smooths the ebbs and flows of global financial conditions and limits the extent of boom-bust credit swings and foreign exchange accumulation/deccumulation cycles. The way the international adjustment mechanism works in principle helps channel fluctuations in price pressures through current account and exchange rate movements. In periods of high growth, cost-push pressures from reduced slack in the economy are partially offset by a strengthened currency, and the significant vigor of domestic demand shifts to the imported components of expenditure. Conversely, in periods of slowdown the current account deficit narrows, the exchange rate weakens, and inflationary pressures over the medium term ease up. If monetary policy is credible, it can actually engage in countercyclical monetary policy, accommodating the real and monetary adjustment to changing global circumstances. The past few decades in Latin America provide a good case study of this standard model of international macroeconomic adjustment. Periods of looser monetary policy in advanced economies (particularly the US), coincided with an upswing in economic growth, increased capital inflows and current account deficits. (Figure 5) Reversal of these circumstances then led to economic slowdowns if not outright recessions. The average Latin American story from this prism hides significant heterogeneity. It is painfully clear that these swings not always, if ever, allowed a smoothing through countercyclical monetary policy reaction. Chile is a good example in which this was the case. Figure 5 d0 Macroeconomic cycle in Latin America, 1994 - 2016 Sources: World Economic Outlook and Bank for International Settlements. Real Exchange Rate (RER) index the simple average of Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Mexico and Per9c. An increase denotes a depreciation. 2016 considers IMF forecasts and information as of August for the RER. The broad contours of the process mentioned above transpired in Chile in a context of sustained price and financial stability. The immediate post GFC period saw a sharp increase in growth, a strengthening currency, and very low inflation, in spite of which monetary policy quickly tightened. Conversely, over the post Taper Tantrum period, growth stalled, the currency weakened, inflation increased, and monetary policy shifted to a stimulative stance. Throughout these ups and downs in the cycle, expected inflation remained strongly aligned with the 3% target. (Figure 6) Figure 6 d0 Macroeconomic cycle in Chile, 2001 - 2016 Source: Central Bank of Chile. The output gap bands reflects the range of different estimates. The prevalence of ultra-expansionary monetary policies in the developed world hinders the direct application of this vision of the international monetary adjustment. I dond5t think we can blame it on a failure of the model, rather it is a challenge to ponder what are the innovative elements we must input and how they affect the international transmission. It may be odd to bring up this subject as original, since d2we were thered3 in the period 2010-2013. But todayd5s circumstance is qualitatively and quantitatively different. Not only have monetary policy rates pierced their theoretical zero lower bound (in the Eurozone, Sweden, Switzerland and Denmark), but huge quantitative expansions (QE) have been added to the short-term interest rate policy by the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan. This has resulted in the yields on sovereign bonds from several advanced economies plummeting. Although the US Federal Reserve is in a different situation, the maintenance for quite longer of a looser monetary policy also is part and parcel of this extraordinary monetary stimulus across the globe. (Figure 7) Figure 7 d0 Monetary policy across advanced economies Short-term interest rates (*) Solid line shows monetary policy rates; dotted lines show overnight deposit rates. Long-term interest rates Source: Bloomberg. Net supply of securities in the Eurozone (*) Includes purchases under the ECBd5s QE program and longer-term refinancing operations (LTROs). Moving sum of 4 quarters. Source: Citi Research. The transmission of this type of monetary easing differs materially from the standard case. Due to market structure, competitive practices, and in some cases regulatory constraints, negative short-term interest rates have not been transmitted fully into equally negative deposit rates for retail bank clients in these economies. Since central banks have also used quantitative easing in a whole set of assets, market interest rates and credit risk premiums have contracted. This mix of policies has implied that the typical positive effect of an expansionary monetary policy on bankd5s interest spreads, consistent with a steepening of the yield curve, has not materialized as strongly in the current juncture. Some even argue that it might be operating inversely.4 4 M. Brunnermeier and Y. Koby (2016), d2The Reversal Interest Rate: The Effective Lower Bound of Monetary Policyd3. On the contrary, the effect of this monetary policy via the exchange rate channel operates with no impediment, or even more powerfully, thanks to the specifics of the quantitative easing process of the central banks. These prevent the yield curve from a steepening that would constrain to some extent the exchange rate pass-through. This has been coupled in some cases by massive forex interventions. The combination of secular stagnation, quantitative easing, and low or negative short terms interest rates, makes the spillover effects from global monetary policy has become lopsided towards disinflation in emerging economies. (Figure 8) Figure 8 d0 Mechanisms of monetary policy transmission under secular stagnation, QE and NIRP I believe this kind of phenomenon is behind the developments of the past year: more expansionary monetary policies in the advanced economies buttress appreciating currencies, but with only a very tepid reaction from capital flows, credit, spending and activity. The disconnect between global interest rates that remain at historic lows, similar to those we experienced in 2010-2012, a real exchange rate that has been appreciating, and lack of capital inflows is telling. The lack of sustained recovery in commodity prices is another reflection of this lopsided international transmission of monetary policy. (Figure 9) Figure 9 d0 Capital flows and the real exchange rate in Latin America Sources: BIS, EPFR One can note that Latin American economies are small and quite integrated. Therefore these financial factors have effects on our domestic financial markets. Specifically, the equilibrium with low real long-term interest rates in the world has also shifted towards our own financial markets, which in several cases display a clear downward trend. (Figure 10) Figure 10 d0 Long term interest rates in Latin America Source: Bloomberg This may signify that stabilizing inflation also requires a lower neutral interest rate. At the Central Bank of Chile we have taken that into consideration into our own forecasting and policy analysis.5 6 5 L.O. Herrera and R. Caputo (2013), d2Efficient CPI-based Taylor Rules in Small Open Economiesd3, BCCh Working Paper 694. 6 L. Ceballos, J. Fornero and A. Gatty (2016), d2Estimaci97n de la tasa de inter8es real neutral en Chiled3, included in Monetary Policy Report, September 2016, Central Bank of Chile. The anemic growth in investment around the world also takes a toll on the countryd5s capital accumulation and economic growth. To the extent that the saving and investment equilibrium in the advanced world tends to generate smaller current account deficitsd1or greater surplusesd1, pressures will push the opposite way in emerging economies, encouraging further exchange rate appreciation but with no commensurate increase in economic activity. Medium term growth challenges for Latin America Looking over the medium term, what kind of effects, beyond the obvious ones, could be expected from secular stagnation on growth in Latin America? To answer that question we need to look at the drivers of growth: trade linkages, capital accumulation, educational attainment. To start, a clear link appears in that the swings in economic growth follow quite closely the swings in the terms of trade in LAC economies. Almost to a hilt, since 1990 years of increasing terms of trade are years of accelerating growth. There are a few exceptions, again in the early nineties, and more recently when the economy has kept on contracting even though the terms of trade recovered somewhat. Moreover, apart from a few years right before the GFC, LAC economies have seen a systematic deficit in the current account. The relationship between capital flows, the current account deficit and growth is not obvious due precisely to the terms of trade. During periods of expansion, capital inflows finance domestic credit flows to investment and consumption, over and above the boost provided by terms of trade gains, whereas in periods of contraction, the plummeting terms of trade imply also the need for increased external finance to limit the extent of contraction in domestic demand. These patterns of growth and the terms of trade are distinct from what can be seen in other regions. A fair comparison is with ASEAN-5 economies. They are at a similar stage of development, they have transited from a periods of authoritarian rule to a higher degree of democratization, and they boast abundant natural resources. They have also shown a markedly fast development of their manufacturing sector. The patterns of growth, terms of trade and the current account are significantly different that in LAC. (Figure 10) Figure 10 d0 Growth, terms of trade and the current account in ASEAN-5 Economic growth has been significantly less volatile than in LAC. After a very quick recovery in the aftermath of the Asian crisis, growth has remained stable within a relatively narrow range of 4 to 6% per year. The GFC did have an impact but it was exceedingly minor. More importantly, the link to terms of trade fluctuations is materially weaker than in the case of LAC. Note that the economic recovery proceeded apace after the Asian crisis even through the terms of trade continued to contract. The follow-up increase in the terms of trade in the years previous to the GFC did not appear to be associated with significant growth acceleration, and as mentioned the impact of the GFC to the terms of trade was significantly larger than to growth. More recently, even though the terms of trade have remained quite stable, economic growth has resumed and is stable. Another striking difference with the patterns in LAC was the turnaround in the current account balances after the Asian Crisis. Whereas in the nineties this grouping of economies experienced current account deficits of around 5% of GDP, after the Asian crisis surpluses have been the norm. Unlike LAC, the current account reversal of the late nineties has been persistent in ASEAN-5. Regarding the underlying determinants of growth, Latin America and the ASEAN-5 economies also display significant differences. In spite of currently having similar levels of GDP per capita, the trend since the early eighties cannot have been different. Whereas the ASEAN economies seem to display the usual convergence story, steadily closing the gap, LAC countries showed divergence, during the lost decade of the eighties, and then a stabilization around a third of the G7 per capita GDP. Note how recent years have erased a sizeable fraction of the relative increase since the start of this century. Figure 11 d0 Per-capita GDP, as % of G7 The underlying factors behind this lackluster average of Latin America can be found both in capital accumulation and in educational attainment. Figure 12 shows that Latin America lags on both counts. The investment rate, as % of GDP, as remained stuck in the low 20d5s, whereas educational attainment has also stagnated since the eighties, at a level around 2/3s of the average years of schooling of G7 economies. ASEAN economies, in contrast, have not only catch up in educational attainment but also have surpassed Latin America as of 2010. Figure 12 d0 Investment and educational attainment* Concluding remarks and some policy implications for Latin America The arguments I have outlined present the challenges Latin America faces in an era of secular stagnation in Advanced Economies. On the one hand, it is undoubtedly the case that the prevalence of a low growth scenario, driven by lackluster investment, poses significant challenges to capital accumulation as a driver of growth in Latin America. Moreover, the implementation of ultra loose monetary policy, as argued here, appears to have limited cyclical upsides for economic growth in the short term, given the lopsided nature of the international monetary transmission mechanism today. Within these dark clouds lie however a few silver linings, in the extent of the adjustment in the macro economy and in societyd5s expectations, and in the validation of the macroeconomic frameworks. In the three and a half years since the Taper Tantrum episode put a sharp end to the idea that emerging economies could decouple from the international monetary transmissions, Latin America has undergone a painful process of adjustment to lower commodity prices, weaker currencies, decelerating growth and contracting investment. Painful as it has been, thanks to the sustained global monetary stimulus, the dreaded d2sudden stopd3 and current account deficit reversal did not materialize. The transition from the heady days of high commodity prices and high growth right after the GFC to the current state of lowered expectations is what lies behind most of the social and political tensions we have seen in Latin America. What is noteworthy is that, with only a few exceptions, the required downshift of societal expectations about what the economy can deliver, in terms of fiscal efforts for redistribution and income support, has occurred within a functioning democratic framework. In my view this is thanks to the overall environment of macroeconomic and financial stability we have witnessed. The inflation targeting and flexible exchange rate frameworks, key to maintain a modicum of monetary policy independence, have mostly proven resilient, whereas rigid exchange rate arrangements have not. Although the weakening exchange rates over 2014-2015 did generate inflation pressures upward, these have mostly reflected the one-off nature of the impact from relative price changes. In the case of Chile, long term inflation expectations remained firmly at the 3% target in spite of a significant jump in inflation from the exchange rate weakening. Figure 13 d0 Inflation and Monetary Policy Stance in Latin America Inflation Monetary Policy Rate Sources: Bloomberg, Central Bank of Chiled5s Survey of Economic Expectations, Central Bank of Per9c. Dotted lines are forecasts. The validation of this monetary framework, in the presence of low interest rates globally and low growth, points towards a gradual dissipation of inflationary pressures. The degree to which this creates some policy space for the easing of monetary policy will vary depending on each economyd5s circumstances. (Figure 13) Note that within the framework of inflation targeting an easing of policy in this environment is not because of exchange rate or short-term growth concernsd1however legitimated1but simply because in a scenario such as this inflation would tend to position itself below the target. Finally, the prevalence of a risk scenario of slow growth, disinflationary pressures and an appreciated exchange rate could generate an important policy dilemma in case that the monetary toolkit was near exhaustion. Of course, this is what we see in various advanced economies, even financially stable ones. Because of the high inflation we have endured across Latin America, the possibility of deflation and reaching the zero lower bound seems quite remote. For the same reason, the level of monetary policy interest rates is also far from the theoretical limits that can be conceived. 7 Therefore, as long as credibility on medium term inflation objectives is preserved, monetary policy in Latin America will have room to take action if necessary. Alternatively, a scenario of asset price inflation, and excessive froth in the credit market, is so far distant thanks to the tepid overall economic tone and the stability of commodity prices. 7 For these reasons the d2beggar-thy-neighbord3 cross-border spillover effects from monetary expansion in the zero lower bound found in Eggertsson, Mehrotra and Summers (2016), d2Secular Stagnation in the Open Economyd3 (NBER Working Paper No. 22172) are not directly applicable, yet, to Latin America. As we have known for a while, achieving macroeconomic and financial stability is not sufficient to successfully tackle the significant long term growth challenges Latin America faces, some of which I have briefly touched upon here. But by avoiding the mayor social dislocations that result financial instability appears to be necessary for such a task. So far, a global environment of secular stagnation, although not positive for growth or investment, does have some supportive elements that keep helping Latin America, at least in the short run. Thank you. Title: Does economic sovereignty still exist?
text: Does economic sovereignty still exist? Latam Russia India China South Africa Mario Marcel Portugal Ireland Les Recontres Economiques en Aix en Provence d2In a World in Turmoil, what is a Nation for?d3 Greece (right scale) Colombia Mexico Chile Peru Brazil Aix-en-Provence, France, 1-3 July Economic sovereignty may capture many dimensions of economic management d0tax policy, economic regulation, competition, labour markets, finance. Still, this panel is focused on macroeconomic policy, or the ability to stabilize the economy through fiscal and monetary policies. The organizers provocatively argue that such policies, delivered at the national level, have become unable to deal with crises that are systemic and global. Of course this assessment takes place against the background of the extended slowdown/recession that started in 2007. This has been an extraordinary period with three crises following each other: (a) the US financial crisis of 2007-2009; (b) the eurozone recession of 2010-2014, and the EME slowdown of 2014 onwards. During this time, world growth has halved compared to the previous ten years, volatility has increased significantly, unemployment in the advanced economies has soared, and deflation has become a real, multi-country concern. The financial sector has been particularly vulnerable and some of its recent wounds are feared to reopen with new shocks. Indeed, finance is the common thread across these three episodes and what makes them truly global. When we speak of systemic and global crises, finance is usually at the core of it. Finance flows and operations donabt recognize borders and national policies can do little about them. Even the re-regulatory zeal prompted by the 2008 crisis has died out, especially in Europe, where major global banks still cannot completely clean their portfolios, despite all the help from governments and regional institutions. As for EMEs, capital flows tend to be very volatile and subject to the changes in risk apetite from investors, independently of national fundamentals prompting major swings in currencies (Figure 1). Figure 1. Capital Flows to EM (annual, USD billions) Source: IMF and EPFR Still, it should be noted that not all economic shocks and crises are systemic and global. There are a number of current developments with a strong idiosyncratic origin. These include the recessions in Brazil, Russia and South Africa; the origins of the Greek crisis, and the Chinese rebalancing d0even if it involves only a slowdown. The recent past also includes critical economic episodes in South East Asia, the dot-com sector in the US, Sweden and Denmark, to name only a few. Brexit is indeed a national-based phenomenon, no matter the justifications given by its promoters. Since many of these episodes had substantial spillovers on other countries one may wonder if an extra dose of globality d0reflected in greater responsibility towards the resto of the Worldd1could have help prevent or mitigate them. Still, the question remains: how much can national policies do to limit the domestic impact of such global events? In my view, there are four factors that are crucial in facing external shocks and minimize their impact, even if no one is fully immune to them: 1. Financial buffers and shock absorbers, that help withstand market turbulence 2. Price flexibility, to speed up national responses 3. A deep and well capitalized financial sector that can absorb part of the costs and limit the spread of malaise to other sectors of the economy 4. A social protection system that can limit social costs and the multiplier effects of shocks into consumption This list should make it clear that if countries cannot prevent an external shock, surely there is still a lot they could do to isolate it and prevent contagion to critical areas of the domestic economy. Moreover, I would argue that many of the recent crisis spread out because of the absence of one or more of the factors listed above. For example, when we speak of the ineffectiveness of fiscal policy, it is frequently due to having a highly indebted public sector from the very start (Italy) with limited tolerance for additional debt, or by governments being fiscally overwhelmed by the bail-out of failing private financial institutions (Ireland, Portugal, Spain) or by the interest bill growing rapidly as the cost of new debt escalates (all the above). Reducing gross debt buildup through more conservative fiscal policies, building Chinese walls between governments and banks and minimizing refinancing or liquidity risks, are very simple strategies to secure a fully operative fiscal policy. Take now monetary policy. Everybody acknowledges that central banks saved the world from a disastrous depression some seven years ago by providing liquidity at a time it was being sucked by financial turmoil and uncertainty. To do so, monetary authorities walked into uncharted territory to support the economy in the face of challenging conditions, like the reduction of money multipliers by banks withholding funds in the light of heightened risk perceptions, uncertainty over the quality of their portfolios or capitalization needs. Monetary policy has also helped gain competitiveness through its effects on exchange rates, even if such gains have proved short-lived due to competing moves elsewhere. As we know, the main challenge in advanced countries today is to avoid deflation, in a context of weak investment, trade and manufacturing growth. There are many countries in the world that manage their economies on the basis of national fiscal and monetary policies. Certainly some of the BRICs mentioned, many EMEs, but also advanced countries that are not attached to any bloc, like Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Corea or Sweden. This last group of countries has something very important in common: they all faced economic crises of their own in the 10-15 years prior to 2007. So it looks that they learned something from it. Their fiscal response to the crisis in 2008-2010 is very telling in this regard (Table 1). Table 1. Fiscal Behaviour of OECD countries 2007-2013 (Percentajes of GDP) Source: Marcel (2013) Prior to the crisis, the US and the Eurozone thrived on the illusion of being protected from internal or external shocks. Regulators were too slow in responding to the challenges posed by new financial products and risk mismanagement and even misinformation. Eurozone countries borrowed at euro spreads under the (lendersab) assumption that they were backed by the stronger economies of the bloc and violated fiscal rules even in good times. EMEs suffered from a similar veil that prevented countries from recognizing their own weaknesses even during the first stages of the long recession. The prolongued commodity boom created the illusion that many of these countries had finally matured to a point where they could afford countercyclical policies, for the first time in their modern economic history. Once they were unable to unwind their expansionary policies after the emergency and the downside of the cycle caught them with high debt and growing inflation, many have had to return to the old procyclical response of cutting spending and raising interest rates. In my view, this illusion of protection is what explains the severity of the economic crisis and what may lead to blame the d2systemd3 for the current state of affairs. A major question in this regard is whether markets suffer from a similar level of myopia that obscures the true vulnerabilities of domestic economies in the face of a thriving economy, regional risk pooling or booming commodity prices. Figures 2a and 2b present the CDS Spreads series from before the financial crisis for Eurozone and LAC countries. It should be evident that up to mid-2009, spreads for Eurozone countries were almost identical, with the exception of Ireland, where a financial and housing bubble exploded at a similar time than in the US. In the case of LAC distinctions have been more marked, with countries differentiating significantly from each other at various stages, partly due to the fact that commodities do not follow identical cycles anyway. Figure 2a: CDS Spreads in Eurozone countries 2007-2015 (basis points) Figure 2b: CDS Spreads in LAC countries 2007-2015 (basis points) Source: Bloomberg So if effective national macro policies are feasible, what are regional economic blocs for? While regional integration offers a number of benefits on the real economy side, macro policy essentially benefits from the pooling of risks and liquidity. This involves a smaller effort in terms of the factors 1-4 listed above. In other words, regional integration lowers the cost of macro management in mild business cycles. But this involves two risks: first, this lowers the pressure to buildup macro defense mechanisms in good times; second, this may create a deep divide among countries in the same regional bloc in the case of substantial opposing balances. In the case of the Eurozone, for example, it suffered from the division between surplus and deficit, creditor and debtor countries throughout the crisis. Without exchange rates to differentiate each other, this left d2internal devaluationd3, that is, the change in relative prices and salaries through deflation, as the only adjustment mechanism. The former illustrates the point that regionalism is not a free lunch, since it should come with substantial requirements on collective action. Regionalism could be used to build policy coherence. This relates not only to institutions (like financial regulation or deposit insurance), but also to limit internal imbalances. The current discourse against British opportunism after Brexit should be extended to many members that profit from benefits while paying little costs for EU membership. In sum, globalization has not necessarily made national macro policies ineffectual, as testified by the reality of many countries in recent years. Price flexibility, fiscal prudency, strong reserves, access to liquidity and a solid financial sector can do a lot to limit, isolate and compensate the impact of external shocks, as demonstrated by the experience of many countries that learned from past crises. Alternatively, countries can take shelter in broader alliances, pooling their risks and resources for more efficient protection. However, regional systems also need to prepare and be ready to react to crises, which, in turn requires effective collective action mechanisms. As usual, there are no free lunches here.

Title: Monetary Policy Report Presentation Before the Finance Commission of the Honorable Senate of the...
text: Logo only PRESENTATION OF THE MONETARY POLICY REPORT TO THE FINANCE COMMITTEE OF THE HONORABLE SENATE OF THE REPUBLIC. . The December 2019 Monetary Policy Report can be found at . Mario Marcel President Central Bank of Chile December 5, 2019 Introduction Mr. Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Senator Ricardo Lagos Weber. Senators members of this Commission, senators. I appreciate the invitation to present the vision of the Council of the Central Bank of Chile on recent macroeconomic developments, their prospects and the implications for monetary policy. This view is contained in detail in the December 2019 Monetary Policy Report (MPR), published this morning. This background also provides the background for the decision taken by the Council at the Monetary Policy Meeting on Wednesday. I must begin by thanking this Committee for having accepted our request to bring forward the delivery of this report, originally planned for next Monday. The country is going through complex times and the economy, as expected, is reflecting them strongly. This is confirmed by the significant fall of Imacec in October, the different sources of information that indicate a significant loss of jobs during November and the abrupt fall in household and business confidence. In such circumstances, it was important to be able to integrate this information, as soon as possible, into a medium-term perspective. The crisis that began on October 18 has been characterized by social demands that have led to the discussion of relevant institutional changes d1such as a new C3onstituci97nd1 and legitimate pressures for social benefits and rights with important fiscal implications. This process, however, has been accompanied by significant and prolonged episodes of violence, which have caused significant disruptions in the productive system, strongly affecting lower activity and weakening employment. Given the objectives and demands that the law imposes on the Central Bank of Chile, we will not enter into the discussion of the causes of the social outbreak, its dynamic manifestations and possible solutions. To this end, the analysis and reflections of various actors and observers of the social and political reality of the country abound. This report will concentrate only on its economic dimensions and, as usual, its implications for macroeconomic policy and monetary policy in particular. We believe that this is an approach that adds value, because the worst thing that can happen to a social and political crisis is that it is combined with an economic crisis, where resources and possibilities to solve problems would be considerably limited and others of equal or greater magnitude would arise. The history of Latin America has too many episodes of this nature to ignore. As we shall see, the macroeconomic outlook brings an additional degree of concern. The magnitude of the impact of the social crisis is comparable to some of the biggest shocks received in the past by the Chilean economy. Cushioning this impact will involve drawing on much of the slack and experience accumulated by economic authorities over the years. Indeed, only such slacks and an adequate economic policy framework will make it possible to cushion, But not to eliminate the likely consequences of the macro scenario on unemployment, growth and inflation. While part of the impact of the social crisis on the economy has to do with the difficulties for the functioning of the productive system, another, very significant, has to do with the financial system. The available information shows a significant increase in uncertainty and a deterioration in confidence that would be amplifying these effects. Financial markets have been stressed by strong movements in prices, which in some cases have gone beyond what is justifiable due to the greater perception of country risk. As a Council, we have taken a number of measures to improve liquidity in pesos and dollars, and we decided to intervene in the foreign exchange market to mitigate high exchange rate volatility and help adjustments occur appropriately. Consistent with the latter and the convergence of inflation to the target, we maintained the MPR at 1.75 percent at the Monetary Policy Meeting we held yesterday. The greater fiscal impulse recently announced, together with the already high expansionary of monetary policy, will help contain the deterioration of the economy, which after a contraction of 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 2019, will grow between 0.5 and 1.5 percent in 2020. While we expect the significant slowdown in growth to widen the activity gap over the monetary policy horizon, putting downward pressure on inflation, the financial impacts of heightened uncertainty, as well as the more persistent effects of the peso's depreciation, will increase inflationary pressures over the policy horizon. Based on this background, we believe that monetary stimulus is adequate to achieve the inflation target, bearing in mind the current state of the fiscal impulse and exchange rate policy. Market expectations, which do not anticipate major adjustments in the MPR and maintain a two-year inflation expectation at 3 percent, are consistent with this diagnosis. It should be noted that the projections of this IPoM are built in a context of greater uncertainty than usual. The baseline scenario assumes a pattern of recovery of the economy that begins incipiently in December, and then continues with a gradual improvement in demand. A key condition for this scenario to be fulfilled is that uncertainty is significantly reduced and that the different economic sectors can resume their production processes. As documented in one of the boxes of this IPoM (Box V.1), evidence of similar episodes in other countries shows that those societies that have reached agreements that improve institutionality and governance can go through these profound changes with limited effects on activity and employment. However, if this scenario does not occur, the evidence suggests a picture for the economy that will be significantly bleaker, where even the joint thrust of monetary and fiscal policy will be insufficient to avoid a recession and persistent rise in unemployment. Let me now describe our baseline projection scenario. Macroeconomic scenario As I indicated at the beginning, the social crisis generated important changes to the macroeconomic scenario. For the time being, it has negatively affected short-term activity. In October, Imacec recorded an annual drop of 3.4 percent, which was 4 percent in the non-mining Imacec, as a result of various disruptions that affected all economic sectors, including the damage and destruction of facilities, difficulties in moving workers and the reduction of operating hours. The sharpest declines were seen in trade, manufacturing production and various service lines, such as education, transportation, business services, and restaurant and hotel activity. Measured with respect to the previous month, and excluding seasonality, the instantaneous deterioration in activity was 6.1% in the non-mining sectors. All this occurred after the economy showed higher growth in the third quarter than in the first half of the year, in line with what was projected in the September IPoM (Graph 1). For November, the available background suggests that the performance of the economy was affected by the persistence of difficulties in operating under normal conditions, especially by the extension of episodes of violence throughout the country and by various impediments to the normal functioning of companies and public services. The impact on activity in November is also confirmed in the IMCE, which in that month showed an abrupt drop in the use of installed capacity. In the case of industry, it decreased to levels comparable to those recorded after the 2010 earthquake (Figure 2). The need to gather a greater number of antecedents regarding the evolution of the economy in recent weeks has led us to resort to new sources of information. Thus, during the third week of November, the Bank conducted a survey among the group of companies interviewed in the Business Perceptions Report (IPN), which reaches about 1,400. This directory considers companies in all regions and economic sectors of the country, with sales volumes and endowments that place them in the category of small, medium and large companies. The survey was conducted between November 19 and 26, accumulating a total of 343 responses. This survey was complemented by telephone interviews with about 40 companies with relevant regional and national representation, in order to have qualitative information in the light of which to better interpret the data obtained by the survey. Likewise, a consultation was carried out among the financial institutions that participate in the IPN d1mostly regional banking officesd1 and those that participate in the Bank Credit Survey (ECB). The results of this survey of information to companies are detailed in one of the boxes of this IPoM (Box III.1), accounting for the effects that the social outbreak has had on various areas of their performance, including activity, employment, investment, prices and credit conditions. In relation to November, these antecedents show that during that month a large majority of the companies consulted were affected by their performance, and a majority of them expect this effect to extend over the next two quarters (Chart 3). It is also striking that a very small number of the companies consulted mentioned that they would increase their endowment in 2020, and in fact the vast majority will either maintain it or reduce it. Regarding the investment planned for 2020, a very low percentage of those who have projects in the portfolio for next year ratified that they would carry them out as planned. On the contrary, most respondents are reviewing their execution (figure 4). In the baseline scenario, it is assumed that activity will have an annual fall of 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter of the year, which will be concentrated in October and November. December should show a somewhat better performance, but there is high uncertainty surrounding that projection. With this, in 2019 the total GDP will accumulate a growth of around 1 percent, considerably below what was expected in September (between 2.25 and 2.75 percent). This projection contemplates that both consumption and investment will have negative annual variations in the last part of 2019, with a weakness especially concentrated in its tradable components. The poor performance in the last quarter of 2019 delivers a low starting level for the economy in 2020. In fact, although it is estimated that quarter by quarter it will grow again, its annual rate of change would again be negative in the first quarter of next year. With this, for the year as a whole, GDP is expected to grow between 0.5 and 1.5 percent. Finally, for 2021 a recovery in growth is assumed as a result of a gradual recovery of the main components of expenditure and production, which, in any case, will be somewhat below the range of 3%-4% foreseen in the September IPoM (Table 1). Considering all these differences, the level of GDP at the end of 2021 would be around 4.5 percent lower than previously expected. The current scenario presents a greater degree of uncertainty than usual, both due to doubts regarding the duration of disruptions, and due to the evolution of the political situation and medium-term fundamentals. A key factor in the future evolution of the economy will be the confidence of households and companies, and its relationship with the performance of the labor market, consumption and investment. On the consumption side, surveys show that people's confidence deteriorated significantly after 18 October. Of note is the fall in perceptions of current and future economic developments, personal economic conditions, employment, and the timing of purchasing durable goods, which is at its lowest levels since records began (March 2002) (Figure 5). Various sources of information suggest that the labor market is already deteriorating. As I already indicated, in the Bank's survey, just over half of respondents believe that their endowment will have some decrease in 2020. On the other hand, compared to the same month of 2018, the figures of the Labor Directorate of November showed an increase of almost 13 percent in the number of labor settlements, which is explained almost entirely by dismissals due to company necessity (graph 6). If the historical relationship between labour demand and activity continues, and if there are no significant changes on the supply side, the unemployment rate could exceed 10 per cent by the beginning of 2020. To the extent that activity improves as expected over the next year, this figure would be gradually reduced, in which the support of monetary and fiscal expansionism would also cooperate. At the statistical close of this IPoM, no remuneration information was available during October. However, a reduction in income from sales commissions, overtime, work shifts that could not be performed and non-salaried workers who were unable to carry out their activities normally is foreseeable. As for investment, its expected evolution for 2020 is corrected significantly, projecting a fall of 4 percent per year in the base scenario. This reflects a significant decline in private non-mining investment. This is consistent with the greater uncertainty and sharp deterioration in business confidence, as reflected in November's IMCE, the higher costs faced by companies in various areas, including the effect of the depreciation of the peso on the cost of imported machinery, and the deterioration of financial conditions, including the fall in the stock market and increases in corporate rates and spreads (Chart 7). The negative impacts on investment are partially offset by the continuation of the large mining investment projects already started, which, according to qualitative information compiled by the Bank, have not been affected by their development after 18 October. The same does not happen in other sectors, where there is a reevaluation of the terms and amounts of investment previously committed, as shown by the Bank's aforementioned survey. The sharp adjustment in private spending will cause the current account deficit to be reduced significantly in 2020, reaching 0.2 percent of GDP, from the figure close to 3 percent that is estimated to close in 2019. The relevance of this adjustment is increased by considering that it occurs in circumstances in which the Government's savings are reduced. Although to a lesser extent, there is also a higher growth in exports, favoured by the real depreciation of the peso. A Box of this MPI (Box V.2) gives an account of how the dynamics of the current account have been in recent years. The recovery in growth expected throughout 2020 will be helped by a monetary policy that will continue to be expansionary, a greater fiscal impulse, the aforementioned recovery in exports and the gradual dissipation of uncertainty and disruptions that have affected the economy. On the fiscal front, the Minister of Finance made a series of announcements on Monday, December 2. These included an agenda of measures to support productive reactivation, including a series of investment programs and support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The resources involved in these measures reach 5 and a half billion dollars in 2020, of which About 3 billion will be financed from next year's budget. At the same time, a consolidated fiscal program for the period 2020-2022 was announced, which covers the resources committed in the newly approved budget plus the expenses in reactivation programs just mentioned and social programs that have been approved after the budget, including a bonus for one million three hundred thousand low-income households. With this, spending growth would be 9.8 percent in real terms compared to the previous year's budget, the structural deficit for 2020 would increase from 1.4 percent of GDP initially presented, to 3 percent of GDP and the effective deficit would increase to 4.4 percent of GDP. The structural deficit will then shrink at a rate of half a percentage point of GDP in 2021 and 2022, to reach 2 percent of GDP in the latter year. Financing for the larger deficit will come from government assets abroad, mostly denominated in foreign currency, and borrowing in foreign currency. With this, more than 11 billion additional dollars will be brought into the country, mostly in the first part of the year. This figure is very similar to the Central Bank's spot sale program, which I will explain in a few minutes, which will practically double the sale of foreign currency in the first months of 2020. As for gross public debt, the Ministry of Finance projections indicate that it would stabilize at around 38 percent of GDP by 2024. The deficit, structural and effective, figures scheduled for 2020 are very similar to those achieved in 2009. This expresses a declared more expansionary fiscal policy, which is complemented by monetary policy to face a significant economic shock, as it did on that occasion. This is reinforced by the concentration of higher expenditures on items with a greater multiplier effect, such as transfers to low-income sectors and investment. The change in the macroeconomic scenario has also been reflected in the evolution of the national financial market. In the days immediately following October 18, the effects were relatively limited. However, in the following weeks there was a deterioration of a set of financial indicators. Thus, the stock market fell, the peso depreciated significantly, interest rates and risk perception increased (Graph 8). As noted in one of the boxes of this IPoM (Box II.1), these movements have been characterized by high volatility that has been related to internal events. For example, the improvement they had after the signing of the agreement for a new constitution or, in the opposite direction, the resurgence of episodes of violence. At the statistical close of this IPoM, foreign markets had not been a major source of volatility. Heightened local uncertainty has begun to affect domestic credit conditions. While interest rates remain at historically low levels, various sources of qualitative information show a tightening of financial conditions. In particular, a special consultation of the Bank Credit Survey shows a significant drop in the perception of demand for credit, a deterioration in delinquencies and a greater restrictiveness of the supply of loans for individuals and companies (figure 9). The greater degree of uncertainty has given rise to strong movements in financial market prices, which in some cases have gone beyond what would be expected from the greater perception of country risk. The Bank has responded to these changes by taking various measures to provide an adequate degree of liquidity to markets and mitigate volatility in key financial prices. These measures are not intended to set "levels" of certain prices, but rather seek to avoid an excessive degree of volatility or abrupt movements that affect the healthy adjustment of the economy and cause concern in markets and people. In particular, it was decided to intervene the exchange market with an amount of up to 20 billion dollars, from Monday, December 2 until May 29, 2020. This will be implemented with a sale of spot dollars for an amount of up to 10 billion dollars and a sale of foreign exchange hedging instruments until a stock of 10 billion dollars is accumulated. The monetary effects of this measure will be sterilized, so that the provision of liquidity in pesos is consistent with the TPM. In the four days following the intervention announcement, exchange rate volatility, which had risen sharply until the previous Thursday, fell significantly (Chart 10). By 2021, GDP is projected to grow between 2.5 and 3.5 percent in the baseline scenario. This means that the disruptions that are affecting the economy will disappear over the course of the coming quarters, together with a reduction in uncertainty affecting consumption and investment decisions. In this scenario, investment will resume expansion rates above those of GDP towards the second half of 2021. The projections just described consider that the international scenario will not provide a significant boost to Chilean growth. The baseline scenario d0 following the sharp downward correction in September d0 continues to expect global growth in the 2020-2021 biennium to be among the lowest in a decade. The projected evolution of the terms of trade deteriorates somewhat compared to September, with copper prices averaging around 2.7 per pound in 2020 and 2021 (Table 2). In the baseline scenario, total inflation is projected to approach 4 percent during the second and third quarters of 2020, while core inflation will occasionally steepen slightly above 3.5 percent by mid-year, largely responding to the idiosyncratic depreciation of the peso, which involves a higher-than-average pass-through to inflation (Chart 11). This, since in these circumstances there are no cushioning factors, such as the fall in dollar prices of imported products that occurs in the face of a global appreciation of the dollar. Indeed, the contraction in fourth-quarter GDP and the weaker outlook for 2020 widen the activity gap, partly offsetting higher inflationary pressures in the tradable component of inflation. However, the recent idiosyncratic depreciation of the Chilean peso limits the space for monetary policy action, with respect to a situation where the weakness of the currency is transversal for all trading partners. Sensitivities and alternatives to the base scenario We estimate that there are scenarios in which growth may be within projection ranges, but require a different TPM trajectory to ensure convergence of inflation to the target. On the one hand, the economy may underperform. This could occur if investment suffers beyond what is contemplated, for example, if large projects in the mining sector are postponed and/or housing investment suffers a more pronounced adjustment. In such a scenario, we could see an even greater increase in unemployment and GDP growth close to the lower values of the projected range, increasing the probability of a recession during 2020 d0 defined as two consecutive quarters with a negative quarterly change in GDP. There are also scenarios where depreciative pressures on the peso intensify, for example, due to a resurgence of external uncertainty and/or a deepening of the internal crisis. Although this scenario would also imply a larger activity gap, it would be accompanied by a depreciation that would increase inflationary pressures. Nor can a scenario be ruled out where labour cost inflexibilities predominate, leading to a further increase in unemployment and inflation, together with a deeper contraction in activity. Although it is also possible that there will be a scenario where uncertainty is reduced and confidence recovers more quickly, we believe that, in the current context, scenarios of greater weakness in activity and the labour market are more likely, although it is more difficult to anticipate their consequences on inflationary dynamics, given the conflicting effects that some of them may have on prices. We expect the nominal Monetary Policy Rate to remain at its current level over the coming months, consistent with the achievement of the inflation target, in a context of increased fiscal stimulus and exchange rate intervention. In any case, monetary policy will be contributing to the recovery, as it is, in real terms, below what was expected in the September IPoM, especially if the comparison extends over several months. The calibration of monetary stimulus will be particularly challenging in the future, and will depend, among other factors, on the evolution of activity, the labour market, the exchange rate and inflation expectations. There are other scenarios where the performance of the economy would escape the projection ranges previously discussed. For example, if the deterioration in consumption and investment fundamentals deepens, demand could contract and precipitate a period of more persistent economic contraction. To the extent that the deflationary pressures associated with this scenariod1in particular the evolution of the activity gapd1dominate inflation dynamics over the policy horizon, this could lead to the use of a significant part of the remaining monetary policy space. It is also possible that the trend growth of the economy may be affected by a more sustained reduction in investment, labour market distortions and/or a deterioration in productivity. In this case, although the monetary impulse required to achieve the goal of Inflation would be lower, convergence would occur with a lower level and pace of economic growth. A particularly worrisome scenario could occur if regulatory changes lead to increases in labor costs significantly above the increase in productivity, in a context of economic weakness. While this could significantly increase unemployment and affect economic growth, increased inflationary pressures would limit the countercyclical role of monetary policy. Final Thoughts The social crisis that our country is facing has implied new and important challenges for all Chileans. We, who perform public functions, are primarily responsible for generating responses, from each of our areas of competence, that help overcome the complex moment that the country is experiencing, avoiding higher costs for the population. As far as the Central Bank of Chile is concerned, in recent weeks we have acted on practically all fronts of our competence. In compliance with our legal mandate to safeguard currency stability and the normal functioning of internal and external payments, we have adopted a number of measures to provide liquidity to the markets and have initiated significant foreign exchange intervention, in order to facilitate price adjustment and reduce exchange rate volatility, preventing this from having additional effects on activity, employment and inflation. In these decisions, attention is usually drawn to the instruments, the operational design, the resources involved. But we must also highlight the challenge demanded by its implementation, which requires a deep knowledge of the financial market, extracting information in real time, designing instruments that ensure efficiency and safeguard the Bank's assets and carrying out the operations themselves in the markets. We have also helped to safeguard the normal operation of financial infrastructures and payment systems, which have operated smoothly. A topic of particular concern in the early days was the retail payments system, partially affected by the destruction of bank branches and ATMs, a problem virtually overcome thanks to coordination with the CMF, banks and securities transport companies. Electronic means of payment, on the other hand, functioned normally. The elaboration of this IPoM has imposed relevant challenges on us. For a long time, our work had been oriented to assess the impacts of external shocks and the internal cycle, always within a relatively gradual evolution. However, today we are facing an internal shock that has suddenly increased uncertainty in many areas. Therefore, measuring its scope and persistence on economic and financial variables is much more complex. This has meant an important challenge in the use of our analysis instruments, the generation of judgments around it and decision making. The challenges start with measuring the immediate impact of the crisis. A month ago, when this had only been a couple of weeks, the expectations of the market regarding what had been the performance of the activity in October pointed to a fall that today we would qualify as slight. Even in the second week of November, the Survey of Economic Expectations showed a fall of the Imacec of 0.4 percent annually, far from the figure we knew on Monday, with a decrease of 3.4 percent. The contrast of both figures shows that when there are strong disruptions in the economy, with a social and political origin, the speed of events can be much higher than normal, while statistical regularities and traditional sources of information can lose value. In fact, bringing forward the presentation of this IPoM has been intended to help fill some of these gaps, so as not to delay the delivery of information that citizens, authorities and markets need. To this end, we have complemented traditional analysis with new data sources and references to other experiences of social disruption. This is especially relevant because not only must we have a diagnosis of what is happening today, but we must also make projections in the midst of a phenomenon that is unprecedented in the Chilean economy. In this way, the Bank has made every effort to generate additional information, review and enrich its projection models, its analysis, and its ability to make appropriate judgments and timely decisions. In this we have built on projects in development, on access and use of microdata databases and market intelligence that are part of our strategic plan. In this task we have also been helped by the greater knowledge we have acquired about the functioning of the labour market, which is part of the same strategy. However, all these efforts and initiatives are not enough to clear the great uncertainty that marks the current moment. Uncertainty that increases in the face of the prolongation of the abnormal conditions in which the country is operating. The combination of monetary and fiscal policy that has been brewing provides important support for the stabilization of the economy, similar to the response to the global financial crisis of 2008-2009. But it is clear that as long as the underlying uncertainty is not resolved, the costs to the economy, and especially to people, will continue to rise. Our baseline scenario considers projections that, if fulfilled, will make the level of output d0 and therefore the level of income and wealth of all Chileans d0 much lower than we had projected only three months ago. But, if a situation in which the economy cannot operate in the right conditions continues, we may be faced with a scenario in which employment, income and people's quality of life are even more affected. For that reason, along with making efforts to contribute from our sphere of responsibility to reduce uncertainty, we believe that there are two immediate challenges, in which we require support from Congress. The first is to close the pending issues of political definition as soon as possible. One One of the great lessons that this crisis has left us is the need to generate broad agreements on issues that are relevant to everyone. In this sense, the agreements on tax reform, the process for a new Constitution and the dispatch of the Budget for 2020, are clear examples of how cooperation in the political world can help reduce uncertainty while providing a medium-term framework for public finances and responses to the most pressing problems of the population. Such agreements not only help to alleviate human and social problems, but also to restore confidence in institutions. The second is that they allow us to concentrate all our efforts on the tasks assigned to us by law: controlling inflation and promoting financial stability. Faced with the possibility of adding new tasks to the Central Bank, we cannot lose sight of the situation facing the country and the consequent need to have all our resources in order to stabilize the economy and finances. This does not mean that the Bank considers that it does not have room to improve its work, contributing, from its sphere of competence, to raising the welfare of the population. I would like to share with you some thoughts on this. First, the experience of these weeks of social crisis shows the relevance of the Bank's main objectives. Many thought, for example, that, after decades of low inflation, this was no longer a concern for the population. However, the fact that the current crisis has been triggered by an increase in the fare of the Santiago Metro and that the cost of living is cited as one of the main causes of citizen unrest, indicates that it is an issue that maintains full d0 or even greater d0 validity. Indeed, when people talk about "cost of living" they include many more elements than the prices of an average basket of consumption, highlighting some particularly sensitive prices, financing costs, indebtedness and income. We believe that this background confirms the importance of maintaining a firm commitment to price stability, since the sensitivity of the population to high inflation rates may actually be greater than in the past, when it was part of their daily lives. Similarly, the fact that 38 years have passed since the last financial crisis does not mean that financial stability is no longer relevant to people. The queues in front of ATMs in the first weeks of the crisis highlights how central the availability of cash is, especially in times of uncertainty. It is also evident the importance of having a healthy financial system, which provides adequate services to the population. We have reiterated on several occasions the importance of maintaining a sense of urgency regarding reforms that allow adequate monitoring of people's debt burden. The volatile behavior of some financial prices, including the exchange rate, also draws our attention to the frictions and nonlinearities that can occur in markets when they are exposed to abrupt changes in risk perceptions. These are especially relevant if one takes into account that the normal operation of the financial system is essential for transactions of all kinds between people, companies and government to function properly. A second lesson concerns the importance of maintaining a sense of urgency about reforms that benefit people and prevent abuse. A few weeks ago we recalled in this Committee that the Bank has been insisting for years on the need to establish a unified register of debts, in a context in which the over-indebtedness of important segments of the population has been based on the ignorance of its true level of commitments with different creditors. We can now confirm that the Executive will soon send a new bill on the matter for discussion in the National Congress. Third, the importance of looking beyond aggregate figures and large averages should be highlighted. Although this is the ecosystem in which macroeconomists normally operate, doing so can lose sight of the reality faced by important sectors of the population and fundamental aspects of the behavior of economic agents. Fortunately, the Central Bank has been developing, for several years, an agenda to obtain and use microdata, which allows to achieve much more granularity in the analysis. Thus, the databases we were using to better understand the behavior of the labor market for macroeconomic analysis have been fundamental to identify and quantify the knock-on effect of the problems faced by some companies most affected by attacks on their infrastructure and shutdowns in recent weeks. A fourth lesson is that the slacks that accumulate in periods of abundance and tranquility must be available for use in periods of crisis. For many years the authorities argued about the importance of these clearances, accumulating and protecting them, while stress analyses evaluated their relevance in more complex scenarios. Many saw in this an excessive zeal or orthodoxy. Now that a crisis has truly been faced, these slacks have been invaluable in cushioning the impact of the crisis and articulating response measures. In this period, the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance have shown determination to use these resources, which will allow the impact of an unprecedented shock to be lessened. The last, but no less important lesson we draw from this period is the need to explain, educate, listen and put yourself in the shoes of others to build the public trust that is so crucial in periods of tension. In this same perspective, it is important to value other disciplines to understand phenomena that, although they have an economic expression, have an origin in other dimensions of the life of a country. A few months ago, before the social outbreak, I said that I did not consider that economists had the patrimony of truth, but that did not stop them from making a contribution to public policy decisions. Such interdisciplinary dialogue and cooperation, based on humility and recognition of a shared task, is especially important today in Chile. The Central Bank will contribute what is in its hands to help build it. Dear Senators, This IPoM is undoubtedly the most difficult since the inflation targeting framework was implemented in Chile. Difficult in its preparation, difficult because of the dimensions of uncertainty and difficult in its message. We are aware that we are not bearers of good news, but we are convinced that the country today needs its Central Bank to speak frankly, honestly and with technical support, because it is from there that it will be able to face the social crisis we are experiencing. The projections of this IPoM speak of falls in activity, large economic losses for some sectors, job losses and enormous challenges for the recovery, especially if it is to occur without further pressure on the cost of living and the well-being of citizens. It is not in our nature to give false hope, or to make people believe that it will be easy to figure things out. Nor can we give the impression that there are unlimited resources and instruments for the economy and the population to go through this turbulent period unscathed. As we pointed out earlier, the authorities and Chileans in general will have to work hard to avoid the most damaging and persistent consequences in unemployment and inflation, which we know would also increase levels of inequality. This is a time when every day of delay has an enormous cost, where we must be able to have an overview and in which, faced with each topic of discussion, we must ask ourselves not only what we can gain, but also how much we can lose. This, especially when those who stand to lose the most are Chileans whose dissatisfaction and demands have awakened these days. Suffice it to say that if unemployment were to stand at around 10 percent and inflation were to steepen to 6 percent d1 double the Central Bank's target d1 the Gini coefficient, which measures inequality in income distribution, would go back 27 years, to the values it exhibited in the early nineties. In sum, dear Senators, I think there is no doubt that we face an enormous challenge. Our economic policy framework has allowed us to react appropriately, maintaining a highly expansionary monetary policy that provides the necessary space for fiscal policy to act strongly. At the same time, we have taken measures, including foreign exchange intervention, to prevent financial markets from experiencing episodes of stress that affect financial conditions for the rest of the economy. But, commitment, cooperation and concrete actions are still required to ensure that the country will overcome this crisis and use it as an opportunity to improve the lives of all its inhabitants. The last few hours have been encouraging in terms of the progress of important initiatives, reaffirming respect for the Constitution. It seems to us that this Commission, where the first of the cross-cutting agreements was reached in response to the crisis, is a particularly appropriate place to reaffirm the value of that commitment to the country, a commitment of which the Central Bank feels a part. Thanks a lot

Este proceso, sin embargo, ha sido acompaado de episodios de violencia, significativos y prolongados, los que han provocado importantes disrupciones en el sistema productivo, incidiendo fuertemente en una menor actividad y debilitando el empleo. Este Informe se concentrar solo en sus dimensiones econmicas y, como de costumbre, sus implicancias para la poltica macroeconmica y la poltica monetaria en particular. Consideramos que este es un enfoque que aade valor, porque lo peor que le puede pasar a una crisis social y poltica es que se combine con una crisis econmica, donde los recursos y las posibilidades para resolver los problemas se veran considerablemente limitados y surgiran otros de igual o mayor envergadura. La historia de Amrica Latina tiene demasiados episodios de esta naturaleza como para ignorarlos. Como veremos, la perspectiva macroeconmica aporta un grado adicional de preocupacin. La magnitud del impacto de la crisis social es comparable con algunos de los mayores shocks recibidos en el pasado por la economa chilena. Amortiguar dicho impacto involucrar recurrir a gran parte de las holguras y a la experiencia acumulada por las autoridades econmicas a lo largo de los aos. De hecho, solo esas holguras y un marco adecuado de poltica econmica harn posible amortiguar, pero no eliminar, las probables consecuencias del escenario macro sobre el desempleo, el crecimiento y la inflacin. Mientras una parte del impacto de la crisis social sobre la economa tiene que ver con las dificultades para el funcionamiento del sistema productivo, otra, muy significativa, tiene que ver con el sistema financiero. Los mercados financieros se han visto tensionados por fuertes movimientos en los precios, que en algunos casos han ido ms all de lo justificable por la mayor percepcin de riesgo pas. Como Consejo hemos adoptado diversas medidas para mejorar la liquidez en pesos y en dlares, y decidimos intervenir el mercado cambiario para mitigar la alta volatilidad del tipo de cambio y ayudar a que los ajustes ocurran de manera adecuada. En coherencia con esto ltimo y la convergencia de la inflacin a la meta, mantuvimos la TPM en 1,75 por ciento en la Reunin de Poltica Monetaria que sostuvimos ayer. El mayor impulso fiscal recientemente anunciado, unido a la ya alta expansividad de la poltica monetaria, ayudar a contener el deterioro de la economa, con lo que luego de una contraccin de 2,5 por ciento en el cuarto trimestre de 2019, crecer entre 0,5 y 1,5 por ciento en 2020. Si bien prevemos que la relevante desaceleracin del crecimiento ampliar la brecha de actividad en el horizonte de poltica monetaria, presionando a la baja a la inflacin, los impactos financieros de la mayor incertidumbre, as como los efectos ms persistentes de la depreciacin del peso, aumentarn las presiones inflacionarias en el horizonte de poltica. En base a estos antecedentes, consideramos que el estmulo monetario es el adecuado para el logro de la meta de inflacin, teniendo presente el estado actual del impulso fiscal y la poltica cambiaria.
