Title: Seminar on OTC Derivatives Global Reform
text: Seeminarr on OOTC DDerivattives GGlobal Reforrm1 Openning remaarks by Enriique Marrshall Membber of thee Board Centraal Bank oof Chile Januuary 28, 2014 1 Opeening remarrks deliveredd by Enriquue Marshall,, member off the board oof the Centrral Bankk of Chile, aat the Seminnar on OTC Derivativess Global Refform, organnized by the Centrral Bank of Chile and TThe Internattional Moneetary Fund, aand held in Santiago (CChile), on Jaanuary 28-30, 2014. I tthank Kevinn Cowan, Gaabriel Apariici and Daniiel Calvo foor their contrributions annd commentss. Good morning everyone. I would like to give a special welcome to our foreign visitors. On behalf of the Governor and the Executive Board of the Central Bank of Chile, I am pleased to open this seminar on OTC Derivatives Global Reform2. We will all agree that nowadays this is a well-timed topic for a seminar. Derivatives are undoubtedly key instruments for risk management among financial and non-financial firms. They are intensively and increasingly used, however, if the regulatory framework does not contain a set of backstops that provide safety guarantees for participants, derivatives impose high risks with potentially adverse consequences on financial markets3. These backstops are essential in markets characterized by large transaction volumes and numerous participants, as those ingredients inevitable lead to a network of highly interconnected financial commitments. This issue has been known for a long time. However, the recent global financial crisis has reminded us that in such circumstances, negative shocks are transmitted at a high speed, with the well-known adverse impacts on the financial system as well as the real economy. Interconnection risks become even more severe when markets operate with insufficient levels of transparency. Opacity limits the capacity of market participants to make informed financial decisions and the ability of regulators to judge intermediariesd5 exposures and risks. OTC derivative markets, the focus of this seminar, often operates under high interconnectedness and a lack of essential information. This explains why they were at the center of the last financial crisis and raised a high level of concern among financial authorities. Exchange traded derivatives markets, on the other hand, did not produce the same level of preoccupation. They were neither an originator of the crisis nor a major transmission channel of financial disruptions. In the aftermaths of the global crisis, the policy response from financial regulators has been to reduce interconnections, increase transparency and introduce more liquidity and capital requirements for financial intermediaries. Simultaneously, regulators have been developing incentives to move 2 OTC is an abbreviation for over the counter. 3 Activity levels in derivatives markets are reported in BIS (2013), d2Triennial Central Bank Survey of interest rate derivatives turnover in April 2013 - preliminary results released by the BISd3, September 2013. derivatives trading from OTC markets towards more formal and organized exchanges, which have mechanisms in place to reduce exposures and mitigate systemic risks. In this new environment, OTC derivatives markets have continued functioning, but actions have been taken in some jurisdictions to use central clearing for most types of derivatives. Such steps have been led under the mandate of the G20 and the coordination of the Financial Stability Board (FSB)4. The US policy response is embedded in Title VII of the Dodd-Frank Act, while the EU has acted through the European Market Infrastructure Regulation (EMIR). In both cases, there is a d2mandatory clearingd3 for standardized OTC derivatives, among numerous others requirements aimed at strengthening infrastructure standards. An important point is that the new rules have effects not only in the jurisdiction where they were issued, but also in other countries. The potential impact of these d2extraterritorial effectsd3 has been a matter of concern for economies that have substantial cross-border derivative positions with institutions in the US and the EU. This is certainly the case of Chile. After moving to a floating exchange rate regime in 1999, derivative markets have grown quickly. Turnover of foreign exchange derivatives has increased from 1.6% of GDP in 1998 to 5.3% of GDP in 2013. The privately run pension system in Chile has played an important role in this development as their cross border positions have risen over time and, to a great extent, they are hedged back to local currency. The corporate sector is also a key player in this market. Given our floating exchange rate regimen, where fluctuations cannot be disregarded, firms are active in reducing currency mismatches using this type of derivatives. The authorities and the market see this positively, as it reflects firms have learned the lesson of past experiences that were so costly for the country. The US regulation has already had an impact at the Chilean market. According to market information, some transactions have migrated from the US to Europe, in order to circumvent regulations. These movements have not had material effects on market participants. However, it raises the need of 4 G20 (2009). d2Leadersd5 Statement, The Pittsburgh Summitd3, September 24-25, 2009. increasing the level of coordination among financial authorities from different jurisdictions. Beyond any concern, we see ahead interesting opportunities to strengthen infrastructure standards in the region. Our assessment show that such standards are even weaker than those the US and other advance economies had previous to the crisis. Indeed, we share the sense of urgency raised by the FSB to address the main infrastructure gaps in order to develop a sound derivative market in this country and the region in general. In Chile, the derivative market is almost exclusively OTC. Volumes, as I mentioned before, have increased but the level of sophistication remains bounded. Most of derivatives being traded are interest rate swaps and non.deliverable forwards with very few intervening currencies. The main market participants are commercial banks, with a market share of around 61%, followed by pension funds, with a share of 19%, and firms and other agents with a 16% of the total.5 In addition, cross border transactions are all non.deliverable. Clearing is being done on a bilateral basis. A month ago, a central counterparty was authorized to clear both OTC and exchange traded derivatives, although it is expected to operate mainly on the latter. There is another central counterparty in process of getting approval, which is expected to start functioning mainly on OTC derivatives at the end of this year, conditional on authoritiesd5 approval. In terms of transparency, the authoritiesd5 access to information on this kind of transactions is still limited. Banks are force to report transactions to the Central Bank, while non-banks entities must inform foreign exchange derivatives and derivatives traded with foreign counterparties. So, the information received at the Central Bank is significant, but it is still insufficient for adequate financial stability surveillance. Let me be more specific on this point. Transactions between non-bank participants at the local level, for instance, are currently not reported to any financial supervisor. In a context of changing global standards, this seminar is very opportune as it comes at a time when every one of us is engaged in setting priorities and 5 Achar87n, M. y J. M. Villena (2011). d2Mercado Cambiario 2000-2010: Comparaci Internacional de Chiled3. Estudios Econmicos Estad92sticos Na1 88, Banco Central de Chile, Septiembre policy actions in connection with the issues that are on table. The program of the seminar has been designed to provide a better understanding of the correct implementation of the new standards, to review experiences of different jurisdictions, and to discuss how to improve coordination among national authorities. This morning, we will have a review by IMF experts on OTC derivatives reforms with references to various countries and regions. This will be followed by presentations on the cases of Brazil and Mexico. Todayabs program will close with a discussion on global vs. local clearing solutions and the role of the third country regulatory framework. Tomorrow, we will review how CPSS-IOSCO principles apply to the OTC derivative context. Then we will have a presentation on Australian experience with supervision and oversight of CCPs and trade repositories. Finally, we will spend the rest of tomorrow and Thursday morning understanding the main elements of US and EU regulation and, particularly, their implications for third countries. Before ending these remarks, I would like to thank the people and institutions that have made possible we meet today at this seminar. First of all, I would like to thank the IMF and the team from MCM for co-hosting this activity with us. Then, I would like to thank all our distinguished speakers for joining us here in Santiago and for the time they have spent in preparing their presentations. Next, I would like to thank the representatives from supervisory authorities and central banks in the region for joining us for this seminar. And last but not least, a word of thank for the people of the Central Bank and, particularly, for the staff of the Financial Policy Division, led with enormous enthusiasm by Kevin Cowan, who have worked hard in organizing this activity.

Title: Introductory remarks
text: Introductory remarks by Vittorio Corbo L., President of the Central Bank of Chile, at the opening session of the Conference on "The Future of the Trade Liberalization in the Americas" Hotel Crowne Plaza, Santiago Monday, March 22, 2004, 9.15 hrs. On behalf of the Central Bank of Chile, I would like to welcome you to the conference on "The Future of Trade Liberalization in the Americas", organized jointly with the World Bank, and in which we have the participation of a very prominent group of policy makers, academics and practitioners from the countries of the region. This conference represents another link in the collaboration between our institution and the World Bank, which has previously materialized in other conferences, such as the one that addressed the relationship between economic growth and natural resources two years ago and the important support given to the development of our Annual Conference in 1998. In particular, I would like to welcome the two people who are with me at this inaugural meeting. At my side is Mrs. Soledad Alvear, Minister of RR.EE. of the Republic of Chile, who has continued and deepened Chile's successful international insertion strategy with the implementation of free trade agreements with important regions and countries of the world. I am also accompanied by Mr. David de Ferranti, Vice-President of the World Bank for Latin America and the Caribbean, responsible for the technical and credit support of that institution to the opening and commercial integration of the region. Undoubtedly, the theme that inspires this conference is of great importance for Chile in particular and the entire American continent in general. Trade openness is one of the most important determinants of long-term economic growth. A more open economy not only makes more efficient use of existing resources, but can also absorb technologies not available within the country; Openness also has a positive effect on the strength of institutions, which is extremely important for sustained economic development. But for these benefits to materialize it is also necessary 2 Progress on other fronts: macroeconomic stability, extensive use of the market, definition and respect of property rights, efficient regulation, development of institutions. The experience of our country is illuminating in this regard. Together with other reforms, the opening of the economy carried out in past decades allowed the country to make a significant jump in its growth rate, reaching an average rate of 7.3% per year between 1985 and 1997, with a substantial improvement in different social indicators and a better capacity to respond to external shocks. After a first stage of unilateral opening in the 1970s, in which it was possible to standardize tariffs for different products, a common tariff rate of 11% was reached in the mid-90s. However, unilateral opening continued to deepen from 1998 onwards, culminating in an overall tariff of 6% from January 2003. In addition, over the past decade Chile has complemented its policy of global openness with active participation in multilateral trade negotiations and through bilateral trade integration agreements. It is also worth mentioning the efforts made in this period of signing agreements that avoid double taxation. With regard to the bilateral strategy, it is worth mentioning the achievement of a significant number of trade agreements in force with countries or regions such as Mexico, Canada, countries of the Andean Community, MERCOSUR and Central American countries. This last strategy has been crowned with the successful negotiation and signing of free trade agreements with the European Union (which entered into force in 2003) and with the United States (in force since January of this year). An FTA has been agreed with Korea that will enter into force next April. The free trade agreement with EFTA countries is also for approval by Congress. These latest agreements are not only important because of the weight of our new partners in the world economy and in Chilean foreign trade, but also because of the multiple non-commercial dimensions they cover. These state-of-the-art free trade agreements are comprehensive because they include agreements ranging from the regulation of flows to 3 investments in public sector procurement, and from the protection of intellectual property rights to greater transparency in changes in public legislation, and from phytosanitary protection to environmental and labor regulation. It is possible that these broad aspects will help to further strengthen the country's institutions and the stability of its economic policies, because they consolidate clear and permanent rules, with the consequent potential benefit represented by access to greater volumes, at lower cost, of external financing. The objectives of carrying out agreements of this type are to increase the opening of the economy, but ensuring better access for Chilean exports to third markets, which would not have higher costs in trade diversion due to the low tariff that Chile has with the rest of the world. This is how one of the important topics of this conference will be to learn about the benefits that following this type of strategy has provided to our country. But the issue is not only relevant to our country. In terms of trade openness, the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean have followed similar paths. In this regard, the adoption of trade agreements within the region stands out, such as the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), MERCOSUR and the recent free trade agreements between Central America and Mexico and the United States (CAFTA-US). These recent subregional agreements represent varying degrees of integration and consideration of broad factors beyond trade in goods, for which we have much to learn from them. In addition, the issue takes on vital importance at a time when the great challenge of creating a free trade agreement between all the countries of the region has arisen, where the discussion of the experience accumulated in existing agreements, the prerequisites, benefits and costs of such agreements, and the analysis of possible alternative policies will be decisive when discussing the convenience and optimal strategy to create a free trade agreement. of the Americas. The general objective of this conference is to contribute to the knowledge about the economic consequences and political conditions of free trade agreements from economic theory and past experiences. Recent history in America allows us to 4 learn from concrete experiences, such as the 10 years of existence of NAFTA and the more than 10 years of MERCOSUR. In addition, from the characteristics of recently implemented treaties, such as the FTAs signed by Chile, inferences can be made about their possible future effects. This conference will cover seven main topics, all of which are of great relevance to trade integration strategies in particular and to economic policies in general. The first topic of the conference is economic growth. Evidence is presented on the impact of trade integration on technology diffusion flows, in the NAFTA experience. In addition, new empirical evidence is presented about the effects of trade agreements on growth in the world in general and in Chile in particular. The importance of this evidence is crucial because achieving higher growth is a central objective of preferential trade agreements d0 and trade theory tells us that the effects of trade agreements on output are ambiguous, varying from case to case. Related to the issue of growth is the question about the possible effects of trade integration on vulnerability to external events and the synchronization of economic fluctuations between trading partners. Evidence in this regard is crucial for the correct design and implementation of stabilizing economic policies. A third theme of the conference is a complete evaluation of the effects of NAFTA, with the presentation of a complete report that the World Bank has made 10 years after the existence of this trade agreement, with a special emphasis on the effects and benefits that NAFTA has had for Mexico. This conference also evaluates preferential trade agreements in comparison with other arrangements. This includes an analysis of different forms of trade integration on poverty in Brazil, the benefits of countries exporting to the U.S. under preferential access conditions, and an analysis of reciprocity in 5 Free trade between rich and poor countries. Understanding these international political economy aspects of trade agreements is key to understanding the relative benefits and costs of pursuing bilateral or regional agreements, or pursuing a unilateral opening strategy. The fifth topic covers the trade and fiscal consequences of free trade agreements, from the perspective of finance and trade ministers and free trade agreement negotiators in the region. Another crucial aspect in Latin America's economic development is the growing and variable flow of foreign investment. The conference will address some important aspects of the incentives for the volume, composition and regional reallocation of foreign capital that different agreements may entail, and the implications these have on the participation of different countries in trade agreements. The seventh aspect concerns the impact of trade integration on poverty and income distribution. Any free trade agreement implies a change in relative prices that generates important sectoral reallocations of productive resources. While it is this aspect that allows the gains of comparative advantage to be exploited and the level of economic efficiency to be increased, the slow reallocation of the labour force, particularly of low-skilled workers, has implications for poverty and inequality levels. The reviewed works provide recent evidence of this aspect, a key contribution to the design of policies that allow a faster transition and lower social cost. The final session will present the main conclusions of the conference, with special emphasis on their implications for future trade policies and negotiations in our hemisphere. The papers presented here are mostly based on agreements reached between different actors in the Americas, including the cases of countries such as Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Mexico and the United States. A good read and rich discussion of 6 Such experiences are essential to improve the design and implementation of future trade agreements, so that our continent can enjoy the economic and social gains of free trade in the near future. Contributing to this discussion is the goal of this conference. I would also like to highlight the relationship that this conference has with the development and policies of the Central Bank of Chile. The openness of the economy and the form it takes affects all areas of the economy and therefore it is necessary for our institution to have a broad understanding of the theme of this conference. The Central Bank's contribution to the advancement of policy-relevant knowledge and research has been important for many years. Part of the Bank's social responsibility is to contribute to economic development through initiatives such as this and others like it, such as the series of annual conferences organized by the Central Bank of Chile, which this year will address the important issue of how developing economies should be insured to better address the external vulnerability to which they are subjected. Therefore, due to the relevance of the topic for the design of future trade opening strategies, this conference is a meeting point for leading leaders and policy makers of the region, including ministers of state, central bank presidents, representatives and executives of international organizations and private companies, academics and researchers of international trade and development. To all of them I extend a very cordial welcome. I would also like to highlight the valuable collaboration of the conference organizers, Daniel Lederman, Senior Economist of the Vice Presidency for Latin America and the Caribbean of the World Bank, and Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel, Economic Research Manager of the Central Bank of Chile. They have been supported by a significant number of officials from both institutions; To all of them I extend my thanks. Thanks a lot.
text_original: Palabras introductorias de Vittorio Corbo L., Presidente del Banco Central de Chile, en la sesin inaugural de la Conferencia sobre El Futuro de la Liberalizacin Comercial en las Amricas Hotel Crowne Plaza, Santiago Lunes 22 de marzo, de 2004, 9.15 hrs. Sin duda el tema que inspira esta conferencia es de gran importancia para Chile en particular y todo el Continente Americano en general. La apertura comercial es uno de los determinantes ms importantes del crecimiento econmico de largo plazo. Una economa ms abierta no slo utiliza de forma ms eficiente los recursos existentes, si no que tambin puede absorber tecnologas no disponibles al interior del pas; la apertura tiene tambin un efecto positivo sobre la fortaleza de las instituciones, lo que es importantsimo para un desarrollo econmico sostenido. Pero para que estos beneficios se materialicen es necesario tambin  avanzar en otros frentes: estabilidad macroeconmica, uso extensivo del mercado, definicin y respeto de los derechos de propiedad, regulacin eficiente, desarrollo de instituciones. La experiencia de nuestro pas es iluminadora en este aspecto. En conjunto con otras reformas, la apertura de la economa llevada a cabo en dcadas pasadas permiti al pas dar un salto significativo en su tasa de crecimiento, alcanzando una tasa promedio de 7,3% anual entre 1985 y 1997, con una mejora sustancial en distintos indicadores sociales y una mejor capacidad de respuesta ante perturbaciones externas. Luego de una primera etapa de apertura unilateral en los aos 1970, en la que se logr uniformar los aranceles para distintos productos, se lleg a una tasa arancelaria comn de 11% a mediados de la dcada de los 90. Sin embargo, la apertura unilateral se continu profundizando desde 1998 en adelante, culminando en un arancel general de 6% a partir de enero de 2003. Adems, durante la ltima dcada Chile ha complementado su poltica de apertura global con una activa participacin en las negociaciones comerciales multilaterales y a travs de acuerdos bilaterales de integracin comercial. Vale la pena mencionar tambin los esfuerzos realizados en este periodo de suscripcin de acuerdos que evitan la doble tributacin. En lo que respecta a la estrategia bilateral cabe destacar el logro de un nmero importante de acuerdos comerciales en vigencia con pases o regiones como Mxico, Canad, pases de la Comunidad Andina, MERCOSUR y pases de Centroamrica. Esta ltima estrategia ha sido coronada con la negociacin y firma exitosa de los acuerdos de libre comercio con la Unin Europea (que entr en vigencia en el ao 2003) y con los Estados Unidos (vigente desde enero del presente ao). Con Corea se ha acordado un TLC que entrar en vigencia el Io de abril prximo. Se encuentra asimismo para aprobacin del Congreso el acuerdo de libre comercio con los pases de EFTA. Estos ltimos acuerdos no son slo importantes por el peso de nuestros nuevos socios en la economa mundial y en el comercio exterior chileno, sino que tambin por las mltiples dimensiones no comerciales que abarcan. Estos tratados de libre comercio de ltima generacin son amplios porque incluyen acuerdos que van desde las regulaciones de los flujos de  inversiones a las compras del sector pblico, y desde la proteccin de los derechos de propiedad intelectual hasta la mayor transparencia en los cambios en las legislaciones pblicas, y desde la proteccin fitosanitaria la regulacin ambiental y laboral. Es posible que estos aspectos amplios ayuden a fortalecer an ms la institucionalidad del pas y la estabilidad de sus polticas econmicas, porque consolidan reglas claras y permanentes, con el consiguiente beneficio potencial representado por un acceso a mayores volmenes, a menor costo, de financiamiento externo. Los objetivos de llevar a cabo acuerdos de este tipo son aumentar la apertura de la economa, pero asegurando un mejor acceso de las exportaciones chilenas a terceros mercados, lo que no tendra mayores costos en desviacin de comercio debido al bajo arancel que tiene Chile con el resto del mundo. Es as como uno de los temas importantes de esta conferencia ser aprender sobre los beneficios que ha brindado a nuestro pas el seguir este tipo de estrategia. Pero el tema no es nicamente relevante para nuestro pas. En materia de apertura comercial, los pases de Amrica Latina y el Caribe han seguido caminos similares. En este sentido destaca la adopcin de acuerdos comerciales dentro de la regin, como el Acuerdo de Libre Comercio de Norteamrica (NAFTA), el MERCOSUR y los recientes acuerdos de libre comercio de Centro Amrica con Mxico y con los Estados Unidos (CAFTA-US). Estos recientes acuerdos subregionales representan distintos grados de integracin y de consideracin de factores amplios que van ms all del comercio de bienes, por lo cual tenemos mucho que aprender de ellos. Adems, el tema toma vital importancia en los momentos en que se ha planteado el gran reto de crear un acuerdo de libre comercio entre todos los pases de la regin, donde la discusin de la experiencia acumulada en los acuerdos existentes, los prerrequisitos, beneficios y costos de tales acuerdos, y el anlisis de las polticas alternativas posibles ser determinante al discutir la conveniencia y la estrategia ptima para crear un acuerdo de libre comercio de las Amricas. El objetivo general de esta conferencia es aportar al conocimiento sobre las consecuencias econmicas y las condiciones polticas de los tratados de libre comercio a partir de la teora econmica y las experiencias pasadas. La historia reciente en Amrica nos permite  aprender de experiencias concretas, como lo son los 10 aos de existencia del NAFTA y los ms de 10 aos del MERCOSUR. Adems, a partir de las caractersticas de tratados recientemente implementados, como los TLC suscritos por Chile, se pueden hacer inferencias acerca de sus posibles efectos futuros. En esta conferencia se cubrirn siete tpicos principales, todos ellos de gran relevancia para las estrategias de integracin comercial en particular y para las polticas econmicas en general. El primer tpico de la conferencia es el crecimiento econmico. Se presenta evidencia acerca del impacto de la integracin comercial en los flujos de difusin tecnolgica, en la experiencia del NAFTA. Adems se presenta nueva evidencia emprica acerca de los efectos de la los tratados comerciales sobre el crecimiento en el mundo en general y en Chile en particular. La importancia de esta evidencia es crucial porque lograr un mayor crecimiento es un objetivo central de los acuerdos preferenciales de comercio - y la teora del comercio nos dice que los efectos de los acuerdos comerciales sobre el producto son ambiguos, variando de caso a caso. Relacionada con el tema del crecimiento es la pregunta acerca de los posibles efectos de la integracin comercial en la vulnerabilidad a eventos externos y a la sincronizacin de fluctuaciones econmicas entre socios comerciales. La evidencia en este aspecto es crucial para el correcto diseo e implementacin de polticas econmicas estabilizadoras. Un tercer tema de la conferencia es una evaluacin completa de los efectos del NAFTA, con la presentacin de un completo informe que ha realizado el Banco Mundial a los 10 aos de existencia de este acuerdo comercial, con un nfasis especial en los efectos y beneficios que ha tenido el NAFTA para Mxico. En esta conferencia tambin se evala a los acuerdos preferenciales de comercio en comparacin con otros arreglos. Esto incluye un anlisis que tendran distintas forma de integracin comercial sobre la pobreza en Brasil, los beneficios de los pases que exportan a EE.UU. bajo condiciones de acceso preferencial y un anlisis de la reciprocidad en acuerdos de  libre comercio entre pases ricos y pobres. Entender estos aspectos de economa poltica internacional de los acuerdos comerciales es clave para entender los beneficios y costos relativos de llevar a cabo acuerdos bilaterales o regionales, o en seguir una estrategia de apertura unilateral. El quinto tema cubre las consecuencias comerciales y fiscales de los acuerdos de libre comercio, desde la ptica de ministros de hacienda y comercio y de negociadores de tratados de libre comercio de la regin. Otro aspecto crucial en el desarrollo econmico de Latinoamrica es el creciente y variable flujo de inversin extranjera. En la conferencia se abordarn algunos aspectos importantes respecto de los incentivos al volumen, a la composicin y a la reasignacin regional de los capitales extranjeros que distintos acuerdos pueden implicar, y las consecuencias que dichos aspectos tienen en la participacin de distintos pases en acuerdos comerciales. El sptimo aspecto a tratar se refiere al impacto de la integracin comercial sobre la pobreza y la distribucin del ingreso. Todo tratado de libre comercio implica un cambio de precios relativos que genera importantes reasignaciones sectoriales de los recursos productivos. Si bien es este aspecto el que permite explotar las ganancias de las ventajas comparativas e incrementar el nivel de eficiencia econmica, la reasignacin lenta de la fuerza de trabajo, en particular de trabajadores de baja calificacin, tiene implicancias en los niveles de pobreza y desigualdad. Los trabajos revisados entregan evidencia reciente de dicho aspecto, aporte clave para el diseo de polticas que permitan una transicin ms rpida y de menor costo social. En la sesin final se presentarn las principales conclusiones de la conferencia, con un nfasis especial en sus implicancias para las polticas comerciales y negociaciones futuras en nuestro hemisferio. Las ponencias presentadas aqu se basan mayoritariamente en acuerdos alcanzados entre distintos actores del continente americano, incluyendo los casos de pases como Argentina, Brasil, Canad, Chile, Mxico y los Estados Unidos. Una buena lectura y nutrida discusin de  dichas experiencias es fundamental para mejorar el diseo y la implementacin de futuros acuerdos comerciales, de manera que nuestro continente pueda gozar en un futuro cercano de las ganancias econmicas y sociales propias del libre comercio. Aportar a esta discusin es la meta de esta conferencia. Quiero destacar tambin la relacin que tiene esta conferencia con el desarrollo y las polticas del Banco Central de Chile. La apertura de la economa y la forma que esta toma incide en todos los mbitos de la economa y por lo tanto es necesario para nuestra institucin el tener un entendimiento amplio del tema de esta conferencia. El aporte del Banco Central al avance del conocimiento y la investigacin relevante para la formulacin de polticas ha sido importante durante muchos aos. Parte de la responsabilidad social del Banco es contribuir al desarrollo econmico a travs de iniciativas como sta y otras similares, como lo es la serie de conferencias anuales que organiza el Banco Central de Chile, la que este ao tratar sobre el importante tema de cmo se deben asegurar las economas en desarrollo para enfrentar de mejor manera la vulnerabilidad externa a las que estn sometidas. Por lo tanto, debido a la relevancia del tema para el diseo de futuras estrategias de apertura comercial, esta conferencia es un punto de reunin de destacados lderes y responsables de polticas de la regin, incluyendo ministros de estado, presidentes de bancos centrales, representantes y ejecutivos de organismos internacionales y de empresas privadas, acadmicos e investigadores del comercio internacional y del desarrollo. A todos ellos les doy una muy cordial bienvenida. Tambin quiero destacar la valiosa colaboracin de los organizadores de la conferencia, Daniel Lederman, Economista Snior de la Vice-Presidencia de Amrica Latina y el Caribe del Banco Mundial, y Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel, Gerente de Investigacin Econmica del Banco Central de Chile. Title: Opening Speech
text: Vittorio Corbo Opening Speech Eighth Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile: "External Vulnerability and Prevention Policies" Tuesday, August 10, 2004, 9.30 AM, Hotel Crowne Plaza, Santiago On behalf of the Board of the Central Bank of Chile, I welcome you to our Eighth Annual Conference and thank the distinguished scholars and practitioners present here for their participation. The theme that brings us together this year is external vulnerability and policies for its prevention. For decades, policymakers have faced the significant challenge of reducing the vulnerability of their economies to external shocks and improving the way policies respond to them. In recent years, increasing financial and trade integration has created great opportunities to improve growth prospects but at the same time has increased the need for policies designed to mitigate economic fluctuations that emerge from greater interconnectedness between economies. The experience of a large number of emerging economies at the end of the past decade shows the importance that the degree of external vulnerability and policies that face adverse external shocks can have, not only on macroeconomic stability but also on medium-term growth. In recent years, the Chilean economy has faced a complicated external scenario. The Asian crisis in the period 1997-1998, the crises in Argentina and Turkey in 2001, the significant global slowdown during 2001-2002, and the current intense volatility in commodity prices are notorious examples of the complex framework in which monetary policy has passed. Although the economic cycle of our economy showed the negative effects of these shocks, it is no less true that the improvement of the economic policy framework, based on the lessons learned in the 1980s and 1990s, allows us to have an institutional design that makes the country less vulnerable to external shocks. Chile's macroeconomic and financial policy framework today is based on three essential pillars. First, there is the inflation-targeting regime as the nominal anchor of the economy. The monetary authority's continued commitment to the inflation target has allowed convergence towards stable inflation at 3%, the center of the inflation target range. This monetary framework has been strengthened by the adoption of a floating exchange rate since 1999. The second pillar of stability is the consolidation of strong fiscal discipline, institutionalized in the adoption in 2000 of the structural surplus rule for the public sector. Finally, macroeconomic and financial stability is underpinned by a sound banking system and a deep and healthy capital market, reflecting efficient regulation and effective supervision. These three pillars of the policy framework have created the foundations for growth and have been instrumental in making Chile's economy less vulnerable to external shocks than it was in the past. Thus, the empirical evidence accumulated in recent years is irrefutable proof of the greater capacity of shock absorption that our economy has achieved. But as in other matters, it is still possible to make progress in reducing the external vulnerability of the Chilean economy. As is tradition, the Central Bank of Chile has been holding an annual conference since 1997 with the objectives of perfecting its own policies and contributing to the development and debate of ideas that allow achieving higher levels of well-being for society. This eighth conference is framed within these principles. This conference will contribute to the development and debate of ideas on the transmission and absorption of financial and real external shocks in small and open economies, the options available to the economic authority to face these shocks and the development of new mechanisms to reduce the vulnerability of these economies to external shocks. From the point of view of economic policy, the interest of the Central Bank of Chile in the theme of this conference lies in the growing role of financial markets d1 domestic and international d1 and external shocks d1 both real and financial d1 in the design and transmission of monetary policy. Increasing financial integration with the world has increased the channels and speed of transmission of shocks between countries. In this context, it is essential to make progress in improving financial markets and designing a set of economic policies that allow emerging economies to reduce their vulnerability to these shocks. This is a challenge shared by central banks, finance ministries and international financial institutions around the world. As established in its organic law, the Central Bank of Chile seeks not only to guarantee the stability of the currency but also the stability of the internal and external payment system of the economy. The objective of currency stability is pursued with a monetary policy aimed at keeping inflation in a range of 2 to 4%, focused on 3%. The objective of stability of the internal and external payment system is cautioned with macroeconomic stability and regulation and supervision aimed at achieving timely identification and appropriate management of risks. The Bank's work to maintain currency stability is made explicit in its Monetary Policy Report (MPR), which serves as a vehicle for explaining the Board's view of recent and expected inflation developments and the consequences for monetary policy, sets out the medium-term framework used by the Council for monetary policy formulation, and provides useful information for the formation of monetary policy expectations. economic agents on the most likely path of inflation and output. This report considers a balance of risks, including those linked to external shocks, for both activity and inflation. With regard to the stability of internal and external payments, the Bank has added a second publication as of August of this year: the Financial Stability Report, which aims to account for the most relevant developments for Chile that affect its financial stability and prospects. It is therefore of great institutional interest to draw lessonsd1from the discussions at this conferenced1on possible policies that, added to the current policy framework, will enable our economy to better cope with these external shocks and develop mechanisms that make it less vulnerable to them. Between today and tomorrow we will discuss these issues with a select group of academics and practitioners. We will begin with the Guest Lecture by IMF Chief Economist Dr. Raghuram Rajan, who will describe the role of international financial institutions in reducing external vulnerability. In the first session of the conference, the stylized facts regarding the impact of external shocks on macroeconomic performance will be described. This section will assess the capacity of both Chile and the rest of the world's economies to withstand adverse real and financial external shocks, such as fluctuations in the terms of trade, growth of the main trading partners, fluctuations in global real interest rates and the flow of capital to the region. In this sense, C8esar Calder97n, Norman Loayza and Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel present international evidence on the impact of trade and financial openness, and its interaction with external shocks on growth and macroeconomic volatility. For their part, Helmut Franken, Eric Parrado and Guillermo Le Fort assess the importance of these external shocks in Chile's economic cycle and the ability of our economy to withstand adverse shocks in recent years. Complementing these works, Fernando Broner and Roberto Rigob97n compare the differences in the volatility patterns of capital flows to emerging and industrial economies, linking these differences to external shocks faced by these economies. The second session, which will run entirely today and tomorrow, will first review international experience with policy responses to external shocks, with special emphasis on the analysis of differences between emerging and developed economies to counter external shocks. Secondly, both the effect of international reserves in the prevention of external crises and the role recently played by the Chilean foreign exchange derivatives market in reducing foreign exchange risk will be evaluated. Third, the determinants and effects of exchange exposure in firms in the Chilean non-financial sector will be discussed. Regarding the first topic -international experience of policy responses to shocks-, Luis Felipe C8espedes, Lian Goldfajn, Phil Lowe and Rodrigo Vald8es analyze the economic policies designed by emerging economies to counteract external shocks compared to policies applied by industrial nations, listing the political and legal obstacles to implementing alternative policies in periods of crisis. Regarding the second topic -role of international reserves in crisis prevention-, Pablo Garc92a and Claudio Soto evaluate the contribution of international liquidity in reducing the risk of a currency crisis, calculating the optimal level of reserves from estimates of crisis probabilities. For their part, Esteban Jadresic and Jorge Selaive analyze the capacity of the foreign exchange derivatives market as a mechanism to reduce exposure to foreign exchange risk by firms as well as volatility of exchange rate fluctuations. Along with them, Kevin Cowan, Erwin Hansen and Luis Oscar Herrera evaluate the response of the private sector to the external shocks faced by the Chilean economy in the late nineties, distinguishing the factors anticipated by firms from those that were difficult to predict or cover. At the end of the Second Session we will have invited Lectures. The first, by Professor Sebasti87n Edwards, will analyze the experience of emerging and transition economies with respect to capital account convertibility and management, as well as the imposition of capital controls, emphasizing the empirical relationship between capital account constraints and vulnerability to external shocks. In the second invited conference, Ernesto Talvi will be in charge of the analysis of the relationship between sudden stops and financial vulnerabilities and their possible consequences on the economies of South America. The final part of the conference, to be held on Wednesday, includes the assessment of possible policy and market instruments that could be developed to reduce external vulnerability. First, Kenneth Kletzer analyzes debt management in at-risk economies, emphasizing the role of contractual innovations that would help smooth the amount of debt obligations in the face of external shocks. Second, Francisco Gallego and Geraint Jones study the role of floating exchange rate regimes as an insurance mechanism against external shocks. And, finally, Ricardo Caballero and Stavros Panageas analyze optimal portfolio strategies in an environment with sudden stops in the inflow of capital, thus offering a practical tool for the management of reserves and investments in emerging economies. You are invited to a debate that I am sure will be fruitful and will provide important lessons for optimal policy-making in an increasingly integrated world. Finally, I would like to highlight the work done by the organizing team of this Annual Conference. Ricardo Caballero, professor at M.I.T, Luis Felipe C8espedes, senior economist at the Bank, and C8esar Calder97n, senior economist at the Bank, have achieved a splendid program and excellent organization of this conference, efficiently assisted by Alvaro Aguirre and M97nica Correa. Thanks a lot.
text_original: Vittorio Corbo Discurso de Inauguracin Octava Conferencia Anual del Banco Central de Chile: Vulnerabilidad Externa y Polticas de Prevencin Martes 10 de agosto 2004, 9.30 AM, Hotel Crowne Plaza, Santiago A nombre del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile, les doy la bienvenida a nuestra Octava Conferencia Anual y agradezco la participacin de distinguidos acadmicos y profesionales aqu presentes. El tema que este ao nos rene es la vulnerabilidad externa y las polticas para su prevencin. Durante dcadas, las autoridades econmicas han enfrentado el importante desafo de reducir la vulnerabilidad de sus economas frente a shocks externos y mejorar la forma en que las polticas responden a ellos. En los ltimos aos, la creciente integracin financiera y comercial ha generado grandes oportunidades para mejorar las perspectivas de crecimiento pero en paralelo ha aumentado la necesidad de contar con polticas diseadas para aminorar las fluctuaciones econmicas que emergen de una mayor interconexin entre economas. La experiencia de un amplio nmero de economas emergentes a fines de la dcada pasada dan muestra de la importancia que puede tener el grado de vulnerabilidad externa y las polticas con que se hace frente a shocks externos adversos, no slo sobre la estabilidad macroeconmica sino tambin sobre el crecimiento de mediano plazo. En los ltimos aos, la economa chilena hizo frente a un complicado escenario externo. La crisis asitica en el perodo 1997-1998, las crisis de Argentina y Turqua en 2001, la importante desaceleracin mundial durante 2001-2002, y la intensa volatilidad actual en precios de materias primas son ejemplos notorios del complejo marco en el cual la poltica monetaria ha transitado. An cuando el ciclo econmico de nuestra economa evidenci los efectos negativos de estos shocks, no es menos cierto que el mejoramiento del marco de poltica econmica, a partir de las lecciones obtenidas en los aos 1980 y 1990, nos permite contar hoy con un diseo institucional que hace al pas menos vulnerable a shocks externos. El marco de polticas macroeconmicas y financieras de Chile se basa hoy en tres pilares esenciales. En primer lugar se encuentra el rgimen de metas de inflacin como ancla nominal de la economa. El compromiso continuo de la autoridad monetaria con la meta de inflacin ha permitido la convergencia hacia una inflacin estable en tomo al 3%, el centro del rango-meta de inflacin. Este marco monetario se ha visto fortalecido por la adopcin de un tipo de cambio flotante desde 1999. El segundo pilar de la estabilidad es la consolidacin de una slida disciplina fiscal, institucionalizada en la adopcin en el ao 2000 de la regla de supervit estructural para el sector pblico. Finalmente, la estabilidad macroeconmica y financiera est apoyada por un sistema bancario slido y un mercado de capitales profundo y sano, reflejo de una regulacin eficiente y una supervisin efectiva. Estos tres pilares del marco de polticas han creado las bases del crecimiento y han contribuido de manera decisiva a que la economa chilena sea hoy menos vulnerable a shocks externos a lo que fue en el pasado. As, la evidencia emprica acumulada en los ltimos aos es prueba fehaciente de la mayor capacidad de absorcin de shocks que ha logrado nuestra economa. Pero como en otras materias, todava es posible avanzar en reducir la vulnerabilidad externa de la economa chilena. Como ya es tradicin, el Banco Central de Chile viene realizando desde el ao 1997 una conferencia anual con los objetivos de perfeccionar sus propias polticas y de contribuir al desarrollo y debate de ideas que permitan alcanzar niveles mayores de bienestar para la sociedad. Esta octava conferencia se enmarca dentro de estos principios. Esta conferencia contribuir al desarrollo y debate de ideas sobre la transmisin y absorcin de shocks externos financieros y reales en economas pequeas y abiertas, las opciones disponibles a la autoridad econmica para enfrentar a estos shocks y el desarrollo de nuevos mecanismos de reduccin de la vulnerabilidad de estas economas a shocks externos. Desde el punto de vista de poltica econmica, el inters del Banco Central de Chile en el tema de esta conferencia radica en el creciente papel de los mercados financieros  nacionales e internacionales y de los shocks externos tanto reales como financieros en el diseo y la transmisin de la poltica monetaria. La creciente integracin financiera con el mundo ha aumentado los canales y la velocidad de transmisin de los shocks entre los pases. En este contexto, resulta primordial avanzar en el perfeccionamiento de los mercados financieros y en el diseo de un conjunto de polticas econmicas que permitan a las economas emergentes reducir su vulnerabilidad a estos shocks. Este es un desafo compartido por bancos centrales, ministerios de hacienda e instituciones financieras internacionales de todo el mundo. Tal como est establecido en su ley orgnica, el Banco Central de Chile busca no slo garantizar la estabilidad de la moneda sino tambin la estabilidad del sistema de pagos interno y externo de la economa. El objetivo de la estabilidad de la moneda se persigue con una poltica monetaria orientada a mantener la inflacin en un rango de 2 a 4%, centrado en 3%. El objetivo de estabilidad del sistema de pagos interno y externo se cautela con la estabilidad macroeconmica y una regulacin y supervisin orientada a lograr una identificacin oportuna y manejo apropiado de los riesgos. La labor del Banco encaminada a mantener la estabilidad de la moneda se explcita en su Informe de Poltica Monetaria (IPoM), el que sirve de vehculo para explicar la visin del consejo sobre la evolucin reciente y esperada de la inflacin y las consecuencias para la poltica monetaria, expone el marco de mediano plazo utilizado por el Consejo para la formulacin de la poltica monetaria y provee informacin til para la formacin de expectativas de los agentes econmicos sobre la trayectoria ms probable de la inflacin y el producto. Este informe considera un balance de riesgos entre ellos los vinculados a los shocks externos tanto para la actividad como para la inflacin. En lo que se refiere a la estabilidad de los pagos internos y externos, el Banco agrega una segunda publicacin a partir de agosto del presente ao: el Informe de Estabilidad Financiera, que tiene por objeto dar cuenta de los desarrollos ms relevantes para Chile que inciden en su estabilidad financiera y sus perspectivas. Es por lo tanto de gran inters institucional obtener leccionesa partir de los debates de esta conferencia sobre posibles polticas que, sumadas al marco de poltica actual, permitan a nuestra economa enfrentar de mejor manera estos shocks externos y desarrollar mecanismos que la hagan menos vulnerable a estos. Entre hoy y maana debatiremos con un selecto grupo de acadmicos y profesionales estos temas. Daremos inicio con la Conferencia Invitada del Economista Jefe del FMI, Dr. Raghuram Rajan, quien describir el rol de las instituciones financieras internacionales en la reduccin de la vulnerabilidad externa. En la primera sesin de la conferencia, se describirn los hechos estilizados en tomo al impacto de los shocks externos sobre el desempeo macroeconmico. Dicha seccin evaluar la capacidad tanto de Chile como del resto de economas del mundo para resistir shocks externos adversos, reales y financieros, como por ejemplo, fluctuaciones en los trminos de intercambio, crecimiento de los principales socios comerciales, fluctuaciones en las tasas reales de inters mundial y el flujo de capitales hacia la regin. En este sentido, Csar Caldern, Norman Loayza y Klaus Schmidt-Hebbel presentan evidencia internacional sobre el impacto de la apertura comercial y financiera, y su interaccin con shocks externos sobre el crecimiento y la volatilidad macroeconmica. Por su parte, Helmut Franken, Eric Parrado y Guillermo Le Fort evalan la importancia de estos shocks externos en el ciclo econmico de Chile y la capacidad de nuestra economa para resistir shocks adversos en los ltimos aos. Complementando estos trabajos, Fernando Broner y Roberto Rigobn comparan las diferencias en los patrones de volatilidad de los flujos de capitales hacia economas emergentes e industriales, vinculando dichas diferencias a shocks externos que enfrentan estas economas. En la segunda sesin, que se desarrollar entere hoy y maana, se revisar, en primer lugar, la experiencia internacional en tomo a las respuestas de poltica ante shocks externos, con especial nfasis en el anlisis de las diferencias entre las polticas que han aplicado economas emergentes y desarrolladas para contrarrestar los shocks externos. En segundo lugar, se evaluar tanto el efecto que juegan las reservas internacionales en la prevencin de crisis externas como el rol desempeado recientemente por el mercado de derivados cambiarios chileno en la reduccin del riesgo cambiario. Tercero, se discutirn los determinantes y efectos de la exposicin cambiara en firmas del sector chileno no-financiero. Con relacin al primer tema -experiencia internacional de respuestas de poltica a shocks-, Luis Felipe Cspedes, lian Goldfajn, Phil Lowe y Rodrigo Valds analizan las polticas econmicas diseadas por economas emergentes para contrarrestar los shocks externos en comparacin con polticas aplicadas por las naciones industriales, enumerando los obstculos polticos y legales para implementar polticas alternativas en periodos de crisis. Respecto del segundo tema -papel de las reservas internacionales en la prevencin de crisis-, Pablo Garca y Claudio Soto evalan la contribucin de la liquidez internacional en la reduccin del riesgo de una crisis cambiara, calculando el nivel ptimo de reservas a partir de estimaciones de probabilidades de crisis. Por su parte, Esteban Jadresic y Jorge Selaive analizan la capacidad del mercado de derivados cambiarios como mecanismo para reducir la exposicin al riesgo cambiario por parte de las firmas as como volatilidad de las fluctuaciones del tipo de cambio. Junto a ellos, Kevin Cowan, Erwin Hansen y Luis Oscar Herrera evalan la respuesta del sector privado a los shocks externos enfrentados por la economa chilena a fines de los aos noventa, distinguiendo los factores anticipados por las firmas de aquellos que fueron difciles de predecir o cubrir. Al final de la Segunda Sesin tendremos Conferencias invitadas. La primera, a cargo del Profesor Sebastin Edwards, analizar la experiencia de las economas emergentes y en transicin con respecto a la convertibilidad y manejo de la cuenta de capitales, as como la imposicin de controles de capital, poniendo nfasis en la relacin emprica entre las restricciones en la cuenta de capitales y la vulnerabilidad a crisis externas. En la segunda conferencia invitada, Ernesto Talvi tendr a su cargo el anlisis de la relacin entre sudden stops y vulnerabilidades financieras y sus posibles consecuencias sobre las economas de Sudamrica. La ltima parte de la Conferencia que se llevar a cabo el mircoles contempla la evaluacin de posibles instrumentos de poltica y de mercado que podran desarrollarse para reducir la vulnerabilidad externa. En primer lugar, Kenneth Kletzer analiza el manejo de deuda en economas con riesgo, enfatizando el rol de innovaciones contractuales que ayudaran a suavizar el monto de obligaciones de la deuda ante shocks externos. Segundo, Francisco Gallego y Geraint Jones estudian el rol de los regmenes cambiarios de flotacin como un mecanismo de seguro contra shocks externos. Y, finalmente, Ricardo Caballero y Stavros Panageas analizan estrategias de portafolio ptimas en un ambiente con sudden stops en el influjo de capitales, ofreciendo as una herramienta prctica para el manejo de reservas e inversiones en economas emergentes. Quedan ustedes invitados a un debate que estoy seguro ser fructfero y permitir obtener importantes lecciones para el diseo ptimo de polticas en un mundo cada vez ms integrado. Finalmente, deseo destacar la labor realizada por el equipo de organizacin de esta Conferencia Anual. Ricardo Caballero, profesor del M.I.T, Luis Felipe Cspedes, economista snior del Banco y Csar Caldern, economista snior del Banco, han logrado un esplndido programa y una excelente organizacin de esta conferencia, asistidos eficientemente por Alvaro Aguirre y Mnica Correa. Muchas gracias.

Title: Presentation of the book "Economy for All"
text: PRESENTATION OF THE BOOK "ECONOMY FOR ALL" Welcome Remarks 14 October 2004 On behalf of the Board of the Central Bank of Chile, I am pleased to welcome you to the presentation of the book "Econom92a Para Todos". The title of the book refers to a function that the bank has decided to assume as a priority issue in its communications policy: to approach different audiences and make them aware of its objectives, the logic of its policies and basic tools to improve the understanding of economic phenomena. We know that, although these matters affect the common citizen, for them information and economic analysis are considered dry and difficult to understand, which often marginalizes them from participating in the discussion and activities around these issues. However, almost all the press, television and radio media include economic information in one way or another, since it crosses all the activities that take place in the country. When these matters are not understood, institutions such as the Central Bank end up being perceived by the general public as unaffordable. For the BC, effective communication with people is highly relevant because a better understanding of its policies gives them greater credibility, effectiveness and efficiency. Even more, as public servants whose decisions affect the well-being of all Chileans, we have a responsibility to deliver as much information as necessary about the rationality of our decisions and the fulfillment of our objectives. This is an integral part of our transparency policy. For this reason, the Bank has made many efforts to provide citizens and markets with open, clear and timely information, with all relevant information on its strategy, evaluation and policy decisions, as well as on its procedures. Among the most important initiatives are: - Publication and presentation to different audiences of the Monetary Policy reports and, more recently, the Financial Stability Report, - formal establishment of regular monetary policy meetings, - press releases and publication of minutes following these meetings, - information on its website , - Technical publications - Public interventions of its main authorities, which are also made accessible through the institutional website. - Also noteworthy is the publication of the BC projection models . - Moreover, the Bank publishes most of its economic research and analysis, and is the third largest central bank in the world in terms of the number of working papers published and demanded, as measured by downloads of such documents via the Internet. To institutionalize all communications tasks, the Bank created in the last year a management dedicated to these tasks. However, we recognize that this hard work of increasing transparency must be complemented by an additional effort to approach those audiences that until now do not know our actions and know little about economics. The understanding of our messages conditions the success of transparency: part of that understanding is achieved through the clarity of the messages and another part thanks to the promotion of the capacity of audiences to understand the basic concepts of economics implicit in our communications. In order to bring us closer to the non-specialist public, the Bank has created a program of activities that we call Economy for the Majority, which seeks to disseminate among different sectors basic concepts of economy and, especially, the work of the Central Bank. The importance that the Central Bank of Chile assigns to achieving this objective explains the profile of the person we invite to support us in the first public activity of this program. It is precisely the Importance that we give to the subject which explains why we have chosen a renowned economist to be the author of this book. Everyone knows that Carlos was my predecessor in the presidency of the bank between 1996 and 2002, perhaps less know that he was previously Vice President of the Central Bank of Chile, then becoming president of this institution for the first time in 1967. His responsibilities have included being Director of the Institute of Economics of the University of Chile, Executive Director of the International Monetary Fund, consultant and member of the Economic Research Evaluation Council at the World Bank, and Project Coordinator and Deputy Executive Secretary of the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC). He is a Commercial Engineer, Master and Ph.D (c) in economics from the U. From Chicago, university professor, who is the author of numerous publications and articles in international books and journals. It is precisely his knowledge of economics, which gives him both his studies and his varied professional experience, which ensures the quality of the contribution that Carlos can make in a program. of activities that promote the dissemination of economic matters, a task that, as I said, the Central Bank of Chile has decided to assume. The book "Economy for All" is a first step in this effort. Its pages explain terms that are alien and complex to many, in a simple and very attractive way. In particular, the illustrations contained therein effectively reflect the concepts that are intended to be introduced through everyday situations. The idea is that both students of the last years of high school, technicians and professionals from areas other than economics, and small and medium entrepreneurs can approach this science in a friendlier way, but no less precise or rigorous. The mentioned program includes other tools that we are developing: - The creation of an educational website, which will include didactic downloads of the book "Economy for All", and an annual contest aimed at high school students that will promote the reading on economic issues and motivate them to consider the economy as a useful tool in their activities; - Likewise, extension talks of Directors are already being held to different audiences, mainly to publicize the Monetary Policy Report and the Financial Stability Report, which are the main communication tools of the Central Bank; - Material is being prepared in the form of minutes that explain in a simple way economic concepts or problems commonly used among experts, which are repeatedly mentioned in the various Bank publications. The objective of these is that a layman in economic matters can be self-taught and within a few months come to understand reports such as the Ipom or the IEF. - A very successful project is that of guided tours of the Bank's places of interest. In the celebration of the National Heritage Day we were surprised to see the enormous interest of people to know this building. On that occasion our bank became one of the most visited points and more than 1500 people went through the collection of banknotes and currencies. The bank believes that this motivation should be used as an instrument for this process of disseminating the most important concepts of economics. Thus, the Economy for the Majority program has strengthened the call and the capacity to attend school visits; It is a progressive project: between June and September we received 20 monthly visits, with 420 students, and between October and December more than 40 visits will arrive on average, so we hope that in this semester another 1,200 students will pass through the bank. The programme expects 200 schools to visit us by 2005. We are convinced that this book will be an important contribution, especially to education and business development in our country, and highlighting again the excellent work done by Carlos Massad, I would like to thank on behalf of the Council the presence of all of you at this ceremony.
text_original: PRESENTACION LIBRO ECONOMIA PARA TODOS Palabras de Bienvenida 14 de octubre de 2004 A nombre del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile tengo el agrado de darles la bienvenida a la Presentacin del libro Economa Para Todos. El ttulo del libro se refiere a una funcin que el banco ha decidido asumir como tema prioritario en su poltica de comunicaciones: acercarse a distintos pblicos y darles a conocer sus objetivos, la lgica de sus polticas y herramientas bsicas para mejorar el entendimiento de fenmenos econmicos. Esto es una parte integral de nuestra poltica de transparencia. Por ello son mltiples los esfuerzos que el Banco ha realizado con el fin de facilitar a la ciudadana y a los mercados, de una forma abierta, clara y oportuna toda la informacin relevante sobre su estrategia, evaluacin y decisiones de poltica, as como sobre sus procedimientos. Tambin cabe destacar la publicacin de los modelos de proyeccin del BC.  Ms an, el Banco publica la mayor parte de su investigacin y anlisis econmico, y es el tercer banco central del mundo en cuanto a nmero de documentos de trabajo publicados y demandados, medido por las bajadas de dichos documentos va internet. La importancia que el Banco Central de Chile asigna al logro de este objetivo explica el perfil de la persona que invitamos a apoyarnos en la primera actividad pblica de este programa. Es justamente la importancia que le damos al tema lo que explica que hayamos elegido a un connotado economista para ser autor de este libro. Todos saben que Carlos fue mi antecesor en la presidencia del banco entre el ao 1996 y el 2002, quiz menos conocen que previamente fue Vicepresidente del Banco Central de Chile, convirtindose luego en presidente de esta institucin por primera vez en 1967. Sus responsabilidades han incluido ser Director del Instituto de Economa de la Universidad de Chile, Director Ejecutivo del Fondo Monetario Internacional, consultor y miembro del Consejo de Evaluacin de Investigaciones econmicas en el Banco Mundial, y Coordinador de Proyectos y Secretario Ejecutivo Adjunto de la Comisin Econmica para Amrica Latina y el Caribe (CEPAL). Se trata de un Ingeniero comercial, master y Ph.D (c) en economa de la U. De Chicago, profesor universitario, que es autor de numerosas publicaciones y artculos en libros y revistas internacionales. Son justamente sus conocimientos de economa, que le dan tanto sus estudios como su variada experiencia profesional, lo que asegura la calidad del aporte que Carlos puede hacer en un programa de actividades que promueven la difusin de materias econmicas, labor que, como dije, el Banco Central de Chile ha decidido asumir. El libro Economa Para Todos es un primer paso de este esfuerzo. En sus pginas se explican trminos que a muchos resultan ajenos y complejos, de una manera simple y muy atractiva. En especial, las ilustraciones en l contenidas reflejan eficazmente los conceptos que se quieren introducir mediante situaciones cotidianas. La idea es que tanto los estudiantes de los ltimos aos de enseanza media, los tcnicos y profesionales de reas distintas a la econmica, y los empresarios pequeos y medianos puedan acercarse a esta ciencia de una manera ms amigable, pero no por ello menos precisa ni rigurosa. El programa mencionado incluye otras herramientas que estamos desarrollando:  La creacin de un sitio web educativo, que incluir bajadas didcticas del libro Economa Para Todos, y un concurso anual dirigido a estudiantes de enseanza media que fomentar la lectura en temas econmicos y los motivar a considerar la economa como una herramienta til en sus actividades;  Asimismo, ya se estn realizando charlas de extensin de Consejeros a distintos pblicos principalmente para dar a conocer el Informe de Poltica Monetaria y el Informe de Estabilidad Financiera, que son las principales herramientas de comunicacin del Banco Central;  Se est preparando material en forma de minutas que expliquen de manera sencilla conceptos o problemas econmicos de uso habitual entre los expertos, los que se mencionan repetidamente en las distintas publicaciones del Banco. El objetivo de stas es que un lego en materias econmicas pueda ser autodidacta y en un plazo de unos pocos meses llegar a comprender informes como el Ipom o el IEF.  Un proyecto muy exitoso es el de las visitas guiadas a los lugares de inters del Banco. En esa oportunidad nuestro banco se convirti en uno de los puntos ms visitados y ms de 1500 personas pasaron por la coleccin de billetes y monedas. El banco piensa que dicha motivacin debe ser aprovechada como instrumento para este proceso de difusin de los conceptos ms importantes de economa. As, el programa Economa para la Mayora ha reforzado la convocatoria y la capacidad de atender visitas de colegios; se trata de un proyecto progresivo: entre junio y septiembre pasado recibimos 20 visitas mensuales, con 420 estudiantes, y entre octubre y diciembre llegarn en promedio ms de 40 visitas, por lo que esperamos que en este semestre pasen por el banco otros 1.200 estudiantes. El programa espera que para el ao 2005 nos visiten 200 colegios. | Estamos convencidos que este libro ser un aporte importante, especialmente a la educacin y al desarrollo empresarial de nuestro pas, y destacando nuevamente el excelente trabajo realizado por Carlos Massad, me gustara agradecer a nombre del Consejo la presencia de todos ustedes en esta ceremonia.

Title: Presentation of Roadmap: Basel II
text: Presentation of Roadmap: Basel II Speech by Mr. Vittorio Corbo, President of the Central Bank of Chile, January 25, 2005 1. Most of the time I have to make a presentation to an audience like this, the main topic is some aspect of monetary policy or the macroeconomic outlook. This is what most people expect from the President of the Central Bank, because he relates this institution to price stability, to the administration of monetary policy and to the analysis of the evolution of activity, inflation and interest rates. 2. In this presentation, however, I want to refer to the other fundamental objective of the BCCh and that is the complement of price stability: financial stability. The Central Bank of Chile, as indicated in its Constitutional Organic Law, aims to ensure the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal and external payments. As we know, and experience at both the international and national levels confirms, financial stability and price stability are two complementary objectives. Price stability is a prerequisite for the proper functioning of the financial system and the payment system, and financial stability is a requirement for price stability. 3. Ensuring the financial stability of the economy implies: "the preservation of the primary functions of credit intermediation and savings in general, the provision of payment services, and the allocation of risks, carried out by financial markets and institutions." In other words, it is about avoiding (or at least reducing the probability of) financial and/or exchange rate crisis situations, and, if they occur, minimizing their costs to the economy. 4. Financial stability has the characteristics of a public good. First, more than other sectors of the economy, the financial system is vulnerable to public trust problems, the effects of which quickly spread between institutions and markets and become systemic problems. Second, problems in the financial sector end up adversely affecting all sectors of the economy, when they lead to a credit crunch. Third, historically, the most costly, deep, and long-lasting recessions have been those that originated from episodes of financial crisis. Without going any further, no one can forget the costs that the banking crisis we suffered in the early eighties meant for the country. 5. On the contrary, a financial system that manages to function in an environment of stability contributes significantly to economic growth. There is abundant evidence to show the positive relationship between economic growth and financial stability and development. If financial institutions are strong and there is confidence in financial infrastructure, capital is more likely to be channeled into the best ideas and projects and improve resource efficiency. 6. The concept of financial stability has gained greater notoriety in recent times. In recent years, most central banks and international financial institutions, such as the IMF and the BIS (Bank for International Settlements), have begun to publish regular reports on financial stability. The BCCh also recently began the publication of its Financial Stability Report, whose objective is to provide a well-founded vision about the financial stability conditions of the Chilean economy. 7. This interest probably has its origin in the greater frequency of financial crises in the world since the 70s. Indeed, between 1945 and 1970 there were almost no episodes of systemic financial crises in the world (although access to credit was limited). Since 1970, with the deregulation and opening of financial systems, there is more access to credit, but there are also more episodes of crisis, whose aftershocks, from time to time, have been felt in our economy. 8. However, there is nothing new about concerns about financial stability for central banks. Central Banks were created precisely to deal with the financial instability caused by repeated episodes of bank insolvency and its systemic consequences. Thus, in their initial stages, Central Banks favored the stabilization of financial markets and their work as lenders of last resort. The concern about what we now understand as monetary policy came later, following the abandonment of the gold standard regime with free movement of international capital and the adoption of fiduciary regimes. 9. The role of the BCCh is complementary to the supervisory and supervisory roles performed by the Superintendencies of the financial area and, in particular, the SBIF with respect to individual banks. Our role, however, is focused on systemic risk, which is consistent with the powers and mandates established for the Central Bank in its Constitutional Organic Law. 10. The BCCh assumes a number of responsibilities in relation to financial stability. Firstly, the implementation of financial crisis prevention policies (or more positively, the promotion of stability); and secondly, crisis management policies (or restoration of stability when it is interrupted). With regard to the first group, it is worth mentioning, for example: a5 Maintain low and stable inflation. An environment of low and stable inflation is much less conducive to fueling cycles of financial euphoria than one of high inflation. a5 Ensure the proper functioning of payment systems, i.e. that institutional arrangements are in place for the efficient functioning of the settlement and clearing of high- and low-value payments. a5 Promote, in coordination with the Superintendencies of the financial area, an adequate environment of prudential regulation, financial supervision and market discipline. a5 Monitor the developments of the financial system and financial markets to identify and prevent situations of risk and instability. This involves promoting informed debate on financial stability issues and providing information to participants in the financial system so that they can develop their own risk diagnoses. This mandate is responsible, for example, for the preparation of our six-monthly Financial Stability Report. a5 Participate in international coordination bodies to promote global financial stability (IMF, BIS and others). 11. On the other hand, with regard to the second group, i.e. crisis management policies: a5 Stabilization of financial markets. The Central Bank is empowered to provide emergency liquidity to the economy, in domestic or foreign currency, through open market operations or foreign exchange operations. a5 Lender of last resort. Only in very exceptional situations can the BCCh grant emergency loans to specific institutions: solvent but illiquid banks, in order to contain a contagion of their problems to the rest of the financial system. 12. With respect to the Bank's powers to modify the regulatory framework, I would like to highlight a number of recent initiatives to modernize and keep financial regulations up to date: a5 First, the modernization of the infrastructure of the country's payment systems, with the implementation last April of a system of gross settlement and real-time of high-value payments, known as RTGS, which is associated with the Intraday Liquidity Facility (FLI). To this is added the upcoming creation of a High Value Payment Clearing House, operated by banks under the regulation of the BCCh and the supervision of the SBIF, and the provisions to interconnect payment systems with the Central Securities Depository and, in this way, achieve standards of Delivery against Payment in securities market transactions. a5 Secondly, the new regulations on liquidity risk management in banking institutions, which became operational last June. These rules place the responsibility of defining the liquidity policy on the board and senior administration of the bank and allow the use of its own models to manage liquidity risks. a5 And thirdly, the reform of the rules on market risks (interest rate and currencies) that banking companies must comply with. I can announce that after a long analysis work with the SBIF and the ABIF these rules have recently been approved by the Central Bank Council and will be published in the coming days to enter into force from next July. a5 The new provisions on market risk management represent an important step in bringing our regulatory framework into line with international market risk management standards and recommendations, taking as a reference the 1996 amendment to the Basel Committee's 1988 Capital Arrangement and the 2004 recommendations on interest rate risk management and supervision incorporated into Pillar II of the New Capital Arrangement (Basel II). In practical terms, this is the first concrete step of this roadmap to Basel II which will then be presented by the Superintendent of Banks and Financial Institutions. 13.
