It should be recognized that this occurred in a context of permanent debate in the profession, about the role of the State and monetary and fiscal policies in the economy. Between 1953 and 1955 the fiscal situation deteriorated further, accelerating inflation to 80% in 1955. In this context, the Government invited the Klein-Saks mission to work on formulating and implementing a macroeconomic stabilization programme. The program included short- and long-term actions to control inflation. Short-term actions in monetary, fiscal, and exchange rate policy, as well as price and wage fixings, helped reduce inflation from just over 80 percent in 1955 to less than 20 percent in 1957. But because long-term stocks never materialized for lack of political support, inflation accelerated again to over 30% in 1958. A new attempt at stabilization was introduced between 1959 and 1961, which focused on the use of a fixed exchange rate as a nominal anchor, complemented by the liberalization of foreign transactions. But inflationary inertia and the expansion of public spending led to a deterioration of the current account and a real appreciation, which ended up unleashing a balance of payments crisis that forced the program to be abandoned at the end of 1961. Another attempt was made in the period 1965-1967, on the basis of income policies and monetary policy planning, but this time it was the fiscal deterioration that forced the program to be abandoned. The history of the last thirty years is known. Inflation accelerated again in the early seventies due to a strong fiscal deterioration, and the use of an exchange rate anchor between 1978 and 1982 ended with the debt crisis, which was associated with a severe contraction of economic activity, the generalized bankruptcy of the financial system and, as a result, a deterioration in fiscal and quasi-fiscal accounts. The Central Bank of Chile played a key role in the intervention of the banks and later in its reconstruction. After 1985, the main concerns were to restore order in the fiscal accounts, normalize external payments, rebuild the financial system, and prevent a pickup in inflation. It was only towards the end of the eighties, with the restoration of order in the fiscal accounts, the growing solidity of the financial system, and the creation of an autonomous Central Bank d0 with a clear mandate to ensure the stability of prices and internal and external payments d0 that it was possible to begin to advance more definitively in the control of inflation. When the autonomous Central Bank began to operate, inflation was around 30% per year. In order to reduce it, the Bank set itself annual inflation targets, which were reduced from year to year. Thus began to take shape what is now known as the inflation targeting scheme, which Chile fully implemented only at the end of 1999, when it announced a permanent target and adopted a floating exchange scheme. The inflation-targeting monetary policy scheme was introduced in the early nineties in some industrialized countries, with the aim of keeping inflation at a permanently low level, with Chile being a pioneer among emerging countries. In this scheme, the anchor for inflation is the publicly announced inflation target. Although the credibility of the scheme depends on the autonomy in the management of its instruments and the determination of the Central Bank to guide monetary policy towards achieving the announced objective, its effectiveness and efficiency depend on the order in the fiscal accounts and the existence of a solid financial system. Today there is broad consensus in the country around these principles, and public institutions work in coordination to maintain the macroeconomic stability that eluded us for so many years. But this consensus, which is shared by many countries, was reached after decades of discussion and bad experiences, not only in Chile, but around the world. The current monetary policy scheme has enabled Chile to continuously reduce inflation, from an annual average of 12.1 per cent in the period 1991-1995, to 4.8 per cent in the period 1996-2000, and to 2.2 per cent in the period 2001-2004. Today Chile has a proven and credible inflation targeting scheme, which includes a floating exchange rate with a deepening market to cover currency risks, orderly fiscal accounts and a robust financial system, and which has completed its integration into international capital markets. As a result, our country is better prepared than at other times in its history to face external and internal shocks , since it has a monetary policy that can be transformed into an effective countercyclical tool. But the tasks of a Central Bank never end. Thus, we need to continue working to better understand the functioning of our economy and, in particular, the transmission mechanisms and the effectiveness of monetary policy. The main task of a Central Bank is to contribute to macroeconomic stability. It is through this stability that the Central Bank facilitates the country's growth. This, by the way, we have learned only in the last thirty years: it was an expensive apprenticeship. Despite having achieved stability, we must make every effort to maintain and consolidate it, strengthening and perfecting the institutional framework so that it does not return to the vices of the past which, as we well know, are easy to gestate, but very difficult to solve. The importance of having the right institutional framework is another lesson we economists have learned, this time in the last ten years. And we must all dedicate ourselves to this task of continuing to strengthen the institutional framework, so that when we celebrate 100 years of the Central Bank we can find a Chile that has already definitively conquered macroeconomic stability, and that thanks to this and the advances in education, innovation and competition has achieved economic development and achieved a better distribution of the fruits of it among all Chileans.
text_original: El Banco Central y La Poltica Monetaria en Chile: Sntesis de Ochenta Aos de Existencia Discurso efectuado por don Vittorio Corbo, Presidente del Banco Central de Chile, en la Cena de Gala ofrecida con motivo del Octagsimo Aniversario del Banco Central de Chile 18 de agosto de 2005 En esta oportunidad, en que celebramos ochenta aos de vida del Banco Central de Chile, quisiera hacer un breve recuento de lo que fueron sus orgenes y lo que han sido los logros alcanzados durante las ocho dcadas pasadas. Si nos remontamos a los albores de la Repblica, o incluso antes, encontramos documentacin que muestra que la escasez de circulante ya era una preocupacin constante. Lo anterior signific que desde muy temprano existi en Chile una necesidad evidente de producir dinero, la que se resolvi inicialmente a travs de una autorizacin de la Corona para que se instalara en el pas una casa de moneda y, posteriormente, siendo Chile una Repblica independiente, a travs de la emisin de billetes por parte de bancos comerciales desde la dcada de 1850. Pero fue en 1860, con la primera Ley de Bancos, cuando empezaron a proliferar los bancos privados, los que estaban autorizados para emitir billetes convertibles en oro. Tambin a partir de esa dcada la preocupacin por la escasez de circulante fue reemplazada por una preocupacin por el control de la emisin de medios de pago, de modo de evitar los efectos nocivos de la inflacin y el quiebre del sistema bimetlico. Y siempre existi la duda de si la emisin deba o no ser centralizada y entregada en forma exclusiva a una entidad nica, fuera sta privada, pblica o mixta. Esta discusin se acenta entre 1921 y 1925, y culmina en un acuerdo poltico para crear un banco central basado en la propuesta de la comisin encabezada por el profesor de la Universidad de Princeton, Edwin Kemmerer. As, el 22 agosto del ao 1925 se crea el Banco Central de Chile, para satisfacer ampliamente la necesidad de dotar al pas de una institucin que estabilice la moneda ..." Al momento de crearse el banco se aprobaron tambin otras dos leyes relacionadas: la ley monetaria y la ley general de bancos. La primera estableci un rgimen de patrn oro; la segunda cre una Superintendencia de Bancos que fiscalizara a los bancos comerciales. Para que el Banco Central pudiese cumplir en mejor forma su cometido, se lo concibi como un ente independiente, con un directorio donde slo tres de sus diez miembros eran nombrados por el Presidente de la Repblica. Los restantes eran designados por los otros accionistas, entidades gremiales y sindicales. A su fundacin, el capital del Estado en el Banco alcanzaba a un poco ms del 20%. El propsito de esta estructura de propiedad y de gobierno corporativo era evitar que el Banco Central pudiese ser capturado por el Gobierno o los bancos comerciales. La institucionalidad establecida a partir de estas leyes sirvi de marco para la evolucin econmica del pas en las dcadas siguientes. En sus primeros aos de operacin, en el marco del rgimen monetario de patrn oro, la inflacin fue reducida y los prstamos al sector pblico no excedieron el lmite legal, que era fijado en funcin de la participacin del Estado en el capital del Banco. Esto fue posible gracias a que la fuerte expansin que exhibi el gasto pblico a fines de la dcada del veinte, fue mayoritariamente financiada en el exterior. El auge exportador, la poltica fiscal expansiva y una poltica monetaria tambin expansiva, en la forma de sucesivas reducciones a la tasa de redescuento del Banco Central, llevaron a un fuerte crecimiento econmico en 1928 y 1929. Pero esto cambi abruptamente con el inicio de la Gran Depresin, la que golpe a Chile con una intensidad sin precedentes. La pronunciada cada de las exportaciones tanto el volumen como los precios deterior la situacin fiscal, redujo el crecimiento y aceler la prdida de reservas. En paralelo, el colapso del financiamiento externo oblig a una fuerte contraccin del dficit en cuenta corriente, la que se hizo muy costosa dado el rgimen de patrn oro. No debe sorprender que en estas circunstancias se iniciara un perodo deflacionario que termin, en julio de 1931, con el abandono del patrn oro en medio de una severa crisis poltica y econmica que dio lugar, por primera vez en nuestra historia, a la suspensin del servicio de la deuda externa. El fin del vnculo con el oro en medio de la Gran Depresin, en todo caso, no fue un fenmeno propio de Chile, pues afect a la mayora de los pases del mundo, incluyendo el Reino Unido (septiembre de 1931) y EE.UU. (1933). Superada la Gran Depresin, entre 1933 y 1938 se vivi un perodo de relativa estabilidad macroeconmica, amparada en una notoria mejora de la situacin fiscal, una poltica monetaria ordenada y la recuperacin de la economa mundial, con una inflacin promedio anual de slo 5,4%. Pero el Banco Central continu otorgando crdito a instituciones pblicas y a la industria del salitre, inicindose un perodo en el que el desarrollo de Chile y la operacin del Banco Central estuvieron dominados por la situacin fiscal. As, entre 1938 y 1952 hubo una fuerte expansin del crdito asociada al financiamiento tanto del sector pblico como del sector privado. El gobierno corporativo del Banco Central, controlado por una mayora de representantes del sector privado hasta 1947, facilit este proceso expansivo de la emisin. Durante la mayor parte de este perodo, la tasa de redescuento del Banco Central se mantuvo en 4,5% anual, mientras la inflacin promedio anual alcanzaba a 17%. Ante la incapacidad de controlar el crecimiento de la emisin, las principales herramientas utilizadas para contener la inflacin fueron la fijacin de precios de bienes, tipos de cambio mltiples, controles de cambio y la poltica de reajuste controlado de los salarios. Como era previsible, estas medidas fueron poco eficaces en el control de la inflacin, e introdujeron distorsiones a los precios relativos, con importantes costos de eficiencia. Cabe reconocer que esto ocurra en un contexto de permanente debate en la profesin, sobre el rol del Estado y de las polticas monetaria y fiscal en la economa. Entre 1953 y 1955 la situacin fiscal se deterior aun ms, acelerndose la inflacin a 80% en 1955. En este escenario, el Gobierno invit a la misin Klein-Saks para que trabajara en formular y poner en prctica de un programa de estabilizacin macroeconmica. El programa incluy acciones de corto y largo plazo para controlar la inflacin. Las acciones de corto plazo en poltica monetaria, fiscal y cambiara, as como las fijaciones de precios y salarios, contribuyeron a reducir la inflacin desde poco ms de 80% en 1955, a menos de 20% en 1957. Pero como las acciones de largo plazo nunca se materializaron por falta de apoyo poltico, la inflacin volvi a acelerarse por sobre 30% en 1958. Un nuevo intento de estabilizacin se introdujo entre 1959 y 1961, el que se centr en el uso de un tipo de cambio fijo como ancla nominal, complementado por la liberalizacin de las transacciones con el exterior. Pero la inercia inflacionaria y la expansin del gasto pblico llevaron a un deterioro de la cuenta corriente y a una apreciacin real, que terminaron por desatar una crisis de balanza de pagos que oblig a abandonar el programa a fines del ao 1961. Otro intento se hizo en el perodo 1965- 1967, sobre la base de polticas de ingresos y una planificacin de la poltica monetaria, pero esta vez fue el deterioro fiscal lo que oblig a abandonar el programa. La historia de los ltimos treinta aos es conocida. La inflacin se volvi a acelerar a comienzos de los setenta debido a un fuerte deterioro fiscal, y el uso de un ancla cambiara entre 1978 y 1982 termin con la crisis de la deuda, la que estuvo asociada a una severa contraccin de la actividad econmica, la quiebra generalizada del sistema financiero y, a consecuencia de lo anterior, un deterioro de las cuentas fiscales y cuasi-fiscales. Al Banco Central de Chile le correspondi un rol clave en la intervencin de la banca y ms adelante en su reconstruccin. Despus de 1985, las principales preocupaciones consistieron en restaurar el orden en las cuentas fiscales, normalizar los pagos externos, reconstruir el sistema financiero, y evitar un repunte de la inflacin. Fue slo hacia fines de los aos ochenta, con el restablecimiento del orden en las cuentas fiscales, la creciente solidez del sistema financiero, y la creacin de un Banco Central autnomo -con un claro mandato de velar por la estabilidad de precios y de los pagos internos y externos-, que se pudo comenzar a avanzar en forma ms definitiva en el control de la inflacin. Cuando comenz a operar el Banco Central autnomo, la inflacin bordeaba el 30% anual. Para lograr reducirla, el Banco se plante objetivos anuales de inflacin, los que se fueron reduciendo de ao en ao. Empezaba as a gestarse lo que hoy se conoce como esquema de metas de inflacin, el que Chile implemento en forma plena recin a fines de 1999, al anunciar una meta permanente y adoptar un esquema de flotacin cambiara. El esquema de poltica monetaria de metas de inflacin fue introducido a comienzos de los noventa en algunos pases industrializados, con el objetivo de mantener la inflacin en un nivel bajo de manera permanente, siendo Chile pionero entre los pases emergentes. En este esquema, el ancla para la inflacin es el objetivo inflacionario pblicamente anunciado. Aunque la credibilidad del esquema depende de la autonoma en el manejo de sus instrumentos y la determinacin del Banco Central para orientar la poltica monetaria hacia el logro del objetivo anunciado, la efectividad y eficacia del mismo dependen del orden en las cuentas fiscales y de que exista un sistema financiero slido. Hoy existe amplio consenso en el pas en torno a estos principios, y las instituciones pblicas trabajan coordinadamente para mantener la estabilidad macroeconmica que nos fue esquiva por tantos aos. Pero a este consenso, que es compartido por muchos pases, se lleg despus de dcadas de discusin y malas experiencias, no slo en Chile, sino en todo el mundo. El esquema de poltica monetaria actual le ha permitido a Chile reducir en forma continua la inflacin, desde un promedio anual de 12,1% en el perodo 1991-1995, a un 4,8% en el perodo 1996-2000, y a un 2,2% en el perodo 2001-2004. Hoy Chile tiene un esquema de metas de inflacin probado y creble, que incluye un tipo de cambio flotante con un mercado cada vez ms profundo para cubrir riesgos cambiarios, cuentas fiscales en orden y un sistema financiero robusto, y que ha completado su integracin a los mercados internacionales de capitales. Como resultado de ello, nuestro pas est mejor preparado que en otros momentos de su historia para enfrentar shocks externos e internos, pues dispone de una poltica monetaria que puede transformarse en una efectiva herramienta anticclica. Pero las tareas de un Banco Central nunca terminan. As, tenemos que seguir trabajando para entender mejor el funcionamiento de nuestra economa y, en particular, los mecanismos de transmisin y la efectividad de la poltica monetaria. La principal tarea de un Banco Central es contribuir a la estabilidad macroeconmica. Es a travs de esta estabilidad que el Banco Central facilita el crecimiento del pas. Esto, por cierto, lo hemos aprendido solo en los ltimos treinta aos: fue un aprendizaje costoso. No obstante haber alcanzado la estabilidad, debemos poner todos nuestros esfuerzos en mantenerla y consolidarla, fortaleciendo y perfeccionando el marco institucional de manera que no se vuelva a los vicios del pasado que, como bien sabemos, son de fcil gestacin, pero de muy difcil solucin. La importancia de contar con un marco institucional adecuado es otra de las lecciones que hemos aprendido los economistas, esta vez en los ltimos diez aos. Y a esta tarea de seguir fortaleciendo el marco institucional debemos abocarnos todos, para que cuando se celebren 100 aos del Banco Central podamos encontramos con un Chile que ya haya conquistado definitivamente la estabilidad macroeconmica, y que gracias a sta y a los avances en educacin, innovacin y competencia haya alcanzado el desarrollo econmico y logrado una mejor distribucin de los frutos de ste entre todos los chilenos.

Title: Presentation to the International Monetary and Financial Committee of the IMF
text: Presentation by Mr. Vittorio Corbo, President of the Central Bank of Chile, to the XII Meeting of the International Financial and Monetary Committee, held in Washington D.C. on September 24, 2005. Thank you, Mr. President. The Managing Director's paper on the Medium-Term Strategy of the International Monetary Fund is a very useful and comprehensive document. I would like to take this opportunity to refer to four specific points that I consider particularly relevant to our discussions. Globalization as an Organizing Principle. First, while the proposals to reform the Fund's work in terms of emerging aspects of the opportunities and challenges of globalization deserve our full support, it is also true that the concept of globalization is too broad, as the Managing Director acknowledges in his proposed agenda, which necessitates some clarification. To improve the Fund's effectiveness and efficiency, it is important that it focus its efforts on its areas of expertise and responsibility: that is, on the macroeconomic and financial aspects of globalization, including both policies and institutions. Monitoring Advanced Economies Second, the Fund needs to find better ways to promote joint efforts by major economies to contribute to an orderly adjustment of large global imbalances. To this end, it will be useful to strengthen the Fund's work in analyzing and advising on global trends and developments in individual countries with a focus on their global consequences, as well as giving more emphasis to the analysis of regional and global issues. However, it is necessary to go beyond improving this analysis, and also think about how to determine more clearly the responsibility of the major economies in the resolution of global imbalances, given the magnitude of the "extemalities" of their actions. A possible step in that direction would be to make the IMFC a central forum for discussion of policy options facing major economies, as well as for exploring ways to find cooperative solutions. Insurance and Financing of Emerging Economies Third, studying and promoting the development of private instruments that could play a role in preventing and alleviating financial crises that have the potential to become systemic crises would be a great opportunity and challenge for the Fund's contribution to crisis prevention and international financial stability. The Fund should actively engage with international financial markets for the development of new financial instruments to provide liquidity in times of difficulty. This effort should be seen as a complement to the start of a second round of discussions on Contingent Credit Lines and precautionary arrangements, which we also support. We must remember that the previous discussion on Contingent Credit Lines was not conducive, not because of disagreement over the ultimate objective of the initiative, but rather because of specific problems in the design of the instrument. In this direction, we also propose that the Fund participate in the development of a clearer set of guidelines to incorporate modern risk management practices into the management of public sector assets and liabilities. While much of this technical work can be done at the country level, Fund involvement is needed to change the perception of "good practice standards," thus facilitating countries' political economy to implement these risk management practices. This is important to improve quality and reduce the cost of decreasing emerging economies' exposure to significant exogenous external fluctuations. Capital Account Liberalization Fourthly, in relation to capital account liberalization, and based on our significant experience in this area, we believe that it is wise to achieve a better understanding of its advantages and dangers and thus minimize the risks and maximize the opportunities it offers. Moreover, we recommend that the Fund develop its analysis and advice on a comprehensive review of the role that building an appropriate macroeconomic policy framework and a well-developed, regulated and supervised financial system play in achieving successful integration into global capital markets.

Title: Award speech
text: Santiago, October 17, 2005. AWARD SPEECH Speech by Vittorio Corbo, President of the Central Bank Award Ceremony, contest, "The economy close" This is a very special day, as we have come together to celebrate the happy culmination of an interesting initiative. We are here to award the winners of the school contest "The Closer Economy", the first of its kind organized by the Central Bank of Chile. Some of you may wonder why an institution like the Central Bank has decided to hold this school competition? The reason is that with the experience accumulated through 80 years of existence and 15 years of autonomy, we have managed to establish a framework of monetary, exchange rate and financial policies, which has contributed to building a solid and internationally integrated economy, with low and stable inflation. Having finally achieved macroeconomic stability, which was very elusive for many years, allows us and at the same time forces us to worry about other relevant and complementary aspects of our daily work, which contribute to consolidating stability and improving the effectiveness of our policies. One of these aspects is to improve society's ability to understand the importance of the Central Bank's objectives and the logic of its policies. In this sense and unlike past decades, central banks around the world have come to the conviction that it is not enough for the monetary authority to provide information about what it does and why it does it; In addition, today it is essential that this information is understood by as many people as possible, in order to contribute to strengthening autonomy and improving the effectiveness of monetary policy. In addition, we want to collaborate from our field in the educational process, contributing to the economic and financial training of Chileans. We believe that for people, knowing and understanding the macroeconomic and financial environment and its perspectives allows them to make better decisions in their domestic environment, contributing to improving their well-being and reducing the uncertainty and risk that surrounds them. Many central banks around the world are aware of this, as are international organizations (OECD) that have begun to develop massive education and extension programs in economic matters. For this we created the "Economy for the Majority" Program, which tries to bring the Central Bank closer to citizens through a website, seminars and other related activities. The first step in this line was the launch of the book "Economy for all", written by Carlos Massad, which in its pages tries in a simple and attractive way to explain concepts and terms that are usually alien to the common people. The next step has been the realization of the school contest "La Econom92a Cerca", for whose award we have met today. The development of this contest has allowed us to live an interesting process, which began last February with the dissemination stage of the contest. At this stage, the support of Mineduc was very important, which through its Enlaces network gave us access to all schools in the country. The answer was certainly surprising: 1246 groups belonging to 503 municipal schools, subsidized and paid throughout Chile, including Easter Island, were registered. From the registered groups, 449 essays were received from the most remote places of Chile, and they addressed in a very creative way the contents proposed by the contest. As an example, I tell you that we received an essay entitled: "Can there be an economy so close in the commune of Hualaihue, if there is no bank branch?" This work was sent by the students of 3or half of the Liceo Hornopir8en of the commune of Hualaihue, in the X region, and was selected among the 11 best essays. The evaluation of the works was certainly one of the most complex stages, not only because of the quantity but also because of the variety of approaches. At this stage we had the collaboration of 10 professionals from the bank, who had the difficult mission of selecting the 11 finalist works. I take this opportunity to thank: Valeria Garc92a, Carolina Grunwald, Carolina Orellana, Felipe Bravo, Luis Figueroa, Alvaro Garc92a, Patricio Jaramillo, Mauricio Larra92n, Fernando Parro and Sergio Rodr92guez, for their time, work and dedication. We share with them the amazement and excitement of trying to look at the economy from angles not usual for us. The next step was to select the 3 best works that have been presented today by their authors to the jury. I refer to the works: - "Impact of the interest rate on family spending", of the Arturo Alessandri Palma Polyvalent High School, A-12, of Providencia; - "Inter8es versus Reito", from the Liceo Carlos Cousi96o Goyenechea, A-45, from Lota, in the VIII Region; and - "A youth conceptual proposal: The student basket", of the Anglo Maip9c School, of Maip9c. The reading of these works and this morning's session, where the different groups made a presentation in front of the jury, has been a tremendously enriching experience, which ratifies my deep conviction, after teaching for many years, that one of the main responsibilities of any society is to educate future generations. Education is the ultimate cause of development and progress, but also the vehicle that allows each human being to fully develop his capacities and, therefore, his personal fulfillment. I would like to conclude by thanking all those who made possible the successful realization of this contest, in particular: The officials and authorities of the Ministry of Education and its Enlaces network; The teachers guide the more than 400 works submitted; The students of the more than 500 schools enrolled, for their enthusiasm and creativity, especially those who are with us today; The officials and authorities of the different municipalities, who selflessly joined this effort; The different Associations of Schools, both subsidized and private, that collaborated in the dissemination of this contest; Central Bank officials who, at different stages of the contest and from different areas of the bank, contributed their time, creativity and effort; Finally, to the counselor of the Central Bank of Chile Mrs. Mar92a Elena Ovalle, who was the executor of this initiative and who, on behalf of the Council, assumed the tasks of supervision and coordination of each and every one of the stages of the contest. I am sure that Mar92a Elena's participation was vital so that today we can celebrate the success achieved in this first version of this School Contest. Thanks a lot.

Title: Speech by the President of the Central Bank of Chile, Vittorio Corbo, in tribute to the Minister of...
text: FAREWELL ADDRESS TO MRS. MARIA ELENA OVALLE, COUNSELOR OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF CHILE Vittorio Corbo 30 November 2005 It is for me to begin this event by expressing, on behalf of this institution, the recognition of one of its members who is serving his term on the Council, in whose honour we have met. If Mar92a Elena Ovalle leaves us today, it is with the personal satisfaction of having completed an entire career dedicated to public service. From her years of work there is a personal mark: Mar92a Elena's professional commitment to deep, reasoned and objective analysis in macroeconomic, monetary and financial matters, the basis of central bank decision-making. Our institutional achievements, in terms of price stability and credibility, have the clear stamp of your personal contribution. However, Mar92a Elena's important contribution to the institutional consolidation of the Central Bank goes beyond the merely technical. I must mention here his great contribution in bringing the Bank closer to the community, in order to promote understanding of its objectives, policies and achievements among citizens. In this area, Mar92a Elena became the promoter, defender and guarantor of the need for the Central Bank of Chile to make an effort to bring the economy closer to society. In other words, to commit the Central Bank to the education of Chileans, within the scope of its competence. Programs such as Econom92a para la Majority, which awarded the best economics essay written by high school students from all over the country, are examples of Mar92a Elena Ovalle's healthy influence among her peers. At the heart of the contribution of Mar92a Elena Ovalle, economist, wife, mother of four children, grandmother of eight grandchildren, lies in having given the country all her experience in the most diverse national contexts and to the Bank in numerous positions, from the area of studies to internal credit management, culminating in 1995 with her appointment as a counselor. He witnessed the evolution of monetary management in our country, its growing complexity and harmony with world developments, as well as the expectations it was generating in increasingly broad sectors of the population. She was able to see, in a pioneering way, that the interlocutors and "clients" of a central bank are not only bankers, financial operators and economists with postgraduate studies, but an increasingly broad set of social actors, exposed to increasingly sophisticated media. Although her name is associated, and to our pride, with this institution, Mar92a Elena Ovalle did not limit herself to making a career in the Central Bank. After a period of eighteen years in the functions just mentioned, she moved to the private financial sector, in which she gained valuable experience in her capacity as manager of the Association of Banks and Financial Institutions, Director of the Guillermo Subercaseaux Institute of Banking Studies, Alternate Governor of the Latin American Federation of Banks and Director of the Economic Policy Commission of the Confederation of Production and Commerce. The highest trade union body of Chilean business. Perhaps my words convey an erroneous notion, in terms of suggesting a professional future free of obstacles. We must also remember that, when Mar92a Elena joined the Central Bank, the role of women in this activity was still very incipient, if not a rarity. Even so, she marked a style and left an imprint that opens the way for future generations of professionals. She was president, without going any further, of the Chilean chapter of the "Women's World Banking". I am sure that many women who are currently pursuing university degrees in the area of social sciences, have as their antecedent Mar92a Elena Ovalle, syndicated by the media as one of the national women leaders. Perhaps a central element of this curriculum, as rich as it is intense, is the fact that Mar92a Elena Ovalle is a person of faith. Of faith in people, faith in country and faith in God. Voracious reader, lover of opera, the countryside and flowers, concerned about the development of women and society. As an example of these convictions: his eldest son Arturo is a priest and follows the example of San Alberto Hurtado, working in the first Jesuit community in the Mapuche world, in the commune of Tir9ca, eighth region. I conclude my words of thanks to Mar92a Elena Ovalle by counting me among those who have had the privilege of working with her. With the members of the Council we can attest to its contribution to the consolidation of monetary policy in Chile and its legitimacy and transparency among economic and social actors. Its stamp is reflected by thoroughness and rigor. Mar92a Elena, your colleagues at the Central Bank of Chile give you the most affectionate farewell. Although we will miss you very much, we are left with the certainty that you will not lower your arms and you will find many ways to continue contributing to the well-being of Chile. Thanks a lot

Title: Oil Price and Monetary Policy
text: OIL PRICES AND MONETARY POLICY Presentation by Mr. Vittorio Corbo, President of the Central Bank of Chile, at the Monetary Club, December 2, 2005. Introduction Since the end of 2003, the price of oil has risen by 75%. Despite its significant magnitude, such an increase was not part of the most likely scenario, although it was part of the possible risks considered by the markets and the different specialized observers. Oil prices have been rising since 1999. For several years, even though the price continued to rise, the market outlook took the increase as transitory. This transit was gradually lost, and we arrived at 2005 where for several months now the expectations implied in future prices indicate that the market expects the price of oil to remain at persistently high levels. croeconomic. The less developed economies, including Chile's, also experienced periods of great turbulence. Global concern regarding this phenomenon is natural. The previous times we saw oil prices like nowd1remember the seventies and eightiesd1the world suffered sharp inflationary increases and economic growth suffered significantly. Never since the post-war period has the global economy been subject to so much volatility in the aftermath of the war. Unlike the sharp rise in prices of the seventies, which responded to a severe restriction of the supply of crude oil by OPEC, today the high price of oil is linked to high demand, which in turn derives from the robust growth of the world economy. This means that the shock occurs in a favorable context of global dynamism, driven by the high growth of large oil consumers such as China, the US and India. Despite being the result of an increase in demand, will we see such a negative outcome again? For various reasons, it seems that the world economy (Chile included) today is better prepared than in the past to face changes of this magnitude in the price of oil. The same historical experience has conveyed lessons to both policy implementers and market participants to avoid making the mistakes that exacerbated the effects of previous oil shocks. Below I will review some of these elements that allow us to expect, as a central scenario, a relatively benign accommodation of the oil shock, but I emphasize that in any case we must be attentive to the possibility that in the future the implications of these prices will be more unfavorable than what we expect today. The most obvious is the effect it has on the purchasing power of households and companies that use oil and derivatives for their consumption or in their production processes. Although this happens whenever the price of a product rises, in the case of oil the effect is exacerbated because the possibilities of replacing it with other products or inputs are very scarce, particularly in the short term. In this way, the rise in oil prices acts as a tax on households and businesses, reducing consumer income, increasing costs and cutting firms' profits. The counterpart to this has been a significant increase in the revenues of oil-exporting countries. How has this income effect been in Chile? Between January 2004 and October of this year, the price of the representative consumption basket, on which the CPI is calculated, rose 6.8%, and a third of the increase is explained by the fuel situation. Oil prices, therefore, have directly reduced the real income of families between 2 and 2.5%, with a minor additional effect through their impact on some regulated tariffs, such as collective locomotion. At the country level, in 2003 we spent 3.1 billion on fuel imports. This year, by comparison, we will spend about 6.4 billion on this concept. This increased spending is equivalent to approximately 2.5% of our national income. However, everything suggests that the effect on growth in Chile has been relatively limited, lower than the income effect. In part, this lower revenue has not translated into a proportional reduction in spending, thanks to the fact that it has been able to accommodate with greater financing. Indeed, although the current account balance is no longer showing the large surpluses of previous years d0 a balance close to balance is expected this year d0 this is largely due to the strong fiscal surplus. The latter has compensated, then, in the aggregate external accounts of the Chilean economy, private financing needs that are substantial, probably in the order of 4 to 5% of GDP. This is more than just an arithmetic exercise. The higher price of oil has not had a contractionary effect of the first order in Chile thanks to the fact that it has coincided with an external environment that in substance remains very favorable. There is a general rise in the prices of basic products, particularly copper, so relevant for the Chilean economy, but also molybdenum and cellulose, among others. Moreover, the cost of external financing has been particularly advantageous, thanks to low international interest rates and the compression of sovereign spreads. Oil-exporting countries have spent much of the increased income on increasing their savings abroad, thus helping to finance current accounts in other economies and thus sustaining global growth. To the extent that nominal wages sought to maintain the purchasing power of households, despite the negative income effect we mentioned, this meant that in the end the higher inflation was the one that reacted to make the adjustment of disposable income. Indeed, if wages begin to adjust to past effective inflation, the increase in fuel prices will become an increase in costs (beyond its direct effect), a compression of margins and greater forward price pressures. In the current circumstances in Chile, to the extent that wages depend more on expectations of future inflation, and these expectations remain well anchored at around 3%, the pass-through to wages and the impact on prices will be less. The lower inflation that occurs, the less monetary policy tightening is needed. Monetary policy reaction The monetary policy reaction to higher oil prices must be understood within the macroeconomic policy framework that exists in Chile. As is well known, it has three fundamental components: (i) A responsible fiscal policy that follows the structural surplus rule; (ii) A credible inflation target based on a range of 3 /-1%; and (iii) A floating policy would change, in which the Central Bank reserves the possibility of intervening in exceptional circumstances. In practice, the main mechanism of shock spread has to do with the same monetary policy action or inaction. In the seventies, the reaction of monetary policy in the main economies was accommodative, motivating a relaxation of monetary conditions in the presence of higher inflation, which in turn led to an additional acceleration of inflation, effective and expected. The lessons of this episode are that monetary conditions should not automatically ease after an inflationary shock, but the opposite. In any case, the same rise in fuel prices weakens activity, and therefore mitigates policy actions, which together with the expected persistence of the shock are important factors when gauging the magnitude of the monetary policy response. The recent increase in the price of oil in the world has occurred in circumstances where major economies had already begun to withdraw monetary stimulus. The weak stage of the global cycle, between 2002 and 2003, has already passed, and the world is showing significant expansion rates. That in itself is reason enough for the very loose monetary conditions to begin to normalize. The additional concern is that this oil shock does not end up affecting inflation expectations for maturities beyond one year and, in this way, causes an increase in the inflationary trend that affects price stability. Something similar has happened in Chile. The gradual increase in the MPR has been implemented thanks to the fact that economic activity and domestic spending have left behind the periods of low expansion between 2001 and 2003. So far, the oil shock has had an impact on the course of monetary policy only insofar as it has reacted to avoid a de-anchoring of inflation expectations in Chile.
