En el corto plazo, la inflacin subyacente del IPCX1, aunque con vaivenes, se proyecta en niveles similares a los actuales. Durante el 2007 y comienzos del 2008, estara marginalmente por sobre 3%, dado un breve crecimiento superior al de tendencia en el 2007 y por el efecto del leve aumento del tipo de cambio real que supone el escenario base. Para la inflacin IPC, en tanto, se proyecta una reduccin paulatina hacia valores incluso por debajo de 3% a fines del tercer y comienzos del cuarto trimestre del 2006, en parte importante por la alta base de comparacin de igual perodo del 2005. En los ltimos meses del ao volvera a aumentar transitoriamente a cifras por encima de 3% anual, para luego mantenerse en torno al centro del rango meta hasta fines del horizonte de proyeccin. El mayor precio esperado para el petrleo en el escenario base tiene su principal impacto sobre la inflacin en el 2006. Aunque ms lentamente que en IPoM anteriores, se espera una convergencia a su precio considerado de largo plazo, lo que lleva a una inflacin proyectada del IPC menor que la del IPCX e IPCX1 el 2007 y principios del 2008. Este escenario es congruente con el supuesto metodolgico de reduccin gradual del impulso monetario en los prximos trimestres con una trayectoria comparable a la implcita en la estructura de tasas de inters de las ltimas dos semanas. Las proyecciones del IPoM se construyen a partir de los eventos que se consideran ms probables y que configuran el escenario base. Como es habitual, existen variadas fuentes de incertidumbre que podran dar pie a resultados diferentes de los supuestos. En el mbito externo, destaca el riesgo de que el precio del cobre sea distinto del proyectado. Podra ser menor, considerando que las alzas recientes se han dado sin cambios adicionales significativos en sus fundamentos. Pero tambin es posible que se den precios superiores, ante un escenario de mayor demanda, especialmente de China e India, y problemas imprevistos en la oferta. Asimismi sobresale el riesgo de que el precio del petrleo se mantenga en los niveles actuales o incluso suba. Este riesgo ha aumentado y podra tener efectos negativos en el crecimiento mundial, as como mayores presiones inflacionarias, lo que ha sido alertado recientemente por el FMI. Si bien se estima que el mundo es hoy menos sensible a los incrementos del precio del petrleo, los altos niveles de las ltimas semanas, y el hecho que el precio ahora tambin est afectado por factores de oferta, podran tener efectos ms significativos que los vistos hasta ahora. El riesgo de un deterioro de las condiciones financieras internacionales sigue presente y se percibe algo mayor. Ello por el aumento de la inflacin en economas desarrolladas, el mayor dinamismo de la demanda interna y el incremento del precio de los combustibles, en un contexto en que las holguras de capacidad se han ido copando ms rpido que lo anticipado, en especial en EE.UU. Por otro lado, los premios soberanos de economas emergentes se han mantenido en niveles inusualmente bajos, lo que mantiene el riesgo de aumentos significativos frente a una eventual reevaluacin del apetito por riesgo de los inversionistas. Esto, por ejemplo, ante un deterioro abrupto de las condiciones de liquidez internacional o una menor disposicin de los inversionistas por tomar posiciones en instrumentos de economas emergentes, en particular de Amrica Latina. Destacan, adems, las muestras de preocupacin que ha dado el mercado por el desempeo de algunas economas especficas en la regin. Mantiene preponderancia el riesgo de un descenso mayor en los precios de activos inmobiliarios en los pases desarrollados, en los que han alcanzado niveles especialmente altos. El consiguiente deterioro de la riqueza de las familias podra llevar a una desaceleracin mayor que la prevista del gasto privado en esas economas, de la actividad de la construccin y, en ltimo trmino, del ritmo de expansin de la actividad mundial. A nivel global, existen varios riesgos menos probables en el corto plazo, pero que de ocurrir tendran un impacto notorio. Contina la posibilidad de ajuste desordenado de los desbalances globales ahorro-inversin, que provocara un deterioro de las condiciones financieras internacionales y una disminucin de la actividad mundial. Adems, los propios desbalances podran acentuar las disputas comerciales a nivel mundial, llevando a un mayor proteccionismo global, con el consiguiente dao al comercio y al crecimiento econmico. Si bien los alcances de la gripe aviar an son desconocidos, podra tener efectos negativos en el crecimiento mundial. Asimismo, permanecen los riesgos geopolticos y de atentados terroristas. Internamente, existen riesgos asociados a la transmisin de las alzas recientes del precio del cobre a la economa. Ello se relaciona con expectativas de que los altos precios perduren, llevando a una demanda interna mayor que la esperada, en un escenario de menor tipo de cambio y mayores presiones inflacionarias. En este cuadro cabra esperar la consiguiente reaccin de la poltica monetaria, para mantener la estabilidad de precios y la sostenibi- lidad del ciclo expansivo. Es incluso posible que las expectativas sobre este tipo de escenario tengan efectos que se manifiesten en el corto plazo a travs de movimientos en los precios financieros clave, o si los agentes privados adelantan sus planes de gasto. Cabe destacar que el precio de referencia del cobre que se establezca para efectos del clculo de los ingresos estructurales del Fisco es un elemento central en la transmisin de cambios en el precio del cobre al resto de la economa a travs del gasto pblico y, por lo tanto, en la probabilidad de materializacin de este riesgo. Ms all de lo anterior, es posible que la desaceleracin que ya se observ en el crecimiento anual de la demanda interna durante el primer trimestre no prosiga segn lo proyectado. Esto, tanto por las favorables condiciones crediticias presentes como por el robusto crecimiento del empleo. Considerando los elevados trminos de intercambio que enfrenta la economa chilena y las dudas de cmo este fenmeno ser absorbido, adems de las excepcionales condiciones financieras internacionales, se estima que existe una mayor incertidumbre respecto de la trayectoria que seguir la demanda interna, la actividad y el tipo de cambio en Chile. Finalmente, los efectos del precio del petrleo y su incierta evolucin futura persisten como un riesgo importante en el mbito interno. Dado que se estima que las holguras de capacidad ya son escasas y desapareceran en los prximos trimestres, es posible que los mayores precios de los combustibles, ya ocurridos o por ocurrir, tengan un efecto ms perceptible sobre la inflacin subyacente que lo visto hasta ahora. El Consejo considera que, evaluadas en conjunto, estas distintas contingencias hacen que el balance de riesgos para el crecimiento est sesgado al alza y equilibrado para la inflacin. El Consejo estar especialmente atento a cmo la economa absorba el inusual escenario de trminos de intercambio que enfrenta, en un contexto de escasas holguras de capacidad y una tendencia inflacionaria y expectativas de inflacin alineadas con el centro del rango meta. De particular inters ser el comportamiento de la demanda interna, de la actividad, de precios clave como los salarios y el tipo de cambio, y sus implicancias para la inflacin proyectada en el horizonte habitual de poltica de 12 a 24 meses.

Title: Global Imbalances and Risks in the World Economy
text: Global Imbalances and Risks in the World Economy Presentation of the President of the Central Bank, Mr. Vittorio Corbo Lioi, at the Seminar of the Center for Public Studies, on July 26, 2006. The external environment for the Chilean economy is unusually favorable. Although fluctuating, the world economy is on track to complete the best three years of growth in the last three decades, with average rates more than a third higher than those observed between 1970 and 2000. Moreover, for the first time in many years, this great global dynamism has been driven by improvements in all regions. The global growth of 2004-2005, driven by a single engine d0 the US d0 is now accompanied by other major players. These include the Eurozone, which is emerging strongly from its lethargy, and China and India, which together represent the same as the US in world GDP to PPP, and which grow at impressive rates that can be maintained over time, given the great potential that remains to be exploited. Thus, this scenario of high growth is also more balanced, which gives lights of greater sustainability. For 2007, a somewhat less strong dynamism is expected than in recent years, although also much more powerful than in the average of the last three decades. External financial conditions, meanwhile, although they show a small deterioration in the latest data, caused by the increase in policy and long-term interest rates in developed economies, remain quite expansionary. This is especially true in the US, whose GDP has been growing for a couple of years above its potential output growth, generating inflationary pressures in an overheated economy, and entering a cycle of increases in the monetary policy rate that, after many increases, is nearing its end. Sovereign prizes in emerging economies also remain unusually low, albeit with a slight increase in recent months. This has resulted in significant reductions in the cost of borrowing that these economies have taken advantage of well to refinance their debts and improve their solvency. Finally, contrary to expectations, commodity prices have reached higher and have remained at these levels for longer than expected. The Bank and market players have had to make continuous adjustments to their projections of the future evolution of these prices but, fortunately in the case of Chile, these have been stronger for our exportable products (copper and molybdenum) than for our importable products (oil), resulting in an improvement in the terms of trade and an increase in the disposable income of its inhabitants. However, this exceptional external scenario is not without risks. On the near horizon, there are concerns about the possibility of high oil prices spreading beyond what was expected and even reach higher levels. Linked to this risk is that inflation in developed countries does not reduce and even increases further, putting an end to the times when the second-round effect of high oil prices was not passed on to prices, and beginning a cycle in which economies with capacity gaps in the capacity covered begin to lose their ability to insulate themselves from inflationary pressures produced by these oil rises, which with new price shocks would worsen the situation. In the longer term, the central concern is how global imbalances will be managed and what their impact will be. We are currently facing an unusually high oil price. Since February 1999, it has almost quadrupled in real terms. Although at first it was thought that this was a transitory cycle similar to the previous ones, over time expectations have been adjusted towards a much more durable cycle with much higher price levels than originally expected. In comparative terms with the cycles lived since 1975, this is today (even before knowing where and when it will end) an abnormal cycle. In length it already doubles the average 28 months of the previous five cycles, and in amplitude the doubling of prices that we have witnessed is much higher than the average increase of 36%. In this context, the Bank and the market have been adjusting their projections upwards. The first projections for 2006 that we made in January 2005 gave a price of 34 dollars a barrel, that is, about half of what is projected today for this year. The same has happened with the projections for 2007. The futures market has also been constantly changing upwards and even reducing its slope, reflecting the expected duration of this cycle. As for the origin of the cycle, unlike that of the late seventies where the problem was one of supply from the OPEC member countries, today the narrowness of the market is due to a demand that has grown a lot in a context of limited and uncertain supply. In addition, it should not be ignored that part of the increase is due to speculation. Hedge funds and commodity trading have increased dramatically over the past four years. On the demand side, the dynamism of large oil consumers such as China and India contributes to a powerful source of higher consumption. Between 1990 and 2003, increased oil consumption by both nations accounted for about one-third of the global increase. Moreover, the rise in prices has not produced the expected adjustment in consumption. The price elasticity of demand is generally low, although it varies by region, being higher in Asian countries and relatively low in the US. Replacement, maintenance, and efficiency gains have been limited. Part of this callousness stems from national tax and subsidy policies, which prevent prices from reflecting shortages, inhibiting the natural adjustment that current prices should produce . On the supply side, the ability to react to price increases is rather slow and limited. First, the largest oil potentials are located in areas of high political instability, which increases the risk premium for new projects and limits the production of active fields. Indeed, to the conflicts related to the missile tests in North Korea and the nuclear dispute in Iran, the conflict between Israel and Lebanon was added, which affects the price of oil by increasing the Likelihood of crude supply cuts. Additionally, if Syria and/or Iran are added to the conflict, the price can jump even higher. On the other hand, new projects take longer to materialize due to the increasing obstacles imposed by environmental regulation. Even if oil extraction increases in the coming months, the limit will come from the inability to process it and therefore in the supply of fuels. That is, the bottleneck is in the refineries. Finally, there have been significant supply cuts due to severe weather events in the Gulf of Mexico. In conclusion, the precarious political stability of oil-producing countries, with the consequent uncertainty regarding possible production increases in the near future, together with the large increase in demand expected from India and China, and the limited reaction of policies that encourage the rationalization of demand, suggest that the tightness of the market will be more durable than initially expected and previous cycles. The good news is that the world today is better prepared to minimize the costs of these oil price shocks. The high credibility in the inflationary objectives that most economies have achieved and the high levels of competitiveness reduce the pass-through to prices. In addition, the greater diversification of suppliers, potential improvements in efficiency of use and substitution towards other energy sources, give lights of hope. In fact, substitutes such as sand and soybean oil are already marketed at acceptable prices today. Finally, to the extent that the composition of the countries' production diversifies and the importance of services in the productive basket increases, the intensity of energy use will be reduced. A second latent risk, related to the previous one, is that inflation increases in developed countries. Until 2005, core and CPI inflation were well contained in the world. Today, increases in the prices of raw and industrial materials and the takeover of capacity slack have been pushing up prices. The US, the Eurozone and Japan have all seen their various measures of inflation increase over the past year, reaching levels that exceed the implicit (US) or explicit (Europe) targets that have been imposed. In fact, in the US, total inflation today exceeds the limit of the monetary authority's comfort zone and exceeds recent Chilean inflation. The case of Europe is even more complicated since having a relatively new central bank that is still building its reputation, agents look only at dirty inflation and its weak credibility contributes to more expeditious transfers at prices. In this context, the central banks of developed countries have begun to reduce the expansionary nature of their monetary policy. In general, those who experienced a period of monetary policy easing between 2001 and 2003 have reversed or are reversing that stimulus. In the US, the rate adjustment began as early as April 2005. At its meeting on June 29, the Fed increased the policy rate by 25 basis points for the seventeenth consecutive time, placing it at 5.25% annually. The latest indicators suggest economic growth is moderating, reflecting cooling in the housing market, the lagged effects of interest rate hikes and energy hikes. On the price side, inflationary risks remain unchanged, although moderating growth helps limit inflation pressures. The market expects that in the remainder of the year it will produce one or two further rate hikes before the normalization cycle ends. In the Eurozone, the ECB began cutting expansionary in December. In July, it maintained the instance rate at 2.75%, but said it will keep a strong watch to ensure that inflationary risks do not materialize. Signs of improved growth prospects in Europe lead to expectations of further increases in the future. The latest to jump on this trend was the Bank of Japan, which after a while of trying unorthodox ways out of recession, began its rate hike cycle recently with it rising to 0.25%. In conclusion, it is clear that inflationary pressures are being felt and may increase with further oil price shocks or a longer cycle. Therefore, it is very likely that it will be necessary to continue cutting the expansionary nature of monetary policy, but with high uncertainty regarding how much and therefore the final effect on activity. If inflationary pressures are underestimated, it lags behind in rate adjustment and allows sharp increases in inflation and rates, with detrimental effects on financial markets. On the other hand, if the adjustments that occur are excessive, then there is a risk of unnecessarily slowing down economic activity. The last risk I want to analyze is one of lower probability, but with final effects that can be of high impact. That is, how global imbalances are resolved. Over the past thirteen years, the US current-account deficit has widened considerably. By 2006 it is expected to reach 6.5% of US GDP and more than 2% of world GDP. So far, this growing deficit has been financed mainly by oil-producing countries, emerging Asia d1 especially China d1 and Japan. Latin America's contribution is negligible. In 2005, the region ran a surplus equivalent to less than 1 percent of the U.S. current-account deficit. However, even if it is not contributing to aggravate imbalances, it may suffer the consequences of abrupt changes in financial prices, caused by this situation, which, in the opinion of many, is unsustainable. The first visions of how the adjustment would occur were colored by the Asian and Mexican crises, so it was expected that the solution to this imbalance would occur abruptly when foreign investors lost interest in keeping American assets in their portfolios, causing a sharp break in the financing of high American consumption. In such a case, US interest rates would rise and the dollar would over-react. Consumption in the U.S. would slow without being offset by increases in other countries, with strong effects on global growth. I think this scenario, very popular until a couple of years ago, is unlikely. The flexibility and depth of financial markets and portfolio decisions in the rest of the world suggest that adjustment should occur much more gradually through softer movements in financial prices. In this case, demand can be expected to move gradually from deficit countries to countries with surplus, and that consumption and asset prices converge smoothly to sustainable paths, as in fact we are already observing. Thus, higher savings in the US and higher consumption and/or investment in the rest of the world lead to a more benign scenario for global growth, where the slowdown in US demand is partly offset by stronger demand from other countries. The gradual nature of this adjustment would benefit if Asia, especially China, made its exchange rates more flexible to produce the necessary reallocation of spending. This greater flexibility would also be beneficial for countries to regain control over their monetary policy. But this benign adjustment would still be accompanied by a moderate slowdown in global growth. An alternative vision of this gradual adjustment is the one made public by a line of research by Chilean economist Ricardo Caballero, who argues that these imbalances are a balancing solution in a world where very dynamic emerging countries have not sufficiently developed their financial markets or attractive investment instruments, while the US has done so with remarkable efficiency. In this case, the adjustment would also be gradual and would occur to the extent that financial markets developed in emerging countries and part of the capital flows returned to their countries of origin when profitable investment alternatives were found. Recent events of rising demand in Japan and the European Union and slowing private consumption and housing markets in the US make a gradual adjustment more likely. However, although with low probability, the risks of an abrupt adjustment are still present and, given the high costs involved, the authorities cannot passively wait for global imbalances to be corrected. Instead, they should promote gradual and cooperative adjustment and take action to reduce the detrimental effects that this adjustment may have on their countries. To promote gradual and cooperative adjustment, savings in the U.S. should be encouraged through fiscal effort and incentives for private savings; encouraging private consumption in Chinad1which now saves more than half of GDPd1through financial sector reforms that improve households' access to credit and expanding social safety nets to reduce household savings out of precaution, such as those proposed at the last Communist Party Congress. Also increase investment in emerging Asiad1which slumped in 1997 and has failed to recover sinced1through incentives for quality investment through structural reforms that increase expected returnsd1improvements to the business environment, labor flexibility, and efficient allocation of resources in the financial market. Asian countries have faced crises with strong accumulations of international reserves, which at current rates and exchange rates are relatively cheap, and even profitable, and with this they hope to avoid a new crisis like that of 97. The bad thing is that they have had a strong expansion of credit (especially China) and that they have neglected reforms in the financial market that would protect them more efficiently from a possible crisis. Finally, it would help this adjustment greatly if the relative value of the dollar were reduced vis-88-vis other currencies, especially China's. Ex-post reactions to minimize the costs of an abrupt adjustment depend on the monetary and exchange rate policy framework. Countries with inflation expectations well anchored at low levels and with limited exchange rate mismatches should let the exchange rate adjust to lead the change in relative prices. "Leaning against the wind" will only generate capital flight, financial instability and a credit shortening. Countercyclical fiscal and monetary policy and a solid local financial system help to face possible international financial crises with reversal of capital flows, with less need to accumulate international reserves. Countries with unanchored inflation expectations face a more complex picture. Real depreciation will be overshadowed by higher inflation or, if currency mismatches of assets and liabilities are large, depreciation will be contractionary by producing significant balance sheet effects. To avoid a major financial crisis in these countries, the only tool available will be fiscal policy and it would be strongly recessionary. Uncertainty about how the adjustment of imbalances will occur has an impact on policy decisions. The monetary policy of emerging countries has limited or no impact on how the adjustment occurs. However, it undoubtedly affects monetary policy decisions, their implementation and effectiveness. The greatest uncertainty must be taken into account when projecting the product and prices. The global scenario also makes it difficult to interpret the impact of monetary policy on demand and inflation. The policies and the healthy and stable macroeconomic environment that Latin American countries have been building have reduced their vulnerability to an adjustment of global imbalances that could be more abrupt than expected. In the last twenty years, and especially in the last five, significant progress has been made in economic policies and outcomes. A tax system never before thought has been achieved, with a notorious example in the Chilean case, but with important improvements in most countries. Inflation rates have fallen from triple-digit annual figures no more than 15 years ago to single-digit levels in recent years. Current accounts have mostly moved to surplus positions and sovereign prizes have fallen to levels never seen before, with the consequent decrease in external financing costs, which has benefited the solvency of countries allowing them to refinance their debts on much better terms. Finally, great strides in the development, supervision and regulation of the financial system have also contributed to significant performance improvements in Latin American countries . However, although Latin America is more resilient than in the past, it is not fully protected and is sensitive to how imbalances are corrected. An abrupt adjustment would increase sovereign prizes, increase the financial burden of the most indebted countries, such as Argentina and Uruguay, and hurt the large suppliers of goods to the US, whose demand would not be absorbed by other countries. Despite increasing diversification, NAFTA partners buy 34% of total Latin American exports (excluding Mexico). Within the region, the most exposed are Mexico and Central America, due to their important commercial relationship with the United States. In conclusion, the world economy presents an exceptionally favorable outlook, where the great novelty is the dynamism of China and India. However, this good international outlook presents significant risks. The most immediate are larger and longer increases in the price of oil, and possible increases in inflation in developed countries. Over a longer horizon, how global imbalances will adjust is another major uncertainty today. However, this appears as less pressing since there are clear signs that gradual adjustments are already beginning to occur, in addition, countries are recognizing that the solution involves many actors and that they need to be coordinated. In addition, countries have been able to implement healthy macroeconomic policies that help make the adjustment softer and the impact less felt. This, without ignoring that they must continue working to strengthen their policies to face a world of greater uncertainty.
text_original: Los Desbalances Globales y los Riesgos en la Economa Mundial Presentacin del presidente del Banco Central, don Vittorio Corbo Lioi, en Seminario del Centro de Estudios Pblicos, el 26 de julio de 2006. El entorno externo para la economa chilena es inusualmente favorable. Aunque con vaivenes, la economa mundial se encamina a completar los mejores tres aos de crecimiento en las ltimas tres dcadas, con tasas promedio ms de un tercio mayores que las observadas entre 1970 y 2000. Adems, por primera vez en muchos aos, este gran dinamismo mundial ha sido empujado por mejoras en todas las regiones. El crecimiento mundial del 2004-2005, impulsado por un solo motor EE.UU. hoy viene acompaado por otros importantes actores. Entre estos destaca la Zona Euro, que est saliendo con fuerza de su letargo, y China e India, que sumadas representan lo mismo que EE.UU. en el PIB mundial a PPC, y que crecen a tasas impresionantes que se vislumbra pueden mantenerse en el tiempo, dado el gran potencial que les queda por explotar. As, este escenario de alto crecimiento es tambin ms balanceado, lo que da luces de mayor sostenibilidad. Para el 2007, se espera un dinamismo algo menos fuerte que en los aos recientes, aunque igualmente mucho ms potente que en el promedio de las ltimas tres dcadas. Las condiciones financieras externas, en tanto, aunque presentan un pequeo deterioro en los ltimos datos, provocado por el aumento de las tasas de inters de poltica y de largo plazo en economas desarrolladas, siguen siendo bastante expansivas. Esto es especialmente cierto en EE.UU., cuyo PIB lleva un par de aos creciendo por sobre el crecimiento de su producto potencial, generando presiones inflacionarias en una economa sobrecalentada, y entrando en un ciclo de alzas de la tasa de poltica monetaria que, luego de muchas subidas, se acerca a su fin. Los premios soberanos en las economas emergentes tambin siguen inusualmente bajos, aunque con un leve aumento en los ltimos meses. Esto ha repercutido en reducciones importantes en el costo de endeudamiento que estas economas han aprovechado bien para refinanciar sus deudas y mejorar su solvencia. Por ltimo, contrariando las expectativas, los precios de productos primarios han llegado ms alto y se han mantenido en esos niveles por ms tiempo de lo esperado. El Banco y los agentes del mercado han tenido que hacer continuos ajustes a sus proyecciones de la evolucin futura de estos precios pero, afortunadamente en el caso de Chile, estos han sido ms fuertes para nuestros productos exportables (cobre y molibdeno) que para nuestros importables (petrleo), dando como resultado una mejora de los trminos de intercambio y un aumento del ingreso disponible de sus habitantes. Sin embargo, este excepcional escenario externo no est exento de riesgos. En el horizonte cercano, preocupa la posibilidad de que los altos precios del petrleo se extiendan ms all de lo esperado e incluso que alcance niveles ms elevados. Ligado a este riesgo est que la inflacin de pases desarrollados no se reduzca e incluso que aumente an ms, poniendo fin a los tiempos en que el efecto de segunda vuelta de los altos precios de petrleo no se traspasaba a precios, y comenzando un ciclo en el que las economas con brechas de capacidad copadas empiecen a perder su capacidad de aislamiento de las presiones inflacionarias producidas por estas alzas del petrleo, lo que con nuevos choques al precio empeorara la situacin. En un plazo ms largo, la preocupacin central est en cmo se ordenarn los desbalances globales y cuales sern sus repercusiones. En la actualidad estamos ante un precio del petrleo inusualmente alto. Desde febrero de 1999 casi se ha cuadruplicado en trminos reales. Si bien al principio se pens que este era un ciclo transitorio similar a los anteriores, en el tiempo se han ido ajustando las expectativas hacia un ciclo bastante ms duradero y con niveles de precios muchsimo ms altos que lo originalmente previstos. En trminos comparativos con los ciclos vividos desde 1975, este es hoy (incluso antes de saber dnde y cundo terminar) un ciclo anormal. En longitud ya duplica los 28 meses promedio de los cinco ciclos previos, y en amplitud la duplicacin de precios que hemos presenciado es muy superior al aumento promedio de 36%. En este contexto, el Banco y el mercado han ido ajustando al alza sus proyecciones. Las primeras proyecciones para el ao 2006 que efectuamos en enero del 2005 daban un precio de 34 dlares el barril, esto es, cerca de la mitad de lo que hoy se proyecta para este ao. Lo mismo ha ocurrido con las proyecciones para el 2007. Tambin el mercado de los futuros ha ido cambiando constantemente hacia arriba e incluso reducido su pendiente, reflejando la duracin esperada de este ciclo. En cuanto al origen del ciclo, a diferencia del de fines de los setenta donde el problema era de oferta desde los pases miembros de la OPEP, hoy la estrechez del mercado obedece a una demanda que ha crecido mucho en un contexto de oferta limitada e incierta. Adems, no hay que desconocer que parte del aumento obedece a motivos de especulacin. Los hedge funds y el comercio de productos primarios han aumentado en forma impresionante en los ltimos cuatro aos. Por el lado de la demanda, el dinamismo de grandes consumidores de petrleo como China e India contribuye con una potente fuente de mayor consumo. Entre 1990 y 2003, el aumento del consumo de petrleo por parte de ambas naciones explica cerca de un tercio del aumento global. Adems, el alza de los precios no ha producido el ajuste esperado del consumo. La elasticidad precio de la demanda es baja en general, aunque vara por regiones, siendo mayor en pases asiticos y relativamente baja en EE.UU. La sustitucin, conservacin, y mejoras de eficiencia han sido limitadas. Parte de esta insensibilidad obedece a polticas nacionales de impuestos y subsidios, que impiden que los precios reflejen la escasez, inhibiendo el natural ajuste que deberan producir los precios actuales. Por el lado de la oferta, la capacidad de reaccin a los aumentos de precios es bastante lenta y limitada. En primer lugar, los mayores potenciales petrolferos se encuentran en zonas de alta inestabilidad poltica, lo que aumenta el premio por riesgo de nuevos proyectos y limita la produccin de yacimientos activos. En efecto, a los conflictos relacionados con las pruebas de misiles en Corea del Norte y la disputa nuclear de Irn, se sum el conflicto entre Israel y el Lbano, que afecta el precio del petrleo al aumentar la probabilidad de recortes al suministro de crudo. Adicionalmente, si se agregan al conflicto Siria y/o Irn, el precio puede saltar aun ms. Por otra parte, los proyectos nuevos toman ms tiempo en materializarse por las crecientes trabas impuestas por la regulacin ambiental. Aun si se aumenta la extraccin de petrleo en los prximos meses, el lmite vendr por la incapacidad de procesarlo y por lo tanto en la oferta de combustibles. Es decir, el cuello de botella est en las refineras. Por ltimo, ha habido importante recortes de oferta por fenmenos climticos severos en el Golfo de Mxico. En conclusin, la precaria estabilidad poltica de pases productores de petrleo, con la consecuente incertidumbre respecto de posibles aumentos de produccin en el futuro cercano, junto con el gran aumento de la demanda que se espera de India y China, y la escasa reaccin de polticas que incentiven la racionalizacin de la demanda, sugieren que la estrechez del mercado ser ms duradera que lo inicialmente esperado y que ciclos previos. La buena noticia es que el mundo est hoy mejor preparado para minimizar los costos de estos choques de precios del petrleo. La alta credibilidad en los objetivos inflacionarios que han logrado la mayora de las economas y los altos niveles de competitividad, reducen el traspaso a precios. Adems, la mayor diversificacin de proveedores, potenciales mejoras de eficiencia de uso y sustitucin hacia otras fuentes de energa, dan luces de esperanza. De hecho, hoy ya se comercializan a precios aceptables sustitutos como petrleo de arena y de soya. Por ltimo, en la medida en que la composicin de la produccin de los pases se vaya diversificando y aumentando la importancia de servicios en la canasta productiva, la intensidad de uso de energa se reducir. Un segundo riesgo latente y relacionado con el anterior, es que aumente la inflacin en los pases desarrollados. Hasta el 2005, la inflacin subyacente y del IPC estaban bien contenidas en el mundo. Hoy, aumentos de precios de materias primas e industriales y copamiento de holguras de capacidad han ido presionando al alza los precios. Tanto EE.UU. como la Zona Euro y Japn han visto aumentar sus distintas medidas de inflacin en el ltimo ao, llegando a niveles que exceden las metas implcitas (EE.UU.) o explcitas (Europa) que se han impuesto. De hecho, en EE.UU. la inflacin total excede hoy el lmite de la zona de confort de la autoridad monetaria y supera la inflacin chilena reciente. El caso de Europa es an ms complicado puesto que al tener un banco central relativamente nuevo que est todava construyendo su reputacin, los agentes miran solo la inflacin sucia y su dbil credibilidad contribuye a traspasos ms expeditos a precios En este contexto, los bancos centrales de pases desarrollados han empezado a reducir la expansividad de su poltica monetaria. En general, los que vivieron un perodo de relajacin de la poltica monetaria entre 2001 y 2003, han revertido o estn revirtiendo ese estmulo. En EE.UU., el ajuste de tasas comenz ya en abril del 2005. En su reunin del 29 de junio, la Fed aument por decimosptima ocasin consecutiva la tasa de poltica monetaria en 25 puntos base, ubicndola en 5,25% anual. En el comunicado seal que los ltimos indicadores sugieren que el crecimiento econmico se est moderando, reflejando el enfriamiento del mercado inmobiliario, los efectos rezagados de los aumentos en la tasa de inters y las alzas energticas. En relacin con los precios, se indica que los riesgos inflacionarios se mantienen, a pesar de que la moderacin del crecimiento ayuda a limitar las presiones sobre la inflacin. El mercado espera que en lo que queda del ao se produzcan una o dos nuevas alzas de tasa antes de dar por finalizado el ciclo de normalizacin. En la Zona Euro, el BCE comenz a recortar la expansividad en diciembre. En julio mantuvo la tasa de instancia en 2,75%, pero seal que mantendr una fuerte vigilancia de tal forma de asegurar que los riesgos inflacionarios no se materialicen. Indicios de mejores perspectivas de crecimiento en Europa llevan a esperar ms aumentos en el futuro. El ltimo en subirse a esta tendencia fue el Banco de Japn, que despus de un tiempo de tratar de maneras poco ortodoxas de salir de la recesin, inici su ciclo de alza de tasas recientemente con un aumento de esta hasta 0,25%. En conclusin, es evidente que las presiones inflacionarias se estn sintiendo y que pueden aumentar con nuevos choques de precios del petrleo o con un ciclo ms duradero. Por ello, es muy probable que se requiera seguir recortando la expansividad de la poltica monetaria, pero con alta incertidumbre respecto de cunto y por lo tanto del efecto final en la actividad. Si se subestiman las presiones inflacionarias, se queda atrs en el ajuste de tasas y se permiten aumentos bruscos de la inflacin y las tasas, con efectos perjudiciales en los mercados financieros. Por otro lado, si los ajustes que se producen son excesivos, entonces se corre el riesgo de frenar innecesariamente la actividad econmica. El ltimo riesgo que quiero analizar es uno de menor probabilidad, pero con efectos finales que pueden ser de alto impacto. Esto es, la forma en que los desbalances globales se resuelvan. En los ltimos trece aos, el dficit de cuenta corriente de EE.UU. ha aumentado en forma considerable. Para el 2006 se espera que alcance el 6,5% del PIB americano y ms del 2% del PIB mundial. Hasta ahora, este dficit creciente ha sido financiado principalmente por pases productores de petrleo, Asia emergente especialmente China y Japn. La contribucin de Amrica Latina es insignificante. En el 2005, la regin tuvo un supervit equivalente a menos del 1% del dficit de cuenta corriente de EE.UU. Sin embargo, aun cuando no est contribuyendo a agravar los desequilibrios, puede sufrir las consecuencias de los cambios abruptos en los precios financieros, causados por esta situacin que, en la opinin de muchos, es insostenible. Las primeras visiones de cmo se producira el ajuste estaban teidas por las crisis asitica y mexicana, por lo que se esperaba que la solucin a este desbalance se produjera abruptamente cuando los inversionistas extranjeros perdieran el inters por mantener activos americanos en sus carteras, provocando un quiebre brusco al financiamiento del alto consumo americano. En tal caso, las tasas de inters de EE.UU. aumentaran y el dlar sobre-reaccionara. Se desacelerara el consumo en EE.UU. sin ser compensado por aumentos en otros pases, con fuertes efectos en el crecimiento mundial. Creo que este escenario, muy popular hasta hace un par de aos, es poco probable. La flexibilidad y profundidad de los mercados financieros y de las decisiones de portafolio del resto del mundo, hacen pensar que el ajuste debiera producirse en forma bastante ms gradual a travs de movimientos ms suaves en los precios financieros. En este caso cabe esperar que la demanda se mueva gradualmente desde pases con dficit a pases con supervit, y que el consumo y precio de activos converjan suavemente a sendas sustentables, como de hecho ya estamos observando. As, el mayor ahorro en EE.UU. y el mayor consumo y/o inversin en el resto del mundo llevan a un escenario ms benigno para el crecimiento mundial, donde la desaceleracin de la demanda de EE.UU. es compensada, en parte, por una demanda ms vigorosa de otros pases. La gradualidad de este ajuste se vera beneficiada si Asia, especialmente China, flexibilizara sus tipos de cambio para producir la necesaria reasignacin del gasto. Esta mayor flexibilidad tambin sera beneficiosa para que los pases retomaran control sobre su poltica monetaria. Pero igual este ajuste benigno estara acompaado de una desaceleracin moderada en el crecimiento mundial. Una visin alternativa de este ajuste gradual es la que ha hecho pblica una lnea de investigacin del economista chileno Ricardo Caballero, quien plantea que estos desbalances son una solucin de equilibrio en un mundo donde pases emergentes muy dinmicos no han desarrollado suficientemente sus mercados financieros ni instrumentos atractivos de inversin, mientras que EE.UU. lo ha hecho con notable eficiencia. En este caso, el ajuste tambin sera gradual y se producira en la medida en que los mercados financieros se desarrollaran en los pases emergentes y parte de los flujos de capitales volvieran a sus pases de origen al encontrar alternativas de inversin rentables. Acontecimientos recientes de aumento de demanda en Japn y la Unin Europea y de desaceleracin del consumo privado y del mercado inmobiliario en EE.UU., hacen ms probable un ajuste gradual. Sin embargo, aunque con baja probabilidad, los riesgos de un ajuste abrupto todava estn presentes y, dado los altos costos que este involucrara, las autoridades no pueden esperar pasivamente a que se corrijan los desbalances globales. Deben, en cambio, promover un ajuste gradual y cooperativo y tomar acciones para reducir los efectos perjudiciales que este ajuste puede tener en sus pases. Para promover un ajuste gradual y cooperativo se debe incentivar el ahorro en EE.UU. mediante un esfuerzo fiscal e incentivos al ahorro privado; incentivar el consumo privado en China que hoy ahorra ms de la mitad del PIB a travs de reformas al sector financiero que mejoren el acceso de las familias al crdito y ampliando las redes de proteccin social para reducir el ahorro familiar por motivo precaucin, como los propuestos en el ltimo Congreso del Partido Comunista. Tambin aumentar la inversin en Asia emergente que se desplom en 1997 y no ha logrado recuperarse desde entonces mediante incentivos a la inversin de calidad a travs de reformas estructurales que aumenten los retornos esperados mejoras al ambiente de negocios, a la flexibilidad laboral y a la asignacin eficiente de recursos en el mercado financiero. Los pases asiticos han enfrentado las crisis con fuertes acumulaciones de reservas internacionales, que a las tasas y cambios vigentes les resulta relativamente barato, e incluso rentable, y con ello esperan evitar una nueva crisis como la del 97. Lo malo que han tenido una fuerte expansin del crdito (especialmente China) y que han descuidado las reformas en el mercado financiero que los protegeran de manera ms eficiente de una posible crisis. Por ltimo, ayudara bastante a este ajuste que se redujera el valor relativo del dlar con respecto a otras monedas, especialmente la china. Reacciones ex post para minimizar los costos de un ajuste abrupto dependen del marco de poltica monetaria y cambiaria. Pases con expectativas de inflacin bien ancladas en niveles bajos y con descalces cambiarios acotados, deberan dejar que el tipo de cambio se ajustara para liderar el cambio en precios relativos. Leaning against the wind solo generar fugas de capitales, inestabilidad financiera y un acortamiento del crdito. Poltica fiscal y monetaria contracclica y un sistema financiero local slido ayudan a enfrentar posibles crisis financieras internacionales con reversin de flujos de capitales, con menor necesidad de acumular reservas internacionales. Los pases con expectativas de inflacin desancladas enfrentan un panorama ms complejo. La depreciacin real ser opacada por mayor inflacin o, si los descalces de monedas de activos y pasivos son grandes, la depreciacin ser contractiva al producir importantes efectos de hojas de balance. Para evitar una crisis financiera mayor en estos pases, la nica herramienta disponible ser la poltica fiscal y sera fuertemente recesiva. La incertidumbre con respecto a cmo se producir el ajuste de los desbalances repercute en las decisiones de poltica econmica. La poltica monetaria de pases emergentes tiene impacto limitado -o nulo- en cmo se produce el ajuste. Sin embargo, ste afecta indudablemente las decisiones de poltica monetaria, su implementacin y efectividad. La mayor incertidumbre se debe tener en cuenta a la hora de proyectar el producto y los precios. El escenario global tambin dificulta la interpretacin del impacto de la poltica monetaria en la demanda y la inflacin. Las polticas y el ambiente macroeconmico sano y estable que han ido construyendo los pases latinoamericanos han reducido su vulnerabilidad ante un ajuste de los desbalances globales que pudiera ser ms abrupto de lo esperado. En los ltimos veinte aos, y especialmente en los ltimos cinco, se han logrado avances significativos en polticas y resultados econmicos. Se ha alcanzado un ordenamiento fiscal nunca antes pensado, con un ejemplo notorio en el caso chileno, pero con mejoras importantes en la mayora de los pases. Se han bajado las tasas de inflacin desde cifras anuales de tres dgitos hace no ms de 15 aos, a niveles de un dgito en los aos recientes. Las cuentas corrientes han pasado en su mayora a posiciones superavitarias y los premios soberanos han bajado a niveles nunca antes vistos, con la consiguiente disminucin de costos de financiamiento externo, que ha beneficiado la solvencia de los pases permitindoles refinanciar sus deudas en condiciones mucho mejores. Por ltimo, grandes avances en el desarrollo, supervisin y regulacin del sistema financiero tambin han contribuido a mejoras importantes de desempeo en los pases de Amrica Latina. Sin embargo, aunque Amrica Latina es ms resiliente que en el pasado, no est totalmente protegida y es sensible a cmo se corrijan los desbalances. Un ajuste abrupto aumentara los premios soberanos, subira la carga financiera de los pases ms endeudados, como Argentina y Uruguay, y se perjudicara a los grandes proveedores de bienes a EE.UU., cuya demanda no sera absorbida por otros pases. A pesar de la creciente diversificacin, los socios del NAFTA compran 34% del total de exportaciones latinoamericanas (excluyendo Mxico). Dentro de la regin, los ms expuestos son Mxico y Amrica Central, por su importante relacin comercial con EE.UU. En conclusin, la economa mundial presenta un panorama excepcionalmente favorable, donde la gran novedad es el dinamismo de China e India. Sin embargo, este buen panorama internacional presenta riesgos importantes. Los ms inmediatos son alzas mayores y por ms tiempo en el precio del petrleo, y posibles aumentos de inflacin en pases desarrollados. En un horizonte ms largo, la forma en que se ajustarn los desbalances globales constituye hoy otra gran incertidumbre. Sin embargo, esta aparece como menos apremiante ya que hay claras seales de que los ajustes graduales ya se comienzan a producir, adems, los pases estn reconociendo que la solucin involucra a muchos actores y que necesitan coordinarse. Adems, los pases han sabido implementar polticas macroeconmicas saludables que ayudan a que el ajuste sea ms suave y que el impacto se sienta menos. Ello, sin desconocer que deben seguir trabajando en fortalecer sus polticas para enfrentar un mundo mayor incertidumbre.

Title: Award of the contest "The Economy + Close"
text: AWARD OF CONTEST "THE ECONOMY CLOSE" Speech by Mr. Vittorio Corbo, President of the Central Bank of Chile. 18 October 2006 Madam Minister of Education Madam Undersecretary for the Economy Mr. Superintendent of Banks and Financial Institutions Members of the Jury Dear teachers and students Ladies and gentlemen It is a source of great satisfaction for me and for the Central Bank of Chile to preside over this ceremony, in which, for the second consecutive year, we successfully completed an initiative that excites us more and more. Today we reward the winners of the school contest "The economy close" that, in its second version, managed to summon students from all regions and the most diverse types of educational establishments in the country. We are more pleased to see that the number of trials received far exceeded that of last year. This gives us a strong stimulus to continue with our objective of bringing the Bank closer to students and the general public, to promote their interest in economic issues, their learning about the role and objectives of our Institution, as well as the understanding of what contribution an autonomous institution like ours can make to the development of the country and the well-being of its inhabitants. Some of you may still wonder why an institution like the Central Bank has decided to hold this school competition? The reason is very simple. Having achieved macroeconomic stability, which was very elusive for so many years, allows us to place more emphasis on our obligation to worry about other relevant and complementary aspects of our daily work, which contribute to consolidating that stability and improving the effectiveness of our policies. One of these aspects is to improve the capacity of Chilean society to understand the importance of the objectives of the Central Bank and the logic of its policies. In this sense, many central banks around the world have come to the conviction that it is not enough for the monetary authority to provide information about what it does and why it does it. Nowadays it is essential that this information is understood by as many people as possible, in order to contribute to strengthening autonomy and improving the effectiveness of monetary policy. One of the ways to achieve this goal is to actively participate in the development of the educational process of Chileans. How? Putting at their disposal tools that allow them to have greater and better access to training in economic and financial issues. Knowing and understanding the macroeconomic and financial environment, as well as its prospects, allows people to make better decisions, not only in the big investment issues, but also at the domestic level. And if people make good decisions, they will have a greater opportunity to improve their well-being and reduce spaces of uncertainty and risk always present in everyday life. Central banks in the world, as well as multilateral organizations and international organizations, have become aware of the need to expand economic training and have also begun to develop massive education and extension programs in these areas. As part of this global trend, the Central Bank of Chile created a few years ago the " Economy for the Majority" Program, which tries to bring closer to This institution to citizens through a website, seminars and other activities. The first step was the launch of the praiseworthy book "Economy for all", written by the former President of the Central Bank, Mr. Carlos Massad and which explains, in a didactic and attractive way, concepts and terms that are usually alien to the common people. The next phase was the realization of the school contest "The economy close" that summons us today, and that in its first version carried out last year had a response and results that surprised us very pleasantly, for the number of participants and for the quality of the work done. We have set ourselves the challenge of continuing to walk along this path of teaching and approaching the population. Our next initiative, which we will launch in 2007, is a new website of "The economy for the majority", which will put in attractive pages and designs and with a language close to all audiences economic issues that seem so complex and that are so relevant to the development of society. We hope that visitors to this website will learn there from the simplest definition of the Central Bank to how it implements its monetary policy . We have also proposed to complement these information tools with workshops for teachers of Social Sciences and History. Our purpose is to train them in basic concepts of economics and finance and in the objectives and functions of this institution, so that they become vehicles of motivation and reliable transmission of these topics to their students and urge and support them in the preparation of the essays for this contest. The second version of the contest "The economy close" culminates today after a process that began last March. As I said at the beginning, its results are highly satisfactory for us. 1,004 groups from 513 subsidized and paid municipal schools throughout the country were registered. Of the registered groups, 520 essays were received from the most remote places of Chile, and whose quality and creativity speaks very well of the human potential that our country is having. I would like to highlight today an exemplary initiative. Among the works presented, we received one presented by a group of students from the Coresol Adult Professional Technical High School, which operates inside the Huachalalume prison in La Serena. Under the title "The problem of controlling inflation in a penitentiary center", they gave us an interesting economic reflection based on the reality that they live in prison, where the acquisition and exchange of products have special characteristics that contrast radically with those of the rest of society. The jury awarded this work fourth place and we wanted to highlight it especially with an honorable mention. The evaluation of the works was certainly one of the most complex stages, not only because of the quantity but also because of the variety of approaches. At this stage we had the collaboration of 29 Bank professionals, who had the difficult mission of making the first pre-selection based on a strict guideline that considered the technical and practical mastery of the topics. They classified 53 works for the second stage that would decide the 10 finalists. I want to express to all the professionals who participated in this evaluation and selection phase our special recognition for the work done. The jury present here today, and which I had the honor of chairing, evaluated the finalist essays following this same rigorous guideline, resulting in the highest scores the three essays that this morning were exposed and defended by their authors. These trials are: . "TPM and financial acceleration from a local approach", by students of IV middle year of the Amalia Err87zuriz School, in Ovalle. . "El fiado y el control de la inflation", by students of IV middle year of the San Agust92n School, in Vi96a del Mar; and . "The role of the Superintendence of Banks in my high school", of students of III middle year of the Commercial Institute of Linares. The reading of these essays and this morning's session, in which the different groups presented and defended their work in front of the jury, has been a tremendously enriching experience. Not only have we been able to share what it has meant for these students to try to look at the economy in a different way and from angles not usual for us, but this also ratifies my deep conviction, after teaching for many years, that one of the main responsibilities of every society is to educate. Education is the priority cause of the development and progress of countries and, at the same time, the exclusive vehicle for human beings to achieve the full development of their own capacities and, therefore, their personal fulfilment. I want to highlight at this ceremony the contribution and enthusiasm put by all those who participated in this successful initiative. Of course, we are committed to continuing it and making an effort to obtain an ever greater participation. I thank all those who made this initiative possible and, in particular, the members of the jury; the authorities of the Ministry of Education; the guiding teachers of the more than 500 works submitted; the participating students, in particular those who are with us today, as well as the officials of the Central Bank. Everyone put their effort, creativity and time to help this contest achieve its objectives and contribute to the economy being closer to the people. THANKS A LOT

Title: X Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile: "Current Account and External Financing"
text: X ANNUAL CONFERENCE OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF CHILE: "CURRENT ACCOUNT AND EXTERNAL FINANCING" Welcome speech delivered by the President of the Central Bank of Chile, Mr. Vittorio Corbo Lioi. 9 November 2006 Dear central bankers, academics and visiting economists. Dear friends, you are very welcome. It is always a source of satisfaction to bring together a group of people with whom you have interests and concerns in common, and if it is a question of sharing two days with the most qualified scholars of the respective topics, we must add the enthusiasm for the injection of vitality and renewal that this area of thought will be receiving . It fills me with pride that we are already celebrating the Tenth Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, which has become a traditional event to discuss ideas relevant to central banking policies and the economic development of our countries. The theme of this conference is the Current Account and External Financing d0 a crucial issue for an economy like Chile's d0 historically very open to global trade in goods, and increasingly integrated into international capital markets. By way of illustration, let me show you two graphs. The first shows the evolution of the sum of exports plus imports over GDP since the mid - 70. As can be seen, as a result of a systematic process of integration, Chile has become very open to foreign trade, both compared to other Latin American economies and to the world average. This other graph shows the sum of our gross international assets and liabilities over GDP. This is a measure of the degree of financial integration of an economy. I would like to highlight three facts here. First, in 2004 Chile's degree of financial integration was well above the average for emerging economies, but still below the average for developed economies. Second, this integration process has accelerated since the mid-90s. And third: although the ratio of more active liabilities to GDP is similar in the nineties and eighties in terms of magnitude, the composition of this total differs substantially, with much greater weight of gross international assets from the mid-90s. Financial integration has the potential to accelerate economic growth, allowing savings from other countries to finance profitable investment projects in Chile that would not otherwise be realized. Let us remember that the current account deficit is nothing more than the gap between investment and national savings . Financial integration also makes it possible to smooth fluctuations in national income and their effects on household consumption and investment, whether these fluctuations respond to changes in the prices of the goods we export and import (as in recent years) or to local events that influence our productivity. For an economy that relies on a limited number of export products, whose prices are also highly volatile, this intertemporal smoothing of consumption is crucial. Thanks to financial integration, it is possible to increase the diversification of the risk of our asset portfolios, a fact that Chilean asset holders have increasingly sought to take advantage of in recent years. In practice, however, these potential benefits of opening the capital account do not always materialize. Emerging economies on average have been characterized by countercyclical current accounts and highly volatile consumption relative to current income: just the opposite of what intertemporal current account theory predicts. Moreover, emerging economies have suffered episodes of instability and in some cases crises, associated with sudden slowdowns in capital flows. Isolating oneself from international financial markets is not an option; d0 the potential benefits are simply too great to be wasted, and innovations in information and communication technology reduce the effectiveness of eventual controls. It is imperative, then, to fully understand the factors that determine international capital flows, from and to emerging economies such as ours. This will allow us to design policy schemes that ensure that these flows increase consumption and decrease volatility, and not the other way around. To put it simply, there are two prevailing views regarding the functioning of international financial markets. The first (emphasizing domestic factors) is that an economy with orderly fiscal accounts, a monetary policy geared towards price stability, and adequate financial regulation can be integrated into international capital markets without exposing itself to external financial shocks. This vision emphasizes that the origin of the volatility associated with capital flows is in each country, with the international financial system being a mere amplifier. In this view, the role of domestic policies is limited to not being a source of shocks. The second view is that the source of the shocks is in the international financial system (either directly or by contagion from other emerging economies). Economies differ in their degree of vulnerability to such shocks d0 by a combination of public policies and structural conditions of the economy. In this vision, the role of public policies is closely related to the decisions made by the private sector and the restrictions it faces. All the recent discussion of exchange rate and term mismatches, as well as optimal reserve decisions and the use of contingent international liabilities is part of this vision. As a Central Bank we have taken an eclectic vision, halfway between both positions. We believe it is essential to have a set of policies that are not sourced. of instability, and that also help to cushion the effects of volatility in international financial markets. Fiscal prudence, an inflation-targeting regime with a floating exchange rate aimed at maintaining price stability, and adequate financial regulation and supervision all contribute to these objectives. Moreover, we have worked to provide tools for the private sector to help it deal with the consequences of volatility in international financial markets. You may wonder why, as the Central Bank, we are interested in the issue of the current account deficit and external financing, especially given the floating exchange rate inflation targeting regime with which we currently operate? The first part of the question is easy. We have a mandate to ensure the normal functioning of internal and external payments. Therefore, to fulfil our mandate, we need to understand both the functioning of international financial markets and the effects of shocks from those markets on our financial system. To illustrate the importance of this, it is enough to recall how our economy was shaken by the fall in international liquidity that followed the Russian Crisis in 1998-99. Closely related to the previous point, are the optimal reserve policies. The volatility of external financingd1and in particular the likelihood of a sudden cut in the flow of fundsd1are key ingredients to consider in the level and composition of international reserves. Capital flows also play an important role in conducting monetary policy towards our inflation target, due to the impact that international financial conditions have on aggregate demand and the price level. For example, a fall in the cost of external financing (such as we have experienced in recent years) is clearly expansive. Finally, as the Central Bank, the organic law attributes to us a set of tools that determines the degree of opening of the financial account. You will remember that in 1998 we lowered the reserve requirement to zero and that in 2001 we eliminated a good part of the remaining restrictions on the entry and exit of capital. But not all of them. Just a few weeks ago the Central Bank authorized the issuance of bonds in pesos by foreigners in the local market . This is a good time to rethink these issues. On the one hand, because the boom in basic prices that we are experiencing in the region is going to end sooner or later, and as a middle-income country, we will need external financing to continue growing. And, on the other, by the situation of "global imbalances" that the world economy is experiencing today. The U.S. current-account deficit raises uncertainty about how it will unravel, and how different policy scenarios and frameworks will affect small, open economies like Chile's. These are unavoidable questions that we must understand. These are the topics that summon us for these two days. It is an ambitious agenda, and the issues are crucial. A first block of the agenda will assess the factors that explain the behavior of capital flows to emerging economies, in particular the extent to which they are caused by internal shocks, external demand shocks, or imperfections in international financial markets. In this block we will have the honor of having the masterful presentation of the renowned economist and friend Guillermo Calvo. We will also have the opportunity to listen and discuss recent economic research by Jaime Guajardo, Gita Gopinath, Graciela Kaminsky and Kevin Cowan. Chris Kent, Juan Pablo Medina and David Moreno will review and analyze the experiences with the current account of different regions in recent decades. Australia and New Zealand are very good references, since they are large exporters of raw materials and follow an inflation targeting scheme with a floating exchange rate, as does Chile. To make the counterpoint, the experience of the countries of East Asia is also presented. Today's and tomorrow's agenda also includes the issue of global imbalances. As we all know and as illustrated in the third chart, since the late nineties, most developing regions have accumulated current account surpluses, while developed economies as a whole d0 and in particular, the United States d0 have exhibited large current account deficits. This situation of imbalance has raised much concern and research in recent times, so our conference will devote a good part of its agenda to exploring whether this situation is transitory or more permanent, as well as the implications that different solutions pose for the Chilean economy. To this end, we have invited important contributors to this debate such as Sebastian Edwards, Mike Dooley, Barry Eichengreen and Roberto Zahler. Another issue that we could not exclude from this forum is the gross international position of assets and liabilities. In line with the recent increase in gross stocks of international assets, the profession has begun to analyse the valuation effect of these stocks and its implications on capital flows. As the bulk of this literature has focused on developed economies d1and in particular the United Statesd1, this conference has wanted to take the issue from the perspective of developing countries, emphasizing questions regarding the interaction between gross stocks and capital flows for Chile. These are the topics of the studies presented by Pierre Olivier Gourinchas and Rodrigo Vald8es. Finally, we will have the opportunity to think about the interrelationship between exchange rate policy, optimal reserves and current account. We will do this in the context of John Williamson's keynote presentation and Joshua Aizenman's study. These two days of analysis of extremely relevant topics with top-level economists would not have been possible without the dedication of Kevin Cowan, Sebasti87n Edwards and Rodrigo Vald8es to think about the issues and people most qualified to address them. In addition the very efficient collaboration of David Rappoport and Monica Correa in the organization was vital. Finally, the fact that presenters and commentators of such a recognized trajectory have agreed to participate, ensures that today and tomorrow will be two days of great benefit. To all of you, dear participants, I wish you a fruitful discussion and much learning.
