Title: Dutch Disease: Evidence and Policy Implications
text: Dutch Disease Symposium The School of Public Policy, University of Calgary, March 7th, 2013 Remarks by Sebasti87n Claro Panel Discussion: Potential policy responses: What are they, and are they necessary? It is a great opportunity to be in this fascinating conference, both because of its high.level participants as well as for the relevance of the theme. The Dutch. disease concept was coined in the mid 1970s to analyze the impact on the Netherlandsd5 economy of the surge in oil prices.1 Since then, the impact of fluctuations in terms of trade and/or capital flows has been often analyzed keeping the Dutch.disease framework in mind: a boom in commodity prices puts an upward pressure on the real exchange rate, affecting the competitiveness position of other tradable sectors not benefited by the boom. In the last decade or so, with the expansion of China and the so.called super cycle in commodities, a revival of this discussion has taken place. The question is whether natural.resource.abundant countries like Canada or Chile are headed toward de.industrialization caused by real exchange rate pressures, and, if so, what policy responses would be needed to counterbalance this phenomenon. What I would like to do in this talk is go over what I see as the main questions that arise: (1) is there evidence of a Dutch disease?, (2) is it really a disease?, and finally, (3) is there room for policies to counter.balance it?. I will try to answer these questions from the perspective of a small developing economy like Chile, and from the point of view of a central banker. 1. Is there evidence of a Dutch disease? The super cycle of commodity prices since the early 2000s has led to a boom in mining exports d1 mainly copper d1, which have increased more than fourfold between 2003 and 2012. In contrast, exports of agricultural and manufactured products grew 150% in the same period (see figure 1). By far, the largest contributor to this difference has been the copper price, which has virtually quadrupled in the last decade. After deflating figures by a sector.specific export price index (see figure 2), the opposite patterns arise: real copper exports have grown 10% in the last nine years, while agricultural and manufacturing exports have grown 80% and 50%, respectively (see figure 3). Overall, we observe a mild effect of the copper boom on Chiled5s exports. There are several explanations for this. First, to some extent other tradable goods produced in Chile d1mainly food and food processed goodsd1 have also been subject to a terms.of.trade shock. At the end, the same forces driving copper prices up have pushed other commodities up. Chiled5s export mix d0 both 1 The Economist, d2The Dutch Diseased3, November 26th, 1977. in agriculture and manufacturing d0 is highly concentrated in natural.resource.intensive products, including beverages, food and fish processing, among others. Also, the capacity constraints in copper production have limited the impact of the change in relative prices on factor reallocation. But at the same time, investments in the mining industry have raised demand for machinery and metal products, a small part of which is located domestically. Finally, although real exchange rate indices at the sector level show an appreciating trend for agricultural and industrial products (see figure 4), these sectors have been able to compensate such forces with high productivity growth. This is especially true in agriculture, where average labor productivity has increased three times faster than in the aggregate. Industry, on the other hand, has had a trend similar to the aggregate while the mining industry has experienced a significant fall in average labor productivity. (See figure 5) This evidence is consistent with the hypothesis d0 though not proof of . that productivity gains could be an endogenous response to competitiveness pressures. This is consistent with the evidence that, at the aggregate level, the appreciation of Chiled5s real exchange rate has been lower than that of other countries. (See table 1). For example, Chiled5s currency is currently 16% more appreciated in real terms than its average level in 2002, while the same numbers for other countries are 56% for Australia, 68% for Brazil, 36% for Canada, 31% for New Zealand and 9% for Peru. Of course, the high intensity of natural.resource.based trade in Chile d1which to some extent has shielded Chile from a Dutch.disease type phenomenond1 reflects the small share that traditional manufacturing sectors that apparently have increasing returns2 (i.e. pharmaceutical, electronic and non.electric machinery, motor vehicles and instruments) have. I will come back to this issue at the end of the talk. Finally, another explanation for the milder appreciation of the real exchange rate is that non. tradable services have experienced very significant productivity growth, limiting the impact on domestic factor prices of demand growth. This brings us to the question of whether this phenomenon requires any policy intervention. 2. Is this really a disease? Usually, the concept of disease is related to the hypothesis that factor reallocation toward natural resources hurts long.run growth because the other tradable sectors have economies of scale or great chances of productivity growth. This reallocation depresses growth by shrinking the 2 Antweiler, W. and D. Trefler (2002), d2Increasing Returns and All that: A View from Traded3, American Economic Review 92(1): 93.119. increasing.returns manufacturing sector. This is the basis of the export.led growth literature, and hence some room for policy action appears to compensate for such externality.3 As we mentioned before, tradable sectors that traditionally have been associated with increasing returns to scale are hardly present in Chiled5s output structure. Also, agriculture and manufacturing have shown a reasonable performance, in part due to higher.than.average productivity growth. Interestingly, the services sector has not only shown a large rate of growth (as expected given the terms.of.trade gains in the economy and the real exchange rate appreciation), but also it has experienced high productivity growth. For example, average labor productivity in Commerce and Financial Services have grown more than twice as fast as in the aggregate. (See figure 6) Similar evidence can be found in construction and telecommunication services, for example. As a consequence, a large flow of foreign direct investment to these sectors in other Latin American countries has taken place. This represents evidence that there is ample room for productivity growth in the services sector and that there is also capacity to d2export technologyd3. This implies that the traditional distinction of tradable and non.tradable sectors that provides the last name to the Dutch phenomena has become increasingly blurry. An interesting book edited by the Inter American Development Bank in 2010 shows that commerce explains a significant share of the productivity gap between Latin America and the developed world. To some extent, it is the distribution/infrastructure sectors which represent a bottleneck for its development. Of course this does not mean that boosting these sectors will necessarily be welfare enhancing, but it does suggest that the expansion of services enhanced by a Dutch.disease phenomenon can be a source of output and productivity growth. This phenomenon need not be exclusive to developing countries. According to Rajan (2010), many export.oriented strategies followed by developed countries d1like Japand1 have ended up protecting highly inefficient domestic.oriented production. These inefficiencies in the provision of services represent a hurdle for long.run growth.4 3. Is there room for policies? 3.1 Structural challenge 3.2 Cyclical challenge In my opinion, the policy question should distinguish two phenomena. A first one is related to the structural changes that a Dutch disease might impose, and their growth implications. A second one is related to cyclical considerations and the role of macro policies. Let me first turn to some structural challenges. 3 Magud, N. and S. Sosa (2010), d2When and Why Worry About Real Exchange Rate Appreciation? The Missing Link between Dutch Disease and Growth,d3 IMF Working Papers 10/271. 4 Rajan, R. (2010), Fault Lines, Princeton University Press. If there is evidence that the appreciating trend of the real exchange rate results from fundamental market forces that affect negatively some increasing.returns sectors, the focus should be on sector.specific policies rather than aggregate policies. Besides the obvious difficulties on providing justification for such interventions, the point I would like to make is that in any case the focus should be on the specific sectors that require assistance and on dealing with the market failures directly. The aggregate impact of fiscal and/or monetary policies in dealing with these phenomena is ineffective. In many developing countries, like Chile, I think the most fundamental question is not about finding those areas in need of protection but rather establishing the institutional setting for using this extraordinary income. In the last several decades, the most harmful policy of developing countries has been the tendency of governments to spend the transitory income d1and much mored1 in transfers that raise government expenditures beyond their medium run possibilities, and that also distort relative prices. After some years, everything is gone, and no fundamental change in the economy has taken place. Now, the region has another opportunity to benefit in the long run from the terms.of.trade windfall. The absence of a traditional IRS manufacturing base in Chile reflects the scarcity of human capital, and the past experiences of protectionism to enhance those sectors proved wrong. For this, it is critical to make sure that the resources are d1over timed1 invested in highly profitable projects rather than consumed. This is what will determine the comparative advantages in the years to come. In Chile, there is a clear deficit in education, which makes the labor force not adequately prepared to confront the challenges of the information society. Investing in quality education is probably the best decision. This has implications both for government programs that promote education within a framework that assures that resources go where they are needed and also to public policies, which should not introduce distortions in the price signal individuals receive for their education decisions. Policies that distort educational wage premium may end up deterring the incentives for people to invest in human capital. Another dimension of this disease d1not originally associated with the Dutch phenomenond1 has a more cyclical aspect. Even if there is no such externality in the tradable sector, a transitory real exchange rate appreciation d1due to exuberant expectations or highly pro.cyclical fiscal policyd1 can have negative consequences in some areas with sector.specific investment (physical of human capital). A transitory contraction/disappearance of an industry might be suboptimal if the forces driving the appreciation will reverse. Again, sectoral policies are called for if such phenomenon is perceived to occur. A second set of questions regarding the Dutch disease are related to its cyclical implications. Because it is very difficult to assess whether a commodity cycle is permanent or transitory, expectations and fiscal (in)discipline could generate a boom that eventually could end up in a debt/financial crisis. This is especially true in a context of weak supervision of the financial system. The vast experience of developing countries with boom/bust cycles suggests that excessive cyclical fluctuations should be deterred. Here, fiscal and monetary policies have a fundamental role to play. A prudent fiscal policy, conservative supervision of the financial sectors and a flexible exchange rate has been a good combination for many countries to deal ex.ante with these boom/bust cycles. The ability of the governments to run surpluses and save the extraordinary revenues has exchange rate implications, and hence it could be seen as a counter.balancing force for a Dutch. disease phenomenon. But it should not. The benefits of a prudent fiscal policy should be evaluated in its own merit, rather than thought of as a mechanism for helping some particular industries. And there is abundant evidence that saving the extraordinary revenues from a terms.of.trade windfall is a sound fiscal policy. Over the medium term, monetary policy is unable to counter.balance the appreciation forces coming from fundamental variables. Some possibility to smooth out the appreciation is possible in the short run, but it has no material effect on the exchange rate trend, which fundamentally determines the de.industrialization forces that might be in place. A loose monetary policy aimed at depreciating the nominal exchange rate will end up in higher inflation. Neither is there strong evidence about the capacity of monetary policies to affect the equilibrium trend in the real exchange rate with capital controls. Although the conceptual case for capital controls is related to the existence of speculative capital flows, the literature has found mixed effects of capital controls on the real exchange rate and capital flows.5 Indeed, it is possible to argue that capital controls d1because of their limited nature and the sophistication of financial markets d1 can end up attracting speculative capital inflows because of the expected capital gains associated with the expected further appreciation of the currency in the context of regular FX interventions. Room for monetary policy interventions appears when the appreciative forces are stronger than what fundamentals suggest. In that case, a monetary intervention can put the exchange rate back on a sustainable path without affecting the inflation rate. In practice, the presence of such bubbles or speculative forces is very difficult to observe. In the current cycle in Chile there is no evidence of 5 Edwards, S (1999), d2How Effective are Capital Controls?d3, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 13(4):65.84, Fall; De Gregorio, J., S. Edwards, and R. Vald8es (2000), d2Controls on Capital Inflows: Do they Work?d3, Journal of Development Economics, 63(1):59.83; Larrain, F (ed), (2000) Private Capital Flows, Capital Controls and Currency Crises: Latin America in the 1990s, University of Michigan Press; Valdes, S., and M. Soto (2000), d2Selective Capital Controls: Theory and Evidenced3, in Private Capital Flows, Capital Controls & Currency: Latin America in the 1990s, F. Larrain (ed.) The University of Michigan Press; Gallego, F., Hernandez, L. and Schmidt.Hebbel, K., (2001), d2Capital Controls in Chile: Were They Effective?d3, in Banking, Financial Integration, and International Crises, L. Hernandez y K. Schmidt.Hebbel (eds). Series on Central Banking, Analysis, and Economic Policies, Central Bank of Chile speculative forces driving the peso beyond what its fundamentals suggest, but this is something for which central banks are always on the lookout. Thank you. Title: Challenges for Financial Stability after the International Financial Crisis
text: Challenges for Financial Stability in the aftermath of the international financial crisis1 Sebastian Claro Member of the Board, Central Bank of Chile August 8 , 2014 The financial crisis of 2008 d0 2009 provoked a significant rearrangement in the regulatory paradigm in the world and an invitation to review the role of the authorities in prudential financial stability. Although the lessons have not been decided, and many of the proposals or regulatory changes have not been tested, it is possible at this point to identify some relevant dimensions for Chile. A good starting point is the comprehensive reform plan to which G20 members have committed. This plan seeks to strengthen the supervision of financial institutions, improve the infrastructure of certain key markets, and deepen the monitoring of financial markets . Part of this debate has been picked up by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, which has proposed a strengthening of micro-prudential requirements for capital, leverage and liquidity. In addition to promoting the incorporation of macro. prudential in banking regulation and supervision, understood as policies that seek to contribute to the stability of the financial system. 2 Although the financial regulation and supervision scheme has worked well in recent decades in Chile, this debate is a good opportunity to review the current situation. Not only because it is valuable in an open and modern country to adapt to certain international standards d0 certainly adjusted to the reality of each country d0 but because In addition, markets will require financial intermediaries to standards similar to those required of international entities. In this presentation I would like to focus on two aspects that are particularly interesting for Chile. They are: ( i) the improvement of regulatory standards in the banking system, and (ii) the improvement of the transaction infrastructure in the financial system. For reasons of time, I will not refer to other aspects that are very relevant in the international discussion and that also have implications for Chile. 1 Speech prepared for the seminar Chilean Investor Forum, Santiago de Chile, The Ritz Carlton. These comments do not necessarily represent the vision of the Central Bank of Chile. I appreciate the collaboration of Gabriel Aparici, Nancy Silva, and Catherine Tornel in the preparation of this document. 2 Beau, Cahn, Clerc y Mojon, Macro.Prudential Policy and the Conduct of Monetary Policy, DTBC 715, Banco Central de Chile These include the regulatory treatment of other non-bank financial institutions, the institutional framework for the protection of financial consumers and the role of monetary policy in safeguarding the stability of the financial system in its interaction with so-called macro-prudential policies. 1. Improvement in the standards of regulation and supervision of banks in Basel 3. a. While the system meets the Basel III minimums on average, available estimates suggest that some banks are under these limits. b. Both for internal policies and market requirements, banks tend to comply with regulatory requirements with ease, so higher legal and regulatory standards will also imply an increase in the required capital. c. The formal incorporation of operational and market risks into capital indicators makes the international comparison more informative. 1.2 Liquidity 1.3 Macro-prudential aspects 1.1 Capital A first relevant dimension of the Basel committee agreement relates to the need to strengthen the capital base of banks. During the crisis, both the level and quality of capital of banks in developed countries could not adequately withstand the deterioration in the quality of the assets, which deepened liquidity problems and threatened the stability of the banking sector. That is why there is a need to deepen regulation in this area. Capital is the first and most important cushion for achieving stability in the value of bank liabilities, and strengthening capital standards helps to reduce risk of runs like that observed in 2008-2009 in developed markets . Certainly it is not the only mechanism, but it has the virtue of tending to greater stability in the value of liabilities while avoiding feeding moral hazard in the decisions of financial institutions. The alternative of promoting a massive assurance of liabilities by tax authorities does not seem promising, and substantive restrictions on the transformation of maturities in the banking system limits the role of promoting the growth of the system financial. The Basel Committee (BCBS) has proposed new , stricter standards for capital. While Basel II set a minimum of 8% for equity measured on assets weighted by credit, market or operational risk, Basel III raises this threshold to 10.5% and includes two new limits: one of 4.5% on risk-weighted assets (APR) for the highest quality capital (called Tier 1: Common Capital and Reserves), and one of 3% when measured on total assets (leverage). In addition, the Basel Committee introduced several capital requirements to mitigate systemic risks arising from exposures between financial institutions, such as capital incentives to use central counterparties when trading OTC derivatives. 3 At the same time, it highlights the extension of capital requirements to institutions considered systemic, referring to those whose failure could have a significant impact on the functioning of the financial system. 4.5 3 4 It also developed a methodology of quantitative and qualitative indicators to identify global systemically important banks (G.SIBs). ( ). For local SIBs, it proposes a similar methodology, replacing global impact variables with economy-specific factors ( ). It is worth mentioning that some proposals go further, introducing structural limitations to the growth of banking (derived from the Dodd-Frank Act in the US, the banking reform in the United Kingdom and the report of the Liikanen commission in Europe). 6 Finally, the Financial Stability Board's recommendations for the efficient resolution of Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs) include the development of Recovery and Resolution Plans, also called "living wills "; consisting of detailed contingency plans to be followed in the event of a relevant liquidity or capital stress scenario 7 The intention to limit the development of large and complex financial institutions that could jeopardize the proper functioning of the financial system seems laudable. it has many complexities, especially for a banking system with few institutions and rather small, as is the case in Chile. Beyond the good intentions that may underpin these proposals, legitimate doubts are raised about the ability of certain institutions to curb systemic risk. without overfeeding the moral hazard implicit in many of these definitions. Moving along this path by strengthening market discipline to achieve an adequate risk assessment by private agents is essential. The assessment of the implications of these capital requirements for Chilean banks is generally positive. The credit risk charges set out in the General Banking Act (LGB) are based on Basel I, but the available estimates, both the level and the The capital quality of the banking system in Chile is, on average, above the minimums defined by Basel III8. On the other hand, although the law does not include charges For operational or market risks, the BCCh's market risk regulations play an additional role, since the SBIF calculates and publishes an estimated indicator of the index capital adequacy that includes market risk , with weights derived from said regulations. Notwithstanding the foregoing, it is important to incorporate reforms in our General Banking Law (LGB), which allow a better adaptation to the solvency requirements defined by Basel III, to the less for the following reasons: 5 Basel III suggests additional requirements for Tier 1 capital of between 1 and 2.5% of APRs, increasing in the degree of "systemic impact" of global systemic banks. 6 See page 45 IEF first semester 2013: 7 8 Share capital and supplementary capital (consisting solely of subordinated bonds) represent more than 8.5% more and 2% of APRs, respectively. The healthy solvency levels of banks in Chile should be seen as an opportunity to move towards new international standards. But its adoption should not limit the strengths of our system. While the Basel accords represent the international consensus, their guidelines have proved not entirely foolproof, especially in the aftermath of the crisis. As an example, we can mention the challenges to the massive use of internal models, introduced in Basel II. In Chile there is only one standard model, and the credit risk weights used are in some cases much higher than those proposed by Basel. 9 Another example is the excessive reliance on ratings given by rating agencies to define capital charges, which has been prohibited in some reviews. regulatory and legal, by example, in the U.S. Chilean regulation has been cautious in several of these matters, and experience suggests keeping some distance from the international border on those issues where domestic experience has been successful. Another aspect to highlight in the regulatory proposals is the importance of adequate liquidity risk management, both for the normal functioning of financial markets and the banking sector. TheBasel Committee revised its Principles for Liquidity Risk Management in Banking and proposed quantitative measures to complement these principles, setting for the first time a international standard . The short-term liquidity coverage ratio (LCR, 30 days) seeks to ensure that banks have sufficient resources to face a stress scenario important, and the net stable financing ratio (NSFR) seeks to ensure a sustainable maturity profile for assets and liabilities in the medium term (1 year). In Chile, the BCCh, by mandate of its Constitutional Organic Law, must regulate the relations between active and passive banking operations. Based on this legal mandate, the current liquidity management regulation, in force since 1999, establishes that 30- and 90-day term mismatches must be less than one and two times the core capital, respectively. As a result of an evaluation of current regulations and international experience, the Central Bank of Chile has presented a series of modifications to the liquidity rules, which are in the process of public consultation. The main objectives sought are: (i) to strengthen liquidity risk management policies in banking, in line with international best practices, (ii) to incorporate the quantitative measures of Basel III as monitoring tools, and (iii) increase the quantity and quality of information available to the supervisor and the market. 9 60% for mortgage loans and 100% for consumption. In the case of companies , according to the rating method, a large company with a high Basel risk rating assigns capital charges close to 0%. However, in Chile it is 100%. Importantly, these changes will be phased in. In particular, and in keeping with this principle, the quantitative measures of Basel III are introduced as monitoring tools and not as normative requirements. The evaluation carried out over a period will allow the Basel criteria to be adapted to the realities of the local market, assessing the need to calibrate the indicators and establish a progressive transition. A final aspect that I would like to highlight in the Basel agreements relates to the incorporation of macro-prudential elements in banking regulation and supervision. 10 The overall objective is to introduce mechanisms that mitigate movements in credit and asset prices , thereby reducing the tendency of the banking system to amplify the cycle. economic through a very pro-cyclical supply of credit. Basel III has several proposals in this regard. The first is the introduction of an anti-cyclical capital buffer. The higher common equity requirement d0 in a range of 0 to 2.5 percent of APRs d0 would apply when the authorities consider that credit growth is causing an unacceptable accumulation of systemic risks. Since this tool has not been tested, it is difficult to define the metric according to which its application and subsequent withdrawal would be justified. In addition, it is complex to define the interaction between the macro-prudential functions themselvesd1usually associated with the role of the central bankd1with respect to micro-prudential supervisory objectives, since increasing capital requirements for macroeconomic needs could be counterproductive from the point of view of a particular bank . Another Basel III proposal, more in the area of solving troubled banks, relates to the establishment of a "capital conservation buffer", which limits or prohibits discretionary distributions of funds, such as profit sharing , when a bank falls below some solvency threshold. While this idea seems useful from a theoretical perspective, it faces practical difficulties, for example, in relation to the risk of the signal delivered to the market by the suspension of dividend payments due to capital "insufficiency" in a bank, and the liquidity problems that could arise. In general, this type of proposal should tend to introduce simple triggers, of a general nature, well calibrated, and where the discretion of the authority is low. This provides greater certainty to participants, minimizes arbitrary decisions, and strengthens supervisor independence. For now, the discussion on this matter is open. Other macro-prudential policies that have been discussed at the international level are related to limiting excessive pro-cyclicality in the demand for credit, especially 10 for the purchase of assets that is highly leveraged. The limits to the ratio of loans to asset values and the debt-to-income ratio are the most discussed. International evidence on the effectiveness of these policies is inconclusive, but generally Several studies suggest that its adoption in several countries has helped to mitigate the pro.cyclility of credit in some cases. 11 Chile has not been very active in the application of this type of measure, but it is worth noting the analysis being carried out by the SBIF to Establish provisions based on the loan-to-guarantee ratio of mortgage loans. 2. Market infrastructure Another lesson of the financial crisis relates to the soundness of the financial infrastructure. The significant development of derivative products to mitigate balance sheet risks resulted in a significant increase in interactions between financial institutions. This ability to transfer the risk of certain positions to other market participants had as its main virtue to disseminate the risk to those participants with greater willingness to maintain it. However, the opacity in the holding of many of these instruments, the possibilities of regulatory arbitrage to achieve lower capital requirements , and the greater counterparty risk derived from these inter-relationships contributed to the paralysis. of important segments of the financial system during the crisis. The lack of information and transparency not only blocked the action of supervisors, but also limited adequate market discipline, which would help to establish prices consistent with the inherent risks of each instrument. Since then, an important effort to make relations between agents transparent and strengthen and mitigate counterparty risks has been part of the international agenda. These efforts cover all markets with relevant transaction volumes, but have focused primarily on derivatives markets, on which I would like to deepen. The greatest need for infrastructure strengthening is seen in OTC derivatives markets. The ideal is that this type of transactions are channeled through trading platforms. An intermediate solution, which emerges from the international discussion, is to maintain the OTC nature of derivatives d0 in cases where their development through exchanges is complex d0 but channeling their transactions through Central Counterparties (CCPs). In some advanced markets, the existence of CCPs and exchanges for trading derivatives has been developing for decades and, during the crisis, it was possible to clearly verify the benefits. of this type of infrastructure. The best known case is that of Lehman Brothers, where the management of its default process presented great difficulties with its 11 See Box IV.1, International Evidence of Macro-prudential Policies Related to the Real Estate Sector, Financial Stability Report, Second Semester 2012, Central Bank of Chile. derivative transactions, except with those of forwards traded through CCPs, where it was possible to determine the net amounts committed in a short time. In contrast, in the Credit Default Swaps (CDS) markets, OTC traded and outside these infrastructures, the situation was very complex and the uncertainty of resolution It lasted for a long time. Motivated by these lessons, the Financial Stability Board (FSB), under the auspices of the G20 agreements, has established six areas relevant to the proper functioning of derivatives markets: the existence of transaction repositories, processing through Central Counterparty Chambers (CCPs), transactions in exchanges or others. platforms, product standardization, margin requirements for multilateral transactions, and capital requirements. In addition, the BIS Specialized Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems, in conjunction with the International Association of Supervisors of financial markets (CPSS12. IOSCO13), established a series of principles for the strengthening of all systemic market infrastructures (Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures). This discussion is of the first order for Chile, since the derivatives markets are almost exclusively OTC, traded bilaterally, without the intermediation of CCPs, and relevant in relation to to other economies. Indeed, contracts in Chile reach almost 7 times GDP, almost three times higher than in Latin American markets (2.4 times) and other emerging economies (2.6 times), although still well below economies advanced (28 times GDP). 14 In addition, compliance with these principles is important not only because adaptation to international standards is an appropriate benchmark in many areas, but because the regulations of Dodd-Frank (United States) and EMIR (Europe) require countries to move in this direction, to maintain a deep financial relationship with entities in those jurisdictions in derivative products. In this sense, the deepening of derivatives operations with the US and Europe depends in part on the best possible adaptation to these new standards. Assessing the degree of compliance with these principles is not easy, as it involves a complex review of the relevant legislations, regulations and internal operating rules of each of the market infrastructures (e.g. Central Counterparty Chambers, Transaction Repositories, Depositories). of Securities, Clearing Houses). In the case of Chile, the degree of progress in several of these areas in the last decade has been significant, considering, for example, the implementation of a 12 Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS). This equipment is equivalent to the BCBS (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on Banking Supervision) which establishes prudential recommendations for Banks. 13 The International Organization of Securities Commissions. 14 Figures to 2013, obtained from Villena and Salinas (2014), "Chilean Exchange Market, an International Comparison: 1998 to 2013," Estudios Econ97micas Estad92sticas 106, Central Bank of Chile. RTGS system in 2004, administered by the BCCH, the private development of an Interbank Chamber of Payments in 2005, the enactment of the securities clearing and settlement law in 2009 and the creation of the first CPC in the country in 2010. Despite these advances, there are areas in which improvements are needed. An important challenge is related to deepening the information provided to the market and the authorities, regarding the possession and exposure in derivatives. Other important aspects are related to the legal and regulatory structure that underpins the operation of CCPs in Chile. For this, it is essential to configure the development of Transaction Repositories (TRs) and analyze in detail the functioning of our legislation on clearing and settlement of securities (Law 20,345). The vision of international experts can be very useful in this area. Among the issues to be analyzed, it is necessary to establish the minimum standards that would allow the constitution of TRs, if they will be obliged and/or incentivized through capital requirements and/or collateral the processing of derivative transactions through CCPs, as well as establishing the criteria and protocols for the recognition of CCPs and other types of international infrastructure. The development of projects in the private sector, both in the stock exchange (CCLV-Derivatives) and banking (Comder) is positive, and must be prosecuted in a context more general institutional development. These advances will certainly require the participation and involvement of the public sector, as well as legal modifications. The Central Bank is committed to advancing this joint effort. 3. Conclusions I want to end with 3 very brief conclusions. First, the discussion about the regulatory lessons of the crisis has been wide-ranging, and many countries are in the process of major reforms. It is necessary to look with caution at this process in that its definitions and implications are in the process of continuous change, but it is at the same time necessary to take advantage of the opportunity and the debate to make a rigorous evaluation of our position. The markets demand it, and the degrees of interconnection of our country with the world also impose the need for best practices. Second, whatever the assessment of best practices and our gaps, the idiosyncrasies of our scheme must be taken into account in order to adapt regulations and laws to our reality. But at the same time, you should not lose sight of the north. Finally, the points I have highlighted in this presentation, which also applies to several others where I have not delved into, suggest that relevant regulatory modifications and legal changes could be required to perfect our architecture in the financial market. This is a far-reaching issue that requires the involvement of public authorities and the private sector.
text_original: Desafos para la Estabilidad Financiera despus de la crisis financiera internacional1 Sebastin Claro Miembro del Consejo, Banco Central de Chile 8 de agosto de 2014 La crisis financiera del 2008  2009 provoc un significativo reacomodo en el paradigma regulatorio en el mundo y una invitacin a revisar el rol de las autoridades en cautelar la estabilidad financiera. Aunque las lecciones no han decantado, y muchas de las propuestas o cambios regulatorios no han sido probadas, es posible a estas alturas identificar algunas dimensiones relevantes para Chile. Un buen punto de partida es el plan comprehensivo de reformas al cul los miembros del G20 se han comprometido. Este plan busca fortalecer la supervisin de instituciones financieras, mejorar la infraestructura de ciertos mercados claves, y profundizar el monitoreo de los mercados financieros. Parte de este debate ha sido recogido por el Comit de Supervisin Bancaria de Basilea, el que ha propuesto un fortalecimiento en los requerimientos microprudenciales de capital, apalancamiento y liquidez, adems de promover la incorporacin de aspectos macro prudenciales en la regulacin y supervisin bancaria, entendidas como polticas que buscan contribuir a cautelar la estabilidad del sistema financiero.2 Aun cuando el esquema de regulacin y supervisin financiera ha funcionado adecuadamente en las ltimas dcadas en Chile, este debate es una buena oportunidad para revisar la situacin actual. No slo porque es valioso en un pas abierto y moderno adecuarse a ciertas normas internacionales  por cierto ajustadas a la realidad de cada pas , sino porque adems los mercados exigirn a los intermediarios financieros estndares similares a los exigidos a entidades internacionales. En esta presentacin quisiera enfocarme en dos aspectos que son particularmente interesantes para Chile. Ellos son: (i) el perfeccionamiento de estndares de regulacin en el sistema bancario, y (ii) el perfeccionamiento en la infraestructura de transacciones en el sistema financiero. Por razones de tiempo, no me referir a otros aspectos que son muy relevantes en la discusin internacional y que tambin tienen implicancias sobre Chile. 1 Discurso preparado para el seminario Chilean Investor Forum, Santiago de Chile, The Ritz Carlton. Estos comentarios no representan necesariamente la visin del Banco Central de Chile. Agradezco la colaboracin de Gabriel Aparici, Nancy Silva, y Catherine Tornel en la preparacin de este documento. 2 Beau, Cahn, Clerc y Mojon, MacroPrudential Policy and the Conduct of Monetary Policy, DTBC 715, Banco Central de Chile Entre ellos destaca el tratamiento regulatorio de otras instituciones financieras no bancarias, la institucionalidad de proteccin al consumidor financiero o el rol de la poltica monetaria en cautelar la estabilidad del sistema financiero en su interaccin con las llamadas polticas macroprudenciales.  Perfeccionamiento en los estndares de regulacin y supervisin de los bancos en Basilea 3. 1.1 Capital Una primera dimensin relevante del acuerdo del comit de Basilea dice relacin con la necesidad de fortalecer la base de capital de los bancos. Durante la crisis, tanto el nivel como la calidad del capital de los bancos de los pases desarrollados no pudieron resistir adecuadamente el deterioro en la calidad de los activos, lo que profundiz los problemas de liquidez y amenaz la estabilidad del sector bancario. Es por ello que aparece la necesidad de profundizar la regulacin en este mbito. El capital es el primer y ms importante colchn para lograr estabilidad en el valor de los pasivos bancarios, y el fortalecimiento de los estndares de capital contribuye a disminuir el riesgo de corridas como la observada el 20082009 en los mercados desarrollados. Por cierto que no es el nico mecanismo, pero tiene la virtud de propender a una mayor estabilidad en el valor de los pasivos al mismo tiempo que evita alimentar el riesgo moral en las decisiones de las entidades financieras. La alternativa de promocionar un aseguramiento masivo de pasivos por parte de las autoridades fiscales no parece prometedora, y restricciones sustantivas a la transformacin de plazos en el sistema bancario limita el rol de promocin del crecimiento del sistema financiero. El Comit de Basilea (BCBS) ha propuesto nuevos y ms estrictos estndares para el capital. Mientras Basilea II fij un mnimo de 8% para el patrimonio medido sobre activos ponderados por riesgo de crdito, mercado u operacional, Basilea III eleva este umbral a 10,5% e incluye dos nuevos lmites: uno de 4,5% sobre activos ponderados por riesgo (APR) para el capital de mayor calidad (llamado nivel 1: capital ordinario y reservas), y uno de 3% cuando se mide sobre activos totales (apalancamiento). Adicionalmente, el Comit de Basilea introdujo varios requerimientos de capital para mitigar los riesgos sistmicos que emanan de las exposiciones entre instituciones financieras, como los incentivos de capital para utilizar entidades de contraparte central al negociar con derivados OTC.3 A su vez, destaca la ampliacin de las exigencias de capital a instituciones consideradas sistmicas, referidas a aquellas cuya falla podra tener un impacto significativo en el funcionamiento del sistema financiero.4,5 3 http://www.bis.org/bcbs/basel3/b3summarytable_es.pdf 4 Asimismo, elabor una metodologa de indicadores cuantitativos y cualitativos para identificar a los bancos de importancia sistmica globales (GSIB). (http://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs255.pdf). Para SIB locales, propone una metodologa similar, reemplazando las variables de impacto global por factores especficos a cada economa (http://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs233.pdf). Cabe mencionar que algunas propuestas van ms all, introduciendo limitaciones estructurales al crecimiento de la banca (derivadas de la Ley DoddFrank en EE.UU., la reforma bancaria en Reino Unido y el reporte de la comisin Liikanen en Europa).6 Finalmente, las recomendaciones del Financial Stability Board para la resolucin eficiente de las Instituciones Financieras Sistmicamente Importantes (SIFIs) incluyen el desarrollo de Planes de Recuperacin y Resolucin, tambin llamados testamentos en vida; que consisten en detallados planes de contingencia a seguir en caso de que se materialice un escenario de estrs de liquidez o de capital relevante7 La intencin de limitar el desarrollo de instituciones financieras grandes y complejas que pueda poner en riesgo el buen funcionamiento del sistema financiero parece loable, pero tiene muchas complejidades, especialmente para un sistema bancario con pocas instituciones y ms bien pequeo, como es el caso de Chile. Ms all de las buenas intenciones que puedan sustentar estas propuestas, se plantean legtimas dudas sobre la capacidad de poner freno al riesgo sistmico de ciertas instituciones sin alimentar de manera excesiva el riesgo moral implcito en muchas de estas definiciones. Avanzar por este camino fortaleciendo la disciplina del mercado para lograr una adecuada evaluacin del riesgo por parte de los agentes privados es fundamental. La evaluacin sobre las implicancias de estas exigencias de capital sobre la banca chilena es en general positiva. Los cargos por riesgo de crdito establecidos en la Ley General de Bancos (LGB) estn basados en Basilea I, pero las estimaciones disponibles, tanto el nivel como la calidad del capital del sistema bancario en Chile se encuentran, en promedio, sobre los mnimos definidos por Basilea III8. Por otra parte, aunque la ley no incluye cargos por riesgos operacional ni de mercado, la normativa de riesgo de mercado del BCCh juega un rol suplementario, ya que la SBIF calcula y publica un indicador estimado del ndice de adecuacin de capital que incluye riesgo de mercado, con ponderadores derivados de dicha normativa. No obstante lo anterior, resulta importante incorporar reformas en nuestra Ley General de Bancos (LGB), que permitan una mejor adaptacin a los requerimientos de solvencia definidos por Basilea III, al menos por las siguientes razones:  Si bien el sistema cumple en promedio con los mnimos de Basilea III, las estimaciones disponibles sugieren que algunos bancos se encuentran bajo dichos lmites.  Tanto por polticas internas como por exigencias de mercado, los bancos suelen cumplir los requerimientos regulatorios con holgura, por lo que mayores estndares legales y regulatorios implicarn igualmente un aumento en el capital exigido. 5 El acuerdo de Basilea III sugiere requerimientos adicionales para el capital de nivel 1 de entre 1 y 2,5% de los APR, crecientes en el grado de impacto sistmico de los bancos sistmicos globales. 6 Ver pgina 45 IEF primer semestre 2013: http://www.bcentral.cl/publicaciones/politicas/pdf/ief2013_1.pdf 7 http://www.financialstabilityboard.org/publications/r_110719.pdf 8 El capital accionario y el capital suplementario (constituido nicamente por bonos subordinados) representan ms de un 8,5% ms y de un 2% de los APR, respectivamente.  La incorporacin formal de los riesgos operacionales y de mercado en los indicadores de capital hace ms informativa la comparacin internacional. Los saludables niveles de solvencia de la banca en Chile deben ser vistos como una oportunidad para avanzar hacia nuevos estndares internacionales. Pero su adopcin no debe limitar las fortalezas de nuestro sistema. Si bien los acuerdos de Basilea representan el consenso internacional, sus directrices han demostrado no ser del todo infalibles, en especial con posterioridad a la crisis. A modo de ejemplo, pueden mencionarse los cuestionamientos al uso masivo de modelos internos, introducidos en Basilea II. En Chile slo existe un modelo estndar, y los ponderadores por riesgo de crdito utilizados son en algunos casos muy superiores a los propuestos por Basilea. 9 Otro ejemplo es la excesiva dependencia de los ratings otorgados por las clasificadoras de riesgo para definir cargos de capital, lo que ha sido prohibido en algunas revisiones normativas y legales, por ejemplo, en EE.UU. La regulacin chilena ha sido cauta en varias de estas materias, y la experiencia sugiere mantener cierta distancia de la frontera internacional en aquellos temas donde la experiencia domstica ha sido exitosa.  Liquidez Otro aspecto a resaltar de las propuestas regulatorias es la importancia de una adecuada gestin del riesgo de liquidez, tanto para el normal funcionamiento de los mercados financieros como del sector bancario. El Comit de Basilea revis su documento de principios para la administracin del riesgo de liquidez en la banca y propuso medidas cuantitativas que complementen estos principios, fijando por primera vez un estndar a nivel internacional. La razn de cobertura de liquidez de corto plazo (LCR, a 30 das) busca asegurar que los bancos cuenten con recursos suficientes para enfrentar un escenario de estrs importante, y la razn de financiamiento estable neto (NSFR) busca asegurar un perfil de vencimientos sustentable para los activos y pasivos en el mediano plazo (1 ao). En Chile, el BCCh, por mandato de su Ley Orgnica Constitucional, debe regular las relaciones entre las operaciones activas y pasivas de la banca. Sobre la base de este mandato legal, la regulacin actual de gestin de liquidez, vigente desde 1999, establece que los descalces de plazo a 30 y 90 das deben ser menores a una y dos veces el capital bsico, respectivamente. Fruto de una evaluacin de la normativa vigente y de la experiencia internacional, el Banco Central de Chile ha presentado una serie de modificaciones a las normas de liquidez, que se encuentran en proceso de consulta pblica. Los principales objetivos buscados son: (i) fortalecer las polticas de gestin del riesgo de liquidez en la banca, en lnea con las mejores prcticas internacionales, (ii) incorporar las medidas cuantitativas de Basilea III como herramientas de monitoreo, y (iii) aumentar la cantidad y calidad de informacin disponible para el supervisor y el mercado. 9 60% para crditos hipotecarios y 100% para consumo. En el caso de las empresas, de acuerdo al mtodo de ratings, a una gran empresa con elevada clasificacin de riesgo Basilea asigna cargos de capital cercanos a 0%. No obstante, en Chile es de 100%. Es importante destacar que estos cambios tendrn una introduccin gradual. En particular, y en atencin a este principio, las medidas cuantitativas de Basilea III se introducen como herramientas de monitoreo y no como requerimientos normativos. La evaluacin que se haga durante un periodo permitir adaptar los criterios de Basilea a las realidades del mercado local, evaluando la necesidad de calibrar los indicadores y establecer una transicin progresiva.  Aspectos macroprudenciales Un ltimo aspecto que quisiera destacar de los acuerdos de Basilea dicen relacin con la incorporacin de elementos macroprudenciales en la regulacin y supervisin bancaria.10 El objetivo general es introducir mecanismos que atenen los movimientos del crdito y precios de activos, reduciendo as la tendencia del sistema bancario a amplificar el ciclo econmico a travs de una oferta de crdito muy procclica. Basilea III tiene varias propuestas en este sentido. La primera es la introduccin de un colchn de capital anticclico. La mayor exigencia de capital ordinario  en un rango de entre 0 y 2,5% de los APR  se aplicara cuando las autoridades consideren que el crecimiento del crdito est ocasionando una acumulacin inaceptable de riesgos sistmicos. Puesto que esta herramienta no ha sido probada, resulta difcil definir la mtrica segn la cual se justificara su aplicacin y posterior retiro. Adems, es complejo definir la interaccin entre las funcin propiamente macroprudenciales usualmente asociada con el rol del banco central respecto de los objetivos microprudenciales de supervisin, ya que el aumento de los requerimientos de capital por necesidades macroeconmicas podras ser contraproducente desde el punto de vista de algn banco en particular. Otra propuesta de Basilea III, ms en el mbito de la resolucin de bancos en problemas, dice relacin con el establecimiento de un colchn de conservacin de capital, que limite o prohba las distribuciones discrecionales de fondos, como el reparto de utilidades, cuando un banco caiga bajo algn umbral de solvencia. Si bien esta idea parece til desde una perspectiva terica, enfrenta dificultades prcticas, por ejemplo, en relacin al riesgo de la seal que entrega al mercado la suspensin del pago de dividendos por insuficiencia de capital en un banco, y los problemas de liquidez que se podran derivar. En general, este tipo de propuestas debe propender a introducir gatillos simples, de carcter general, bien calibrados, y donde la discrecionalidad de la autoridad sea baja. De esa manera se provee de mayor certidumbre a los participantes, se minimizan las decisiones arbitrarias, y se fortalece la independencia del supervisor. Por ahora, la discusin en esta materia est abierta. Otras polticas macroprudenciales que se han discutido a nivel internacional dicen relacin con limitar la excesiva prociclicalidad en la demanda de crdito, especialmente 10 http://www.bis.org/publ/bcbs189.pdf para la compra de activos que est muy apalancada. Los lmites a la razn entre prstamos y valor de los activos y a la razn deudaingreso son los ms discutidos. La evidencia internacional sobre la efectividad de estas polticas no es concluyente, pero por lo general diversos estudios sugieren que su adopcin en varios pases ha contribuido a mitigar la prociclicalidad del crdito en algunos casos.11 Chile no ha sido muy activo en la aplicacin de este tipo de medidas, pero cabe destacar el anlisis que est realizando la SBIF para establecer provisiones en funcin de la razn prstamogaranta de los crditos hipotecarios.  Infraestructura de mercado Otra de las lecciones de la crisis financiera dice relacin con la solidez de la infraestructura financiera. El significativo desarrollo de productos derivados para mitigar riesgos en el balance produjo un aumento importante en las interacciones entre instituciones financieras. Esta capacidad de trasladar el riesgo de ciertas posiciones hacia otros participantes del mercado tena como principal virtud diseminar el riesgo hacia aquellos participantes con mayor disposicin a mantenerlo. Sin embargo, la opacidad en la tenencia de muchos de estos instrumentos, las posibilidades de realizar arbitraje regulatorio para lograr menores exigencias de capital, y el mayor riesgo de contraparte derivado de estas interrelaciones contribuy a la paralizacin de importantes segmentos del sistema financiero durante la crisis. La falta de informacin y transparencia no solo bloque la actuacin de los supervisores, sino que tambin limit una adecuada disciplina de mercado, que contribuyera a establecer precios coherentes con los riesgos inherentes de cada instrumento. Desde entonces, un esfuerzo importante por transparentar y fortalecer las relaciones entre agentes y mitigar los riesgos de contraparte ha sido parte de la agenda internacional. Estos esfuerzos comprenden a todos los mercados con volmenes de transacciones relevantes, pero se han focalizado principalmente en los mercados de derivados, tema sobre el cul quisiera profundizar. La mayor necesidad de fortalecimiento de infraestructura se observa en los mercados de derivados OTC. El ideal es que este tipo de transacciones se canalicen a travs de plataformas burstiles. Una solucin intermedia, que surge de la discusin internacional, es mantener la naturaleza OTC de los derivados en los casos en que su desarrollo a travs de bolsas es complejo , pero canalizando sus transacciones a travs de Entidades de Contraparte Central (ECCs). En algunos mercados avanzados, la existencia de ECCs y bolsas para transar derivados se ha venido desarrollando por dcadas y, durante la crisis, fue posible verificar con claridad los beneficios de este tipo de infraestructuras. El caso ms conocido es el de Lehman Brothers, donde la gestin de su proceso de default present grandes dificultades con sus 11 Ver Recuadro IV.1, Evidencia Internacional de Polticas Macroprudenciales vinculadas al sector inmobiliario, Informe de Estabilidad Financiera, Segundo Semestre 2012, Banco Central de Chile. operaciones de derivados, excepto con aquellas de forwards transadas a travs de ECCs, donde fue posible determinar los montos netos comprometidos en corto tiempo. En contraposicin, en los mercados de Credit Default Swaps (CDS), transados OTC y fuera de estas infraestructuras, la situacin fue muy compleja y la incertidumbre de la resolucin se extendi por largo tiempo. Motivados por estas lecciones, el Financial Stability Board (FSB), al alero de los acuerdos del G20, ha establecido seis reas relevantes para el buen funcionamiento de los mercados de derivados: la existencia de repositorios de transacciones, procesamiento a travs de Cmaras de Contraparte Central (CCPs), transacciones en bolsas u otras plataformas, estandarizacin de productos, requerimientos de margen para transacciones multilaterales, y requerimientos de capital. Adems el Comit especializado en sistemas de pagos y liquidacin del BIS, en conjunto con la asociacin internacional de supervisores de mercados financieros (CPSS12 IOSCO13) , establecieron una serie de principios para el fortalecimiento de todas las infraestructuras sistmicas de mercado (Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures). Esta discusin es de primer orden para Chile, ya que los mercados de derivados son casi exclusivamente OTC, transados bilateralmente, sin la intermediacin de ECCs, y relevantes en relacin a otras economas. En efecto, los contratos en Chile alcanzan casi 7 veces el PIB, casi tres veces superior al de mercados latinoamericanos (2,4 veces) y otras economas emergentes (2,6 veces), aunque an bastante por debajo de economas avanzadas (28 veces el PIB).14 Adems, el cumplimiento de estos principios es importante no slo porque la adecuacin a normativas internacionales resulta un benchmark apropiado en muchas materias, sino porque las regulaciones de DoddFrank (Estados Unidos) y EMIR (Europa) exigen a los pases avanzar en esta direccin, para mantener una relacin financiera profunda con entidades de esas jurisdicciones en productos derivados. En este sentido, la profundizacin de las operaciones de derivados con EE.UU. y Europa depende en parte de la mejor adaptacin posible a estos nuevos estndares. Evaluar el grado de cumplimiento de estos principios no es fcil, ya que implica una compleja revisin de las legislaciones relevantes, regulaciones y reglas de funcionamiento interno de cada una de las infraestructuras de mercado (por ejemplo, Cmaras de Contraparte Central, Repositorios de Transacciones, Depositarios de Valores, Cmaras de Compensacin). En el caso de Chile el grado de avance en varios de estos mbitos en la ltima dcada ha sido significativo, considerando por ejemplo la implementacin de un 12 Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS). Este equipo es equivalente al BCBS (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Comitee on Banking Supervision) que establece las recomendaciones prudenciales para Bancos. 13 The International Organization of Securities Commissions. 14 Cifras a 2013, obtenidas de Villena y Salinas (2014), Mercado Cambiario Chileno, una Comparacin Internacional: 1998 a 2013, Estudios Econmicos Estadsticos 106, Banco Central de Chile. Sistema LBTR en 2004, administrado por el BCCH, el desarrollo privado de una Cmara de Pagos Interbancarios en 2005, la promulgacin de la ley de compensacin y liquidacin de valores en 2009 y la creacin de la primera CCP en el pas en 2010. No obstante estos avances, existen reas en las cuales son necesarios perfeccionamientos. Un desafo importante dice relacin con profundizar la informacin entregada al mercado y las autoridades, en cuanto a la tenencia y exposicin en derivados. Otros aspectos importantes estn relacionados con la estructura legal y reglamentaria que sustenta el funcionamiento de las ECCs en Chile. Para ello, es fundamental configurar el desarrollo de Repositorios de Transacciones (TRs) y analizar en detalle el funcionamiento de nuestra legislacin sobre compensacin y liquidacin de valores (Ley 20.345). La visin de expertos internacionales puede resultar muy til en esta materia. Entre los temas a analizar, es necesario establecer los estndares mnimos que permitiran constituir TRs, si se obligar y/o incentivar a travs de requerimientos de capital y/o colaterales el procesamiento de transacciones de derivados a travs de CCPs, as como establecer los criterios y protocolos para el reconocimiento de CCPs y otros tipos de infraestructura internacionales. El desarrollo de proyectos en el sector privado, tanto de la bolsa de comercio (CCLVDerivados) como de la banca (Comder) es positivo, y deben encausarse en un contexto ms general de perfeccionamiento institucional. Estos avances requerirn por cierto el concurso e involucramiento tambin del sector pblico, as como modificaciones legales. El Banco Central est comprometido con avanzar en este esfuerzo conjunto.  Conclusiones Quiera terminar con 3 conclusiones muy breves. Primero, la discusin sobre las lecciones regulatorias de la crisis ha sido muy amplia, y muchos pases se encuentran en proceso de reformas importantes. Es necesario mirar con cautela este proceso en cuanto a que sus definiciones e implicancias estn en proceso de continuo cambio, pero es al mismo tiempo necesario aprovechar la oportunidad y el debate para hacer una rigurosa evaluacin de nuestra posicin. Los mercados as lo exigen, y los grados de interconexin de nuestro pas con el mundo tambin imponen la necesidad de contar con las mejores prcticas. Segundo, cualquiera sea la evaluacin sobre las mejores prcticas y nuestras brechas, se debe tener en cuenta la idiosincrasia de nuestro esquema para adecuar las normativas y las leyes a nuestra realidad. Pero al mismo tiempo, no debe perderse de vista el norte. Por ltimo, los puntos que he destacado en esta presentacin, lo que tambin se aplica a varios otros donde no he profundizado, sugieren que relevantes modificaciones regulatorias y cambios legales podran ser requeridos para perfeccionar nuestra arquitectura en el mercado financiero. Este es un tema de largo alcance que requiere del concurso de las autoridades pblicas y del sector privado.

Title: Cooperation and Financial Integration between Chile and China
text: Cooperation and Financial Integration between Chile and ChinaI I Speech prepared for the seventh meeting of the China-Chile Business Council, held at the Marriott Hotel, Santiago, Chile, May 26, 2015, on the occasion of the official visit to Chile of the Premier of China, Mr. Li Keqiang. Sebastian Claro Board Member, Central Bank of Chile 26 May 2015 I sincerely appreciate the invitation to this important business meeting, especially as it represents a very valuable opportunity to share with you some reflections on the Central Bank's vision for financial integration with China. As is public knowledge, the Central Bank of Chile announced yesterday important agreements in this area with the Central Bank of the People's Republic of China (PBC), and I have thought it profitable on this occasion to share with you some reflections on the context in which these agreements are framed, as well as to deepen their implications. China's role as a trading power is beyond dispute, and our own experience proves it: China is today our main trading partner. In addition, China's role in the international financial and monetary system is now in a process of increasing deepening. The edges of this process are varied, from the creation of new regional and multilateral development financing arrangements and balance-of-payments stabilization, through the development of offshore RMB markets, to the possible incorporation of the RMB into the IMF's special drawing rights basket. These different dimensions arise from the effort of financial integration and opening of the capital account, which places China in an expectant position regarding its role in the coming decades. Due not only to the size but also to the degree of interconnectedness with the world that China has, this process presents very significant opportunities and challenges for the rest of the world. A first dimension of these opportunities is related to the possibility of using the Renminbi (RMB) as a payment currency in international trade. So far, the depth of China's international trade is not commensurate with the low percentage of it that is determined and paid in RMB. In recent years, however, the RMB's share of international trade payments has risen rapidly and significantly, and according to Swift reports, at the end of 2014 the RMB was positioned within the 5 most used currencies in international trade, after the U.S. dollar. the Euro, the Pound and the Yen, accounting for just over 2% of international trade payments. The advantages of trading with China by paying or receiving RMB can be very large, being able to translate, for example, into better conditions with local clients, in decreases in transaction costs, or in improvements in the management of currency risks, among others. Naturally, the possibility and benefits for companies in the rest of the world to pay or receive RMB are directly related to the possibility of holding financial positions in that currency and accessing deep markets. This brings us to the second major challenge: the opening of the financial account in China allows the diversification of sources of financing and investments of Chinese abroad, as well as foreigners in China. The government of China, and its Central Bank, have been making concrete efforts to expand foreign investors' access to RMB financial assets in the onshore market, both directly and through offshore platforms, enhancing access to RMB instruments and facilitating their use through ensuring their convertibility. In turn, systematic efforts have been made to develop liquid and deeper RMB markets in different countries. At present, the use of the RMB in Chile is negligible, which is not related to the intensity of our trade with China. In turn, there are also no RMB-denominated financial products or securities available in Chile, and the exposure of financial agents to RMB-denominated assets is very low. This, more than being a problem, is a sample of the existing space for the use of the RMB in Chile to expand, considering the global context of financial openness in China and Chile's bilateral trade surplus with China, which potentially constitutes an important source of liquidity in RMB for the domestic market. It should be noted that as part of the diversification of the investment of its International Reserves, the BCCh has taken positions in RMB for some time. Currently, about 3% of the Reserves are invested in RMB. This is a process initiated in 2011, with investments made in the offshore market, both in short-term bank deposits and in debt instruments issued by the Chinese government in Hong Kong, and which continued in 2014 with an investment in the onshore market through a program offered by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS, for its acronym in English). The Agency Agreement recently signed with the PBC to be able to invest directly in the onshore interbank bond market will allow greater diversification and depth of these investments. At the Central Bank of Chile we are confident that the deepening of the process of financial opening in China will bring important benefits to Chilean companies and investors in the future. According to our legal mandate, the Central Bank of Chile has the obligation to ensure the normal functioning of internal and external payments. Taking the first steps to promote the development of RMB payments that are safe, efficient and affordable represents a significant contribution in this regard. That is why we have taken the decision to deepen the integration ties with the Central Bank of the People's Republic of China, taking precisely concrete steps to facilitate the use of the RMB in commercial transactions with China, as well as to promote the possibilities of investment in RMB-denominated instruments. It is in this context that the recently signed agreements must be understood. The Memorandum of Understanding (Mol92) signed by both Central Banks encourages cooperation in this area in a substantial way. On the one hand, a permanent dialogue is established and communication channels are determined for the exchange of aggregated information on financial operations that are carried out in RMB in the local market. Also, and more importantly, the Mol92 contemplates that the PBC will designate an RMB Clearing Bank (RMB Clearing Bank ). The PBC has entered into similar agreements with other central banks, such as Germany, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia. Chile is the first Latin American country to have such an agreement. The designation of the RMB Clearing Bank will be made exclusively by the Chinese authorities, since it will grant a bank established in Chile access to the PBC's high-value payment system. This will allow it to offer various services in Chile, subject to Chilean legislation and regulations, such as making payments and transfers to and from China, without the need to previously go through the offshore currency market. This should result in a reduction in transaction costs associated with these operations, as well as ensuring liquidity in the nascent RMB/CLP market. Subject also to the corresponding regulations, Banco Compensatorio may also offer RMB-denominated financial products to Chilean participants, which should also contribute to greater use of that currency and promote the exposure of Chilean agents to the RMB. Strictly speaking, today it is already possible for Chilean companies to denominate, receive or pay RMB in their commercial transactions with China, as well as it is feasible for financial institutions to have positions in that currency. However, this must be done through other offshore centres, which makes them difficult to access and limits the development of an RMB/CLP market. The appointment of a Compensatory Bank will facilitate the development of this market directly in Chile, increasing the possibilities for Chilean financial and non-financial companies. Finally, in the future, the existence of a Compensatory Bank in Chile could encourage local financial institutions to offer RMB-denominated products, as has happened in other countries. Along with the signing of the MoU, the Central Bank of Chile and the Central Bank of the People's Republic of China also signed a Bilateral RMB/CLP Swap Line Agreement , which will allow both institutions to ensure the availability of the counterparty's currency in their country. The line agreed with the PBC is for an amount of RMB 22 billion or CLP 2,200 billion, and has a duration of 3 years, extendable. There are more than 30 countries whose central banks have negotiated similar lines with the PBC in the last 3 or 4 years. This agreement, which grants substantial access to RMB for the Central Bank of Chile, fulfills the objective of providing confidence to the domestic market that, in case of any situation of financial friction that hinders the normal financing of external payments, there may be a liquidity facility of last resort to which local financial institutions can resort so that these payments are not interrupted. Certainly, this complements a set of instruments already available by the Central Bank of Chile to face a situation of international financial stress. Considering the size of China, we believe this line is a relevant contribution to financial stability. In addition, the authorities in China have granted Chile an initial quota of RMB 50 trillion (equivalent to approximately USD 8 billion) in its program called "Renminbi Qualified Foreign Institutional Investor" (RQ. FII), which allows Qualified Foreign Institutional Investors to invest directly in that country's stock market. This is an important announcement, both because of its content and because Chile is the first country in Latin America to obtain a quota in that program. Direct access to financial markets in China for institutional investors established in Chile, such as banks, pension funds and insurance companies, mutual funds and investment funds, among others, grants more expeditious access to a broad set of RMB financial instruments. This generates significant benefits in terms of reducing transaction costs in currencies and diversification, and increases the possibilities for the financial system in Chile to become a regional financial investment platform in China. To access this quota, financial institutions must apply for individual quotas with the authorities in China, then access debt and equity markets in China using RMB obtained in the offshore market. It should be noted that the government and corporate bond market in China is the third largest in the world, and the stock market the second largest, a history that alone shows the possibilities that the Chinese market offers to foreign investors. I would like to conclude by emphasizing that with these agreements, the Central Bank of Chile is helping to lay the foundations for facilitating the use of the RMB in international trade and financial investments, and for the development of an RMB/CLP market. We appreciate the willingness of the authorities in China to strongly strengthen financial ties with the region through Chile. Having said that, it is important to emphasize that it will ultimately be the proactivity of financial and non-financial companies that will determine the success of this process. The deepening of financial relations with China, and the taking advantage of the opportunities that are beginning to open up for Chilean companies, will depend on the initiative of the private sector. We trust that the agreements signed will be a contribution to enabling private sector actors to extract in the medium term the benefits associated with the internationalization of the RMB. Thanks a lot.

Debido no solo al tamao sino al grado de interconexin con el mundo que tiene China, este proceso presenta oportunidades y desafos muy significativos para el resto del mundo. Una primera dimensin de estas oportunidades dice relacin con la posibilidad de utilizar el Renminbi (RMB) como moneda de pago en el comercio internacional. Hasta ahora, la profundidad del comercio internacional de China no se condice con el bajo porcentaje de ste que se determina y paga en RMB. En los ltimos aos, sin embargo, la participacin del RMB en los pagos de comercio internacional ha subido de manera rpida y significativa, y de acuerdo a los reportes de Swift, a fines del 2014 el RMB se posicion dentro de las 5 monedas ms usadas en el comercio internacional, despus del Dlar de EE.UU., el Euro, la Libra y el Yen, representando algo ms del 2% de los pagos de comercio internacional. Las ventajas de comerciar con China pagando o recibiendo RMB pueden ser muy grandes, pudiendo traducirse, por ejemplo, en mejores condiciones con clientes locales, en disminuciones de costos de transaccin, o en mejoras al manejo de riesgos de moneda, entre otros. Naturalmente, la posibilidad y los beneficios para empresas en el resto del mundo de pagar o recibir RMB estn en directa relacin con la posibilidad de mantener posiciones financieras en esa moneda y de acceder a mercados profundos. Esto nos lleva al segundo gran desafo: la apertura de la cuenta financiera en China permite la diversificacin de fuentes de financiamiento e inversiones de chinos en el exterior, as como de extranjeros en China. El gobierno de China, y su Banco Central, han estado realizando esfuerzos concretos para ampliar el acceso de inversionistas extranjeros a activos financieros en RMB en el mercado onshore, tanto directamente como a travs de plataformas offshore, potenciando el acceso a instrumentos en esa moneda y facilitando su uso a travs de asegurar su convertibilidad. A su vez, se han hecho esfuerzos sistemticos para desarrollar mercados lquidos y ms profundos de RMB en diferentes pases. En la actualidad, la utilizacin del RMB en Chile es nfima, lo que no guarda relacin con la intensidad de nuestro intercambio con China. A su vez, tampoco existen productos o valores financieros denominados en RMB disponibles en Chile, y la exposicin de los agentes financieros a activos denominados en RMB es muy baja. Esto ms que ser un problema, es una muestra del espacio existente para que el uso del RMB en Chile se expanda, considerando el contexto global de apertura financiera en China y el supervit comercial bilateral de Chile con China, lo que constituye potencialmente una importante fuente de liquidez en RMB para el mercado domstico. Cabe destacar que como parte de la diversificacin de la inversin de sus Reservas Internacionales, el BCCh ha tomado posiciones en RMB desde hace algn tiempo. En la actualidad, cerca del 3% de las Reservas se encuentran invertidas en RMB.
