El Acuerdo de Agencia suscrito recientemente con el PBC para poder invertir directamente en el mercado interbancario de bonos onshore permitir una mayor diversificacin y profundidad de estas inversiones. En el Banco Central de Chile confiamos que la profundizacin del proceso de apertura financiera en China traer importantes beneficios a las empresas e inversionistas chilenos en el futuro. De acuerdo a nuestro mandato legal, el Banco Central de Chile tiene la obligacin de velar por el normal funcionamiento de los pagos internos y externos. Dar los primeros pasos para promover el desarrollo de pagos en RMB que sean seguros, eficientes y asequibles, representa un aporte significativo en este sentido. Es por ello que hemos tomado la decisin de profundizar los lazos de integracin con el Banco Central de la Repblica Popular de China, dando precisamente pasos concretos para facilitar el uso del RMB en transacciones comerciales con China, as como promover las posibilidades de inversin en instrumentos denominados en RMB. Es en este contexto en que deben ser entendidos los acuerdos recientemente firmados. El Memorndum de Entendimiento (Mol, por su sigla en ingls) firmado por ambos Bancos Centrales fomenta la cooperacin en esta materia de manera sustancial. Por un parte, se establece un dilogo permanente y se determinan canales de comunicacin para el intercambio de informacin agregada sobre operaciones financieras que se lleven a cabo en RMB en el mercado local. Tambin, y ms importante, el Mol contempla que el PBC designar a un Banco Compensatorio de RMB (RMB Clearing Bank por su sigla en ingls). El PBC ha suscrito acuerdos similares con otros bancos centrales, como los de Alemania, Reino Unido, Canad y Australia. Chile es el primer pas latinoamericano en contar con un acuerdo de este tipo. La designacin del Banco Compensatorio de RMB corresponder realizarla exclusivamente a las autoridades chinas, toda vez que en virtud de ella se le entregar a un banco establecido en Chile acceso al sistema de pagos de alto valor del PBC. Esto le permitir ofrecer diversos servicios en Chile, sujetndose a la legislacin y normativa chilena, tales como realizar pagos y transferencias desde y hacia China, sin que sea necesario pasar previamente por el mercado de divisas offshore. Esto debiera dar lugar a una reduccin en los costos de transaccin asociados a estas operaciones, adems de garantizar liquidez en el naciente mercado de RMB/CLP. Sujeto igualmente a las regulaciones correspondientes, el Banco Compensatorio tambin podr ofrecer productos financieros denominados en RMB a participantes chilenos, lo que tambin debiera contribuir a una mayor utilizacin de esa moneda y a promover la exposicin de agentes chilenos al RMB. Estrictamente hablando, hoy ya es posible para empresas chilenas denominar, recibir o pagar RMB en sus transacciones comerciales con China, as como tambin es factible para entidades financieras tener posiciones en esa moneda. Sin embargo, ello debe efectuarse a travs de otros centros offshore, lo que dificulta su acceso y limita el desarrollo de un mercado RMB/CLP. La designacin de un Banco Compensatorio facilitar el desarrollo de este mercado directamente en Chile, aumentando las posibilidades para empresas chilenas financieras y no financieras. Por ltimo, en el futuro, la existencia de un Banco Compensatorio en Chile podra incentivar a las instituciones financieras locales a ofrecer productos denominados en RMB, como ha ocurrido en otros pases. Junto con la firma del MoU, el Banco Central de Chile y el Banco Central de la Repblica Popular China tambin suscribieron un Acuerdo Bilateral de Lnea Swap en RMB/CLP, la que permitir a ambas instituciones asegurar la disponibilidad de la moneda de la contraparte en su pas. La lnea acordada con el PBC es por un monto de RMB 22 mil millones o de CLP 2.200 miles de millones, y tiene una duracin de 3 aos, prorrogables. Existen ms de 30 pases cuyos bancos centrales han negociado lneas similares con el PBC en los ltimos 3 o 4 aos. Este acuerdo, que otorga un acceso cuantioso a RMB para el Banco Central de Chile, cumple con el objetivo de proveer confianza al mercado domstico que, en caso de existir alguna situacin de friccin financiera que trabe el normal financiamiento de los pagos externos, podr existir una facilidad de liquidez de ltima instancia a la que podrn acudir las instituciones financieras locales para que esos pagos no se interrumpan. Por cierto que esto complementa un conjunto de instrumentos ya disponibles por el Banco Central de Chile para enfrentar situacin de stress financiero internacional. Considerando el tamao de China, creemos que esta lnea es una contribucin relevante para la estabilidad financiera. Adicionalmente, las autoridades en China han otorgado a Chile una cuota inicial de RMB 50 billones (equivalentes aproximadamente a USD 8.000 millones) en su programa denominado "Renminbi Qualified Foreign Institutional Investor" (RQ.FII), que permite a Inversionistas Institucionales Extranjeros Calificados invertir directamente en el mercado de valores de ese pas. Este es un anuncio importante, tanto por su contenido como porque Chile es el primer pas en Amrica Latina que obtiene una cuota en ese programa. El acceso directo a los mercados financieros en China para inversionistas institucionales establecidos en Chile, como bancos, fondos de pensiones y compaas de seguros, fondos mutuos y fondos de inversin, entre otros, otorga un acceso ms expedito a un conjunto amplio de instrumentos financieros en RMB. Esto genera importantes beneficios en cuanto a reduccin de costos de transaccin en monedas y diversificacin, y aumenta las posibilidades para que el sistema financiero en Chile se convierta en una plataforma regional de inversin financiera en China. Para acceder a esta cuota, las instituciones financieras deben postular a cuotas individuales con las autoridades en China, accediendo luego a mercados de deuda y acciones en China usando RMB obtenidos en el mercado offshore. Cabe notar que el mercado de bonos de gobierno y corporativos en China es el tercero ms grande del mundo, y el mercado accionario el segundo ms grande, antecedentes que por s solos muestran las posibilidades que el mercado chino ofrece a inversionistas extranjeros. Quisiera finalizar recalcando que con estos acuerdos, el Banco Central de Chile est contribuyendo a sentar las bases para facilitar el uso del RMB en el comercio internacional y en inversiones financieras, y para el desarrollo de un mercado RMB/CLP. Valoramos la disposicin de las autoridades en China de potenciar fuertemente los vnculos financieros con la regin a travs de Chile. Habiendo dicho esto, es importante recalcar que ser finalmente la proactividad de las empresas financieras y no financieras lo que determinar el xito de este proceso. La profundizacin de las relaciones financieras con China, y el aprovechamiento de las oportunidades que se comienzan a abrir para las empresas chilenas, dependern de la iniciativa del sector privado. Confiamos en que los acuerdos suscritos sern una contribucin para que los agentes del sector privado puedan extraer en el mediano plazo los beneficios asociados a la internacionalizacin del RMB. Muchas gracias.

Title: The new normal in China and Latin America
text: The New Normal in China and Latin America1 Sebastian Claro Vice President, Central Bank of Chile September 22 , 2015 I sincerely appreciate the invitation to this seminar. For now, the Pontificia Universidad Cat97lica de Chile has been my home for several years, and it is always a pleasure to be here. On the other hand, the set of exhibitors gives a special highlight to this debate. I would especially like to highlight the presence of outstanding UCSD researchers who are with us today, such as Barry Naughton, from whom I personally have learned a lot from reading their research. Finally, the subject that brings us together is not only of utmost importance, but sometimes of extreme ignorance, so a meeting like this is very valuable. The focus of my presentation will be the impact on Latin America of the so-called "new normal" in China. After decades of very high growth, China is approaching growth rates around 6% by the end of this decade and a number closer to 5%. in 10 years, with a lower boost in investment and exports, and a greater role for domestic consumption. 2 This is a very relevant change, and certainly the news in recent months account for the difficulties of this convergence. The essence of my presentation is to share with you some ideas on why the new normal in China means a new normal for Latin America. To this end, I have chosen three aspects that I consider fundamental. China's dividend A first aspect I have called the "China dividend ", and it is born from the observation of the regional reality in the early 2000s that I have emphasized earlier. 3 In 2003, economists Carmen Reinhart, Ken Rogoff and Miguel Savastano published a paper entitled "Debt Intolerance"4, where they analyzed the levels of external debt.GDP.GDP). that could be considered safe or tolerable. In this paper, the critical level of debt depended on both fundamental economic variables and the historical payment behavior of countries of their financial commitments. The main conclusion was that tolerable debt levels were low, and that countries in the region had debt levels that brought them dangerously close to the abyss. The response to the Asian crisis had left debt levels in a dangerous area. 1 Speech prepared for the seminar "China and Latin America in the Asian Century", organized by the UC Center for Asian Studies and the University of California San Diego, held in Santiago de Chile, September 22, 2015. The comments do not necessarily represent the view of the board of the Central Bank of Chile. 2 See S. Claro, 2012, "Chinese economy, what comes forward?", Economics and Management UC 72:8.12, published based on the presentation at the V Chile-China Business Meeting, June 2011, in honor of Xi Jinping's visit to Chile. See also Fand, C., and I. Roberts, 2015, "Potential Growth and rebalancing in China", Bulletin Reserve Bank of Australia, June Quarter. 3 Ver discurso ante el UCLA Anderson Latin American Annual Conference 2010. 4 Reinhart, C., K. Rogoff y M. Savastano, 2003, "Debt Intolerance," Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, 34(1):1.74. Naturally, the debate on the macroeconomic implications of this situation was not long in coming. According to the authors: "For countries with intolerable debt, maintaining access to international financial markets becomes problematic unless debt go down quickly. To assess how this "deleveraging" can occur, we examine how, historically, emerging economies have managed to lower their high debt levels. We analyze episodes of large changes in external debt levels, falling more than 25 percentage points of GDP in three years. Of the 21 cases identified in the group of middle-income countries since 1970, nearly two-thirds of the cases had some form of default or restructuring. of debt. Only in one case d0 Swaziland in 1985 d0 was the country able to substantially lower external debt levels as a result of high growth." In the early 2000s, unless a miracle occurred, default seemed to be just around the corner for a number of countries in the world. the region. But miracles exist. And China was one of them. The strong boom in commodity prices since the middle of the last decade allowed countries in the region to run persistent current account surpluses in a relatively short time. Thus, China's strong expansion significantly eased external and fiscal accounts in Latin America. As an example, in 2002 Brazil's public debt exceeded 80% of GDP, and in 2007 it was almost 30 percentage points lower. In the past, this miracle would have been wasted, but this time countries had more robust macroeconomic policy frameworks, saving some of the windfall, prudently managing the capital flows that They inevitably reached the financial systems, and allowed the fluctuation of currencies, which had created so much trouble in the past. Thus, a combination of good luck and good policies explains the easing in the fiscal and external accounts in several countries of the region. Moreover, as Figure 1 shows, since the mid-2000s the countries of Latin America, as well as other emerging countries, have had growth rates much higher than those of the main developed economies, something not observed since Mid-1980s. Thus, the commodity super cycle not only relieved the heavy backpacks of debt but also contributed to a strong expansion of investment and activity. The "new normal" in China marks the end of the period of extraordinary commodity price booms, and thus raises the question of how prepared economies are of the region to face it. The region is facing strong investment adjustment and lower growth rates , and concerns naturally arise about how much of the growth in The last 10 years were due to structural reasons and what part can we explain as a result of the commodity boom. This question is fundamental because in the current context, an erroneous vision that greatly emphasizes cyclical aspects in the slowdown runs the risk of postponing productivity agendas that enhance the growth in the medium term, and instead can contribute to generating macroeconomic imbalances and stressing fiscal accounts. And I dare to anticipate that this time another China will not appear on the road. Trading Patterns A second aspect to highlight is related to the change in the productive structure that this phenomenon demands. China's penetration of world markets over the past 20 years has been overwhelming, especially in less skilled labor-intensive sectors, where China has natural comparative advantages that have also been enhanced by a policy of attracting foreign investment and capital subsidies for domestic enterprises that have contributed to further skew Chinese exports towards labour-intensive goods . 5 The strong competition of products imported from China to domestic industries has been the subject of analysis on multiple occasions. 6 Its impact has been heterogeneous. In developed countries, such as the United States, lower-skilled labor-intensive industries account for a smaller percentage of employment and manufacturing output. And even in cases where U.S. firms have faced direct competition from Chinese exporters, evidence shows that U.S. firms were able to "escape" the competition from China with increases in productivity, product quality, exports and movements towards more sophisticated goods. 7 In Latin America there is a higher percentage of companies whose production has a relevant degree of substitution with Chinese products, so the impact of Chinese imports has been older. This is especially clear in Central America and Mexico. The case of Chile is interesting, and somewhat different from the rest of the countries, since the process of trade opening and liberalization in Chile began in the mid-1970s, which meant that many industries where Chile did not It had comparative advantages diminished in relevance or simply disappeared during the 1980s. Thus, the commercial expansion in China since the mid-1990s generated an impact on a much smaller percentage of the domestic industry, and the availability of cheaper products was directly beneficial to consumers. Even so, the evidence shows that in those industries where there was a meeting of Chilean companies with Chinese competitors, the former were not able to react like their North American peers, but rather negatively affected employment and increased their probability of dying. 8 The conjecture behind this evidence is that the lower levels of productivity, human capital and innovation in an economy like Chile's hinder the process of upgrading or differentiation required to face the competition from cheaper and increasingly quality Chinese products. This discussion takes on utmost importance going forward, as the end of the commodity cycle induces, and demands, a movement of resources from natural resource sectors to 5 Claro, S., 2009, d2FDI Liberalization as a Source of Comparative Advantage in Chinad3, Review of Development Economics 13(4): 740.753. 6 See articles on Latin America and China in Integration and Trade No. 24, 2006. 7 A.B. Bernard, A., J.B. Jensen y P.K. Schott, 2006, d2Survival of the best fit: Exposure to low.wage countries and the (uneven) growth of U.S. manufacturing plantsd3, Journal of International Economics 68(1): 219d0237. 8 e7lvarez, R., y S. Claro, 2009, d2David Versus Goliath: The Impact of Chinese Competition on Developing Countriesd3, World Development 37(3):560d0571 Other sectors. In Chile, the last commodity cycle resulted in a very substantial increase in the share of mining investment in GDP in a context where non-mining investment had a declining trend over GDP (figure 2). Consistent with this, since the mid-2000s d0 with the exception of the year marked by the international financial crisis d0 the economies of the region had a strong real appreciation of their currencies. In Chile, this sharply raised unit labor costs in dollars, as shown in Figure 3, driving the movement of resources into mining. This phenomenon, which is associated with the concept of Dutch disease discussed in the literature,9 should be reversed in the coming years, boosting production and exports in industries. different from raw materials. The depreciation of currencies in the countries of the region effectively contributes to the fall in dollar costs , thus increasing their competitiveness. Two observations arise here on which I would like to elaborate briefly. On the one hand, this process requires employment mobility and investment reallocation, among others. These processes are slow and sometimes costly to achieve, and it is therefore key to establish adequate conditions to facilitate it and not hinder it. Especially in a context where competition from Chinese products in broad industrial sectors is increasingly intense, the flexibility of domestic industry to adapt, innovate and reinvent itself is crucial in light of the aforementioned evidence. On the other hand, the more traditional idea of industrialization is somehow obsolete with the advent of outsourcing as a method of production, and with the possibility of exporting technologies and services. The main rationale for why Dutch disease is a disease rests on the idea that tradable industries are hurt by the natural resource boom. They have economies of scale or higher productivity growth , while the expansion of service sectors d0 presumably with lower potential for productivity growth d0 would not be a source of growth. Evidence in Chile shows that the services sector has had strong momentum in recent years, not only in terms of its size d0 something to be expected given the growth of the country d0 but also for its strong growth in productivity. For example, average labour productivity in the trade and financial services sectors has risen more than twice as much as in the aggregate (see Figure 4), and similar evidence may be found in the construction and communications services sectors. The export of services and technology d0 either directly or through foreign direct investment flows d0 has been a distinctive pattern of growth in Chile in Chile . The last decade, and in my opinion gives an important window of possibilities forward, since the service sector is a niche without major competition from China and with a strong deficit in Latin America. 9 Corden, W. Thus, low productivity in the distribution and infrastructure sectors is a bottleneck for the development of the region. This phenomenon is not exclusive to emerging countries. El dividendo de China Un primer aspecto lo he denominado el dividendo de China, y nace de la observacin de la realidad regional a comienzos de los 2000s que he enfatizado con anterioridad.3 El ao 2003 los economistas Carmen Reinhart, Ken Rogoff y Miguel Savastano publicaron un trabajo titulado Debt Intolerance4, donde analizaban los niveles de deuda externaGDP que podan considerarse seguras o tolerables. Patrones Comerciales Un segundo aspecto a destacar dice relacin con el cambio en la estructura productiva que este fenmeno exige. Title: Some thoughts on exchange rate policy in China
text: Some reflections on exchange rate policy in China1 Sebasti87n ClaroVice President, Central Bank of ChileJune 10, 2016 I would like to begin by thanking the Monetary Club of the Finis Terrae University, which since 1992 has become one of the main spaces for debate on public policy and economics in Chile. On this occasion, we are interested in exchange and monetary management in China. The past year has seen a significant increase in exchange rate volatility in China, against a backdrop of deep financial reforms. If until a few years ago the news from China was almost exclusively focused on its impact on world markets for goods and raw materials, recent quarters show that China is already a major player in global financial markets. In this presentation, I would like to share with you some ideas to understand the phenomenon of financial openness in China, and to better monitor its monetary and exchange rate management. Given the short time, my plan is to focus on five points that I consider central to understanding the management of exchange rate and monetary policy. 1. China is in a process of economic slowdown after decades of double-digit growth. One of the questions that have arisen in this regard is to what extent this phenomenon reflects adverse cyclical conditions or whether it reflects a structural change in China's growth capacity. The comparison with other experiences in Asia is informative and the conclusion is simple: China is reaching levels of per capita income that, in the cases of Japan and South Korea several decades ago, were followed by significant and fairly rapid changes in their growth rates. 2 In these cases, within five years countries grew 3 to 4 percent less than their averages over the previous two decades. (See Figure 1) The fundamental explanation for this phenomenon, beyond the characteristics of each country, is the natural convergence as a result of the decline in the profitability of investment and the evidence that productivity improvements are slower as countries approach the frontier of knowledge and best practices. Is China different? The trajectory of savings and investment in China suggests it could be. As Table 1 shows, their high levels of savings and investment d0 much higher than those observed in Japan and Korea at similar levels of development d0 could suggest that the profitability of capital accumulation in China is still very high, which justifies the postponement of consumption and the maintenance of high savings rates. 1 Presentation at Club Monetario, Finis Terrae University, Hotel Ritz Carlton Santiago, June 10, 2016. 2 See Claro, S, 2012, Chinese Economy: What's Coming Forward?, Administration and Economics UC 72: 8.12. Evidence suggests rather that these high savings and investment rates in China reflect the problems facing the economy, rather than its strength. There is evidence that levels of return on investment are very low, and that discretion in the allocation of capital is becoming increasingly problematic. From the beginning of its transition, China decided on a gradual strategy that, among other things, promoted strong support for investment in state-owned enterprises. In this way, it avoided a significant collapse in the activity of companies with evident technological backwardness in a context of growing openness to foreign investment. The need to boost capital accumulation required a high rate of domestic savings, given limited access to external financing. Over time, the Chinese authorities favored a system of favoring domestic savings as a mechanism for financing investment, and not external savings that could lead to financial dependence. The promotion of domestic savings and the government's need to control the banking system, providing it with cheap financing and influencing the allocation of credit, quickly led China to converge to a scheme with increasing trade openness d0 whose most significant milestone is the entry into the WTO in 2001 d0 but with strong limitations on capital movements. Thus, the only instrument of mass savings in China was bank deposit at very low nominal rates. In this context, the fixed exchange rate policy implemented from the mid-1990s was key to consolidating a scheme that induced domestic savings and allowed banks to be financed generously. 2. There are many reasons to explain China's high savings rates. 3 The macroeconomic scheme that has relied on capital account control and the fixed/controlled exchange rate scheme designed by the Central Bank of China (PBoC) is one of them. To deepen on this we must recognize the validity of the Monetary Scheme to the Balance of Payments, developed by the philosopher and economist David Hume in the mid-eighteenth century, and widely applied to the case of China by Michael Mussa. 4 First, it is necessary to emphasize that the growth of the economy in China and the shift from an agricultural economy to a modern economy have produced an immense growth in the demand for money in China. In a closed capital account context, where there is no access to external financing, and with a fixed exchange rate, the only way for agents in China to obtain such funds is to save, and generate a trade surplus whose returns are settled in the Central Bank in exchange for RMB. Thus, part of the accumulation of reserves and the current account surplus reflects a permanent excess demand for money that induces savings. In a flexible exchange rate scheme, this pressure would result in an appreciation of the RMB, a fall in nominal income, and the disappearance of the monetary imbalance. 3 Ver, por ejemplo, Modigliani, F. y Shi L., 2004, The Chinese Saving Puzzle and the Life.Cycle Hypothesis, Journal of Economic Literature 42(1):145.170. 4 Mussa, M, 2007, IMF Surveillance over Chinad5s Exchange Rate Policy, Peterson Institute for International Economics. But it is difficult to think that the massive accumulation of reserves by the PBoC, which in 2014 reached almost 4 trillion dollars (see figure 2), responds exclusively to an unsatisfied demand for money. The current account surplus has also been due to other considerations that are not related to a monetary imbalance, and the inflows of "autonomous" capital, derived for example from the access of foreign capital in the form of Foreign Direct Investment have generated a significant increase in the availability of foreign currency in China. 5 In this case, with a fixed exchange rate and a closed capital account, there is a mechanism of self-correction of imbalances, where through changes in relative prices massive movements of capital are contained and changes in savings rates are induced. The intuition is simple: the pressure on the accumulation of reserves to defend parity in response to capital inflows or excessive saving generates monetary expansion that causes downward pressure on interest rates, higher nominal spending, and upward pressure on inflation that contributes to appreciating the real exchange rate. These mechanisms increase domestic spending and reduce incentives for capital inflows, gradually correcting the original imbalances. Authorities in China have helped block these automatic adjustment mechanisms. From the early part of the 2000s, when current account surpluses and capital inflows manifested themselves strongly, the PBoC developed an active sterilization policy, both with the issuance of bonds but especially through a very substantial increase in reserve requirements for banking institutions, as shown in Figure 3. 6 This sterilization, in a context of massive control of state banks and financial repression, made it possible to finance the accumulation of reserves without massive monetary issuance, thus maintaining strong incentives for savings and a surplus current account. 3. Thus, the control of capital flows and the management of monetary and exchange rate policy have been functional to the objectives of promoting high levels of savings in China. However, beyond the obvious success of China's transformation process, the benefits of these policies have been diminishing over time. The reasons are several. On the one hand, the passage of time became clear that investment flows did not necessarily finance profitable projects, so bank liabilities began to lose value. On the other hand, the control of the financial system, required to manage financing flows according to criteria different from the traditional ones of profitability/risk, induced, little by little d0 and especially after the global financial crisis of 2008/2009 d0 the appearance of non-bank financial intermediaries that have dismantled the initial scheme based on state banks without competition in raising resources. Added to this are the rising costs for banks of sterilization in a scheme with almost zero depth in bond and equity markets. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the strong accumulation of reserves in the context described above has meant a sacrifice in terms of consumption that is increasingly costly. This is especially clear in a context of lower growth rates and higher income levels that demand higher levels of consumption from the population. 5 Ver Hatzvi, E., J. Meredith y W. Nixon, 2015, Chinese Capital Flows and Capital Account Liberalisation, RBA Bulletin, December. 6 Bank of China (Hong Kong), 2015, Comparison of China and USd5 Bank Reserves and Their Implications, Economic Review, February. This evaluation has led to a slow transition in terms of modifying some aspects of the macro-financial scheme. For now, as shown in Figure 4, already from 2006 the PBoC gradually allowed a sustained appreciation of RMB against the dollar, partly accommodating massive capital inflows and easing current account pressures. The crisis of 2008/2009 produced a parenthesis in this regard, but the underlying picture since 2007 can be described as one where China favored the gradual appreciation of its currency. Even so, reserve accumulation continued strongly. It was from 2011, and clearly since 2013 with the arrival of the current administration led by Xi Jinping, when China began to show signs of a more substantive transformation of some aspects of its exchange and financial management. There are many reform projects in this area. In others, they include: (i) the liberalization of interest rates, which have allowed the banking system to accommodate the competition of the shadow financial system, (ii) greater flexibility in the determination of the exchange rate, and (iii) efforts to promote financial openness d0 both for income and capital outflows. 7 These efforts were accompanied by a substantive plan for labor market reforms, local government financing, and reforms of state-owned enterprises. While progress in the latter areas has been slow, some of the reforms in the financial system have been implemented more quickly. For example, interest rates were liberalized, there has been greater openness to cross-border portfolio flows, progress has been made in facilitating the convertibility of the RMB and its use in international payments, and a scheme of greater floating of the RMB was deepened. Thus, even though the accumulation of reserves continued until the beginning of 2014, its rate of expansion was clearly lower than that observed until 2011, showing that some of the mechanisms that in the past had deepened current account surpluses and capital inflows were relaxed. For example, after peaking in late 2011, bank reserve requirements have fallen steadily (see Figure 5), while the ease of holding deposits abroad for Chinese firms eased balance-of-payments pressure. Certainly, many other phenomena also explain the change in trend in foreign exchange inflows since 2012, but it is clear that the effort to make the exchange market more flexible and allow greater capital flows establishes a new paradigm on the management of exchange rate policy in China. 7 Prasad, E, 2016, Chinad5s Economy and Financial Markets: Reforms and Risks, Hearings before the US.China Economics and Security Review Commission. 4. The difficulties we have seen in recent quarters begin when the market view of the growth prospects in China and how attractive assets are in that country changes. The slowdown in activity and the hidden costs of the tremendous stimulus package to deal with the 2008-09 crisis, as well as weak external demand, led to a shift in the valuation of assets in China, particularly the RMB, in mid-2013 and prompted massive capital outflows. By the way, this phenomenon was not exclusive to China, but common to many developing countries. (See Figures 6 and 7) In the old scheme, with strong capital controls and fixed exchange rates, this phenomenon would have resulted in a limited loss of international reserves and a lower current account surplus. However, and in full transition to a new macro-financial scheme, the pressure on reserves may be much greater given the space for capital outflows, both through regular channels and the traditional mechanisms of over-invoicing of imports, for example. In turn, signals of greater exchange rate flexibility gave the PBoC the possibility of accommodating capital outflows with a depreciation of the RMB. However, the authorities have favored a gradual adjustment in the value of the RMB, a massive sale of international reserves, as can be seen in Figure 8, and some hesitant measures about the ease of regular mechanisms for international capital movements. Rather than calming the doubts of the markets, the sharp fall in international reserves (although they are partly explained by the global appreciation of the dollar), doubts about exchange rate management and expectations of a greater adjustment have deepened doubts about the situation in China in recent quarters, feeding back capital outflows. 8 Indeed, there is widespread debate about the depth of this problem. For some authors, the pressure of capital flows exists, but it does not represent an imminent threat to the balance of payments in China. 9 5. However, China has already taken substantial and partly irreversible steps towards a more flexible exchange rate scheme and an open capital account, with more room for capital movements. I would like to conclude with two very brief reflections on the implications of this process. On the one hand, just as the rest of the world has an unmet demand for Chinese assets d0 beyond conjunctural considerations d0 the Chinese also have an unmet demand for assets in the rest of the world. The space for diversifying investments is very broad, and they have ample benefits. 8 For example, there is evidence that Chinese exporting and importing companies have an active management of their balance sheets based on their expectations about the evolution of the RMB (Hatzvi, E., J. Meredith and W. Nixon, 2015, Chinese Capital Flows and Capital Account Liberalisation, RBA Bulletin, December.) See also Eichengreen, B., 2016, China's Exchange Rate Trap, Project Syndicate, Feb 9. 9 Lardy, N., 2016, Renmimbi Series Part 4: The Outlook for the Renmimbi, China Economic Watch, Peterson Institute for International Economics. A second aspect is that the opening of the capital account and the flexible exchange rate inevitably give greater room for volatility of flows and asset prices. Developed countries and many emerging countries are direct witnesses to these movements. China is not used to this volatility, and the rest of the world is not used to this news from China either. It's time to get used to it. Thank you.
text_original: Algunas reflexiones sobre poltica cambiaria en China1 Sebastin Claro Vicepresidente, Banco Central de Chile 10 de Junio, 2016 Quisiera partir agradeciendo la invitacin al Club Monetario de la Universidad Finis Terrae, que desde 1992 se ha convertido en uno de los principales espacios de debate sobre poltica pblicas y economa en Chile. En esta oportunidad, nos rene el inters el manejo cambiario y monetario en China. En el ltimo ao hemos sido testigos de un significativo aumento en la volatilidad cambiaria en China, en un contexto de profundas reformas financieras. Si hasta hace pocos aos las noticias de China estaban casi exclusivamente centradas en su impacto sobre mercados mundiales de bienes y de materias primas, los ltimos trimestres dan cuenta que China es ya un jugador importante en los mercados financieros mundiales. En esta presentacin quisiera compartir con ustedes algunas ideas para entender el fenmeno de apertura financiera en China, y para lograr un mejor seguimiento de su manejo monetario y cambiario. Dado el breve tiempo, mi plan es enfocarme en cinco puntos que considero centrales para entender el manejo de la poltica cambiaria y monetaria.  China se encuentra en un proceso de desaceleracin econmica despus de dcadas de crecimiento a dos dgitos. Una de las preguntas que han surgido en este sentido es en qu medida este fenmeno refleja condiciones cclicas adversas o si ms bien es reflejo de un cambio estructural en la capacidad de crecimiento en China. La comparacin con otras experiencias en Asia es informativa y la conclusin es simple: China est alcanzando niveles de ingreso per cpita que, en los casos de Japn y Corea del Sur hace varias dcadas, fueron seguidos por cambios significativos y bastante rpidos en sus tasas de crecimiento.2 En estos casos, en un plazo de cinco aos los pases pasaron a crecer entre 3 o 4 por ciento menos que sus promedios en las dos dcadas anteriores. (Ver figura 1) La explicacin fundamental para este fenmeno, ms all de las caractersticas propias de cada pas, es la natural convergencia como consecuencia del decaimiento en la rentabilidad de la inversin y de la evidencia que las mejoras en productividad son ms lentas a medida que los pases se acercan a la frontera del conocimiento y de las mejores prcticas. Es China diferente? La trayectoria del ahorro y la inversin en China sugieren que podra serlo. Como muestra la tabla 1, sus altos niveles de ahorro e inversin  muy superiores a los observados en Japn y Corea en niveles similares de desarrollo  podran sugerir que la rentabilidad a la acumulacin de capital en China es todava muy alta, lo que justifica la postergacin de consumo y la mantencin de altas tasas de ahorro. 1 Presentacin en Club Monetario, Universidad Finis Terrae, Hotel Ritz Carlton Santiago, Junio 10, 2016. 2 Ver Claro, S, 2012, Economa China: qu viene hacia adelante?, Administracin y Economa UC 72: 812. La evidencia sugiere ms bien que estas altas tasas de ahorro e inversin en China son reflejo de los problemas que enfrenta la economa, ms que de su fortaleza. Existe evidencia que los niveles de retorno a la inversin son muy bajos, y que la discrecionalidad en la asignacin del capital est siendo crecientemente problemtica. Desde el comienzo de su transicin, China decidi una estrategia gradual que, entre otras cosas, promova un fuerte soporte a la inversin en empresas estatales. De esta manera, evitaba un colapso significativo en la actividad de empresas con evidente atraso tecnolgico en un contexto de creciente apertura a la inversin extranjera. La necesidad de potenciar la acumulacin de capital exigi una alta tasa de ahorro domstico, dado el limitado acceso a financiamiento externo. Con el paso del tiempo, las autoridades chinas privilegiaron un sistema de favoreci el ahorro interno como mecanismo de financiamiento de la inversin, y no el ahorro externo que podra acarrear dependencia financiera. La promocin del ahorro interno y la necesidad por parte del gobierno de controlar al sistema bancario, proveyndolo de financiamiento barato e influyendo en la asignacin del crdito, hizo que China convergiera rpidamente a un esquema con una creciente apertura comercial  cuyo hito ms significativo es la entrada a la OMC el 2001 , pero con fuertes limitaciones a los movimientos de capital. As, el nico instrumento de ahorro masivo en China era el depsito bancario a tasas nominales muy bajas. En este contexto, la poltica de tipo de cambio fijo implementada a partir de mediados de los 1990s fue clave para consolidar un esquema que induca al ahorro interno y permita financiar a los bancos de manera generosa.  Existen muchas razones para explicar las altas tasas de ahorro en China.3 El esquema macroeconmico que ha descansado en el control de la cuenta de capitales y en el esquema cambiario fijo/controlado diseado por parte del Banco Central de China (PBoC) es uno de ellos. Para profundizar sobre esto debemos reconocer la vigencia del Esquema Monetario a la Balanza de Pagos, desarrollado por el filsofo y economista David Hume a mediados del siglo XVIII, y aplicado ampliamente al caso de China por Michael Mussa.4 Primero, es necesario destacar que el crecimiento de la economa en China y el paso de una economa agrcola a una economa moderna han producido un inmenso crecimiento en la demanda por dinero en China. En un contexto de cuenta de capitales cerrado, donde no existe acceso a financiamiento externo, y con tipo de cambio fijo, la nica manera para los agentes en China de conseguir tales fondos es ahorrando, y generando un supervit comercial cuyos retornos son liquidados en el Banco Central a cambio de RMB. As, parte de la acumulacin de reservas y del supervit de la cuenta corriente refleja un permanente exceso de demanda por dinero que induce al ahorro. En un esquema cambiario flexible, esta presin repercutira en una apreciacin del RMB, una cada en el ingreso nominal y en la desaparicin del desequilibrio monetario. 3 Ver, por ejemplo, Modigliani, F. y Shi L., 2004, The Chinese Saving Puzzle and the LifeCycle Hypothesis, Journal of Economic Literature 42(1):145170. 4 Mussa, M, 2007, IMF Surveillance over Chinas Exchange Rate Policy, Peterson Institute for International Economics. Pero es difcil pensar que la masiva acumulacin de reservas por parte del PBoC, que en 2014 alcanz casi 4 trillones de dlares (ver figura 2), responda exclusivamente a una demanda por dinero insatisfecha. El supervit de la cuenta corriente tambin ha obedecido a otras consideraciones que no dicen relacin con un desequilibrio monetario, y los ingresos de capitales autnomos, derivados por ejemplo del acceso de capitales extranjeros en la forma de Inversin Extranjera Directa han generado un aumento importante en la disponibilidad de divisas en China.5 En este caso, con tipo de cambio fijo y cuenta de capitales cerrada, existe un mecanismo de autocorreccin de desequilibrios, donde a travs de cambios en precios relativos se contienen movimientos masivos de capital y se inducen cambios en las tasas de ahorro. La intuicin es simple: la presin a la acumulacin de reservas para defender la paridad en respuesta a una entrada de capitales o a un ahorro excesivo genera una expansin monetaria que provoca una presin bajista en las tasas de inters, un mayor gasto nominal y una presin al alza en la inflacin que contribuye a apreciar el tipo de cambio real. Estos mecanismos aumentan el gasto interno y disminuyen los incentivos a la entrada de capitales, corrigiendo gradualmente los desequilibrios originales. Las autoridades en China han contribuido a bloquear estos mecanismos de ajuste automtico. Desde la primera parte de los 2000s, cuando los supervits en la cuenta corriente y las entradas de capital se manifestaron con fuerza, el PBoC desarroll una poltica activa de esterilizacin, tanto con la emisin de bonos pero especialmente a travs de un incremento muy sustantivo en los requerimientos de reservas a las instituciones bancarias, como se observa en la figura 3.6 Esta esterilizacin, en un contexto de control masivo de la banca estatal y de represin financiera, permiti financiar la acumulacin de reservas sin una masiva emisin monetaria, manteniendo as fuertes incentivos al ahorro y a una cuenta corriente superavitaria.  As, el control a los flujos de capital y el manejo de la poltica monetaria y cambiaria han sido funcionales a los objetivos de promover altos niveles de ahorro en China. Sin embargo, ms all del evidente xito que ha tenido el proceso de transformacin de China, los beneficios de estas polticas han ido disminuyendo en el tiempo. Las razones son varias. Por un parte, el paso del tiempo fue dejando claro que los flujos de inversin no necesariamente financiaban proyectos rentables, con lo que los pasivos bancarios comenzaron a perder valor. Por otro lado el control del sistema financiero, requerido para manejar los flujos de financiamiento de acuerdo a criterios diferentes a los tradicionales de rentabilidad/riesgo indujo, poco a poco,  y especialmente despus de la crisis financiera global de 2008/2009  la aparicin de intermediarios financieros no bancarios que han desarticulado el esquema inicial basado en bancos estatales sin competencia en la captacin de recursos. A esto se suman los crecientes costos para los bancos de la esterilizacin en un esquema con casi nula profundidad en mercados de bonos y acciones. Por ltimo, y quiz ms importante, la fuerte acumulacin de reservas en el contexto antes descrito ha significado un 5 Ver Hatzvi, E., J. Meredith y W. Nixon, 2015, Chinese Capital Flows and Capital Account Liberalisation, RBA Bulletin, December. 6 Bank of China (Hong Kong), 2015, Comparison of China and US Bank Reserves and Their Implications, Economic Review, February. sacrificio en trminos de consumo que resulta crecientemente costoso. Esto es especialmente claro en un contexto de menores tasas de crecimiento y niveles de ingreso ms alto que demandan de la poblacin niveles de consumo mayores. Esta evaluacin ha llevado a una transicin pausada en cuanto a modificar algunos aspectos del esquema macro financiero. Por de pronto, como se observa en la figura 4, ya a partir de 2006 el PBoC permiti gradualmente una apreciacin sostenida de RMB respecto del dlar, acomodando en parte las masivas entradas de capital y aliviando las presiones sobre la cuenta corriente. La crisis de 2008/2009 produjo un parntesis en este sentido, pero el panorama de fondo desde 2007 puede ser descrito como uno donde China favoreci la apreciacin gradual de su moneda. Aun as, la acumulacin de reservas continu fuertemente. Fue a partir del 2011, y con claridad desde 2013 con la llegada de la actual administracin liderada por Xi Jinping, cuando China comenz a dar seales de una transformacin ms sustantiva de algunos aspectos de su manejo cambiario y financiero. Los proyectos de reformas en este mbito son mltiples. En otros, destacan: (i) la liberalizacin de las tasas de inters, que han permitido al sistema bancario acomodarse a la competencia del sistema financiero en las sombras, (ii) una mayor flexibilidad en la determinacin del tipo de cambio, y (iii) los esfuerzos por promover la apertura financiera  tanto para ingresos como para salidas de capital.7 Estos esfuerzos vinieron acompaados de una plan sustantivo de reformas en los mercados laborales, en el financiamiento de gobiernos locales, y de reformas a empresas estatales. Mientras el avance en estos ltimos aspectos ha sido lento, algunas de las reformas en el sistema financiero se han implemento con mayor rapidez. Por ejemplo, se liberalizaron las tasas de inters, ha existido mayor apertura a los flujos transfronterizos de portafolio, se ha avanzado en facilitar la convertibilidad del RMB y su uso en pagos internacionales, y se profundiz un esquema de mayor flotacin del RMB. As, aun cuando la acumulacin de reservas continu hasta comienzos de 2014, su tasa de expansin fue claramente menor que la observada hasta 2011, dando cuenta que algunos de los mecanismos que en el pasado haban profundizado los supervit de la cuenta corriente y la entrada de capitales fueron relajados. Por ejemplo, despus de alcanzar su mximo a fines del 2011, los requerimientos de reservas bancarias han cado sostenidamente (ver figura 5), mientras que la facilidad para mantener depsitos en el exterior para las empresas chinas disminuy la presin sobre la balanza de pagos. Por cierto que muchos otros fenmenos tambin explican el cambio de tendencia en las entradas de divisas a partir de 2012, pero resulta evidente que el esfuerzo para flexibilizar el mercado cambiario y permitir mayor flujos de capital establece un nuevo paradigma sobre el manejo de la poltica cambiaria en China. 7 Prasad, E, 2016, Chinas Economy and Financial Markets: Reforms and Risks, Hearings before the USChina Economics and Security Review Commission.  Las dificultades que hemos observado en los ltimos trimestres comienzan cuando cambia la visin de mercado sobre las perspectivas de crecimiento en China y sobre cun atractivo resultan los activos en ese pas. La desaceleracin de la actividad y los costos ocultos del tremendo paquete de estmulo para enfrentar la crisis de 200809, as como la debilidad de la demanda externa produjeron hacia mediados de 2013 un cambio en la valoracin de los activos en China, en particular el RMB, e impulsaron una salida masiva de capital. Por cierto este fenmeno no fue exclusivo a China, sino comn a muchos pases en desarrollo. (Ver figuras 6 y 7) En el esquema antiguo, con fuertes controles de capital y tipo de cambio fijo, este fenmeno se hubiese traducido en una prdida acotada de reservas internacionales y en un menor supervit de la cuenta corriente. Sin embargo, y en plena transicin hacia un nuevo esquema macro financiero, la presin sobre las reservas puede ser mucho mayor dado el espacio para las salidas de capital, tanto a travs de canales regulares como los tradicionales mecanismos de sobrefacturacin de importaciones, por ejemplo. A su vez, las seales de mayor flexibilidad cambiaria entregaban al PBoC la posibilidad de acomodar las salidas de capital con una depreciacin del RMB. Sin embargo, las autoridades han privilegiado un ajuste gradual en el valor del RMB, una masiva venta de reservas internacionales, como se puede observar en la figura 8, y algunas medidas dubitativas sobre la facilidad de los mecanismos regulares a los movimientos internacionales de capital. Ms que calmar las dudas de los mercados, la fuerte cada en reservas internacionales (aunque en parte se explican por la apreciacin global del dlar), las dudas sobre el manejo cambiario y las expectativas de un ajuste mayor han profundizado en los ltimos trimestres las dudas sobre la situacin en China, retroalimentando las salidas de capital.8 Por cierto que existe un amplio debate acerca de la profundidad de este problema. Para algunos autores, la presin de flujos de capitales existe, pero no representa una amenaza inminente a la balanza de pagos en China.9  Con todo, China ya ha realizado pasos sustantivos y en parte irreversibles hacia un esquema cambiario ms flexible y una cuenta de capitales abierta, con mayor espacio para los movimientos de capital. Quisiera terminar con dos reflexiones muy breves sobre las implicancias de este proceso. Por una parte, as como el resto del mundo tiene una demanda insatisfecha por activos chinos  ms all de las consideraciones coyunturales , los chinos tambin tienen una demanda insatisfecha por activos en el resto del mundo.
