Title: Financial Stability and the Role of the Central Bank
text: FINANCIAL STABILITY AND THE ROLE OF THE CENTRAL BANK Rodrigo Vergara* * Speech given on the occasion of the Launch of the Center for Regulation and Macrofinancial Stability of the Faculty of Economics and Business of the University of Chile, March 30, 2012, CasaPiedra. President Central Bank of Chile March 2011 I thank you for the invitation to participate in this event and congratulate the Faculty of Economics and Business of the University of Chile, and Guillermo Larra92n in particular, for the initiative to create this Center for Regulation and Macro-Institutional Stability. Its focus, financial stability, is undoubtedly a major issue. Events - both in recent years and so many others throughout history - have proved this. The contribution of the University in generating research in this area is very welcome by all of us who are faced with decision-making and policy design in this area. The concern for financial stability is at the origin of central banking, this having been the main motivation for the creation of the first central banks in Sweden and the United Kingdom. Both in these cases and in the creation of the Federal Reserve in the US at the beginning of the twentieth century, the main logic of these institutions was to provide a function of lender of last resort, which would allow to contain runs and the consequent banking crises that from time to time hit these economies. In the twentieth century, with the abandonment of the gold standard, monetary policy emerged as a key tool to stabilize economic activity. However, it could also generate inflation. This put the objective of macroeconomic stability in general, and price stability in particular, as one of paramount importance for central banks. Concerns about financial stability remained, but in many jurisdictions it lost the relevance that the development of financial systems demanded. The recent global financial crisis has restored interest in financial issues and has led to a greater presence of such considerations in the work of central banks. So far, the nature of monetary and financial stability policies is such that the former tends to have greater visibility than the latter. While monetary policy involves periodic action by the Central Bank that is widely commented on by the specialist public, financial stability policies are less visible. This, because some of them act by their mere presence as mechanisms that avoid crises, so hearing little about them is good news; Others, meanwhile, immediately involve a smaller circle, such as the issuance of regulations. In the Chilean case, the original institutional design installed the supervisory function in a superintendence independent of the Central Bank. Despite this, the issuing institute maintained and maintains a leading role in financial stability issues. In this sense, the LOC was a landmark in setting the BCCH a mandate that covers both price stability and the normal functioning of the payment system. I. Functions of the Central Bank in Financial Stability As I've mentioned so far, the role of lender of last resort is a key function of any central bank. This is a role that, similar to deposit insurance, acts more through its existence as a possibility than through its effective use. Indeed, the common knowledge of the members of the system of the existence of this facility avoids actions motivated by beliefs of liquidity problems in specific institutions. Secondly, the Central Bank regulates an important part of the actions of banks and cooperatives. In particular, the regulatory scope defined in Article 35 of its Constitutional Organic Law refers to the collection of deposits from the public, especially sight deposits. It also regulates financial intermediation and sets limits on the ratio of assets to liabilities of the aforementioned institutions. It authorizes readjustment systems for credit operations and dictates rules for companies that issue and operate credit cards. Finally, it determines the reserve that deposit-taking entities must constitute. Third, the Bank administers the real-time interbank payment system, and must authorize the regulations to which payment and securities clearing systems must be subject. The legislator has also entrusted the Central Bank with other functions in the financial field, such as establishing, within the limits defined by law, parameters for portfolio investment by pension funds. Similarly, it regulates the investments of the unemployment fund and establishes the limits of investment abroad for Insurance Companies. The Banking Law establishes that the Central Bank must regulate housing financing mechanisms d0 including the so-called "mortgage bonds" d0 and pay the demand deposits in case of liquidation of an entity. II. Recent developments and current challenges Within this framework, the Central Bank has been adapting the way it implements its mandate to the changing reality of the financial environment. These changes have been particularly intense in recent decades. The developed world embarked on a wave of financial deregulation, particularly in the last decade of the twentieth century. Some symbolic milestones are the policy known as the "Big Bang" or liberalizing regulatory reform in the United Kingdom in the mid-2s eighties, and the abolition of the Glass-Steagall law in the US in 1999. This law prevented the same institution from carrying out commercial and investment banking operations. Its abolition expanded the range of operations of banks and allowed mergers that gave rise to large institutions. This implied strong changes in the financial landscape, which were characterized by a trend towards a greater volume of financial operations, greater complexity in contracts and products, an expansion in the range of operations of certain intermediaries, greater concentration, and greater international financial connections. Although there was no equivalent deregulation in Chile, the financial system did experience strong and sustained growth. This is due to several factors, such as the greater internationalization of banking, and the growth of institutional investors, in particular Pension Funds and Life Insurance Companies. At the international level, the change in the environment generated new visions of how central banks should perform their functions in this area. One vision that was installed is that it seems that the solidity of the system can no longer be guaranteed by the solidity of institutions considered individually. Intermediaries are increasingly exposed to common shocks either through direct links between them or through participation in the markets themselves. As a reaction to this new reality, in the late nineties some central banks began to publish systemic risk analyses through financial stability reports. These are motivated by the recognition of the importance of system aggregate analysis to monitor the occurrence of risks. Chile's Central Bank adopted this vision early, publishing its first Financial Stability Report in 2004. These reports analyze the system as a whole and warn of possible imbalances and vulnerabilities of agents and intermediaries to these imbalances. Another consequence of a deeper and more complex financial system was initiatives to strengthen payment systems. In 2004, the Central Bank launched the real-time interbank gross settlement system and the regulatory framework for the operation of high-value clearing houses. The financial crisis that began to manifest itself in August 2007 and peaked in September 2008 was a challenge for governments, regulators and central banks around the world, particularly in the developed world. In the major economies, decisions had to be taken in very short terms of intervention and rescue of institutions that involved huge budgetary commitments. Institutions such as 3 the Bank of England had to de facto resume a role of banking supervision that they had abandoned about ten years ago. Our financial system was not fundamentally affected by the recent international crisis. However, the uncertainty generated at the most acute moment of it did affect liquidity in both foreign and domestic currencies. Given this, and acting based on its mandate to preserve the stability of internal and external payments, the Central Bank implemented policy measures to address this situation. The financial crisis undoubtedly intensified the importance of financial stability issues on the agenda of regulators, supervisors and central banks. One lesson has been the need to strengthen regulatory and supervisory frameworks. In Chile, an important step has been the recent creation of the Financial Stability Board. This forum allows to give a greater formality to the transmission of risk visions and to the cooperation in the analysis in a system that increases its complexity. This Committee will allow a fluid coordination between those who are in charge of supervising the most important sections of the Chilean financial system. On the other hand, the international financial crisis revealed the risks of a financial system where, as a result of the growing complexity and interconnection, a set of financial entities that are systemically relevant appear. For this reason, regulatory initiatives have emerged that seek to strengthen financial institutions, especially systemic ones. It is in this context that the Central Bank has important challenges and tasks for the near future. One of them is to improve the coordination mechanisms that have been established with the various superintendencies so that regulations and supervision acquire the comprehensive approach they require. The efforts made to establish good regulation for the clearing and payments of financial securities, for example, mark the path in which we must persevere forward. Another task of the first order for our country is to gradually advance in the adoption of international standards of banking regulation - specifically, the recommendations of the Basel Committee on both capital and liquidity requirements. Chilean banking regulations have been central to ensuring the normal functioning of the Chilean financial system in recent decades. In fact, the level and quality of banking capital in Chile should facilitate the adoption of such standards. It is also worth remembering that some of the elements that have been incorporated in Basel III have always been present in Chilean regulation, such as leverage requirements and the possibility of differentiating capital requirements in the face of bank mergers. However, the external and internal events of recent years, the increasing sophistication and international integration of the Chilean financial system and the 4 A conviction to maintain a degree of consistency with international standards makes it prudent for the regulations to be brought into line with the recommendations emanating from the Basel Committee. I reiterate my congratulations to the Faculty of Economics and Business of the University of Chile for this initiative. Much water has passed under the bridge of financial development since the creation of the first central banks. Today, the complexity of financial stability determines that it is a responsibility shared by different institutions. I am confident that the research of this new Centre will help all of us with responsibilities for financial stability to better understand the issue and make policy decisions towards this goal. Thanks a lot.
text_original: ESTABILIDAD FINANCIERA Y ROL DEL BANCO CENTRAL Rodrigo Vergara Presidente Banco Central de Chile Marzo 2011 Agradezco la invitacin a participar de este evento y felicito a la Facultad de Economa y Negocios de la Universidad de Chile, y a Guillermo Larran en particular, por la iniciativa de crear este Centro de Regulacin y Estabilidad Macrofmanciera. Su foco, la estabilidad financiera, es sin duda un tema de primer orden de importancia. Los eventos - tanto de los ltimos aos como tantos otros a lo largo de la historia - as lo han demostrado. El aporte de la Universidad en generar investigacin en esta rea es muy bienvenido por todos quienes nos vemos enfrentados a la toma de decisiones y al diseo de polticas en este mbito. La preocupacin por la estabilidad financiera est en el origen de la banca central, habiendo sido esta la motivacin principal de la creacin de los primeros bancos centrales en Suecia y en el Reino Unido. Tanto en estos casos como en la creacin de la Reserva Federal en EE.UU. a comienzos del siglo XX, la principal lgica de estas instituciones era la de proveer de una funcin de prestamista de ltima instancia, que permitiera contener corridas y las consecuentes crisis bancarias que cada cierto tiempo azotaban a esas economas. En el siglo XX, con el abandono del patrn oro, la poltica monetaria surge como una herramienta clave para estabilizar la actividad econmica. Sin embargo, tambin poda generar inflacin. Esto puso al objetivo de estabilidad macroeconmica en general, y de precios en particular, como uno de importancia capital para los bancos centrales. La preocupacin por la estabilidad financiera se mantuvo, pero en muchas jurisdicciones perdi la relevancia que el desarrollo de los sistemas financieros exiga. La reciente crisis financiera global ha restablecido el inters por los temas financieros y ha llevado a una mayor presencia de consideraciones de esta ndole en el quehacer de los bancos centrales. Hasta ahora la naturaleza de las polticas monetaria y de estabilidad financiera es tal que la primera suele tener mayor visibilidad que la segunda. Mientras que la poltica monetaria conlleva una accin peridica del Banco Central que es ampliamente comentada por el pblico especialista, las polticas de estabilidad financiera son menos visibles. Esto, debido a que algunas de ellas actan por su sola presencia como mecanismos que evitan crisis, por lo que escuchar poco de ellas es una buena noticia; otras, en tanto, involucran en lo inmediato a un crculo ms pequeo, como la emisin de normativa. En el caso chileno, el diseo institucional originario instal la funcin de supervisin en una superintendencia independiente del Banco Central. No obstante esto, el instituto emisor mantuvo y mantiene un rol de primer orden en temas de estabilidad financiera. En ese sentido, la LOC fue seera al fijarle al BCCH un mandato que cubre tanto la estabilidad de precios como el normal funcionamiento del sistema de pagos. I. Funciones del Banco Central en Estabilidad Financiera Como he mencionado hasta ahora, el rol de prestamista de ltima instancia es una funcin clave de cualquier banco central. Este es un rol que, de manera similar a los seguros de depsito, acta ms a travs de su existencia como posibilidad que a travs de su uso efectivo. En efecto, el conocimiento comn de los miembros del sistema de la existencia de esta facilidad evita acciones motivadas por creencias de problemas de liquidez en instituciones especficas. En segundo lugar, el Banco Central regula una parte importante del accionar de bancos y cooperativas. En particular, el mbito regulatorio definido en el artculo 35 de su Ley Orgnica Constitucional se refiere a la captacin de depsitos del pblico, en especial los depsitos vista. Tambin regula la intermediacin financiera y establece lmites a la relacin entre activos y pasivos de las instituciones mencionadas. Autoriza sistemas de reajustes para operaciones de crdito y dicta normas para las empresas que emiten y operan tarjetas de crdito. Finalmente, determina el encaje que deben constituir las entidades captadoras de depsitos. En tercer lugar, el Banco administra el sistema de pagos interbancarios en tiempo real, y debe autorizar los reglamentos a los que deben sujetarse los sistemas de pago y compensacin de valores. Asimismo, el legislador ha confiado al Banco Central otras funciones en el mbito financiero, como la de fijar, dentro de lmites definidos por la ley, parmetros para la inversin de cartera de los fondos de pensiones. De manera similar, reglamenta las inversiones del fondo de cesanta y establece los lmites de inversin en el exterior para las Compaas de Seguros. La Ley de Bancos establece que el Banco Central debe reglamentar los mecanismos de financiamiento de vivienda -incluyendo los denominados bonos hipotecarios -, y pagar los depsitos vista en caso de liquidacin de una entidad. II. Evolucin reciente y desafos actuales Dentro de este marco, el Banco Central ha ido adaptando el modo de implementar su mandato a la realidad cambiante del entorno financiero. Estos cambios han sido particularmente intensos en las ltimas dcadas. El mundo desarrollado se embarc en una ola de desregulacin financiera, en particular en la ltima dcada del siglo XX. Algunos hitos simblicos son la poltica conocida como Big Bang o reforma regulatoria liberalizadora en el Reino Unido a mediados de los aos 2 ochenta, y la abolicin de la ley Glass-Steagall en EE.UU. en 1999. Esta ley impeda que una misma institucin pudiese realizar operaciones de banca comercial y de inversin. Su abolicin ampli el rango de operaciones de los bancos y permiti fusiones que dieron origen a instituciones de gran tamao. Esto implic fuertes cambios en el paisaje financiero, que se caracterizaron por una tendencia hacia un mayor volumen de operaciones financieras, una mayor complejidad en los contratos y productos, una ampliacin en el rango de operaciones de determinados intermediarios, mayor concentracin, y mayores conexiones financieras internacionales. Si bien en Chile no hubo una desregulacin equivalente, el sistema financiero s experiment un crecimiento fuerte y sostenido. Esto por diversos factores, como la mayor intemacionalizacin de la banca, y el crecimiento de inversionistas institucionales, en particular Fondos de Pensiones y Compaas de Seguros de Vida. A nivel internacional, el cambio en el entorno gener nuevas visiones de cmo los bancos centrales deban desempear sus funciones en este tema. Una visin que se instal, es que pareciera que la solidez del sistema ya no puede garantizarse por la solidez de instituciones consideradas individualmente. Los intermediarios estn cada vez ms expuestos a shocks comunes ya sea por vnculos directos entre ellos, como por participacin en los mismos mercados. Como reaccin a esta nueva realidad, a fines de los noventa algunos bancos centrales comenzaron a publicar anlisis de riesgos sistmicos a travs de informes de estabilidad financiera. Estos se motivan en el reconocimiento de la importancia del anlisis del agregado del sistema para monitorear la aparicin de riesgos. El Banco Central de Chile adopt tempranamente esta visin, publicando su primer Informe de Estabilidad Financiera en 2004. En estos informes se analiza el sistema en su conjunto y se advierte sobre posibles desequilibrios y vulnerabilidades de agentes e intermediarios ante estos desequilibrios. Otra consecuencia de un sistema financiero ms profundo y complejo, fueron las iniciativas de robustecimiento de los sistemas de pagos. El Banco Central puso en marcha en 2004 el sistema de liquidacin bruta de pagos interbancarios en tiempo real, y el marco reglamentario para la operacin de cmaras de compensacin de alto valor. La crisis financiera que comenz a manifestarse en agosto de 2007 y que llegara a su peak en septiembre de 2008, fue un desafo para gobiernos, reguladores y bancos centrales de todo el mundo, en particular del mundo desarrollado. En las principales economas se tuvieron que tomar en plazos muy cortos decisiones de intervencin y rescate de instituciones que involucraban compromisos presupuestarios enormes. Instituciones como 3 el Banco de Inglaterra tuvieron que retomar de facto un rol de supervisin de la banca que haban abandonado haca unos diez aos. Nuestro sistema financiero no se vio afectado en lo fundamental por la crisis internacional reciente. No obstante, la incertidumbre generada en el momento ms agudo de ella s afect la liquidez tanto en moneda extranjera como en moneda domstica. Ante esto, y actuando en base a su mandato de preservar la estabilidad de los pagos internos y externos, el Banco Central implemento medidas de poltica para enfrentar esta situacin. La crisis financiera, sin duda, intensific la importancia de los temas de estabilidad financiera en la agenda de reguladores, supervisores y bancos centrales. Una leccin ha sido la necesidad de fortalecer los marcos de regulacin y supervisin. En Chile un paso importante ha sido la reciente creacin del Consejo de Estabilidad Financiera. Este foro permite dar una mayor formalidad a la transmisin de visiones de riesgo y a la cooperacin en el anlisis en un sistema que aumenta su complejidad. Este Comit permitir una coordinacin fluida entre quienes estn cargo de supervisar a las secciones ms importantes del sistema financiero chileno. Por otra parte, la crisis financiera internacional revel los riesgos de un sistema financiero donde, producto de la creciente complejidad e interconexin, aparecen un conjunto de entes financieros que son sistmicamente relevantes. Por ello han surgido iniciativas regulatorias que buscan robustecer a las instituciones financieras, en especial a las sistmicas. Es en este contexto el Banco Central tiene desafos y tareas importantes para el futuro prximo. Una de ellas es perfeccionar los mecanismos de coordinacin que se han establecido con las distintas superintendencias con el objeto de que las regulaciones y la supervisin adquieran el enfoque comprehensivo que requieren. Los esfuerzos desplegados para establecer una buena regulacin para la compensacin y pagos de los ttulos financieros, por ejemplo, marcan el camino en el que debemos perseverar hacia delante. Otra tarea de primer orden para nuestro pas es avanzar gradualmente en la adopcin de los estndares internacionales de regulacin bancaria - en concreto, las recomendaciones del Comit de Basilea tanto en requerimientos de capital como de liquidez. La normativa bancaria chilena ha sido central en asegurar el normal funcionamiento del sistema financiero chileno en las ltimas dcadas. De hecho, el nivel y la calidad del capital de la banca en Chile debiesen facilitar la adopcin de dichos estndares. Tambin vale la pena recordar que algunos de los elementos que se han incorporado en Basilea III siempre han estado presentes en la regulacin chilena, como por ejemplo los requerimientos de apalancamiento y la posibilidad de diferenciar requerimientos de capital ante fusiones bancarias. Sin embargo, los eventos externos e internos de los ltimos aos, la crecientemente sofisticacin e integracin internacional del sistema financiero chileno y la 4 convenciencia de mantener cierto grado de consistencia con los estndares internacionales, hace prudente que la normativa se ponga en lnea con las recomendaciones emanadas del Comit de Basilea. Reitero mis felicitaciones a la Facultad de Economa y Negocios de la Universidad de Chile por esta iniciativa. Mucha agua ha pasado bajo el puente del desarrollo financiero desde la creacin de los primeros bancos centrales. Hoy, la complejidad de la estabilidad financiera determina que es una responsabilidad compartida por distintas instituciones. Estoy seguro de que las investigaciones de este nuevo Centro nos ayudarn a todos los que tenemos responsabilidades en la estabilidad financiera a entender mejor el tema y a tomar decisiones de poltica en pos de este objetivo. Muchas gracias.

Title: The 14th General Review of Quotas and the Relationship of the Central Bank of Chile with the Monetary Fund...
text: Logo only L A 14bb R EVISION G ENERAL DE C UOTAS Y LA RELACIeeN DEL BANCO C ENTRAL DE CHILE CON EL FONDO MONETARIO INTERNACIONAL. Rodrigo Vergara President Central Bank of Chile April 11, 2012 .Presented to the special session of the Finance Committee of the Chamber of Deputies in order to initiate discussion of the bill authorizing the Central Bank of Chile to subscribe to an increase in Chile's quota in the International Monetary Fund (IMF) (Bulletin No. 8217-05). Mr Chairman of the Finance Committee of the Chamber of Deputies, Deputy Ernesto Silva, Members who are members of the Finance Committee, On behalf of the Council of the Central Bank of Chile (BCCh), I thank you for the invitation to this session of the Finance Committee, to give our vision on this bill that authorizes the BCCh to subscribe to the increase in the quota that corresponds to the Republic of Chile, within the framework of the 14th General Review of Quotas of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). I would like to take this opportunity to provide this Committee with background on the role of quotas in the governance and functioning of the IMF, as well as the international context in which this particular quota increase occurs. In addition, I will make a brief review of the different dimensions involved in the relationship of the Central Bank with the IMF, which go beyond the strictly financial relationship associated with the increase in quotas. According to its Articles of Agreement, to which Chile participated as one of the original 35 signatory countries at the Bretton Woods meeting in 1944, the IMF is an institution whose source of permanent financing is constituted by the quotas paid by the member countries. Currently, the total amount of quotas is 238 billion Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), equivalent to US371 billion, which are distributed among the different IMF member countries according to the size of their economy, their degree of openness, the variability of their foreign trade, and their level of international reserves. Thus, quotas fulfill a double role. On the one hand, the IMF's permanent lending capacity through its credit facilities is directly related to the volume of quotas, and each member's quota is the basic measure for accessing IMF resources in the event of balance of payments problems. On the other hand, quota largely determines each country's voting power in decisions made by IMF governors and boards. It should be noted that IMF quotas are regularly reviewed under General Quota Reviews. The most recent increases in IMF quotas were carried out in 1991 and 1999, both of which were submitted to the Congress of the Republic for approval under a procedure similar to the current one. Chile's current quota is 856.1 million SDRs (US1.33 billion), equivalent to a 0.359% share of the total. Our country has regularly learned about quotas in the IMF as a clear sign of our commitment to fulfilling our obligations as members of the international monetary system within the framework of a State policy. The 14th General Review of Quotas, approved by the IMF governors in 2010, takes place in a context in which the global economy has undergone important changes, which have implied a significant increase in the weight of emerging countries, with the corresponding decrease in industrialized economies. In addition, the scale of the external financing needs of IMF members, both emerging and some advanced, after the 2008 financial crisis increased significantly. It is in this context that IMF governors agreed, on the one hand, to double the total size of quotas to 476.8 billion SDRs, equivalent to US742 billion, and, on the other hand, to significantly increase the relative weight of emerging economies. This agreement seeks that the quota increase is materialized during 2012. The following figure shows how the entry into force of the 14th revision modifies the distribution of quotas, and therefore the voting power and eventual access to financing. OVERVIEW OF THE 14TH QUOTA REVIEW Source: International Monetary Fund In the case of Chile, the 14th revision allows its quota to increase to 1,744 million SDRs, equivalent to US2,712 million, for which parliamentary approval is required. Because quotas are part of the BCCh's international reserves, I will explain in greater detail below how this quota increase is constituted. The constitution of the quota increase in the IMF is materialized with 25% in foreign currency and 75% in local currency. Thus, of the total quota increase, the Central Bank will be responsible for paying approximately 222 million SDRs (US342 million) as a proportion in foreign currency, which implies a change in the composition of its international reserves. The remainder of the quota is constituted in local currency, through an accounting account in the assets and an equivalent account in the liabilities of the Bank. Therefore, if the bill under discussion is approved, once this quota increase is known, the level of international reserves will increase by about 666 million SDRs (US1,024 million). The financial return on the portion of international reserves represented by quotas is linked to the IMF-set SDR interest rate, which is an average of short-term interest rates on U.S., German, Japan, and British government bonds . As noted earlier, quota is not only a measure of capital contribution, but also the basic measure of Chile's access to IMF financing. Informing the increase in quotas will allow the country to have additional relevant external financing in cases of balance of payments crisis, equivalent to a multiple of the quota. For example, an access level of 600 percent of quotad1which corresponds to a standard access level for a stand-by facilityd1would be equivalent under the 14th revision to 10.464 billion SDRs (US16.224 billion), but only 5.137 billion SDRs (US7.963 billion) if the current quota is maintained . The increase in quotas is also associated with an increase in Chile's relative share of voting power in the IMF, from 0.359% to 0.366%. While this represents a marginal increase in total quotas, it constitutes a significant increase in Chile's relative voting power in the Southern Cone's jurisdiction over the IMF, where Chile participates alongside Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Peru, and Uruguay. The jurisdiction's agreement on the distribution of positions has allowed Chile to hold the position of Executive Director of the IMF in one biennium in each of the last decades, which is proportional to its relative quota. The Executive Board is composed of 24 directors and is chaired by the Managing Director. The Executive Director is responsible for conducting the day-to-day work of the IMF in terms of its administration and budget, financing, lending through existing instruments, reviewing lending instruments, and defining general policies for conducting IMF surveillance . Likewise, as part of this agreement, Chile has been responsible for representing the countries of the Southern Cone before the International Monetary and Financial Committee, which is the IMF's highest discussion body and is responsible for providing guidance to the work of the IMF every six months at the Annual Meetings and Spring Meetings of that Committee. which I will attend next week in Washington. My predecessor represented the Southern Cone Chair as Governor before the International Monetary and Financial Committee in 2010 and 2011, each time issuing a statement with Chile's position on the agenda of issues of each meeting. These statements are public knowledge and are published on the website of the Central Bank . Having already covered the financial relationship through quotas and its importance for our participation in the IMF, I would like to present below some additional dimensions involved in the Central Bank's relationship with the IMF. These include IMF surveillance of member economies and the provision of technical assistance. Under the IMF's Articles of Agreement, all members are subject to an annual review of their economic policies under the consultation process of Article IV of the Articles of Agreement. This involves the visit of an IMF mission, which meets with economic authorities and private sector counterparts, with the objective of preparing a report that is presented to the IMF Board for discussion. Subsequently, subject to the authorization of the Chilean economic authorities, this report is published by the IMF on its website, and is also disclosed on the institutional websites of the BCCh and the Ministry of Finance. In addition, the IMF and the World Bank conduct a joint assessment of member countries' financial system through the Financial System Assessment Program (FSAP ), which is conducted on a regular basis, and aims to assist governments, central banks, and supervisory authorities in understanding and improving financial systems. In the case of Chile, the first evaluation was carried out in 2004, and the second in 2011, in both cases, with broadly favorable results consistent with Chile's solid financial situation. The IMF also provides the possibility of reviewing compliance with international standards through its Program for the Review of Compliance with Standards and Codes (ROSCs), in which our country has participated in the Banking Supervision, Transparency of Monetary and Financial Policy, and Securities Regulation (2004); Money and Asset Laundering and Terrorist Financing (2005); Data Dissemination (2001, 2007) and Fiscal Transparency (2003 and 2005 ). The IMF has also provided a number of technical assistance missions on various issues of importance to the Central Bank as well as to the Government. These technical assistance missions are carried out at the request of the member country, and constitute an important source of support in terms of technical knowledge on specific topics. I wish to emphasize the fact that the IMF remains the international financial institution par excellence, as it plays a key role in supporting countries facing balance of payments problems. Learning from the lessons of the past, the IMF has made its lending instruments significantly more flexible, for example through precautionary liquidity provision instruments, which has allowed countries such as Mexico, Colombia, and Poland to face the crisis with the possibility of shifting resources through the Flexible Credit Line they maintain with the IMF. There is also a process for reviewing the Fund's performance, which is conducted regularly by the IMF's Independent Evaluation Office, and then issues stand-alone reports on IMF activities. A recent report reviewed the failures of the bank's supervisory activities during the recent financial crisis, and suggested possible improvements that are in the process of being incorporated. The relationship of the Republic of Chile with the IMF, since its inception, has been based on a State policy. The Chilean economy has also been an example of the correct application of macroeconomic and financial policies. Although it is not possible to be immune to international shocks in the globalized economy, macroeconomic and financial stability has been maintained in Chile in the face of complex situations at the global level since 2008. This resilience has been widely recognized at the IMF. In conclusion, I wish to reiterate the readiness of the Central Bank of Chile and its Council, if the draft is approved by Parliament, to inform the IMF quota increase, as a clear demonstration of the commitment we have to fulfilling our obligations as members of the international monetary system within the framework of the State policy followed since the IMF was established. Thank you very much, and I remain at your disposal to clarify any doubts.
text_original: LA 14 REVISIN GENERAL DE CUOTAS Y LA RELACIN DEL BANCO CENTRAL DE CHILE CON EL FONDO MONETARIO INTERNACIONAL Rodrigo Vergara Presidente Banco Central de Chile 11 de abril de 2012 Presentado ante la sesin especial de la Comisin de Hacienda de la Cmara de Diputados con el objeto de iniciar la discusin del proyecto de ley que autoriza al Banco Central de Chile a suscribir un aumento de la cuota correspondiente a Chile en el Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI) (Boletn N 8217-05). Seor Presidente de la Comisin de Hacienda de la Cmara de Diputados, diputado Ernesto Silva, seores diputados miembros de la Comisin de Hacienda: A nombre del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile (BCCh), les agradezco la invitacin a esta sesin de la Comisin de Hacienda, para dar nuestra visin sobre este proyecto de ley que autoriza al BCCh a suscribir el aumento de la cuota que le corresponde enterar a la Repblica de Chile, en el marco de la 14 Revisin General de Cuotas del Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI). Deseo aprovechar esta oportunidad para proveer a esta Comisin de los antecedentes sobre el rol que cumplen las cuotas en la gobernabilidad y funcionamiento del FMI, as como el contexto internacional en que se da este aumento de cuotas en particular. Adems, har una breve revisin de las distintas dimensiones que involucra la relacin del Banco Central con el FMI, que van ms all de la relacin estrictamente financiera asociada al aumento de cuotas. Segn establece su Convenio Constitutivo, al que Chile concurri como uno de los 35 pases signatarios originales en la reunin de Bretton Woods en 1944, el FMI es una institucin cuya fuente de financiamiento permanente la constituyen las cuotas que enteran los pases miembros. En la actualidad, el monto total de cuotas es de 238 mil millones de Derechos Especiales de Giro (DEG), equivalentes a US$371 mil millones, las que se distribuyen entre los distintos pases miembros del FMI segn el tamao de su economa, su grado de apertura, la variabilidad de su comercio exterior y su nivel de reservas internacionales. As, las cuotas cumplen un doble rol. Por un lado, la capacidad de prstamo permanente del FMI a travs de sus facilidades crediticias est en directa relacin con el volumen de las cuotas, y la cuota de cada miembro es la medida bsica para acceder a recursos del FMI en caso de enfrentar problemas en la balanza de pagos. Por otro, la cuota determina en gran medida el poder de voto de cada pas en las decisiones que toman los gobernadores y el Directorio del FMI. Cabe sealar que las cuotas del FMI se revisan regularmente bajo las Revisiones Generales de Cuotas. Los aumentos ms recientes de cuotas del FMI se llevaron a cabo en los aos 1991 y 1999, siendo en ambos casos sometidos a la aprobacin del Congreso de la Repblica bajo un procedimiento similar al actual. La cuota actual de Chile es de 856,1 millones de DEG (US$1.330 millones) que equivalen a una participacin del 0,359% del total. Nuestro pas ha enterado regularmente las cuotas en el FMI como una clara muestra del compromiso que tenemos con el cumplimiento de nuestras obligaciones como miembros del sistema monetario internacional en el marco de una poltica de estado. La 14 Revisin General de Cuotas, aprobada por los gobernadores del FMI en el ao 2010, se da en un contexto en que la economa global ha experimentado cambios importantes, que han implicado un significativo aumento del peso de los pases emergentes, con la correspondiente disminucin de las economas industrializadas. Adems, la escala de las necesidades de financiamiento externo de los pases miembros del FMI, tanto emergentes como algunos avanzados, luego de la crisis financiera del 2008, se increment de manera muy significativa. Es en este contexto que los gobernadores del FMI acordaron, por un lado, duplicar el tamao total de las cuotas a 476,8 mil millones de DEG, equivalentes a US$742 mil millones, y, por otro lado, aumentar de manera relevante el peso relativo de las economas emergentes. Este acuerdo busca que el aumento de cuota est materializado durante el ao 2012. La figura siguiente muestra cmo la entrada en vigor de la 14 revisin modifica la distribucin de cuotas, y por tanto del poder de voto y acceso eventual a financiamiento. SINOPSIS DE LA 14 REVISIN DE CUOTAS Pases que aumentan su cuota relativa Pases que disminuyen su cuota relativa Pases que mantienen su cuota relativa Fuente: Fondo Monetario Internacional En el caso de Chile, la 14 revisin permite aumentar su cuota hasta 1.744 millones de DEG, equivalentes a US$2.712 millones, para lo cual se requiere la aprobacin parlamentaria. Debido a que las cuotas son parte de las reservas internacionales del BCCh, a continuacin explicar con un mayor grado de detalle cmo se constituye dicho aumento de cuotas. La constitucin del aumento de cuotas en el FMI se materializa con 25% en moneda extranjera y 75% en moneda local. Por lo tanto, del aumento total de cuotas, al Banco Central le corresponder enterar aproximadamente 222 millones de DEG (US$342 millones) como proporcin en moneda extranjera, lo cual involucra un cambio en la composicin de sus reservas internacionales. El resto de la cuota se constituye en moneda local, a travs de una cuenta contable en los activos y una cuenta equivalente en los pasivos del Banco. Por lo tanto, de aprobarse el proyecto de ley en discusin, una vez enterado este aumento de cuota, el nivel de reservas internacionales se incrementar en alrededor de 666 millones de DEG (US$1.024 millones). El retorno financiero de la fraccin de las reservas internacionales representado por las cuotas est vinculado a la tasa de inters de los DEG que fija el FMI, la cual es un promedio de las tasas de inters de corto plazo sobre los bonos de gobierno de EE.UU., Alemania, Japn e Inglaterra. Tal como seal anteriormente, la cuota no es solo una medida del aporte de capital, sino tambin la medida bsica de las posibilidades de acceso al financiamiento del FMI por parte de Chile. El enterar el aumento de cuotas le permitir al pas contar con financiamiento externo relevante adicional en casos de crisis de balanza de pagos, equivalente a un mltiplo de la cuota. Por ejemplo, un nivel de acceso de 600% de la cuota que corresponde a un nivel de acceso tipo para una facilidad crediticia Stand-By equivaldra, bajo la 14 revisin, a 10.464 millones de DEG (US$16.224 millones), pero a solo 5.137 millones de DEG (US$7.963 millones) si se mantiene la cuota actual. El aumento de las cuotas tambin tiene asociado un aumento de la participacin relativa de Chile en el poder de voto en el FMI, desde un 0,359% a un 0,366%. Si bien esto representa un aumento marginal en el total de cuotas, constituye un aumento relevante del poder de voto relativo de Chile en la jurisdiccin del Cono Sur ante el FMI, donde Chile participa junto a Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Per y Uruguay. El acuerdo de dicha jurisdiccin sobre distribucin de cargos le ha permitido a Chile tener el cargo de Director Ejecutivo del FMI en un bienio en cada uno de los ltimos decenios, lo que es proporcional a su cuota relativa. El Directorio Ejecutivo est compuesto por 24 directores y es presidido por el Director Gerente. El Director Ejecutivo tiene la responsabilidad de la conduccin del quehacer diario del FMI en cuanto a su administracin y presupuesto, financiamiento, otorgamiento de prstamos a travs de los instrumentos vigentes, revisin de los instrumentos de prstamos y definicin de polticas generales para la conduccin de las actividades de supervisin del FMI. Asimismo, como parte de dicho acuerdo, a Chile le ha correspondido representar a los pases de la Silla del Cono Sur ante el Comit Monetario y Financiero Internacional, que es el ente mximo de discusin del FMI y est encargado de proveer orientacin al quehacer del FMI cada seis meses en las Reuniones Anuales y en las Reuniones de Primavera de dicho Comit, a las cuales asistir la prxima semana en Washington. A mi antecesor le correspondi representar a la Silla del Cono Sur en calidad de Gobernador ante el Comit Monetario y Financiero Internacional el 2010 y el 2011, emitiendo cada vez una declaracin con la posicin de Chile sobre la agenda de temas de cada reunin. Dichas declaraciones son de conocimiento pblico y se encuentran publicadas en el sitio web del Banco Central. Habiendo ya cubierto la relacin financiera a travs de las cuotas y su importancia para nuestra participacin en el FMI, a continuacin deseo presentar algunas dimensiones adicionales que involucra la relacin del Banco Central con el FMI. Estas incluyen las actividades de supervisin del FMI a las economas de los pases miembros y la provisin de asistencia tcnica. De acuerdo con lo establecido en el Convenio Constitutivo del FMI, todos los pases miembros estn sujetos a una revisin anual de sus polticas econmicas que se lleva a cabo bajo el proceso de consulta del Artculo IV del Acuerdo Constitutivo. Este involucra la visita de una misin del FMI, la que se rene con las autoridades econmicas y contrapartes del sector privado, con el objetivo de elaborar un informe que se presenta al Directorio del FMI para su discusin. Posteriormente, sujeto a la autorizacin de las autoridades econmicas chilenas, dicho reporte es publicado por el FMI en su sitio web, y se divulga tambin en los sitios web institucionales del BCCh y del Ministerio de Hacienda. Adicionalmente, el FMI y el Banco Mundial llevan a cabo una evaluacin conjunta del sistema financiero de los pases miembros a travs del Programa de Evaluacin del Sistema Financiero (FSAP por su sigla en ingls), las que se realizan de manera peridica, y tienen como objetivo asistir a los gobiernos, bancos centrales y autoridades supervisoras en el entendimiento y mejoramiento de los sistemas financieros. En el caso de Chile, la primera evaluacin se llev a cabo el 2004, y la segunda el 2011, en ambos casos, con resultados ampliamente favorables y congruentes con la slida situacin financiera de Chile. El FMI tambin provee la posibilidad de revisar el cumplimiento de estndares internacionales a travs de su Programa de Revisin de la Observancia de Estndares y Cdigos (ROSC) dentro del cual nuestro pas ha participado en los de Supervisin Bancaria, Transparencia de la Poltica Monetaria y Financiera y Regulacin de Valores (2004); Lavado de Dinero y Activos y Financiamiento del Terrorismo (2005); Diseminacin de Datos (2001, 2007) y Transparencia Fiscal (2003 y 2005). El FMI tambin ha provisto diversas misiones de asistencia tcnica en diversos temas de importancia para el Banco Central as como para el Gobierno. Dichas misiones de asistencia tcnica se materializan a peticin del pas miembro, y constituyen una fuente importante de apoyo en cuanto a conocimiento tcnico en temas especficos. Deseo recalcar el hecho de que el FMI sigue siendo la institucin financiera internacional por excelencia, ya que juega un rol fundamental en el apoyo de pases que enfrentan problemas de balanza de pagos. Aprendiendo de las lecciones del pasado, el FMI ha flexibilizado significativamente sus instrumentos de crdito, por ejemplo mediante instrumentos de provisin de liquidez de carcter precautorio, lo que ha permitido que pases como Mxico, Colombia y Polonia hayan podido enfrentar la crisis con la posibilidad de girar recursos a travs de la Lnea de Crdito Flexible que mantienen con el FMI. Tambin existe un proceso de revisin del actuar del FMI, que la Oficina de Evaluacin Independiente del FMI realiza en forma regular, y luego emite informes autnomos sobre las actividades del Fondo. Un informe reciente revis las fallas de las actividades de supervisin de la entidad durante la reciente crisis financiera, y sugiri posibles mejoras que estn en proceso de ser incorporadas. La relacin de la Repblica de Chile con el FMI, desde sus inicios, ha estado basada en una poltica de Estado. La economa chilena ha sido, adems, un ejemplo de correcta aplicacin de polticas macroeconmicas y financieras. Aunque no es posible ser inmune a los embates internacionales en la economa globalizada, s se ha logrado mantener la estabilidad macroeconmica y financiera en Chile frente a la seguidilla de situaciones complejas a nivel global desde el ao 2008. Esta resiliencia ha sido reconocida ampliamente en el FMI. En conclusin, deseo reiterar la disposicin del Banco Central de Chile y de su Consejo a, si el proyecto es aprobado por el Parlamento, enterar el aumento de cuota en el FMI, como una clara muestra del compromiso que tenemos con el cumplimiento de nuestras obligaciones como miembros del sistema monetario internacional en el marco de la poltica de Estado seguida desde que se constituy el FMI. Muchas gracias, y quedo a su disposicin para aclarar cualquier duda.

Title: The Productivity Challenge
text: Logo only THE PRODUCTIVITY CHALLENGE. Rodrigo Vergara President Central Bank of Chile November 2012 . Presentation prepared for the seminar Economic and Business Vision 2012-2013, organized by SOFOFA and the Universidad del Desarrollo and held in Santiago on November 6, 2012. Introduction I want to thank you for the invitation to speak at this seminar organized by Sofofa and the Universidad del Desarrollo. It is always good to take advantage of instances like this to present our vision about the Chilean economy and the challenges that lie ahead. Especially at the present time, when we see contradictory signals between the international situation that remains difficult and a domestic economy that remains solid and dynamic. The world is going through a complex scenario as a result of the legacy of the financial crisis, and this situation will continue to accompany us for a long time. The Chilean economy has managed to maintain its dynamism and is growing strongly, offsetting the effects of the crisis in Europe thanks to relatively favourable terms-of-trade conditions and access to external financing and the boost in domestic demand. However, we are a small economy open to the rest of the world, so it would be illusory to think that we can isolate ourselves from what happens outside our borders. In fact, although to a lesser extent than expected, the scope of the external crisis is becoming evident, for example, with lower exports to crisis areas such as Europe. It would be unwise to think that, following the recent measures taken by the authorities of the developed countries, the risks on the external front have diminished significantly, and that is why we constantly reiterate them in our presentations as I am doing here today. On the other hand, we face our own internal challenges. There are those of the short term, related to the economic cycle, and also other more relevant, medium and long term, which are related to our economic and social development. We have been successful and we have achieved important things in recent decades in terms of macroeconomic soundness and in terms of the well-being of our people, but there is still a long way to go and we must continue to persevere for development. The Central Bank is traditionally identified with the conjuncture and with the economic cycle, because it is the horizon in which monetary policy operates. However, for us it is important to have a long-term view of the Chilean economy, because this gives us a context to interpret the conjunctural situations and guide our decisions. In my presentation, I will review some of the productivity challenges we face in order to maintain high growth rates over time. I will start with a description of what we have done in the last twenty-five years and then focus on some of the key elements that will allow us to continue to grow steadily. I do not intend to be exhaustive in the enumeration and analysis of these elements (this would give for a much longer presentation), but only to highlight some challenges that frequently appear in our analyses. Nor will I completely exclude the most circumstantial analysis, I just want to say that in this presentation the longer-term issues will have a special dedication. Twenty-five years of economic history In the last twenty-five years the Chilean economy has made significant progress. During this period, output grew at an average annual rate of 5.6 per cent, GDP per capita increased 2.7 times its 1986 level, and poverty levels have fallen substantially (figure 1). The comparison of our development is also very favorable when we look at ourselves with respect to the rest of Latin America. Adjusted for purchasing power parity, Chile's GDP per capita has increased 5.2-fold since 1986, outperforming all countries in the region (Figure 2). These results have been the result of a set of economic and social policies and, indeed, of the efforts of all Chileans. At the macroeconomic level, Chile has based its development on several pillars. First, serious, predictable, and responsible fiscal policy. Copper surpluses began to be saved in the mid-80s with the so-called Copper Compensation Fund and from the year 2000, with a structural rule that guides spending and leads to savings in periods of bonanza to use them in periods of weakness. It should be noted that the Chilean treasury today has a gross debt of only 10% of GDP and a negative net debt when incorporating the resources accumulated in sovereign funds and other instruments. This fiscal position is remarkable in today's world where much developed economy has particularly high debt levels, which are, in fact, part of their current crisis (Figure 3). Second, a monetary policy based on an inflation target, with an autonomous central bank that has a clear mandate for price stability. Third, an exchange rate policy based on the floating of the exchange rate. This float, adopted in 1999, is key to accommodating the different shocks it faces. An economy like Chile's. We have seen in the past that fixed or semi-fixed exchange rates caused major problems for our economy. Fourth, sound regulation and supervision of the financial system. Finally, there is a growing commercial and financial opening of the economy, which has allowed entry to a large number of markets and has expanded business possibilities for the country. The favorable results of this scheme are evident. As I mentioned, over the past twenty-five years GDP averaged 5.4% annual growth, which compares to the average increase of 2.5% over the previous twenty-five years. GDP per capita in 2011 was 2.7 times that of 1986, while by 1970 GDP per capita was 1.6 times that of 1940. Inflation has averaged 3.3% annually this century, compared with nearly 32% between 1950 and 1970. The advances I mentioned have not gone unnoticed by the rest of the world. These achievements motivated, for example, that a few years ago we were invited to be part of the select group of member economies of the OECD, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. In addition, several international rankings prepared by prestigious institutions also account for the progress we have made in the last 25 years in different areas. In aspects such as competitiveness, economic freedom or macroeconomic performance, we are among the best emerging economies and even outperform some advanced economies in others (Chart 4). All these figures speak of the success we have had as a country in achieving development that allows a better quality of life for all. However, we still have a long way to go to reach development. Moreover, the section we have left is difficult because it requires a special additional effort. It requires maintaining the good we have done, but at the same time adapting with the necessary modifications to the new reality we live in as a country with an increasingly high per capita income and, in addition, adapting to an ever-changing international reality. There are many examples of countries that have had historic opportunities like the ones we have today in Chile and that have missed it. But there are also successful cases, which are the ones we must follow (I recommend reading Acemoglu and Robinson's book "Why Nations Fail?"). In any case, we must be clear that it is up to us and only on us to take advantage of this opportunity. Let me I then make some reflections on some of the challenges we have in terms of competitiveness. Competitiveness challenges Chile is today located in a privileged place in Latin America. The levels of social and economic development are much higher than those of several countries in the region. But this cannot make us fall into conformism. When we compare ourselves with developed economies, we realize that our country still has a long way to go to achieve a better level of development. Per capita income is still below the OECD average, our poverty rates remain above those of those countries, and we still have significant challenges in terms of income distribution and equality of opportunity (Figure 5). To this, we must add elements such as a quality of education that appears at persistently low levels every time it is measured in competitiveness rankings and that, by the way, is also related to income distribution. Hence the importance of the efforts being made in this area. Topics such as levels of investment in research and development and procedures for starting a business also appear with room for improvements in international rankings, although regarding the latter, in recent years there have been important advances in the number of days needed to do so. The fundamental question is what can we do not stop the progress we have sustained in recent decades? As I mentioned a few moments ago, the more successful you get, the harder it is to move forward: the old idea of diminishing marginal returns. I believe that a key area on which we must focus our efforts is to continue to improve the competitiveness of our economy. How do we achieve this? There are several things they contribute. The first, and certainly fundamental, is the very innovative and productive force of our economy. Chile's growth in the last twenty-five years has been accompanied by a significant change in our productive and export structure. In nominal terms, the share of mining in exports is still very relevant and, in fact, this has increased in recent years as a result of the high price of copper. However, industrial exports have increased their relevance from figures below 10% of total shipments abroad in the sixties to values of the order of 30% or more in recent years (figure 6). This has allowed not only a significant growth of companies that are dedicated to export but also in the number of products exported from Chile. For reference, in 1990 the number of products exported was around 2,800. In 2011 that figure slightly exceeded 5,000. On the other hand, the economic crisis in developed economies has had a limited effect on Chilean exports, mainly due to the diversification of products and markets to which we have access today. In the sixties, 90% of national exports went to Europe and the United States; in 2011 this proportion fell to 30% and diversification into other economies, mainly China, increased significantly (Figure 7). Thus, the number of countries to which exports increased significantly, from 109 in 1990 to 192 in 2011. This shows that to continue to be successful it is necessary to continue with the process of diversification of both products and markets. Continuing to diversify our export basket and expand the destination markets requires creativity and innovation to adapt to the new demands and special requirements of new markets. Another relevant issue related to competitiveness is related to the real exchange rate. As we said in the September Monetary Policy Report, the real exchange rate is at the low end of values consistent with their long-term fundamentals. Remember that the Central Bank's policy is one of exchange rate flexibility, but we reserve the right to intervene when conditions warrant it. These conditions are related to the accumulation of reserves (which in today's scenario appears to be less evident) and to the misalignment of the real exchange rate with respect to its fundamentals, which is subject to periodic evaluation. It is important to look for ways that allow us to continue increasing our competitiveness and access more markets and with better conditions for our exporters. Here, I will dwell on a few points. A first point I would like to mention in the area of improving competitiveness is that of energy costs. This has been a hotly debated topic with edges in different ways. One dimension of the issue is that, according to OECD data, measured in dollars and adjusted for Parity of purchasing power, the cost of industrial electricity increased in Chile by 35% between 2003 and 2011. More importantly, compared to the rest of the countries in this group, this cost went from being 6% below the median in 2004 to being 35% higher in 2011. On the other hand, the price of gasoline shows no substantive differences (figure 8). The evolution of the cost of electricity makes it highly necessary to advance in the development of a balanced energy matrix, which reduces costs in this area and allows Chilean companies to be more competitive. It is not a direct matter of our competence, but we call on those who have responsibilities in this area to take the appropriate initiatives and leadership to avoid further delaying the necessary investments that must be made in this sector. A second issue is the cost of labour. In recent quarters, we have seen a significant narrowing of the labour market. Unemployment has remained at low levels and nominal wages are growing at annual rates of the order of 6 to 7%, growth that is related to the productivity increases I mentioned a few moments ago and to the greater demand for labour that has been observed. The background information we received from various productive sectors, both in Santiago and in regions, shows that the difficulty in hiring workers has remained, and has even increased significantly in certain sectors and regions of the country, leading to significant increases in wages. This is especially high in the north of the country and in areas such as mining, construction and agriculture. In addition, according to this background, the phenomenon has been moving southwards, although still limited to specific activities and trades. Certainly, it is very positive that workers' income levels are increasing, and to the extent that the economy as a whole is doing well, that must be reflected in an increase in employment and wages. One important area where our economy must continue to advance is in bringing women into the workforce. We have seen significant increases, but we have not yet reached levels of participation comparable to those of developed economies. Between the mid-nineties and 2011, the percentage of women in the workforce went from just under 40 to 56%. In OECD member countries, this share is 64%, while in the main developed countries it reaches almost 70%. Undoubtedly, all initiatives that facilitate women's access to Work is welcome and you must continue to persevere so that more of them join the workforce. The same for the maintenance and incorporation into the workforce of the elderly and young people. Another very significant element is the one referring to the skills of our workforce, particularly in relation to their education. Certainly, this has been a country issue in recent years, as there are justified demands for improvements in this area. It is important to achieve a quality educational system that rewards capabilities and adds significant value to all its participants. In this regard, initiatives in this direction are welcome. To the extent that we have a more and better trained and suitable workforce, our path to development will be more expeditious. Improving infrastructure is also part of the task of competitiveness. Although there have been important advances in this area, there are still sectors that present relevant competitive disadvantages in relation to other countries, due to inadequate infrastructure that increases costs such as transport, which in themselves are already greater products of our geographical reality. Let me now briefly analyse the situation. Recent developments in the Chilean economy Our growth projections have been revised upwards over the past year, and we went from expecting growth for 2012 of between 4 and 5% in September last year, to projecting one between 4.75 and 5.25% in our latest Monetary Policy Report. The latest background suggests that we could be at the top of that range. But, as we have constantly repeated, the risks on the international stage are very high. In recent weeks there have been important advances that seem to establish a roadmap to solve the fundamental problems facing the Eurozone and that, in addition, show greater clarity and political will to act than a few months ago. Intentions to move towards a banking and fiscal union in the region are certainly key to a definitive solution. In addition, the approval of the ESM and the announcement of the OMT programme help to ease tensions in financial markets. Undoubtedly, the path that the Eurozone must follow will be full of obstacles, with political and institutional negotiations that generate conflicts and frictions, even more so considering the growing social tensions that the weakened growth outlook causes. Thus, it is not possible to rule out that the turbulence in the financial markets will resurface with greater intensity in the future. The fiscal discussion that the United States must make is also a matter of concern and may also be the source of new tensions in the financial markets. The series of subsidies and temporary tax cuts in that economy are coming to an end and the lack of an agreement to prevent the so-called fiscal cliff from being triggered can translate into a fiscal adjustment of significant magnitude. Private estimates suggest that, if there is no agreement, GDP growth in 2013 could be reduced by around 2 percentage points due to that effect alone. In addition, they will also soon have to face again the discussion on the limit of public debt that would be reached at the beginning of 2013. The evolution of growth in emerging economies also deserves special attention, since they are the ones that have made it possible to maintain a global growth rate that does not differ much from its average of the last 20 years. Thus, for 2012 the IMF estimates a global growth of 3.3% that compares with the average of 3.5% in the previous 20 years. The signs of slowdown that we had been observing in China require closer monitoring of the effects that a slowdown in that economy can have not only on the dynamism of global growth, but also on the price of raw materials, and especially copper. However, the latest news suggests that the slowdown in some relevant emerging economies such as China and Brazil could be entering a breaking point. The picture in Chile contrasts with what is observed in the rest of the world. The effects of the weakened external scenario have been tenuous and the economy continues to perform strongly, with activity growing around trend rates. However, he highlighted the dynamism of domestic demand, whose growth projections exceed those of GDP for both 2012 and 2013. So our estimates suggest that the current account deficit will widen next year from just over 3% to just over 4% of GDP. However, if the dynamism of domestic demand is maintained d0 and indeed, the most recent indicators of consumption point to greater strength of thisd1we could be generating vulnerabilities for our economy that may require difficult adjustments later on, particularly considering the complex international scenario. Hence, the importance of maintaining moderate spending and being fully aware of the risks we face. Spending that is not moderated leads to larger deficits, which are possible to finance as long as conditions remain favorable. But what would happen if the price of copper has sharp falls? Or if there is a sharp deterioration in external financial conditions? Certainly, this would be quickly transmitted to domestic markets. We have seen this in the past, even with a Chilean financial system that is very solid. In such a scenario, the costs of maintaining debts grow, families' incomes suffer, and so does their wealth. To the extent that the current account deficit is higher, or more persistent, the possibility that a deterioration in the external scenario will be transmitted more strongly to domestic conditions also grows. Moderation in spending is everyone's job. From the private sector, through decisions that prudently evaluate their future income prospects and the debt obligations they are assuming, with adequate risk management and based on real and not too optimistic assumptions, based on the boom of recent years. From the public sector, in the construction of a balanced budget that allows us to cover the needs and desires of the population, but without neglecting that part of the success we have had as a country is based on a fiscal policy that has been and must continue to be serious and responsible. In this regard, we value the achievement of the structural deficit target of 1% one year ahead of schedule. On the part of those in charge of financial supervision, to maintain close monitoring that allows actions to be taken to avoid the incubation of dangerous imbalances. In the case of the Central Bank, with a monetary policy that has been prudent and must remain so, which has managed the risks of the current external scenario, but which also faces the medium-term risks that the state of the Chilean economy imposes on inflation. Also, with a constant review of regulatory aspects that allow better risk management by the financial and private sector. Thus, to the extent that there is an increase in these risks, it is possible to think about prudential measures to mitigate them. Finally, I cannot fail to refer to price developments. Annual CPI inflation and the core inflation measure excluding food and energy, IPCSAE, remain below 3%. Although there are no perceived risks to inflation in the short term, the difference between goods and services inflation persists, the latter more closely linked to the state of capacity slacks. This highlights the medium-term risk for this variable, since maintaining a buoyant activity and demand may continue to intensify the use of installed capacity and generate inflationary pressures that move away from the target. Allow me to make a final thought. Final Thoughts Without a doubt, we face a challenging scenario. In the last twenty-five years we have taken a remarkable step forward as a country. We have grown, we have decreased poverty, we have raised our quality of life. But much remains to be done. We are far from reaching the state of development that we all want, and the paths to it are neither easy nor obvious. Chile's progress has been based on the innovation capacity of our people, taking advantage of the opportunities presented to us and striving to do our best in pursuit of our objectives. Thus, we have managed to enter world markets and be recognized as a serious, proven country with an institutionality that provides a reliable framework in which initiatives can be developed. Continuing to move forward and improve our competitiveness is based on continuing on this path. The economic policy framework we have built has also been very important. Highly valued fiscal responsibility; sound regulation and supervision of the financial system; greater trade and financial integration; the clarity and coherence in the anti-inflationary objective of the autonomous Central Bank and the validity of the exchange rate float as an adjustment instrument, reserving by the way the possibility of intervening in exceptional situations and the opening to the outside of the economy. Finally, I think it is important to highlight the importance of looking optimistically to the future. In the last two and a half decades we have managed to build a better country, certainly not yet good enough that we all wanted, but we have come a long way. The next few years can also be great Progress, but achieving further development depends on our ability to stay on the right track. The demands are many and many of them fully valid, so we must work to satisfy them. However, it is impossible to do so, at least not in full, in the short term without creating imbalances that sooner rather than later would be paid dearly. There are many aspects of our country that are very valuable and that we must preserve and increase. Being more competitive in an increasingly complex world depends on us, on the changes we can make, but also on the conviction in the pillars that have led us to success in these years. Thanks a lot.
