Es as como a las restricciones regulatorias al descalce cambiarlo en instituciones financieras se ha sumado el desarrollo de mecanismos de cobertura. Esto es lo que permite evitar que an en un contexto de significativa devaluacin del peso, como en 2014 y en la actualidad, ste genere grandes costos para los agentes econmicos y riesgos para la estabilidad financiera. Por ltimo, estos marcos de poltica monetaria y financiera no buscan imponer una camisa de fuerza al accionar del Banco, que pudiera limitar la posibilidad de articular medidas excepcionales ante situaciones tambin excepcionales. Es as como en los ltimos meses el Banco ha aplicado medidas extraordinarias para reducir la volatilidad y asegurar liquidez para reducir el impacto de ajustes de portafolio ante un aumento significativo de la incertidumbre. Con ello se ha protegido el proceso de formacin de precios, los flujos de pagos y el acceso al crdito. Para ello, el Banco ha recurrido a opciones contempladas en los propios marcos de poltica o en su Ley Orgnica. Lo anterior no significa, por cierto, que la economa chilena pueda salir indemne de shocks tan importantes como los que hoy se observan. Sera irresponsable dar una sensacin de total inmunidad, especialmente cuando parte de los shocks tienen un origen interno. No obstante, s podemos asegurar que el Banco cuenta con instrumentos para responder a nuevos desafos que enfrente el pas y que su Consejo tiene la voluntad y disposicin para usarlos en funcin de su potencial efectividad, de la naturaleza de los problemas que se enfrenten y del bienestar de los chilenos. Por eso, al presentar estos documentos, podemos decirle al pas que puede esperar de nosotros honestidad, profesionalismo y decisin, tanto en momentos normales como en momentos de tensin. Esto es as porque el Banco Central de Chile no trabaja para intereses econmicos estrechos, ni para un sector poltico, ni para un modelo determinado, sino para el conjunto del pas. Este es el verdadero sentido de nuestra autonoma. Los documentos que hoy presentamos son una buena demostracin del ejercicio de la misma. Muchas gracias.

Title: Presentation of the Monetary Policy Report June 2020
text: PRESENTATION OF THE MONETARY POLICY REPORT TO THE FINANCE COMMITTEE OF THE HONORABLE SENATE OF THE REPUBLIC * *No Monetary Policy Report June 2020 can be found at . Mario Marcel President Central Bank of ChileJune 17, 2020 Introduction Mr. Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Senator Jorge Pizarra. Senators members of this Commission, senators. I appreciate the invitation to present the vision of the Council of the Central Bank of Chile on recent macroeconomic developments, their prospects and the implications for monetary policy. This view is contained in detail in the June 2020 Monetary Policy Report (IPoM), published this morning. This background also provides the background for the decision taken by the Council at the Monetary Policy Meeting on Tuesday. At the beginning of April, when we presented our previous IPoM to this Commission, the country was beginning to face the effects of Covid-19. At that time, the health authority had decreed various health containment measures and people began to adopt social distancing practices. Today, the number of people who have fallen ill with Covid-19 has increased significantly, as well as those who, unfortunately, have lost their lives as a result of it, which has led the authorities to escalate restrictions to achieve control of the pandemic. When we presented our previous Report, we anticipated that the suspension of many activities or the drastic reduction of them as a result of quarantines and other restrictions on the mobility and interaction of people, would cause a rapid contraction of economic activity. What we then had to estimate with little information and many assumptions has been ratified in the figures that have emerged. This contraction has deepened and prolonged over the past two months, while the economic authorities have been trying to mitigate its most damaging effects by reducing the cash deficits of households and firms and ensuring a flow of credit to the latter. The health struggle to control the spread of the virus has thus been accompanied by the fight to prevent its direct impact on companies' revenues from spreading to other companies, workers and the financial system. The situation that Chile is going through is not far from what has happened in other countries, nor from what is happening in much of Latin America. The evolution of the Covid-19 pandemic and the actions taken to contain it constitute an unprecedented and large-scale shock to the global economy. The projections that I will present to you in a few moments consider that Chile will have this year the largest economic contraction in 35 years, while various international organizations predict that for the world it will be the worst result in an even longer period. Historical evidence shows that countries struggle to recover when they suffer significant recessions. However, it is not obvious how applicable this experience is to the current situation. The origin of the shock we face today has no economic or financial origin. What we are experiencing today is a health crisis for which we have few precedents to accurately anticipate its economic consequences and in which public policies have acted considerably more aggressively. A relevant element of these experiences is that when the initial shock becomes a financial problem, costs grow substantially and its effects are much more persistent. That is why this time, central banks and governments around the world have placed special emphasis on preventing the sharp fall in the incomes of individuals and companies from translating into a problem of financial insolvency. In the case of the Central Bank of Chile, we have strongly intensified the monetary impulse, bringing the MPR to its technical minimum. Along with this, we have taken various measures to ensure liquidity in the markets and facilitate the delivery of credit to companies. In fact, given the greater deterioration shown by the economy as a result of the pandemic, at yesterday's Monetary Policy Meeting we announced the implementation of unconventional measures to intensify the monetary impulse and preserve financial stability. These measures include a second stage of the Conditional Financing Facility to Increase Placements (FCIC), to ensure the continuity of the flow of credit to companies, and a program of purchase of financial assets, to reactivate other sources of credit to the economy. The future challenges of this crisis are enormous. Since the nature of this is different from previous recessionary episodes, the speed of its recovery depends on factors beyond the purely economic. How the epidemic evolves locally and globally, how people behave in the future and whether there will be more or less permanent structural reallocations are all issues of great relevance but still do not have a clear answer. In any case, the fiscal policies to protect employment that are being deployed d0 in the world, and in Chile in particular d0 aim immediately to mitigate the loss of income of people and in the future, to allow a rapid reactivation. In this sense, the greater fiscal impulse that will be verified with the Emergency Plan agreed between the Government and this enlarged Finance Commission is very important. Monetary policy is called to play an important role in providing the necessary liquidity to support different programs to support individuals and companies. But you also need to understand the limits it has. For this reason, close coordination between monetary and fiscal policy is more essential than ever. We have been doing this and an example of this has been the complementarity between the liquidity provided by the FCIC and the guarantees provided by FOGAPE and FOGAIN. The new fiscal measures agreed by the government and the monetary and financial measures approved by the Bank's Board at yesterday's RPM reflect this joint and complementary effort to support the economy and the living conditions of the population. I will now turn to describe our assessment of the economic outlook and its risks. Macroeconomic scenario Since January, Covid-19 has been spreading rapidly around the world, shifting the focus of infections and the strictness of mandatory and voluntary containment actions between continents. Thus, after the appearance of the virus in China, the epicenter of infections moved during March and April to Europe and the United States, and from May it is located in Latin America. Thus, while some Asian countries have already gradually returned to normal throughout the second quarter, in Europe and the United States it is still an incipient process, and Latin America d0 including Chile d0 is in its phase of greatest confinement (graph 1). The evolution of economic indicators has reflected these changes. At the beginning of the year, China's data showed significant falls in consumption and investment, with first-quarter GDP declining by around 7 percent, the first decline since the seventies. More recent data, consistent with the reduction in infections and restrictions on mobility, indicate rebounds in several dimensions. Europe, where the peak of infections occurred later, had significant falls in its activity in the first quarter, observing historical collapses in various indicators during March and April. In recent weeks, quarantines were lifted in several countries and the gradual reopening of various activities began. In the United States, the economic figures for March and April had sharp falls, and a process of reopening has already begun, although there the number of infections is still high and the latest data show a rebound in some states (graph 2). Latin America, as I mentioned, is going through the most complex phase of the pandemic, with more limited resources to contain it. Several countries continue to record daily records for infections and deaths. In Chile, after a downward trend in April, infection rates began to accelerate during May, forcing the imposition of more restrictive health containment measures and other adjustments in the strategy followed. In this sense, the quarantine that has been extended since mid-May for a large part of the Metropolitan Region and its recent extension to an important part of the Valpara92so Region stands out. As a result, the proportion of the population affected by quarantines rose from just under 30 percent at the end of April to just over 40 percent today. The unprecedented nature of this situation makes it particularly difficult to make projections, since they depend largely on factors that escape economic analysis. In the immediate term, a significantly larger contraction is expected in the second quarter. After the fall at the end of last year, the economy recovered somewhat faster than expected, until the country's entry into phase 4 of the pandemic brought with it a set of control measures that strongly affected activity from the second half of March, which led to a fall in activity of 3.1 percent annually. The impact was greatest in April, when activity contracted by around 14 percent annually. As expected, the economic sectors where personal contact is predominant in the development of the activity were the most affected, in particular commerce, restaurants and hotels, transport and various personal services (Figure 3). The implementation of stricter quarantines means that the deterioration in activity was greater in May and June, so the activity records for those months will probably be more negative than in April. Thus, between May and June the GDP generated in the affected communes went from 36 to almost 46 percent of the total. Private expectations have picked up on this deterioration. The June Economic Expectations Survey estimated that in May the IMACEC would have fallen 15.5 percent annually, while sharply reducing its projection for the second quarter, from a fall of the order of 7 percent annually in the May measurement to one of 13 percent annually in June (Graph 4). While the biggest deterioration in activity has probably already occurred, the evolution of the disease and the number of new infections make it difficult to estimate how long it will take to observe a recovery, until the stricter containment measures begin to be relaxed. It is added that once these measures are lifted, it is not known with certainty if there will be outbreaks, how people's behavior will evolve and what their impact will be on the performance of different economic sectors. The experience of other countries could give some approximation of the health and economic response to the reopening of cities. However, these processes are still recent enough to detect patterns clearly, and it is not evident how the singularities of social, climate and environmental behavior can affect Chile's relative performance in this dimension. Finally, the outlook for demand will depend on the impact of high uncertainty and loss of household and business income. In the central scenario, it is assumed that quarantines will be reduced during the third quarter and a gradual reopening of the economy will be achieved, thus allowing a gradual improvement in activity and the labor market. In any case, this considers that part of the social distancing practices d0 mandatory and voluntary d0 will continue to be present for several quarters, so the activity of some economic sectors will take longer to return to the levels prior to the beginning of the pandemic. In this way, the economy will begin to recover in the second part of 2020, although it will not yet reach levels of activity comparable to those of the beginning of the year. In fact, it is expected that only by mid-2022 will the activity levels of the third quarter of 2019 be equalized. The projections are subject to a much higher level of uncertainty than usual, which implies that changes in their communication are made in this IPoM, similar to what other central banks have done (Table 1). On normal occasions, the width of the growth range for the current year would be reduced to 0.75 percentage points, while it would remain at 1 percentage point for the following year, all this applying a criterion based on historical projection errors. Instead, this IPoM reflects the high uncertainty by increasing the width of the projection range for GDP in 2020 and 2021 to 2 and 1.5 percentage points, respectively. For 2022, the width of the projection range remains at one percentage point, considering that by that time some relevant uncertainties will have already been cleared. The variables of the macroeconomic framework in the central scenario d0 consumption and investment, among others d0 continue to be published with a timely estimate, but the informative value of both these projections and the growth ranges is clearly lower than usual. Taking into account the above criteria, the Council estimates that in 2020 total GDP will contract between 5.5 and 7.5 per cent, while during 2021 and 2022, the economy will recover, registering growth between 4.75 and 6.25 per cent and between 3 and 4 per cent, respectively (Graph 5). In the framework of the central scenario, consumption will contract by about 4 percent in 2020, mainly due to its private component. After the sharp fall in the second quarter, this projection assumes that households will continue to be affected by lower incomes and high uncertainty, elements that are tempered by social protection measures, such as the Emergency Family Income and fiscal support programs focused on the most vulnerable. In recent months, there has been a significant loss of jobs d1 some of them temporary d1 and a reduction in income, a factor that has also combined wage adjustments and the reduction in workers' working hours. The deterioration of the labour market has been significant in recent months. Voluntary and mandatory health actions have had important effects. On the one hand, they have led to a large drop in company sales and a sharp reduction in demand for work, especially in sectors whose activities are developed more intensively based on contact between people. On the other hand, the need to confine oneself d0 voluntarily or involuntarily d0 to avoid contagion has prevented many people from carrying out their work activities on a regular basis. Although the rapid adoption of teleworking has mitigated some of this shock, only some activities are adaptable to a remote work scheme, so these physical restrictions are still very relevant. A striking case of these effects has been the sharp fall in self-employment, which regularly acts as a buffer in times of economic contraction, but which has been prevented from operating by health restrictions, accounting for about half of the job losses when the figures are compared year after year (graph 6). In this context, the national unemployment rate increased to 9 percent in the INE Survey for the February, March and April quarter. Other measurements, which are not directly comparable, such as that of Universidad de Chile for Greater Santiago or that of the Catholic University place it above that level, reaching double-digit values. In the case of the INE, although the increase in unemployment reflects the significant loss of jobs that has occurred in several economic sectors, its increase has been less than the reduction in the employment rate (measured as a percentage of the working-age population). In the rolling quarter ended in April, this stood at 52.7 percent, with a sharp drop in the last record that places it between 5 and 6 percentage points below what was observed throughout 2019. Comparatively, this fall in employment is much higher than the increase in the unemployment rate, which until April was of the order of 2 percentage points. The reason for this difference is a sharp increase in inactivity (Figure 7). In fact, data from the INE survey show that more than 95 percent of those who lost their jobs in the last mobile quarter moved into this category. This means that they are people who, despite being unemployed, and wanting one, are not actively looking for it. This can be explained in part because the set of health restrictions prevents people from carrying out paid work and even the search for a new job. Factors such as quarantines and school closures could support this hypothesis. Another plausible reason is discouragement: the process of looking for a job could grind to a halt for a while, not only because it involves costs, but also because there might be a perception that there aren't enough job openings available. In fact, the Bank's Internet Job Vacancies index shows an annual drop of 65 percent annually in May. Another important adjustment factor in the labour market has been the Employment Protection Act. This allows the temporary suspension of the employment relationship in companies whose activities were totally or partially affected by health restrictions, allowing the worker to access Unemployment Insurance funds. The program has had a massive use, and as of June 7, more than 610,000 workers had benefited from the Law. Its use has been especially important in sectors such as Construction and Commerce, Restaurants and Hotels, reaching about 20 percent of workers in the sector (figure 8). Unlike traditional unemployment, this measure makes it possible to preserve the contractual relationship with the employer. Going forward, to the extent that infections decrease and the economy is able to start, there should be a significant, although incomplete, recovery in incomes, which should be reflected in consumption. On the one hand, self-employment should develop again as soon as stricter health containment measures are reduced. Something similar should happen with workers covered by the Employment Protection Act. If this happens, there would be an increase in income that would help reactivate the economy. In the meantime, the Emergency Plan agreed between the government and this Commission will significantly extend compensatory transfers to households, increasing their coverage, amount and duration. If this manages to reduce uncertainty about future incomes, it can also help a recovery in consumption. In the central scenario, investment will contract by around 16 percent in 2020. This performance is explained by a sharp contraction in investment in the non-mining sectors due to the tightness and constraints of corporate cash flows and the very high uncertainty. In addition, the postponement of the execution of major projects in 2020 is added. By 2021 and 2022, a rebound in investment is expected, considering that by then the uncertainties will have been cleared or reduced, large investment projects will resume their development and the government will increase public investment in infrastructure and housing as part of the agreed Emergency Plan. It remains to be determined how companies will adjust to the higher level of indebtedness that is being generated to cover current financing needs (figure 9). Another factor that adds uncertainty is the fear that, once the health emergency is over, episodes of violence will resurface that cause significant disruptions in economic performance. The effect of high uncertainty on projections is also observable globally. As in the case of Chile, projections for global growth this year have had a significant downward adjustment in recent months. In the central scenario of this IPoM, the Council estimates that global GDP would fall in the order of 4.5 percent this year, growing 4.4 percent in 2021 and 4.5 percent in 2022 (Chart 10). Regarding the current account, a surplus of 0.8 percent of GDP is projected this year (0.3 percent in March). Behind this revision is a contraction in imports and exports that is expected to be deeper than in March, but with a more marked adjustment in the case of the former. This, in line with the significant decrease expected in domestic spending, which will not be fully counteracted by the Government's greater dissavings. The increase in the terms of trade, in particular the revision of the price of copper, also affects the correction. The price of copper would average about 2.65 a pound in the period 2020-2022, the same period in which oil would average about 43 a barrel, when considering the Brent/WTI average. The significant upward adjustment in the price of copper means that over the projection horizon the terms of trade are higher than estimated in March and provides support for exports and mining investment (Graph 11). Containing and overcoming the economic damage caused by the pandemic has required a significant and coordinated effort by the economic authorities. In several countries, central banks are using unconventional tools and governments have put in place substantial fiscal support packages for households and firms. In the main, the measures have been aimed at providing credit and liquidity that avoids the rupture of relations between companies, their suppliers, customers and workers. Achieving this is key to reducing the persistence of the effects of the crisis. The decision and timeliness in action of the world's fiscal and monetary authorities has been one of the main factors that has contributed to reversing the marked deterioration of financial markets at the beginning of the pandemic. Beyond the recent ups and downs, compared to the second half of March, most financial variables show an improvement: stock markets have recovered, long-term interest rates and risk rewards have fallen and most currencies have appreciated against the dollar. Added to this is the increase in the price of raw materials, including copper. In Chile, from mid-March to date, various State authorities have implemented measures to support households and businesses. The Government has provided resources in the order of 17 billion dollars, aimed, among other objectives, at protecting employment, supporting household income and injecting liquidity into the productive system. Added to this will be the recently agreed Emergency Plan for the Protection of Family Income and Economic and Employment Reactivation. This contemplates a fund of up to 12 billion dollars for the next twenty-four months. These resources will initially be used to reinforce transfers to the most vulnerable sectors through the Emergency Family Income. A reinforcement of the Employment Protection Law, the Unemployment Insurance and the realization of support for formal independent workers are added. Subsequently, the resources of this fund will be used to support economic reactivation through plans to support jobs and investment. The agreement provides for this additional effort to be transitory and to be followed by fiscal consolidation in the medium term, in order to prevent public debt from exceeding 45 percent of GDP. The central projection scenario considers the effects of this Plan on economic growth between 2020 and 2022 in general terms. More specific estimates of their impacts can be made once their details are approved in Congress. The situation of companies has also been of particular concern, in particular because encouraging the delivery of credit to those that are solvent, but face significant liquidity problems due to the pandemic, will reduce the negative effects of the current situation, avoiding bankruptcies that result in permanent and unnecessary losses of productive capacity and employment. To this end, the Central Bank established the Financing Facility Conditional on Increasing Placements (FCIC). This is an instrument that provides commercial banks with additional resources to lend to households and businesses. Access to this facility is supported by eligible collateral and is determined based on the recent behavior of commercial and consumer credit, with special emphasis on that granted to small businesses. As of June 11, banks had used 83 percent of the facility, with some of them already reaching the available ceiling. The combination of this facility with the guarantees provided by the government through FOGAPE and the relaxation of rules of the Commission for the Financial Market, have led commercial credit to grow at annual rates of the order of 11 percent real in May, which are compared with the values around 6.5 percent that showed until February (graph 12). This is expressed in the use of credit lines, massive rescheduling and a significant flow of credits in installments for the financing of working capital, especially relevant for small and medium-sized companies. This countercyclical behaviour of aggregate commercial credit, together with the increase in the share of credit going to smaller firms, makes a significant difference compared to other recessionary periods. However, the worsening of the negative effects of the pandemic on the economy has raised the financial requirements of companies, so the Council considered it necessary to launch a second stage of the FCIC. It will commit funds of another 16 billion. In addition, it considers the strengthening of incentives for the delivery of bank credit to small and medium-sized enterprises, and to non-bank credit providers, which will be combined with the improvement of the guarantee schemes of the Covid-19 lines, committed in the agreement between government and parliamentarians. Some details of this measure are shown in Table 2. Finally, since the beginning of the social crisis, the Bank has developed various liquidity and asset purchase operations, which have helped reduce frictions in portfolio adjustments as a result of changes in risk perceptions, have contained increases in long-term rates and have helped to avoid the paralysis of non-bank credit channels. The special asset purchase program announced yesterday aims to deepen these measures. In particular, in its first month of validity this program will contemplate an amount of 1,500 million dollars, which will be destined to the purchase of assets currently eligible for the Bank d0 Central Bank bonds and bank bonds. Regarding inflation, it fell to 2.8 percent annually in May, influenced by the significant fall in fuel prices. Core inflation d0 measured by the CPI without volatiles d0 remains at values of the order of 2.5 per cent per annum. Of note is a somewhat larger increase in food prices, combining supply and demand factors, such as drought, logistical problems arising from movement restrictions and increased demand for some commodities. I would like to highlight that from this IPoM we have made a change in the core inflation indicator that we consider most relevant. This is a process that began to be reported in December last year, when a box and a methodological note on its measurement were published. This box compared various indicators, including the CPI and the CPI without volatiles, concluding that the latter better reflected the underlying behavior of inflation. Although its current levels differ, in fact the IPCSAE is closer to 2 percent, its medium-term dynamics should not be very different1. V The change in the indicator through which core inflation is interpreted is not new. Over the last few years For 20 years, the Bank has used indicators such as the CPI (CPI without fuels and without fresh fruits and vegetables), the CPI 1 (CPI without energy and perishable foods) and the CPI (CPI without energy and without food). This is a practice that is also carried out by other central banks and that should be continuous over time. Returning to the projection, the sharp increase in the activity gap in the second quarter, together with the more recent appreciation of the peso, significantly reduces inflationary pressures. In the central scenario, inflation will fall to around 2 percent by the end of this year, with it projected that only towards the end of the policy horizond1the second quarter of 2022d1will it be around 3 percent annually (Chart 13). In this scenario, monetary policy will remain in a highly expansionary position for the time necessary to ensure the convergence of inflation to the 3 percent target over a two-year horizon, and to support financial stability. This will also boost demand and activity. Consistent with this, at the June Meeting, we decided to maintain the MPR at 0.5 percentd1which corresponds to the current estimate of its technical minimumd1we noted that, in the central scenario, it would remain at that level for at least the two-year policy horizon, and we ordered the application of non-standard measures equivalent to up to 10 percent of GDP (Chart 14). In addition, we indicate that the eventual expansion and/or adoption of these or other measures would be evaluated in accordance with the needs of the economy and the legal powers of the Bank. As always, there are sensitivity scenarios where the evolution of the macroeconomic situation could require adjustments to the monetary impulse. On this occasion, these scenarios respond to different assumptions of how the pandemic and the subsequent recovery of the economy will behave. First, there could be a more benign scenario in which the evolution of the virus is more favorable, implying a faster rebound in activity in the second part of the year, allowing a more vigorous recovery in consumption and investment. On the other hand, there could also be a more pessimistic scenario, for example, because quarantines must be extended into the second half of the year. This would lead to activity being hit harder, extending the weakness of consumption and investment. In the most benign scenario, the greater dynamism from the third quarter of this year would lead to an earlier closing of the activity gap, which would support a somewhat earlier inflationary convergence. On the contrary, the negative scenario would imply a more unfavourable and persistent evolution of the gap, with a more lasting weakness of inflationary pressures. In line with the high uncertainty and difficulty of assigning a specific probability to each scenario, the Board considers that both the balance of risks for growth and inflation is balanced. The difficulty in differentiating the probability of occurrence of sensitivity scenarios from that of the central scenario is also reflected in the exceptional expansion of the projection range for 2020 and 2021. However, scenarios that may be even more negative than those proposed deserve special attention. The magnitude of the effects of the pandemic is significant and although the monetary and fiscal authorities have implemented an unprecedented set of measures, it is not possible to ensure that the size or duration of the damage does not exceed what was assumed, which could put financial stability at risk. In such a situation, with the policy rate already at its technical minimum, the Bank may need to make extreme use of its policy instruments. In this regard, the Council particularly appreciates the Commission's support for a constitutional and legal reform that extends the powers of the Institution to act in exceptional situations where the preservation of financial stability especially requires it. During the last forty years Chile has faced three recessionary periods, one in the early eighties, product of the external debt crisis and the bankruptcy of local banks, another in the late nineties, product of the Asian crisis and another at the end of the decade of the two thousand, product of the global financial crisis. Each of these episodes has particularities that differentiate it from the others, either by the origin of the crisis, the prevailing policy framework and response capacity, as well as the synchrony of the effects between countries. The current situation bears little relation to any of these periods, both because its origin is not economic, its effect has a synchrony never before seen between economies, and the public policy framework has a greater response capacity than in the past. Even so, the cost to the country of the current crisis will be high, and some sectors will require significant adjustments in the face of more lasting changes in their conditions and modes of operation. In response to the change of scenery, the Council deepened its monetary impulse, committing to maintain it for a long period of time and to increase it through unconventional channels if this is necessary for the achievement of the objectives of controlling inflation and maintaining financial stability. Final Thoughts When in mid-2019 the External Evaluation Panel that examined the Bank's performance in conducting monetary and financial policy over the past few years recommended improving our preparedness for sudden and extreme shocks, our first reaction was some skepticism. Our economy had weathered the international financial crisis of 2008-2009 quite well. Was it then necessary to go back to the eighties to look for parameters with which to elaborate tests of financial stress, evaluate our policy instruments and the space for monetary and fiscal policy? Wasn't it enough to have a policy framework that had already worked at complex junctures for almost twenty years? A short time later we were faced with two successive episodes that qualify precisely as sudden and extreme shocks: an internal social crisis and a pandemic. None originated directly in the economy, but with an immediate and profound impact on activity. surrounded by a drastic increase in uncertainty, encouraging changes in the behavior of investors, companies, workers and households. Despite failing to fully respond to the panel's recommendation, the Central Bank had previously taken some initiatives that laid the groundwork for better addressing these situations. Among them, the creation of a corporate risk management; progress with the Commission for the Financial Market in the implementation of the new General Banking Law; access to databases and the ability to understand the microeconomics behind the behavior of large aggregates; strengthening market intelligence mechanisms; updating emergency protocols, improving communications and strengthening business continuity systems. All these elements were useful to respond to the challenges imposed on us by these events. The Central Bank was able to articulate innovative and large-scale responses to shocks that far exceeded the previous turbulence. Within days, if not hours, liquidity measures were taken; Without complexes, it was decided to intervene in the market to change it; Within weeks, an innovative program was launched to ensure an adequate response of bank credit to monumental cash deficits in companies. All this by committing resources on an unprecedented scale. Although it is not easy to add things up, the total resources mobilized or committed by the Bank in the last eight months are close to 20 percent of GDP. However, the key to these responses was not only these technical and administrative aspects. More important was the professionalism and commitment of our staff; coordination with other relevant actors, such as the Ministry of Finance and the CMF, and a sense of responsibility to citizens, particularly the conviction that we could not let families and businesses experience a catastrophe similar to the crisis of the early eighties. Those of us who have enough years to have lived that experience, know the human pain and the social cost of a crisis that affected millions of homes for years; a crisis in which the debate between intervention and automatic adjustment deepened the damage to the economy; where people feared the loss of life savings; where the multiplication of bankruptcies and mass layoffs were faced without protection systems for the unemployed; in which scarce public resources had to be devoted to rescuing banks and financial institutions and then restricted for years to recover public finances. Beyond its immediate effects, the wounds of this crisis took decades to heal. Today Chile and its economy are very different. But those of us who hold state responsibilities have to make sure that people notice that. It is not enough to follow and cite the usual statistics, built on averages and generated with the cadence required by methodological rigor. In these eight months we have had to go out and look for information, quantitative, qualitative and disaggregated, to capture and better understand the reality of the country, and reflect it in our decisions. For this very reason, we know that it is useless to leave things halfway. Recovering the economy from shocks such as those we are experiencing is a complex task, which must be followed until the end. It is not enough to make decisions and commit resources: we must worry about their implementation, generate complementarities with the measures of other authorities; Evaluate, adjust, and scale them if necessary. That is why, faced with a prolongation of health restrictions as a result of the spread of contagion, yesterday we adopted unconventional measures for about 10 percent of GDP, practically doubling the contribution of the Central Bank to the containment of the crisis, on the one hand, and to the preparation for a subsequent recovery. on the other. While dealing with these responsibilities, we must not lose sight of the substantive lessons. First, despite the advances of recent decades, we are still an emerging country, with weaknesses and vulnerabilities that affect important segments of society and the productive system. Our institutions may be stronger than those of some peers, but they are not yet strong enough to inspire the confidence to contain increased uncertainty in the face of unexpected events or to sufficiently protect those who need it most. That is why, as I just mentioned, public policies cannot be based only on averages, it is necessary to look at the complete distribution, recognizing inequality. Second, we need to be prepared for adverse events, including those we don't even know about. Asia-Pacific countries, from New Zealand to Korea, coped better with Covid-19 because for decades they prepared to face epidemics caused by unknown viruses. In Chile and Latin America we must better prepare not only for this, but to better face economic and social emergencies, improving our social protection systems and regulatory frameworks and the capacity to mobilize credit. This will prevent the spread of damage in a sector or a dimension of our economy. This, of course, includes recomposing, as soon as possible, the fiscal and financial slack accumulated over decades, and which have given us space to act today, but also strengthening social protection systems and their capacity to act in systemic crises. Finally, we must recognize that technical capacity and creativity are not enough to replace organization, cooperation and dialogue. In this episode we have found that there is no single actor who can solve the country's most pressing problems and that when someone tries to do so, they soon make mistakes that weaken their reliability. At this juncture, the autonomy of different institutions has not been an obstacle to cooperation and coordination. It has been shown that, just as when cooperation happens everyone wins, when it does not occur, no one can win. This Finance Commission has highlighted the merits of dialogue and cooperation, even among those who think very differently and may have discrepancies at other junctures, an example that should be recognized and thanked for the country. In short, Mr President, honourable Senators, this crisis, which is still far from over, and which has not necessarily ruled out the social crisis of October, leaves us with a lesson in humility: knowing that we are exposed to events that we cannot control, that we do not know everything and that we are responsible to millions of people for whom a good or bad policy decision can make an enormous difference. In short, if humility motivates us to do things better, it can also make us stronger in the face of the unforeseen situations we face as a country. Thanks a lot 18 Jul. 19 Jul. text_original: Presentacin del informe de Poltica Monetaria ante la Comisin de Hacienda del Honorable Senado de la Repblica Mario Marcel Presidente Banco Central de Chile 17 de junio de 2020 Introduccin Seor Presidente de la Comisin de Hacienda del Senado, Senador Jorge Pizarra. Senadores miembros de esta Comisin, senadoras y senadores. Agradezco la invitacin para presentar la visin del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile sobre los desarrollos macroeconmicos recientes, sus perspectivas y las implicancias para la poltica monetaria. Esta visin est contenida en detalle en el Informe de Poltica Monetaria (IPoM) de junio de 2020, publicado esta maana. Asimismo, estos antecedentes aportan el trasfondo para la decisin adoptada por el Consejo en la Reunin de Poltica Monetaria de ayer martes. A comienzos de abril, cuando presentamos nuestro anterior IPoM ante esta Comisin, el pas comenzaba a enfrentarse a los efectos del Covid-19. En ese momento, la autoridad sanitaria haba decretado diversas medidas de contencin sanitaria y las personas comenzaban a adoptar prcticas de distanciamiento social. Hoy, el nmero de personas que han enfermado del Covid-19 ha aumentado significativamente, as como las que, lamentablemente, han perdido la vida como producto de ella, lo que ha llevado a las autoridades a escalar las restricciones para lograr el control de la pandemia. Cuando presentamos nuestro anterior Informe, anticipamos que la suspensin de numerosas actividades o la drstica reduccin de ellas como producto de las cuarentenas y otras restricciones a la movilidad e interaccin de las personas, provocara una rpida contraccin de la actividad econmica. Lo que entonces debimos estimar con poca informacin y muchos supuestos se ha visto ratificado en las cifras que han do surgiendo. Esta contraccin se ha do profundizando y prolongando en los ltimos dos meses, al tiempo que las autoridades econmicas hemos estado intentando mitigar sus efectos ms nocivos por la va de reducir los dficits de caja de hogares y empresas y asegurando un flujo de crdito a estas ltimas. La lucha sanitaria por controlar la propagacin del virus ha sido acompaada as por la lucha para evitar que su impacto directo sobre los ingresos de las empresas se propague a otras empresas, a los trabajadores y al sistema financiero. La situacin por la que atraviesa Chile no dista de lo que ha sucedido en otros pases, ni tampoco de lo que est ocurriendo en buena parte de Amrica Latina. La evolucin de la pandemia del Covid-19 y las acciones adoptadas para su contencin constituyen un shock sin precedentes y de gran magnitud para la economa mundial. Las proyecciones que les presentar en unos momentos consideran que Chile tendr este ao la mayor contraccin econmica en 35 aos, mientras que diversos organismos internacionales prevn que para el mundo ser el peor resultado en un lapso an ms largo. La evidencia histrica muestra que a los pases les cuesta reponerse cuando sufren recesiones significativas. Sin embargo, no es evidente cun aplicable es esta experiencia a la situacin actual. El origen del shock que enfrentamos hoy no tiene un origen econmico o financiero. Lo que hoy vivimos es una crisis sanitaria de la que tenemos pocos precedentes para anticipar con precisin sus consecuencias econmicas y en la cual las polticas pblicas han actuado de manera considerablemente ms agresiva. Un elemento relevante de estas experiencias es que cuando el shock inicial se transforma en un problema financiero, los costos crecen sustantivamente y sus efectos son mucho ms persistentes. Por eso esta vez, los bancos centrales y los gobiernos alrededor del mundo hemos puesto un especial nfasis en evitar que la brusca cada de los ingresos de las personas y empresas se traduzca en un problema de insolvencia financiera. En el caso del Banco Central de Chile, hemos intensificado fuertemente el impulso monetario, llevando la TPM a su mnimo tcnico. Junto con ello, hemos adoptado diversas medidas para asegurar la liquidez en los mercados y facilitar la entrega de crdito a las empresas. De hecho, ante el mayor deterioro que muestra la economa producto de la pandemia, en la Reunin de Poltica Monetaria de ayer anunciamos la implementacin de medidas no convencionales para intensificar el impulso monetario y preservar la estabilidad financiera. Estas medidas incluyen una segunda etapa de la Facilidad de Financiamiento Condicional al Incremento de las Colocaciones (FCIC), para asegurar la continuidad del flujo de crdito a las empresas, y un programa de compra de activos financieros, para reactivar otras fuentes de crdito a la economa. Los desafos futuros de esta crisis son enormes. Dado que la naturaleza de esta es distinta a episodios recesivos anteriores, la velocidad de su recuperacin depende de factores que escapan a lo puramente econmico. Cmo evolucione la epidemia en el plano local y mundial, cmo sea el comportamiento de las personas en el futuro y si habr reasignaciones estructurales ms o menos permanentes, son todos temas de gran relevancia pero que an no tienen una respuesta clara. En todo caso, las polticas fiscales de proteccin del empleo que se estn desplegando en el mundo, y en Chile en particular apuntan en lo inmediato a mitigar la prdida de ingresos de las personas y hacia adelante, a permitir una reactivacin rpida. En tal sentido, resulta muy importante el mayor impulso fiscal que se verificar con el Plan de Emergencia acordado entre el Gobierno y esta Comisin de Hacienda ampliada. La poltica monetaria est llamada a jugar un rol importante en proveer la liquidez necesaria para respaldar distintos programas de apoyo a las personas y empresas. Pero tambin es preciso entender los lmites que tiene. Por esta razn, ms que nunca es fundamental una estrecha coordinacin entre la poltica monetaria y fiscal. As lo hemos estado haciendo y un ejemplo de ello ha sido la complementariedad entre la liquidez aportada por el FCIC y las garantas aportadas por FOGAPE y FOGAIN. Las nuevas medidas fiscales acordadas por el gobierno y las monetarias y financieras, aprobadas por el Consejo del Banco en la RPM de ayer son reflejo de este esfuerzo conjunto y complementario por apoyar la economa y las condiciones de vida de la poblacin. Ahora pasar a describirles nuestra evaluacin del panorama econmico y sus riesgos. Escenario macroeconmico A partir de enero, el Covid-19 ha ido propagndose rpidamente alrededor del mundo, trasladando el foco de los contagios y la estrictez de las acciones de contencin obligatorias y voluntarias entre continentes. De este modo, tras la aparicin del virus en China, el epicentro de los contagios se traslad durante marzo y abril a Europa y Estados Unidos, y a partir de mayo se ubica en Amrica Latina. As, mientras algunos pases asiticos ya han retomado gradualmente la normalidad a lo largo del segundo trimestre, en Europa y Estados Unidos es un proceso an incipiente, y Amrica Latina incluido Chile est en su fase de mayor confinamiento (grfico 1). La evolucin de los indicadores econmicos ha reflejado estos cambios. A comienzos de ao, los datos de China mostraron cadas significativas del consumo y la inversin, con un PIB del primer trimestre que tuvo un descenso anual del orden de 7 por ciento, el primer retroceso desde la dcada de los setenta. Datos ms recientes, acordes con la reduccin de los contagios y las restricciones a la movilidad, sealan repuntes en varias dimensiones. Europa, donde el peak de contagios se produjo ms tarde, tuvo cadas significativas de su actividad en el primer trimestre, observndose desplomes histricos en diversos indicadores durante marzo y abril. En las ltimas semanas, se levantaron las cuarentenas en varios pases y se comenz con la reapertura gradual de diversas actividades. En Estados Unidos, las cifras econmicas de marzo y abril tuvieron fuertes cadas, y ya ha comenzado un proceso de reapertura, pese a que all el nmero de contagios an sigue siendo elevado y los ltimos datos muestran un repunte en algunos estados (grfico 2). Amrica Latina, como mencion, est atravesando por la fase ms compleja de la pandemia, con recursos ms limitados para contenerla. En varios pases se continan registrando rcords diarios de contagios y fallecimientos. En Chile, luego de una tendencia decreciente en abril, las tasas de contagio comenzaron a acelerarse durante mayo, obligando a la imposicin de medidas de contencin sanitaria ms restrictivas y otros ajustes en la estrategia seguida. Resalta en este sentido la cuarentena que se extiende desde mediados de mayo para gran parte de la Regin Metropolitana y su reciente ampliacin a parte importante de la Regin de Valparaso. Con ello, la proporcin de la poblacin afectada por cuarentenas pas de algo menos de 30 por ciento a fines de abril a algo ms de 40 por ciento en la actualidad. Lo indito de esta situacin hace particularmente difcil realizar proyecciones, pues ellas dependen en gran parte de factores que escapan del anlisis econmico. En lo inmediato, se prev una contraccin significativamente mayor en el segundo trimestre. Tras la cada de fines del ao pasado, la economa se recuper algo ms rpido que lo previsto, hasta que el ingreso del pas a la fase 4 de la pandemia trajo consigo un conjunto de medidas de control que afectaron con fuerza la actividad a partir de la segunda quincena de marzo, lo que llev a una cada de la actividad de 3,1 por ciento anual. El impacto fue mayor en abril, cuando la actividad se contrajo del orden de 14 por ciento anual. Tal como se esperaba, los sectores econmicos donde el contacto personal es predominante en el desarrollo de la actividad fueron los ms afectados, en particular el comercio, restaurantes y hoteles, transporte y varios servicios personales (grfico 3). La implementacin de cuarentenas ms estrictas implica que el deterioro de la actividad fue mayor en mayo y junio, con lo que los registros de actividad de esos meses sern probablemente ms negativos que el de abril. As, entre mayo y junio el PIB que se genera en las comunas afectadas pas de 36 a casi 46 por ciento del total. Las expectativas privadas han recogido este deterioro. La Encuesta de Expectativas Econmicas de junio estim que en mayo el IMACEC habra cado 15,5 por ciento anual, mientras que redujo marcadamente su proyeccin para el segundo trimestre, desde una cada del orden de 7 por ciento anual en la medicin de mayo a una de 13 por ciento anual en junio (grfico 4). Si bien el deterioro mayor de la actividad probablemente ya ocurri, la evolucin de la enfermedad y el nmero de nuevos contagios hace difcil estimar cuanto tiempo demorar en observarse una recuperacin, hasta que comiencen a flexibilizarse las medidas de contencin ms estrictas. Se suma que una vez levantadas dichas medidas, no se sabe con certeza si existirn rebrotes, cmo evolucionar el comportamiento de las personas y cul ser su impacto en el desempeo de distintos sectores econmicos. La experiencia de otros pases podra dar alguna aproximacin de la respuesta sanitaria y econmica a la reapertura de las ciudades. Sin embargo, estos procesos son an recientes como para detectar patrones con claridad, y no es evidente cmo las singularidades del comportamiento social, del clima y del medio ambiente pueden afectar el desempeo relativo de Chile en esta dimensin. Por ltimo, las perspectivas para la demanda dependern del impacto de la alta incertidumbre y la prdida de ingresos de hogares y empresas. En el escenario central se asume que las cuarentenas se reducirn durante el tercer trimestre y se lograr una reapertura gradual de la economa, permitiendo as una mejora paulatina de la actividad y el mercado laboral. En todo caso, esto considera que parte de las prcticas de distanciamiento social obligatorias y voluntarias seguirn presentes por varios trimestres, por lo que la actividad de algunos sectores econmicos tardar ms en retomar los niveles previos al comienzo de la pandemia. De esta manera, la economa comenzar a recuperarse en la segunda parte de 2020, aunque no alcanzar an niveles de actividad comparables a los de principios de ao. De hecho, se prev que solo hacia mediados de 2022 se equipararn los niveles de actividad del tercer trimestre de 2019. Las proyecciones estn sujetas a un nivel de incertidumbre mucho mayor al habitual, lo que implica que en este IPoM se hagan cambios en su comunicacin, de manera similar a lo que han hecho otros bancos centrales (tabla 1). En ocasiones normales, el ancho del rango de crecimiento para el ao en curso se reducira a 0,75 puntos porcentuales, mientras que se mantendra en 1 punto porcentual para el ao siguiente, todo esto aplicando un criterio basado en los errores histricos de proyeccin. En lugar de ello, en este IPoM se recoge la elevada incertidumbre aumentado el ancho del rango de proyeccin para el PIB de 2020 y 2021 a 2 y 1,5 puntos porcentuales, respectivamente. Para 2022, el ancho del rango de proyeccin se mantiene en un punto porcentual, considerando que para esas fechas ya se habrn despejado algunas incertidumbres relevantes. Las variables del encuadre macroeconmico en el escenario central consumo e inversin, entre otros sigue publicndose con una estimacin puntual, pero el valor informativo tanto de estas proyecciones como de los rangos de crecimiento es claramente menor al habitual. Tomando en cuenta los criterios anteriores, el Consejo estima que en 2020 el PIB total tendr una contraccin entre 5,5 y 7,5 por ciento, mientras que durante 2021 y 2022, la economa ir recuperndose, registrando crecimientos entre 4,75 y 6,25 por ciento y entre 3 y 4 por ciento, respectivamente (grfico 5). En el encuadre del escenario central, el consumo se contraer cerca de 4 por ciento en 2020, principalmente por su componente privado. Tras la fuerte cada del segundo trimestre, esta proyeccin asume que los hogares continuarn afectados por la baja de los ingresos y la elevada incertidumbre, elementos que son morigerados por las medidas de proteccin social, como el Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia y los programas de apoyo fiscal enfocados a los ms vulnerables. En los ltimos meses, se ha observado una importante prdida de puestos de trabajo alguna parte de ellos transitoria y una reduccin de los ingresos, factor en que tambin se han conjugado ajustes de los sueldos y la disminucin de las jornadas laborales de los trabajadores. El deterioro del mercado laboral ha sido relevante en los ltimos meses. Las acciones sanitarias voluntarias y obligatorias han tenido importantes efectos. Por un lado, han llevado a una gran cada de las ventas de las empresas y a una fuerte reduccin en la demanda por trabajo, en especial en los sectores cuyas actividades se desarrollan ms intensivamente en base al contacto entre personas. Por otro lado, la necesidad de confinarse voluntaria o involuntariamente para evitar el contagio ha impedido que muchas personas puedan desarrollar sus actividades laborales de forma habitual. Aunque la adopcin rpida del teletrabajo ha permitido mitigar parte de este shock, slo algunas actividades son adaptables a un esquema de trabajo remoto, por lo que estas restricciones fsicas siguen siendo muy relevantes. Un caso llamativo de estos efectos ha sido la fuerte cada que muestra el empleo por cuenta propia, que regularmente acta como amortiguador en pocas de contraccin econmica, pero que se ha visto impedido de operar por las restricciones sanitarias, pasando a explicar cerca de la mitad de la prdida de empleos cuando se comparan las cifras ao a ao (grfico 6). En este contexto, la tasa de desocupacin nacional aument hasta 9 por ciento en la Encuesta del INE para el trimestre febrero, marzo y abril. Otras mediciones, que no son directamente comparables, como la de Universidad de Chile para el Gran Santiago o la de la Universidad Catlica la ubican por sobre ese nivel, alcanzando valores de dos dgitos. En el caso del INE, si bien el aumento de la desocupacin refleja la importante prdida de empleos que se ha dado en varios sectores econmicos, su incremento ha sido menor a la reduccin en la tasa de ocupacin (medida como porcentaje de la poblacin en edad de trabajar). En el trimestre mvil terminado en abril, esta se situ en 52,7 por ciento, con una cada brusca en el ltimo registro que la ubica entre 5 y 6 puntos porcentuales por debajo de lo observado a lo largo de 2019. Comparativamente, esta cada de la ocupacin es bastante superior al aumento en la tasa de desocupacin, que hasta abril era del orden de 2 puntos porcentuales. La razn de esta diferencia es un fuerte aumento de la inactividad (grfico 7). De hecho, los datos de la encuesta del INE muestran que ms del 95 por ciento de quienes perdieron su empleo en el ltimo trimestre mvil, pasaron a esta categora. Esto significa que son personas que pese a estar sin empleo, y querer uno, no lo estn buscando activamente. Esto puede explicarse en parte porque el conjunto de restricciones sanitarias impide que las personas puedan desarrollar labores remuneradas e incluso la propia bsqueda de un nuevo empleo. Factores como las cuarentenas y el cierre de los colegios, podra apoyar esta hiptesis. Otra razn plausible es el desaliento: el proceso de bsqueda de un trabajo podra detenerse por un tiempo, no solo porque implica costos, sino tambin porque podra existir la percepcin de que no hay suficientes ofertas laborales disponibles. De hecho, el ndice de Vacantes Laborales en Internet que produce el Banco muestra una cada de anual de 65 por ciento anual en mayo. Otro factor de ajuste importante en el mercado laboral ha sido la Ley de Proteccin del Empleo. Esta permite la suspensin temporal de la relacin laboral en empresas cuyas actividades fueron afectadas total o parcialmente por restricciones sanitarias, permitiendo al trabajador acceder a fondos del Seguro de Cesanta. El programa ha tenido un uso masivo, y al 7 de junio se haban acogido a la Ley ms de 610 mil trabajadores. Su uso ha sido especialmente importante en sectores como Construccin y Comercio, Restaurantes y Hoteles, alcanzando a cerca del 20 por ciento de los trabajadores del sector (grfico 8). A diferencia del desempleo tradicional, esta medida permite conservar la relacin contractual con el empleador. Hacia adelante, en la medida que los contagios disminuyan y se logre poner en marcha la economa, debera producirse una recuperacin importante, aunque incompleta de los ingresos, lo que debera reflejarse en el consumo. Por un lado, la ocupacin por cuenta propia debera volver a desarrollarse en cuanto las medidas de contencin sanitaria ms estrictas vayan reducindose. Algo similar debera ocurrir con los trabajadores incorporados a la Ley de Proteccin del Empleo. De darse esto, se producira un aumento de los ingresos que ayudara a reactivar la economa. En el intertanto, el Plan de Emergencia acordado entre el gobierno y esta Comisin extender significativamente las transferencias compensatorias a los hogares, elevando su cobertura, monto y duracin. Si esto logra reducir la incertidumbre sobre los futuros ingresos puede ayudar tambin a una recuperacin del consumo. En el escenario central, la inversin se contraer en torno a 16 por ciento en 2020. Este desempeo se explica por una fuerte contraccin de la inversin de los sectores no mineros debido a las estrecheces y restricciones de los flujos de caja corporativos y la altsima incertidumbre. Se suma la postergacin de la ejecucin de los grandes proyectos en 2020. Hacia 2021 y 2022, se prev un repunte de la inversin, considerando que para entonces ya se habrn despejado o aminorado las incertidumbres, los grandes proyectos de inversin retomarn su desarrollo y el gobierno elevar la inversin pblica en infraestructura y vivienda como parte del Plan de Emergencia acordado. Resta por determinar cmo las empresas se ajustarn al mayor nivel de endeudamiento que se est generando para cubrir las actuales necesidades de financiamiento (grfico 9). Asignacin La entrega de fondos de la FCIC2 estar vinculada a la dinmica de crditos Covid, as como tambin aquellos otorgados a oferentes de crdito no bancarios (OCNB). Este se fijar como el monto de crditos en cuotas entregados a este tipo de instituciones durante 2020 (promedio enero a mayo). Colaterales Los fondos que se giren de la FCIC2 deben ser respaldados con colaterales elegibles. Para estos efectos se considerarn todos los incluidos en FCIC1, ms crditos de la cartera comercial de evaluacin individual clasificada en categora A4.  Con todo, los crditos categora A4 podrn ser utilizados como colaterales hasta un 50% del uso de la FCIC completa (1 y 2). Condiciones financieras Se mantienen las que rigen para el caso de la FCIC1, es decir, TPM con pagos mensuales. Title: Launch of the book "Use of Macroeconomic Models in the Central Bank of Chile"
text: Launch of the book " Use of Macroeconomic Models in the Central Bank of Chile"Opening remarks by Mario Marcel, President of the Central Bank of Chile March 22, 2021, via online - Santiago, Chile Dear colleagues and friends, welcome to the launch of the book "Use of Macroeconomic Models in the Central Bank of Chile". The objective of this book is to present the current state of the instruments available to the Central Bank for the construction of projections and the role of models within the decision-making process of the Council. This book is published in a complementary way to the document that updated the monetary policy framework of the Central Bank of Chile, published in March 2020. Also, this book updates a previous version that was published in 2003, although more than an update, it is a new version much more complete and detailed. On the one hand, it describes the process of using the models with a great level of detail, highlighting the stages, information, and communication between the staff and the Council. On the other hand, it includes not only models of reduced form, but also details the structural models, which, given their strong theoretical foundation, allow a great variety of analysis and understanding of the different channels and mechanisms behind the numbers. Finally, this book is accompanied by references where each model is described in depth and with a more technical analysis, and is also accompanied by the codes of the most important general equilibrium models used by the bank, the MSEP and XMAS, so that the most technical users can see the detail of the operation of these models and do their own exercises. Meaning of the book and how it is framed in the BCCh's transparency and accountability policy The publication of this book is part of the effort to increase transparency in the monetary policy decision-making process of the Central Bank of Chile, which complements other transparency mechanisms in the decisions and actions of the institution. This exercise is in line with international best practices on transparency according to the International Monetary Fund's 2020 Central Bank Transparency Code and good practices promoted by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). The information documented in this book is comparable to the documentation of models and projection processes of the central banks of Norway and England and can be considered superior to those of other central banks that are international reference such as those of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Sweden and the Federal Reserve of the United States. For the more general reader, who wants to understand the objectives and instruments of the BCCh, the new documents Monetary Policy of the Central Bank of Chile are available in the Framework of Inflation Targeting and Financial Policy of the Central Bank of Chile. If you are also looking to learn about which models are specifically used in the monetary policy framework, you can refer to the Model Book where the process in which they are dealt with is described in detail and a non-technical description of each model. For readers interested in the technical dimension, each model described in the book is supported by documents referenced in the book and written mostly by Bank economists, where all the technical characteristics such as equations and details of their estimation are detailed. Finally, for a specialist audience that wants to execute the codes, estimate the models, and perform quantitative exercises, the publication of the book is accompanied by the publication of the codes Central Bank of Chile March 2021 computational of the two most used general equilibrium models in the Bank. With this, we hope to deliver the tools that enable a clear understanding of the way in which decisions are made and the instrumental models that the Bank has. The models presented in this book are not necessarily the final word on the subject. As we live in a world where the most important questions and analyses are changing over time, and economic analysis must adapt to shocks of non-economic origin, new modeling discoveries are developed day by day, so the models used by the Central Bank are constantly in a process of revision and updating. Which will undoubtedly give rise to new versions of this book in the future. The Model Book in the context of the recommendations made by the Independent Evaluation Panel The publication of this book of models, together with the codes to reproduce its operation, also seek to increase the effectiveness of monetary policy. Indeed, in a policy framework of prospective inflation targeting such as that prevailing in Chile, compliance with these targets cannot be verified by simply observing the current or past CP. Hence the importance of being able to verify whether the monetary policy stance is consistent with the convergence of inflation to the target over the 24-month policy horizon, an issue that requires the use of models, starting with those used by the Bank itself. This issue was noted by the Independent Evaluation Panel that analyzed the Bank's performance in achieving its institutional objectives. Within its recommendations regarding Monetary Policy, the Panel emphasized the need to better communicate its policy decisions, making transparent the judgments applied to the base projections, their sensitivity and assumptions, involving in the response not only the respective Division but also the Board. This is how these recommendations have been considered in the book we are launching today, placing the Central Bank of Chile within a select group of central banks of advanced economies with high standards of transparency. The structure of this volume reflects the practice accumulated during the last years in the development and use of Central Bank models. The book begins by describing the roles of models in the Bank, specifically during monetary policy decisions, and also explains the role of judgment in this process. Chapter 2 details the main instances in which the use of macroeconomic models is required. This includes the IPoM, presented four times a year, where a thorough analysis of the current and expected state of the economy is carried out; and published one day after the March, June, September and December Monetary Policy Meetings. In the remaining four Meetings, the projections of the international and domestic scenario of the short term are updated. Chapters 3 and 4 discuss the process of analysis and projections, and describe the models used in the Bank. These models can be grouped differently according to the criteria used: frequently used main models and satellite or auxiliary models; models for international analysis and models for national analysis; or models focused on the short term and models focused on the medium and long term. Finally, in Chapter 5, the guidelines for a future modeling agenda that is consistent with the latest empirical and theoretical developments and that, in addition, aims to achieve a better understanding of the effects of monetary policy, the determinants of inflation, and its interaction with employment, the evolution of the financial market and other economic variables. Final words and thanks In conclusion, I would like to thank all those who contributed to the preparation of this document. In particular, I thank the teams of the Macroeconomic Analysis and International Analysis Departments for their contributions and the Economic Modeling Department of the Economic Studies Management for their contributions and organization, as well as the outstanding economists who will comment on the chapters of the Model Book. ***

Title: Financial Stability Report First Semester 2021. Mario Marcel, President
text: bench central Chile FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT PRESENTATION BEFORE THE FINANCE COMMITTEE OF THE HONORABLE SENATE OF THE REPUBLIC * * The Financial Stability Report of the first half of 2021 can be found in . bcentr to .el. Mario Marcel, President Solange Berstein, Financial Policy Division Manager Central Bank of Chile May 05, 2021 Madam Chair of the Senate Finance Committee, Senator Ximena Rinc97n, Senators members of this Committee, Senators, I welcome the invitation to present the vision of the Council of the Central Bank of Chile on recent developments in the financial sector and implications for financial stability. In accordance with the provisions of its Constitutional Organic Law, the Central Bank of Chile is responsible for "ensuring the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal and external payments." The latter is directly associated with our concern for financial stability. In this context, the preface of the Financial Stability Report (or FSI) points out that financial stability exists when the financial system performs its functions normally or without relevant disruptions, even in the face of adverse temporary situations. The monitoring carried out by the Central Bank of Chile on financial stability is complementary to that carried out by specialized supervisors, being an element of independent analysis regarding the attributions and functions that correspond to them in relation to the entities subject to their control. The vision presented today is contained in detail in the IEF for the first half of 2021, available, from today morning, on the website of the Central Bank of Chile. FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT MAY 2021 central bank Chilc8 The Financial Stability Report Greot Pc8oce TD Work GertfflrtJtch Financial Policy of the Central Bank of Chile a5 The CBC aims to ensure the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal payments and External. To meet this second objective, it must safeguard the stability of the financial system within the perimeter of its legal powers, implemented from a macro-financial perspective. a5 Financial stability exists when the system performs its functions normally or without significant disruptions, even in the face of adverse temporary situations. The identification of potential risk events, vulnerabilities and mitigators, along with the evaluation of the impact on the financial system, are at the center of the financial policy analysis of the Central Bank of Chile (BCCh). a5 The BCCh conducts its financial policy by seeking to contribute, within its sphere of competence, to the stability of the financial system. This has been deepening and gaining stability in recent decades due, in part, to the Development of financial policy tools and their proper application. This in turn has contributed to the effectiveness of monetary policy and increased the resilience of the economy to disruptive events. a5 The Bank implements its financial policy through joint and coordinated actions with the supervisor and regulator. In particular, the BCCh issues and administers financial regulation, prepares reports and issues opinions on the impact of potential legal or regulatory changes regarding which you are consulted. To this is added the eventual exercise of the role of lender of last resort for banking companies and other liquidity management tools. Oo It is important to emphasize that the IEF differs from the Monetary Policy Report (MPR) in that, while the latter is built around a projection of the most likely economic scenario, the IEF analyzes events of lower probability of occurrence, but plausible, that may affect the stability of the financial system. Likewise, while the Bank is directly responsible for monetary policy decisions from the IPoM, the policy implications that can be derived from the IEF are not necessarily its responsibility. For this reason, it is important to discuss the IEF with regulators, the government, the National Congress and market agents. a5 The Financial Stability Report (FSB) is the main means through which, since 2004, the BCCh communicates its assessment of the main risks to financial stability in the country, their origins, propagation mechanisms, vulnerabilities and mitigators. a5 The IEF differs from the Monetary Policy Report (MPR) in that, while the latter is built around a projection of the most likely economic scenario, the IEF analyzes events of lower probability of occurrence, but plausible, that may affect the stability of the financial system. a5 Likewise, while the Bank is directly responsible for monetary policy decisions from the IPoM, the policy implications that can be derived from the IEF are not necessarily its responsibility. Portal reason, it is important to discuss the IEF with regulators, the government, the National Congress and market agents. a5 The focus of the IEF is financial stability, so it is inevitable that the bulk of its content refers to the financial system or the implications that the performance of other actors or markets could have on it. This focus responds to the institutional mandate of the BCCh, which does not mean underestimating the importance of other dimensions of the country's economic and social life. a5 Historical and comparative experience shows that financial crises have a direct and lasting impact on countries, often absorbing substantial public resources for their resolution. Therefore, safeguarding stability and preventing financial crises is a task that contributes to the well-being and progress of the country. What does this IEF tell us? The slack accumulated over the years, along with a deep financial market and the action of the authorities, have been essential to confront the greatest threat to financial stability in recent decades. The economy, after reaching its lowest point in the middle of last year, is in recovery due to policy action, the vaccination process and a better economic scene. The vulnerabilities, while significant, are smaller than six months ago. The most vulnerable households and businesses have reduced their ability to face unfavorable future scenarios, increasing their risk of default. Abrupt adjustments in financial conditions in some of the largest economies could have negative effects, especially in countries lagging behind in their economic recovery. Since the previous FSI, global financial conditions have remained supportive and global activity is showing signs of recovery, while substantial supportive policies remain in many economies. At the local level, the action of different authorities including the Central Bank of Chile (BCCh), and the prudent operation of the financial sector, allowed to contain the risks to financial stability, derived from the unusual shock generated by the Covid-19 pandemic. Thus, unlike previous crises, the cost of financing has remained low, non-performing loans remain contained and credit has continued to flow, albeit with a recent slowdown. In this context, activity shows a significant recovery after the deep contraction of the second quarter of 2020, allowing a large part of companies, households and banks to have greater strength to withstand stress scenarios than what was estimated in the previous IEF. However, the situation continues to deteriorate compared to two years ago, since credit users d0 households, non-financial companies and government d0 have seen their wealth situation eroded as a result of greater leverage or use of savings, especially in sectors whose activity has been more sensitive to mobility restrictions. Banks, for their part, have made large provisions to reflect the increased risk of their credit portfolios, compressing their profits. Going forward, various risk factors persist due to the unusual shock caused by the pandemic and the uncertainty regarding its evolution. In this sense, abrupt adjustments in long-term rates in developed economies, or deterioration in emerging economies, which fail to keep pace with the international recovery, may affect local financing conditions. The main challenge for economies such as Chile, where the process of vaccination and economic recovery is advancing, will be to achieve an adequate balance between policies that underpin such growth and the necessary recomposition of financial slacks towards the medium term.
