Dear Senators, It will not escape your attention that in this presentation we have talked a lot about institutions and financial markets, banks, companies, investors, balance sheets. This is not the product of an unconscious bias, but simply to comply with the Bank's institutional mandate to safeguard financial stability. It is therefore inevitable that the bulk of a financial stability report refers to the financial system or the implications that the performance of other actors or markets could have on it. However, this does not mean that workers, women, small businesses or youth are absent from this analysis. Historical and comparative experience shows that financial crises have a direct and lasting impact on countries. Likewise, its resolution, when it compromises the solvency of financial institutions, absorbs substantial resources with a high opportunity cost in social and infrastructure programs. Therefore, safeguarding stability and preventing financial crises is a task that contributes to the well-being and progress of the country. In the last World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund estimated that, were it not for the rapid and vigorous policy response of the economic authorities to the Covid-19 shock, the recession would have been three times deeper than it did in 2020. To a large extent, this difference is explained because the authorities' interventions not only cushioned the impact of the crisis on workers' incomes and company operations, but also because they prevented the shock from spreading to the financial sector, from where it would have reverted to the economy with more uncertainty, bankruptcies and massive job losses. If we applied this simple 1:3 ratio in Chile, we would conclude that, in the absence of the policy response we have had, this shock would have had an impact equivalent to about 17 points of GDP, very similar to the cumulative fall in activity in the 1982-83 crisis. Thus, the fiscal, monetary, financial and regulatory policy response has also contributed to reducing the potential impact of the crisis by a third, largely preventing its spread to the financial system. This does not mean minimizing the magnitude of the crisis that the economy has suffered, much less its impact on people, but aims to emphasize that the preservation of financial stability is strongly related to the stability of the economy and the well-being of people. For that very reason, we need to stay vigilant, identify new risks and vulnerabilities, and cooperate in developing mitigators. Although we think that the most critical point of the crisis was reached in mid-2020 and we have begun a recovery that limits the vulnerabilities of economic agents, the risks are still far from disappearing and we could not forgive that, after having gone through such a difficult period, we failed the country in the last stretch. This IEF has that special meaning. We remain at your disposal for questions and comments. bench central Chile FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT MAY 2021 Thanks a lot. * * *

Title: Monetary Policy Report December 2021. Mario Marcel, President.
text: bench central Chile PRESENTATION OF THE MONETARY POLICY REPORT TO THE FINANCE COMMITTEE OF THE HONORABLE SENATE OF THE REPUBLIC * *No Monetary Policy Report of December 2021 can be found at . Mario Marcel President Central Bank of ChileDecember 15, 2021 Introduction Madam President of the Senate Finance Committee, Senator Ximena Rinc97n. Senators members of this Commission, Senators, I appreciate the invitation to present the vision of the Council of the Central Bank of Chile on recent macroeconomic developments, their prospects and implications for monetary policy. This view is contained in detail in the December 2021 Monetary Policy Report (IPoM), published this morning. This background provides the background for the decision taken by the Council at the Monetary Policy Meeting on Tuesday. The IPoM that we present today shows that, in recent months, the economy has remained on a path of strong expansion led by private consumption. With this, growth in 2021 will exceed what was expected in September, closing the year with activity levels significantly higher than those prior to the crisis, as well as its estimated potential. On the other hand, inflation has continued to rise, standing at over 6.5 percent annually in November, a figure explained mainly by the extraordinary expansion of domestic demand and the depreciation of the peso caused by local factors. These have been added to global phenomena such as increased global demand, disruptions in international value chains for goods due to the pandemic and rising commodity prices. Likewise, higher inflation has lasted long enough to risk second-round effects through the indexation of contracts and wage increases. The costs of inflation on the economy are already visible, and have become one of the main economic concerns of households and businesses. The containment of inflation is, at this time, a priority to alleviate the situation of those who were already the ones who suffered the most with the first blows of the Covid-19 crisis. To this end, it is necessary to withdraw the measures to stimulate domestic demand deployed during the emergency, given that, after it, they are pressuring prices rather than boosting activity. On the fiscal side, this means that public spending will be adjusted to the budget approved for 2022, initiating a path of convergence towards sustainable debt levels in the medium term, in line with the proposals of the Autonomous Fiscal Council. On the monetary side, after having gone from its technical minimum to 4 percent in the second half of 2021, the Council estimates that the MPR should continue to increase in the short term, to be above its nominal neutral value d0 which is consistent with the inflation target of 3 percent d0 for much of the monetary policy horizon. This adjustment in fiscal and monetary policies will help to gradually close the activity gap, helping to ensure that recent inflationary dynamics do not have a persistent impact on the price formation process. We highlight in this IPoM that the risks around this scenario are relevant, given the deterioration of the local capital market and the persistent uncertainty. This has led to significant increases in long-term interest rates and a lower appetite for Chilean financial assets, which has not allowed an adjustment of the economy as in past episodes and will represent a growing obstacle to investment. Added to this are risks of deteriorating external financial conditions as the major economies respond to rising inflation. I will now turn to our assessment of the economic outlook and its risks. Macroeconomic scenario Since the previous IPoM, economic activity has continued to exhibit great dynamism, which has even exceeded what was expected in September when the projections of the IPoM already considered a significant upward correction of the growth forecast for this year. Thus, after the pre-crisis level of activity was exceeded in the second quarter, in the third quarter GDP accelerated its quarterly expansion, reaching 21 percent annualized. At the beginning of the fourth quarter, October's Imacec grew 15 percent in twelve months (17 percent annually for the non-mining part), although with lower monthly expansion speeds than previously observed. Private consumption has continued to be the most dynamic component of spending, growing 27.5 percent year-on-year in the third quarter. On the supply side, this has been reflected in the continued expansion of the trade sector and the acceleration of services. With this, GDP not only recovered pre-pandemic levels, but continued to accelerate in the third quarter, a behavior that was even more noticeable in consumption (graph 1). Annual CPI inflation continued to rise in recent months, reaching 6.7 percent in November. He highlighted the rise in volatile prices d1 including energy d1 whose annual rate of change has climbed rapidly and reached 10.5 percent in the penultimate month of the year. Although the core CPI d0 which excludes volatile ones d0 showed a more limited annual expansion rate (4.7 percent), it has also increased steadily during 2021 and is at its highest level in the last six years. Within the core CPI, the annual change in the price of goods exceeds that of services, however, both have had an upward trajectory during the year (Graph 2). In the case of services, it should be considered that some prices and administered rates have not presented increases in accordance with their usual readjustability rules for several quarters. In fact, when these items are excluded from service inflation, their annual rate of change is significantly higher. The recent rise in inflation has been accompanied by a significant rise in expectations of future inflation. The different indicators d0 surveys and prices of financial assets d0 suggest that annual CPI inflation will end 2021 in figures close to 7 percent, at the same time that they have been increasing their forecasts for a year term, approaching values of the order of 5 percent. Although private expectations contemplate a downward trend in inflation towards 2023, they are still above 3 percent over the twenty-four-month term (Chart 3). The main cause of the higher price increases has been local factors. The projections of the central scenario that I will show you in a few moments consider that the average annual inflation of the fourth quarter of this year will reach figures of the order of 6.5% per year, which represents an increase of 3.6 percentage points compared to the annual inflation that was registered in the last quarter of 2020. Of this increase, more than three quarters are associated with local factors, be they the behavior of demand or the impact of the idiosyncratic depreciation of the peso. External factors are of much lesser relevance (Figure 4). Chile stands out as one of the countries where the currency has depreciated the most, where policies have been implemented to support the most significant incomes, where there is a greater increase in private consumption and where the increase in inflation is among the highest (graph 5). As shown in one of the boxes in this IPoM, a more formal statistical analysis indicates that global and local factors have played a different role in the evolution of inflation in different countries. In these results, the local factor has had a relevant weight in the increase in inflation without volatile in Chile and the US, while, in others, such as France, global or common factors between economies have been more important. It is necessary to emphasize that, although the contribution of the global factor is relevant for most economies, this does not mean that in these countries the origin of inflation is completely imported, but rather that it has been caused by a factor that is common to several economies globally, such as the relatively synchronized opening of economies after the most complex part of the pandemic. The dynamism of spending has led Chilean GDP growth to be among the highest in the world for 2021, has caused the economy to operate well above its short-term capacity and that accumulated cost pressures are exacerbated (graph 6). An unequivocal reflection of the excess domestic demand is the largest current account deficit, despite a high copper price and the significant depreciation of the peso. Of note is the high current account deficit measured at trend prices, which will reach 6.7 percent of GDP this year. Thus, the strong increase in national income in 2021 d0 thanks to the cyclical recovery and the increase in the price of copper d0 has been more than offset by the behaviour of private and public consumption, depressing national savings. This is how the consumption of durable goods has already accumulated several quarters of expansion at very significant rates, exceeding by more than 60 percent the level registered before the social crisis and the pandemic. Consumption of non-durable goods and services rose significantly in the third quarter. The sum of the various extraordinary contributions to household liquidity d0 resources provided by the State and withdrawals from pension funds d0 yields a total of close to US85 billion between 2020 and 2021, equivalent to 34 percent of last year's GDP. Most of the resources that have not yet been consumed are still in current accounts and people's sight, which allows us to anticipate that the higher expenditure will persist in the coming quarters (figure 7). In the labour market, people's labour supply has put a brake on the recovery in employment, leading to higher nominal wage growth than in 2020. Vacancies have had a significant increase throughout the year, which has been reflected in an increase in employment compared to the fall it accumulated in mid-2020. In fact, formal salaried employment has already recovered to its pre-pandemic level, while the less formal categories are in this process (Figure 8). According to November's IPN, supply constraints are evident in a wide range of sectors, especially in lower-skilled jobs. According to INE data, there are around one million more inactive than in January 2020 and the willingness to work more hours is at historic lows. While the labour participation rate has narrowed the gap from its pre-pandemic level, women and people over 55, as well as those under 25, still lag significantly, a phenomenon also seen in several other economies (Figure 9). Investment continued to recover in the third quarter, with significant dynamism in all its lines. The machinery and equipment component maintained high growth, especially for industrial use and cargo vehicles. In construction and other works, the reactivation of building projects and engineering works related to mining has been key. In fact, according to the third-quarter CBC cadastre, 2021 investment is among the highest in the last five years (figure 10). The macroeconomic scenario has been marked by the sharp deterioration of local financial conditions in the last year. Behind this phenomenon there are multiple factors, among which the impact of massive liquidations of pension savings and the persistence of political-legislative uncertainty stand out. These phenomena, added to the greater volume of bond issues by the Treasury to finance the increase in the deficit of 2021, have put special pressure on the fixed income market. As a result, there has been a significant rise in long-term interest rates, double that observed in a group of comparable economies. Thus, with a high degree of volatility, the yield on 10-year bonds in pesos (BTP-10) has risen in the order of 300bp during 2021 (graph 11). As discussed in one of the boxes in this Report, a significant part of the increase in long-term interest rates is explained by a greater perception of risk (Figure 12). Rising long-term interest rates are having a visible impact on individuals and businesses. It has had an impact on the loss of value of the most conservative pension funds, on continuous redemptions of type 3 mutual funds and on the rise in the cost of mortgage loans and other long-term financing instruments. Short-term rates have also shown significant increases in recent months, linked to the change in the stance of monetary policy. This factor, however, has had less relevance for long-term rates. High uncertainty and increased risk perceptions around the Chilean economy have reduced appetite for local and long-term assets. In this context, the preference for foreign currency assets has increased, with greater demand for deposits and current accounts in dollars and for financial instruments that invest abroad, a phenomenon that has occurred transversally. Likewise, the outflows of financial capital from residents in Chile that have been observed since 2019 have persisted. In fact, between October 2019 and October of this year, households and companies accumulated an outflow of around 30 billion dollars (graph 13). Thus, despite the high price of copper and the higher rate differential, the Chilean peso has had a significant depreciation (of almost 18 percent) during 2021. For its part, the level of the real exchange rate is much higher than its average of the last two decades (Chart 14). The increase in the cost of banking funding, together with the greater degree of uncertainty regarding the evolution of the economy, have contracted the supply of credit in a context in which demand also remains contained. The Bank Credit Survey (ECB) and the IPN report that uncertainty regarding the economic environment and the rise in banks' funding costs are the main reasons behind the greater restrictions on financing in all loan portfolios. For the housing segment, in particular, there is an increase in the required foot and the shortening of credit terms, among others. Demand for credit, meanwhile, is held back by both high liquidity and sustained uncertainty (Chart 15). The baseline projections described in the next section reflect the negative impact of these factors on the future investment outlook. Externally, although the world economy continues to recover from the impacts of the pandemic, the data of recent months have shown less dynamism than expected. Activity in the third quarter was weaker than projected in major economies. Beyond the ups and downs in the control of the pandemic, demand remains dynamic while supply has denoted growing problems. These include disruptions in supply chains resulting from remaining constraintsd1some of which have intensified in several economies most recentlyd1increased shortages and prices of various raw materials, and labor markets that remain tight in the face of a slow recovery in labor supply (Figure 16). Inflation has continued to rise globally, both in developed and emerging economies, changing the perception of the transience of the inflationary phenomenon. The sustained high level of global demand for goods, in the face of a supply whose capacity to respond remains limited, has continued to push the prices of various raw materials and key goods and services, such as freight. Several developed countries have seen significant surprises in recent months' data, and in some of them annual inflation has reached levels not seen for more than a decade. This trend has also occurred in emerging countries, especially in Latin America (Figure 17). In any case, as I mentioned at the beginning, the increase in inflation has been very heterogeneous between countries, being greater in economies where stimulus policies have been more significant. In this context, an increasing number of monetary authorities have announced, initiated or continued the withdrawal of monetary stimulus. The Federal Reserve slowed the pace of its asset purchases, and recent statements by its authorities have signaled the possibility of an acceleration of the withdrawal of stimulus. Among commodity exporters, Norway and New Zealand have started raising rates in recent months. In Latin America, where significant exchange rate depreciations are recorded, Colombia has already begun the cycle of increases and Brazil and Chile accelerated it in recent months. The European Central Bank is one of the few that maintains its transitory view of inflation and its commitment to the expansionary nature of its policies, largely due to a less aggressive behavior of inflation (Graph 18). Projections of the central stage The central projection scenario sees total CPI inflation remaining at around 7 percent for a few months, only to begin to decline in the second quarter of 2022 and stand at 3 percent within the two-year policy horizon. In the short term, the projection is revised upwards compared to September in response to the sustained dynamism of activity and spending, the additional depreciation of the peso, the already registered increase in energy prices, the upward inflation surprises of recent months and the effect of indexation. For core inflation, it is expected to reach slightly above 6% by the first half of 2022, driven by indexation and the pass-through of exchange rate depreciation (Chart 19). Towards the medium term, a key assumption for the convergence of inflation to the target is the resolution of the imbalances presented by the Chilean economy. The record suggests that in the third quarter of 2021 the economy operated widely d0 in the order of 5 percent d0 above its potential level. In the central scenario, this gap will gradually close from the first quarter of 2022, returning to levels around zero between the end of next year and the beginning of 2023 (figure 20). The closing of the activity gap means the end of the massive transfer programs of the Treasury motivated by the health emergency, as well as the extraordinary withdrawals of pension funds. This scenario also includes a tighter monetary policy and assumes a return of two-year inflation expectations to the 3 percent target. Even so, the central scenario maintains levels of uncertainty above historical levels, which has a particular impact on investment and job creation. In this scenario, the economy is forecast to grow between 11.5 and 12.0 percent in 2021. This range is above the estimate in September (between 10.5 and 11.5 percent), reflecting the aforementioned greater dynamism in activity and spending, with significant revisions in private consumption and investment in machinery and equipment. Between 2022 and 2023, the annual expansion rates of the economy will have a significant reduction, as a result of considerably more demanding bases and in a manner consistent with the expected change in macroeconomic momentum and the closing of the activity gap. Thus, by 2022 and 2023, the economy is projected to grow between 1.5 and 2.5 percent, and between 0.0 and 1.0 percent, respectively. Negative quarterly growth rates are likely to occur on this trajectory, although the level of activity that the economy will reach at the end of the projection period will be very similar to that expected in the June and September Reports (Chart 21). The high base of comparison, the extinction of direct fiscal transfers, the use of accumulated liquidity in recent quarters, the withdrawal of the monetary impulse and the tighter financial conditions will lead to a contraction in private consumption over the next two years, concentrated in durable consumer goods. In the central scenario, private consumption will fall 0.2 percent in 2022 and 1.5 percent in 2023, explained by a substantial reduction in the consumption of durable goods after its strong accumulation during 2021. Gross fixed capital formation will also perform weakly over the next two years, with tighter financial conditions resulting from structural changes in the local capital market, as well as the persistence of greater uncertainty, playing a key role. The central scenario assumes that investment will decline by 2.2 percent in 2022, then increase marginally in 2023 (Table 1). In these projections, public investment and the drag of large projects will not be enough to offset the impact of local uncertainty and high long-term interest rates on other components of private investment. The effect of the depreciation of the peso and the poor performance of the stock market is added, as well as the limited prospects for expansion of the local economy for the next biennium. In fact, various sources of information indicate lower investments for the next two years. The central scenario assumes that fiscal policy will be implemented in accordance with the approved budget for 2022 and that in the following years it will follow the path of convergence outlined therein. This implies a significant drop in spending derived from the end of massive transfer programs motivated by the health emergency. This will lead to a significant reduction in the effective and structural fiscal deficits next year. In the medium term, the scenario assumes that the trajectory presented in the last Public Finances, which would be consistent with a gradual convergence to sustainable public debt levels, consistent with the recommendations of the Autonomous Fiscal Council. The central scenario considers that towards the end of the projection horizon the TCR will continue to be above its averages of the last fifteen to twenty years. Since the previous IPoM, the exchange rate has increased again, reaching values around 840 per dollar at the statistical close of this Report. At the same time, the real exchange rate is around 110 in its index 1986100. The return to historical levels of real exchange rates will be limited by changes in national savings generated over the past two years, which will make investment more dependent on external financing. The baseline also foresees lower external momentum over the next two years. The average growth of Chilean trading partners is reduced to 3.6 percent (4 percent in September) for the period 2022-2023. While developed economies continue to present a favorable outlook, the US is expected to have less expansionary fiscal and monetary policy than expected, reducing its growth prospects. In emerging economies, high inflation and a less expansionary monetary policy anticipate a scenario of lower growth. In China, uncertainty about the prolongation of bottlenecks, energy shortages and the slowdown in the real estate sector suggest less dynamism. The terms of trade will remain high, although lower than in the September IPoM. This, with projections for the price of copper that do not present major changes, while those of oil are somewhat higher: on average, US 3.83 per pound and US 68 per barrel for 2022-2023 (table 2). Sensitivity scenarios The central scenario is based on a set of assumptions regarding the economic environment, the behaviour of agents and the orientation of policies. On these assumptions, sensitivity exercises can be carried out that, while maintaining GDP growth around the expected ranges, require somewhat different monetary policy action. Thus, there are scenarios where the evolution of domestic spending could give way to trajectories that take the MPR in opposite directions, marking the lower and upper limits of the MPR corridor. On the one hand, the adjustment of private consumption from its current high levels could take longer than expected or be less intense, which would delay the closing of the activity gap by generating additional inflationary pressures. Such a scenario would require a more contractionary monetary policy, placing the MPR at the upper bound of the rate corridor. On the other hand, a scenario in which the persistent uncertainty that has affected the Chilean economy in recent quarters causes a more negative effect on consumption and investment than anticipated cannot be ruled out either. In this situation, medium-term inflationary pressures would be reduced, leading to monetary policy that would return faster to levels around neutral. This scenario marks the lower boundary of the TPM corridor. A scenario where idiosyncratic uncertainty eases would lead to a decrease in short-term inflationary pressures , which have been largely determined by exchange rate developments, while increasing the dynamism of activity in the medium term. In this context, it is expected that a less contractionary monetary policy will be required than in the central scenario. The set of these scenarios forms the TPM corridor presented in each IPoM (figure 22). The current rate corridor is shifting higher compared to September, in response to higher inflationary pressures built up in recent months. At the same time, the corridor is narrowing, given the need for faster rate hikes to avoid the accumulation of second-round effects on prices and a persistence of expectations above the inflation target. Thus, for a significant period, the lower edge of the current corridor is above the nominal neutral MPR for inflation of 3 percent. Risk scenarios In addition to sensitivity exercises, risk scenarios are analyzed in which changes in the economy would be more significant and where the reaction of monetary policy would exceed the limits of the corridor for the MPR. Domestically, the main risk remains that the evolution of public finances is not clear about their stabilization in the long term. In such a situation, greater spending pressures than expected in the central scenario would be observed, along with a more significant deterioration in the local financial market and the value of the peso. In such a situation, higher inflationary pressures would lead to the need for an increase in the MPR above the upper limit of the corridor, yet inflation may not be able to converge to the policy target within the two-year horizon. Externally, the main risk relates to the possibility of a hasty withdrawal of monetary stimulus in the US amid the apparent weakness of the Chinese economy. A scenario in which the inflationary outlook in the US becomes complicated could lead the Federal Reserve to withdraw stimulus more aggressively, significantly deteriorating financial conditions for emerging economies. Its negative effects could be amplified by the weakness that the Chinese economy has recently shown and the financial problems in some of its large companies. A scenario like this would aggravate the negative effects on external demand and commodity prices, leading to a fall in activity that would quickly turn the activity gap negative. In such a scenario, the MPR could be below the lower limit of the corridor. Monetary policy stance At its October and December Meetings, the Board adjusted the MPR faster than expected in the central scenario of the September MPR, responding to the increased risks to the convergence of inflation to the target. On the one hand, domestic demand has shown a very high dynamism, which has led to the activity gap, after closing more quickly towards the middle of the year, being at much more positive levels than expected in the second half of this and early next year. On the other hand, effective inflation data surprised to the upside for several months, with market expectations that have increased in both the short and medium term. In fact, in the two-year term, the expectations measured in surveys and those measured in the prices of financial assets are above 3 percent. In addition, the deterioration of the domestic capital market and the persistent uncertainty observed during this year have caused, which has caused a significant depreciation of the peso. The projections of this IPoM consider that the economy requires an adjustment of spending in 2022 and 2023 to undo the imbalances incubated in recent times. Monetary policy will cooperate in this, taking the MPR to a higher level than indicated in the September IPoM. In the central scenario, the Board estimates that the MPR will continue to increase in the near term, to be above its nominal neutral level d0 which is consistent with the 3 percent inflation target d0 for much of the monetary policy horizon. With this, the activity gap will gradually close, helping to ensure that recent inflationary dynamics do not have a persistent impact on the price formation process. The convergence of inflation to the target is important not only for the fulfillment of the Central Bank's mandate, but also to alleviate the economic situation of households, which have previously suffered the impact of the Covid-19 crisis. Although the required adjustment may generate negative figures of seasonally adjusted quarterly variation at some point in the next two years, it should be noted that the level of activity will be higher than projected in September for much of 2022 (graph 20). Likewise, the most important adjustment in spending will occur in the consumption of durable goods, offsetting the strong accumulation they had in 2021. The likelihood of activity declines could subside significantly if uncertainty and pressures on the capital market are reduced. Over the past few months, several expectations indicators show that market players expect inflation to be above 3 percent by the end of the two-year monetary policy horizon, as opposed to the central bank's inflation target. So far, there is no evidence that this is influencing the dynamics of inflation, which, together with the significant slowdown expected for the economy and a monetary policy that responds to changes in the scenario, is sufficient to guarantee the convergence of inflation within the next two years. However, in a scenario where inflation expectations remain high and make it difficult for inflation to converge over the policy horizon, further increases in the MPR will be necessary in the short term. In any case, as always, the implementation of monetary policy will be contingent on the effects of new information on the projected dynamics for inflation. Final Thoughts Dear President, Senators, The presentation of this IPoM is the first public activity that I carry out as in the framework of the second period that I will exercise as President of the Central Bank of Chile, after the appointment with which the President of the Republic honored me. It represents, therefore, an opportunity to make some reflections on the challenges that I had to face together with the Board and the Staff of the Bank during the five years of my first term and the new challenges that lie ahead. The five years that have just ended have been unusually intense, both in terms of content and the environment in which the Bank's work has taken place. In terms of content, it is clear that in the last two years we have faced three overlapping crises which, having originated in non-economic factors, have affected economic activity, the financial system and prices on an unprecedented scale and sequence. This prompted us to give, from the beginning, equally unprecedented answers. Thanks to its institutional autonomy, the Central Bank of Chile was the first to respond to the shocks suffered by the economy, articulating in the whole period, about 25 measures aimed at cushioning its impact, preventing its spread to other areas and facilitating subsequent recovery. An update of the study we presented in the September IPoM indicates that credit stimulus measures, articulated in conjunction with the Ministry of Finance and the CMF, were the ones that contributed most to mitigating the impact of the Covid-19 crisis on the economy in 2020 and the first three quarters of 2021 (table 3). The latter also speaks to the importance of coherent and coordinated action of monetary policy, fiscal policy, and financial regulation when the economy faces unusually adverse circumstances. It is important to note, however, that these crises and consequent effects not only demanded a response from the Bank in the macroeconomic and financial spheres, but also extended to all areas of our institutional work. Thus, along with operationalizing many of the measures through interventions in specific markets, we also had to respond to a significant increase in demand for cash, the need to generate real-time data for decision-making, and inform citizens and markets more clearly about the situation of the economy in times of great uncertainty. With regard to the conditions in which this work was developed, like many other institutions and organizations, we were affected by the health restrictions adopted to control the pandemic. In particular, the quarantines for the commune of Santiago, which totaled the equivalent of seven and a half months, forced the Central Bank to operate from the homes of officials distributed throughout the city and even outside it, and not from its institutional building. The teleworking of 700 people, performing the regular and additional functions was possible thanks to the extraordinary support of the IT area and the human resources management area. Although it is almost inevitable to focus attention on the challenges imposed by the crisis, the work of the last five years did not begin or end with it. During the years leading up to the social outbreak, we had to deal with an economy with low growth, deflationary risks, global trade conflicts, and the need to strengthen the banking system. In the same way, the demands of the population in terms of information and means of payment, as well as technological progress did not stop during the crisis, and demanded concrete responses from the Central Bank. How was the Institution able to cope with the immediate challenges of the crisis, the follow-up of previous problems and the parallel advancement of society and technology? First, we have a clear navigation chart d0 the Strategic Plan 2018-2022. As I have highlighted on other occasions in this instance, it was prepared with the participation of all levels of the Bank and considering the perceptions of our main reference groups, with the purpose of materializing a vision of how it could strengthen the confidence of citizens in a context of accelerated changes. This gave us the willingness and the instruments to adapt quickly to disruptive changes in the country's scenario, responding in a timely and effective manner to an unprecedented crisis, without abandoning longer-term tasks. Second, we strengthened our ability to act as a team. During this time we have had a stable and committed Council, which has been able to incorporate and promote new visions, always focused on our mandates and faculties. Cooperation and cohesion have also been strengthened with the changes in the organizational structure adopted in 2018, which generated a solid line of divisional management that covers both economic and support areas related to operations, treasury, technology, communications and human resources. This was especially timely at a time when the Central Bank has been sued in every dimension of its work. Third, we never lost sight of the fact that the Bank's main asset is the people who work there. In the course of the crisis, we intensified internal dialogue and exchange with experts on issues further from our competence. When this was no longer possible in person, we turned to technology, which also helped us keep work teams connected. In this way, intensifying and adapting the means to link and communicate, we tried to ensure that in the course of the pandemic no one felt alone, helpless or powerless in the face of what was happening in the country. Today I can say with legitimate pride that we have risen to the occasion. We have led actions to contain the impact of the crisis. We have strengthened confidence in the institution in a time of questioning. We have kept the team united and motivated. This has been reflected in various external evaluations, as well as in personal and institutional recognitions1. But the most important thing for us is the significant increase in knowledge of the Bank among citizens. A survey conducted this year reveals that the proportion of people who have heard of or know the Bank rose from 54 to 90 percent between 2017 and 2021 (Figure 23). The fact that the Bank is going to face the next four years with the same President of the previous five may suggest the idea of continuity without major changes, but it would be misleading. Changes in the environment will continue to be very important, and the Bank must be able to adapt to them, even from leadership positions. Responding to the trust that citizens have placed in the institution d0 and sustaining that trust over time d0 forces us to be prepared to adapt to scenarios that mutate in an accelerated and often surprising way. The challenges will come first and foremost from the economy itself. There is still a long way to go for the country to fully recover from the crisis and reach a new balance that takes into account the structural transformations that have occurred in recent years, on the one hand, as well as those that can be promoted by the new political authorities that will take office next March. In this context, the Central Bank of Chile still has a very important task: that of controlling inflationary pressures in a way that facilitates d0 and does not hinder d0 the full rearrangement of the economy. A second source of change is given by the ongoing constitutional process. In our appearance before the Commission on Justice Systems, Autonomous Control Bodies and V During 2021, two relevant evaluations were published for the Bank: the review of institutional transparency practices based on the Central Bank Transparency Code of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the Stability Assessment of Chile's Financial System, a program developed jointly by the IMF and the World Bank, both with very positive feedback for the Bank and recommendations for improvement that are already being implemented. Likewise, the Institution was ranked 10th among the best companies to work for in Chile in the Great Place to Work (GPTW) ranking. At the same time, it ranked 5th among the entities that promote and enhance female employment in the GPTW Women. Finally, it was ranked above benchmark for organizations in Chile in the Values Barometer of the Business Generation Foundation. Constitutional Reform of the Constitutional Convention, an instance that is addressing the issue of the Central Bank, we stated that our aspiration was to have the best future institutional framework, having opportunities for improvement with respect to the current regulations. To contribute to the discussion, we delivered to the commission a dossier with 10 documents, several of which correspond to comparative analyses with respect to other central banks in the world on issues such as institutional mandates, dimensions of autonomy, powers, accountability and coordination with the government. Once the regulations for the Central Bank are approved along with the rest of the new constitutional text, there will still be the task of adapting the Organic Law, including matters that the Convention has considered proper to it. Thirdly, the evolution of the digital economy will require answers and the leadership of the Central Bank, particularly with regard to means of payment. Thus, for example, the security, speed and interoperability of retail digital means of payment, incorporated into the so-called 4-part model, will be important. The Bank will also have to take care of the implications arising from the eventual approval of the Fintech Law, among which the regulation of so-called stablecoins, or digital currencies with capital backing, stands out. Finally, the Institution shall take a position on the need and conditions for the issuance of its own digital currency. All these issues, some of which are already under development and organized around what we have called the Central Bank's Digital Agenda, will be addressed in an institutional position paper (White Paper), which will be published next March. Fourth, the Bank will need to fully address the challenges that climate change and ecosystem developments pose to the economy. While these challenges can be addressed within the Bank's current mandate, powers, and competencies, it is clear that, to be most effective, it will be necessary to focus on the dimensions where it adds the most value and can complement the work of other institutions. To this end, the Bank has already joined the Global Network of Regulators for Green Finance (NGFS) and the Natural Capital Committee formed by the Ministry of the Environment of Chile. Similarly, work has begun to regularly generate carbon emissions accounts and estimate Chile's natural capital. Finally, there are many issues on which, despite significant progress, the work is not yet complete. These include strengthening the Bank's ties with society and the groups most relevant to the institution, enriching the link with all regions of the country, and promoting diversity at all levels and levels of the organization. All these issues, and some others, will be reflected in the Strategic Plan 2023-2027, which will be developed in the course of next year. This work will continue to be motivated by making the Central Bank of Chile a reliable institution for Chileans, reinforcing its character as a key entity for the development of the country and exercising our autonomy with responsibility, judgment and creativity at the service of a better quality of life. Senators. This occasion is special not only because of the topics I have just discussed, but because this is the last presentation of an IPoM that will be attended by two outstanding participants of the last decade. I am referring, first of all, to our Vice-President, Joaqu92n Vial, who at the beginning of next February completes his term as Director. He will be replaced by Luis Felipe Cespedes, whose nomination was recently ratified by the Senate. Secondly, this will also be the last presentation of the IPoM in which Senator Carlos Montes will participate. Regardless of their different location at this table, both are carriers of an extensive career of commitment to good public policies, in which they have made great contributions to the country. We have met Joaquin many times, alternating first in the Directorate of Budgets and then coinciding in the Council of the Central Bank. I have had to interact with Carlos in the legislative process for 32 years, usually in the Commissions of Finance of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, where I have always found him seeking and encouraging him to go further, demanding more from imagination, analysis and ability. Joaquin's prudence and Carlos' ambition are two attributes, apparently contradictory, that have nevertheless contributed to improving public policies in our country. Personally, I want to tell you that I will miss you in this instance, but that I have no doubt that we will meet in others, as has happened before. Thank you very much for your attention and now we look forward to listening to your comments and answering your questions. text_original: banco central Chile Presentacin del informe de Poltica Monetaria ante la Comisin de Hacienda del Honorable Senado de la Repblica Mario Marcel Presidente Banco Central de Chile 15 de diciembre de 2021 Introduccin Seora Presidenta de la Comisin de Hacienda del Senado, Senadora Ximena Rincn. Senadores miembros de esta Comisin, Senadoras y Senadores, Agradezco la invitacin para presentar la visin del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile sobre los desarrollos macroeconmicos recientes, sus perspectivas e implicancias para la poltica monetaria. Esta visin est contenida en detalle en el Informe de Poltica Monetaria (IPoM) de diciembre de 2021, publicado esta maana. Estos antecedentes aportan el trasfondo para la decisin adoptada por el Consejo en la Reunin de Poltica Monetaria de ayer martes. El IPoM que les presentamos hoy da cuenta de que, en los ltimos meses, la economa se ha mantenido en una senda de fuerte expansin liderada por el consumo privado. Con esto, el crecimiento de 2021 superar lo previsto en septiembre, cerrando el ao con niveles de actividad significativamente superiores a los previos a la crisis, as como a su potencial estimado. Por su lado, la inflacin ha seguido aumentando, ubicndose en noviembre por sobre 6,5 por ciento anual, cifra explicada fundamentalmente por la extraordinaria expansin de la demanda interna y la depreciacin del peso causada por factores locales. Estos se han agregado a fenmenos globales como el aumento de la demanda mundial, las disrupciones en las cadenas de valor internacional de bienes a causa de la pandemia y las alzas de los precios de las materias primas. Asimismo, la mayor inflacin se ha prolongado lo suficiente como para arriesgar efectos de segunda vuelta a travs de la indexacin de contratos e incrementos salariales. Los costos de la inflacin sobre la economa ya son visibles, y se han transformado en una de las principales preocupaciones econmicas de hogares y empresas. La contencin de la inflacin es, en este momento, una prioridad para aliviar la situacin de quienes ya fueron los que ms sufrieron con los primeros embates de la crisis del Covid-19. Para ello es necesario retirar las medidas de estmulo a la demanda interna desplegadas durante la emergencia, dado que, pasada sta, estn presionando los precios antes que dinamizar la actividad. Por el lado fiscal, esto supone que el gasto pblico se ajustar al presupuesto aprobado para 2022, iniciando una senda de convergencia hacia niveles de deuda sostenibles en el mediano plazo, en lnea con las propuestas del Consejo Fiscal Autnomo. Por el lado monetario, despus de haber transitado en la segunda mitad de 2021 desde su mnimo tcnico hasta 4 por ciento, el Consejo estima que la TPM deber seguir aumentando en el corto plazo, para ubicarse por sobre su valor neutral nominal aquel que es coherente con la meta de inflacin de 3 por ciento durante gran parte del horizonte de poltica monetaria. Este ajuste de las polticas fiscal y monetaria contribuir a que la brecha de actividad se cierre gradualmente, colaborando a que la dinmica inflacionaria reciente no tenga un impacto persistente sobre el proceso de formacin de precios. Destacamos en este IPoM que los riesgos en torno a este escenario son relevantes, dado el deterioro del mercado de capitales local y la persistente incertidumbre. Esto ha provocado alzas significativas de las tasas de inters de largo plazo y un menor apetito por activos financieros chilenos, lo que no ha permitido un ajuste de la economa como en episodios pasados y representar un obstculo creciente para la inversin. A ello se agregan riesgos de deterioro de las condiciones financieras externas como respuesta de las principales economas al alza de la inflacin. Reflexiones finales Estimada Presidenta, Senadoras y Senadores, La presentacin de este IPoM es la primera actividad pblica que llevo a cabo como en el marco del segundo perodo que ejercer como Presidente del Banco Central de Chile, luego de la designacin con la que me honrara el Presidente de la Repblica. Representa, por tanto, una oportunidad para hacer algunas reflexiones sobre los desafos que me toc enfrentar junto al Consejo y el Staff del Banco durante los cinco aos de mi primer mandato y los nuevos retos que se vislumbran a futuro. Los cinco aos que acaban de culminar han sido inusualmente intensos, tanto por el contenido como por el entorno en que se ha desarrollado el trabajo del Banco. En lo que respecta al contenido, es evidente que en los ltimos dos aos hemos enfrentado tres crisis superpuestas que, habindose originado en factores no econmicos, han afectado a la actividad econmica, el sistema financiero y los precios a una escala y en una secuencia indita. Esto nos impuls a dar, desde un comienzo, respuestas igualmente inditas. Gracias a su autonoma institucional, el Banco Central de Chile fue el primero en responder a los shocks que sufri la economa, articulando en el conjunto del perodo, cerca de 25 medidas orientadas a amortiguar su impacto, evitar su propagacin a otros mbitos y facilitar la recuperacin posterior. Una actualizacin del estudio que presentamos en el IPoM de septiembre indica que las medidas de estmulo al crdito, articuladas en conjunto con el Ministerio de Hacienda y la CMF, fueron las que ms contribuyeron a mitigar el impacto de la crisis del Covid-19 sobre la economa en 2020 y los primeros tres trimestres de 2021 (tabla 3). Esto ltimo habla tambin de la importancia de una accin coherente y coordinada de la poltica monetaria, la poltica fiscal y la regulacin financiera cuando la economa enfrenta circunstancias inusualmente adversas. Es importante resaltar, sin embargo, que estas crisis y consecuentes efectos, no solo demandaron una respuesta del Banco en el mbito macroeconmico y financiero, sino que se extendieron a todos los mbitos de nuestro quehacer institucional. Es as como, junto con operacionalizar muchas de las medidas mediante intervenciones en mercados especficos, tambin debimos responder a un aumento significativo de la demanda por efectivo, a la necesidad de generar datos en tiempo real para la toma de decisiones, e informar con mayor claridad a la ciudadana y los mercados sobre la situacin de la economa en momentos de gran incertidumbre. En lo que respecta a las condiciones en que se desarroll este trabajo, como muchas otras instituciones y organizaciones, nos vimos afectados por las restricciones sanitarias adoptadas para controlar la pandemia. En particular, las cuarentenas para la comuna de Santiago, que totalizaron el equivalente a siete meses y medio, obligaron a que, durante buena parte de los ltimos dos aos, el Banco Central operara desde los hogares de funcionarias y funcionarios distribuidos por toda la ciudad y an fuera de ella, y no desde su edificio institucional. El teletrabajo de 700 personas, desempeando las funciones regulares y adicionales fue posible gracias a un extraordinario apoyo del rea de informtica y de la de gestin de recursos humanos. Aunque es casi inevitable fijar la atencin en los desafos que impuso la crisis, el trabajo de los ltimos cinco aos no comenz ni termin con sta. Durante los aos previos al estallido social, debimos lidiar con una economa con bajo crecimiento, riesgos deflacionarios, conflictos comerciales globales y la necesidad de fortalecer el sistema bancario. Del mismo modo, las exigencias de la poblacin en materia de informacin y medios de pago, as como el avance tecnolgico no se detuvieron durante la crisis, y demandaron respuestas concretas del Banco Central. Cmo pudo la Institucin hacerse cargo de los desafos inmediatos de la crisis, el seguimiento de problemas previos y el avance paralelo de la sociedad y la tecnologa? En primer lugar, contamos con una carta de navegacin clara -el Plan Estratgico 2018-2022. Como lo he destacado en otras oportunidades en esta instancia, ste se prepar con participacin de todos los estamentos del Banco y considerando las percepciones de nuestros principales grupos de referencia, con el propsito materializar una visin de cmo ste podra fortalecer la confianza de la ciudadana en un contexto de cambios acelerados. Esto nos dio la disposicin y los instrumentos para adaptarnos rpidamente a cambios disruptivos del escenario del pas, respondiendo de manera oportuna y efectiva a una crisis indita, sin por ello abandonar tareas de ms largo plazo. En segundo lugar, fortalecimos nuestra capacidad para actuar en equipo. Durante este tiempo hemos contado con un Consejo estable y comprometido, que ha sido capaz de incorporar y promover nuevas visiones, siempre centrados en nuestros mandatos y facultades. La cooperacin y la cohesin tambin se han fortalecido con los cambios en la estructura organizacional adoptados en 2018, que generaron una slida lnea de gerencias divisionales que abarcan tanto las reas econmicas, como las de apoyo, relacionadas con las operaciones, tesorera, tecnologa, comunicaciones y recursos humanos. Esto fue especialmente oportuno en un momento en que el Banco Central ha sido demandado en todas las dimensiones de su quehacer. Tercero, nunca perdimos de vista que el principal activo del Banco son las personas que all se desempean. En el curso de la crisis, intensificamos el dilogo interno y el intercambio con expertos en temas ms lejanos a nuestras competencias. Cuando ello ya no fue posible de modo presencial, recurrimos a la tecnologa, la que tambin nos ayud a mantener conectados a los equipos de trabajo. De esta manera, intensificando y adecuando los medios para vincularnos y comunicarnos, procuramos que en el curso de la pandemia nadie se sintiera solo, desamparado o impotente frente a lo que ocurra en el pas. Hoy puedo decir con legtimo orgullo que hemos estado a la altura de las circunstancias. Hemos liderado las acciones para contener el impacto de la crisis. Hemos fortalecido la confianza en la institucin en una poca de cuestionamientos. Hemos mantenido unido y motivado al equipo de trabajo. Esto se ha reflejado en diversas evaluaciones externas, as como en reconocimientos personales e institucionales1. Pero lo ms importante para nosotros, es el significativo aumento del conocimiento del Banco entre la ciudadana. Es as como una encuesta realizada este ao, revela que la proporcin de las personas que ha escuchado hablar o conoce al Banco se elev desde 54 a 90 por ciento entre 2017 y 2021 (grfico 23). El que el Banco vaya a enfrentar los prximos cuatro aos con el mismo Presidente de los cinco previos puede sugerir la dea de continuidad sin mayores cambios, pero sera equvoco. Los cambios en el entorno seguirn siendo muy importantes, y el Banco deber ser capaz de adecuarse a ellos, incluso desde posiciones de liderazgo. Responder a la confianza que ha depositado la ciudadana en la institucin y sostener dicha confianza en el tiempo obliga a estar preparados para adaptarnos a escenarios que mutan de manera acelerada y muchas veces sorpresiva. Los desafos vendrn en primer lugar de la propia economa. An resta mucho para que el pas se recupere plenamente de la crisis y alcance un nuevo equilibrio que considere las transformaciones estructurales que se han producido en los ltimos aos, por una parte, as como aquellas que pueden impulsar las nuevas autoridades polticas que asumirn en marzo prximo. En este contexto, el Banco Central de Chile tiene an una tarea muy relevante: la de controlar las presiones inflacionarias de un modo que facilite y no entorpezca el pleno reacomodo de la economa. Una segunda fuente de cambios est dada por el proceso constitucional en marcha. En nuestra comparecencia a la Comisin sobre Sistemas de Justicia, rganos Autnomos de Control y V Durante 2021 se publicaron dos evaluaciones relevantes para el Banco: la revisin de prcticas institucionales de transparencia basadas en el Cdigo de Transparencia de Bancos Centrales del Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI), y la Evaluacin de la Estabilidad del Sistema Financiero de Chile, programa desarrollado en conjunto por el FMI y el Banco Mundial, ambas con retroalimentacin muy positiva para el Banco y recomendaciones de mejora que ya se estn implementando. Asimismo, la Institucin se ubic en el lugar 10 entre las mejores empresas para trabajar en Chile en el ranking Great Place to Work (GPTW). Al mismo tiempo, ocup el 5 lugar entre las entidades que promueven y potencian el empleo femenino en el GPTW Mujeres.
