Title: Chilean economy Economic Outlook and Outlook
text: Chilean Economy-Situation and Outlook. Presentation by Mrs. Mar92a Elena Ovalle, Counselor of the Central Bank of Chile, held at the SERNAM of Temuco and at the University of Temuco, October, 1998. I. Introduction For more than a decade, economic policies have been developed with a seal of commitment to macroeconomic and financial stability. In this period, a solid position of solvency and external liquidity has accumulated, a trajectory of sustained reduction in inflation has been achieved, in a context where the financial system is in healthy conditions, the surplus in the fiscal accounts has been constant and public indebtedness is at minimum levels. It is these strengths that allow us to face the current situation with confidence, but at the same time, they represent a high and demanding standard, which must be taken care of to maintain the privileged position occupied by the Chilean economy among the emerging countries of the world. 1. A decade of sustained and high growth. Average GDP growth in the period 1986-1997 was 7.6%. Output growth in 1997 was 7.1% and by 1998 it is expected to be about 5%. The GDP per capita of our country is US 5,500 (1997). According to World Bank measurements, in which a methodology approved between countries is used is just under US 10,000, the highest in Latin America. One of the greatest achievements of economic policy is the decline in single-digit inflation, without sacrificing growth or damaging the country's external position (1997 6%, 1998 4.5%, 1999 4.3%). It is the8th year of declining inflation and 5th year of single-digit inflation. These figures are unprecedented in Chile. The main objective of the Central Bank is price stability, setting gradual targets for reducing inflation. Its medium-term goal is to reach industrial country rates, this is about 3% per year. The decline in inflation is more significant considering that it has been achieved with steady growth, low unemployment and healthy external accounts. 2. The International Scenario and its Impact on the Chilean Economy. Global growth for the next 2 years has experienced a progressive deterioration. Growth of 2.0 per cent is expected in 1998 and 2.5 per cent in 1999, conditional on the start of a recovery process in Japan. The causes of the decline in growth in the world are mainly the Asian crisis, the gradual slowdown in the US and a more significant slowdown in Latin American economies, while the European economies remain the same as in 1997 and the same is expected for 1999. There are significant risks that do not rule out lower global growth, which are: a. Further deterioration of Japan's economy. b. New mistrust of Asian economies and waves of contagion to other emerging economies. c. Faster slowdown of the US economy or a slowdown in European economies d. Possibility of a drastic correction in US and European stock price. The external scenario described has various effects on the Chilean economy, which are transmitted mainly through changes in the flows of the current account and capital account of the balance of payments. In the current account the The consequences of the external crisis are manifested in changes in the prices and quantities of trade in goods and services. In the capital account, a distinction can be made between changes in investment capital flows and external financing to Chile and variations in the demand for international assets from domestic agents. (a) Effect on the terms of trade The slowdown in the global economy has reduced the dynamism of demand for major commodities. Indeed, the dollar prices of primary goods have fallen by more than 20% in the last twelve months. In particular, the price of copper fluctuated around 75 cents per pound during 1998. In the current external scenario, it is prudent to assume that for the remainder of this year and part of next, the situation will not change significantly. The medium-term outlook, meanwhile, is more optimistic, with values closer to one dollar a pound. On the other hand, the external crisis has also led to reductions in the dollar prices of other raw materials and processed products in the economies most affected by the crisis. Chile is favored by this fact, both for its effect on the current account and for the moderation in domestic inflationary pressures. During the period from January to July of this year, the average price of imports, measured in dollars, has fallen about 5.0% compared to the same period of the previous year. However, this situation cannot be projected for the future, considering that it is less likely that there will be additional decreases in the price of raw materials and, in addition, that the dollar will continue the pace of international appreciation that it has shown in the course of the last year. In sum, the reduction in the terms of trade of the Chilean economy will reach about 10% for this year, which subtracts from national income the equivalent of two percentage points, and has a negative impact on the deficit of the trade balance estimated at US 1,400 million. Part of this larger deficit is counterbalanced by the reduction in profits of foreign copper companies. (b) Effects on trade volumes Chilean export volumes increased by 7.3 per cent during the period January to July 1998 over the same period last year. The volume of copper exports grew by 14.5% and exports other than copper grew by 2.2% in the reporting period. These figures show that the effect of the external crisis on real exports is smaller than that observed in other periods of slowdown in international activity, such as those in 1991 and 1993. The reason for this is the substantial geographical reorientation of Chilean exports. Indeed, it is observed that in the period from January to July of this year, in respect of the same months of In 1997, the volume exported to Asia decreased by 7.9 per cent, while that of the rest of the world grew by 15.4 per cent, a phenomenon observed to varying degrees for all categories of goods. (c) External financing flows The third effect of the global crisis is the reduction in capital and financing flows into the country. During the first half of 1998, there was a significant decrease in portfolio investment from abroad. In any case, the sum of medium and long-term capital reached US 4,700 million in the first half of the year, substantially higher than the current account deficit in the same period and very similar to the flows received in previous years in relation to GDP. In turn, the greater preference of international investors for currencies, markets and instruments considered safer, has led to a general increase in the cost of external financing of emerging economies. However, it should be noted that these increases have been lower than those registered in other economies in the region and, in absolute terms, the cost of external financing for Chile remains well below the average for Latin America. Importantly, interest rates in industrial countries, especially long-term ones, have tended to decline. On the other hand, during this year, an important characteristic of the Chilean economy has been the accumulation of assets abroad. There has been a very significant movement in the capital account during 1998 stemming from increased demand for international assets by the private banking and non-banking sector. This movement has meant an increase in outflows for investments from Chile abroad d0 direct investments, portfolio investments and accumulation of other short-term assets d0 which in this period total just over US 4,400 million. These portfolio adequacy movements have been influenced by the greater degree of uncertainty in the international economy and the depreciation in the value of the peso over the last few months, reacting through a greater demand for assets that allow exchange risk hedging, as well as an increase in interest in taking advantage of greater international diversification of the asset portfolio. Conclusions 1. The international situation is complex and there is uncertainty about its future evolution, about its depth, time frame and form that the recovery will take. 2. The high degree of financial and real integration of the country with the rest of the world must be recognized and, therefore, the risks on the future evolution of the Chilean economy and projections. 3. Within the possible scenarios, there could be a limited reduction in the price of copper, new financial turbulence in international markets and a more marked slowdown in exports. As a result, domestic policies should exhibit a greater degree of flexibility and favour prudence and austerity. 4. At this moment there have been events that allow us to look more optimistically at the external situation, such as the lowering of rates in the US and England, the election of Cardoso in Brazil and the consensus that exists between international institutions and the unusual countries to take concrete measures to face the crisis. II. Situation of the Chilean Economy I think it is important to visualize what happened to remember what was the situation of the Chilean economy prior to the Asian crisis. There was a strong dynamism of domestic demand, which must be recognized as a constant feature of the decade. The increase in the total investment rate (33% of GDP) was not accompanied by a similar increase in national savings (22% of GDP). Another way of looking at the same is the widening of the current account deficit, the reduction of which is one of the Central Bank's major concerns. In the 2nd half of 1997, domestic demand expanded by over 12% compared with the 2nd half of 1996, while GDP grew by 9% per year in the same period (import growth was 20%). Part of this spending drifted to domestic markets, generating more dynamic GDP growth and a narrowing of the labor market, bringing the unemployment rate below historical trend, while nominal wages continued to grow at the same time. 8% per year. The excellent results of the national economy during the last 10 years had generated an atmosphere of optimism for the development of new projects by companies (strong growth of internal and external sales, increase in productivity). At the same time, from the perspective of consumers (increase in private income, real wages and employment, decrease in unemployment rate and reduction in inflation), together with optimism, generated greater momentum to spending. In turn, the deepening of the domestic capital market, together with greater access to international financial markets, provided the necessary funds to validate these spending decisions and decouple to a greater degree the investment decisions of companies and families from their ability to save. The needs of large companies to finance investment projects with their own resources had decreased, the financial system has expanded into new segments, in particular loans to individuals. This generated a growing pressure for funds in the domestic credit market, driving up domestic interest rates and, at the same time, a greater use of external savings (current account deficit). In turn, the strong interest of international investors to participate in the Chilean economy, even paying the reserve, provided the necessary resources to finance the deficit. In 1997, the economy received net external resources in the order of 10% of GDP, almost double the financing requirements of the cta.cte deficit. As of the4th quarter of 1997, the application of an effort to contain domestic demand to bring it towards levels in line with the new external scenario became imminent. The macroeconomic programme implemented since January 1998 aims to reduce the current account deficit over a limited period of time, without jeopardizing the medium-term equilibria of the economy. Economic policy consistent with these objectives is based on the restrictive stance of monetary and fiscal policies. It is important to recognize that one of the consequences of external turbulence is the natural uncertainty that occurs among private actors about the policies of authority. The macroeconomic programme that had been defined by the end of 1997 needed to be adapted to the new realities. This fact generates a series of interactions between the market and the authority, where on the one hand legitimate doubts are opened regarding the prevailing policies and on the other, the new signals delivered by the authority must gain credibility. This has been one of the most relevant elements in the application of monetary policy this year and is manifested in two facts. First, the Central Bank's firm decision to maintain the inflation target at all times as a basis for ordering the rest of macroeconomic policies and as a signal for private sector decisions. Second, the greater effort to coordinate fiscal and monetary policy. In the absence of these two fundamental options, uncertainties would have increased rather than decreased. 1. Pillars of Macroeconomic and Financial Stability One of the reasons why our country has been less affected than other emerging economies, as mentioned at the beginning, has been because of the solidity and firmness of the fundamentals of the Chilean economy. I would like to make a brief review of these fundamentals. 1.1. Solvency and external liquidity. Chile has a solid position of solvency and international liquidity. Over the last decade, Chile's solvency and external liquidity indicators have shown a highly favourable evolution, a trajectory that has been accompanied by a gradual process of financial internationalization of the Chilean economy. Proof of this has been the magnitude of capital flows to or from Chile, the degree of international integration of financial markets, the unification of exchange markets, the level of country-risk assigned by specialized agencies to our economy, as well as the spread of rates obtained by the main Chilean companies when contracting long-term external financing. Although these indicators have shown a somewhat more unfavorable evolution during the last year due to external financial turbulence, this process has not weakened the solvency and external liquidity bases of the Chilean economy. Indeed, the weight of external debt for the Chilean economy is lower than that of the rest of the Latin American economies and that of Asian countries. Graph na13 shows that the ratio of external debt, net of international reserves, to GDP is highly favorable for our country compared to the countries of Latin America and Asia. This strength is the result of the economic policy carried out in recent years, which has had as one of its objectives, the achievement of a current account deficit in line with the most permanent sources of financing. Therefore, our policy has defined as an explicit objective the maintenance of current account deficits that average a value between 4% and 5% of GDP. Although in the current conjuncture this is higher than this value, this is understood in the context of the weakened international scenario and the bank's policy of dealing with it with a combination in which adjustment and financing are roughly combined in parts. Next year, with the fiscal effort announced at the end of September, it will be possible to return to the range estimated as reasonable. Liquidity and external vulnerability indicators are also very favourable to the Chilean economy; They clearly reflect a differentiation with respect to the rest of the countries that have been, in one way or another, touched by the crisis, the service of the external debt as a percentage of GDP, shows that Chile does not have the same vulnerability as other countries in Latin America and Asia. The same is indicated by the number of months of imports covered by international reserves and short-term debt as a percentage of total debt. Chile's sovereign risk is A- according to Standard & Poor's, and BAA1 according to Moody's, which corresponds to the best ranking for Latin American countries. It can be seen that it has been getting better and better. Chile is one of the thirty countries considered strongest by the International Monetary Fund, among the 182 member countries of the fund. Chile is a creditor of the fund, the second largest creditor in relation to its quota. In conclusion, we can point out that the Chilean economy is in a solid international financial position. The Central Bank has no foreign debt. Short-term debt is small, and maturities of medium- and long-term debt next year and next year do not reach 1/6 of our reserves. The above indicators are an important test of the strength of our external sector, both in absolute terms and in comparative terms with other economies. 1.2. Soundness of the Financial System Our financial system is sound and consolidated. During the course of recent years the Chilean financial system has tended towards a progressive consolidation, deepening in the domestic market, developing new products - factoring, leasing, securitization, among others - and internationalizing. The deepening of Chile's financial system is substantially greater than that of other Latin American and Asian countries. In fact, the ratio of money to quasi-money to GDP reaches 40%, a figure that is almost double that of some of our neighbors, also significantly exceeding that of Asian economies, such as Korea, the Philippines and Indonesia Total placements in relation to GDP in Chile are 2 times higher than in the average of the three largest Latin American countries. Chile's stock market assets, as a proportion of GDP, are between four and five times greater than that of its next country in Latin America. Another strong point of the Chilean financial system, which is frequently mentioned by international analysts, is the strength of its regulation and the quality of supervision carried out by the Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions. In fact, solvency indicators, such as the level of capitalization and the proportion of the portfolio that is overdue, confirm this assertion. The level of capitalization of the financial system, measured according to the Basel indicator, as of July this year is 11.5% of risk-weighted assets, almost 2% more than last year, and higher than that recommended as an international standard. The non-performing loan portfolio as a percentage of total loans remained at levels considered very good in July, this is around 1.2%, well below those of other emerging and still developed economies. Moreover, the provisions on placements far exceed that figure. In terms of financial performance, during the first half of this year the bank showed a solid position, with a profitability indicator that reached annualized levels close to 14% in July. Likewise, the growth of placements in twelve months, although declining, currently remains above 12%, while commercial placements grow at a rate close to 17% per year. In conclusion, the Chilean economy has a solid and well-capitalized financial sector, which allows us to look calmly at future developments, the current external crisis has confirmed once again that it is not enough to maintain macroeconomic balances. The financial sector is also required to be efficient and strong. The first, so that it makes a good allocation of credit resources, and the second, so that a credit crisis does not occur at the first symptom of slowdown in the economy. 1.3. Fiscal Soundness Fiscal management is serious and responsible. During the nineties, the management of fiscal policy has made it possible to balance and strengthen public finances, reaching an average global surplus of 1.8% of GDP and substantially reducing public debt. In addition, the government's fiscal policy objective has been to achieve high and stable savings rates, which on average have been 4.5% of GDP and which have made public savings one of the most stable components of national savings. This level of public savings has become the main source of financing for public investment, replacing gradually external indebtedness and reducing financial dependence on external cycles. These high levels of savings have been possible thanks to an adequate control of current expenditure which, although it has grown, on average, above the product, has been healthily financed, given the high rates of increase in public revenues, especially tax collection. The advantages of having accumulated fiscal surpluses over the years are manifold. Today, the economy has greater flexibility to manage domestic interest rates because increases in these do not significantly affect the fiscal budget, agents know this. Therefore, in Chile, a policy of high interest rates has more credibility than in other countries, which facilitates the adjustment process. According to the latest figures provided, in the second half of 1998 fiscal expenditure will grow by 3.5%, which will register 5.5% for the year (figure above the growth of output). On the other hand, given the current situation, government revenues from copper will decrease by 46.4% this year. For 1999 the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to create opportunities for the most vulnerable groups by maintaining a fiscal policy adjusted to support economic stability, so that public spending will be 2.8% for 1999 including pension readjustment (1.5%), while the central government's current account surplus will be 3.5% of GDP and the overall 0.2%. 1.4. Strength of the Real Sector The real sector is also strong. One of the most remarkable facts of the nineties is the high growth of investment, which has led the Chilean economy to levels of investment never seen in its economic history. Indeed, gross fixed capital formation averaged 27.6 percent of GDP over the period 1990-97, measured at constant prices. Moreover, it continues to show a continuous upward trend, becoming one of the fundamental pillars of our country's economic growth. The other factor that has sustained the high growth of this decade is the increase in employment and the quality of the workforce. Indeed, during the decade, the rate of job creation reached an average rate of around 2.5% per year, and the level of unemployment reached an average rate of around 7%. In turn, incorporating the increase in quality, the quality-corrected workforce has had an average growth of around 4% in the period. To measure the growth of the quality of the labor force, the Central Bank has constructed an index that reflects changes in its composition according to its educational level, measured in years of education and weighted according to relative wages. Thus, this index grows as the relative importance of the more educated workforce increases. This fact is directly related to the issue of productivity and real wages. Wages have grown at an average rate of between 3% and 4%, consistent with the trend growth in labor productivity. The aforementioned indicators reflect the significant development of the Chilean business and labor sector. This has been widely pointed out in the world rankings of competitiveness, highlighting its managerial and entrepreneurial capacity, the growing degree of technical training of executives, entrepreneurs, and workers, as well as its innovative attitude. These important aspects can be reaffirmed with the figures provided by Prochile, an institution that has provided a great service to the country, referring to different aspects of the export sector. For example, the number of exporting firms has increased from 3,462 in 1989 to 5,841 in 1997, of which 83.2% are firms exporting less than US1 million annually. Similarly, the number of products exported has also increased significantly: from 1,490 in 1989, 3,771 products were shipped abroad in 1997. The dynamism of our exports has been a constant throughout the last decade. Proof of this is that during this year the destinations of our exports have been reoriented towards those markets with greater thrust in the current situation. Indeed, volumes to Asia have decreased significantly and increased to the rest of the world. It is also important to highlight the growth of non-traditional exports that in the current situation have grown by 11% in volumes during the first half of the year, compared to the same period last year. The current situation that our economy is experiencing is an important test of the capacity of the Chilean business sector, in the sense that it has to move with enough agility in the face of the changing situation of the markets, in order to maintain its sales in more competitive conditions. The fundamentals of the real economy are solid, we have productive capacity, an educated workforce and an entrepreneurial capacity that has proven capable of leading development and weathering previous crises. 1.5. Strength of Institutions and Policies. We have strong institutions, which work. The international recognition achieved by the Chilean economy over the last few years has been largely supported by the solidity and prestige achieved by its institutions. In particular, the autonomy of the Central Bank has been a key element both in the setting of the main macroeconomic goals and in the reception by the market of the policies implemented by the authority. Our main commitment to the country's economy is to ensure the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal and external payments, being the exclusive competence of this entity the determination of monetary and exchange policies. Notwithstanding this independence or autonomy of the policies of the Central Bank, coordination with the Ministry of Finance is given important privilege in all those areas of macroeconomic work that merit it, seeking with these coordination bodies the general consensus of policies. The rigor and technical capacity of the institutions that carry out the economic policy of our country, as well as the solidity of other regulatory entities, facilitate the understanding and compliance with the rules and policies taught by the authority. This is a great asset that our country has, which allows the efforts made by the technical teams to be correctly implemented in practice. Another important element to highlight at this point is related to the transparency of the policies implemented. Indeed, from 1997 onwards, a summary extract of the minutes corresponding to the quarterly monetary policy meetings began to be published, as a way of making known in greater detail the framework on which monetary and exchange rate policies are being made in the country. These publications are added to the usual summaries of council meeting minutes that are delivered with a lag. The Central Bank now has a frequently updated website where you can find the latest available information, advisory agreements and key documents, as well as speeches and public statements by the bank's authorities. As a rule, all official speech will be on the website at the time of issue, so that there is no privileged access to the bank's information. Our institutions are strong and internationally recognized. This solidity is supported by recent international recognition of the low level of possible corruptions in the Chilean institutional system. 2. Chilean Economy 1998 and Outlook 1999. 2.1. Objectives and Policies The difficult times facing the global economy, as well as our own economy, have required a dose of greater discipline and prudence in the formulation of objectives and greater flexibility in the implementation of policies. Within the new international economic circumstances, the Central Bank seeks as its main objective to maintain the macroeconomic and financial stability of the country. To this end, it has reaffirmed its commitment to the process of gradual reduction of inflation and with the firm intention of bringing the current account deficit to a sustainable level in the medium and long term. Achieving these objectives will result in an economic growth rate consistent with the adverse external scenario. Achieving the above objectives requires that monetary and exchange rate policy instruments be applied firmly and consistently, and that fiscal policy be adjusted to the times. Likewise, the cost of achieving these objectives depends crucially on the credibility of the policies implemented by the economic authority. Everyone knows that the greater the credibility in macroeconomic policies, the less sacrifice there will be in terms of slowing economic growth, employment and wages. Premature easing of adjustment policies or overreactions in the exchange rate would only ruin the stability achieved over a decade and lead the country to a longer period of lower growth, higher unemployment, and higher inflation. The external crisis and its negative impact on the terms of trade and the supply of external financing, as well as the increase in demand for foreign assets, in a context of strong domestic demand pressures, made the application of a demand containment effort inevitable at the beginning of this year. to bring the current account deficit to levels in line with the new international scenario. Subsequently, and in a complementary manner, both the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance have taken a series of measures aimed at reinforcing the firm commitment to medium- and long-term economic stability. Among the main measures adopted this year are the application of a tighter monetary policy from January, together with a greater degree of flexibility in the management of liquidity and more active participation in the foreign exchange market by the Central Bank. Subsequently, towards the end of June, at a time of great uncertainty, the implementation of a narrower band was announced as a guide for the exchange rate, the provision of new hedging instruments would exchange rate and the reduction of reserve requirements would change it to capital inflows to 10%. Although the adjustment in global spending has proceeded well, the Chilean financial market was involved in episodes of high volatility of the interbank rate, volatility that was transmitted to the other interest rates in the market. This necessitated an improvement in the policy mix in place since 25 June in order to adequately preserve macroeconomic stability. On September 16, the Central Bank Council resolved to address more aggressively the excessive volatility of market interest rates, while deciding to incorporate some technical modifications to the exchange rate band, with the aim of granting greater flexibility to the administration of monetary, exchange rate and fiscal policies. In particular, it was decided to make the purposes of the short-term monetary policy more explicit, raising the instance rate to 14% of the variation of the UF, a value that, although unusually high, is lower than that shown by the interbank rate in the weeks prior to the measure. In exchange rate matters, the limit of the band was modified, expanding it to /-3.5% with respect to the dollar agreement. A gradual extension of the band was incorporated, as an additional measure, until December 31 of this year, until it is in a range of /-5%. Another element incorporated was the elimination for this year of the discount for external inflation to the dollar rule agreement, which will also be indexed by the inflation target. The complex external situation was also addressed through the capital account via the elimination of the exchange reserve for all capital inflows. This measure goes in direct support to the private sector in everything that says related to the financing of investment projects. The combination of measures taken on September 16 was aimed at facilitating the normalization of interest rates, thereby reducing the pressure on financial markets in recent weeks. After the measures adopted in September and thanks to the consolidation of the adjustment underway together with the positive reaction of the market manifested through more stable and declining rates, the Board of the Central Bank last Tuesday (13/10/98) decided to reduce the instance rate by 200 basis points from 14% to 12%. The Central Bank will manage liquidity so that the interbank interest rate fluctuates around the new instance rate, thus allowing the normalization of market interest rates. However, the bank will continue to maintain flexibility, both in terms of liquidity management and in setting the instance rate, so as to continue to adequately cope with the changing and unstable international environment. The measures taken during this year and the general behavior that the Central Bank has had during this period have taken into account the fact that in recent months we have been faced with periods of strong financial turbulence in economies such as Japan and Russia. Therefore, the management of a more flexible policy instrument, together with the necessary condition of being constantly alert to possible changes in the international environment, allow greater efficiency in achieving the objectives set by the authority. The announced commitment to limit the growth of public spending in 1999 to a growth of 1.5% and 2.8%, including the readjustment of pensions that is significant, is a sign that helps to dispel doubts, especially in a year with presidential elections. This commitment and its fulfillment are highly valued by the Central Bank. The more that can be done in this field, the faster the necessary adjustment of the economy can be completed. 2.2. Outlook The most recent record indicates that the main economic variables, such as inflation, growth and external accounts, move in the desired direction within limits considered reasonable, given external circumstances. This background supports the macroeconomic program presented to the Senate for this and next year, based on the consolidation of these trends. In the first place, the inflation rate must continue on a path of gradual reduction, in the short term, this commitment is expressed in achieving the inflation target set for this year. It should be noted that inflation rates in 12 months at the end of September and October this year are likely to be close to, and still below, the annual target. However, uncertainties remain about the results in November and December, and macroeconomic policies will be geared towards around /-4.3% in 1999, with continued progress towards price stability in the coming years. Second, the current account deficit in 1998 is estimated to reach around 5.15 billion, but on a path of reduction towards next year, to around US4 billion in 1999 (4% to 5% of GDP), helped by recent announcements of a tighter fiscal budget. We are in the process of revising these figures based on the new fiscal budget and the IMF's new projections for the global economy. Thirdly, the adjustment trend in domestic demand is expected to deepen during the second half of this year, so that it will continue to grow at a very moderate pace, around 1.5 per cent in 1999. The observed and expected slowdown in final sales, lower prices for export raw materials, the increase in long-term interest rates and the higher cost of importing machines and equipment are factors that should accentuate the adjustment of fixed investment in the second half of 1998, a trend that would continue in 1999. Finally, the expected trend in external demand, which has so far helped to dampen economic growth, is expected to break down from the second half of this year and also in 1999, in order to act as a source of impetus for global demand. This expectation is based on two elements. On the one hand, the verification of very important growth rates for some products such as copper exports (due to the entry into operation of new projects and expansion of existing ones) and, possibly, the partial recovery of fishmeal production. On the other hand, the accentuation, in the second half of 1998 and, especially in 1999, of the adjustment trend in imports, with growth projected below GDP. Despite the expected recovery in net exports, GDP growth in 1999 would be significantly lower than the 5 per cent projected for this year as a result of the adjustment in domestic demand. This result, although close to half of the trend growth of the last decade, is adequate considering the complex external scenario. Global absorption, or expenditure, on the other hand, would grow by about 5.5% in 1998, and by about 1.5% in 1999. Even with the moderate expansion expected for this year and next, the average economic growth of this decade will be the highest this century. Although our economy faces a complicated situation associated with the global crisis faced by the vast majority of the world's emerging economies, we must emphasize that the Chilean economy has a solid financial situation and its fundamentals remain firm. III. Conclusions The Chilean economy is facing difficult times. Although its fundamentals are solid, the external crisis with its negative effects on foreign trade and the capital account, forces us to moderate the pace of economic growth until stability is restored in international markets. The fragility of the global economy requires discipline and prudence in the formulation of economic objectives and flexibility in policy implementation. In this context, the economic policy mix has been aimed at achieving a prudent mix between increased external financing and correction of the level of domestic spending. The actions of the Central Bank have sought to promote an orderly adjustment of relative prices and avoid a deterioration in the trend of reducing inflation. Despite short-term risks, the medium-term fundamentals of the Chilean economy remain solid and it is possible in the future to achieve the successful performance of the last decade, ultimately the potential growth of the economy depends on a capacity for investment in human and physical capital, incorporation of new technologies and development of new products and reinvestment. The fixed investment rate is the highest since historical records exist, progress is observed in the educational level of the labor force and new sectors begin to appear that take the lead in economic growth. The structure of flexible markets and a greater effort to save will allow high and sustained growth, at the same time as the deficit of the cta.cte. do not exceed prudent limits in the range of 4% to 5% of GDP. In conclusion, we are living a difficult time that we hope to leave behind in the coming months. The challenges of the current situation will allow us to demonstrate, once again, that the Chilean economy has been built on solid foundations, which allow us to cope with these crises.
