Title: Financial Risks and the Central Bank
text: RIESGOS FINANCIEROS Y EL BANCO CENTRAL Jos8e de Gregorio. President Central Bank of Chile August 2008 Good morning. Welcome to this meeting organized by the Central Bank of Chile for directors and representatives of the banking administration and supervisory bodies of the financial system. The analysis and discussion on the proper management of financial risks is a permanent task of banking. However, today it takes on a particularly relevant nuance as a result of the problems that are affecting developed economies. On the one hand, it is appropriate to assess whether banks' financial risk management policies are prudent and in line with the times. It should be remembered that it is precisely times of financial stress that test the risk management policies and strategies of institutions and those responsible for them, their directors and senior executives. On the other hand, the lessons that have been decanted from the international crisis should lead us to evaluate our regulation and the business practices of banking in general. That is why today we see it as important to share some reflections and participate with you in an open discussion on this topic. At the present juncture I could not think of another person better prepared to join us in the discussion than our guest of honor. Governor Kroszner is an international authority on these matters, both from his prolific activity as an academic and professor at the University of Chicago business school and from his participation from the Federal Reserve in the current financial crisis. Your vision will be very enriching for those of us who participate in this meeting. Most recently, Governor Kroszner has represented the Federal Reserve on the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and the Financial Stability Forum. In this presentation I will first refer to the role of the Central Bank in the stability of our financial system. I will then discuss some of the challenges for banking in the current context and finally make some comments on the lessons that the recent international financial crisis throws for the regulation and conduct of our financial system. The Role of the Central Bank The Central Bank of Chile has a constitutional mandate to ensure the normal functioning of internal and external payments. At the heart of this mandate is the stability of banking. . Discurso inaugural en el High Level Meeting on Risk Management in Banking Institutions, Santiago, 29 de agosto de 2008. Webelieve that the main tool for achieving this stability objective is an appropriate macroeconomic policy framework. The inflation targeting scheme enables inflationary control over a reasonable time horizon consistent with price stability. The floating exchange rate regime allows to accommodate external shocks with a lower cost in employment and product, and at the same time avoids the exchange insurance that has been so costly for Chile in the past. The monetary and exchange rate policy scheme adopted in Chile are key to reducing the vulnerability of the economy to the effects of this crisis, but we are not immune and we have a responsibility to ensure that disruptions are as few as possible, although the recent difficulties caused by high inflation show that this task is neither easy nor cost-free. The delivery of timely and adequate information and the analysis of the potential financial threats facing the economy is a second tool in the post of financial stability. Our Financial Stability Report is the main communication instrument for this. Importantly, as the recent financial crisis shows, even if individual risk analysis is done carefully and rigorously, an inadequate assessment of systemic risks can end up weakening financial institutions excessively. This monitoring must be permanent, not only in times of stress, because many times sudden disruptions would not have been if the appropriate variables had been monitored. The third axis of action of the Central Bank with respect to financial stability is in the regulations of the payment system, the market and liquidity risks faced by banks, and aspects related to the financial integration of the Chilean economy. As a general principle, the Bank has sought to facilitate both international integration and financial innovation, always ensuring that this does not undermine its stability mandate. In terms of regulation of market and liquidity risks, we are in line with the recommendations of international best practices. On the other hand, increases in the maximum limits of investment abroad for AFPs have recently been authorized within the maximum ranges established in Legislative Decree 3,500, after a careful evaluation of the effects of a potential exit of the AFPs and bearing in mind that the purpose of the regulation is not short-term macroeconomic management but the welfare of the affiliates, with due protection for stability. The authorization, with safeguards, of the netting of derivative positions is another example of promoting the financial integration of our market. This seeks to expand flexibility in the taking of derivative positions without undermining the powers of the Central Bank and the SBIF to take preventive actions in cases of bank illiquidity. As for the internal payments system, we have come a long way together with you in recent years. However, we have pending challenges in payment and clearing systems with external agents. As the Chilean economy advances in its integration process, these challenges will increase. Counterparty risk in international financial transactions has become extremely evident since August Last year, and only the determined intervention of the Fed and other central banks of developed countries has prevented a major systemic crisis. This is where we must move forward in the short term. Let me emphasize that the Central Bank does not operate in isolation in preserving financial stability. This is a shared mission between the Central Bank, the superintendencies of the financial sector, the Ministry of Finance and crucially the private sector. Each of those involved addresses financial stability from our areas of action. Central bankers and supervisors around the world highlight the contribution to financial stability that the full implementation of Basel II will deliver. This framework for measuring capital requirements and banking supervision will allow risk and capital levels to be aligned more reasonably. That is why we see with great interest the progress made by the Superintendency of Banks in this area and the intention of the Ministry of Finance to incorporate this modernization of banking legislation in MK III. We have, together with supervisors and the Ministry of Finance, a role in the regulation, monitoring and execution of mitigating actions in case of severe imbalances. The private sector, meanwhile, has an equally important role to play through self-regulation, prudence and market discipline. It is precisely the complementary action of regulators, supervisors and private agents, which seeks to maintain a climate of stability in a financial system that has maintained very good financial indicators, and that contributes, in this way, to the proper functioning of our economy. In this area, the current economic situation brings a series of challenges for Chilean banks in the short and medium term. Let me take the opportunity to point out the three challenges that I consider to be the most important facing banking these days. Challenges for Banking First, and as you well know, the world's major financial centres continue to show a high level of fragility. This fragility is manifested in the weakened capital situation of major financial intermediaries, and uncertainty about the value of their assets. As a result of this uncertainty, the level of activity in various financial markets remains depressed, while the liquidity market among financial intermediaries continues to show high premiums and difficulties in their operation. On the other hand, the housing markets of several developed economies are in a phase of strong contraction, with significant slowdowns or falls in price, which feeds a vicious circle of greater losses, lower capital and lower activity in these markets. We know that a fall in the price of housing, beyond its direct effect on the construction sector, should have limited effects on activity. But when it contaminates the financial sector, the credit channel can significantly exacerbate the business cycle, as we see in some industrialized countries. This is how the main risk to the stability of the financial system that we identified in our last Financial Stability Report d0 the risk of a credit crunch of the supply of external capital for the Chilean economy d0 remains valid. That is why we are in a process of accumulation of reserves, pre-announced and mechanical, so as not to alter the functioning of monetary policy. The second major challenge for banks is the domestic macroeconomic environment of high inflation and higher interest rates. The Central Bank will persist in its efforts to ensure inflationary dynamics consistent with the objective of price stability. As we noted in the communiqu8e of our last monetary policy meeting, in the most likely scenario, additional adjustments will be necessary to ensure the convergence of inflation to the target. We do this with the certainty that the solvency and liquidity of Chilean banks has allowed the Central Bank to implement a tightening of monetary policy without disruption to financial stability. The third challenge for national banks is that of increasing financial integration. On the one hand, the interim reform once again extends the limits of investment abroad for pension funds, passing the global maximums to 60% and 80% in October of this year and next. In the medium term, these limits imply a qualitatively different domestic financial system from the one we have become accustomed to in the last 20 years. In it, pension funds invest a substantial fraction of their portfolio abroad and domestic agents finance a growing fraction of their investment or consumption with external savings. In this scheme, banking plays the fundamental role of intermediating these external resources to companies and consumers, as it does in many highly integrated developed economies. Given the extension of AFP limits, there was legitimate concern about the high dependence of some banks on financing them. This concentration of funding sources could translate into higher liquidity risk. However, we believe that the situation has been properly managed by the industry, taking the necessary safeguards to deal with this situation, and we believe that these safeguards will continue to be taken to the extent that the limits of investment abroad are extended and the existing gaps are filled. Added to the above is the package of measures announced a couple of weeks ago by the Ministry of Finance in the context of MKIII, which seeks to eliminate some of the remaining obstacles to the entry of foreign capital into the Chilean economy and advance in the internationalization of the peso. Within this package of measures, the Ministry of Finance asked the Central Bank to evaluate the authorization of international financial operations in pesos, in order to internationalize the peso. This is an issue that we are evaluating carefully, in order to allow the potential efficiency gains that this measure may entail with the possible risks to stability. On a closely related issue, and continuing with a strategy initiated in 2005, the Central Bank is interested in participating in mechanisms for settling exchange transactions, among which a possible incorporation of the Chilean peso into CLS stands out. Some Lessons from the Subprime Crisis I would like to share with you some thoughts on the lessons of the financial crisis in the financial markets of the United States and some European countries. We must start by recognizing that liquidity risks should never be ignored. Reliance on short-term funding sources, especially wholesale investors, to finance illiquid assets exposes leveraged financial intermediaries to loss of confidence and runs. These are not necessarily withdrawals of deposits, as happened in the case of Northern Rock, but can also be an investor run, as happened with Bear Stearns, a fact that threatened the insolvency of other banks in the United States until the Fed intervened decisively in their rescue and in the expansion of liquidity provision for investment banks. At the Central Bank, we are closely following the international discussion regarding the liquidity risk regulations that have been generated as a result of the crisis. The rescue of Bear Stearns, as well as the toolkit recently approved by the US Congress to support Fanny Mae and Freddy Mac, has once again opened the old debate about the moral hazard of bailout policies. In developing countries we know this, and in Chile we have examples of policies that encourage careless risk management, generating instability. We are very aware of the need to act in a manner consistent with the incentive structure so that this does not happen. The subprime crisis has also opened a debate about the risks of financial innovation. From the outset, it reminds us that higher levels of sophistication do not guarantee the normal functioning of the financial system. A minimum level of regulation, control and monitoring is required. Here in Chile, it took some time before banks were authorized to issue options. And they are only authorized if banks demonstrate that they have adequate financial risk management policies. I believe that progress must be made in the innovation processes, they are very positive, but we must move forward with the proper safeguards. It is important to implement regulatory changes gradually, seeking the adequate delivery of information and transparency in order to ensure adequate monitoring of the risks involved. It is also crucial to carefully review the incentives and potential conflicts of interest posed by the new instruments and processes. Another lesson has to do with the role, at this point essential, that financial risk control and management systems fulfill. A true financial risk control and management system starts with the definition of policies at the highest level, the board, the involvement of senior management in monitoring and monitoring, and, ultimately, the development of an organizational culture that is capable of adequately combining profitability and leadership objectives with prudence and risk sensitivity. Some of these features have been gradually incorporated into our regulation. In this same area, an issue that is at the center of the discussion of financial reforms in developed countries is the global incentive structure of financial intermediaries. Several analysts have argued that the system of Executive compensation, coupled with the subordination of the risk management divisions to the detriment of commercial areas, had to do with the expansion of real estate credit in the United States to clients with minimal probability of payment. I believe that this is an issue that all actors in the financial system must follow closely. It is well known that the board and senior management play a crucial role in the design, implementation and monitoring of these policies and strategies. This has been established in multiple documents discussing best management practices, published by the BIS, the IIF and other international organizations. This is how the board and senior management must have an accurate view of the nature of the risks facing their institution and the coherence between those levels of risks and the level of capital available to face their eventual materialization. These and other observations were highlighted by the Senior Supervisors Group in March 2008 to the Financial Stability Forum, in an effort to distinguish those banks that have behaved appropriately during the current crisis1. On the contrary, the difficult times that banking institutions are experiencing in the United States and other important developed countries are largely explained by the failure to comply with some of these basic premises on financial risk management. The role played by risk rating agencies in the subprime crisis also appears as an important corollary of the current crisis. This is a complex issue, due to the sophistication of some financial instruments, but especially because of the incentives with which the rating agencies operate. The progress that the SBIF has been taking in the wake of the adoption of Basel II d0 and the role of classifiers in this framework d0 lead to this being a discussion that we must follow with extreme attention. Final Comments The current crisis illustrates the importance of not ignoring the macroeconomic environment. The combination of global imbalances, high levels of savings looking for assets to invest in, and low interest rates are often at the center of financial crises. In these scenarios, the incentives to take excessive risks are greater and the powers to detect risky actions are clouded by irresponsible euphoria. This is how many of the triggers of the present crisis are not as novel as many of us believed in its beginnings, dizzy by a sea of new acronyms for financial instruments that only channeled more traditional foundations frequently immersed in financial crises of our history. There is certainly more technology involved, but the origins are similar. Fortunately, we have not observed these problems in Chile, where we have a deep and prudent financial system. We learned from our mistakes and a severe financial crisis nearly 25 years ago. But this should not lead us to complacency, and we should all 1 Senior Supervisors Group on Risk Management Practices, d2Observations on Risk Management Practices during the Recent Market Turbulenced3, We must strive to maintain the health and efficiency of our financial system. When financial crises are added to the business cycle, the costs are immeasurable. As a result of the current problems, there will be more regulation in international financial markets and everyone, even those of us who are not at the centre of the difficulties, should watch carefully. The existence of massive problems of moral hazard, opacity and new ways of complying with the requirement of central banks to provide liquidity is leading to a review of regulatory frameworks at the international level. We must be aware that increased regulation leads to finding ways around it, which may end up threatening financial stability. Going forward, uncertainty is abysmal. We are in a very complicated scenario. We are facing the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression and an inflationary shock only comparable to that of the seventies. Both events alone can have important consequences, but together, their implications can be disastrous. Fortunately, the decisive action of the world's main central banks, as well as flexible policy frameworks with a strong commitment to stability, limits the most adverse scenarios, but uncertainty persists. For our part, the current scheme of economic policies, the prudential regulatory framework, the equity situation of banks, and the solvency levels of the Chilean economy, should facilitate an eventual adjustment to increasingly restrictive conditions. Undoubtedly, a significant external deterioration would have a negative impact on the Chilean economy. However, our analysis suggests that the Chilean financial system is prepared to face this deterioration without becoming a source of risk or volatility that threatens financial stability. You play an important role in preserving stability, a role that we hope you will continue to fulfill and strengthen. Thanks a lot.
text_original: RIESGOS FINANCIEROS Y EL BANCO CENTRAL Jos De Gregorio Presidente Banco Central de Chile Agosto 2008 Muy buenos das. bienvenidos a esta reunin organizada por el Banco Central de Chile para directores y representantes de la administracin de la banca y de los organismos supervisores del sistema financiero. El anlisis y la discusin sobre el manejo adecuado de los riesgos financieros es una tarea permanente de la banca. Sin embargo, hoy toma un matiz especialmente relevante a raz de los problemas que estn afectando a las economas desarrolladas. Por un lado, resulta oportuno evaluar si las polticas de gestin de los riesgos financieros de la banca son prudentes y acordes con los tiempos que corren. Cabe recordar que son justamente los tiempos de stress financiero los que ponen a prueba las polticas y estrategias de manejo de riesgos de las instituciones y a los responsables de ellas, sus directores y altos ejecutivos. Por otro, las lecciones que se han ido decantando de la crisis internacional debiesen llevarnos a evaluar nuestra regulacin y las prcticas de negocios de la banca en general. Es por ello que hoy vemos como importante compartir algunas reflexiones y participar con ustedes en una discusin abierta sobre este tema. En la actual coyuntura no podra pensar en otra persona mejor preparada para acompaarnos en la discusin que nuestro invitado de honor. El gobernador Kroszner es una autoridad internacional en estas materias, tanto desde su prolfica actividad como acadmico y profesor de la escuela de negocios de la Universidad de Chicago como por su participacin desde la Reserva Federal en la actual crisis financiera. Su visin ser muy enriquecedora para los que participamos en esta reunin. En lo ms reciente, el gobernador Kroszner, ha representado a la Reserva Federal en el Basel Committee on Banking Supervision y en el Financial Stability Forum. En esta presentacin me referir primero al rol del Banco Central en la estabilidad de nuestro sistema financiero. Luego discutir algunos de los desafos para la banca en el contexto actual y finalmente har algunos comentarios sobre las lecciones que la reciente crisis financiera internacional arroja para la regulacin y conducta de nuestro sistema financiero. El Rol del Banco Central El Banco Central de Chile tiene un mandato constitucional de velar por el normal funcionamiento de los pagos internos y externos. En el centro de este mandato est la estabilidad de la banca.  Discurso inaugural en el High Level Meeting on Risk Management in Banking Institutions, Santiago, 29 de agosto de 2008. Creemos que la principal herramienta para lograr este objetivo de estabilidad es un adecuado marco de poltica macroeconmica. El esquema de metas de inflacin posibilita el control inflacionario en un horizonte de tiempo razonable y coherente con la estabilidad de precios. El rgimen de flotacin cambiaria permite acomodar shocks externos con un menor costo en empleo y producto, y a la vez evita los seguros cambiarios que tan costosos han resultado para Chile en el pasado. El esquema de poltica monetaria y cambiaria adoptados en Chile son claves para reducir la vulnerabilidad de la economa ante los efectos de esta crisis, pero no estamos inmunes y nos cabe una responsabilidad en velar porque las disrupciones sean las menores posibles, aunque las recientes dificultades provocadas por la elevada inflacin muestran que esta tarea ni es fcil ni est exenta de costos. La entrega de informacin oportuna y adecuada y el anlisis de las amenazas financieras potenciales que enfrenta la economa es una segunda herramienta en post de la estabilidad financiera. Nuestro Informe de Estabilidad Financiera es el principal instrumento de comunicacin para ello. Es importante destacar, que tal como la reciente crisis financiera nos demuestra, aunque el anlisis de riesgos individuales sea hecho con cuidado y rigor, una inadecuada evaluacin de los riesgos sistmicos puede terminar debilitando excesivamente a las instituciones financieras. Este monitoreo debe ser permanente, no solo en momentos de stress, pues muchas veces las disrupciones repentinas no lo habran sido de haberse estado monitoreando las variables adecuadas. El tercer eje de accin del Banco Central respecto de la estabilidad financiera es en la normativa del sistema de pagos, de los riesgos de mercado y de liquidez que enfrenta la banca, y de aspectos vinculados con la integracin financiera de la economa chilena. Como principio general el Banco ha buscado facilitar tanto la integracin internacional como la innovacin financiera, velando siempre de que ello no atente contra su mandato de estabilidad. En materia de regulacin de los riesgos de mercado y de liquidez estamos en lnea con las recomendaciones de mejores prcticas internacionales. Por otra parte, recientemente se han autorizado aumentos de los lmites mximos de inversin en el exterior para las AFPs dentro los rangos mximos establecidos en el D.L. 3.500, luego de una cuidadosa evaluacin de los efectos de una potencial salida de las AFPs y teniendo presente que el propsito de la regulacin no es el manejo macroeconmico de corto plazo sino que el bienestar de los afiliados, con el debido resguardo a la estabilidad. La autorizacin, con resguardos, del neteo de posiciones de derivados es otro ejemplo de promocin de la integracin financiera de nuestro mercado. Con ello se busca ampliar la flexibilidad en la toma de posiciones de derivados sin menoscabar las atribuciones del Banco Central y de la SBIF para tomar acciones preventivas en casos de iliquidez bancaria. En cuanto al sistema de pagos internos, hemos avanzado mucho en conjunto con ustedes en aos recientes. No obstante, tenemos desafos pendientes en los sistemas de pagos y compensacin con agentes externos. Conforme la economa chilena avance en su proceso de integracin estos desafos se van a incrementar. El riesgo de contraparte en transacciones financieras internacionales se ha hecho en extremo evidente desde agosto del ao pasado, y slo la decidida intervencin de la Fed y dems bancos centrales de los pases desarrollados ha evitado una crisis sistmica mayor. Es aqu donde debemos avanzar en el corto plazo. Permtanme enfatizar que el Banco Central no opera aislado en la preservacin de la estabilidad financiera. Esta es una misin compartida entre el Banco Central, las superintendencias del sector financiero, el Ministerio de Hacienda y en forma crucial el sector privado. Cada uno de los involucrados abordamos la estabilidad financiera desde nuestros mbitos de accin. Banqueros centrales y supervisores de todo el mundo destacan el aporte a la estabilidad financiera que entregar la plena implementacin de Basilea II. Este marco de medicin de los requerimientos de capital y de supervisin bancaria permitir alinear de una manera ms razonable los niveles de riesgo y de capital. Es por ello que vemos con sumo inters los avances que ha realizado la Superintendencia de Bancos en la materia y el propsito del Ministerio de Hacienda de incorporar esta modernizacin de la legislacin bancaria en el MK III. Tenemos, junto con los supervisores y el Ministerio de Hacienda, un rol en la regulacin, monitoreo y ejecucin de acciones mitigadoras en caso de desajustes severos. Al sector privado, en tanto, le corresponde un papel igualmente importante a travs de la autorregulacin, la prudencia y la disciplina de mercado. Es precisamente la actuacin complementaria de reguladores, supervisores y agentes privados, la que procura la mantencin de un clima de estabilidad en un sistema financiero que ha mantenido muy buenos indicadores financieros, y que contribuye, de esta manera, al buen funcionamiento de nuestra economa. En este mbito, la coyuntura econmica actual trae una serie de desafos para la banca chilena en el corto y mediano plazo. Djenme tomar la oportunidad de sealar los tres desafos que considero son los ms importantes que enfrenta la banca en estos das. Desafos Para la Banca En primer lugar, y como ustedes bien saben, los principales centros financieros del mundo continan mostrando un alto nivel de fragilidad. Esta fragilidad se manifiesta en la situacin de capital debilitada de importantes intermediarios financieros, y de incertidumbre acerca del valor de sus activos. Producto de esta incertidumbre, el nivel de actividad en diversos mercados financieros permanece deprimido, mientras que el mercado de liquidez entre los intermediarios financieros continua mostrando altas primas y dificultades en su operacin. Por su parte, los mercados de vivienda de varias economas desarrolladas estn en una fase de fuerte contraccin, con importantes desaceleraciones o cadas de precio, lo que alimenta un crculo vicioso de mayores prdidas, menor capital y menor actividad en dichos mercados. Sabemos que una cada en el precio de las viviendas, ms all de su efecto directo sobre el sector construccin debiera tener efectos acotados sobre la actividad. Pero cuando este contamina el sector financiero, el canal del crdito puede exacerbar significativamente el ciclo econmico, tal como lo observamos en algunos pases industrializados. Es as como el principal riesgo para la estabilidad del sistema financiero que identificamos en nuestro ltimo Informe de Estabilidad Financiera --el riesgo de un credit crunch de la oferta de capital externo para la economa chilena-- sigue vigente. Es por ello que estamos en un proceso de acumulacin de reservas, pre-anunciado y mecnico, de manera de no alterar el funcionamiento de la poltica monetaria. El segundo gran desafi para la Banca es el ambiente macroeconmico interno de elevada inflacin y mayores tasas de inters. El Banco Central persistir en su esfuerzo de asegurar una dinmica inflacionaria coherente con el objetivo de estabilidad de precios. Tal como sealramos en el comunicado de nuestra ltima reunin de poltica monetaria, en el escenario ms probable sern necesarios ajustes adicionales para asegurar la convergencia de la inflacin a la meta. Esto lo hacemos con la certeza de que la solvencia y liquidez de la banca chilena ha permitido al Banco Central implementar un endurecimiento de la poltica monetaria sin trastornos sobre la estabilidad financiera. El tercer desafo para la Banca nacional es el de la creciente integracin financiera. Por un lado, la reforma provisional amplia una vez ms los lmites de inversin en el exterior para los fondos de pensiones, pasando los mximos globales a 60% y 80% en octubre de este ao y el prximo. En el mediano plazo estos lmites implican un sistema financiero domstico cualitativamente distinto del que nos hemos acostumbrado en los ltimos 20 aos. En l, los fondos de pensiones invierten una fraccin sustancial de su portafolio en el exterior y los agentes domsticos financian una fraccin creciente de su inversin o consumo con ahorro externo. En este esquema, la banca juega el rol fundamental de intermediar estos recursos externos a empresas y consumidores, tal como lo hace en muchas economas desarrolladas altamente integradas. Ante la ampliacin de lmites de las AFPs hubo una legtima preocupacin por la alta dependencia de algunos bancos del financiamiento de ellas. Esta concentracin de las fuentes de financiamiento se podra traducir en un mayor riesgo de liquidez. Sin embargo, estimamos que la situacin ha sido administrada adecuadamente por la industria, tomando los resguardos necesarios para hacer frente a esta situacin, y consideramos que dichos resguardos se seguirn tomando en la medida que se amplen los lmites de inversin en el exterior y se copen las holguras existentes. Se suma a lo anterior el paquete de medidas anunciadas hace un par de semanas por el Ministerio de Hacienda en el contexto de MKIII, que busca eliminar algunas de las restantes trabas a la entrada de capitales externos a la economa chilena y avanzar en la internacionalizacin del peso. Dentro de este paquete de medidas, el Ministerio de Hacienda solicit al Banco Central evaluar la autorizacin de operaciones financieras internacionales en pesos, a modo de internacionalizar el peso. Este es un tema que estamos evaluando con detencin, a modo de permitir las potenciales ganancias de eficiencia que esta medida puede conllevar con los posibles riesgos a la estabilidad. En un tema estrechamente relacionado, y continuando con una estrategia iniciada el 2005, el Banco Central est interesado en la participacin en mecanismos de settlement de transacciones cambiarias, entre las que destaca una posible incorporacin del peso chileno a CLS. Algunas Lecciones de la Crisis Subprime Quisiera compartir con ustedes algunas reflexiones respecto a las lecciones que arroja la crisis financiera por la cual atraviesan los mercados financieros de los Estados Unidos y algunos pases europeos. Debemos partir por reconocer que los riesgos de liquidez nunca deben ser ignorados. La dependencia de fuentes de financiamiento de corto plazo, en especial de inversionistas mayoristas, para financiar activos ilquidos expone a los intermediarios financieros apalancados a prdidas de confianza y corridas. Estas no necesariamente son retiros de depsitos, como sucedi en el caso de Northern Rock, sino que tambin puede ser una corrida de inversionistas, como ocurri con Bear Stearns, hecho que amenaz con la insolvencia a otros bancos de los Estados Unidos hasta que la Fed intervino decididamente en su rescate y en la ampliacin de provisin de liquidez para bancos de inversin. En el Banco Central estamos siguiendo con detencin la discusin internacional respecto a la normativa del riesgo de liquidez que se ha generado a raz de la crisis. El rescate de Bear Stearns, as como el paquete de herramientas aprobada recientemente por el Congreso norteamericano para apoyar a Fanny Mae y Freddy Mac, ha abierto una vez ms el viejo debate sobre el riesgo moral de polticas de salvataje financiero. En los pases en desarrollo sabemos de esto, y en Chile tenemos ejemplos de polticas que alientan un descuidado manejo de los riesgos, generando inestabilidad. Estamos muy concientes de la necesidad de actuar de manera coherente con la estructura de incentivos para que ello no ocurra. La crisis subprime tambin ha abierto un debate respecto de los riesgos de la innovacin financiera. De partida, nos recuerda que mayores niveles de sofisticacin no garantizan el normal funcionamiento del sistema financiero. Se requiere un mnimo nivel de regulacin, control y monitoreo. Ac en Chile, pas algn tiempo antes de autorizar la emisin de opciones por los bancos. Y solo estn autorizadas si los bancos demuestran que tienen adecuadas polticas de administracin de riesgos financieros. Creo que debe avanzarse en los procesos de innovacin, ellos son muy positivos, pero hay que avanzar con los debidos resguardos. Es importante implementar cambios normativos en forma gradual procurando la adecuada entrega de informacin y transparencia a modo de asegurar un adecuado monitoreo de los riesgos involucrados. Es crucial, adems, revisar con detencin los incentivos y posibles conflictos de inters que planteen los nuevos instrumentos y procesos. Otra leccin tiene que ver con el rol, a estas alturas imprescindible, que cumplen los sistemas de control y gestin de los riesgos financieros. Un verdadero sistema de control y gestin de riesgo financiero parte por la definicin de polticas al ms alto nivel, el directorio, por el involucramiento de la alta administracin en el seguimiento y monitoreo, y, a fin de cuentas, por el desarrollo de una cultura organizacional que sea capaz de combinar adecuadamente los objetivos de rentabilidad y liderazgo con la prudencia y la sensibilidad al riesgo. Algunas de estas caractersticas han sido incorporadas gradualmente en nuestra regulacin. En este mismo mbito, un tema que est en el centro de la discusin de reformas financieras en pases desarrollados es la estructura global de incentivos de los intermediarios financieros. Varios analistas han argumentado que el sistema de compensaciones a los ejecutivos, sumado a la subordinacin de las divisiones de gestin de riesgos en desmedro de las reas comerciales, tuvieron que ver con la expansin del crdito inmobiliario en los Estados Unidos a clientes con mnima probabilidad de pago. Creo que este es un tema que todos los actores del sistema financiero debemos seguir con atencin. Es bien sabido que el directorio y la alta administracin juegan un rol crucial en el diseo, implementacin y monitoreo de estas polticas y estrategias. As ha quedado establecido en mltiples documentos que discuten las mejores prcticas de gestin, publicados por el BIS, el IIF y otros organismos internacionales. Es as como el directorio y la alta administracin deben tener una visin precisa de la naturaleza de los riesgos que enfrenta su institucin y de la coherencia entre esos niveles de riesgos y el nivel de capital disponible para enfrentar su eventual materializacin. Estas y otras observaciones fueron destacadas por el Senior Supervisors Group en marzo de 2008 al Financial Stability Forum, en un esfuerzo por distinguir aquellos bancos que se han comportado adecuadamente durante la crisis actual1. Por el contrario, los momentos difciles que estn viviendo las instituciones bancarias en los Estado Unidos y de otros importantes pases desarrollados, se explican en buena medida por el incumplimiento de algunas de estas premisas bsicas sobre gestin de riesgos financieros. El rol que jugaron las clasificadoras de riesgo en la crisis subprime aparece tambin como importante corolario de la crisis actual. Este es un tema complejo, por la sofisticacin de algunos instrumentos financieros, pero en especial por los incentivos con los que operan las clasificadoras. Los avances que ha ido tomando la SBIF en post de la adopcin de Basilea II --y el rol de las clasificadoras en este marco-- llevan a que esta sea una discusin que debemos seguir con extrema atencin. Comentarios Finales La crisis actual ilustra la importancia de no ignorar el entorno macroeconmico. La combinacin de desbalances globales, elevados niveles de ahorro buscando activos donde invertir, y bajas tasas de inters, son frecuentemente centro de crisis financieras. En estos escenarios, los incentivos a tomar riesgos excesivos son mayores y las facultades para detectar acciones riesgosas se nublan por una euforia irresponsable. Es as como muchos de de los elementos desencadenantes de la presente crisis no son tan novedosos como muchos cremos en sus inicios, mareados por un mar de acrnimos nuevos para instrumentos financieros que tan solo canalizaron fundamentos ms tradicionales frecuentemente inmersos en crisis financieras de nuestra historia. Sin duda hay mayor tecnologa envuelta, pero los orgenes son similares. Afortunadamente, esos problemas no los hemos observado en Chile, donde tenemos un sistema financiero profundo y prudente. Aprendimos de nuestros errores y de una severa crisis financiera hace casi 25 aos. Pero ello no nos debe llevar a la complacencia, y todos 1 Senior Supervisors Group on Risk Management Practices, Observations on Risk Management Practices during the Recent Market Turbulence, http://www.newyorkfed.org/newsevents/news/banking/2008/rp080306.html debemos procurar mantener la salud y eficiencia de nuestro sistema financiero. Cuando al ciclo econmico se le agregan crisis financieras, los costos son inconmensurables. Como resultado de los problemas actuales, habr ms regulacin en los mercados financieros internacionales y todos, incluso quienes no estamos en el centro de las dificultades, debemos observar con atencin. La existencia de masivos problemas de riesgo moral, opacidad y nuevas formas de cumplir con el requerimiento de los bancos centrales de proveer liquidez est llevando a una revisin de los marcos regulatorios a nivel internacional. Debemos estar concientes de que la mayor regulacin conduce a la bsqueda de formas de evitarla, lo que puede terminar amenazando la estabilidad financiera. Hacia delante, la incertidumbre es abismante. Estamos en un escenario muy complicado. Enfrentamos la peor crisis financiera desde la Gran Depresin y un shock inflacionario solo comparable con el de los aos setenta. Ambos eventos por si slo pueden tener importantes consecuencias, pero en conjunto, sus implicancias pueden ser desastrosas. Afortunadamente, la decidida accin de los principales bancos centrales del mundo, as como marcos de poltica flexibles y con un frreo compromiso con la estabilidad, acota los escenarios ms adversos, pero la incertidumbre persiste. Por nuestra parte, el actual esquema de polticas econmicas, el marco de regulacin prudencial, la situacin patrimonial de la banca, y los niveles de solvencia de la economa chilena, deberan facilitar un eventual ajuste a condiciones crecientemente restrictivas. Sin duda que un deterioro externo relevante tendra un impacto negativo en la economa chilena. Sin embargo, nuestro anlisis sugiere que el sistema financiero chileno est preparado para enfrentar este deterioro sin convertirse en una fuente de riesgo o volatilidad que amenacen la estabilidad financiera. Ustedes juegan un rol importante en preservar la estabilidad, rol que esperamos sigan cumpliendo y reforzando. Muchas gracias.

Title: Monetary Policy Report
text: PRESENTATION OF THE FIRST REPORT OF THE FIRST ONE OF THE PUBLIC BEFORE THE HONORABLE SENADO OF THE REPUBLICAN Jos8e De Gregorio President Central Bank of Chile September 11, 2008 Mr. President of the Senate, Senator Adolfo Zald92var Larra92n, Senators, I thank the Council of the Central Bank of Chile for inviting you to present our Monetary Policy Report (IPoM). This presentation coincides with the annual account of the Council of the Central Bank to the Senate, where we present our vision of the recent macroeconomic and financial events of the Chilean economy, as well as its prospects. For decades, our country suffered the disastrous consequences of macroeconomic instability on our development possibilities. External crises followed each other regularly and inflation was high and volatile, a scourge present in the lives of all Chileans. With everyone's efforts, as a country we managed to achieve stability by the middle of the last decade, when we reached single-digit annual inflation records. This has had a significant impact on the well-being of Chileans, especially among the poorest. Since the turn of the century, this stability has been reflected in a mature inflation-targeting regime, which has contributed, decisively, to increasing the resilience of the Chilean economy to external shocks. We therefore have the responsibility to preserve this environment of stability, as it is a necessary condition for a path of sustained progress. Today, the main threat to this environment of stability is the inflationary landscape we face. Inflation is the main problem affecting the Chilean economy. Although the origin of our inflationary problem is mainly external, it is our responsibility as a Central Bank to prevent this adverse situation from becoming a persistent phenomenon, because it will only increase the costs of returning to stability. The inflationary scenario facing Chile has deteriorated drastically in recent months. In addition to the high inflation that was appreciated in the first four months of the year, new increases in food and fuel prices were added, and a greater degree of spread to other prices. Thus, contrary to what was forecast in our May IPoM, inflation reached 9.5% annually in the middle of the year, significantly increasing the risks for its convergence to the target over a horizon of two years. years. This has led to significant increases in inflation expectations in its various measures and has also led to a significant increase in public concern about this issue. The rise in inflation in Chile has not been an isolated event. A significant number of economies, developed and emerging, have seen their annual inflation rates rise sharply in the past year. There are certainly a variety of explanations as to why our inflation and that of the rest of the world have reached the levels they are at today, and part of what I will do in this session of the Honorable Senate will be to present to you the facts that have led us to this situation. It should be noted, however, that, as a Council, we have no doubt that the only way inflation will return to target within two years is with an unambiguous monetary policy response: that is, its tightening, as we have already done in recent months. I will begin, then, by briefly reviewing the international panorama, and then continue with the internal scenario. The International Stage The world economy is going through a very complex situation. Never in modern economic history has there been such a sharp coincidence of such diverse factors. Overall, the inflationary situation is unfavorable for almost all economies in the world. However, while developed economies are going through a serious financial crisis and experiencing a slowdown in output, emerging economies are going through a scenario of sustained growth for several years now. This explains why, while monetary policy in developed economies has had a limited reaction to higher inflation, the outlook in emerging economies, including Chile, is diametrically opposite (Chart 1). I would like to go into more detail about these facts. The financial crisis facing developed economies, particularly the United States, is going through today. It is estimated that the losses of banks, only due to the subprime crisis, would reach about 950 billion dollars, almost what Chile produces in five years. It's hard to find another financial crisis of this size since the Great Depression. Its origins are associated with the huge global imbalances that we have mentioned in several previous reports, as well as with the accelerated expansion of credit towards sectors with low or no payment capacity, in a context of low interest rates and an aggressive search for returns in the financial markets. To this was added a bubble in the real estate market and a process of financial innovation characterized by high degrees of opacity and weaknesses in risk classification processes. The end of this period of credit expansion has resulted in a significant slowdown in economic activity in advanced countries. To be sure, many issues remain about the long-term implications of the recent bailouts of financial institutions, as well as the persistence of the turbulence. But at least the risks of a systemic financial collapse appear to have been controlled in time. In the past, problems of the magnitude of today's would have quickly had very severe repercussions around the world. Today, however, the world economy continues to grow. Today, the commitment that exists almost everywhere in the world is to macroeconomic stability, which is reflected in the adoption of measures to mitigate the consequences of a financial crisis and inflationary problems, allowing the world economy to grow at rates comparable to the robust growth of the first half of this decade. Thus, the regional composition of growth has changed, and the experience of developed and emerging economies is very mixed. Indeed, emerging economies, particularly those in Asia, continue to cycle with high economic growth. The high expansion of the global economy was particularly strong in the biennium 2006-2007, in which the world grew at an average of 5% per year. This good performance of the world economy has had consequences, because as happens in any country where growth exceeds its potential, inflationary pressures have been created in the world. Price increases have been greater in those goods where demand growth has been higher and where supply has had a slower reaction, such as food and oil. This inflationary shock is only comparable to the one that occurred before the acceleration of inflation in the mid-seventies. That is why an anticipated action, which prevents this inflation from increasing and prolonging, is key to avoiding adjustments of the magnitude of those observed in the eighties. From the point of view of the report we are presenting today, the main conclusion that for us derives from the international scenario is that in the period 2008-2010 the external environment will not contribute to the generation of slack at the internal level. According to the consensus scenario among analysts, during the projection horizon, global growth will maintain a dynamism above the average of the last twenty years. The increase in global activity for the biennium 2008-2009 will be similar to that projected in the May IPoM, and for 2010 it will increase again (Table 1). It follows that the demand factors that have led to the increase in the prices of raw materials and staple foods will not provide relief. Nor that the supply experiences a sufficient increase to significantly reduce external price levels. This means that, in the scenario considered most likely, oil and food prices will not see significant changes for the next two years, so although they will not constitute a source of inflation in the projection horizon, they will not help to reduce cost levels either. Thus, we project that oil will average values. About 115 a barrel for the next two years, while copper will decline slightly to average 300 cents a pound in 2010 (Table 2). As always, we cannot rule out alternative scenarios. Much of the global growth that the market consensus forecasts for the next two years rests on the fact that this decoupling between the growth of emerging and developed economies will continue. However, it is difficult to find a period with such a dispersion of regional growth as today, posing risks to the favourable global growth outlook (Chart 2). In addition, our baseline scenario considers that the global inflationary problem will be solved without requiring monetary adjustment and global growth comparable to that experienced in the early eighties. The truth is that, if these assumptions do not occur, the scenario we will face will be, in all likelihood, negative in terms of global growth and access to external financing. In recent days, we have seen a drop in the price of oil and an increasing discussion about the strength of the global economy, which may suggest greater external weakness than we consider in our baseline scenario. Certainly, a lower oil price would help us, not only because it has a direct implication on the CPI but also, as I will discuss later, because it reduces the production costs facing the national economy. However, experience teaches us that we cannot rest the convergence of inflation on the assumption that we will be helped by a price over which we have no control and which, moreover, is subject to extreme volatility. As an example, in early 2007 oil fluctuated between 50 and 60 per barrel, and implied distributions in option prices gave a probability close to 10 percent of a scenario in which the price would exceed 90 by the end of 2008 (figure 3). Today, however, expectations implicit in options indicate that a 40% probability is assigned to the value of oil above 130 a barrel by the end of the year. Although we cannot rule out more adverse scenarios, in which a very slow recovery of the developed world begins to drag the economies most dependent on their exports to developed countries, I want to end my presentation on the international scenario on a positive note. Although we are not immune to global events, the degrees of vulnerability to which we were accustomed in the past have been reduced. Good macroeconomic management has certainly contributed to this. But the resilience of the world economy to current problems is also due to the degrees of development that have been achieved, in particular the flexibility and integration that have accompanied the progress of recent decades. In Latin America, the debate is no longer how to contain the financial, fiscal and balance of payments crises, but how to reduce the impact of the current adverse scenario, in order to continue with a process of sustainable development, without That there are still economies vulnerable to falls in commodity prices. At the conclusion of our reserve accumulation process, the international liquidity position of the Chilean economy will have strengthened. For everyone, then, the great challenge remains to reduce inflation and preserve the price stability that we worked so hard to conquer. The internal scenario Internally, inflation over the past year has been characterised by a sustained increase not only in the CPI, but also in all indicators of inflationary trend and those that eliminate from their measurement the most volatile prices or those most affected by external shocks (Graph 4). In recent months, the main novelty of the inflation figures has been the presence of a greater degree of inflationary spread, a phenomenon that was triggered with unexpected force from May. In the May-July quarter, inflation accumulated an increase of 3.8 percentage points, while our projections included in the May IPoM were 1.3 percentage points. In just two and a half months after the release of our May Report, 2.5 percentage points of deviation in the inflation projection accumulated. This was a novelty not only for us. It was also for private expectations, considering what they projected at the time we published the May IPoM. In that report we expected inflation to be 4.7% by December of this year, while the median of the expectations survey placed it at 4.4%. The Board has reacted decisively to this drastic deterioration in the inflation outlook, increasing the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) by 200 basis points since June, totalling an increase of 325 basis points since mid-2007 and noting that the future trajectory of the MPR includes additional adjustments to ensure the convergence of inflation to the target. There are some particular factors that may directly explain some of this higher inflation, such as the price of oil, which in May-July averaged 130 a barrel, peaking at nearly 150 sometime in July. However, there are other factors of domestic origin and much more complex to elucidate, such as the further spread of external shocks to domestic prices. In the coming years, I will present our vision regarding some of the determinants of the increase in inflation in the last year. On the side of imported inflation we have observed a notable increase. The External Price Index relevant to the Chilean economy is projected to increase 14% this year, well above the average of 4.6% for the period 2000-2007. The Rises International food prices have had a significant impact on domestic food prices, which explains four percentage points of annual CPI inflation as of August 2008. To this is added the aforementioned increase in the price of oil, the magnitude of whose transfer to the domestic market has varied among its different derivatives. In the case of gasoline, the authority has decided to mitigate the impact on the cost for the consumer through various measures, including the cut in the specific tax and the injection of resources into the Fuel Price Stabilization Fund. Thus, while in international markets the price of gasoline has increased by just under 50% in the last year, the consumer price in Chile has risen a little more than 10%. Liquefied gas, paraffin and diesel oil have seen larger increases. As of last August, 1.4 percentage points of annual inflation are a direct consequence of the rise in fuel prices. It also highlights the increase in the cost of electricity since mid-2007, mainly caused by the scarcity of water resources and natural gas and aggravated by the increase in the cost of diesel oil (figure 5). As of August, the direct effect of higher electricity tariffs on the CPI is equivalent to 0.6 percentage points of annual inflation. According to the background available so far, which we report in a box of our IPoM, the increase in energy costs verified in the first half of 2008 d1considering the higher cost of electricity and oild1 could have an impact of the order of two percentage points on the cost structure of the economy. Its direct effect on inflation is debatable and several assumptions must be taken to estimate it, but assuming that margins are constant, this could explain an increase in inflation of equal magnitude. Special mention should be made of the evolution of the exchange rate and the policy of accumulation of reserves. As I pointed out before, the international financial scenario has been very uncertain since the first months of this year, and the estimated costs for the Chilean economy, if more adverse scenarios materialize, could reach significant dimensions. Therefore, in April we decided to start a program of accumulation of reserves for 8,000 million dollars. We did so with the aim of strengthening our international liquidity position, at a time when the peso seemed to have strengthened beyond its fundamentals, and therefore a bubble may be forming . It was certainly a difficult decision, as it was being made at a complex time from the inflationary point of view. A time when a lower exchange rate helped dampen domestic inflationary pressures. In fact, raising rates and initiating the intervention process could have encouraged speculation in favor of the peso. However, our assessment was that the first-quarter inflation news, which justified maintaining the MPR, allowed us to accommodate a somewhat higher exchange rate, without causing higher costs for inflation. That is, it was a time when financial, exchange and, above all, inflationary conditions allowed it. Moreover, given external uncertainty, the reserve accumulation programme constitutes a strong investment in stability. Consequently, and as we mentioned in our communiqu8es and then in the IPoM of May, we perceived that a depreciation of the exchange rate could be accommodated by the evolution of inflation. This did not happen in practice, as the inflationary outlook deteriorated, but financial uncertainties, particularly the implications of the current crisis on financing emerging economies, have not abated. From April to date, the nominal exchange rate has depreciated. Immediately following the announcement of the reserve purchase program, the parity increased between 15 and 20. Later, together with a series of changes in the evaluation of the performance of developed economies, fluctuations in the price of raw materials d0 especially copper and oil d0 and local news of inflation and activity, the parity continued to depreciate, reaching between 510 and 525 per dollar in the two weeks prior to the statistical close of this IPoM, and exceeding by about 13% the levels corresponding to the IPoM of May. The multilateral exchange rate depreciated 11% in the same period. In any case, it is difficult to allocate a significant part of this increase to intervention. However, the current level of the nominal exchange rate is not very different from that of a year ago, so its effect in twelve months on imported inflation in pesos is not relevant (Graph 6). It cannot be ruled out that the exchange rate has played some role in the higher inflation of recent months. In particular, because there are prices of regulated goods where the exchange rate is one of the indicators used in their setting. However, the intervention has been carried out in a mechanical and transparent manner, without any exchange rate objective, so as to maintain the full capacity to modify the MPR if the inflationary outlook so requires. And that's how, finally, it happened. In relation to aggregate demand, the information available for the third quarter is consistent with the prospects that the annual expansion of the economy in the second half of the year will significantly exceed that of the first half of 2008. With this, the base projection scenario considers that the economy will grow this year between 4.5 and 5.0%. This growth scenario and the dynamism shown by activity, particularly in sectors other than natural resources, suggest that capacity gaps are lower than previously expected. This set of higher cost pressures, both internal and external, in an economy with less slack than expected and with domestic demand that has continued to grow strongly, may have favoured a greater persistence of high inflation and the spread of different shocks to other prices. In fact, the measure of inflation that excludes food and energy prices from the CPI contributed to August just under three percentage points of inflation, in circumstances that in the period 2001-2006 contributed, on average, slightly less than half of that figure. The baseline scenario of this MPI assumes that annual CPI inflation will begin to fall towards the target in the course of 2009. In the coming years, I will present to you the factors that our estimates will bring inflation back to target within two years. Two-year inflation projection The baseline scenario of this IPoM considers that annual CPI inflation will reach the inflation target of 3% during 2010. The basis for this projection is that activity will lose momentum, growing by around one percentage point less than its trend over the projection horizon, which is consistent with a GDP expansion of between 3.5 and 4.5% during 2009, with a balance of risks that, given the possible alternative events, is skewed to the downside. The baseline scenario assumes a reduction in the annual growth rate of domestic demand for 2009. Private consumption will continue to slow, investment will reduce its very high annual growth rate, and public spending will also increase at lower rates than this year, in line with recent announcements by the Ministry of Finance and the limits imposed by the structural surplus rule. This trajectory of activity, determined by the impact of a restrictive monetary policy and the aforementioned normalisation of the pace of expansion of demand, considers that the natural resources sectors will grow more than the rest of the economy (Table 3). The baseline scenario of this IPoM considers that inflation expectations and future wage dynamics will be in line with compliance with the target. This is consistent with annual unit labour cost growth, currently between 7 and 9 per cent per year, returning to levels consistent with the target over the projection horizon. Contributing to this dynamic will be the fact that future wage increases are moderate, not fully reflecting the increase in past inflation, but rather considering as a fundamental determinant that inflation will return to target within a limited period of time. Similarly, the baseline scenario assumes that price decision-making is based on a target-aligned inflation expectation. If expectations are higher than the target, the dose of monetary policy required to lower them will be higher. I want to emphasise that, even if inflation expectations are close to target, it is perfectly possible that the rate will have to be raised further. For now, several measures of two-year inflation expectations remain at levels above 3% (Chart 7). However, in recent days we have seen a decline in inflation expectations calculated on the basis of financial asset prices. This fact, if it persists, is undoubtedly positive, but we must point out that monetary policy is not determined mechanically from the observation of some specific variables, but from our own projections and risk assessments regarding future inflationary dynamics (Chart 8). As working assumptions, the baseline scenario assumes that in the long term the real exchange rate (CRR) is similar to its current level, with short-term dynamics consistent with monetary policy developments. This arises from the consideration that, unlike what was assessed in May, the current level of the TCR is at the top of the range of values that are considered consistent with its long-term fundamentals. It is also considered that the MPR will follow a trajectory that in the short term will be greater than that deduced from the different measures of expectations of the private sector, in force in the two weeks prior to the statistical closure of this IPoM. This, in order to generate the necessary slack to achieve the convergence of inflation to the target (Graph 9). Thus, in the base scenario it is projected that the CPI will end 2008 with an annual variation of 8.5%, which with ups and downs, especially in the first quarter of 2009, will fall to 4.9% at the end of next year. The convergence of inflation to the target will continue in 2010, with annual CPI inflation projected to be 3% for the third quarter of 2010 (Table 4). This CPI trajectory sees the spread of recent inflationary shocks as relatively persistent. In fact, by the end of the projection horizon, the main source of higher inflation is the share of the CPI that discounts food and energy (Figure 10). Around our baseline scenario, there is a set of situations that may lead to inflation projections differing from what has been indicated. On this occasion, taking into account the possible alternative events, the Board considers that the balance of risks for inflation is skewed upwards in the short term, but balanced in the projection horizon. Final considerations The origin of our inflationary problem is external, but the current situation is also due to internal developments, in particular further spread. It is normal for a cost shock to have some degree of spillover to the rest of the prices. In fact, our monetary policy scheme is based on a two-year target, in part because it recognizes that there are events whose repercussions do not dissipate quickly, but which, by their nature, do not merit significant neutralization by monetary policy. However, it is the task of monetary policy, as the Council considers in its decisions, to prevent an unexpected and undesirable increase in inflation from being perpetuated and propagating more than prudent over time. As I have pointed out in this presentation, there is a set of factors that can explain this phenomenon. Further indexation of prices and wages could be occurring in response to high inflation, as some case-by-case evidence might indicate. On the other hand, inflation expectations increased, particularly over shorter horizons, which could put pressure on pricing. A more depreciated exchange rate from April to date, but, in any case, not very different from the one that We projected a year ago, it could also have resulted in higher inflation. It is added that the capacity gaps are somewhat smaller than anticipated. In relation to this last point, I want to emphasize that inflation depends primarily on slacks, and not directly on domestic demand. However, we cannot rule out that strong domestic demand may have facilitated the pass-through of cost shocks to the prices of goods and services. The increase in energy costs can also be considered to have generated significant cost pressures, which have been difficult to absorb without generating some price changes . It is not possible, with the history accumulated so far, to specify exactly the relative importance of these factors in the greatest spread, and there may be other factors that we do not yet have the capacity to appreciate. However, its monetary policy implications leave for little doubt and the Council has therefore been tightening monetary policy, which we hope will continue. While the Central Bank orients its policies towards achieving a medium-term, rather than short-term, inflation objective, part of the success of its task is to ensure that inflationary pressures that could affect the credibility and inflationary anchor of the economy are not incubated. Thus, to the extent that it continues to assess that the spread of past inflationary shocks puts at risk the convergence of inflation to the target over a two-year horizon, the Council will necessarily take additional monetary policy actions to correct these imbalances. The Council reaffirms its commitment to conduct monetary policy so as to reduce the current high inflation towards 3% over the policy horizon. This is essential to align inflationary dynamics with the objective of price stability. The future trajectory of the MPR includes additional adjustments to ensure convergence of inflation to the target, at a pace that will depend on new information that accumulates and its implications for projected inflation.
