Title: Implementation of transparency policies and practices: the case of the Central Bank
text: Implementation of transparency policies and practices: the case of the Central Bank I I Inaugural conference of the XXIV Plenary Assembly of the Permanent Academic Conference of Accounting Research (CAPIC), developed at the Universidad Austral de Chile, under the theme: "Accounting and Financial Markets. Reciprocal influence between Financial Information and Markets", on October 24, 2013. Enrique Marshall Board MemberCentral Bank of ChileValdivia, November 2013 1. Introduction I appreciate the invitation to participate in the opening ceremony of this Permanent Academic Conference on Accounting Research 2013 that takes place under the slogan "Accounting and Financial Markets. Reciprocal Influence between Financial Information and Markets". I concur with the greatest consideration for the discipline you practice. During my professional career I have been able to see, on many occasions, how much it can contribute to the understanding of the Economic and financial phenomena its correct accounting representation. When the Central Bank decided to apply reserve requirements to external loans in the nineties, the regulations applicable to banks had to be drafted. We had no experience on how to do it. We went around a thousand times exploring solutions. I remember perfectly that the use of the "T" accounts was what made it easier for us to find a satisfactory formula. But I have not come to talk about lace, much less about the "T" account. What I would like to do on this occasion is to share with you some experiences on the application of transparency policies and practices in the Central Bank of Chile, a public institution whose actions have relevant effects on financial markets and ultimately on the economy as a whole. According to its Constitutional Organic Law (LOC), the Central Bank is mandated to ensure the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal and external payments. In other words, its task is to make inflation low and stable over time and, along with this, to ensure that banks, providers of means of payment, adequately provide the services required by people and companies. To meet this objective, the Central Bank has three types of powers Main. There are first those that relate to the conduct of the policies entrusted to it, among which the monetary policy. Then there are the powers to dictate financial and exchange rules, which is known as the exercise of regulatory power. And finally there are those that are related to his quality as a banker of commercial banks and that allow him to carry out operations with the latter, among which are the reception of deposits, the granting of liquidity credits and the purchase and sale of dollars. The law defines the Central Bank as an institution of a technical nature and, consistent with this, provides it with autonomy for the fulfillment of its mandate. Consequently, its policies and decisions are not subject to subsequent review, but they are subject to requirements for information and transparency in the terms provided for by its Organic Statute. Its superior administration is handed over to a Council made up of five members appointed by the President of the Republic, with the prior approval of the Senate, following a procedure that seeks to ensure a balance of visions within it. In fact, during the same presidential administration, only two of the five members of the Council are renewed. Autonomy imposes on the Central Bank an important challenge in the sense of earning the trust of citizens. For this reason, it has sought to implement good institutional practices and high standards of transparency in all its areas of action, as a policy driver, as a regulator and as a banker. The Central Bank is a key reference in the field of economic and financial activities. Their decisions, carefully processed by the markets, affect interest rates and yields and the prices of financial assets. That influence is direct in money markets, although more so. indirect, mainly via expectations, in medium- and long-term debt markets and other financial markets. To ensure that these Positive effects require that the decisions of the Central Bank be taken in a transparent, credible and predictable policy framework. It must be recognized that progress in transparency has been widespread in recent years, both in the field of public institutions and in private companies. The 2008 Transparency Law is a good example of this. Its enactment enshrined the principle of transparency of the civil service and regulated the procedures for the access to information and its exceptions in all organs of the State. In the private sector, the developments that have taken place in recent times have been marked by the accounting scandals of the beginning of the last decade and then by the global financial crisis. At the local level, the crisis in La Polar has also had significant repercussions. All this taught us or, rather, reminded us that opacity has associated costs that can be very high. The important thing, in any case, are the lessons learned. In this perspective, progress has been appreciable. Regulation and supervision have become more demanding and markets have raised the requirements they impose on issuers of publicly offered securities. With this frame of reference, I would like to comment on four specific initiatives that the Bank has adopted in recent years and that reflect the effort made to raise institutional and transparency standards. Two of them are related to his role as a policy driver and the other two, to institutional aspects or matters. 2. Introduction of a policy regime monetary based on inflation targeting. The first initiative concerns monetary policy. At the end of 1999, the Bank formally introduced an inflation targeting regime. This involved moving in the direction of having a policy rule and reducing the margins of discretion in the conduct of monetary policy. An annual inflation target of 3% with a tolerance margin of 1% is explicit. It should be noted that this is a goal that has technical foundations and is in line with those established in other emerging economies. Along with this, monetary policy criteria and principles were made explicit and decision-making procedures were established, which were enshrined in written and widely disseminated documents. This sought to generate confidence and credibility in the New policy framework. In addition, the practice of reviewing monetary policy on a monthly basis at a meeting specially cited for that purpose was adopted. To ensure an adequate level of transparency, a document containing the background information based on publicly available information that the Bank's technical teams bring to the attention of the Board was released the day before. This is complemented by a Document released the day after the meeting containing the graphs and tables used to formulate the diagnosis and base the decision. The aim is for analysts and the general public to have all known and processed background information in view. On the same day of the meeting, a short press release is delivered informing about the decision taken and its main rationale. Eleven working days later, a more complete minute is released containing a detail of the arguments put forward, the policy options considered, and the vote of each of the members of the Council. This regime has been in operation for nearly 15 years and its results have been perfectly satisfactory. Inflation, although it has deviated from the target, has generally behaved consistently with it. To a large extent, these deviations have been caused by factors over which monetary policy has no control, such as the rise in the price of oil in international markets. Under this policy scheme, it is key that the market maintains confidence that the authority will take the actions so that inflation is maintained or converges to the target within a horizon of two years. Therefore, the Central Bank follows very closely the behavior of inflation expectations, particularly those of the medium term. In this perspective, it should be noted that these expectations have, as a rule, remained at consistent with the 3 per cent target. Positive effects of the monetary policy regime can be seen at the same time in the behavior of the rates of return on long-term debt securities. I refer specifically to securities issued by the Central Bank and the Public Treasury. These long-term rates contain, among other elements, market expectations about the future path of short-term rates and thus the expected path for inflation. The level of these rates and their behavior in the face of changes in the internal or external scenario reflect the greater or lesser degree of soundness of the policy framework and the market's confidence in the results that will result from its implementation. However, rates such as those we observe today for long-term peso securities would have been unthinkable two decades ago and would not have been achieved without this policy framework having been implemented and, above all, without having achieved a high level of degree of confidence on the part of the market. This inflation-targeting regime is complemented by a free- floating exchange rate system, which does not rule out the possibility of intervening in exceptional circumstances and concludes that the benefits of doing so outweigh its costs. In recent years, the Bank has exercised this option, first in 2008 and then in 2011. However, in both cases, the intervention was subjected to a program that was reported in detail, so that from the beginning it was known what the total amount of purchases to be made would be and how they would be distributed over time. This made it possible to reduce uncertainty and maintain a reasonable harmony with the rest of the policies in place. 3. Preparation and dissemination of the Financial Stability Report (FSR). The second initiative is related to financial stability, which is an area in which the Central Bank performs relevant functions, although complementary to those performed by the superintendencies of the financial sector. Since 2004, the institution has been preparing and disseminating a report every six months that gives an account of its vision on financial stability. This report describes the main financial developments that have taken place in recent times. It reviews the financial situation of relevant actors such as the Government, households and companies. Additionally, it analyzes in detail the position of the banking system, including its main risks and vulnerabilities. Having this diagnosis is intrinsic to the Bank's tasks. With a greater or lesser degree of sophistication, this is something that has always been done. In reality, the innovation has been the preparation and dissemination of a document that seeks to share this diagnosis with the market and the general public. The IEF has found a good reception from analysts and the general public. Are Several of the issues raised that have aroused Attention in the last time. One of them is the prevention that was formulated on dynamism reached by the real estate and construction sector. The aim of this was not to affect a development that has objective foundations, but to warn about the risks that all this entails for banks and other entities that provide maintenance with public resources. The aim was for these risks to be well incorporated into credit decisions. 4. Application of international standards for the preparation and dissemination of their states Financial. The two initiatives I have mentioned so far have been related to the role of the Central Bank as Conductor of public policies. The one I will describe below is of an institutional nature and relates to the preparation and disclosure of financial statements. The law establishes that the Council of the Central Bank, after a favorable report from the Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions (SBIF), will issue the rules regarding the requirements and general conditions that the annual financial statements must meet. The law adds that these financial statements must have the opinion of external auditors, appointed by the Council, from among those that appear in the SBIF registry. In the past, the Central Bank prepared its balance sheet using criteria that did not always coincide with generally accepted principles in Chile. An important divergence occurred with the exchange rate of accounting representation. The Central Bank, by its very nature and the functions it fulfils, normally incurs a significant mismatch of currencies, because it maintains among its assets reserves in dollars and other currencies that have as counterparty, among its liabilities, the current currency, the deposits of the banks and, in circumstances such as the current ones, issues of securities in local currency. The magnitude of this mismatch has varied over time, but in certain periods it has reached very significant amounts, as is the case today. In the distant past, when no monetary correction was applied, this mismatch coupled with the permanent Depreciation of the national currency, gave rise to surpluses that reflected an illusion rather than a reality. This was rectified but new challenges arose over time. In the early nineties, for example, the representation of assets and liabilities in foreign currency was done applying the dollar agreement, which at first seemed reasonable. The problem arose when the dollar of Market began to show an increasing deviation from the dollar of accounting representation. The The only reasonable path, in those circumstances, was Abandon the dollar agreement criterion and start using the market dollar. Without ignoring their Accounting effects, that was the path followed from 1998. Thus, over the years, divergences were reduced, partly because the applicable rules were adjusted and, in part, because transactions subject to special rules left the Bank's balance sheet, as was the case with assets relating to subordinated debt. The decision to move towards international standards was taken in 2007 and effectively implemented from FY2009. There were several considerations that were taken into account to take that step. International norms appeared as the recommended standard at the global level. Most countries were implementing them or had announced that they would transition to them. For financial institutions, these appeared as a necessary complement to prudential regulations, such as those recommended by the Basel Committee. Central banks around the world were also beginning to join this trend. And finally, the SBIF had issued instructions for local financial institutions to avail themselves of them. It was quite clear that the Central Bank, as the governing body of the local financial system, could not exempt itself from such a widespread movement. The change in accounting standards gave rise to an internal convergence project that took about two years. Its execution was advised by our external auditors and overseen by the newly created Audit and Compliance Committee. (CAC), to which I shall refer later. This project first included reviewing the experiences of other central banks; the analysis of the main rules applicable to the Central Bank, and the identification of the information systems that would be affected by the changes. The divergences resulting from the application of the new criteria were then surveyed and their significance or materiality was assessed. This showed that the most relevant divergences occurred in the valuation of international reserves and securities issued in the local market. The criterion that was agreed was not to make exceptions except in those operations that had originated in special laws and that were related to episodes of financial crisis experienced prior to the entry into force of the current LOC. One carefully analyzed issue was that of monetary correction. The decision was taken to suspend its application in order to conform to international standards. However, it was noted that this should not affect the applicable legal rules, especially with regard to the calculation of the statutory capital and the distribution of the annual surplus to the Treasury. Therefore, although equity is presented in the financial statements without monetary correction, its value adjusted for monetary correction is recorded through a note for the purposes of compliance with said legal precepts. As planned, as of 2009, the financial statements began to be prepared in accordance with international financial reporting standards in all that their application does not compromise the specific legal provisions that govern the Central Bank and that relate to the fulfillment of its public functions. If there are discrepancies, the rules that prevail are those approved by the Council, which are transparent in the financial statements. The most relevant discrepancy that remains in force is that related to the credits originated due to the liquidation of Sinap, which represent around 4% of the Bank's total assets according to the 2012 financial statements. For greater transparency, since 2009, these and other operations originating from specific legal norms are presented in a separate item of internal credit operations that relate to the permanent functions of the bank. In addition, it should be noted that in the presentation of the financial statements, some statements, such as cash flow, exchange of equity and comprehensive income statements, have been replaced by notes on changes in the monetary base and reserve assets, and by the presentation of comparative income statements. The application of the new rules implied a positive effect on results of the order of US 300 million, calculated at the exchange rate of accounting representation of the year 2008. This is an important figure, but rather reduced compared to the total assets and liabilities of the Central Bank, which at that date reached a sum of the order of US 29 billion and that at the end of 2012 reached US 48 billion. It is true that the public interest in the Bank is not, as a rule, centred on its balance sheet, which is, moreover, difficult to read and interpret. However, it cannot ignore the challenge of providing financial statements that adequately reflect its operations and the results derived from them. First, because the financial information contained in these statements, to the extent that it meets conditions of validity, reliability and timeliness, facilitates the monitoring and evaluation of the macro-financial policies applied. And secondly because the Bank It currently has a weakness of assets. The benefits of seigniorage, that is, the income derived from the exercise of the exclusive power to issue new currency or working capital, will allow this situation to be overcome and restore the patrimonial balance. However, the current equity position must be carefully monitored and the application of the highest accounting standards contributes positively to this. 5. Creation of the Audit Committee and Compliance. The last initiative I would like to comment on is the establishment of ACC, which is closely related to the preparation and disclosure of financial statements. In 2007, the Council decided to set up such a Committee. There was intense discussion about his composition, objectives and functions and, above all, on its relations with the Council. The analysis was informed of the experiences of various central banks in the developed world. A much-debated point was whether one or more Council members should sit on this committee. As the Council is small in size and has normally functioned as a single body, with no division of functions or tasks, it was finally decided to form it with three external members. The appointments are made by the Council and have a duration of three years, with the possibility of renewal only once. To ensure a reasonable degree of continuity in its operation, nominations or renewals are made once each year. Without limitation, the appointments have sought to bring to the Committee knowledge and experience in the legal, operational and accountant. It may be noteworthy that the name Audit and Compliance Committee has been used. As the Central Bank is an organ of the State, with a mandate of the highest level, it seemed important to also incorporate this dimension referring to compliance with the applicable legal norms. According to its statutes, the Committee is an advisory body to the Council, which performs the following functions: a) Report on the effectiveness of systems and internal control procedures of the institution. b) Evaluate and report on the equity and reputational effects involved in fulfilling the Bank's obligations. c) Assess the reliability, completeness, and timeliness of information that is part of states Financial. d) Coordinate with the Office of the Comptroller General, that is, with the Internal Comptroller's Office, with regard to the function it performs. e) Propose the hiring of external auditors. f) Give your opinion about the organization and procedures of the internal comptroller's office and evaluate the external auditors. The Committee has authority to access the Bank's management team and to request any information or background information necessary for the performance of its functions. In practice, their main interaction is with managers, the prosecutor and the auditor or comptroller. internal. Nevertheless, the Committee maintains a direct relationship with the Board of the Bank, to which it must report on the results of its management. With this in mind, it may propose or recommend the adoption of certain policies or rules to safeguard Bank interests. It may also raise the advisability or appropriateness of conducting any investigation or analysis regarding the contingencies or irregular situations that it warns. The Committee must meet regularly at least 4 times a year, but may also hold extraordinary sessions. In practice, the number of meetings has been of the order of 7 per year. It follows that this Committee is in line with the recommendations that flow from the specialized literature and with the practices followed in the most advanced countries. It is perfectly consistent with the concept of an audit committee contained in the instructions issued by the SBIF for its application in the banking system. It also coincides with many of the functions assigned to the Directors' Committee by the Companies Act, although the latter is guided by the objective of providing protection to minority shareholders rather than by the exercise of comprehensive oversight over risk management and internal control. Despite having only six years of operation, the Audit and Compliance Committee of the Central Bank has become a benchmark for other institutions both in the country and abroad. The interest in learning about this experience has been growing. It is worth mentioning that people who completed their terms as members of the Committee have been recruited to audit committees of other entities. This reflects the value attached not only to the professional quality of each of them but also to the experience accumulated in the Central Bank. 6. Final Comments The initiatives to which I have referred in this presentation demonstrate the efforts made by the Central Bank to implement transparency policies and practices with the consequent benefits that this entails for the functioning of financial markets and the economy as a whole. All this has been done in a coherent manner and seeking to achieve its different functions and areas of action. However, I do not want to leave a complacent vision. We recognize that there are tasks ahead. International financial reporting standards, for example, are still applied with exceptions. Therefore, in this and other areas, improvements and refinement will be required in the future. The important thing, in any case, is to persevere in the policies and practices applied in these years.

La ley establece que el Consejo del Banco Central, previo informe favorable de la Superintendencia de Bancos e Instituciones Financieras (SBIF), dictar las normas relativas a los requisitos y condiciones generales que debern cumplir los estados financieros anuales. La ley agrega que estos estados financieros debern contar con la opinin de auditores externos, designados por el Consejo, de entre aquellos que figuren en el registro de la SBIF. En el pasado, el Banco Central prepar su balance aplicando criterios que no siempre coincidan con principios generalmente aceptados en Chile. Una divergencia importante es la que se produca con el tipo de cambio de representacin contable. El Banco Central, por su propia naturaleza y las funciones que cumple, incurre normalmente en un significativo descalce de monedas, porque mantiene entre sus activos reservas en dlares y otras divisas que tienen como contraparte, entre sus pasivos, el circulante, los depsitos de los bancos y, en circunstancias como las actuales, emisiones de ttulos en moneda local. La magnitud de este descalce ha variado a lo largo del tiempo, pero en determinados perodos ha alcanzado montos muy significativos, como ocurre en la actualidad. En el pasado lejano, cuando no se aplicaba correccin monetaria, este descalce unido a la permanente depreciacin de la moneda nacional, daban origen a excedentes que reflejaban una ilusin ms que una realidad. Ello fue rectificado pero con el transcurso del tiempo surgieron nuevos desafos. A principios de los aos noventa, por ejemplo, la representacin de los activos y pasivos en moneda extranjera se haca aplicando el dlar acuerdo, lo que en principio pareca razonable. El problema surgi cuando el dlar de mercado comenz a mostrar una creciente desviacin respecto del dlar de representacin contable. El nico camino razonable, en esas circunstancias, era abandonar el criterio del dlar acuerdo y comenzar a utilizar el dlar de mercado. Sin desconocer sus efectos contables, ese fue el camino que se sigui a partir del ao 1998. As, con el transcurso de los aos, las divergencias se fueron reduciendo, en parte, porque se ajustaron las normas aplicables y, en parte, porque las operaciones sometidas a normas especiales salieron del balance del Banco, como ocurri con los activos relacionados con la deuda subordinada. La decisin de moverse hacia normas internacionales se adopt en 2007 y se implemento efectivamente a partir del ejercicio 2009. Varias fueron las consideraciones que se tuvieron presente para dar ese paso. Las normas internacionales aparecan como el estndar recomendado a nivel global. La mayora de los pases las estaban aplicando o haban anunciado que transitaran hacia ellas. Para las instituciones financieras, estas aparecan como un necesario complemento de las regulaciones prudenciales, como las recomendadas por el Comit de Basilea. Los bancos centrales alrededor del mundo tambin comenzaban a sumarse a esta tendencia. Y finalmente, la SBIF haba dictado instrucciones para que las instituciones financieras locales se acogiesen a ellas. Era bastante claro que el Banco Central, en su calidad de entidad rectora del sistema financiero local, no poda exceptuarse de un movimiento tan generalizado. El cambio de normas contables dio origen a un proyecto interno de convergencia que tom alrededor de dos aos. Su ejecucin cont con la asesora de nuestros auditores externos y con la vigilancia del recin creado Comit de Auditora y Cumplimiento (CAC), al cual me referir ms adelante. Este proyecto contempl primeramente la revisin de las experiencias de otros bancos centrales; el anlisis de las principales normas aplicables al Banco Central, y la identificacin de los sistemas de informacin que se veran afectados por los cambios. Luego se efectu un levantamiento de las divergencias que se producan como resultado de la aplicacin de los nuevos criterios y se procedi a evaluar su significacin o materialidad. Ello puso en evidencia que las divergencias ms relevantes se producan en la valoracin de las reservas internacionales y de los ttulos emitidos en el mercado local. El criterio que se acord fue no efectuar excepciones salvo en aquellas operaciones que se haban originado en leyes especiales y que se relacionaban con episodios de crisis financiera vividos con anterioridad a la entrada en vigencia de la actual LOC. Un tema cuidadosamente analizado fue el de la correccin monetaria. La decisin que se adopt fue suspender su aplicacin para adecuarse a las normas internacionales. Sin embargo, se dej constancia de que ello no deba afectar las normas legales aplicables, especialmente en lo relativo al cmputo del capital estatutario y a la distribucin del excedente anual al Fisco. Por ello, si bien el patrimonio es presentado en los estados financieros sin correccin monetaria, se deja constancia a travs de una nota de su valor ajustado por correccin monetaria para efectos del cumplimiento de dichos preceptos legales. Como estaba planificado, a partir de 2009, los estados financieros comenzaron a ser elaborados de acuerdo con normas internacionales de informacin financiera en todo aquello en que su aplicacin no compromete las disposiciones legales especficas que rigen al Banco Central y que se relacionan con el cumplimiento de sus funciones pblicas. De existir discrepancias, las normas que priman son las aprobadas por el Consejo, las que son transparentadas en los estados financieros. La discrepancia ms relevante que permanece vigente es la que se relaciona con los crditos originados con motivo de la liquidacin del Sinap que representan alrededor del 4% del total de activos del Banco segn los estados financieros 2012. Para mayor transparencia, desde el ao 2009, estas y otras operaciones originadas en normas legales especficas se presentan en una partida separada de las operaciones de crdito interno que se relacionan con las funciones permanentes del banco. Aparte de ello, habra que sealar que en la presentacin de los estados financieros se han reemplazado algunos estados, como el de flujo de efectivo, el de cambio del patrimonio y de resultados integrales por notas sobre las variaciones de la base monetaria y de los activos de reserva, y por la presentacin de estados de resultados comparados. La aplicacin de las nuevas normas implic un efecto positivo sobre resultados del orden de US $ 300 millones, calculado al tipo de cambio de representacin contable del ejercicio 2008. Esta es una cifra importante, pero ms bien reducida comparada con los activos y pasivos totales del Banco Central, que a esa fecha alcanzaban a una suma del orden de US $ 29 mil millones y que al cierre del ejercicio 2012 llegaban a los US$ 48 mil millones. Es cierto que el inters pblico que concita el Banco no est centrado, por regla general, en su balance, que por lo dems es difcil de leer e interpretar. Sin embargo, ste no puede soslayar el desafo de proveer estados financieros que reflejen adecuadamente sus operaciones y los resultados que de ellas se derivan. Primero porque la informacin financiera contenida en dichos estados, en la medida que cumpla condiciones de validez, confiabilidad y oportunidad, facilita el seguimiento y evaluacin de las polticas macro- financieras aplicadas. Y segundo porque el Banco registra actualmente una debilidad patrimonial. Los beneficios del seoreaje, esto es, los ingresos derivados del ejercicio de la potestad exclusiva de emitir moneda o circulante nuevo, permitirn superar este cuadro y restablecer el equilibrio patrimonial. Sin embargo, la actual posicin patrimonial debe ser monitoreada con atencin y a ello contribuye positivamente la aplicacin de los ms altos estndares contables.  Creacin del Comit de Auditora y Cumplimiento. La ltima iniciativa que quisiera comentar es la creacin del CAC que se relaciona estrechamente con lo sealado en materia de preparacin y divulgacin de los estados financieros. El ao 2007, el Consejo decidi constituir dicho Comit. Se discuti intensamente sobre su composicin, objetivos y funciones y, sobre todo, sobre sus relaciones con el Consejo. Para iluminar el anlisis se recurri a las experiencias de varios bancos centrales del mundo desarrollado. Un punto muy debatido fue si uno o ms miembros del Consejo deban formar parte de este comit. Como el Consejo es de tamao reducido y ha funcionado normalmente como un cuerpo nico, sin divisin de funciones o tareas, se opt finalmente por conformarlo con tres miembros externos. Las designaciones son efectuadas por el Consejo y tienen una duracin de tres aos, existiendo la posibilidad de renovacin solo por una vez. Para asegurar un razonable grado de continuidad en su funcionamiento, las nominaciones o renovaciones se realizan una cada ao. Sin que ello constituya una limitacin, los nombramientos han procurado llevar al Comit conocimientos y experiencias en los mbitos legal, operacional y contable. Puede llamar la atencin que se haya usado la denominacin de Comit de Auditora y Cumplimiento. Como el Banco Central es un rgano del Estado, con un mandato del ms alto nivel, pareci importante incorporar tambin esta dimensin referida al cumplimiento de las normas legales aplicables. De acuerdo con sus estatutos, el Comit es un rgano asesor del Consejo, que cumple las siguientes funciones:  Informar sobre la eficacia de los sistemas y procedimientos de control interno de la institucin.  Evaluar e informar sobre los efectos patrimoniales y de reputacin involucrados en el cumplimiento de las obligaciones del Banco.  Evaluar la confiabilidad, integridad y oportunidad de la informacin que forma parte de los estados financieros.  Coordinarse con la Revisora General, esto es, con la contralora interna, en lo que respecta a la funcin que sta realiza.  Proponer la contratacin de los auditores externos.  Emitir su opinin sobre la organizacin y procedimientos de la contralora interna y evaluar a los auditores externos. El Comit tiene autoridad para acceder al equipo gerencial del Banco y requerir cualquier informacin o antecedente necesario para el cumplimiento de sus funciones. En la prctica, su principal interaccin es con los gerentes, el fiscal y el revisor o contralor interno. No obstante ello, el Comit mantiene una relacin directa con el Consejo del Banco, al cual debe informar sobre los resultados de su gestin. En esa perspectiva, puede proponer o recomendar la adopcin de determinadas polticas o normas para cautelar los intereses del Banco. Tambin puede plantear la conveniencia o procedencia de conducir cualquier investigacin o anlisis respecto de las contingencias o situaciones irregulares que advierta. El Comit debe reunirse en forma ordinaria por lo menos 4 veces al ao, pero puede celebrar tambin sesiones extraordinarias. En la prctica el nmero de sesiones ha sido del orden de 7 por ao. De lo sealado se desprende que este Comit est en lnea con las recomendaciones que fluyen de la literatura especializada y con las prcticas seguidas en los pases ms avanzados. Es perfectamente coherente con el concepto de comit de auditora contenido en las instrucciones impartidas por la SBIF para su aplicacin en el sistema bancario. Coincide tambin con muchas de las funciones que la ley de sociedades annimas le asigna al Comit de Directores, si bien ste ltimo tienen una orientacin marcada por el objetivo de brindar proteccin a los accionistas minoritarios ms que por el ejercicio de una vigilancia integral sobre la gestin de riesgos y el control interno. A pesar de tener solo seis aos de funcionamiento, el Comit de Auditora y Cumplimiento del Banco Central se ha constituido en un referente para otras instituciones tanto en el pas como en el exterior. El inters por conocer de esta experiencia ha sido creciente. Valga mencionar que las personas que completaron sus perodos como miembros del Comit han sido reclutadas para integrar comits de auditora de otras entidades. Ello refleja el valor que se le asigna no solo a la calidad profesional de cada uno de ellos sino tambin a la experiencia acumulada en el Banco Central.  Comentarios Finales Las iniciativas a las que me he referido en esta presentacin ponen de manifiesto los esfuerzos desplegados por el Banco Central por aplicar polticas y prcticas de transparencia con los consiguientes beneficios que ello conlleva para el funcionamiento de los mercados financieros y de la economa en su conjunto. Todo ello se ha hecho en forma coherente y procurando alcanzar sus distintas funciones y mbitos de actuacin. Sin embargo, no quisiera dejar una visin complaciente. Reconocemos que existen tareas por delante. Las normas internacionales de informacin financiera, por ejemplo, se aplican todava con excepciones. Por ello, en este y otros mbitos, se requerirn mejoras y perfeccionamiento en el futuro. Lo importante, en todo caso, es perseverar en las polticas y prcticas aplicadas en estos aos.

Title: The Challenge of Financial Education
text: The Financial Education Challenge1 Enrique Marshall Vice President Central Bank of Chile May 2014 1 Presentation made within the framework of an activity organized by the Coopeuch Foundation and held on May 28, 2014 in Santiago. I appreciate the comments of Rosario Celed97n, lawyer of the Central Bank, to a previous version of this document. In any case, this is the sole responsibility of its author and does not bind the Board of the Central Bank of Chile. I am grateful for the invitation of the Coopeuch Foundation to participate in this activity whose objective is to reflect on the challenges of financial education in our country. I begin by recognizing that this is an issue that is of significant importance for achieving inclusive financial development that rests on solid foundations. Financial education has gained increasing interest in the field of public policy. The G-20 included it in its work agenda after the global financial crisis. Along the same lines, the OECD, an organization that brings together countries with the highest standards in public policies and of which Chile has been a full member since 2010, established a special program on this matter. 2 Most advanced countries and a growing group of developing countries have established national strategies in this area. Central banks and financial supervisors have designed and implemented special financial education programmes, which are reported on their respective websites. 3 On a different, but no less important, level, banks, credit unions and, in general, financial service providers have become concerned about this issue and 2 The documents and activities deployed by the OECD can be consulted on its website: . 3 Reflections on financial education on the part of central bank governors can be find in Bernanke Ben S. (2012) and Vergara, R. (2012). are developing relevant educational actions. 4 All of this is very welcome. There are powerful reasons why financial education has come to the fore. The crisis of 2008-9 exposed a reality that had been brewing for some time. I am referring to the massification of financial products and services and their increasing complexity. The crisis also showed that these trends, in the absence of safeguards, generate conditions for the commission of excesses. Over the past few decades, access to financial services has expanded significantly in virtually every country in the world. Chile has not been the exception, which is clearly visualized in graph No. 1. Not many years ago, services were a privilege of some. But that has been changing. Of course, there is still a long way to go, but the massification of benefits has advanced a lot and will continue to do so. Soon, the instruments have become sophisticated and increasingly difficult to understand. This poses a huge challenge because segments of the population accessing services for the first time have lower levels of schooling and therefore less prepared to make financial decisions. 4 A recent paper illustrating banks' approach to this issue is found in Awad (2014). With regard to the sophistication of products and services, a trend that has been observed in recent years is that the contracts associated with the benefits have become longer and more complex and therefore more difficult to read and understand in all their details. The new trends in consumer protection lead to give an increasing weight to the contracts signed by the parties, but this raises the need to have a certain capacity for reading comprehension which, as we know, is not a sufficiently generalized skill in the population. In this context, financial education has emerged as a public policy instrument aimed precisely at reducing this gap or asymmetry between suppliers and customers. But what should we understand by financial education? In the specialized literature there are several definitions. According to the OECD, financial education is: "the process by which financial consumers/investors improve their understanding of financial products, concepts and risks, and, through information, instruction and/or objective advice, develop the skills and confidence to become more aware of financial risks and opportunities, make informed decisions, know where to go for help and take any effective action to improve their economic well-being." 5 The implicit assumption in this is that financial education would lead to better financial decisions by individuals and families and, as a result, to a better functioning of the financial system as a whole. But we must be realistic. Education can help reduce the gaps we have discussed, but it cannot solve all problems. Nor can it act alone or in isolation. To be effective, it must do so in conjunction with other actions and policies that aim at the same goal of achieving healthy financial inclusion. We must recognize that financial inclusion and financial education are two sides of the same coin. They are inseparable goals. It is striking that this has not been visualized with the same clarity in the past. We made great strides in inclusion, but we belatedly realized that this had to be accompanied by adequate financial education. But the task does not end there. Healthy inclusion requires, in addition to good prudential regulations, an adequate consumer protection framework, effective supervision or control and something very important. 5 Definition from OECD (2005). "Improving Financial Literacy. Analysis of Issues and Policies." Paris. December. Spanish version taken from CAF, Development Bank of Latin America (2013). "Financial education in Latin America and the Caribbean. Current situation and prospects". Public Policies and Productive Transformation Series No. 12 / 2013. important, such as the responsible marketing of products and services by suppliers. The use of financial instruments undoubtedly entails relevant benefits for the population. Credit, for example, is a means that opens up opportunities, such as access to own housing and durable consumer goods, to mention two types of operations common in the segment of natural persons. But the use of these financial tools comes with costs and risks, which must be properly weighed. Therefore, when financial decisions are made, the possibility of making mistakes, facing unexpected contingencies and incurring failures cannot be ruled out. Financial vulnerability and over-indebtedness are precisely manifestations of outcomes of this type, with very relevant implications for the people directly involved and their respective family groups. What financial education aims to do is reduce the likelihood that people will make such mistakes and failures. The global financial crisis of 2008-9 taught us, additionally, that failures can have systemic implications, either because the amounts involved reach very high levels, as happened with the sub-prime crisis, or because those affected represent a fraction significant of the total population, although the amounts are not so significant. When the decisions are mostly correct, the proper functioning of the financial system is reaffirmed. When this is not the case, questions arise about its efficiency and, finally, about the role it is fulfilling. The generalization of failures is a wake-up call about the functioning of the system, beyond any consideration of the impact that these failures may or may not have on its solvency. It is common to associate financial education with financial instruction or literacy. The latter refers to the knowledge and management of basic financial concepts and techniques, which allow, for example, to compare the effective cost of two or more credit operations or distinguish between a nominal interest rate and an inflation-adjusted interest rate. To be sure, these are very desirable domains or skills, but I have doubts that they point well to what the great mass of the population requires. Moreover, these financial technicalities suppose, as a necessary condition, a certain handling of mathematics, which is not always present in the population as a whole. This implies that progress along these lines has limitations. In any case, my impression is that the main challenge of financial education is not in this field, but in what is related to the development of attitudes, behaviors and practices that encourage good financial decisions. The ultimate goal is for people to approach financial issues responsibly and to manage to manage their personal finances well. That is the best way to achieve good results and that they last over time. The challenge of financial education crosses different groups and subgroups of the population, each of which has its own needs. However, there is considerable agreement that the task must begin with children and young people, who gain experience with financial products at an increasingly young age. But, the most important thing is that the actions that are deployed between them can be very effective in the medium and long term. In this perspective, the first responsibility undoubtedly lies with parents and guardians. These must support their respective children and wards in the formation of attitudes, behaviors and practices for a healthy future development in the field of their personal finances. In the same vein, schools, lyceums and universities can make a positive contribution. By the way, introducing elements of financial education at these levels is not an easy task and will require overcoming several challenges. I mention, as examples, the search for space in a school curriculum already quite full of content, the training of teachers or instructors, and the production of support material that facilitates the achievement of the educational objectives pursued. 6 I also see an important role for financial institutions in approaching children and young people to provide them with a good and healthy familiarity with financial instruments. This would serve to complement and bring to practical the financial education they receive in the classroom or within their families. For several reasons, many of them acceptable, there is a certain resistance on the part of institutions to establish relations with minors. This is something that should be reviewed. In any case, this preferential attention for children and young people should not lead to disregarding the needs of the adult population, which is the one that exercises most of the demand for financial products and services at present. Along these lines, a particularly important issue, which is assigned high priority in advanced countries, is that of saving for retirement and old age with all the implications that this entails. I use these distinctions to formulate a more general reflection. Financial education programs should be designed and implemented with the 6 On the relationship between financial education and school curriculum see Honorato, M. (2014). characteristics and needs of the different groups to which they are addressed. It is not possible to think of a single model of universal validity. The contents, approaches and methodologies may well vary from case to case. In this perspective, it seems important to me to open up to the use of modern techniques supported by the use of telephony and the internet. This can be key to reaching the world of children and young people. We must recognize, however, that we still know little about what works and what does not work well in terms of financial education. There is a growing number of financial education programs worldwide and they are beginning to emerge in our country as well, but the available evidence is still insufficient to draw conclusive lessons. For the time being, the important thing is to facilitate the emergence and development of initiatives by the different stakeholders, promote the exchange of experiences, and ensure that these can be rigorously evaluated to draw lessons. 7 Financial service providers have begun to venture into the field of financial education with a wide range of proposals. 8 All of this is very valuable. Without 7 A good summary of the state of education in the world is provided by Xu, Lisa and Bilal Zia (2012). A diagnosis on the same topic but referring specifically to Latin America is found in CAF, Development Bank of Latin America (2013). 8 Financial institutions with massive benefits generally have sections on financial education on their respective websites. However, a very positive contribution would be to intensify their efforts in order to reduce the complexity of the products and services they offer in a massive way and, along with it, to increase the information about them. This would reduce the gap between suppliers and customers and increase transparency and competition. The challenge posed to financial education would become much more realistic. This recommendation, by the way, does not exclude the possibility that the offer for customers with higher degrees of education is much more sophisticated. On the level of financial education in our country, the evidence we have is still partial and does not allow us to formulate a complete and finished diagnosis. However, the available figures paint a bleak picture, where significant gaps appear. I would like to refer to some of this background. In order to measure the degree of knowledge of the population on basic financial issues and facilitate comparisons, standardized tests have been designed and applied in several countries and in different population groups within them. The comparative results of these measurements are not auspicious for our country, as evidenced in graph No. 2. As can be seen in it, Chile appears with scores comparable to those of other developing countries, but well below those obtained by developed countries. The Central Bank regularly conducts a Household Financial Survey, which makes it possible to collect relevant information on the financial situation at the household level. Taking advantage of this instrument, it was possible to carry out an evaluation of the information that individuals or households handle about their finances. In terms of credit, people appear well informed about the monthly fee they must pay and the term of their respective obligations. However, they show a high ignorance about the effective interest rate associated with their operations. As shown in graph No. 3, the figures of ignorance of the interest rate exceed 70% in consumer loans and 60% in mortgage loans. In social security matters, there are also shortcomings. According to figures from the aforementioned survey and summarized in graph No. 4, only 37% of households say they know the balance of their capitalization account, and about 55% know in which fund their savings are. This lack of information or knowledge about the pension system is also reported by the Social Protection Survey (EPS) carried out by the Undersecretariat of Social Security. According to figures from the 2009 version, which are summarized in graph No. 5, a high Percentage of the population does not know key aspects of the system such as, for example, the percentage of remuneration that is deducted and paid monthly in the pension fund, or how pensions are calculated in the current pension system. The figures of both the EFH and the EPS also show that the deficiencies in financial education, although they cross all groups of society, tend to be greater in the segments with less formal education and lower incomes. 9 Regarding the topic that summons us, an additional antecedent that seems very revealing to me is the one referring to the practice of saving in our country. The World Bank has a database on financial inclusion that allows comparisons between countries. A number of indicators include one that accounts for the percentage of the population that practices saving. The reference is not to the amount of savings, but simply to the use of this instrument for financial decision-making or with financial implications or scope. There is some evidence that financial education is positively related to the practice of saving. With this framework of analysis, we made a comparison between Chile and the rest of the countries. The results, presented in Figure 8, 9 Evidence of this is found in the 2011-12 Household Financial Survey and in the Microdata Center of the Department of Economics of the University of Chile (2010). See graphs Na16 and Na17 in this document. They show that the savings practice indicators of our country are relatively low, comparable to those of other developing countries, but much lower than those of developed countries. These results are not encouraging if we take into account that the per capita income of our country is higher than the average of those of emerging economies. All these antecedents, although partial, highlight that there is a gap between advances in financial inclusion, which cannot be unknown, and levels of financial education, which appear in principle rather low, considering the degree of development of our country. Therefore, the steps that have been taken in recent years to adequately face the challenge of financial education are auspicious. A very important one was the constitution of the Working Group on Financial Education with the participation of actors from the public and private sectors. This led to the first international seminar on the subject at the beginning of last year, which aimed to review international recommendations and the experiences of other countries, learn what is being done in Chile at different levels and articulate a network of relationships among interested actors and, based on all this, lay the foundations for a national financial education strategy. The interest aroused by this seminar He highlighted that there are many actors in the public and private sectors that are deploying educational actions with varied focus and oriented to different target audiences. The initiatives under way are multiple, the challenge is to articulate them around certain principles or guidelines and to promote a fruitful exchange of experiences, which allows us to know what works well and what works less well in this field. Along the same lines, we should highlight the initiative that creates the Advisory Commission for Financial Inclusion and Education, formed by the Minister of Finance, who will chair it; the Minister of Social Development; the Minister of Economy, Development and Tourism; the Minister of Education; the Minister of Labour and Social Security; and the Minister Secretary-General of the Presidency. This Commission would have the permanent advice of the Central Bank by virtue of the provisions of article 4 of its Organic Law. The Ministry of Education has also undertaken action in this field. In the course of 2013 it carried out a public consultation process aimed at incorporating topics of financial education in the curricular bases of the basic and intermediate levels. That should provide important elements for moving along these lines. In the medium term it will be very interesting to see the effects of these initiatives through international performance tests school, some of which plan to incorporate measurements on financial education. 10 The Central Bank usually adopts a macro or systemic view of economic and financial phenomena, however this has not been an obstacle to develop some specific educational actions that are worth mentioning. These are part of the program called "Central in your Life", launched last year, but which includes initiatives that have been carried out for several years. 11 These include the economics and finance essay competition for high school students, which has been very successful considering the participation achieved. During the last 9 years, the program has summoned almost 30 thousand students from about 2,200 educational establishments from all over the country. Starting this year, the contest will be audiovisual works that answer the question: What is inflation and why is it important to keep it low and stable? This innovation seeks to achieve a better harmony with the world of young people. The objectives of the "Central en tu Vida" program are to disseminate the role played by the Central Bank in the development of the economy among non-experts in the field; Educate the population on issues 10 See Honorato M. (2014). 11 More details about this program can be found in economic and financial activities that are more directly related to its institutional work; and make a contribution to the task of having better informed citizens with sufficient capacity to properly manage their personal finances. With this, the Central Bank makes a contribution that adds to the many others that are being made in the country for the sake of a common goal, which is to raise the level of economic and financial education of the population. 12 I conclude by reiterating some of the concepts made earlier. Financial education has acquired relevance for public policies with the massification of financial products and services. The main objective pursued with financial education is to favor good financial decisions by individuals and families, with the benefits that this entails for their own well-being. These good decisions also contribute to strengthening the proper functioning of financial activity and, in this way, to the efficient performance of the economy as a whole. For all these reasons, I share the view that financial education has a very important role and, therefore, deserves the opportunity to demonstrate how much it can contribute to healthy financial development. 12 The Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions (SBIF) has developed two portals on financial education: and . En esa misma lnea, la OECD, organizacin que agrupa a los pases con los ms altos estndares en polticas pblicas y de la cual Chile es miembro pleno desde 2010, dispuso un programa especial sobre esta materia.2 La mayora de los pases avanzados y un grupo creciente de pases en desarrollo han establecido estrategias nacionales en este campo. Los bancos centrales y los supervisores financieros han diseado y puesto en aplicacin programas especiales de educacin financiera, de los cuales se informa en sus respectivos portales electrnicos.3 En un plano distinto, pero no menos importante, los bancos, las cooperativas de ahorro y crdito y, en general, los prestadores de servicios financieros han comenzado a preocuparse por este tema y 2 Los documentos y actividades desplegadas por el OECD pueden ser consultados en su portal internet: www.oecd.org/finance/financial-education. 3 Reflexiones sobre educacin financiera de parte de los gobernadores de bancos centrales se pueden encontrar en Bernanke Ben S. (2012) y Vergara, R. (2012). estn desarrollando acciones educativas relevantes.4 Todo ello es muy bienvenido. Existen poderosas razones para que la educacin financiera haya saltado a un primer plano. La crisis de los aos 2008-9 dej al descubierto una realidad que se vena gestando desde haca tiempo. Me refiero a la masificacin de los productos y servicios financieros y a su creciente complejidad. La crisis puso en evidencia, adems, que estas tendencias, en ausencia de resguardos, generan condiciones para la comisin de excesos. En el curso de las ltimas dcadas, el acceso a los servicios financieros se ha extendido significativamente en prcticamente todos los pases del orbe. Chile no ha sido la excepcin, lo que se visualiza con claridad en el grfico N1. No muchos aos atrs, los servicios eran un privilegio de algunos. Pero ello ha ido cambiando. Por cierto queda todava bastante camino por recorrer, pero la masificacin de las prestaciones ha avanzado mucho y lo seguir haciendo. Enseguida, los instrumentos se han sofisticado y resultan cada vez ms difciles de entender. Ello plantea un enorme desafo porque los segmentos de la poblacin que acceden por primera vez a los servicios cuentan con menores niveles de escolaridad y por tanto con menor preparacin para tomar decisiones financieras. 4 Un documento reciente que ilustra la aproximacin de los bancos a este tema se encuentra en Awad (2014). A propsito de la sofisticacin de los productos y servicios, una tendencia que se ha observado en lo ltimos aos es que los contratos asociados a las prestaciones se han tornado ms largos y complejos y por tanto ms difciles de leer y entender en todos sus detalles. Las nuevas tendencias en materia de proteccin de los consumidores conducen a entregarle un creciente peso a los contratos suscritos por las partes, pero ello plantea la necesidad de contar con cierta capacidad de comprensin de lectura que como sabemos, no es una habilidad suficientemente generalizada en la poblacin. En este contexto, la educacin financiera ha surgido como un instrumento de poltica pblica orientado precisamente a reducir esa brecha o asimetra entre proveedores y clientes. Pero, qu debemos entender por educacin financiera? En la literatura especializada se encuentran varias definiciones. Segn la OCDE, la educacin financiera es: el proceso por el cual los consumidores/inversionistas financieros mejoran su comprensin de los productos financieros, los conceptos y los riesgos, y, a travs de informacin, instruccin y/o el asesoramiento objetivo, desarrollan las habilidades y confianza para ser ms conscientes de los riesgos y oportunidades financieras, tomar decisiones informadas, saber a dnde ir para obtener ayuda y ejercer cualquier accin eficaz para mejorar su bienestar econmico.5 El supuesto implcito en ello es que la educacin financiera conducira a mejores decisiones financieras por parte de las personas y las familias y, como resultado, a un mejor funcionamiento del sistema financiero en su conjunto. Pero debemos ser realistas. La educacin puede ayudar a reducir las brechas que hemos comentado, sin embargo no puede resolver todos los problemas. Tampoco puede actuar sola o aisladamente. Para ser efectiva lo debe hacer en conjunto con otras acciones y polticas que apunten al mismo objetivo de lograr una sana inclusin financiera. Debemos reconocer que inclusin financiera y educacin financiera son dos caras de la misma moneda. Son objetivos inseparables. Llama la atencin que esto no se haya visualizado con la misma claridad en el pasado. Avanzamos mucho en inclusin, pero advertimos con tardanza que sta deba ir acompaada de una adecuada educacin financiera. Pero la tarea no termina all. Una sana inclusin requiere adems de buenas regulaciones prudenciales, de un adecuado marco de proteccin de los consumidores, de una eficaz supervisin o fiscalizacin y de algo tambin muy 5 Definicin proveniente de OECD (2005). El uso de instrumentos financieros conlleva sin duda beneficios relevantes para la poblacin. El crdito, por ejemplo, es un medio que abre oportunidades, como el acceso a la vivienda propia y a los bienes de consumo durables, por mencionar dos tipos de operaciones habituales en el segmento de las personas naturales. Pero el uso de estas herramientas financieras trae aparejado costos y riesgos, que deben ser adecuadamente ponderados. Por ello, cuando se adoptan decisiones financieras la posibilidad de cometer errores, de enfrentar contingencias inesperadas y de incurrir en fracasos no puede ser descartada. La vulnerabilidad financiera y el sobreendeudamiento son manifestaciones precisamente de desenlaces de ese tipo, con implicancias muy relevantes para las personas directamente involucradas y sus respectivos grupos familiares. Lo que pretende la educacin financiera es reducir la probabilidad de que las personas incurran en ese tipo de errores y fracasos. La crisis financiera global de 2008-9 nos ense, adicionalmente, que los fracasos pueden tener implicancias sistmicas, ya sea porque los montos involucrados alcanzan niveles muy altos, como ocurri con la crisis sub-prime, o bien porque los afectados representan una fraccin significativa del total de la poblacin, aunque los montos no resulten tan significativos. Cuando las decisiones son mayoritariamente acertadas, el buen funcionamiento del sistema financiero se ve reafirmado. Cuando ello no es as, surgen interrogantes sobre su eficiencia y, finalmente, sobre el rol que est cumpliendo. La generalizacin de los fracasos es un llamado de alerta sobre el funcionamiento del sistema, ms all de cualquier consideracin sobre el impacto que esos fracasos pueden o no tener sobre su solvencia. Es comn asociar educacin financiera con instruccin o alfabetizacin financiera. Esta ltima est referida al conocimiento y manejo de conceptos y tcnicas financieras bsicas, que permiten, por ejemplo, comparar el costo efectivo de dos o ms operaciones de crdito o bien distinguir entre una tasa de inters nominal y una tasa de inters ajustada por inflacin. Sin duda, estos son dominios o habilidades muy deseables, pero tengo dudas que apunten bien a lo que requiere la gran masa de la poblacin. Por lo dems, estos tecnicismos financieros suponen, como condicin necesaria, cierto manejo de las matemticas, lo que no siempre est presente en el conjunto de la poblacin. Esto implica que avanzar en esa lnea tiene limitaciones. En todo caso, mi impresin es que el principal desafo de la educacin financiera no est en ese campo, sino en aquello que se relaciona con el desarrollo de actitudes, conductas y prcticas que favorezcan la adopcin de buenas decisiones financieras. El objetivo ltimo es que las personas se aproximen con responsabilidad a los temas financieros y que logren hacer un buen manejo de sus finanzas personales. Esa es la mejor forma de lograr buenos resultados y que stos perduren en el tiempo. El desafo de la educacin financiera cruza a distintos grupos y subgrupos de la poblacin, cada uno de los cuales tiene sus propias necesidades. Sin embargo, existe bastante coincidencia en que la tarea debe comenzar con los nios y los jvenes, que adquieren experiencia con los productos financieros cada vez a ms temprana edad. Pero, lo ms importante es que las acciones que se desplieguen entre ellos pueden resultar muy efectivas en el mediano y largo plazo. En esa perspectiva, la primera responsabilidad la tienen sin duda los padres y apoderados. Estos deben apoyar a sus respectivos hijos y pupilos en la formacin de actitudes, conductas y prcticas para un sano desenvolvimiento futuro en el mbito de sus finanzas personales. En esa misma lnea, las escuelas, liceos y universidades pueden efectuar una positiva contribucin. (2014). caractersticas y necesidades de los distintos grupos a la cual se dirigen. No es posible pensar en un modelo nico de validez universal.
