Recall that gross domestic product (GDP) grew 7.2% that year. To postulate that the subsequent reduction of the instance rate to 6.5% caused, in less than six months, an acceleration of more than 15% of domestic spending, is to assign an unusual power to monetary policy, so we must discard this movement of rates as the central argument in the overexpansion of spending. Our studies indicate that domestic demand received a strong stimulus from the huge capital inflows that were registered that year (over 10% of GDP), partly attracted by relatively high domestic interest rates and exchange rate stability, and also by favorable business expectations in the country. Towards the last quarter of 1997, a dilemma arose between relatively high rate levels (relative to international rates) that attracted external capital, despite the reserve requirement, and tended to pressure the floor of the exchange rate band, and signs of rapid recovery in domestic spending that required a tilt to tighten monetary policy. This dilemma originated in part in a duality of purposes maintained by the Central Bank: on the one hand, to maintain controlled spending in order to meet inflation targets; and on the other, avoiding an appreciation would change beyond the band. Finally, at the beginning of 1998, faced with a capital account with lower flows and with an inverse exchange rate trend (to depreciation), the rate of instance was raised, privileging the usual mechanism of transmission of monetary policy. It should be added that fiscal policy maintained in the period the expansionary instance that it had brought since 1996, which may have contributed to the phenomenon. Indeed, the indicators of fiscal impulse and cyclical effect of the public budget indicate that 1997 was an expansionary year, while budget execution shows a strong increase on the expenditure side just in the fourth quarter of 1997. It is at this moment that the first speculative attack against the peso and a rapid escalation of the exchange rate manifest itself. What were the policy options in that context? One option, followed by several of the Asian countries a little earlier, was to "loosen ties", unanchor the exchange rate, inflation expectations and eventually inflation itself, without initially tightening monetary policy and then, later, cooling inflationary pressures with restrictive monetary and fiscal policies. The other was to first cool the trajectory of spending (by immediately tightening monetary policy), propose a limited defense of the peso, ensure that inflation expectations are kept at bay, and then allow a more pronounced exchange adjustment. Both options inevitably had a real cost, both because of the effect of real shocks and because of the greater uncertainty that was beginning to set in in financial markets. In the Central Bank, we chose the second policy option, because it offered, in the medium term, lower costs for the national economy. This is based on the fact that, according to historical experience, increases in the exchange rate have a significant inflationary impact on a highly indexed economy such as Chile's. Indeed, different estimates show a pass-through coefficient of 50% after one year, which means that a nominal depreciation of 1% translates into 0.5% additional inflation within the indicated period. There is also evidence that this coefficient is procyclical. For example, in a period when the economy is growing above its potential, the transfer can reach 70%. Thus, an additional depreciation of 10% in January 1998 would have generated 7% additional inflation, driving us back to double-digit inflations. But regardless of these calculations, in the conditions of increasing uncertainty that developed, the risk of nominal anchor loss was latent if a sudden and significant depreciation was allowed. This led to an increase in inflation substantially higher than discussed above. In an environment without a nominal anchor, the pass-through ratio is close to 100% and, if there is a late reaction from the authorities, interest rates must finally rise further to avoid an explosion of inflation. This situation was generated because releasing the exchange rate after it had been in practice almost fixed or appreciating for a long time could produce a drastic change in the conditions of arbitrage and risk perceptions in the market that alter portfolio composition decisions and artificially raise the exchange rate. In other words, one could maximize the likelihood that an open and costly overreaction would change in the context of an overheated economy. On the other hand, the credibility of the Central Bank's policy commitment to macroeconomic stability was also at stake if, faced with the first serious difficulty of the decade, the objectives of macroeconomic equilibrium were easily abandoned. On the contrary, what was done was to follow a strategy that minimized the risk of nominal anchor loss. It cannot be overlooked that the adoption of this strategy initially had some difficulties linked to the perception of the market in the face of the commitment of some authorities with respect to it. In addition, and due to difficulties inherent to the fiscal administration, the necessary cuts in public spending were implemented much later than the dates on which they were announced, so that in practice the fiscal execution was expansionary until well into the year, thus contributing to additional pressure on interest rates during the first quarters of 1998. Towards the beginning of June of that year, a new speculative attack against the peso was brewing, based on projecting a prolongation of the deterioration in the prices of primary products (especially copper) and the apparently low response of domestic demand and imports in the face of the more contractionary monetary policy. The prospects of a growing current account deficit, which private analysts projected to be close to 8% of GDP, made the market bet that the peso should continue to depreciate. This form of adjustment also found an echo in several union, academic and political instances, even within the government. A substantial increase in the minimum wage over the next three years had been announced shortly before. With this threatening picture looming and with the prospect of a strong inflationary resurgence still in force, the moderation of the forces that pressured the peso appeared as the most immediate anchor to placate the uncertainty associated with high exchange rate volatility and keep under control the expectation of an uncontrolled and crisis scenario. The exchange intervention of those days cooperated to the necessary portfolio adjustment carried out by the private sector, providing the foreign currency to reduce the significant exchange rate mismatch observed by that sector. However, it was not enough to eliminate expectations of a sharp depreciation of the peso. Faced with this reality, it became necessary to explicitly narrow the band would change the way of "pruning" the most extreme expectations, even at the cost of regressing in terms of the reverse trend that this band brought since the beginning of the decade. The more explicit and firm commitment to the stability of the peso (within the fluctuation limits allowed by the new band), was initially successful in appeasing exchange rate pressures, which allowed a moderation of market interest rates that moved towards instance rate levels. In that context, however, came the Russian moratorium and the enormous stir it caused in all global financial markets. The consequences of this new crisis in the immediate future were: substantial increases in the cost of external financing for emerging economies, drastic falls in the stock markets in the world, new falls in the prices of primary products and indications of significant restrictions on access to credit for Latin American economies. In particular, the surcharge on the cost of external financing for Chilean companies reached levels above 500 basis points, with respect to equivalent US Treasury securities. Internally, the effect was an increase in interest rates beyond expectations, to impulses of speculative demand for currencies that led some institutions to use resources beyond prudence to acquire dollars. At all times, global liquidity was sufficient to finance the economy, but tended to concentrate, which led the Central Bank to modify the monetary reserve requirements. Surcharge External FinancingChilean Companies Certainly, these developments were not deliberately sought, but were the result of a serious aggravation of the external scenario in all its lines. It is a mistake to assess monetary policy on the basis of its effect on spending and growth, without taking into account the enormous financial uncertainty generated after the Russian crisis. The real dilemma was how to manage that uncertainty, whether through the exchange rate or through interest rates. The picture was so uncertain that in any case there would have been extraordinary and uncontrolled increases in financial prices. The decision in the margin was initially to allow a combination of policies that emphasized a greater adjustment in interest rates and a more controlled adjustment in the exchange rate, and then reverse the order as the external situation cleared and domestic markets calmed down. The second way, to leave all the adjustment to the exchange rate, entailed an immediate cost in terms of more inflation and loss of credibility, but even more, the risk of a much deeper and lasting recession going forward to stop an economy on the verge of a balance of payments crisis and overheated with respect to its possibilities. - General reflections It has been pointed out that the Central Bank's fears of a significant inflationary resurgence from a change of control last year were unfounded, since there has ultimately been a nominal depreciation close to 20%, and inflation has remained strictly within the ranges defined by the annual targets. This statement is erroneous. The nominal depreciation has been accompanied by a reduction in domestic demand pressures that have prevented its direct pass-through to prices. In addition, international prices have been falling by significant magnitudes, and beyond expectations, since the beginning of last year, due to the appreciation of the dollar against major currencies and the economic contraction in Asia. In the absence of a contraction in domestic demand, accompanied by mostly fortuitous external deflation, coupled with market conviction of the firmness of the authorities' commitment to protecting macroeconomic stability, inflation would be substantially higher today. Worse still, we would be in the initial stages of a much deeper adjustment, coupled with that high inflation and serious difficulties in accessing international financial markets. Viewed from a positive perspective, the effective adjustment of the economy has made it possible to move in the direction of greater exchange rate flexibility and to accommodate a depreciation of the peso consistent with the new external scenario. In other words, in the long run a marked change in the exchange rate (nominal and real) has not been prevented, but this change has been made to occur at a more propitious time. No one today can ignore that the recession that we have just begun to overcome has been more intense and profound than predicted even by the most pessimistic of analysts some six or eight months ago. However, it is important to clarify that the serious worsening of the external scenario between August of last year and well into the first quarter of this year, made an economic contraction inevitable. Taking into account the direct effects of external shocks and the average response of macroeconomic policy to these shocks, it explains most of Chile's GDP variability (up to two-thirds in the case of demand-sensitive GDP). Thus, effective external shocks and the typical or average (not effective) policy reaction indicate that the twelve-month growth projected for the last quarter of last year and the first quarter of 1999 would have been negative. With two quarters of negative growth we would have technically been in a recession anyway, according to this projection, and not a simple slowdown as some claim. The greater effective fall observed with respect to the projected one, on the other hand, is due to a series of factors impossible to be foreseen, among which we must mention: the prolongation of the drought, the concentration of the fiscal adjustment in the last quarter of 1998, the Brazilian crisis in January and its recessionary impact on the region and an increase of more than 80% in the international price of oil so far in the future. 1999. Only the direct and indirect effects of drought account for one point of growth in the first half of this year. The recession we have gone through, moreover, is not a phenomenon that occurs only in Chile. All of Latin America, almost without exception, is in a strongly contractionary phase, which in some cases began clearly last year, while in others it began strongly only in 1999. However, the size of the external shock that Chile faced in this period, that is, the sum of the fall in terms of trade and the surcharges on the cost of external financing measured as a percentage of GDP, was much higher than that observed in most countries, being surpassed only by Venezuela. It is possible that, with the advantage of knowing the story once it has occurred, today some of the measures adopted seem more debatable. Today we know that the United States and international financial markets did not face a picture of credit collapse as feared after the collapse of the investment fund Long Term Capital Management; we also know that the financial impacts of the devaluation of the Brazilian real were relatively limited and that Asia has been taking the necessary measures, and that we will probably see a recovery of its growth next year. One can always speculate that this or that set of alternative measures would have led to a smaller recession without having fallen into a destabilization of the economy. The policy measures adopted at each moment were those that appeared to be the most consistent with that defense, according to the information available and the assessment of possible risks in the face of alternative policies. There is no doubt that they were policies to deal with an emergency situation. In situations like the ones we have experienced, fine-tuning management tends to lose meaning and requires instead clear and firm signals of where you are going. The US Federal Reserve itself reacted to the Russian crisis by changing its monetary policy twice in a row in less than 60 days, although the situation of domestic demand did not justify it, as a way to face a situation of external convulsion. As always happens when a crisis is overcome, we have all learned something that will serve us well for the future. One of those lessons is that the Central Bank's commitment to macroeconomic stability is not only to be fulfilled in times of plenty, but also when the economy faces severe external scenarios. Inflation is not a solution to solve anything and, on the contrary, it is only an obstacle to growth and development. More generally, despite the critical external scenario, the Central Bank's policies never abandoned their guiding principles: not only did inflation continue to be reduced, but a situation of controlled current account deficit was preserved, the process of financial integration abroad continued, and new modernizations to financial regulation were introduced. The policies of the Central Bank. A vision of the future As the uncertainty generated by the turbulent external scenario experienced last year has diminished and macroeconomic stability consolidates, the Central Bank's policies have taken a course of greater normality, although always guided by the same four guiding principles mentioned above. The circumstances are today, however, different from those that existed when the Asian crisis broke out, so policies have also been adapted to the current and probable future scenarios. - Exchange rate flexibility For example, important steps have been taken towards greater exchange rate flexibility. The reference band has been extended daily in a pre-announced way, so that today it has an amplitude of more than 22% from floor to ceiling, a figure that will be even greater as time goes by. Likewise, the Central Bank has not intervened in the changed market since the beginning of last February, when it did so very marginally, in order to facilitate that it is the market that directly determines this price. There are three crucial elements that currently enable this direction of exchange rate policy. First, last year's strong defense of macroeconomic stability created enough room to reduce the risk of a sharp pass-through of possible substantial depreciations of the peso to domestic inflation. The strategy of a cooler economy as a necessary condition for subsequent depreciation is consistent with a larger floating margin of exchange rate in the context of inflation-targeted monetary management. The second element is the reversal of the trend towards real appreciation brought by the peso before the crisis, which has implied a substantial portfolio realignment of non-bank private agents, many of whom were heavily disshoveled as of January last year. This situation is much more balanced today, and in general the expectation of a more volatile exchange rate forces, today, a position of less average mismatch. The Central Bank has cooperated in this development by promoting, together with the Superintendency of Banks, a series of regulatory innovations that will significantly deepen, in a schedule already begun, the risk coverage markets (of currencies, interest rates and terms) at the level of the banking industry. This effort is part of the Central Bank's interest in developing financial markets as complete and fluid as possible. In recent times, the range of derivative products that can be developed by financial institutions in the local market, among themselves or with third parties established in the country or abroad has expanded. In this way, futures, forwards, swaps and combinations of these on national and foreign currency, local and foreign interest rates and authorized readjustability units are currently authorized. Likewise, in response to the demand of banks and financial companies for financial instruments at various maturities and interest rates, in June of this year financial institutions were authorized to sell or assign Readjustable Promissory Notes with Payment in Coupons (PRC) and Readjustable Promissory Notes in Dollars (PRD) in installment form, from a coupon or the part corresponding to the rights thereof. Recently, a new type of document has been created, the Optional Readjustable Issue Coupon, in UF and dollars, exchangeable for PRD and PRC, in order to facilitate the transaction of the coupons, and thus give greater liquidity and depth to the market and improve the information of the yield curve. This allows the interest rate derivatives market to deepen. In addition and in order to limit the various risks facing the banking business, the Central Bank introduced important modifications to the regulations on active and passive relations in foreign currency and terms, while creating the matching of interest rates. The limits on mismatches between foreign currencies were modified and the regulations on term matching were improved in order to limit the liquidity risk of banks. Likewise, the adjustment of interest rates was incorporated, which limits the risk of operations in national and foreign currency in the face of fluctuations in interest rates. Although the agenda in this area will always be under permanent review, the progress achieved is remarkable. Going forward, and to the extent that the recent reforms are properly assimilated, the implementation of non-linear derivatives (options) in the banking industry will be studied. Likewise, an attempt will be made to facilitate that Chilean companies can issue debt securities in pesos or UF abroad. It is important to highlight that, as a result of the development of these more complex financial risk hedging instruments, the risk of exchange rate depreciations being strongly transferred to domestic inflation is significantly reduced. This has possibly been the case in Australia and New Zealand in recent years. The third element we would like to highlight concerns the fact that the Central Bank has also continued in this time the process of integration of local financial and capital markets into the rest of the world. In this field, in the last two years the necessary steps have been taken to facilitate an adequate diversification of the investment portfolio of banks and institutional investors. With regard to banking, the range of operations feasible to carry out abroad was expanded, which, as a result of the new regulations, have increased more than tenfold in the period December 1997 to June 1998, reaching on the latter date just over US 1,800 million. At the same time, the regulations governing the financing of foreign trade operations between third countries were relaxed and the carrying out of commercial credit operations directed abroad was authorized. Likewise, in order to promote greater diversification of the portfolio of pension funds and insurance companies, the global investment limits of these institutions abroad were increased. Thus, as of last June, the total investments of pension funds abroad amounted to 12.4% of their value, a figure that compares with 3.3% observed a year ago. The reserve requirement for capital inflows was also reduced to zero, as a way to alleviate the cost to the domestic private sector of the increase in spreads that has characterized the unfavorable external scenario. Looking ahead, although it is not entirely ruled out that this reserve requirement rate could rise if necessary, we believe that the flexibility itself would change and the development of more elaborate risk hedging instruments will make its use less likely. In short, very significant steps have been taken to make viable a scheme of increasing exchange rate floating. This approach seems today to be the most appropriate for the future in order to have the exchange rate as an adjustment valve without the risks that were faced last year. - Inflation targeting and monetary policy In this environment of greater exchange rate flexibility, we want to reaffirm the key role played by the inflation target as a nominal anchor of the Chilean economy and confirm the Central Bank's commitment to the inflation targeting scheme as a framework for its monetary policy. However, the current levels of inflation (3.8% in twelve months to June) place us very close to where we want to go in this area or to what we could call a regime state. This means that we are approaching a situation where, rather than reducing inflation year by year, it is necessary to maintain inflation rates within the parameters defined for this state of regime. In this context, the possibility of extending the horizon of fixation beyond one year and emphasizing more a range than a punctual and precise figure is being studied, although we have not yet taken a decision on the matter. A move in this direction would be, moreover, consistent with the greater flexibility that would change. We must make it clear that a decision of this nature should not be confused with the intention of achieving a faster economic recovery or lower unemployment rates by accepting higher inflation. Modern economic history proves time and again that voluntarist attempts to increase employment while tolerating higher inflations have inevitably failed. They have only succeeded in raising inflation, and more often than not they have ended up with even higher unemployment rates when governments react by tightening their macroeconomic policies to control the inflationary resurgence. In the end, more tolerance for inflation only brings less economic growth, and so our own historical experience shines. In our country, the relationship between the five-year averages of GDP growth and the inflation rate from 1950 to 1999 is negative, which is in some ways further evidence that the "Phillips curve" does not work, especially in a country with generalized indexing. Inflation and Growth Chile 1950-1999 annual rate of change of GDP., and logarithm of the annual increase in inflation (pilx %) In the Chilean case, the idea of increasing employment by hundreds of thousands of new jobs by paying only a minimum cost of one or two points more inflation is completely wrong. First, this dilemma is totally false in the medium term. Moreover, large increases in employment levels and a reduction in inflation can coexist. For example, between 1990 and 1997 inflation fell from 27.3 per cent to 6.0 per cent, while the level of employment increased at an average rate of 2.5 per cent per year. Second, if one even thinks that there is indeed a positive relationship between inflation and employment in the short term, in an environment in which the nominal anchor is lost, this relationship can be transformed into a negative one. An escalation of inflation-devaluation is completely useless as a way to create jobs and may rather destroy them. The experience of Chile in 1982 and of Asian countries in 1997-1998 shows that depreciation can often be contractionary. If the financial sector is substantially affected by a depreciation, there is no way to generate new jobs. Finally, if this positive short-term relationship exists, it is important to size it correctly. What does exist is the theoretical possibility of absorbing a shock with alternative policy combinations, in particular, interest rates and/or exchange rates. Technically, it is said that different policy rules generate different results in terms of employment variability and inflation. However, the real possibilities of taking advantage of this positive relationship are very limited, since it is unstable, and during periods of turbulence it is very difficult to graduate an intermediate outcome of interest rates and exchange rates. As we have already indicated, in crisis scenarios it usually ends up in more extreme gross solutions, where the monetary authority, as was done last year in our country, tries first of all to minimize the risks of ending up in a solution of high inflation, financial disorder and, finally, more unemployment. In any case, and given the trajectory that inflation currently shows, it is perfectly feasible that next year there will be a substantial increase in employment as the economic recovery consolidates and, at the same time, inflation remains within a declining trajectory with respect to the target set for this year. In other words, under no circumstances is it necessary to tolerate higher inflation in the year 2000 in order to achieve increases in employment. A greater degree of flexibility in target parameters is only needed to accommodate the floating exchange rate regime. While we recognize the effects of monetary policy on the exchange rate in current and future circumstances, I do not want this to be interpreted as a refusal by the Central Bank to maintain an extremely vigilant attitude towards the behaviour of domestic demand. This is absolutely necessary for macroeconomic stability. On the other hand, it is also important to reiterate that it is not for the Central Bank to have a precise objective with respect to the real exchange rate. The policy mix chosen may affect the nominal exchange rate, but its effect on the real exchange rate is very transitory. The latter, the true relevant parameter for production and expenditure decisions, can be affected more permanently by other policies related to State administration, which are linked to national savings and the productivity of productive factors. The contribution that an increase in public savings can make, for example, is an important element to consider. Any measure taken in this direction from next year will be positive for the future growth prospects of the Chilean economy. Conclusions I would not like to end without reiterating my conviction that future analyses of this episode will be carried out with more information, more time and also less passion. Some specific errors may be detected in some measures taken, but I am sure that the central axis of policies, the preservation of macroeconomic stability, will not be questioned. It is this achievement that today allows us to look confidently to the future, to foresee a significant recovery in economic activity, investment and employment next year, with inflation that is definitely stationary at rates comparable to those of developed countries and with comfortable external accounts. This basic requirement of progress is the floor on which the new political authorities will be able to build the future, continuing or initiating the modernizations in the different areas of national work that are required to maintain the impetus of growth and development observed in the decade that ends. In the ten years ending at the end of 1999, the Chilean economy, despite the current difficulties, will show impressive results: the highest average economic growth rate of the century, permanently declining inflation approaching levels of stability, a solid financial system, a strengthened and orderly external sector, more than sufficient external reserves, and social development indicators that put our country at the head of the continent. It is a good starting point to start the new century. The Central Bank of Chile, independent in these ten years, is associated with these results.

Como ocurre siempre que se supera una crisis, todos hemos aprendido algo que nos ser til para el futuro. Una de esas lecciones es que el compromiso del Banco Central con la estabilidad macroeconmica no slo est para cumplirse en las pocas de abundancia, sino tambin cuando la economa enfrenta severos escenarios externos. La inflacin no es una solucin para resolver nada y, al contrario, slo es un obstculo para el crecimiento y el desarrollo. Ms en general, a pesar del crtico escenario externo, las polticas del Banco Central no abandonaron nunca sus principios ordenadores: no slo se continu reduciendo la inflacin, sino que se preserv una situacin de dficit controlado de la cuenta corriente, se continu el proceso de integracin financiera al exterior y se introdujeron nuevas modernizaciones a la regulacin financiera. Las polticas del Banco Central. Una visin de futuro A medida que la incertidumbre generada a raz del convulsionado escenario externo vivido el ao pasado ha do disminuyendo y que se consolida la estabilidad macroeconmica, las polticas del Banco Central han tomado un curso de mayor normalidad, aunque siempre guiadas por los mismos cuatro principios ordenadores mencionados con anterioridad. Las circunstancias son hoy, sin embargo, distintas a las que haba cuando se desencaden la crisis asitica, por lo que tambin las polticas se han ido adaptando a los actuales y probables futuros escenarios. - Flexibilidad cambiara Por ejemplo, se han dado pasos importantes hacia una mayor flexibilidad cambiara. La banda de referencia se ha do ampliando diariamente en forma preanunciada, de modo que hoy tiene una amplitud superior a 22% desde el piso al techo, cifra que ser an mayor conforme pasa el tiempo. Asimismo, el Banco Central no ha intervenido en el mercado cambiado desde comienzos de febrero pasado, cuando lo hizo muy marginalmente, de manera de facilitar que sea el mercado quien directamente determine este precio. Hay tres elementos cruciales que permiten en la actualidad esta direccin de la poltica cambiara. Primero, la firme defensa de la estabilidad macroeconmica realizada el ao pasado cre el espacio suficiente como para disminuir el riesgo de un fuerte traspaso de eventuales depreciaciones sustanciales del peso a inflacin domstica. La estrategia de una economa ms fra como una condicin necesaria para una depreciacin posterior es coherente con un margen mayor de flotacin cambiara, en el contexto de una administracin monetaria guiada por metas de inflacin. El segundo elemento lo constituye la reversin de la tendencia a la apreciacin real que traa el peso antes de la crisis, lo que ha implicado un sustancial reacomodo de cartera de los agentes privados no bancarios, muchos de los cuales estaban fuertemente descalzados a enero del ao pasado. Esa situacin es mucho ms balanceada en la actualidad, y en general la expectativa de un tipo de cambio ms voltil obliga, hoy en da, a una postura de menor descalce promedio. El Banco Central ha cooperado a este desarrollo impulsando, junto a la Superintendencia de Bancos, una serie de innovaciones regulatorias que profundizarn significativamente, en un cronograma ya iniciado, los mercados de cobertura de riesgos (de monedas, tasas de inters y plazos) a nivel de la industria bancaria. Este esfuerzo se inscribe en el inters del Banco Central en desarrollar mercados financieros lo ms completos y fluidos posible. En el ltimo tiempo se ha ampliado la gama de productos derivados que pueden desarrollar las instituciones financieras en el mercado local, entre s o con terceras partes establecidas en el pas o en el exterior. De esta forma, en la actualidad se encuentran autorizados los futuros, forwards, swaps y combinaciones de stos sobre moneda nacional y extranjera, tasas de inters locales y extranjeras y unidades de reajustabilidad autorizadas. Asimismo, como respuesta a la demanda de bancos y sociedades financieras por instrumentos financieros a diversos plazos y tasas de inters, en junio del presente ao se facult a las instituciones financieras para que puedan vender o ceder Pagars Reajustables con Pago en Cupones (PRC) y Pagars Reajustables en Dlares (PRD) en forma fraccionada, a partir de un cupn o de la parte correspondiente a los derechos del mismo. Recientemente se ha creado un nuevo tipo de documento, el Cupn de Emisin Reajustable Opcional, en UF y en dlares, canjeables por PRD y PRC, con el objeto de facilitar la transaccin de los cupones, y as dar mayor liquidez y profundidad al mercado y mejorar la informacin de la curva de rendimientos. Esto permite profundizar el mercado de derivados de tasa de inters. En forma complementaria y con el objeto de acotar los diversos riesgos que enfrenta el negocio bancario, el Banco Central introdujo importantes modificaciones a la normativa sobre relaciones activas y pasivas en moneda extranjera y de plazos, en tanto cre el calce de tasas de inters. Se modificaron los lmites a los descalces entre monedas extranjeras y se perfeccion la normativa referida al calce de plazos, con el fin de limitar el riesgo de liquidez de la banca. Asimismo, se incorpor el calce de tasas de inters que limita el riesgo de las operaciones en moneda nacional y extranjera ante fluctuaciones en las tasas de inters. Aunque la agenda en esta materia siempre estar en permanente revisin, los avances logrados son notables. Hacia adelante, y en la medida que las recientes reformas se asimilen adecuadamente, se estudiar la implementacin de derivados no lineales (opciones) en la industria bancaria. Asimismo, se intentar facilitar que las empresas chilenas puedan emitir ttulos de deuda en pesos o UF en el exterior. Es importante resaltar que, como resultado del desarrollo de estos instrumentos ms complejos de cobertura de riesgos financieros, disminuye notoriamente el riesgo de que las depreciaciones cambiaras se trasladen con fuerza a la inflacin interna. Este posiblemente ha sido el caso de Australia y Nueva Zelanda en los ltimos aos. El tercer elemento que queremos destacar se refiere al hecho de que el Banco Central tambin ha continuado en este tiempo el proceso de integracin de los mercados financieros y de capitales locales al resto del mundo. En este campo, en los ltimos dos aos se han dado los pasos necesarios para facilitar una adecuada diversificacin de la cartera de inversiones de la banca e inversionistas institucionales. Con relacin a la banca, se ampli la gama de operaciones factibles de efectuar con el exterior, las que, producto de la nueva normativa, se han incrementado en ms de diez veces en el perodo diciembre 1997 a junio 1998, alcanzando en esta ltima fecha poco ms de US$ 1.800 millones. Al mismo tiempo, se flexibiliz la normativa que regula el financiamiento de operaciones de comercio exterior entre terceros pases y se autoriz la realizacin de operaciones de crdito comercial dirigidas al extranjero. Asimismo, con el fin de favorecer una mayor diversificacin del portafolio de los fondos de pensiones y compaas de seguros, se aumentaron los lmites globales de inversin de estas instituciones en el exterior. As, a junio ltimo, el total de inversiones de los fondos de pensiones en el exterior ascendi a 12,4% del valor de los mismos, cifra que se compara con 3,3% que se observaba un ao atrs. Tambin se redujo el encaje a los influjos de capitales a cero, como una forma de aliviar el costo al sector privado nacional del incremento en los spreads que ha caracterizado el desfavorable escenario externo. Hacia futuro, aunque no es del todo descartable que esta tasa de encaje pudiera subir si fuera necesario, creemos que la propia flexibilidad cambiara y el desarrollo de instrumentos ms elaborados de cobertura de riesgo cambiarlo harn menos probable su utilizacin. En sntesis, se han dado pasos muy significativos para hacer viable un esquema de creciente flotacin cambiara. Este enfoque parece hoy como el ms adecuado de cara al futuro en orden a contar con el tipo de cambio como una vlvula de ajuste sin los riesgos que se enfrentaron el ao pasado. - Metas de inflacin y poltica monetaria En este ambiente de mayor flexibilidad cambiara, queremos reafirmar el rol clave que juega la meta de inflacin como ancla nominal de la economa chilena y confirmar el compromiso que tiene el Banco Central con el esquema de metas de inflacin como marco de su poltica monetaria. No obstante, los actuales niveles de inflacin (3,8% en doce meses a junio) nos sitan muy cerca de donde queremos llegar en esta materia o a lo que podramos llamar un estado de rgimen. Esto significa que nos aproximamos a una situacin donde, ms que requerirse reducir la inflacin ao a ao, se necesita mantener tasas de inflacin dentro de los parmetros definidos para este estado de rgimen. En este contexto, estn en estudio la posibilidad de extender el horizonte de fijacin ms all de un ao y enfatizar ms un rango que una cifra puntual y precisa, aunque an no hemos tomado una decisin en la materia. Un movimiento en esta direccin sera, adems, coherente con la mayor flexibilidad cambiara. Debemos dejar en claro que una decisin de esta naturaleza no se debe confundir con la intencin de conseguir una reactivacin econmica ms rpida o menores tasas de desempleo aceptando una inflacin mayor. La historia econmica moderna demuestra una y otra vez que los intentos voluntaristas de aumentar el empleo tolerando inflaciones ms altas, han resultado indefectiblemente en fracaso. Slo han conseguido aumentar la inflacin, y la mayora de las veces han terminado con tasas de desempleo an mayores cuando los gobiernos reaccionan endureciendo sus polticas macroeconmicas para controlar el rebrote inflacionario. Al final, ms tolerancia a la inflacin slo trae menos crecimiento econmico, y as lo lustra nuestra propia experiencia histrica. En nuestro pas, la relacin entre los promedios quinquenales del crecimiento del PIB y de la tasa de inflacin desde 1950 a 1999 es negativa, lo que constituye de alguna forma una evidencia ms de que la "curva de Phillips" no funciona, y menos en un pas con indizacin generalizada Inflacin y Crecimiento Chile 1950-1999 tasa de variacin anual del PIB., y logaritmo del incremento anual de la inflacin (pilx %) En el caso chileno, la dea de aumentar el empleo en cientos de miles de nuevos puestos pagando slo un costo mnimo de uno o dos puntos ms de inflacin, es completamente errnea. En primer lugar, esta disyuntiva es totalmente falsa en el mediano plazo. Es ms, pueden coexistir grandes aumentos en los niveles de empleo y una reduccin en la inflacin. Por ejemplo, entre 1990 y 1997 la inflacin disminuy desde 27,3% a 6,0%, mientras que el nivel de empleo aument a un ritmo promedio de 2,5% por ao. Segundo, si se piensa incluso que efectivamente existe una relacin positiva entre inflacin y empleo en el corto plazo, en un ambiente en que se pierde el ancla nominal, esta relacin se puede transformar en negativa. Una escalada de inflacin-devaluacin es completamente intil como forma de crear empleos y puede ms bien destruirlos. La experiencia de Chile en 1982 y de los pases asiticos en 1997-1998, muestra que una depreciacin puede muchas veces ser contractiva. Si el sector financiero ve sustancialmente afectada su fortaleza con una depreciacin, no hay manera de generar nuevos empleos. Por ltimo, en caso de existir esta relacin positiva de corto plazo, es importante dimensionarla correctamente. Lo que efectivamente existe es la posibilidad terica de absorber un shock con combinaciones de poltica alternativas, en particular, tasas de inters y/o tipo de cambio. Tcnicamente se dice que distintas reglas de poltica generan distintos resultados en en cuanto a variabilidad de empleo e inflacin. Sin embargo, las posibilidades reales de aprovechar esta relacin positiva son muy limitadas, pues ella es inestable, y durante perodos de turbulencia es muy difcil graduar un resultado intermedio de tasas de inters y tipo de cambio. Como ya hemos indicado, en escenarios de crisis normalmente se termina en soluciones gruesas ms extremas, donde la autoridad monetaria, como se hizo el ao pasado en nuestro pas, intenta antes que nada minimizar los riesgos de terminar en una solucin de alta inflacin, desorden financiero y, finalmente, ms desempleo. De cualquier modo, y dada la trayectoria que muestra la inflacin en la actualidad, es perfectamente factible que el prximo ao se observe un incremento sustancial en el empleo conforme se consolida la recuperacin econmica y, al mismo tiempo, se mantenga la inflacin dentro de una trayectoria declinante respecto de la meta planteada para este ao. En otras palabras, bajo ningn punto de vista se requiere tolerar una inflacin ms alta en el ao 2000 para conseguir aumentos en materia de empleo. Slo se necesita un grado mayor de flexibilidad en los parmetros de la meta para acomodar el rgimen de creciente flotacin cambiara. Aunque reconocemos los efectos que tiene la poltica monetaria sobre el tipo de cambio en las actuales y futuras circunstancias, no quiero que esto se interprete como una renuncia del Banco Central a mantener una actitud extremadamente vigilante frente al comportamiento de la demanda interna. Esto es absolutamente necesario para la estabilidad macroeconmica. Por otra parte, tambin es importante reiterar que no corresponde al Banco Central un objetivo preciso respecto del tipo de cambio real. La combinacin de polticas escogida puede afectar al tipo de cambio nominal, pero su efecto sobre el tipo de cambio real es muy transitorio. Este ltimo, el verdadero parmetro relevante para las decisiones de produccin y gasto, puede ser afectado en forma ms permanente por otras polticas relacionadas con la administracin del Estado, y que se vinculan al ahorro nacional y a la productividad de los factores productivos. La contribucin que puede hacer, por ejemplo, un aumento del ahorro pblico al respecto resulta un elemento importante a considerar. Cualquier medida que se tome en esta direccin a partir del prximo ao ser positiva para las perspectivas de crecimiento futuro de la economa chilena. Conclusiones No quisiera terminar sin reiterar mi conviccin de que los anlisis que se hagan en el futuro sobre este episodio se realizarn con ms informacin, ms tiempo y tambin menos pasin. Podrn detectarse algunos errores puntuales en algunas medidas tomadas, pero estoy seguro que el eje central de las polticas, la preservacin de la estabilidad macroeconmica, no sern puestos en duda. Es este logro el que hoy da nos permite mirar con confianza hacia el futuro, prever una recuperacin importante de la actividad econmica, la inversin y el empleo el prximo ao, con una inflacin que se estaciona definitivamente en tasas comparables a las de los pases desarrollados y con cuentas externas holgadas. Este requisito bsico de progreso es el piso sobre el cual las nuevas autoridades polticas podrn edificar el futuro, continuando o iniciando las modernizaciones en las distintas reas del quehacer nacional que se requieren para mantener el mpetu de crecimiento y desarrollo observado en la dcada que termina. En los diez aos que concluirn a fines de 1999, la economa chilena, a pesar de las dificultades actuales, mostrar resultados impresionantes: la tasa de crecimiento econmico promedio ms alta del siglo, inflacin permanentemente declinante que se acerca a los niveles de estabilidad, un sistema financiero slido, un sector externo fortalecido y en orden, reservas externas ms que suficientes, e indicadores de desarrollo social que ponen a nuestro pas a la cabeza del continente. Es un buen punto de partida para iniciar el nuevo siglo. El Banco Central de Chile, independiente en estos diez aos, est asociado a estos resultados.

Title: Presentation of the Annual Report 1999
text: Presentation by the President of the Central Bank of Chile to the Senate on the Occasion of the Presentation of the 1999 Annual Report I. Introduction A year ago, the global economic and financial scenario was volatile and highly uncertain due to the crisis in Asia and the collapse of markets following the Russian debt moratorium. Most emerging economies, and especially the economies of the Latin American region, faced strong capital outflows, while the cost of their external financing increased and the price of their assets and commodities collapsed. International organizations made successive downward revisions to their growth projections for the world economy, and various negative developments occurred one after another in international financial markets. In recent months, the situation in global financial markets has improved very significantly and external risk factors have been narrowing, but the negative consequences for global activity of this turbulent period have become evident. The international economy has continued on a trajectory of slow growth driven only by the dynamism of the United States of America (US), commodity prices are just beginning to change their negative trend and Latin America has entered a recessionary period. Due to this complex scenario, the Chilean economy has gone through a period of contraction, although milder than that of the vast majority of countries in the region. A year ago, a rapid decline in growth was expected, inevitable as a result of the real costs of the international crisis as they were then seen. However, in the second half of last year, the crisis intensified beyond expectations, with a further decline in the terms of trade, higher external financing more expensive, higher capital outflows and an exacerbation of speculative pressures against the peso, which kept domestic interest rates high for longer than could be expected. This set of factors caused a greater than expected adjustment in domestic demand, to which were added the strong cyclical effects of the drought on supply, causing a 2.9% decrease in output during the first half of the year, a significant increase in the unemployment rate and a slowdown in inflation and a decrease in the current account deficit that has been faster than anticipated. In 1999, once the main risks on the external front had been identified, macroeconomic policies adopted an expansionary stance with a view to consolidating a process of recovery in economic growth in a context of stable inflation and external balance. Indeed, favourable inflation and current account results indicate that risks on these fronts are currently very low. On the other hand, various indicators of production and demand point to the stabilization in the trajectory of the economy during the first half of this year and some, although still weak, point to a recovery in growth for the second half of the year. The projections and targets presented in this Report are based on the consolidation of these trends. This exhibition is organized in two parts. The first relates to the internal and external economic context that prevailed between the second half of 1997 and the beginning of this year, explaining the policies implemented by the Central Bank during this period and the results obtained. The second part deals with macroeconomic targets, policies and projections for the coming years. II. Central Bank Policies in the Face of the External Crisis 1. The international crisis and its impact on the Chilean economy As is known, the crisis that erupted after the devaluation of the Thai Baht in July 1997 had already spread by the end of that year to most Asian markets. These countries entered a deep financial crisis and then a sharp contraction of their domestic demand, which greatly reduced their imports from other regions of the world, including Chile. At the same time, and as a direct consequence, world economic activity and trade increasingly suffered, while commodity prices, including copper, adjusted sharply downwards. The unexpected over-expansion of domestic demand during the second half of 1997 was mainly caused by the huge capital inflows recorded that year (over 10% of GDP) and, to a lesser extent, by the stimulus of fiscal policy in that period. Monetary policy gradually moderated until the third quarter of that year, although the strong expansion in domestic demand cannot be attributed mainly to this, due to its small magnitude. The main fact is that by the last quarter of 1997 the trajectory of domestic demand was clearly unsustainable in itself, especially in the face of the adverse external scenario that was taking shape at the beginning of 1998. In these circumstances, the first speculative attack on the peso and a rapid escalation of the exchange rate in January 1998 took place. 2. The Central Bank's policies in the face of the crisis In such a context, the policy options were essentially twofold: first, to allow an immediate upward correction of the exchange rate without initially tightening monetary policy. This option implied that inflationary pressures should be cooled later with tight monetary and fiscal policies. The second is to first cool the trajectory of spending (by immediately tightening monetary policy), to propose a limited defense of the peso, and then to allow an orderly changed adjustment. The analysis of the different scenarios that was carried out with all the information available at that moment of time indicated, on the one hand, that sudden and uncontrolled increases in the exchange rate, according to our historical experience, would have a significant inflationary impact on a highly indexed and conjuncturally over-expanded economy such as the Chilean economy towards the end of 1997. Moreover, a drastic change in the arbitrage conditions and risk perceptions of economic agents would have abruptly altered their decisions on portfolio composition, further depreciating the exchange rate, in a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy. In these conditions of increasing uncertainty it was impossible to guarantee that the changed market would not overreact as happened in the Asian economies in 1997. The risk of loss of nominal anchor was latent, which would have created an even greater sense of crisis and mistrust and would probably have led to the need for even tighter interest rate policies in order to restore stability. On the other hand, the credibility of the Central Bank's policy commitment to macroeconomic stability was also at stake in this period. In fact, this credibility would have been lost if, faced with the first serious difficulties of the decade, the objectives of macroeconomic equilibrium were easily abandoned. It cannot be overlooked that the adoption of this strategy initially had some difficulties linked to the market's perception of the commitment of important players to it. In fact, initially the maintenance of the inflation target at 4.5% for the year was questioned, while the reduction in the rate of growth of public spending was fully manifested only in the last quarter of the year. Finally, a substantial increase in the minimum wage was announced over the next three years during the same period. In this context there came, in June of that year, a new speculative attack against the peso. Faced with a threatening situation and with the prospect of a strong inflationary resurgence still in force, the moderation of the forces that pressured the peso appeared again as the most immediate alternative to placate the uncertainty associated with high exchange rate volatility. The intervention that would change from those days cooperated to the necessary portfolio adjustment carried out by the private sector, providing the necessary instruments to reduce the still significant change mismatch observed by that sector. However, this was not enough to eliminate expectations of a sharp depreciation of the peso, before which it became necessary to explicitly narrow the exchange band in order to give a more robust signal. The most explicit and firm commitment to the stability of the peso (within the fluctuation limits allowed by the new band) was initially successful in appeasing exchange rate pressures and moderating market interest rates. But the situation became more complex with the Russian default and the enormous stir it caused in all global financial markets, which was followed, as a sequel, by the collapse of the investment fund Long Term Capital Management in the US. The consequences of this new crisis in the immediate future were: substantial increases in the cost of external financing for emerging economies, drastic falls in stock markets around the world, new declines in the prices of primary products and indications of significant restrictions on access to credit for Latin American economies. All these developments were the result of a serious and growing aggravation of the external scenario in all its lines. It should be noted that, in circumstances such as these, other economies where greater variability or changed adjustment was allowed did not avoid significant increases in their interest rates or strong adjustment in global spending. 3. Results of the policies implemented The strategy followed by the Central Bank has allowed an orderly depreciation of the nominal exchange rate (close to 24% between October 1997 and August of this year) while inflation has remained within the ranges defined by the annual targets. It should be noted that 100 basis points of increase in this award represent in the short term an additional cost of about 220 million dollars per year for the country; This cost rises to about 340 million annually if the increase in the prize is sustained for an extended period of time. It is undeniable that the recession during the first quarters of 1999 has been more intense than anticipated six or eight months ago. However, it is important to clarify that the serious worsening of the external scenario between August of last year and well into the first quarter of this year, made the economic contraction inevitable. In fact, the effects of external shocks explain most of the fall in GDP in Chile in 1999, which added to other factors such as the prolongation of the drought, the fiscal adjustment cycle in 1998, the Brazilian crisis of January of this year and its recessionary impact on the region, and the 100% increase in the international price of oil so far in 1999, They help explain the retraction experienced during this year. Indeed, adding the direct impact of the decline in the terms of trade and the increase in the cost of external financing, the size of the external shock reached about 3% of GDP, being surpassed only by Venezuela until before the recent increase in oil prices. The recession that Chile is going through, moreover, is a phenomenon that occurs in almost all of Latin America. Considering the size of Chile's external shock, the growth result in 1998-1999, measured in relative terms of that shock, is probably the best of Latin American countries. A. Finally, in absolute terms, the change in the inflation rate observed in Chile in 1997-1999 is similar to that observed in other countries, so it is not possible to argue that excessive anti-inflationary zeal prevailed in Chile. This argument has no theoretical or empirical support. The so-called "Phillips curve" does not work, especially in a country with widespread indexing like Chile. Modern economic history allows us to study abundant real cases in which the attempt to increase employment while tolerating higher inflation inevitably failed. On the contrary, in the Chilean case, the evidence shows that in the medium term increases in employment levels can coexist with reductions in the inflation rate. For example, between 1990 and 1997 inflation fell from 27.3 per cent to 6.0 per cent, while the level of employment increased at an average rate of 2.5 per cent per year. In summary, in the last biennium the Chilean economy has faced the worst external scenario in more than fifteen years. Under these conditions it was inevitable to assume a cost in terms of output and higher unemployment. The policies applied were strictly necessary to maintain a degree of global equilibrium in a context of excess spending, lower income and less external financing. It is legitimate to discuss whether alternatives existed and what their advantages and costs were, but it should not be lost sight of the fact that their impact would have been only marginal in the face of the magnitude of the external shock. Once the necessary adjustments have been made, the outlook for the future is favourable. IV. Recent Economic Developments and Outlook 1999 and 2000 I turn now to recent economic developments, the inflation target and the main macroeconomic projections for the period 1999-2000. International economy The international situation is still complex, but its prospects anticipate an improvement in international conditions relevant to Chile. Indeed, over the next year there would be greater dynamism in external demand and an improvement in the terms of trade, positive factors that would be partially attenuated by the increase in the cost of international credit associated with the monetary adjustment policy that the Federal Reserve has been applying in the US. This improvement in the external scenario, however, is not without threats. Among the main risk factors are the magnitude of possible additional increases in interest rates in the US and their negative impact on the growth of the US and world economy, and the reappearance of financial turbulence in Latin American markets as a result of the difficult situation that most of the economies of the region are going through. Financial Markets On the domestic front, financial conditions have moved this year towards a clearly expansionary stage, creating appropriate financial conditions to promote a gradual recovery in domestic demand and economic growth. Market rates have been adjusted in coherence with the decrease in the monetary instance rate, reducing the cost of domestic credit, although long-term interest rates have been reduced to a lesser extent, an evolution related to the recent increase in long-term returns in international financial markets. The value of the peso has shown greater fluctuations over the last year and in net terms a depreciation of the peso has been observed. Indeed, between September 1997 and the end of last August, the peso had depreciated by more than 8% in real terms. Finally, despite the situation experienced by the country's economy during the first half of this year, banks maintained a solid position. Indeed, the indicator of return on annualized capital reached levels of the order of 12% in July; Non-performing loans as a percentage of total loans have stabilized at around 1.7%, which does not represent a risk factor for financial stability; and the wealth of the financial system, as measured by the Basel indicator, has increased in the recent period. With regard to the possible financial effects of the turn of the millennium, it should be noted that the Central Bank has the tools and information systems that allow adequate and timely administration of the increased liquidity that the financial sector may require. The Central Bank considers that the measures adopted, both by the authorities and by the commercial banks themselves under the coordination of the Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions, are sufficient guarantee for the various economic agents to operate with complete normality in the face of the turn of the millennium. Fiscal policy Fiscal policy has been a countercyclical boost to aggregate demand during 1999 and it is estimated that by the end of the year the fiscal accounts will show a deficit result. This development is mainly linked to the position of the business cycle. Likewise, the Government has undertaken to send a budget for next year with an increase in spending with macroeconomic impact that is 3.3% higher in real terms than that contemplated in the 1999 Budget Law, and that is lower than the expected growth of GDP and current revenues of the Treasury in 2000. The proposed ceiling has the virtue of bringing the result of the fiscal accounts closer to more balanced levels, an essential element for the future development of the Central Bank's policies. Indeed, the potential consolidation of a situation of persistent fiscal deficit would lead in the medium term to increased permanent pressures on domestic demand and the deficit in the current account of the balance of payments, which would ultimately raise the level of interest rates and imply a reduction in the real exchange rate. 4. Product, Expenditure and Employment Developments on the external front, which accentuated the need for adjustment policies, played a key role in slowing the pace of growth of the Chilean economy in 1999. GDP contracted by 2.9% during the first half of this year. However, the acute drought experienced by the country during the 1998/1999 season and its effects on supply, estimated at about one percentage point of GDP in the first half of the year, equivalent to one third of the contraction recorded, also contributed to this result. Employment showed a reduction of 1.5% in the first half of the year compared to the same period of the previous year, while the unemployment rate has registered a significant increase in the same period. These developments respond to the concentration of economic adjustment in employment-intensive sectors, such as industry and construction; the slow trend of moderation shown by the pace of growth in nominal and real wages throughout most of 1998 and 1999, and the unusual increase observed in the labour force. Unemployment in our country today reaches high levels, comparable to those of the countries of the European Union. However, it is important to emphasize that the Chilean economy is not going through a structural problem of unemployment such as the one that has affected the largest economies in Europe over the last two decades, but that it is a primarily transitory and cyclical situation. Projections for future developments in demand and output indicate a gradual recovery in growth in the remainder of 1999 and beyond. International conditions are better than in the past and are expected to continue on a recovery path towards the year 2000, while monetary and fiscal conditions are currently expansionary. Leading indicators, such as recent developments in the most liquid monetary aggregates, My industrial sales and trade indicators, Sales Rational Chamber of Commerce (CNC) Effective and quarterly moving averages seasonally adjusted series They point to a recovery in economic growth in the second half of the year. And new home sales Department Sales Effective and quarterly moving averages seasonally adjusted series they have received the strong boost from lower interest rates and the tax incentive program launched by the Government last June. Progress in the public works concession program should also generate a significant increase in investments in road works over the next year and an increase in investments in ports and health companies is expected as a result of the incorporation of private capital into these sectors. In addition, the recovery of mining investments is anticipated as a result of the initiation or expansion of a series of copper exploitation projects. Finally, the implementation of the municipal employment programmes recently announced by the Government will help increase private sector incomes and improve consumer expectations. The revised background indicates that the level of activity would begin to move on an expansion trajectory in this second half of the year and, towards the last quarter, the growth rate would be clearly positive. The growth of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the year as a whole would be practically zero, while domestic demand would show an estimated contraction of around 7%. The consolidation of the recovery trajectory would allow the economy to reach a growth rate of around 5% over the next year, an estimate that is consistent with the range of forecasts of various private analysts. This trajectory would be led by the recovery in domestic demand, estimated at around 7.5%. Net external demand d0 that is, the difference between real exports and imports d0 would show a moderation, mainly as a result of the recovery in purchases abroad and, to a lesser extent, the slowdown in the pace of expansion of copper exports. The projected result for next year's growth rate is consistent with a gradual but vigorous process of recovery in domestic demand and employment, the consolidation of which will allow the economy to grow at sustainable rates and around its potential in the coming years. 5. Inflation: Prices and Wages During 1999, inflation has fallen faster than anticipated. As a consequence of the impact of the economic cycle on price formation and lower external inflation. The same has happened in the world's economies as a whole. Indeed, according to the International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook, for all advanced economies, the average inflation rate would reach 1.4 per cent in 1999, compared with a projection of 1.7 per cent a year ago and with the 2 per cent rates observed until 1997. Similarly, for developing economies as a whole, an average rate of 7 per cent is expected, compared with a projection of 8.3 per cent in October 1998 and an inflation rate of 10.3 per cent in October 1998. Wages have continued to slow gradually, albeit at a slower pace than other prices, resulting in real increases despite falling employment and national income. The future evolution of the inflation rate should remain on a path of relative stability in the coming months, which would imply that by the end of the year annual rates similar to those registered at the end of August and below the target set for this year will be observed. It should be noted that the validity since last January of the new basket used in the calculation of the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which better reflects current consumption habits, has circumstantially allowed a calculation of inflation more than half a percentage point below what would have resulted with the old basket. For next year, there are conflicting elements that need to be considered for the inflation projection. On the one hand, the low inflation achieved this year will keep the usual inertial impulse contained in a wide range of prices of goods and services. Likewise, a gradual recovery rate of economic activity and the slack that exists in terms of employment and installed capacity should contribute to moderate demand pressures not pushing inflation. On the other hand, higher external inflation in a context of relative exchange rate stability, together with the recovery of marketing margins in some sectors, especially imported goods, will be factors of upward pressure on prices. In particular, the 6.6 per cent annual increase in the wholesale price index should be noted, partly as a result of the depreciation of the peso, a pressure that has not been reflected in final marketing prices. All in all, core inflation measures and market and analyst prospects are focused on around 3.5%, although with a still wide dispersion. The latter should not be surprising given the greater uncertainty that can be associated with a turning point in a cycle as acute as the current one. The inflation rates observed today and those reasonably projected for the near future are very close to those that have prevailed on average during the present decade in the industrial countries as a whole, 2.9% per year in the period 1990-1998. It can be said that the inflationary containment program that has encouraged the Central Bank of Chile in recent years is moving to a different stage. By prioritizing a gradual but persistent reduction in inflation, year after year, the movements will be in the direction of privileging the maintenance of a low and more stable inflation environment, around parameters such as those currently observed. In accordance with the above, on this occasion it has been considered appropriate to advance in the consolidation of the inflation targeting scheme by establishing an explicit target with a horizon greater than one year and the adoption of a precise range within which inflation should evolve from the end of next year. These modifications are due to a number of considerations. In the first place, maintaining an environment of low and stable inflation is the main contribution that the Central Bank can make to the country's development. Under current conditions, when much of the way towards this goal has already been traveled, it is opportune to deliver an explicit and permanent signal of commitment to price stability. Second, it is advisable to adopt a target with a greater amplitude in order to accommodate events of high probability of occurrence that affect inflation in the short term but do not alter its medium- and long-term trend. Third, the extension of the horizon is also appropriate to adequately reflect the lags that characterise the impact of monetary policy on price developments and to moderate possible effects on activity. Finally, the specification of the inflation target must reconcile the permanent purpose of price stability with the operation of an environment of greater exchange rate flexibility that can generate transitory pressures on inflation, both upwards and downwards. Specifically, the Central Bank, with the agreement of the Ministry of Finance, has decided to set an inflation target of 3.5% for the year 2000 and simultaneously a range of 2 to 4% per year as a medium-term inflation target to be in force indefinitely from 2001. In the future, that range may be altered, but always respecting the central purpose of maintaining a low inflation environment. The expected trajectory for inflation over the coming year reflects the balance between the forces outlined above. Inflation is expected to remain stable or could show a slight rebound over the next year as sales grow and margins recover, but it is estimated that these effects would be essentially transitory and would not affect its more permanent trend. In turn, the announced range between 2 and 4% establishes the limits within which this variable must be located from December next year and the central value of this range, 3%, constitutes the operational goal that guides monetary policy over time. Transient deviations from the inflationary trend from this central value are tolerable but only to the extent that they do not go beyond the established range and can be expected with reasonable certainty in a period between 12 and 24 months, in which most of the effects of monetary policy on prices are visible, Inflation would return to 3%. That is, both the upper and lower bound of the range are exceptional values for inflation and not targets per se. Likewise, monetary policy actions will be based on the expected evolution of inflation and not on its recent evolution, so even if inflation is within the defined range, it may be necessary to act preventively to avoid the accumulation of future deviations. At the same time, transitory movements in inflation outside this range may not require policy action if there is a well-founded presumption that they are of very short duration. 6. Balance of Payments Finally, with regard to the external accounts, in the second half of 1998 and so far this year, the trade balance and the current account showed a rapid correction as a result of the decline in domestic demand. Current Account and Trade Balance as a percentage of GDP, rolling years (%) This result is mainly explained by the significant contraction of purchases abroad, while the quantities exported grew at an annual rate of more than 8%. However, the current account deficit is estimated to reach around 1.5% of GDP by the end of the year, or around US1 billion, and it is anticipated that over the next year there will be a widening of the current account deficit, mainly due to a strong recovery in the value of imports (16%) to restore diminished inventories and respond to the expected growth in domestic demand. In the medium term, macroeconomic and financial policies must continue to be consistent with maintaining an adequate position of solvency and external liquidity of the Chilean economy, which ensures the normal development of international payments. This translates into maintaining adequate exchange rate flexibility that reflects the risks and trends that are present in the market, that facilitates the consolidation of the process of financial integration with the outside world and that contributes to avoiding unsustainable deteriorations in the current account deficit. 7. Future Direction of Central Bank Policies Mr. President, Senators, The set of goals and projections for the coming year reflect the prudence necessary to face a period like the current one. The inflation target of 3.5% for 2000 and the target range for the coming years are consistent with a realistic forecast of future domestic price growth in a context of recovery in the economy's dynamism throughout 2000. If policies were oriented towards achieving a higher level of inflation, it would only be possible to raise the inflationary expectations of economic agents, without managing to increase the rate of growth of the economy within a sustainable trajectory.
