A combination of expansionary macroeconomic policies such as the current one is adequately targeted to achieve these results and the external environment is appropriate. However, the realization of this set of projections and targets is not without risk. Among the external risk factors are the monetary adjustment process that the Federal Reserve has been implementing in the US and the eventual reappearance of financial turbulence in Latin American markets. Domestic risks include the degree of uncertainty about the speed of recovery in demand: in the case of private consumption, as a result of higher unemployment and the higher burden of personal debt; and investment, as a result of a possible wait by some agents for definitions of the programs and equipment of the future Government. Similarly, a factor of care is the future trajectory of fiscal accounts. The policy toolkit will retain the flexibility to adapt to the above and future events. Important steps have been taken in recent months to improve the Central Bank's policy framework. First, progress towards greater exchange rate flexibility should be noted. The reference band has been expanding daily in a pre-announced manner and the Central Bank has not intervened in the interbank market over the last six months. This development has been made possible by the discipline achieved in the control of inflation, a substantial rearrangement of the portfolio of private non-bank agents towards a situation with fewer exchange rate mismatches and the expansion of risk coverage markets (currencies, interest rates and terms) at the level of the banking industry. In the current circumstances, considering that the conditions are in place to accelerate the ongoing program of incorporating increasing degrees of exchange rate flexibility, the Central Bank recently decided to suspend its formal commitment to intervene in the exchange rate market to sustain the limits of the exchange rate band. In addition, it resolved that the interventions that could be carried out will be made only in exceptional cases, a situation in which the reasons that were taken into account for making the decision to intervene will be explained. To facilitate the transparency of this policy, the Central Bank will provide biweekly, but with some lag, disaggregated information on the holdings of international reserves and their changes. All of the above will allow a freer floating of the exchange rate and, as a consequence, degrees of greater monetary autonomy that, in turn, will facilitate in the future the administration of potential external turbulence. In any case, the "dollar agreement" will continue to be calculated and published according to the current rule as a medium-term reference for the market and for the contracts still in force that use it. Secondly, the Central Bank has continued in this time the process of integrating local financial and capital markets into the rest of the world. The range of foreign banking operations was expanded and the overall limits on overseas investment by pension funds and insurance companies were increased. The reserve requirement for capital inflows was also reduced to 0% as a way to relieve the domestic private sector of the cost of the increase in risk awards that has characterized the unfavorable external scenario. Thirdly, the consolidation of the inflation targeting scheme by incorporating characteristics of a longer-term situation, such as the extension of the setting horizon beyond one year and the definition of a range, will make it possible to deal more effectively with the inevitable fluctuations presented by internal and external economic conditions. V. Final Words In the ten years ending at the end of 1999, the Chilean economy, despite the current difficulties, will show impressive results: the highest average economic growth rate of the century, inflation that is already converging to the levels of the industrial countries, a solid financial system, a strengthened and orderly external sector, abundant external reserves and social development indicators that put Chile at the head of the continent. It is a good starting point to strengthen the recovery of the economy and employment levels, thus initiating the new century. However, our relatively small and open economy will continue to be subject to the influences of the world economy. The present crisis is in the process of being overcome, but others will come in the future that will test the solidity of the fundamentals of the Chilean economy, imposing inevitable costs on it in terms of output and employment. Faced with this risk, it is necessary to make progress in establishing a mechanism for the protection of the unemployed that, without rigidizing the labour market, better distributes the costs of adjustment among the members of our national community. The efforts that are now being made are transitory, and the task of seeking a more permanent mechanism is pending, the existence of which, in addition, would contribute to giving a more countercyclical character to public policies.

Frente a este riesgo, resulta necesario avanzar en el establecimiento de un mecanismo de proteccin de los desempleados que, sin rigidizar el mercado laboral, distribuya mejor los costos del ajuste entre los miembros de nuestra comunidad nacional. Los esfuerzos que ahora se hacen tienen carcter transitorio, y est pendiente la tarea de buscar un mecanismo ms permanente cuya existencia, adems, contribuira a dar un carcter ms anticclico a las polticas pblicas.

Title: Reflections on the Transmission of Monetary Policy
text: Reflections on the Transmission of Monetary Policy Presentation by Carlos Massad, President of the Central Bank of Chile, at the Panel of the Third Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, September 20, 1999. I would like to begin this presentation by reviewing Chile's experience with monetary policy transmission mechanisms in recent years. I will then make some reflections on some issues, which, because of their importance for economic policy, deserve further analysis. I conclude with a mention of the main challenges facing the Bank's policies in the near future. 1. Transmission mechanisms in Chile Economic theory concludes that there are several channels of transmission of monetary policy, which operate simultaneously, and whose relative importance is variable, depending on the specific characteristics of the economy. In a small and open economy like Chile's, it is possible to recognize 5 channels of transmission of monetary policy: (i) the traditional direct channel rates - expenditure / activity - wages - inflation; (ii) the credit channel, in which aggregates have an impact over the effect of rates; (ic1) the exchange rate channel, which directly affects inflation through the price of tradable goods and indirectly through its effects on activity and price of non-tradable goods; (iv) the channel of asset prices, such as stock and real estate prices, that affect people's wealth and aggregate demand; and (v) the channel of expectations about future monetary policy, which affects all variables that are determined considering the future (Jorward-looking). Central among these is expected future inflation, and therefore the credibility of the authority with respect to its specific targets and macroeconomic policy in general. Until 1997, the mechanisms of transmission (i) and (v), traditional via taxes and credibility and expectations, were privileged in Chile. In effect, the exchange rate band, as well as the capital account regulations, were aimed at limiting the exchange rate channel. Inflation control was based on the control of aggregate demand. During the last years the credit channel was not considered directly either, although the deep supervision and monitoring that is carried out on the state of the banking can be considered as a way of having kept this channel clear of problems. As Chile is an economy where there is still limited access to stock markets, the asset price channel (iv) is of secondary importance. Looking ahead, however, we will have to worry increasingly about this channel. After the international crisis of 1997-1998 and its repercussions on the Chilean economy and on the policy framework applied by the Central Bank, the channels of transmission of monetary policy in Chile have undergone some modifications. These will be seen more clearly as the changes in macroeconomic institutions that we have made settle. Three major changes have been implemented since mid-1998. First, the capital account has been further opened through the reduction to zero of the reserve requirement rate on the entry of certain categories of capital. Second, the process of making the exchange market more flexible has been completed, suspending all commitment to the previous exchange rate band. From now on, the market will be the agent in charge of determining the value of the currency. The Central Bank will only intervene in exceptional cases, a situation in which the reasons that were taken into account for taking such a decision will be explained. And thirdly, a new inflation-targeting system has been announced which will take effect from 2001. The new target will have an annual inflation range of 2 to 4%, but will not be tied to a period of 1 calendar year (as it has been since 1991 and until 2000) but will have a medium-term time horizon. This inflation targeting scheme, new for Chile, is used by most countries whose monetary regime is based on inflation targeting. Its adoption by us is due to the fact that the level of inflation has finally converged to a level that is considered adequate and permanent. The point targeting system, of annual evaluation, had great merits in allowing us to reduce inflation in a persistent, gradual, orderly and sustainable manner. However, in a regime scheme it is no longer necessary to continue to reduce inflation. Rather, it requires a scheme that is capable of maintaining anti-inflationary discipline and credibility and, at the same time, allows adequate flexibility to limit to a minimum the collateral effects of monetary policy on variability in output and employment. However, with this new policy scheme, the exchange-rate-based transmission mechanism is no longer a closed channel. On the contrary, changes in the position of monetary policy are directly reflected on the exchange rate, and thus on inflation and activity. We must now think that monetary policy has an additional transmission channel. A not minor problem, however, is the impact of an appreciation on aggregate spending. Experience indicates that appreciations can be strongly expansive, so we must maintain a great deal of caution with this mechanism; But it also indicates that a fast-growing country, with higher productivity gains than its main trading partners, tends to experience a degree of real appreciation of its currency in the medium term. Strong short-term appreciations induced by massive capital inflows are not desirable, while more moderate growth-induced appreciations are necessary and difficult to avoid. It is also a fact that there will be a somewhat higher frequency volatility. The international evidence is clear in this regard: flotation systems have a rate of change that moves more day by day. Over longer horizons, however, the opposite is true: exchange rate volatility is lower in flexible exchange rate systems. This occurs because misalignments are less common to change them under these latter systems. We should also note that maintaining a longer inflation assessment horizon allows for temporary changes in the exchange rate to be accommodated without monetary policy reactions. Moreover, the very mechanisms of hedging against short-term exchange risk will prevent movements in the price of the dollar from being transferred to inflation as easily as they did in the past. 2. Some thoughts on the mechanisms of transmission Let me now make four reflections concerning transmission mechanisms in a small, open and developing economy. These refer to the existence of nonlinearities, the existence of asymmetries, the role of expectations and credibility, and the lags with which monetary policy operates. 2.1. Existence of nonlinearities We usually describe the transmission mechanisms of monetary policy through linear models, in which a stable relationship between instruments and operational objectives is maintained. A classic example is the estimation of an aggregate demand equation (an IS curve) and an inflation acceleration equation (a Phillips curve), both completely linear. But in practice there are problems of nonlinearities that significantly complicate the economic diagnosis and the execution of monetary policy. For example, the credit channel causes a strongly contractionary monetary policy to have proportionately greater effects than the effects of a moderately contractionary policy or an expansionary policy. The well-known reason is this: when interest rates are abnormally high for extended periods, the domestic payments system may suffer with loss of confidence and the financial system may enter a cycle of excessive caution to lend. Thus, it is possible that linear prediction ends up underestimating the contractionary effects on the economy. Additionally, there are problems at the empirical level to estimate the magnitude of nonlinear effects, because few episodes of this nature are recorded. But there are not only problems with non-linear effects in the case of transmission through interest rates. There are also powerful nonlinear effects in the exchange rate transmission channel, which in turn can generate effects on the credit channel. In fact, a violent nominal depreciation can strongly weaken, and even bankrupt, the financial system, generating a recession of proportions. The experience of the southern cone in the early eighties and the more recent experience of East Asia show that if there is sufficient exposure would change a disorderly depreciation can generate a catastrophe. In that case, moreover, it is difficult to avoid high interest rates. Thus, a central bank may be faced with a complex dilemma if the country suffers a major adverse shock that requires a significant exchange rate correction. A central bank must choose between two paths with potential, powerful, and relatively unknown nonlinear effects. The problem is even more complex if one considers that the margin for fine tuning in times of turbulence is limited, that disagreements between relevant actors are maximized and that, in addition, there may be hysteresis effects, in which after nonlinear effects operate, it is more difficult to make the economy function normally. High debt stocks and a weakened financial system make a vigorous recovery difficult. Faced with this dilemma, global experience indicates that central banks in countries with exchange rate flexibility have initially opted for a combination of accommodating devaluation pressures and raising their interest rates. For the medium term, limiting the intensity of this dilemma is key. Two types of policies that help this purpose are a correct incentive policy and the promotion of markets to trade risk. For example, central banks should avoid systematically placing themselves in leaning against the wind positions in the foreign exchange market. This invites speculation, reflected in agents taking positions of currency mismatch. The new institutional framework that we have in Chile precisely avoids this type of situation. On the insurance markets side, we have also made previous substantive progress, deepening the coin derivatives market. 2.2 Existence of asymmetries A second aspect that complicates the operation of transmission mechanisms and the conduct of monetary policy is the existence of asymmetries, i.e. qualitative differences in the economy's responses or in policy responses to positive and negative shocks. This point is different from that of nonlinearities but is intimately related to it. An example of asymmetry is presented through the asset price mechanism. Asset price hikes can lead to speculative bubbles that sooner or later will burst. For central banks, the dilemma arises here as to whether or not to intervene with a restrictive monetary policy in order to prevent the development of the possible bubble. However, the consensus among central bankers d0 endorsed by a recent study by Bernanke and Gertler d0 is to refrain from intervening in cases of asset price inflation that does not translate into consumer price inflation, and to do so only when asset price inflation fuels an excessive increase in aggregate demand. jeopardising the stability of consumer prices. However, some central banks (such as the US Federal Reserve) have made it explicit that they would intervene through rapid reductions in their interest rates to prevent a collapse of their economies when violent declines in asset prices occur (stock market crash). This reflects a clear asymmetry in the policy response to a particular transmission mechanism. It should also be noted that this asymmetry can cause a situation of moral hazard, encouraging agents to over-invest in stocks d0 and therefore to overappreciate the values in the stock markets d0 in the expectation that monetary policy will rescue them from a crash. 2.3 The importance of expectations and credibility The third point I want to draw attention to is the importance of expectations, trust and credibility. Inflation has an inertial component, especially in Chile where there is massive indexation. But inflation is also a variable that considers the future (forward-looking) due to the inflationary effects of exchange movements and, more importantly, a proportion of price formation depends on the conditions that agents foresee for the future, especially inflation itself. Thus, credibility about future policies directly affects the chances of controlling inflation today, because if lower inflation is expected tomorrow, lower inflation will also be today. Not only does today's monetary policy matter, but its entire expected future sequence. Hence the importance of adopting an inflation target based on a strict, steady-state range, pre-announced for the indeterminate future. Moreover, it has been established that greater credibility allows the economy to move to a relationship between the variability of inflation and the most appropriate employment. That is, with greater credibility it is less expensive to control a given inflationary shock. It is then of first importance to win, maintain and take care of credibility. I think there are two different, but related, dimensions to the issue of credibility. On the one hand there is the problem of expectations about the actions the authority will take to bring the economy back to its steady state, given a proposed set of goals. In this case credibility is eroded if authority is more aggressive, and, above all, if it is weaker than expected (an additional symmetry). I am convinced that our Bank has gained in credibility, precisely in the most difficult moments. On the other hand there is the problem that appears when there are doubts about the goals themselves. If at the first moment of difficulty the targets are changed, specifically the inflation target, we enter a perverse circle in which the present and future control of inflation becomes more difficult. In this case, the credibility of the target weakens and expectations of future inflation increase. The latter ends up pushing up current inflation. It is because of this second credibility problem that it is important that there is a broad consensus within society, and between it and the Central Bank, on the medium-term inflation target. If any doubt that the targets will be maintained is dispelled, it facilitates the control of inflation. This commitment to the inflation target does not mean pursuing a more aggressive monetary policy. On the contrary, with high credibility, there is room to relax the speed at which shocks that deviate the inflation rate from the medium-term target are absorbed. 2.4 Lags and monetary policy Four decades ago, Friedman taught us that there are long and variable lags in the effects of monetary policy. For example, estimates show that in Chile, on average, it takes between 3 and 12 months for a change in policy to affect the level of activity, and even longer for it to affect inflation. As mentioned above, there are also nonlinearities and asymmetries, in the sense that the economy's reaction to a reduction in interest rates is, again on average, more vigorous than its reaction to an increase in interest rates. The problem of lags arises not only with respect to the effects of monetary policy, but also in terms of the real-time availability of information relevant to policy decisions. Today we know with certainty only the performance of economic activity a few months ago, counting only on estimates of activity for the period. present. With inflation the problem is less serious, but even here there is a lag. What implications do these restrictions have on monetary policy? I would like to refer to two issues on this occasion. specific: (i) to the classic question about whether politics should be more or less active if these lags exist, and (i)to the problem that We face when the private sector underestimates lags. Regarding the appropriate level of monetary policy activism, let us first recall Brainard's old recommendation: there is room for politics, but it must be less activist or more cautious. Newer work tends to reaffirm this conclusion. For example, if you are not sure about the actual lag that exists and follow a monetary policy rule that depends on the gap between projected inflation and target inflation, it is more appropriate for the rule to be less active, with greater consideration of the future (i.e., more forward looking). In this case the rule is more robust in the sense of achieving a more efficient border between inflation and unemployment variability. Similarly, studies show that if a bias is chosen, the central bank is better off thinking it is harder to control inflation. On the other hand, the gradual and persistent reduction of the inflation rate in an environment of long inflationary history and generalized indexation requires being very demanding in the fulfillment of the annual targets. Hence the importance, and the important consequences for the conduct of monetary policy, of having reached an inflation rate close to that of the steady state. Something similar is demonstrated from real-time data constraints. For example, it has been established that the policies followed by the Fed during the Burns and Volcker eras are not diametrically different from those that a simple rule of John Taylor (present at this conference) would recommend. The key is that at the time of making decisions they did not have an adequate estimate of the gap between GDP and its potential. Counterfactual exercises show that the performance of the US economy would have been better if the rule used had been simpler and focused on controlling inflation (or nominal output). The policy conclusion is that the chances of successfully fine-tuning are limited. With regard to other problems generated by long and variable lags, I would like to draw attention to the consequences of the private sector making errors in its assessment and/or estimation. I am specifically thinking about what can happen if private actors overestimate how quickly monetary policy is transmitted even though they have doubts about its effectiveness. In this case it is easy to generate a crisis of confidence and credibility, even reaching a speculative attack. The problem is that authority cannot and should not remain idle, having to face this lack of credibility, sometimes generating unwanted effects in other areas of the economy. The example of what happened in mid-1998 in Chile illustrates this situation. It had already been 5 months since monetary policy had tightened to cope with overspending and violent worsening external conditions. However, estimates for the annual current account deficit were as high as 8% of GDP. The resulting mistrust generated one of the speculative attacks we had to face during 1998. The problem is that the overspending did indeed subside later than many expected, albeit with costs in activity that could have been avoided in some proportion had there been greater confidence. This is certainly not a trivial problem to address, but it is a distortion of unsuspected consequences. The educational work that a central bank must do to describe how the economy works is key in this regard. To the extent that transmission mechanisms are discussed in a transparent and open manner, these games, which are certainly negative-sum, will be avoided. 3. Remaining Challenges The Central Bank of Chile has consolidated its policy framework through four key measures adopted over the past year: a5 Strengthening risk management in the financial system. a5 The substantial liberalization of capital inflows. a5 the adoption of a flexible changed system. a5 the adoption of an inflation target expressed in a range of 2 to 4% for the medium term, in line with the convergence of Chilean inflation at stationary levels. These measures constitute a significant strengthening of monetary policy, also implying changes in the relative weightings of the policy transmission channels. To further strengthen the credibility of this policy framework, the Central Bank faces three complementary challenges: 1. Contribute to a better understanding of transmission mechanisms, 2. Increase public disclosure of statistical information and methods of analysis and projection used by the Central Bank, and 3. Increase the transparency of the Central Bank's projections and policy decisions through the publication of regular and more frequent macroeconomic policy reports. References Bernanke, B. y M. Quiero comenzar esta exposicin revisando lo que ha sido la experiencia de Chile con los mecanismos de transmisin de la poltica monetaria durante los ltimos aos. Luego realizar algunas reflexiones en torno a algunos temas, que por su importancia para la poltica econmica, merecen mayor anlisis. Finalizo con una mencin a los principales desafos que enfrentan las polticas del Banco en el futuro prximo.  Mecanismos de transmisin en Chile La teora econmica concluye que existen diversos canales de transmisin de la poltica monetaria, que funcionan en forma simultnea, y cuya importancia relativa es variable, dependiendo de las caractersticas especficas de la economa. En una economa pequea y abierta como la chilena, es posible reconocer 5 canales de transmisin de la poltica monetaria: (i) el canal tradicional directo tasas - gasto/actividad - salarios - inflacin; (ii) el canal del crdito, en que los agregados tienen un impacto por sobre el efecto de las tasas; (i) el canal del tipo de cambio, que afecta directamente a la inflacin a travs del precio de los bienes transables e indirectamente a travs de sus efectos en actividad y precio de los bienes no transables; (iv) el canal de los precios de activos, como los precios de las acciones y de los bienes races, que afectan la riqueza de las personas y la demanda agregada; y (v) el canal de las expectativas sobre la futura poltica monetaria, que afecta todas las variables que se determinan considerando el futuro (Jorward-looking). Entre stas es fundamental la inflacin futura esperada, y por lo tanto, la credibilidad que tenga la autoridad respecto de sus metas especficas y de la poltica macroeconmica en general. Hasta 1997 se privilegiaron en Chile los mecanismos de transmisin (i) y (v), tradicional va tasas y de credibilidad y expectativas. En efecto, la banda cambiara, as como las regulaciones de la cuenta de capitales, se orientaban a limitar el canal (i) de tipo de cambio. El control de la inflacin se basaba en el control de la demanda agregada. Durante los ltimos aos el canal del crdito tampoco fue considerado de manera directa, aunque la profunda supervisin y monitoreo que se realiza sobre el estado de la banca puede considerarse como una manera de haber mantenido este canal despejado de problemas. Por ser Chile una economa donde existe todava un acceso limitado a los mercados de valores, el canal (iv), de precios de activos, tiene una importancia secundaria. Hacia el futuro, sin embargo, deberemos preocuparnos crecientemente de este canal. Luego de la crisis internacional de 1997-1998 y sus repercusiones sobre la economa chilena y sobre el marco de polticas aplicadas por el Banco Central, los canales de transmisin de la poltica monetaria en Chile han tenido algunas modificaciones. Estas se vern con mayor claridad en la medida que se asienten los cambios en la institucionalidad macroeconmica que hemos realizado. Son tres los cambios ms importantes implementados desde mediados de 1998. Primero, se ha abierto an ms la cuenta de capitales a travs de la reduccin a cero de la tasa de encaje a la entrada de ciertas categoras de capitales. Segundo, ha culminado el proceso de flexibilizacin del mercado cambiarlo, suspendindose todo compromiso con la anterior banda cambiara. En adelante, el mercado ser el agente encargado de determinar el valor de la divisa. El Banco Central slo intervendr en casos excepcionales, situacin en la cual se explicarn las razones que se tuvieron a la vista para tomar tal decisin. Y tercero, se ha anunciado un nuevo sistema de metas de inflacin que regir a partir del ao 2001. La nueva meta tendr un rango de inflacin anual de 2 a 4%, pero no estar atada a un perodo de 1 ao calendario (como lo ha estado desde 1991 y hasta el ao 2000) sino que tendr un horizonte temporal de mediano plazo. Este esquema de meta de inflacin, nuevo para Chile, es el que utiliza la mayora de los pases cuyo rgimen monetario est basado en metas de inflacin. Su adopcin por nosotros obedece a que el nivel de inflacin finalmente ha convergido a un nivel que se considera adecuado y permanente. El sistema de metas punto, de evaluacin anual, tuvo grandes mritos al permitirnos disminuir la inflacin en forma persistente, gradual, ordenada y sostenible. Sin embargo, en un esquema de rgimen ya no es necesario seguir disminuyendo la inflacin. Ms bien se requiere de un esquema que sea capaz de mantener la disciplina y la credibilidad antiinflacionaria y que, al mismo tiempo, permita la flexibilidad adecuada para limitar a un mnimo los efectos colaterales de la poltica monetaria sobre la variabilidad en el producto y el empleo. Ahora bien, con este nuevo esquema de polticas, el mecanismo de transmisin basado en el tipo de cambio deja de ser un canal clausurado. Por el contrario, cambios en la posicin de la poltica monetaria se reflejan de manera directa sobre el tipo de cambio, y as sobre la inflacin y la actividad. Debemos pensar ahora que la poltica monetaria tiene un canal de transmisin adicional. Un problema no menor, sin embargo, es el impacto de una apreciacin sobre el gasto agregado. La experiencia indica que las apreciaciones pueden ser fuertemente expansivas, por lo que debemos mantener una gran cuota de cautela con este mecanismo; pero tambin indica que un pas que crece con rapidez, con incrementos de productividad mayores que los de sus principales socios comerciales, tiende a experimentar un grado de apreciacin real de su moneda en el mediano plazo. Apreciaciones fuertes en el corto plazo inducidas por ingresos masivos de capitales no son deseables, mientras que aquellas ms moderadas, generadas por el crecimiento son necesarias y difcilmente evitables. Es un hecho, adems, que existir una volatilidad cambiara de frecuencia algo mayor. La evidencia internacional es clara en este sentido: los sistemas de flotacin tienen un tipo de cambio que da a da se mueve ms. A horizontes ms largos, sin embargo, sucede lo contrario: la volatilidad cambiara es menor en sistemas de cambio flexible. Ello ocurre porque son menos comunes los desalineamientos cambiarlos bajo estos ltimos sistemas. Debemos observar, adems, que el hecho de mantener un horizonte de evaluacin de la inflacin ms largo permite acomodar modificaciones transitorias en el tipo de cambio sin reacciones de poltica monetaria. An ms, los propios mecanismos de cobertura contra el riesgo cambiarlo de corto plazo evitarn que los movimientos del precio del dlar se traspasen a inflacin con la facilidad que lo hacan en el pasado.  Algunas reflexiones sobre los mecanismos de transmisin Permtanme ahora hacer cuatro reflexiones relativas a los mecanismos de transmisin en una economa pequea, abierta, y en desarrollo. stas se refieren a la existencia de no-linealidades, a la existencia de asimetras, al rol de las expectativas y de la credibilidad, y a los rezagos con que opera la poltica monetaria. 2.1. Existencia de no linealidades Usualmente describimos los mecanismos de transmisin de la poltica monetaria a travs de modelos lineales, en los que se mantiene una relacin estable entre los instrumentos y los objetivos operacionales. Un ejemplo clsico es la estimacin de una ecuacin de demanda agregada (una curva IS) y de una ecuacin de aceleracin de la inflacin (una curva de Phillips), ambas completamente lineales. Pero en la prctica existen problemas de no linealidades que complican significativamente el diagnstico econmico y la ejecucin de la poltica monetaria. Por ejemplo, el canal del crdito hace que una poltica monetaria fuertemente contractiva tenga efectos proporcionalmente mayores a los efectos de una poltica moderadamente contractiva o una poltica expansiva. La razn, muy conocida, es la siguiente: cuando las tasas de inters son anormalmente altas por perodos prolongados, el sistema de pagos domstico puede resentirse con prdida de confianza y el sistema financiero puede entrar en un ciclo de exceso de cautela para prestar. As, es posible que la prediccin lineal termine subestimando los efectos contractivos sobre la economa. Adicionalmente, existen problemas a nivel emprico para estimar la magnitud de los efectos no lineales, porque se registran pocos episodios de esta naturaleza. Pero no slo se presentan problemas con efectos no lineales en el caso de la transmisin a travs de las tasas de inters. Tambin existen poderosos efectos no lineales en el canal de transmisin del tipo de cambio, el que a su vez puede generar efectos sobre el canal del crdito. De hecho, una depreciacin nominal violenta puede debilitar fuertemente, y hasta hacer quebrar, el sistema financiero generando una recesin de proporciones. La experiencia del cono sur a comienzos de los ochenta y la ms reciente del este asitico demuestran que si existe suficiente exposicin cambiara una depreciacin desordenada puede generar una catstrofe. En ese caso, adems, es difcil evitar tasas de inters elevadas. As, un banco central se puede ver enfrentado a un dilema complejo si el pas sufre un shock adverso de importancia que requiere de una correccin cambiara significativa. Un banco central debe escoger entre dos caminos con potenciales efectos no lineales, poderosos y relativamente desconocidos. El problema es an ms complejo si se considera que el margen para hacer sintona fina en momentos de turbulencia es limitado, que los disensos entre los actores relevantes se maximizan y que, adems, pueden existir efectos de hysteresis, en que luego de que operan los efectos no lineales, es ms difcil hacer funcionar normalmente a la economa. Los elevados stocks de deuda y un sistema financiero debilitado dificultan una recuperacin vigorosa. Ante este dilema, la experiencia mundial indica que los bancos centrales en pases con flexibilidad cambiara han optado inicialmente por una combinacin de acomodo de presiones de devaluacin y aumento de sus tasas de inters. Para el mediano plazo es clave limitar la intensidad de este dilema. Dos tipos de polticas que ayudan a este propsito son una poltica de incentivos correcta y la promocin de mercados para transar riesgo. Por ejemplo, los bancos centrales deben evitar colocarse sistemticamente en posiciones en contra-del-viento (leaning against the wind) en el mercado cambiado. Esto invita a la especulacin, reflejada en que los agentes toman posiciones de descalce de monedas. La nueva institucionalidad cambiara que tenemos en Chile precisamente evita este tipo de situaciones. En el lado de los mercados de seguros tambin hemos realizado avances sustantivos previos, profundizando el mercado de derivados de monedas.  Existencia de asimetras Un segundo aspecto que complica la operacin de los mecanismos de transmisin y la ejecucin de la poltica monetaria es la existencia de asimetras, vale decir, diferencias cualitativas en las respuestas de la economa o en las respuestas de poltica ante shock positivos y negativos. Este punto es distinto al de las no linealidades pero est ntimamente relacionado con l. Un ejemplo de asimetra se presenta a travs del mecanismo de los precios de activos. Alzas de precios de activos pueden desembocar en burbujas especulativas que tarde o temprano reventarn. Para los bancos centrales se presenta aqu el dilema de si intervenir o no con una poltica monetaria restrictiva a fin de prevenir el desarrollo de la eventual burbuja. No obstante, el consenso entre banqueros centrales --refrendado por un estudio reciente de Bernanke y Gertler-- es abstenerse de intervenir en casos de una inflacin de precios de activos que no se traduzca en una inflacin de precios al consumidor, y hacerlo solamente cuando la inflacin de precios de activos alimenta un incremento excesivo en la demanda agregada, poniendo en peligro la estabilidad de los precios al consumidor. No obstante, algunos bancos centrales (como Reserva Federal de los EE.UU.) han hecho explcito que intervendran a travs de reducciones rpidas en sus tasas de inters para evitar un colapso de sus economas cuando se produzcan disminuciones violentas de precios de activos (crash de las bolsas de valores). Esto refleja una clara asimetra en la respuesta de poltica respecto de una mecanismo de transmisin particular. Tambin cabe notar que esta asimetra puede provocar una situacin de riesgo moral, incentivando a los agentes a sobre-invertir en acciones y por tanto a sobre-apreciar los valores en las bolsas ante la expectativa de que la poltica monetaria los rescatar de un crash.  La importancia de las expectativas y de la credibilidad El tercer punto sobre el cual quiero llamar la atencin es la importancia de las expectativas, la confianza y credibilidad. La inflacin tiene un componente inercial, especialmente en Chile donde existe masiva indizacin. Pero tambin la inflacin es una variable que considera el futuro (forward-looking} por los efectos inflacionarios que tienen los movimientos cambiarlos y, ms importante an, una proporcin de la formacin de precios depende de las condiciones que los agentes prevean hacia el futuro, especialmente la inflacin misma. As, la credibilidad sobre las polticas futuras afecta directamente las posibilidades de controlar la inflacin hoy, pues si se espera una menor inflacin maana, menor tambin ser la inflacin de hoy. No slo importa la poltica monetaria de hoy, sino que toda su secuencia futura esperada. De ah la importancia de adoptar una meta de inflacin basada en un rango estricto, de estado estacionario, pre-anunciada para el futuro indeterminado. An ms, se ha establecido que una mayor credibilidad permite llevar la economa a una relacin entre variabilidad de la inflacin y del empleo ms adecuada. Esto es, con mayor credibilidad es menos costoso controlar un shock inflacionario dado. Es entonces de primera importancia ganar, mantener y cuidar la credibilidad. Pienso que existen dos dimensiones distintas, aunque relacionadas, en el tema de la credibilidad. Por un lado est el problema de expectativas sobre las acciones que realizar la autoridad para llevar a la economa de vuelta a su estado estacionario, dado un conjunto de metas propuesto. En este caso la credibilidad se erosiona si la autoridad es ms agresiva, y, sobre todo, si es ms dbil de lo esperado (una simetra adicional). Tengo el convencimiento que nuestro Banco ha ganado en credibilidad, precisamente en los momentos ms difciles. Por otro lado est el problema que aparece cuando existen dudas sobre las metas mismas. Si al primer momento de dificultad se cambian las metas, especficamente la meta de inflacin, se entra en un crculo perverso en que el control presente y futuro de la inflacin se hace ms difcil. En este caso la credibilidad en la meta se debilita y las expectativas de inflacin futura aumentan. Esto ltimo termina por presionar la inflacin presente al alza. Es por este segundo problema de credibilidad que es importante de que exista un amplio consenso al interior de la sociedad, y entre sta y el Banco Central, sobre la meta de inflacin de mediano plazo. Si se disipa toda duda respecto de que las metas sern mantenidas, se facilita el control de la inflacin. Este compromiso con la meta de inflacin no significa seguir una poltica monetaria ms agresiva. Por el contrario, con alta credibilidad, existe espacio para flexibilizar la velocidad a la cual se absorben shocks que desvan la tasa de inflacin de la meta de mediano plazo.  Rezagos y poltica monetaria Hace ya cuatro dcadas que Friedman nos ense que existen rezagos largos y variables en los efectos de la poltica monetaria. Por ejemplo, las estimaciones muestran que en Chile, en promedio, pasan entre 3 y 12 meses para que un cambio en poltica afecte el nivel de actividad, y an ms para que afecte a la inflacin. Como mencionamos arriba, existen adems no linealidades y asimetras, en el sentido de que la reaccin de la economa a una rebaja de tasas de inters es, nuevamente en promedio, ms vigorosa que su reaccin a un incremento de ellas. El problema de los rezagos no slo se presenta respecto de los efectos de la poltica monetaria, sino que tambin en cuanto a la disponibilidad en tiempo real de informacin relevante para las decisiones de poltica. Conocemos hoy con certeza slo el desempeo de la actividad econmica de algunos meses atrs, contando slo con estimaciones de actividad para el perodo presente. Con la inflacin el problema es menos grave, pero an en este caso se presenta un rezago. Qu implicaciones tienen estas restricciones sobre la poltica monetaria? Me quiero referir en esta oportunidad a dos temas especficos: (i) a la pregunta clsica sobre si la poltica debe ser ms o menos activa si existen estos rezagos, y (i) al problema que enfrentamos cuando el sector privado subestima los rezagos. Respecto del nivel adecuado de activismo de la poltica monetaria recordemos primero la antigua recomendacin de Brainard: existe espacio para hacer poltica, pero sta debe ser menos activista o ms cauta. Trabajos ms nuevos tienden a reafirmar esta conclusin. Por ejemplo, si no se est seguro sobre el rezago efectivo que existe y se sigue una regla de poltica monetaria que depende de la brecha entre la inflacin proyectada y la inflacin meta, es ms adecuado que la regla sea menos activa, con mayor consideracin del futuro (es decir, ms "forward looking"). En este caso la regla es ms robusta en el sentido de lograr una frontera ms eficiente entre variabilidad de inflacin y desempleo. Del mismo modo, los estudios muestran que, de escoger un sesgo, es mejor que el banco central piense que es ms difcil controlar la inflacin. Por otra parte, la reduccin gradual y persistente de la tasa de inflacin en un ambiente de larga historia inflacionaria e indizacin generalizada, requiere ser muy exigente en el cumplimiento de las metas anuales. De aqu la importancia, y las destacadas consecuencias para la conduccin de la poltica monetaria, de haber alcanzado una tasa de inflacin cercana a la del estado estacionario. Algo similar se demuestra a partir de las restricciones de datos en tiempo real. Por ejemplo, se ha logrado establecer que las polticas seguidas por el FED durante las pocas de Burns y de Volcker no son diametralmente diferentes a las que una simple regla de John Taylor (presente en esta conferencia) recomendara. La clave est en que al momento de tomar decisiones no contaban con una estimacin adecuada de la brecha entre el PIB y su potencial. Ejercicios contrafactuales muestran que el desempeo de la economa de EE.UU. habra sido mejor si la regla utilizada hubiese sido ms simple y focalizada en el control de la inflacin (o el producto nominal). La conclusin de poltica es que las posibilidades de realizar con xito una sintona fina son limitadas. Respecto de otros problemas que generan los rezagos largos y variables, quiero llamar la atencin sobre las consecuencias derivadas de que el sector privado cometa errores en su apreciacin y/o estimacin. Especficamente estoy pensando lo que puede suceder si los agentes privados sobreestiman la rapidez con que se transmite la poltica monetaria aunque tienen dudas respecto de su efectividad. En este caso es fcil que se genere una crisis de confianza y credibilidad, llegndose incluso a un ataque especulativo. El problema es que la autoridad no puede ni debe quedarse de manos cruzadas, teniendo que enfrentar esta falta de credibilidad, a veces generando efectos no deseados en otras reas de la economa. El ejemplo de lo sucedido a mediados de 1998 en Chile grfica esta situacin. Ya haban pasado 5 meses desde que la poltica monetaria se haba endurecido de manera de hacer frente al exceso de gasto y el empeoramiento violento de las condiciones externas. Sin embargo, las estimaciones para el dficit anual de cuenta corriente llegaban al 8% del PIB. La desconfianza derivada gener uno de los ataques especulativos que debimos enfrentar durante 1998. El problema es que el exceso de gasto efectivamente cedi ms tarde de lo que muchos esperaban, aunque con costos en actividad que se podran haber evitado en alguna proporcin de haber existido una mayor confianza. Ciertamente ste no es un problema trivial de abordar pero constituye una distorsin de consecuencias insospechadas. La labor de educacin que debe hacer un banco central respecto de describir cmo funciona la economa es clave en este sentido. En la medida en que se discuta de manera transparente y abierta sobre los mecanismos de transmisin se evitarn estos juegos que ciertamente son de suma negativa.  Desafos Pendientes El Banco Central de Chile ha consolidado su marco de polticas a travs de cuatro medidas fundamentales adoptadas durante el ltimo ao:  El fortalecimiento del manejo de riesgos en el sistema financiero.  La substancial liberalizacin de la entrada de capitales.  la adopcin de un sistema cambiado flexible.  la adopcin de una meta de inflacin expresada en un rango de 2 a 4% para el mediano plazo, acorde con la convergencia de la inflacin chilena a niveles estacionarios. Estas medidas constituyen un fortalecimiento significativo de la poltica monetaria, implicando, tambin, cambios en las ponderaciones relativas de los canales de transmisin de la poltica. Para fortalecer an ms la credibilidad de este marco de polticas, el Banco Central enfrenta tres desafos complementarios:  Contribuir a una mejor comprensin de los mecanismos de transmisin,  Incrementar la divulgacin pblica de informacin estadstica y mtodos de anlisis y proyeccin utilizados por el Banco Central, y  Incrementar la transparencia de las proyecciones y de las decisiones de poltica del Banco Central, a travs de la publicacin de informes de poltica macroecnomica regulares y de mayor frecuencia. Title: The outlook for the Chilean economy and the new monetary policy scheme
text: The outlook for the Chilean economy and the new monetary policy scheme Presentation by Carlos Massad, President of the Central Bank of Chile, at a breakfast conference organized by ASIMET, March 30, 2000. I would like to thank the Association of Metallurgical and Metalworking Industries (ASIMET) for its invitation and take this opportunity to make a presentation on recent developments and prospects for the Chilean economy. The central ideas I want to share with you are the following: The process of reactivating the Chilean economy is on track and there are no major risks on this front. At present, the central concern of the Issuing Institute and what I will call "new monetary policy scheme", revolves around achieving a healthy and lasting recovery of the economy in a context of low and stable inflation. I. - Recent developments in the economy 1. Throughout 1999, the monetary policy promoted by the Central Bank adopted an openly expansionary position, with successive reductions in the monetary instance rate, which ended 1999 at its lowest level of the decade. At the changed level, the greater stability of national and international financial markets, the greater possibilities for portfolio diversification, the possibility of having greater and better risk hedging mechanisms and inflationary control, were fundamental elements that created the propitious circumstances to progressively introduce the expansion of the limits of exchange rate fluctuation. This ended at the beginning of September in the indefinite suspension of the formal commitment by the Central Bank to intervene in the exchange market through the suspension of the limits of the exchange rate band. This greater exchange rate flexibility means in practice greater degrees of freedom for the actions of the market and the monetary authority. 2. Overall, the policies pursued by the Central Bank in 1999, together with an expansionary fiscal policy, which actively favoured the implementation of special labour recruitment programmes and tax incentives for the purchase of housing, were intended to stimulate the process of recovery and consolidation of economic growth in a context of external balance and low and controlled inflation. This is how, despite the fact that the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) experienced an annual decrease of the order of 1% last year, towards the end of the second quarter a slow recovery of activity began to be evident, which has continued in the following periods. Indeed, according to the evolution of the Monthly Indicator of Economic Activity (Imacec), activity expanded in the order of 5% annually during last December and January. Consistent with the recovery in growth, there has been a significant reduction in unemployment, from a peak of 11.5% at its worst, the rolling quarter ended in August last year, to a level of 8.1% in the rolling quarter ended in February of this year. In general terms, the economic activity indicators clearly indicate a process of recovery, with growth in economic activity expected to be close to potential growth through the year 2000 and to gradually approach the level of activity. 7. Indeed, projections for domestic demand indicate that an increase will be observed in the coming months after the contraction recorded during 1999. Towards the end of last year, private consumption showed a recovery that is expected to continue during the year 2000. Specifically, in the fourth quarter of 1999 sales of new cars grew 13.7%, sales of supermarkets (INE) experienced an increase of 8.5%, retail sales rose 5% and additionally, sales of durable consumer industrial goods increased 11.4%. Going forward, this trend is expected to continue, although not necessarily at the same speed; The increase in both asset prices and earned income has led to an easing of consumer liquidity constraints and increased optimism among agents. This is confirmed by the various consumer confidence indicators available on the market. In addition to the above elements associated with the reactivation of domestic demand, there is an increase in the replenishment of inventories, a phenomenon characteristic of the reactivation phases of the economic cycle. External demand will also pick up during 2000, since the international scenario is more favourable this year in terms of economic growth. Indeed, the external environment has continued to improve in recent months, so that world GDP growth in 1999 exceeded expectations and the rate of global expansion is projected to average around 4 per cent annually from this year. This forecast is based on the consolidation of the recovery already observed in the countries of Europe, Japan and emerging Asia, and, to a lesser extent, in Japan; at the beginning of an expansion phase in the economies of Latin America led by Chile, Brazil and Mexico, according to the IMF, and in a gentle and controlled moderation of the growth of the North American economy. It is expected that during the current year external demand will put favorable pressure on the recovery of commodity prices, especially the price of copper, for which an average price during the year of 81 cents per pound (BML) is estimated. 9. At the same time, the external financial position of the Chilean economy has strengthened significantly over the last year, both in absolute terms and in relation to other emerging economies. The current account of the balance of payments closed in almost equilibrium in 1999, the economy maintained its country risk rating d1 the best of Latin American countries d1 and the sovereign spread decreased considerably, while the solvency, liquidity and external debt ratios remain in a privileged position within emerging economies. The trend in demand, both domestic and external, also favours a gradual pick-up in investment during the 2000 and 2001. The increase in the price of major exports, the improvement in the external scenario and the greater optimism recorded by opinion polls regarding economic growth in the current biennium are elements that positively affect investment. In addition, there are other specific factors that are also favorable, such as the concentration of investments in infrastructure associated with bidding processes for road and urban works; new investments in sanitary works and the partial continuation, during the year 2000, of the tax incentive for the acquisition of new DFL-2 housing. Gross fixed capital formation, estimated at 26.7 per cent of GDP in 1999, will rise to an estimated figure of almost 28 per cent in 2000. 11. Fiscal policy had an expansionary effect on aggregate demand in 1999, with the balance of fiscal accounts deteriorating sharply as a result of the fall in tax revenues associated with the contractionary economic cycle. The results for last year as a whole point to a fiscal deficit of 1.5% of GDP. Public spending with impact Direct macroeconomic on aggregate demand, which represents just over 20% of domestic spending, showed a cumulative growth of 5.7% over the past year. In contrast, current tax revenues showed a decrease of 3.3%, in which the fall in tax collection of items associated with the economic cycle such as VAT, import duties and income tax stands out. Overall, fiscal policy had an expansionary effect on demand during 1999. 12. The prospects that can be deduced from the budget approved for this year point to an improvement in the fiscal position based on moderate growth in public spending and the recovery of tax revenues, consistent with the expected growth of the economy. Overall, fiscal policy is expected to have a slightly contractionary effect on demand during 2000 as a result of a growth rate in fiscal expenditures below the rate of growth in potential GDP and a significant recovery in tax revenues. The new authorities have also emphasized that fiscal policy will be geared towards recovering and consolidating a structural fiscal surplus of the order of 1 percent of GDP over the medium term, which will imply a restrictive fiscal policy during this and next year. 13. Even after the recent increases, the monetary policy interest rate maintains a slightly expansionary stance on aggregate demand. This is possible because, despite the greater recovery recorded by the economy, there are spaces for demand to grow more rapidly in the short term due to the slack in the installed capacity of companies, in the labor market and in the external accounts. However, this growth must necessarily converge in the medium term towards potential or else inflationary pressures will be generated on the demand side. II.- Inflation Outlook and Supply Shocks 14. During 1999, inflation declined sharply, falling below the previous year's target at the end of the period. The business cycle, both in Chile and abroad, was the predominant important cause of the decline in inflationary trends during 1999. The moderation in price behavior was widespread. The non-tradable component of trend inflation increased by 3.1 per cent, more than four percentage points below that observed in 1998. In addition, the contraction of the labor market through the decrease in occupational supply produced a moderating effect on wage adjustments and on the cost of personal services included in the CPI basket. Thus, the prices of professional services, health, education, recreation and housing (rents) significantly reduced their rate of change during 1999 in response to the economic cycle. On the other hand, the international cycle favoured the moderation of imported inflation, which meant that the dollar prices of manufactures and raw materials fell between 1998 and 1999, partially offsetting the weakening of the peso. The trend tradable price index closed 1999 with a growth rate of 0.9 per cent, more than three percentage points lower than at the end of 1998. The prices of durable items such as clothing, white goods and electronics, showed negative or almost zero variations during the period. The decrease in the dollar price of these products, which come mostly from Asia, compensated for the depreciation of the peso, to which was added the decrease in marketing margins due to the growing gap between consumer demand and the expansion of installed capacity in the trade and distribution sector. 16. On the other hand, the Wholesale Price Index (MPI) experienced an acceleration in its rate of growth, ending 1999 with an annual increase of 13.5%, mainly explained by the evolution of the nominal exchange rate during the year. The behavior of this index is relevant for the future determination of the CPI, although partially. In the Chilean case, the relationship between the MPI and the CPI is quite weak, with the predictive capacity of wholesale prices over the CPI being very limited. It should be noted that the increase in the MPI during the last third of the year reflected the increase in the price of international raw materials and the depreciation of the peso in the same period, a situation that, with regard to the exchange rate, was reversed at the beginning of 2000. However, the past evolution of the MPI is nevertheless considered to be an element of care to be taken into account in the future trajectory of inflation. 17. From the analysis within the index, the item that showed the greatest price increases was mining, particularly copper and oil. In the case of oil, since last September significant increases have been consolidated, which even strengthened in the latter part of last year and the first two months of 2000, when the average price was around US27 a barrel. Projections indicate that the price of oil would fall during the current year to be around US 25 a barrel on average for the year. The price of crude oil has fallen in the last two weeks. After the last OPEC meeting and the projected increase in production, the price was around US 24 per barrel. This price may vary in the future. 18. The evolution of fuel prices becomes the most important specific factor in the future trajectory of inflation in the current conjuncture, and therefore is where the element of greatest risk for future price developments lies. The adverse shock associated with the increase in the price of oil affects the price of gasoline and other derivatives and, therefore, the price of transport in general, although in an attenuated and gradual manner due to the operation of the Oil Price Stabilization Fund (FEPP). Increases in other regulated prices, such as drinking water, are also anticipated for this year, although with less impact on the CPI basket. 19 With regard to the inflation target for the year 2000, no changes are contemplated, since fluctuations in the price of crude oil are considered transitory, with inflation trending in the medium term within the target range of 2% to 4%. A detailed analysis of future inflation developments and possible risk scenarios will be provided on the occasion of the Monetary Policy Report to be published in mid-May. III. - Review of the main macroeconomic projections 20. The vigorous performance of the world's leading economies in recent months and the consequent rebound in commodity prices have meant a more favorable scenario for our economy in general and for Chilean exports in particular. Thus, since mid-1999, significant increases have been observed in the prices of the main exported products, mainly in the case of copper and pulp. 21. At the present juncture, imports have been the slowest recovering, with a stronger recovery beginning only in the recent months of 2000. This year is expected to expand foreign sales in line with the pace of reactivation of domestic demand, all of which suggests a surplus trade balance during the first quarter of this year, which will mean a projection of US700 million for the total of 2000, a figure that compares favorably with a neutral balance projected in September 1999. 22. Consistent with this expected improvement in the trade balance for this year, a smaller deficit in the current account of the balance of payments of the same magnitude is expected, which will lead to a deficit of the order of 2.0% of GDP by the end of the year. 2000, within the range considered as healthily financeable by our economy. 23. In terms of activity, the improved external situation, together with a greater use of the resources that were idle during the last recession, are determining elements of the recent evolution of our economy and lay the foundations for a greater boost of growth in the future. This is how for this year a GDP expansion of between 5.5% and 6.0% is estimated, higher than that estimated six months ago. 24. It should be noted that this higher GDP growth could have been even higher, without the increase in oil prices that began in 1999 and that affects us to this day. Estimates of the real effects on our economy of this increase will depend on the future evolution of the markets. Indeed, if the announced reduction occurs towards the end of the year, the impact in macroeconomic terms will be quite limited, reaching only a few tenths of lower growth. If, on the other hand, the highest levels of the recent past are maintained for a long time, the effect may become greater, close to 1% lower GDP growth. The evolution of the yield curve in recent months, as well as the decline in long-term interest rates after the last hike in the monetary interest rate, are consistent with an outstanding reputation for meeting its objectives and with very high credibility in relation to the inflation targets that the Central Bank has forged over its years. of autonomy. Consequently, our institution, faced with the current situation, will continue to monitor in detail the evolution of both prices and expectations. The increase in oil prices, a phenomenon that is considered strictly transitory and that will certainly disappear in the medium term, should not translate into a permanent deterioration in inflation expectations and the credibility of monetary policy. T7. Although the responsibility for controlling inflation lies directly with the Central Bank, the various agents of the economy also have to participate in this process, with prudent management of spending and price and wage adjustments. There is no doubt that controlling inflation is a national purpose, since low and stable inflation defends the incomes of the weakest, allows for more confident planning for the future, more easily shaping expectations, ensuring better functioning markets, and laying the foundations for sound and sustainable economic growth over time. Thus, when inflation rises above what is desired, the implementation of a strong adjustment process is required, which usually means a slowdown in growth with large costs for all. Economic policy in general, and monetary policy in particular, should seek to avoid or minimize, as far as possible, such costs. 28. Hence the importance of moving with priority towards closing the fiscal imbalances observed recently, since increases in public savings allow lower interest rates to be maintained, consistent with a greater expansion of private economic activity. As is widely known, the responsible management of public spending is a fundamental pillar of economic success. 29. Thus, to the extent that fiscal accounts tend to be in surplus, it contributes to sustainable economic growth and that traumatic adjustments are not required later. In addition, the application of a tighter fiscal policy during this and next year, as ratified by the new authorities of the Ministry of Finance, will help decisively to moderate the possible pressures that will be generated on inflation. It also helps to ensure that the effect of temporary price adjustments does not feed back into the spiral of inflationary expectations in the coming months. 30. Likewise, the reduction of the fiscal deficit will facilitate greater competitiveness of Chilean products in foreign markets, through the permanence of a higher real exchange rate. Because of the aforementioned elements and the position in the cycle in which our economy finds itself, I consider that the restoration of fiscal balance, as the government has indicated, is a priority issue that the government's economic policy must consider during this year and next. The government and the Minister of Finance need, and deserve, the support of the whole country to decisively maintain their policy objectives in this field. 31. Monetary policy, in coordination with fiscal policy, should promote and create the conditions for achieving economic growth objectives on their trend trajectory in a context of low and stable inflation, within the medium-term objective objective. It is useful to emphasize that important institutional changes introduced in the recent past also contribute to the achievement of the latter objective, resulting in greater exchange rate flexibility and an increasing opening of the capital account, which we hope to continue to improve, with due prudence, from now on. 32. I would also like to stress that, on the basis of experience, it has been possible to establish smooth and constructive coordination between the Ministry of Finance and the Central Bank. IV. New monetary policy scheme of the Central Bank 33. During the nineties, in compliance with the constitutional mandate of the Central Bank to ensure price stability, year after year inflation targets were set, increasingly low. One-off targets have been very useful in reducing inflation over the past decade and in building an increasing degree of credibility. We have already reached an inflation rate close to the state of regime. This implies that monetary policy must now look not at day-to-day events, but at the medium term. It is no longer necessary to further reduce inflation each year, but to maintain inflation rates within defined parameters. It is in this context that the new monetary policy scheme emphasizes for inflation a medium-term horizon of setting the target (beyond one year) and a range value rather than a punctual and precise figure. 34. The extension of the horizon for setting the one-year target towards the medium term forces the Central Bank to place greater emphasis on carrying out projection exercises and monitoring the behavior of private agents' expectations about future inflation. Several studies confirm that rules of behavior of a Central Bank that are based on expectations and predictions of the future evolution of inflation are more efficient because they reduce the variability of both inflation and output. Simply put, these rules incorporate the fact that there are lags in the transmission of monetary policy and therefore act with adequate anticipation. 35. The selection of a range and not a specific objective for inflation allows to accommodate various types of impacts in such a way that inflation has a margin of fluctuation in the short term without the Central Bank being forced to be excessively active in order not to deviate temporarily from the target. The use of a range is a recognition that there is a degree of uncertainty about the behavior of the economy and about the lag with which monetary policy acts on inflation; It is a recognition that there is always the possibility of phenomena affecting the economy and inflation, which are impossible to anticipate. 36. This new monetary policy scheme provides the necessary flexibility to evaluate these phenomena and act taking into account the repercussions they cause on the economy. However, the proper functioning of the new monetary policy scheme requires avoiding that the effect of external or internal shocks is concentrated in a single market. In the recent past, limited by the operation of exchange rate bands and their effect on the assessment of private risks, the Central Bank was not in a position to distribute the effect of unexpected events in several markets. Now, after careful preparatory work that took almost two years, it has become possible to introduce floating exchange rates which, together with responsible fiscal policy, eases the burden that fell only on the interest rate. The new monetary policy scheme is consistent with a system of greater exchange rate flexibility, such as the one that exists today in the Chilean economy. 37. This scheme recognizes that the interest rate is not an efficient instrument to deal with the first-round effects, or impact, of inflationary pressures originating in cost increases. However, the interest rate should be used, with due caution, to convey clear signals that the Central Bank will not facilitate the generalization of such pressures. If monetary policy were to accommodate all reactions to specific cost pressures, we would inevitably fall into the old trap of the price-wage spiral driven by indexation and the reactions of every sector that believes it has a degree of monopoly power over the market. Some of these reactions have been made public in recent weeks, and it is my duty to draw attention to them and the dangers involved. 38. I must make it clear that a decision not to intervene when effective inflation is within the target range should not be confused with inactivity, or with the intention of achieving a supposed faster economic recovery or lower unemployment rates by accepting higher inflation. It is essential to reiterate that modern economic history clearly demonstrates that attempts to increase employment while tolerating higher inflations have resulted in failure. Thus, keeping GDP growth at rates close to potential output growth is consistent with low and stable inflation. Ultimately, the level of inflation depends on monetary policy and the expectations of agents, that is, on the credibility of the objectives set by the Central Bank. 39. The evolution of the CPI through the year 2000 will surely show smaller and smaller month-to-month increases from mid-year, although increases in 12 months will reflect this trend clearly only later. For inflation targeting purposes, it is more appropriate to consider a measure of inflation that excludes first-round cost pressures, as the core CPI does. When looking at longer maturities, such as the current 12- to 24-month horizon of the new monetary policy scheme, the difference between the two indices, total CPI and core CPI, tends to disappear. But in month-to-month analysis, such differences can lead agents to unnecessary confusion. I must say it clearly: for the new monetary policy, what matters are the trends in the middle horizon, and the policy will be decided according to them and the signals you want to give to the market. 40. For this reason, the Board of the Central Bank has decided to publish a quarterly Monetary Policy Report, which will explain its view on medium-term trends in the inflation rate, and the probabilities that recorded inflation will deviate from these trends. For this very reason, we have agreed to shorten the period of delay in the publication of minutes of our discussions. Indeed, greater transparency, like floating exchange rates, is an indispensable ingredient of the new monetary policy scheme. The first Monetary Policy Report will be delivered in May to the Senate Finance Committee and to the public. V. -Conclusions 41. Before concluding, I would like to reiterate that the recovery of the economy is already underway, as the economic activity indicators are showing a clear positive evolution. Additionally, on the side of the international scenario, good news is also expected regarding world economic growth, which favors the growth prospects in our country in the near future. 42. At the domestic level, the monetary policy interest rate continues to be slightly expansionary in terms of its impact on demand, consistent with the slack in the degree of use of the economy's resources and in a context where a contractionary fiscal policy is expected during the year. This situation means that domestic demand can temporarily grow faster than output. In the medium term, however, this growth should be progressively closer to the economy's potential, in such a way as to avoid incubating unwanted inflationary pressures. 43. The new monetary policy scheme applied by the Central Bank, in coordination with other economic policies, will seek in the current situation that economic growth continues on a healthy path, with low and stable inflation, for which it will act with an anticipative and preventive nature, consistent with this purpose and with due anticipation.
