Title: 10 Years of Inflation Targeting: Design, Performance and Challenges
text: Welcome Remarks by Mr. Carlos Massad to the Fourth Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile: " 10 Years of Inflation Targeting: Design, Performance and Challenges" It is my pleasure to kick off the Fourth Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile. This conference is aimed at the analysis of monetary regimes based on inflation targeting and therefore touches on a topic of special interest to the growing number of countries that have adopted them. Already in November 1964, in his presentation on the state of the Public Treasury, the recently appointed Minister of Finance and President of the Central Bank of Chile, Sergio Molina, publicly announced explicit decreasing inflation targets for 1965, 1966 and 1967. It also announced that monetary policy, as well as wage and public spending policies, would be geared towards achieving these goals. Four months later, a policy of changing the "crawling peg" was initiated. The political difficulties of 1967 led to the failure to meet the inflation target of that year and to a less ambitious policy in the following years, although the "crawling peg" remained until 1970. In 1990, New Zealand and Chile made public announcements of explicit inflation targets, now with independent central banks. Currently, there are about 20 countries that govern their monetary management with explicit inflation targeting schemes, and numerous countries in various regions of the world are considering the adoption of this system. There are good reasons why inflation-targeting regimes are becoming popular. First, these systems have allowed a significant reduction in the level and volatility of inflation, as well as a decrease in the "sacrifice" in terms of output implied by the processes of reducing inflation. Second, explicit inflation-targeting regimes have given central banks a more precise mandate and generated a clearer and more transparent monetary management process. At the same time, the institutional framework of these central banks has been strengthened, since the inflation targeting system requires technical autonomy and a solid capacity for analysis for the correct use of monetary policy instruments. No doubt central banks have also become stronger by having to account for clear and well-defined responsibilities. The inflation-targeting regime is very demanding in terms of economic analysis capacity. It is based on the management of the monetary policy instrument (for example, the interest rate) in such a way as to bring a projection of future inflation to be within a range or at a predetermined point, within a set period. The existence of gaps between policy action and the reaction of the economy obliges the monetary authority to anticipate the evolution of economic variables and to operate on the basis of projections of the future performance of those linked to inflation. In addition, the monetary authority is constrained to conduct its policy in an environment of inevitable uncertainty about the nature and intensity of the impacts that the economy will face. It is partly for this reason that Lars Svensson prefers to refer to this system as the projected inflation targeting regime. In this way, projections, and not certainties, is what the monetary authority has at its disposal to direct its policies and fulfill its responsibilities. The effectiveness of monetary policy will therefore depend on the quality of economic analysis linking policy instruments to the ultimate objectives of monetary action. In principle, this economic analysis should be able to correctly project the effects of changes in the policy instrument on both economic activity and the price level. This projection should not only involve the effects understood in a general way, but should also specify their magnitude, duration and behavior over time. To achieve this end, adequate knowledge of the transmission channels of monetary policy and the behavior of the economy is essential. The monetary authority must know not only the regularities common to all economies but also the particularities of its own, such as its degree of indexation, its relative price flexibility, its seasonality, its fiscal position, and its dependence on external conditions. It is true that to some extent the conduct of monetary policy is an "art", but it would be incorrect to say that it is based only on intuitions. The conduct of monetary policy approaches rigorous science insofar as it is based on models of quantification of effects and probabilistic analysis. It is precisely this conviction that leads us to promote and sustain an event like the one we are starting today. By sponsoring a conference on inflation-targeting monetary schemes, we are motivated not only by an academic attraction but also by a keen interest in improving the techniques of our craft, which is still very much artisanal. The improvement of these techniques is a task that never ends. All the studies presented at this conference will provide an original contribution, ranging from theoretical analyses to purely empirical works. Its authors, whose participation we appreciate, are university academics and researchers from central banks of high qualification and international recognition. In addition, discussion and discussion of ideas at the conference will benefit from the participation of a select group of commentators and a specialized audience. The work of Sterne, and of Mishkin and Schmidt-Hebbel, will introduce the topic of inflation targeting schemes by pointing out their primary characteristics and their international propagation. For their part, the contributions of Gal92, and of Parrado and Velasco, will deal with the optimal design, in terms of objectives and policy responses, of an inflation-targeting regime in contexts of incomplete flexibility of wages and relative prices. Most studies will emphasize aspects relevant to open economies, and some, such as Debelle and Wilkinson, will refer specifically to the case of economies in transition to a low level of inflation. The work of Blejer, Leone, Rabanal, and Schwartz will touch on institutional aspects when studying the implementation of inflation-targeting policies in countries with adjustment programs supported by the International Monetary Fund. The studies by Kumhof, Corbo, Landerretche and Schmidt-Hebbel will assess the performance of inflation-targeting regimes in achieving price stability and economic activity objectives, particularly in comparison with the results obtained by alternative regimes. On the other hand, McCallum will speak about one of the new, and somewhat unexpected, dangers facing monetary policy, namely the lack of liquidity in contexts of excessively low or negative inflation rates. We will also have interesting case studies. The experiences of New Zealand and Chile, countries with a long history of inflation-targeting monetary schemes, will be addressed by works by Drew and Garc92a, Herrera and Vald8es. The shorter but no less interesting Brazilian experience with inflation targeting will be discussed in the study by Bogdanski, Goldfajn and Tombini. The conference will continue with a panel of deputy central bank governors, consisting of Ryzard Kokoszczynski of the Central Bank of Poland, Murray Sherwin of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, Eugenio Domingo Solans of the European Central Bank, and Han Goldfajn of the Central Bank of Brazil. They will share with us their experiences from their unique perspective as monetary policymakers. The closing remarks and conclusions will be presented by the Vice President of the Central Bank of Chile, Jorge Marshall. We therefore have two days of intense work and interesting debate. And what better way to start them than with the presentations that follow in this inaugural session. Jacob Frenkel, former economic adviser and director of economic research at the IMF, former brilliant Governor of the Bank of Israel and current Chairman of Merryll Lynch's Government Advisory Group and International Institutions Group, will present his vision on inflation targeting, exchange rates and monetary policy. Then, Felipe Morand8e, manager of the research division of the Central Bank of Chile, will speak about the past and future of monetary policy in our country. It is good and appropriate that we have a historical and, if I may, introspective presentation of the Central Bank of Chile, especially now that we celebrate 75 years of existence of this institution. With this, I begin the Fourth Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile and extend a fraternal welcome to the foreign and national participants who today honor us with their presence.
text_original: Palabras de Bienvenida del Sr. Carlos Massad a la Cuarta Conferencia Anual del Banco Central de Chile: "10 Aos de Metas de Inflacin: Diseo, Desempeo y Desafos" Es un placer para m dar inicio a la Cuarta Conferencia Anual del Banco Central de Chile. Esta conferencia est dirigida al anlisis de regmenes monetarios basados en metas de inflacin y, por lo tanto, toca un tema de inters especial para el nmero creciente de pases que los han adoptado. Ya en noviembre de 1964, en su exposicin sobre el estado de la Hacienda Pblica, el recientemente designado Ministro de Hacienda y Presidente del Banco Central de Chile, Sergio Molina, anunciaba pblicamente metas explcitas de inflacin decrecientes para 1965, 1966 y 1967. Anunciaba tambin que la poltica monetaria, as como las polticas de salarios y de gasto pblico, se orientaran al logro de estas metas. Cuatro meses despus, se iniciaba una poltica cambiara de "crawling peg". Las dificultades polticas del ao 1967 llevaron al incumplimiento de la meta de inflacin de ese ao y a una poltica menos ambiciosa en los aos siguientes, aunque el "crawling peg" se mantuvo hasta 1970. En 1990, Nueva Zelandia y Chile hicieron anuncios pblicos de metas explcitas de inflacin, ahora con Bancos Centrales independientes. En la actualidad, son alrededor de 20 los pases que rigen su conduccin monetaria con esquemas explcitos de metas de inflacin, y numerosos pases en diversas regiones del mundo estn considerando la adopcin de este sistema. Hay buenas razones por las que los regmenes de metas de inflacin se estn haciendo populares. En primer lugar, estos sistemas han permitido una reduccin significativa en el nivel y la volatilidad de la inflacin, as como una disminucin del "sacrificio" en trminos de producto que implican los procesos de reduccin de la inflacin. En segundo lugar, los regmenes basados en metas explcitas de inflacin han dotado a los bancos centrales de un mandato ms preciso y han generado un proceso de conduccin monetaria ms claro y transparente. A la vez, la institucionalidad de estos bancos centrales se ha visto fortalecida, ya que el sistema de metas de inflacin requiere de una autonoma tcnica y de una capacidad slida de anlisis para la correcta utilizacin de los instrumentos de poltica monetaria. Sin duda los Bancos Centrales tambin se han hecho ms fuertes al tener que rendir cuentas de responsabilidades claras y bien delimitadas. El rgimen de metas de inflacin es muy exigente en materia de capacidad de anlisis econmico. Se basa en el manejo del instrumento de poltica monetaria (por ejemplo, la tasa de inters) de manera tal de llevar una proyeccin de la inflacin futura a ubicarse dentro de un rango o en un punto predeterminado, en un plazo establecido. La existencia de desfases entre la accin de poltica y la reaccin de la economa obliga a la autoridad monetaria a anticipar la evolucin de las variables econmicas y a operar sobre la base de proyecciones del desempeo futuro de aquellas ligadas a la inflacin. Adicionalmente, la autoridad monetaria est constreida a conducir su poltica en un ambiente de inevitable incertidumbre sobre la naturaleza y la intensidad de los impactos que enfrentar la economa. Es en parte por esta razn que Lars Svensson prefiere referirse a este sistema como el rgimen de metas proyectadas de inflacin. De esta manera, proyecciones, y no certidumbres, es lo que la autoridad monetaria tiene a su disposicin para dirigir sus polticas y cumplir con sus responsabilidades. La eficacia de la poltica monetaria depender, por lo tanto, de la calidad del anlisis econmico que relacione los instrumentos de poltica con los objetivos finales de la accin monetaria. En principio, este anlisis econmico debiera ser capaz de proyectar correctamente los efectos de los cambios en el instrumento de poltica tanto sobre la actividad econmica como sobre el nivel de precios. Esta proyeccin debiera no slo involucrar los efectos entendidos de manera general, sino que tambin debiera precisar su magnitud, duracin y comportamiento en el tiempo. Para lograr este fin, es imprescindible un conocimiento adecuado de los canales de transmisin de la poltica monetaria y del comportamiento de la economa. La autoridad monetaria debe conocer no slo las regularidades comunes a todas las economas sino tambin las particularidades de la suya propia, como por ejemplo su grado de indizacin, su flexibilidad de precios relativos, su estacionalidad, su posicin fiscal, y su dependencia de las condiciones externas. Es verdad que en alguna medida la conduccin de la poltica monetaria es un "arte", pero sera incorrecto decir que ella se basa slo en intuiciones. La conduccin de la poltica monetaria se aproxima a una ciencia rigurosa en la medida en que se fundamenta en modelos de cuantificacin de efectos y de anlisis probabilstico. Es justamente esta conviccin la que nos lleva a promover y sustentar un evento como el que hoy iniciamos. Al patrocinar una conferencia sobre esquemas monetarios de metas de inflacin, nos motiva no slo una atraccin acadmica sino tambin un agudo inters por mejorar las tcnicas propias de nuestro oficio, que todava tiene mucho de artesanal. El mejoramiento de estas tcnicas es una tarea que no termina nunca. Todos los estudios presentados en esta conferencia entregarn una contribucin original, incluyendo desde anlisis tericos hasta trabajos netamente empricos. Sus autores, cuya participacin agradecemos, son acadmicos universitarios e investigadores de bancos centrales de elevada calificacin y de reconocimiento internacional. Asimismo, la discusin y el contraste de deas en la conferencia se vern beneficiados por la participacin de un grupo selecto de comentaristas y una audiencia especializada. Los trabajos de Sterne, y de Mishkin y Schmidt-Hebbel, introducirn el tema de esquemas de metas de inflacin sealando sus caractersticas primordiales y su propagacin internacional. Por su parte, las contribuciones de Gal, y de Parrado y Velasco, tratarn del diseo ptimo, en cuanto a objetivos y respuestas de poltica, de un rgimen de metas de inflacin en contextos de incompleta flexibilidad de salarios y precios relativos. La mayora de los estudios enfatizarn aspectos relevantes para economas abiertas, y algunos, como el de Debelle y Wilkinson, se referirn de forma especfica al caso de economas en transicin hacia un nivel bajo de inflacin. El trabajo de Blejer, Leone, Rabanal, y Schwartz tocar aspectos institucionales al estudiar la implementacin de polticas de metas de inflacin en pases con programas de ajuste apoyados por el Fondo Monetario Internacional. Los estudios de Kumhof, y de Corbo, Landerretche y Schmidt-Hebbel, evaluarn el desempeo de los regmenes basados en metas de inflacin en cuanto al logro de los objetivos de estabilidad de precios y de actividad econmica, particularmente en comparacin con los resultados obtenidos por regmenes alternativos. Por otra parte, McCallum disertar sobre uno de los nuevos, y algo inesperados, peligros que enfrenta la poltica monetaria, a saber, la falta de liquidez en contextos de tasas de inflacin excesivamente bajas o negativas. Tendremos tambin interesantes estudios de casos. Las experiencias de Nueva Zelandia y Chile, pases con una larga historia de esquemas monetarios de metas de inflacin, sern tratadas por sendos trabajos de Drew y de Garca, Herrera y Valds. La ms corta pero no menos interesante experiencia brasilea con metas de inflacin ser discutida en el estudio de Bogdanski, Goldfajn y Tombini. La conferencia continuar con un panel de vice-gobernadores de bancos centrales, conformado por Ryzard Kokoszczynski del Banco Central de Polonia, Murray Sherwin del Banco de Reserva de Nueva Zelandia, Eugenio Domingo Solans del Banco Central Europeo, e Han Goldfajn del Banco Central de Brasil. Ellos compartirn con nosotros sus experiencias desde su singular perspectiva de formuladores de poltica monetaria. Las palabras de clausura y conclusiones sern presentadas por el Vicepresidente del Banco Central de Chile, Jorge Marshall. Nos esperan, entonces, dos das de intenso trabajo e interesante debate. Y qu mejor manera de iniciarlos que con las presentaciones que vienen a continuacin en esta sesin inaugural. Jacob Frenkel, ex consejero econmico y director de investigacin econmica del FMI, ex brillante Gobernador del Banco de Israel y actual Presidente del Grupo Asesor de Gobiernos y del Grupo Instituciones Internacionales de Merryll Lynch, nos presentar su visin sobre metas de inflacin, tipos de cambio y poltica monetaria. Luego, Felipe Morand, gerente de la divisin de estudios del Banco Central de Chile, disertar sobre el pasado y futuro de la poltica monetaria en nuestro pas. Es bueno y apropiado que tengamos una presentacin histrica y, si me permiten, introspectiva del Banco Central de Chile especialmente ahora que celebramos 75 aos de existencia de esta institucin. Con esto, doy por iniciada la Cuarta Conferencia Anual del Banco Central de Chile y extiendo una fraternal bienvenida a los participantes extranjeros y nacionales que hoy nos honran con su presencia.

Title: External Financial Stability and the Internationalization of the Peso
text: External Financial Stability and the Internationalization of the Peso Presentation by Carlos Massad, President of the Central Bank of Chile, at the International Conference "The World Economy: Perspectives and Oportunities", January 18, 2001. Introduction I would like to thank the Center for International Economics Studies of the University of Maryland and the Institute of Economics of the Catholic University of Chile for their invitation and take this opportunity to reflect on what it means for a small and open economy like Chile's to live in a world that is characterized by an increasing integration of its markets and that at the same time is affected by Strong volatilities. It is not for me to present or debate theories. In my presentation, I will refer to the strategy of insertion of the Chilean economy within international markets, the progress made in the macroeconomic and financial sphere, some of the pending challenges and the role of the Central Bank in this task. The Chilean economy is relatively small and needs to integrate with the rest of the world to grow. We need international markets to sell those products in which we have competitive advantages, and we require international capital, relatively more abundant in developed countries, in order to finance our economic growth. However, the history of our country and other developing countries records numerous episodes in which changes in the international scenario trigger economic crises, sometimes of great magnitude. We believe that the appropriate response should not be to limit openness to the outside world but to seek to improve it. The adverse effects of international crises on developing economies are often the result of situations of incomplete integration, de facto or de jure, in which the full potential of international economic relations in terms of diversification and hedging is not exploited. This means that our strategy to take full advantage of the benefits of globalization is based on the fact that countries must move forward by removing obstacles and creating the conditions that allow the exchange of a wide variety of international commercial and financial contracts. Greater integration will also allow the country to better manage the risks that globalization inevitably generates. The possibility of making these contracts depends in an important way on the confidence that the rest of the world has in the country's institutions and, in particular, in its currency. This suggests that, as we will see in this presentation, successful economic integration with the rest of the world is a gradual path, in which building credibility in the country, its institutions and its economy is fundamental. Economic integration and risk diversification Integration with the rest of the world affects the stability of the national economy, both in the commercial and financial spheres. First, trade openness to the rest of the world leads to specialization in the structure of production and generates risks associated with fluctuations in the terms of trade. The vulnerability of the economy to such shocks depends on how diversified the export structure is, and on the possibility of diversifying these risks among products, markets and currencies in international financial markets. For many years, the Chilean economy's export earnings depended mainly on the price of copper. For example, three decades ago, almost 80% of our exports corresponded to this mineral, and its ownership was concentrated in the hands of the State, so its fluctuations affected the nation's budget one by one. Since the eighties, three profound changes have taken place. On the one hand, total exports have increased considerably as a percentage of GDP, reducing the dependence of export earnings on copper sales (Chart 1). The share of copper exports in the total has declined from 76 per cent in 1970 to 41 per cent in 2000, while the share of industrial exports, which now outnumber copper, has risen sharply. Moreover, in the nineties, a significant part of the expansion of copper mining has been realized through foreign investment projects, which also diversifies risk and reduces the impact of price fluctuations on national income. In addition, the destinations of our exports have diversified. For example, in 1970, 14% went to the US, 60% to Europe, 11% to Latin American countries, and only 13% to countries in Asia and Oceania. In 2000, our exports were distributed 18% to the USA, 27% to Europe, 22% to Latin America and 32% to Asia and Oceania. Figure 1. Composition of Exports . Copper . Agricultural . Industrial Central Bank of Chile However, the concentration of our exports on primary products and natural resources is still very marked, and it is likely that this situation will persist over time. We have considerable comparative advantages in these products and it is efficient to seek to exploit them in international markets. This implies that progress in the diversification of international risk must also be sought in the financial area. On the financial front, an important development in recent years has been the increase in Chilean investment abroad. This reflects the exploitation of the possibilities of international risk diversification offered by the opening of the capital account. Indeed, the rules governing investment abroad have been relaxed since 1992, when prior authorization for investments with funds from the informal exchange market was eliminated. The stock of foreign investment has increased considerably since then (Figure 2), reaching approximately 31% of GDP at the end of 2000. Figure 2. Chilean Investment Stock Abroad Central Bank of Chile Consistent with this policy of openness has been the extension of the limits on foreign investment by institutional investors, particularly AFPs. In 1992, AFPs were authorized to invest abroad for a maximum of 1.5% of their fund. The authorized limits have been gradually increased to 16% today. The AFPs hold 12% of the fund in investments abroad, close to 7% of GDP. However, while opening up the opportunity to diversify risks, the greater connection with international financial markets can also introduce other sources of instability as a result of the greater degree of dependence on external financing, and the unforeseen remittances that its offer sometimes experiences for reasons external to the country. Recent experience indicates that international financial crises tend to spread rapidly. In the event of a crisis, uncertainty is high and international investors often move abruptly and together. These sudden movements usually have negative effects of magnitude in the economies that suffer them, which multiply if the initial financial situation is weak. While all open economies may face destabilizing financial shocks, experience suggests that the consequences are often substantially more devastating in developing economies than in developed economies. This is easy to appreciate when comparing the effects of the breakdown of the European Monetary System in 1992, for example, with the experiences of Chile in 1982 or Mexico in 1994, and more recently in the Asian crisis. Among the determining factors is the structure of countries' external financing. When there is insufficient credibility among investors regarding the stability of currencies, the only long-term financing that companies and other institutions obtain is in foreign currency. However, the assets and projects of many of these companies are denominated in local currency. The simultaneous combination of currency mismatches and maturities in the financial or corporate sector can be lethal in the context of an international financial crisis. Term mismatches can induce dramatic adjustments in relative prices, and currency mismatches mean that a depreciation of the national currency significantly affects the balance sheet vulnerability of financial and non-financial corporations. In effect, your liabilities will increase without an increase in assets, which implies capital losses. In turn, these capital losses are propagated to the local economy through real and financial markets. Business losses result in a decrease in their ability to carry out investment projects and generate employment, and reduce the quality of credit from local banks. In turn, they will have to reduce the scale of their loans in order to meet capital requirements, which negatively impacts economic activity. Chile's External Financial Vulnerability Overall, the external financial vulnerability of the Chilean economy has been drastically reduced in recent years. First, the Chilean economy maintains a relatively comfortable position in terms of its solvency and external liquidity, as reflected in international risk ratings and the premium paid by sovereign bonds in international markets. (Figure 3) Over the past few years, the current account deficit of the balance of payments, the increase in our international liabilities, has remained within prudent limits, while average output and export growth has been high. (Figure 4) Secondly, debt maturities have been extended, and the share of foreign investment has also increased, so that the international liquidity position of the Chilean economy is very solid. Thus, the share of medium- and long-term debt increased from 75 per cent in 1990 to 81 per cent in November 2000, including the increase in medium- and long-term private debt. In fact, in 1990 it represented 22% of total debt, while in November 2000 it reached 70%. (Figure 5) Figure 5. Composition by Term of External Debt . External Debt of l.P . External Debt of CP Central Bank of Chile Third, the Central Bank has considerable liquidity in international resources to deal with a crisis of magnitude. Net International Reserves (Figure 6) amounted to US 14,741 million at the end of 2000, while its external indebtedness is zero and it is a creditor of international organizations such as the IMF. These trends reflect that the economy is in an adequate position in terms of its solvency, international liquidity and international investor confidence. However, the exposure to the changed risk is still large and this is a challenge that we must face. Chile's external indebtedness occurs almost entirely in foreign currency. Currently, more than 95% of it is denominated in United States dollars. This is not the situation of countries with higher levels of development than Chile. In developed countries, the external financing structure has a larger component in terms of local currency. This determines that the patrimonial effects of the appreciations or devaluations of their currencies are minor. The following chart (Chart 7) shows the currency composition of Australia's and New Zealand's external financing. The similarities of these economies with Chile are several: both are small and open economies, have an export structure based on raw materials, maintain a net debt position with international markets, a significant part of their investment is financed externally, have floating exchange rates and an inflation-targeting monetary regime. However, the difference in the composition of external indebtedness is remarkable. In both cases, external indebtedness in national currency is about 40% of the total. Figure 7. Currency Composition of External Debt a5 I lied 1 localOther. Mbnnlax Central Bank of Chile Diversification helped these economies overcome the consequences of the 1997 Asian crisis. At the starting point, both economies had a significant degree of exchange rate flexibility to adjust their international competitiveness in the face of the reduction of their markets, without fearing consequences for their financial stability. How to reduce our external financial vulnerability? Faced with this reality, what measures can the authority take to generate a more stable financial environment? A first task is to achieve policies that promote macroeconomic stability and credibility in the value of the national currency. In this regard, the Chilean economy has an appropriate institutional framework through an autonomous Central Bank and a responsible fiscal policy. The inflation targeting scheme used by the Central Bank has managed to consolidate low and stable inflation rates, and anchor expectations around 3% per year, the established target. A second task is to achieve regulation and supervision conducive to a sound financial system. A weak financial system has a high probability of going into crisis in the face of a major external shock. A crisis in the financial system will reduce credit in the economy, which will imply a reduction in economic activity and, probably, distrust in the value of the currency. The fact that the financial system has overcome the recent Asian crisis without major problems shows that the work of the Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions and the Central Bank, in the context of modern legislation that has emphasized safeguarding the capital base of banks, has been successful in providing an adequate regulatory framework as well as in supervising compliance with this framework. A third task concerns making the risk transparent to change it. Since September 1999, our economy has been in a free-floating regime, where any interventions by the Central Bank in the foreign exchange market must be informed to the public both in the amounts involved and in the reasons that justify this intervention. This option has not been used. It is necessary to emphasize once again that it was only possible to leave the exchange rate free after careful preparation of the regulatory framework. Along with gradually strengthening banking regulation and supervision, which allowed an important development of the activities allowed to banks, the Central Bank, in close collaboration with the SBIF, began to introduce regulations aimed at limiting and expanding the coverage of risks assumed by banks, but providing greater flexibility in the type of operations, in particular derivative products, which banks can carry out both abroad and in Chile. These measures include credit derivatives, forwards, futures and swaps of interest rates, currencies and readjustability units, repos in foreign currency and the introduction of zero coupon bonds of the Central Bank. In short, these measures contribute to completing all possible transactions on the market. That is, gradually, the Central Bank has prepared the ground in the financial field by providing the necessary tools so that private agents are the ones who form a financial risk profile, using the hedging instruments available in the market. In fact, although it may be of less relevance to the market, the accounting system used in the Central Bank had to be modified by a mechanism for valuing assets and liabilities external to the market exchange rate (observed exchange rate). This change can probably be considered as the first step in the institutional arena to adopt the change of exchange rate policy regime. Subsequently, important reforms were made to the capital account regulations, which sought greater openness and flexibility in the movements of foreign and domestic capital in and out of entry. For example, banks were authorized to operate foreign exchange forwards; to finance foreign currency operations in international trade, including between third countries, and to carry out cross-border financial placements and investments in a growing range of countries, companies and instruments. These activities may be very natural in developed countries, but they could have generated greater exchange rate volatility, in a context where policymakers were trying to suppress volatility, rather than learning to live with it. As noted, in this free-floating environment, the risks are assumed entirely by the private sector, which generates incentives to hedge against these risks. Similarly, the level of the exchange rate reflects relevant information that may affect its value, so that discrete movements, reflecting adjustments to accumulated misalignments of importance in the exchange rate, become less likely. The debate about the advantages and disadvantages of a fixed exchange rate system versus a variable exchange rate system is well known and still present today. On this point I will limit myself to pointing out that with the changes listed above, I believe that the Central Bank has contributed decisively to "sincere" the risk of changing it in the financial and hedging operations of the real sector. On the other hand, in a fixed exchange rate system, the private sector is somewhat distracted from its main activity and assumes excessive risk, often not calculated, betting on some reaction from the Central Bank, which ultimately generates significant adjustment costs due to the mismatches that occur in this dynamic. We believe that a free exchange rate system, together with a sound regulatory framework, minimizes these adjustment costs, allowing the financial system to operate within a range of greater stability in terms of its local and foreign currency positions. Finally, on this subject, I must point out that the introduction of a floating exchange rate regime has not meant excessive volatility in this price. Thus, after more than a year of free floating of our currency, its volatility has been quite moderate, being lower than that of the Mexican peso, the Brazilian real, and even lower than the volatility of currencies of developed countries such as the Japanese yen and the euro, in relation to the US dollar (see Table 1). In 1996, the peso-dollar and UF-dollar forward operations in the formal market represented 70% of GDP, while in October 2000 these operations reached US 100,208 million, equivalent to 144% of the estimated GDP for that year. Figure 8. Dollar Forward Transaction Amount in MCE Central llancn of Chile Another step is to broaden the base of foreign investors willing to invest and issue debt in local currency. Since 1998, the Central Bank authorized the issuance of borrowing in local currency abroad and, more recently, the tax differential that affected the interest on foreign debt in national currency has been eliminated to match the conditions of debt in foreign currency. In recent months we have seen incipient steps in the development of an international market of weights or UF's. Last year, the World Bank issued a bond in UF for 105 million dollars, and subsequently, the Central Bank of Uruguay made a second issue for a similar amount, while other international issuers have announced their intention to carry out operations in UF or pesos. The presence of these instruments helps to generate an international market that facilitates the diversification of changed risk in Chile. Indeed, these issues allow institutional investors in Chile, who have a natural demand for instruments denominated in UF as well as their liabilities, to access investments in this currency, but without the need to continue concentrating their credit risk in Chilean companies. At the same time, foreigners can transfer the exchange risk they absorb when issuing debt in UF, transferring it to Chilean companies that are indebted in foreign currency and that wish to reduce their exchange exposure. In this way, we achieve a better combination of risk and return for all participants. To the extent that local companies achieve adequate conditions of long-term financing in local currency, the financial health of the Chilean economy is also strengthened. Finally, an issue that has been present in the economic policy debate in recent years concerns restrictions on capital inflows, such as reserve requirements and the permanence requirement. These measures were maintained as long as there was a large influx of capital into the Chilean economy, and at the same time, the lack of adequate matching standards in the financial market and a mixed exchange rate regime did not help the private sector to voluntarily control its exposure to exchange risk. Regulations played an important role in helping to limit the volume of capital inflows and extending the maturity of external borrowing. However, in the current context of international financial markets, it would be counterproductive to use these restrictions. Moreover, considering the progress made domestically in terms of stabilizing inflation around its long-term target, floating exchange rates, establishing a fiscal rule, developing exchange rate hedging markets, and matching rules we must continue to move in the same direction of greater international financial integration.

En el punto de partida ambas economas tenan un grado importante de flexibilidad cambiara para ajustar su competitividad internacional frente a la reduccin de sus mercados, sin temer consecuencias sobre su estabilidad financiera. Cmo disminuir nuestra vulnerabilidad financiera externa? Frente a esta realidad, qu medidas puede tomar la autoridad para generar un ambiente financiero ms estable? Una primera tarea es lograr polticas que propicien la estabilidad macroeconmica y la credibilidad en el valor de la moneda nacional. Al respecto, la economa chilena cuenta con una institucionalidad apropiada a travs de un Banco Central autnomo y una poltica fiscal responsable. El esquema de metas de inflacin que ha utilizado el Banco Central ha logrado consolidar tasas de inflacin bajas y estables, y anclar las expectativas en torno al 3% anual, la meta establecida. Una segunda tarea es lograr una regulacin y supervisin conducente a un sistema financiero slido. Un sistema financiero dbil tiene una alta probabilidad de entrar en crisis ante un shock externo de magnitud. Una crisis en el sistema financiero reducir el crdito en la economa lo que implicar una reduccin de la actividad econmica y, probablemente, desconfianza en el valor de la moneda. El hecho de que el sistema financiero haya superado la reciente crisis asitica sin mayores problemas demuestra que la labor de la Superintendencia de Bancos e Instituciones Financieras y del Banco Central, en el contexto de una legislacin moderna que ha puesto nfasis en el resguardo de la base de capital de la banca, ha sido exitosa en la provisin de un marco regulatorio adecuado as como en la supervisin del cumplimiento de este marco. Una tercera tarea se refiere a transparentar el riesgo cambiarlo. A partir de septiembre de 1999 nuestra economa se encuentra en un rgimen de flotacin libre, donde las eventuales intervenciones del Banco Central en el mercado de divisas deben ser informadas al pblico tanto en los montos involucrados como en las razones que fundamentan esta intervencin. Esta opcin no se ha utilizado. Es necesario destacar una vez ms que slo fue posible dejar libre el tipo de cambio luego de una cuidadosa preparacin del marco regulatorio. Junto con fortalecer gradualmente la regulacin y supervisin bancaria, lo que permiti un importante desarrollo de las actividades permitidas a los bancos, el Banco Central, en estrecha colaboracin con la SBIF, comenz a introducir normativas destinadas a acotar y ampliar la cobertura de los riesgos asumidos por los bancos, pero entregando una mayor flexibilidad en el tipo de operaciones, en particular de productos derivados, que la banca puede realizar tanto en el exterior como en Chile. Dentro de estas medidas destacan, los derivados de crdito, los forwards, futuros y swap de tasas de inters, monedas y en unidades de reajustabilidad, los repos en moneda extranjera y la introduccin de los bonos cero cupn del Banco Central. En breve, estas medidas contribuyen a completar el conjunto de operaciones posibles en el mercado. Es decir, en forma gradual, el Banco Central, ha preparado el terreno en el plano financiero entregando las herramientas necesarias para que sean los agentes privados quienes conformen un perfil de riesgo financiero, utilizando los instrumentos de cobertura disponibles en el mercado. De hecho, aun cuando puede ser de menor relevancia para el mercado, el sistema de contabilidad utilizado en el Banco Central tuvo que ser modificado por un mecanismo de valoracin de activos y pasivos externos al tipo de cambio de mercado (tipo de cambio observado). Este cambio, probablemente se puede considerar como el primer paso en el mbito institucional para adoptar el cambio de rgimen de poltica cambiara. Posteriormente, se hicieron importantes reformas a la normativa de la cuenta de capitales, las que buscaban una mayor apertura y flexibilidad en los movimientos de entrada y salida del capital extranjero y nacional. Por ejemplo, los bancos fueron autorizados para operar con forwards de moneda extranjera; para financiar operaciones en moneda extranjera de comercio internacional, incluso entre terceros pases y para efectuar colocaciones e inversiones financieras transfronterizas en una gama creciente de pases, empresas e instrumentos. Estas actividades pueden ser muy naturales en pases desarrollados, pero podran haber generado mayor volatilidad cambiara, en un contexto donde las autoridades intentaban suprimir la volatilidad, en lugar de aprender a convivir con ella. Como se seal, en este ambiente de flotacin libre, los riesgos son asumidos enteramente por los privados, lo que genera los incentivos para cubrirse de estos riesgos. Del mismo modo, el nivel del tipo de cambio refleja la informacin relevante que puede afectar su valor, de tal modo que los movimientos discretos, que reflejan ajustes ante desalineaciones acumuladas de importancia en el tipo de cambio, se hacen menos probables. El debate sobre las ventajas y desventajas de un sistema de tipo de cambio fijo versus un sistema de tipo de cambio variable es bastante conocido y sigue presente hoy en da. Sobre este punto me voy a limitar a sealar que con los cambios enumerados previamente, creo que el Banco Central ha contribuido decisivamente a "sincerar" el riesgo cambiarlo en las operaciones financieras y de cobertura del sector real. En cambio, en un sistema de tipo de cambio fijo, el sector privado en cierta forma se distrae de su principal actividad y asume un riesgo excesivo, muchas veces no calculado, apostando a alguna reaccin del Banco Central, lo que finalmente genera importantes costos de ajuste debido a los descalces que se producen en este dinmica. Creemos que un sistema de tipo de cambio libre, junto con un slido marco normativo, minimizan estos costos de ajustes, permitiendo al sistema financiero desenvolverse dentro de una rango de mayor estabilidad en trminos de sus posiciones en moneda local y extranjera. Por ltimo, en relacin con este tema, debo sealar que la introduccin de un rgimen de tipo de cambio flotante no ha significado una volatilidad excesiva en este precio. Es as como luego de ms de un ao de flotacin libre de nuestra moneda, su volatilidad ha sido bastante moderada, siendo menor que la del peso mexicano, del real brasileo, e incluso menor que la volatilidad de monedas de pases desarrollados como el yen japons y el euro, con relacin al dlar americano (ver Tabla 1). Las operaciones forward peso- dlar y UF-dlar en el mercado formal representaban en 1996 un 70% del PIB, en tanto que a octubre de 2000 estas operaciones alcanzaron a US$ 100.208 millones, lo que equivale a un 144% del PIB estimado para ese ao.
