Esto permitir cambiar el rostro en gran parte de las regiones, retomar un mayor dinamismo econmico y hacer crecer a nuestro pas posiblemente por sobre lo que se proyecta en este Informe, si la economa mundial retoma la senda de una clara recuperacin.  Profundizacin y modernizacin del Sistema Financiero nacional  La conduccin futura de la poltica monetaria bajo el esquema de metas de inflacin requiere que se modernice la institucionalidad regulatoria del sistema financiero chileno. Una economa sana requiere mantener un sector bancario slido y seguro que asigne fondos a los prestatarios en una adecuada combinacin de riesgo-retorno para asegurar el funcionamiento eficiente del sistema de pagos.  La justificacin de un sistema basado en la regulacin se sustenta en posibles fallas del mercado, tales como la existencia de informacin asimtrica o el riesgo moral. Un sistema moderno de supervisin contempla diversos aspectos: nfasis en la regulacin prudencial; la creacin de incentivos para que el mercado supervise las instituciones financieras; procedimientos adecuados para solucionar situaciones de inestabilidad financiera; transparencia para que el mercado de capitales funcione a travs de estndares de control; y funcionamiento de las instituciones privadas que contribuyan a la eficacia del mercado, como clasificadores de riesgo y auditores externos. Sistema de Supervisin Moderno Regulacin prudencial. Incentivos al mercado para supervisin. Procedimientos adecuados. Mayor transparencia. Instituciones privadas contribuyen a la eficacia (clasificadores de riesgo, auditores externos). Informe de Poltica Monetaria, Septiembre 2001 30  Luego de la crisis de los aos '80 una vez recuperada la estabilidad y solvencia del sistema, la institucionalidad regulatoria enfrent nuevos desafos asociados al proceso de globalizacin y de insercin e integracin internacional de la economa, a la consolidacin de los agentes financieros y a la sofisticacin de nuevos productos.  Las principales reformas financieras dictadas por las autoridades reguladoras en los ltimos aos pueden resumirse en aquellas que propenden a acotar de mejor forma los riesgos financieros, complementadas por la autorizacin de nuevas operaciones bancarias.  Un elemento adicional en la profundizacin del mercado financiero se obtiene, indirectamente, con la decisin del Banco Central de utilizar una tasa nominal de inters como tasa de poltica monetaria. Esto permitir un mejoramiento de la estructura de activos y pasivos no slo del mismo Banco Central, sino adems del sector financiero privado en la medida que se mejoran los calces de monedas que cada sector posee en sus portafolios. Ello redundar en un beneficio para todos los agentes del sector financiero y para la economa como un todo.  La internacionalizacin de la banca puede implicar un fuerte aumento de la eficiencia del sector financiero. Aparecen nuevos servicios, mayor innovacin financiera, mejor aprovechamiento del capital de un banco y una mayor diversificacin del riesgo. En consecuencia, aparecen nuevas fuentes de crecimiento y se promueve el desarrollo de la exportacin de servicios.  Sin embargo, con la internacionalizacin surgen algunos riesgos, y se requiere adoptar medidas que permitan mantenerlos acotados. Para ello se han planteado un conjunto de mecanismos, tales como la regulacin de la inversin de los bancos en el exterior.  En los ltimos aos, en el sistema financiero chileno se han desarrollo una serie de innovaciones en productos. El pas cuenta ahora con un mercado desarrollado de colocaciones de consumo, comerciales, de comercio exterior e hipotecarias. Existe un amplio mercado de instrumentos de renta fija y variable, incluyendo pactos de retrocompra ampliamente utilizados por el Banco Central en el manejo de liquidez del mercado interbancario.  No obstante, recientemente el Banco Central ha procedido a ampliar la gama de productos vinculados a pagos, ahorro y manejo de riesgos financieros, autorizando la emisin de dinero electrnico, y la operacin de nuevos productos derivados que facilitan el manejo de los riesgos financieros. Dentro de stos ltimos destacan los futuros en monedas, tasas de inters locales e internacionales, y determinadas formas de instrumentos forwards y swaps. Asimismo, se levant el requisito de autorizacin previa para operar con derivados de tasas de inters con el exterior.  A su vez, el Banco Central ha ayudado a profundizar y completar mercados mediante la emisin de instrumentos reajustables segn las variaciones del tipo de cambio, los que permiten cubrir riesgos cambiarlos y canjear pagars pagaderos en cupones por pagars cero cupn, satisfaciendo la demanda por instrumentos de largo plazo. Para un desarrollo ms eficiente del mercado cambiarlo, tambin se han autorizado prstamos interbancarios y pactos entre instituciones financieras en moneda extranjera.  No obstante, el vertiginoso crecimiento de los instrumentos financieros, en particular los derivados, puede potenciar los riesgos a que se enfrenta el sistema financiero. Por ello, ha sido necesario acotar la toma de riesgos excesivos que las instituciones bancarias enfrentan por la toma de posicin neta en moneda extranjera.  En la actualidad, la mayora de los riesgos que enfrentan los bancos se encuentra adecuadamente controlada, sean stos riesgos de monedas, de tasas de inters, de inflacin, de liquidez o de contagio. El Banco Central ha introducido paulatinamente importantes mejoras a la normativa sobre calce de activos y pasivos en diversas monedas, plazos y tasas de inters.  Pblicamente se ha informado acerca de la reforma y modernizacin del sistema de pagos que prepara el Banco Central. Este proyecto tiene como objetivo fundamental establecer mecanismos de liquidacin ms eficientes y seguros. En sus aspectos centrales la reforma busca asegurar que los riesgos de liquidacin de pagos entre las instituciones financieras sean debidamente asumidos y cautelados por las mismas instituciones, evitando que stos se transfieran al resto del sistema financiero, al pblico o al Banco Central. La posibilidad de realizar transferencias electrnicas en tiempo real y contra saldos disponibles permitir eliminar una parte sustancial de los riesgos presentes en la liquidacin de pagos.  El avance en la modernizacin de nuestro sistema financiero requiere de pasos adicionales, que se ven facilitados por dos hechos recientes, vinculados entre s: la consolidacin de inflaciones anuales bajas y estables, y la nominalizacin de la tasa de inters de poltica monetaria.  Uno de los pasos adicionales, sobre el cual se est haciendo un riguroso estudio, se refiere al pago de intereses sobre obligaciones a la vista y cuentas corrientes. Este es un tema que debe ser abordado con el suficiente cuidado de tal forma de cautelar la coherencia con el resto de la regulacin financiera. Otros aspectos se refieren a la normativa de las libretas de ahorro y las reformas en marcha al sistema de pagos. Asimismo, creemos necesario se inicie una revisin global del esquema de garantas a los depsitos que funciona desde 1986 en el pas, y que resulta conveniente replantear a la luz de estas modernizaciones.  La actual normativa financiera del Banco Central permite el pago de intereses y reajustes sobre obligaciones a plazo, pero prohbe dicho pago sobre captaciones del pblico a menos de 30 das, que se consideran a la vista en la Ley General de Bancos.  La autorizacin de pago de intereses sobre ciertas obligaciones a la vista es una iniciativa que tiene una serie de ventajas desde el punto de vista de la eficiencia y competencia del sistema financiero. Sin embargo, es necesario conciliar esta necesidad de mayor competencia y eficiencia con el esquema de garantas vigente.  Se debe considerar que el pago de intereses sobre obligaciones vista probablemente aumenta la base sobre la cual se aplica la garanta del Banco Central. Adems, un rgimen en que stas se benefician del pago de intereses y adems se garantizan a todo evento, podra incentivar graves distorsiones en el sistema. En efecto, al eliminar el necesario balance entre rentabilidad y riesgo, se crea un riesgo moral que ser particularmente evidente en el caso de instituciones que pudieran exhibir problemas de solvencia y por ende de mayor riesgo.  En lnea con lo anterior, se estima necesario avanzar en un examen crtico del esquema vigente de garanta y seguro de depsitos. Ello debera llevar al diseo de mecanismos ms eficientes de proteccin a los depositantes, lo que se traducir en un sistema ms sano y eficiente, y en el que se cautelen debidamente los problemas de riesgo moral a que estn afectos muchos de estos mecanismos. Esta iniciativa debe abordarse en un trabajo conjunto entre el Banco Central, la SBIF y el Ministerio de Hacienda.  El sistema de regulacin y supervisin actual tiene slidas bases. Sin embargo, los sistemas financieros y sus regulaciones se ven enfrentados a continuos procesos evolutivos. La creciente complejidad de los sistemas, en conjunto con la mayor internacionalizacin de la banca, requiere que la regulacin prudencial descanse cada vez ms en la autorregulacin por parte de los mismos entes financieros.  El mismo mercado, y las propias instituciones financieras organizadas, deben ser capaces de proveer elementos de disciplina para el correcto funcionamiento del sector financiero, para lo cual es indispensable perseverar en la entrega de informacin relevante, oportuna y confiable para el pblico.  Esto ha significado cada vez un mayor nivel de capacidades gerenciales adecuadas a los nuevos tiempos y de un compromiso primordial por parte de los directores de las instituciones financieras. As se han dado pasos concretos para aumentar los niveles de transparencia y profesionalizacin de las decisiones.  Ello, no obstante, requiere la vigilancia permanente y efectiva por parte de las autoridades monetaria y bancaria.  En este contexto general, me complace informar al H. Senado que hemos concluido un acuerdo preliminar con el Ministerio de Hacienda para transformar parte de la deuda en dlares del Fisco con el Banco Central en deuda en pesos. Esto ayudar a resolver el dficit patrimonial del Banco Central, y ser una importante contribucin al fortalecimiento institucional del Banco. Este acuerdo debe ser presentado prximamente al Congreso para su sancin legal.  Finalmente, no puedo dejar de hacer un comentario adicional sobre los terribles acontecimientos de ayer en los Estados Unidos. Lamentamos profundamente las vctimas causadas y los daos infligidos. Pero ms all del dolor de ayer y de hoy, habr seguramente otras consecuencias que hoy es difcil prever. Hemos hecho un anlisis interno en el Banco Central de las posibles consecuencias, y mantenemos una evaluacin minuto a minuto de la situacin de los mercados y de sus perspectivas. El actual esquema de polticas macroeconmicas es el mejor para enfrentar esta coyuntura, y estamos preparados para adoptar las medidas que puedan resultar necesarias para minimizar los efectos de esta tragedia sobre la economa chilena. Ya hemos dispuesto, en el da de ayer medidas necesarias para asegurar un funcionamiento ordenado de los mercados financieros y otorgar una adecuada provisin de liquidez acorde con las necesidades en estas especiales circunstancias. Asimismo, el Banco Central mantendr una mirada atenta en el mercado cambiado, con el fin de adecuar sus operaciones a los requerimientos por cobertura de riesgo y liquidez en moneda extranjera, cuidando evitar que se produzcan efectos financieros perturbadores en ese mercado.

Title: Foreign Financial Integration and Capital Market Development
text: Foreign Financial Integration and Capital Market Development Presentation by the President of the Central Bank of Chile, Carlos Massad, at the Seminar "Capital Market Reform: More Growth and Investment for Chile". Santiago, 28 November 2001. The reform of the capital market, approved by the H. National Congress and recently promulgated by H.E. the President of the Republic, is the theme that brings us together in this Seminar. The relevance of this matter for the future development of the Chilean economy has motivated the Ministry of Finance and the Central Bank of Chile to jointly organize this meeting. With this reform, decisive progress is being made towards the further development of the national financial market and its process of integration into international markets is deepened. I. MONETARY POLICY OUTLOOK IN CHILE Chile is a small economy. It represents just 0.5% of global GDP. The capitalization of our stock market is equivalent to less than 0.4% of its similar in the United States, just over 2% of the UK stock market and less than 13% of its similar in Spain. The above figures illustrate our small relative size. Consequently, Chile has no destiny if it does not look at the world as its market. We need to aim for full integration with world markets, both commercially and financially. This means making better use of these markets. On trade, our tariff barriers are low and continue to be reduced. Financially, we are beginning to enter the process of globalization. Chile is interested in globalization, understood as an increasingly interconnected world. However, globalization increasingly exposes us to external shocks. Hence, we need a policy scheme that is functional to globalization but at the same time facilitates the absorption of external impacts. This, in turn, requires flexibility across markets to minimize the private and social costs of inevitable adjustments in the face of a rapidly changing world. That is the direction in which we have moved in the field of monetary policy. The current monetary policy scheme has five components: a) Floating free exchange rate b) Permanent inflation targets c) Unrestricted exchange rate movements d) Capital movements with minimum regulations e) Nominalization of short-term interest rates, especially the monetary policy rate. Arriving at this scheme was not easy, but what happened in 1998-99 proved us right: trying to maintain an exchange rate within a band does not help absorb external impacts, such as that of the Asian crisis, or internal impacts, such as the excess of expenses of our economy. But achieving flexibility in the foreign exchange market required careful preparation, which had been going on since 1997. This culminated in the floating of the peso in September 1999. A little more than two years after the implementation of the floating exchange rate regime, its effects have been extremely positive: it has contributed considerably to improving the maneuverability of monetary policy in a volatile external environment, while this process has been accompanied by a deepening of the exchange market and the use of risk hedging mechanisms. Already in 1999 the transition from annual inflation target points to a permanent target range was announced: we had managed to bring inflation to levels that do not damage the economy or affect the incomes of the poorest, after 10 years of efforts and for the first time in seventy years. Exchange restrictions, meanwhile, began to be phased out, culminating in April 2001. The policy interest rate was nominalized as of August 9 of this year, in order to make it directly comparable with the rates in force in the rest of the countries of the world and better regulate international capital movements. At the same time, it allows us to induce an increasing nominalization of the short-term variables currently indexed; This will prevent transitory inflationary impacts from becoming semi-permanent through their transfer to the entire economy through indexed variables. Finally, tax restrictions on capital movements have been lifted in the recently enacted Capital Market Reform Law. We now have a policy framework that allows us to look more confidently at our economic relationship with the world, and to move forward with confidence in the negotiation of opening and integration schemes that contain elements of reciprocity and mutual benefit. This does not mean that we are immune to external events. We will suffer, or benefit, from its consequences. But it does mean that we will be able to absorb the possible negative effects of such events at lower private and social costs. Sometimes, we will have to use transitory policies, such as the exchange intervention we announced in August of this year, but they will not change either the direction or the direction of the monetary policy scheme that is in operation. II. RELEVANCE OF HAVING A FINANCIAL SYSTEM DEVELOPED International financial integration is a natural step to strengthen and deepen the Chilean financial market, so that it offers different instruments and forms of financing to the real sector. I would like to say a few words about the importance of having a developed and diversified financial system. A diversified financial system offers its participants different forms of financing, each of which is better suited to different types of projects, firms and industries. Bank financing is best provided in industries whose information is expensive to acquire, but easy to interpret, and where there are real assets that serve as collateral. Venture capital financing is more appropriate for emerging industries, without tangible assets and a lot of human capital, where know-how is in the process of being built. Traditional stock market financing is justified in consolidated industries, where know-how and information are standardized and relatively easy to interpret. On the other hand, the different types of financing complement each other. The possibility of accessing market financing fosters banking competition and limits intermediation margins. In turn, many financial innovations arise from the banking industry and evolve from "tailor-made" products to standardized financial products that can also be traded in a standardized way on the stock exchanges. Diversified financial development also reduces the financial vulnerability of the economy. One type of financing acts as a backup system when the other has problems. When liquidity disappears from markets in periods of financial volatility, bank financing keeps payments and investment going. And in recessionary periods, when bank credit tends to be more restrictive due to risk problems, market financing can channel the impact of more expansionary monetary policies. Similarly, a solid domestic financing base makes the economy less vulnerable to fluctuations in external financing, which is more subject to financial contagion problems or volatile perceptions of sovereign risk. III. INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL INTEGRATION International financial integration is a necessary step to strengthen and deepen the Chilean financial market and improve our capacity to absorb external shocks. However, for financial mobility associated with further integration to be a positive factor, it must be accompanied by a stable macroeconomic environment and appropriate prudential regulation. In this regard, the policies of the Central Bank have followed the criteria of gradualness and prudence: the first, based on the necessary sequence between the development of the domestic financial market and its capacity to face and manage the new risks of international financial integration, and the second, in response to the recognition of the risks of international capital mobility, especially those resulting from unexpected changes of significant magnitude in capital flows. The Central Bank has taken important steps towards international financial integration, adopting measures to make international capital mobility a means of strengthening financial market development. These measures include, first, those relating to capital account liberalization. As will be recalled, in recent years the reserve requirement for foreign capital flows to the country was reduced to 0%, the requirement of a minimum stay of one year of foreign capital in the country in order to be repatriated was eliminated, external debt instruments denominated in pesos were made operational, the percentages of investment abroad of pension fund assets were expanded, insurance companies and mutual funds, to name a few. These measures culminated last April with the elimination of all exchange restrictions and the simplification of the remaining processes, measures fully consistent with the floating exchange rate already in operation. Greater financial integration must also be accompanied by information and transparency policies. The Central Bank, based on the premise that information is one of the most efficient instruments to face the imperfections of the markets, has oriented its actions to improve transparency in its economic policy decisions and in the delivery of increasingly complete information. An example in this area is the publication of the IPOM, which presents the Central Bank's vision on the recent evolution of the economy and the prospects in a two-year moving horizon. This report gives greater transparency to the fundamentals of monetary policy decisions. Another example is advance information on the dates of monetary policy meetings and the publication of minutes of the Council minutes. At the international level, Chile has signed the IMF's special data publication program, which establishes standardized criteria on periodicity and format of information, as well as the publication of the international investment position, which presents information on the stocks of assets and liabilities of the economy as a whole and for four subsectors: General Government, Monetary Authority, Banking Sector and other sectors. Other next steps in terms of external financial integration concern compliance with international codes and standards that have emanated from the initiatives for the "new international financial architecture". Although these are recommendations to date, to the extent that the international financial community pays more attention to them, they are quasi-mandatory, or there is a risk that the cost of international credit will become more expensive. In this area, some of the most important initiatives concern: a5 Market infrastructure: Basic principles for systemically important payment systems and others related to settlement risk in securities and foreign exchange markets. The Central Bank is in a process of modernization in this area in accordance with the best international systems and procedures; a5 financial regulation and supervisory standards, including the Basel capital standards, which are under international review, as well as the basic principles of banking, securities and insurance, and consolidated supervision. IV. CAPITAL MARKET REFORM The law that reforms the capital market, recently promulgated and that has motivated this meeting, contains central aspects that liberalize and perfect the national financial market. The set of measures adopted, in the tax and institutional fields, contribute significantly to the further development of our market, through effective integration with the outside, the removal of obstacles to liquidity in financial markets and new financing alternatives. This will mainly benefit investors, both domestic and foreign, and companies, which will have more options for access to the capital market, thus favoring greater financial integration with the outside world and greater diversification of our financial system. It is not for me to analyse this reform in detail. I would just like to point out that this is a new major step towards greater international financial integration and towards the further development of our capital market. However, the success of the reform is based on the consolidation of a healthy macroeconomic environment. In this sense, maintaining price stability and the sustainability of fiscal policy are permanent challenges that will strengthen our process of financial integration with the outside world and deepen our capital market.
text_original: Integracin Financiera con el Exterior y Desarrollo del Mercado de Capitales Exposicin del Presidente del Banco Central de Chile, Carlos Massad, en el Seminario Reforma al Mercado de Capitales: Ms Crecimiento e Inversin para Chile. Santiago, 28 de noviembre de 2001. La reforma al mercado de capitales, aprobada por el H. Congreso Nacional y promulgada recientemente por S.E. el Presidente de la Repblica, constituye el tema que nos rene en este Seminario. La relevancia de esta materia para el desarrollo futuro de la economa chilena ha motivado al Ministerio de Hacienda y al Banco Central de Chile a organizar en forma conjunta este encuentro. Con esta reforma, se avanza decididamente hacia un mayor desarrollo del mercado financiero nacional y se profundiza en su proceso de integracin a los mercados internacionales.  PERSPECTIVAS DE LA POLITICA MONETARIA EN CHILE Chile es una economa pequea. Representa apenas el 0,5% del PIB mundial. La capitalizacin de nuestro mercado burstil equivale a menos del 0,4% de su similar en Estados Unidos, a poco ms del 2% del mercado burstil del Reino Unido y a menos del 13% de su similar en Espaa. Las cifras anteriores ilustran nuestro reducido tamao relativo. En consecuencia, Chile no tiene destino si no mira al mundo como su mercado. Necesitamos apuntar a una integracin plena con los mercados mundiales, en lo comercial y lo financiero. Ello implica aprovechar mejor esos mercados. En lo comercial, nuestras barreras arancelarias son bajas y siguen reducindose. En lo financiero, comenzamos a entrar en el proceso de globalizacin. A Chile le conviene la globalizacin, entendida como un mundo cada vez ms interconectado. Sin embargo, la globalizacin nos expone cada vez ms a los impactos provenientes del exterior. De aqu que necesitemos un esquema de polticas funcional a la globalizacin pero que a la vez facilite la absorcin de los impactos externos. Esto, a su vez, requiere flexibilidad en todos los mercados para minimizar los costos privados y sociales de los inevitables ajustes ante un mundo rpidamente cambiante. Es esa la direccin en la que hemos avanzado en el campo de la poltica monetaria. El actual esquema de poltica monetaria tiene cinco componentes:  Tipo de cambio libre flotante  Metas de inflacin permanentes  Movimientos cambiarios sin restricciones  Movimientos de capitales con regulaciones mnimas  Nominalizacin de las tasas de inters de corto plazo, especialmente la tasa de poltica monetaria. Llegar a este esquema no fue fcil, pero lo ocurrido en 1998-99 nos dio la razn: pretender mantener un tipo de cambio dentro de una banda no ayuda a absorber impactos externos, como el de la crisis asitica, o internos, como el exceso de gastos de nuestra economa. Pero llegar a la flexibilidad en el mercado cambiario requera cuidadosa preparacin, la que se vena realizando ya desde 1997. Esto culmin con la flotacin del peso en setiembre de 1999. A poco ms de dos aos de la implementacin del rgimen de flotacin cambiara, sus efectos han sido extremadamente positivos: ha contribuido considerablemente a mejorar la capacidad de maniobra de la poltica monetaria en un entorno externo voltil, al tiempo que este proceso ha ido acompaado de una profundizacin del mercado cambiario y del uso de mecanismos de cobertura de riesgos. Ya en 1999 se anunci el paso de las metas punto anuales de inflacin a una meta rango de carcter permanente: habamos logrado llevar la inflacin a niveles que no daan la economa ni afectan los ingresos de los ms pobres, despus de 10 aos de esfuerzos y por primera vez en setenta aos. Por su parte, las restricciones cambiaras se comenzaron a eliminar gradualmente, proceso que culmin en abril de 2001. La tasa de inters de poltica se nominaliz a partir del 9 de agosto de este ao, con el fin de hacerla directamente comparable con las tasas vigentes en el resto de los pases del mundo y regular mejor los movimientos internacionales de capitales. A la vez, nos permite inducir una creciente nominalizacin de las variables de corto plazo actualmente indizadas; ello permitir evitar que impactos inflacionarios transitorios se transformen en semipermanentes a travs de su traspaso a toda la economa mediante las variables indizadas. Finalmente, las restricciones de tipo tributario a los movimientos de capitales se han levantado en la ley de Reforma del Mercado de Capitales recientemente promulgada. Contamos ahora con un esquema de polticas que nos permite mirar con ms confianza nuestra relacin econmica con el mundo, y avanzar con seguridad en la negociacin de esquemas de apertura e integracin que contengan elementos de reciprocidad y beneficio mutuo. Esto no significa que seamos inmunes a los acontecimientos externos. Sufriremos, o nos beneficiaremos, de sus consecuencias. Pero s significa que podremos absorber con menores costos privados y sociales los eventuales efectos negativos de tales acontecimientos. En ocasiones, tendremos que usar polticas transitorias, como la intervencin cambiara que anunciamos en agosto de este ao, pero ellas no cambiarn ni la direccin ni el sentido del esquema de polticas monetarias que est en operacin.  RELEVANCIA DE CONTAR CON UN SISTEMA FINANCIERO DESARROLLADO La integracin financiera internacional es un paso natural para fortalecer y profundizar el mercado financiero chileno, de modo que ste ofrezca diferentes instrumentos y formas de financiamiento al sector real. Quiero referirme brevemente a la relevancia de contar con un sistema financiero desarrollado y diversificado. Un sistema financiero diversificado ofrece a sus partcipes distintas formas de financiamiento, cada una de las cuales se acomoda mejor a distintos tipos de proyectos, firmas e industrias. El financiamiento bancario se presta mejor en aquellas industrias cuya informacin es cara de adquirir, pero fcil de interpretar, y donde hay activos reales que sirven de garantas. El financiamiento de capital de riesgo es ms apropiado para industrias emergentes, sin activos tangibles y mucho capital humano, donde el know-how est en proceso de construccin. El financiamiento en bolsa tradicional se justifica en industrias consolidadas, donde el know-how y la informacin se encuentran estandarizados y sta es relativamente fcil de interpretar. Por otra parte, los distintos tipos de financiamiento se complementan unos con otros. La posibilidad de acceder a financiamiento de mercado fomenta la competencia bancaria y limita los mrgenes de intermediacin. A su vez, muchas innovaciones financieras surgen de la industria bancaria y van evolucionando desde productos a la medida a productos financieros estandarizados que se pueden transar en forma tambin estandarizada en las bolsas. Asimismo, un desarrollo financiero diversificado disminuye la vulnerabilidad financiera de la economa. Un tipo de financiamiento acta como sistema de respaldo cuando el otro presenta problemas. Cuando desaparece la liquidez de los mercados en perodos de volatilidad financiera, el financiamiento bancario mantiene en marcha los pagos y la inversin. Y en perodos recesivos, cuando el crdito bancario tiende a ser ms restrictivo por problemas de riesgo, el financiamiento de mercado puede canalizar el impacto de polticas monetarias ms expansivas. Del mismo modo, una base slida de financiamiento domstico hace a la economa menos vulnerable a las fluctuaciones del financiamiento externo, el que est ms sujeto a problemas de contagio financiero o percepciones voltiles del riesgo soberano.  INTEGRACIN FINANCIERA INTERNACIONAL La integracin financiera internacional es un paso necesario para fortalecer y profundizar el mercado financiero chileno y mejorar nuestra capacidad para absorber impactos externos. Sin embargo, para que la movilidad financiera asociada con una mayor integracin sea un factor positivo, debe estar acompaada de un ambiente macroeconmico estable y de una regulacin prudencial adecuada. En este sentido, las polticas del Banco Central han seguido los criterios de gradualidad y de prudencia: el primero, fundamentado en la necesaria secuencia entre el desarrollo del mercado financiero interno y su capacidad para enfrentar y administrar los nuevos riesgos de la integracin financiera internacional, y el segundo, en respuesta al reconocimiento de los riesgos de la movilidad internacional de capitales, especialmente los que se derivan de cambios inesperados y de magnitud significativa en los flujos de capitales. El Banco Central ha dado pasos importantes para la integracin financiera internacional, adoptando medidas que permiten hacer de la movilidad internacional de capitales un medio para fortalecer el desarrollo del mercado financiero. Entre estas medidas, cabe mencionar, en primer trmino, aqullas relativas a la liberalizacin de la cuenta de capitales. Como se recordar, en los ltimos aos se redujo a 0% el encaje a los flujos de capitales extranjeros al pas, se elimin la exigencia de permanencia mnima de un ao de los capitales externos en el pas para poder ser repatriados, se hicieron operativos los instrumentos de deuda externa denominados en pesos, se ampliaron los porcentajes de inversin en el exterior de los activos de fondos de pensiones, compaas de seguros y fondos mutuos, por citar algunas. Tales medidas culminaron en abril pasado con la eliminacin de todas las restricciones cambiaras y la simplificacin de los procesos restantes, medidas plenamente consistentes con la flotacin cambiara ya en operacin. Una mayor integracin financiera tambin debe estar acompaada de polticas de informacin y transparencia. El Banco Central, basado en la premisa que la informacin es uno de los instrumentos ms eficientes para enfrentar las imperfecciones de los mercados, ha orientado sus acciones a mejorar la transparencia en sus decisiones de poltica econmica y en la entrega de informacin cada vez ms completa. Un ejemplo en esta materia es la publicacin del IPOM, que presenta la visin del Banco Central sobre la evolucin reciente de la economa y las perspectivas en un horizonte mvil de dos aos. Este Informe da mayor transparencia a los fundamentos de las decisiones de poltica monetaria. Otro ejemplo es la informacin anticipada sobre las fechas de las reuniones de poltica monetaria y la publicacin de las minutas de las actas del Consejo. A nivel internacional, Chile ha suscrito el programa especial de publicacin de datos del FMI, que establece criterios estandarizados sobre periodicidad y formato de la informacin, as como la publicacin de la posicin de inversiones internacionales, que presenta informacin de los stocks de activos y pasivos de la economa como un todo y de cuatro subsectores: gobierno general, autoridad monetaria, sector bancario y los dems sectores. Otros pasos siguientes en materia de integracin financiera con el exterior se refieren al cumplimiento de los cdigos y estndares internacionales que han emanado de las iniciativas para la nueva arquitectura financiera internacional. Aunque a la fecha se trata de recomendaciones, en la medida que la comunidad financiera internacional les presta ms atencin, tienen un carcter de cuasi-obligatorias, o se corre el riesgo de que el costo del crdito internacional se encarezca. En este mbito, algunas de las iniciativas ms importantes se refieren a:  infraestructura de mercados: principios bsicos para sistemas de pagos con importancia sistmica y otros relacionados con el riesgo de liquidacin en los mercados de valores y moneda extranjera. El Banco Central se encuentra en un proceso de modernizacin en esta rea acorde con los mejores sistemas y procedimientos internacionales;  estndares de regulacin financiera y supervisin, dentro de los cuales destacan las normas de capital de Basilea, que estn en proceso de revisin a nivel internacional, as como los principios bsicos de regulacin bancaria, valores y seguros, y supervisin consolidada.  REFORMA AL MERCADO DE CAPITALES La ley que reforma al mercado de capitales, recientemente promulgada y que ha motivado el presente encuentro, contiene aspectos centrales que liberalizan y perfeccionan el mercado financiero nacional. El conjunto de medidas adoptadas, en los mbitos tributarios e institucionales, contribuyen de manera significativa a un mayor desarrollo de nuestro mercado, a travs de una efectiva integracin con el exterior, la remocin de trabas a la liquidez de los mercados financieros y nuevas alternativas de financiamiento. Ello beneficiar mayoritariamente a los inversionistas, tanto nacionales como extranjeros, y a las empresas, que tendrn ms opciones de acceso al mercado de capitales, favoreciendo, de esta manera, una mayor integracin financiera con el exterior y una mayor diversificacin de nuestro sistema financiero. No me corresponde analizar en detalle esta reforma. Slo quiero sealar que ella constituye un nuevo gran paso hacia una mayor integracin financiera internacional y hacia un mayor desarrollo de nuestro mercado de capitales. No obstante, el xito de la reforma se basa en la consolidacin de un ambiente macroeconmico sano. En este sentido, mantener la estabilidad de precios y la sustentabilidad de la poltica fiscal son desafos permanentes que permitirn fortalecer nuestro proceso de integracin financiera con el exterior y profundizar nuestro mercado de capitales.

Title: Monetary Policy Effectiveness in Chile and Outlook
text: Effectiveness of Monetary Policy in Chile and Outlook PRESENTATION BY CARLOS MASSAD A., PRESIDENT OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF CHILE, HELD AT THE BREAKFAST CONFERENCE, ORGANIZED BY THE ASSOCIATION OF METALLURGICAL AND METALWORKING INDUSTRIES A. G. (ASIMET), ON MARCH 28 , 2002. Introduction The objective of this presentation is to examine the issue of the effectiveness of monetary policy in Chile. First of all, we will mention the role and importance of monetary policy and the real privilege we have as a country to be able to use it as a countercyclical instrument and to discuss it. We will then examine, from a conceptual and empirical point of view, the transmission mechanisms of monetary policy and the expected effects of changes in interest rates. We will also analyse the experience of 2001 with monetary policy and the transmission of the rate cuts in the first half of the year. At the end of this presentation we will analyze macroeconomic perspectives for this year. Monetary policy in Chile has had to face situations of great complexity since 1997, when the Asian crisis broke out. In addition to facing a complicated external outlook, including serious financial problems in emerging economies in the years 1998-1999, a strong oil shock in 2000 and a recession or a great slowdown in the main industrialized economies during 2001 also complicated economic management. For its part, the economic policy framework has varied in substantial respects. This is how the exchange rate floats freely, we have a target range for inflation, the process of opening the capital account is completed and fiscal policy is guided by a pre-announced rule. In the area of financial policy, mention should be made of the nominalization of monetary policy in August 2001, the deepening of the market for hedging instruments and the recent authorization of interest payments on current accounts. To this is added a great reform to the domestic capital market. It is clear that a lot has happened over the past four years. In part, as a consequence of the magnitude of these shocks and changes, but also because of the importance that society attaches to monetary policy, this process has not been without debate. The discussion has revolved around multiple aspects, ranging from the instruments and objectives of policy, to the very existence of transmission from monetary policy to its objectives, what has been called the effectiveness of policy. Undoubtedly, what has happened with macroeconomics during 2001 has fueled the discussion on the effectiveness of monetary policy, two being the most relevant facts that are used in this debate. The first is that in recent quarters the actual growth of output has turned out to be substantially lower than anticipated by both the authorities and the various market analysts. The exact size of the projection revisions has varied by source, but the sign is the same. As usual, moreover, during periods when there is a surprise d0 in this case unpleasant d0 growth projections are systematically adjusted, giving the perception of an endless process. The historical data are revealing: in September 2000, private projections considered growth of 5.8% for 2001, while in May 2001 these projections had been adjusted to 4.2%, figures that compare with an effective growth of 2.8% according to the new national accounts. The Central Bank's projections did not have a different trajectory (Table 1). The estimates made in late 2000 and early 2001 were not whimsical, but were based on an expected recovery in external demand, an expected increase in the terms of trade, a decline in long-term interest rates, and relative greater financial stability in emerging economies. They were, however, presented as a downward correction from previous projections, partly due to the finding of less dynamic domestic demand than anticipated. The second relevant fact in this discussion is that monetary policy was more expansionary during 2001. Indeed, considering both the signs of slowing domestic demand and the worsening growth prospects of our trading partners, the Central Bank successively lowered the interest rate during the first half of 2001. This is how the rate was cut five times, from UF 5% in January to UF 3.5% in June. This was in addition to a 50 basis point cut in August 2001, when the first signs of weak domestic demand were felt (Chart 1). The level of interest rates remained unchanged during the second half of 2001, although August saw the most important step in the process of nominalization of monetary policy by setting the policy rate in nominal terms. Then, a new process of interest rate cuts began during the first quarter of this year. Thus, between January and March, the policy interest rate has decreased by 175 basis points. The set of reductions in monetary policy interest rates over the past fifteen months has served as the basis for an intense discussion regarding the effectiveness of monetary policy. In light of the observed results, many wonder if the interest rate cuts served or if monetary policy really has relevant effects. Some have even argued that it is useless, that everything is a "problem of expectations". It is interesting to remember that in 1997 there was a similar discussion when consumption was expanding rapidly and some people claimed that raising the interest rate had no effect and, therefore, did not serve to regulate its growth. It was considered that monetary policy could have paradoxical effects: that in order to control the expansion of spending, the interest rate had to be lowered. Today, there are those who argue that to stimulate spending you have to raise it. The role of monetary policy The central role of monetary policy is to maintain price stability, a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for achieving macroeconomic stability. There is consensus, both theoretically and practically, that high inflation only harms the growth capacity of economies, with costs that, moreover, are paid in greater proportion by the poorest. Latin America is unfortunately full of examples that corroborate this. However, in the process of maintaining low and stable inflation, monetary policy also assumes a role of stabilizing output, particularly when there are shocks that affect both activity and inflation in the same direction. Thus, monetary policy can also have countercyclical effects on activity. In order to reduce the variability of inflation, output and employment volatility can also be reduced . This is the case we face, for example, when private spending weakens, negatively affecting both growth and inflation prospects. But there are also more difficult-to-address shocks, in which the synchrony of the effects on activity and inflation does not continue. It is clear, in this sense, that monetary policy is not capable of solving all the problems facing the economy. For example, an excessive rise in wages, inconsistent with productivity gains, is a dilemma that monetary policy cannot accommodate without jeopardizing stability objectives. This is why wage policy is, in itself, a key component of the economic policy framework. Another fact that exemplifies this type of more complex disturbance is a sudden change in the price of oil. In this case, monetary policy must adjust the speed with which it acts, distinguishing changes in the price level that happen all at once, from those persistent that signify genuine inflation, and, in this way, limit the real effects of the policy reaction. Of course, all this is always based on the premise that inflationary control is inescapable. In addition to the complications of being able to recognize the type of shock to the economy, monetary policy faces other difficulties: there is uncertainty about the size and persistence of the observed shocks, the size of the productive capacity gaps in the economy is not known with certainty, and, as is well known, Monetary policy takes time to transmit, which also varies, as does the magnitude of the effect of a given policy change. However, despite these difficulties, there are more benefits than costs of maintaining an active monetary policy in a country like Chile. The benefit of reducing the volatility of inflation, and the reduction, albeit partial, of the volatility of activity levels amply justify the existence of a monetary policy that seeks to deal with the most relevant deviations. It is also important to recognize that the type of discussion at hand is something that only some emerging economies agree to. Chile is a privileged country in this regard because, thanks to the solidity and consistency of its institutions and macroeconomic policy, it has the possibility to discuss the most appropriate degree and effectiveness of countercyclical monetary policy. In the vast majority of countries, the discussion is another: How to limit the destabilizing effects of macroeconomic policy. In fact, we have been able to pursue an expansionary monetary policy, while others are prevented from doing so. Our interest rate today is the lowest in Latin America, and the growth rate is among the highest among emerging countries. In our country, during the last 17 years, a solid position of solvency and external liquidity has been accumulating, together with the sustained reduction of inflation in an environment where a healthy financial system and balanced fiscal accounts have prevailed. All these elements have meant the widespread recognition of the main economies and institutions of the globe and the clear differentiation with respect to the vast majority of emerging economies. The soundness of its macroeconomic fundamentals, external solvency, fiscal soundness, that of the financial system and that of institutions and policies are the pillars on which the Chilean economy is based. The set of reforms implemented over the last decades meant a significant increase in the growth potential of the Chilean economy, along with contributing to rapidly reduce national poverty indicators. Thus, during the last 16 years, the Chilean economy experienced average annual gross domestic product (GDP) growth rates of around 6.0%, which has allowed us to move to the category of upper-middle-income country (figure 2). In inflationary matters, during the nineties, the high degree of commitment against inflation formally assumed by the Central Bank from obtaining its autonomy, meant the reduction of the variability of inflation and its level from around 30%, to values that fluctuate in a range of 2 to 4%, comparable to those of industrialized economies. This has been possible thanks to a policy that, over the past eleven years, has used the interest rate as a policy instrument, and has been widely supported and believed by the market (Figure 3). Another distinctive feature of the Chilean economy has been persistent fiscal discipline. Indeed, for much of the nineties this discipline has meant the achievement of surpluses or very moderate deficits. This commitment to fiscal responsibility made it possible to balance and strengthen public finances, since it facilitated the reduction of public debt significantly, although in some years spending with macroeconomic effect tended to rise more than desirable. It is also worth mentioning as a key milestone in the Chilean economy, the fact that since 2000 a fiscal policy rule has been established based on the maintenance of a structural surplus equivalent to 1% of GDP each year (Figure 4). In addition to the above, Chile's solvency and international liquidity position gradually strengthened during the nineties. This has allowed Chile to consolidate a gradual process of financial and commercial internationalization of its economy, even in the midst of the complex and turbulent international scenario that emerging economies have had to face in recent years. Structural changes, such as the floating exchange rate regime, the removal of restrictions on capital flows, and capital market reform are important steps in this process. The levels reached by the current account deficit in recent years are clear evidence of a sound external accounts from a macroeconomic perspective, which are projected to continue beyond, with higher economic growth rates (Chart 5). This strong position has resulted in a marked differentiation of Chile from other economies in the region, remaining since 1995 at the best level of risk classification in Latin America (A-) and with sovereign risk premium levels well below the rest of the emerging economies (Graphs 6 and 7). For its part, the financial system has tended towards a progressive consolidation and deepening in the domestic market and towards internationalization, incorporating new productsd1factoring, leasing, securitization, among othersd1and regulation that has allowed it to increase its level of exposure in other economies. The removal of barriers to both capital inflows and outflows has been an essential element in the development of the financial system. On the other hand, the improvement of the derivatives market and risk hedging products has allowed the exchange market to deepen and make it more flexible. Another notable point of the Chilean financial system, highly valued nationally and internationally, refers to the strength of the regulatory framework and the quality of supervision carried out by the Superintendency of Banks and Financial Institutions. In fact, solvency indicators, such as the level of capitalization and the proportion of the non-performing portfolio, confirm this statement. The level of capitalization of the financial system in January 2002, measured according to the Basel indicator, is 14.5% of risk-weighted assets, which, although it includes the surpluses of 2001, is well above what is recommended as an international standard (8%). Non-performing loans, meanwhile, remain at levels below 2% (Chart 8). The aforementioned pillars make up a fundamental part of the asset that our nation possesses and that when it comes to comparisons make it so different from the vast majority of emerging economies. For this reason, these are achievements on which we cannot compromise, with a view to inserting Chile within the context of the main economies of the world, hopefully in the not too distant future. Transmission mechanisms and effects of monetary policy From this framework of stability and solvency, it is possible to analyze, from the conceptual and empirical point of view, how monetary policy is transmitted in an economy such as Chile's (Table 2). The theory indicates that there are several channels through which monetary policy is transmitted over aggregate demand, output, and inflation. The traditional explanation of the way monetary policy operates on the economy is based on the fact that movements in the central bank's interest rate have effects on other interest ratesd1for example, the placement rates of the banking systemd1which in turn influences consumption and investment decisions. These aggregates, in turn, affect aggregate demand and prices. This direct effect can be complemented by other transmission mechanisms, such as the role played by the financial market through the volume of loans it grants (the so-called credit channel), the effect on growth and inflation expectations of monetary policy, and the way in which the movement in interest rates affects the prices of different assets in the economy. In the latter case, the changes produced by monetary policy in the exchange rate and in the price level of other assets, and, in this way, in wealth, stand out. Exchange rate movements, in turn, affect the cost of imported goods and the relative competitiveness of productive sectors, which in turn has an impact on net external demand. These transmission channels are not independent mechanisms, but interrelated phenomena that will operate simultaneously and jointly in the face of a certain variation in interest rates. The net final effect will be given by the combination of factors such as the sensitivity of investment and consumption to the cost of funds, the distribution of assets in the economy, the depth and diversification of the financial market, among others. It is possible to expect, in any case, that the traditional mechanism and the effect of changing it will be mechanisms of relevance in an economy such as Chile's, although the effects of monetary policy vary over time. Beyond this conceptual analysis, it is important to note that the various empirical studies carried out for the Chilean economy during the last decade show that, on average, monetary policy has clear effects on the level of activity and inflation. Certainly these studies have differences in the estimated magnitudes of these effects, but together they allow to refute the argument of irrelevance of monetary policy. [Rosende and Herrera (1991), Vald8es (1997), Parrado (2001), Garc92a (2001), Bravo and Garc92a (2002).] It is also interesting to corroborate that the estimates of the effects of monetary policy made for Chile do not differ significantly from the estimates made for other countries. Monetary policy does not seem to be more or less effective in Chile than in other countries with similar institutional and economic development. In this regard, it is worth highlighting a survey conducted by economists from our Central Bank to a group of other central banks, and in which each bank was asked about the impact on activity and inflation of a change in monetary policy interest rates of 100 basis points during a quarter [Schmidt-Hebbel and Tapia (2002)]. The central banks surveyed have, without exception, a policy regime like ours based on inflation targeting and floating exchange rate rates. The results are categorical: in the face of a reduction in interest rates, both economic activity and inflation increase. And, even more interestingly, the magnitudes of the reaction of each economy are similar and the magnitudes estimated for Chile are not especially different from those estimated for other countries. The only thing that stands out in the case of our country is the relative greater persistence with which inflation reacts, an issue that is undoubtedly related to the levels of indexation that still prevail in the economy (Table 3). While it seems clear that monetary policy has on average the effects discussed above, it should be noted that the actual impact of monetary policy often differs from the typical reaction expected. This happens both in the temporal dimension d1there are changes in interest rates more effective than othersd1 and in the dimension of economic agentsd1 the same change in the interest rate generates heterogeneous effects at the level of sectors, companies and people. Some factors behind this heterogeneity are: (i) the dissimilar and changing capacity of companies to access alternative end-of-life sources; (i) the different equity effects that generate changes in the exchange rate; (iii) the variable capacity of enterprises to pass on cost changes to final prices; and (iv) the quantity and characteristics of the portfolio of investment and consumption projects whose materialization may be affected by monetary policy. The experience of the period 2000-2001 From the background described, it is possible to analyze what happened during 2001 and whether, indeed, as some have argued, monetary policy has not had effects. The first thing is to note a question of elementary logic. Just as it cannot be inferred that the opening of umbrellas causes rain d0 even if we see both phenomena occurring at the same time d0 observing lower than expected output growth, while there are reductions in the policy interest rate, does not allow us to conclude that monetary policy is ineffective. In fact, in light of the evidence described, there were other factors that negatively influenced the evolution of economic activity. With regard to monetary policy, the various intermediate indicators show that it did indeed play an expansionary role in 2001. For example, the amount of nominal money expanded on average 15.3% per year, while total nominal placements in domestic currency increased by 10%. Both figures are clearly higher than the sum of GDP growth and average inflation that reached 6.4%. In fact, over the past year there have been several distinguished analysts who criticized the expansion of money as exaggerated. A trend that also ratifies this monetary expansion is that shown by the interest rates of the different documents issued by the Central Bank. For example, documents readjustable to 8 and 20 years ended the year 2000 with averages somewhat below UF 6%. By the end of 2001, they had reached UF 4.8% and 5.3% rates, respectively (Figure 9). On the other hand, the reaction also confirms the expansionary nature of the policy, although the observed depreciation was influenced by the terms of trade and regional turbulence. In any case, the real exchange rate increased by more than 12 per cent on average during 2001, which undoubtedly influenced the 9.7 per cent increase in export volumes observed during the year (figure 10). A more interesting exercise is to ask what would have happened to economic activity if interest rates had not fallen during 2001, that is, if they had been 150 basis points higher at the end of 2001. I think it's very difficult to argue that the situation would have been better. In fact, based on the projection models usually used by the Central Bank, which consider the effect of both short-term and long-term interest rates, and the impact of the real exchange rate on net external demand, it is possible to say that if monetary policy had not reacted during the first half of 2001, Chilean output would have grown at most 1.8% and not 2.8% observed. If monetary policy had an expansionary bias and we argue that it was effective, what then explains the lower than projected increase in activity? The most important explanations lie in a very different evolution of key external variables than anticipated and a considerably weaker than expected behavior of domestic expenditure. The evolution of activity in the United States and other industrialized countries, the terrorist attacks of September 2001 and the regional financial situation had a negative impact on growth prospects (Table 4). The figures speak for themselves. World growth expected for 2001 was 4.2 per cent in September 2000, eventually resulting in 2.2 per cent. In the case of our trading partners, the revision is even more dramatic: from an expected growth of 3.6% we went to just 1%. The price of copper was 15 cents lower than expected, the price of oil only one dollar lower than anticipated, and the terms of trade instead of increasing 2.4% decreased 7%. It is not easy to accurately measure the effect of all these events, but they could certainly explain several less points of growth. Suffice it to say that income increased only 0.5% in real terms last year, with a negative impact due to lower terms of trade compared to 2000 equivalent to 2.8% of GDP. In addition to this negative external environment, during 2001 domestic demand had a slowdown trajectory, ending the last quarter with a fall of 4.9% in 12 months, which implied that on average it decreased 0.7%. Certainly, the almost zero expansion of national income explains part of this fall, but developments that negatively influenced investor and consumer confidence also contributed, such as the financial turbulence observed in the region, with a direct impact on the exchange rate, the successive worsening of the world economic outlook throughout the year. and an unemployment rate that remained at high levels. There is no doubt that expectations play a role. But it is real facts that contribute to its formation or deformation, including negative external circumstances. Transmission of monetary policy at lending interest rates: 2000-2001 So far we have argued that monetary policy has been effective. A different question, however, is whether this was as effective as it could potentially be. As everyone knows, there has been a strong public discussion about the degree and speed of pass-through that has existed between the cuts in the monetary policy rate and the rates charged by the banking industry. Or bviamente, to the extent that the transfer of rates is more expeditious and involves more customers, monetary policy has greater power, at least as far as the traditional interest-expenditure rate channel is concerned. The analysis of the pass-through of interest rates faces at least two difficulties. The first is that the debate tends to confuse the transfer of the reductions that took place during the end of 2000 and the first half of 2001 with the cuts of the last three months. In the following analysis, I will concentrate on assessing whether the reductions for the second half of 2000 and the first half of 2001 have actually been carried over. It is precisely the analysis of this transfer that is relevant to evaluate the degree of effectiveness of monetary policy over the past year. The second complication is given by the difficulties of comparison generated by nominalization. Because in August 2001 the monetary policy rate was changed as a prize over the variation of the unit of promotion (UF) to a strictly fixed rate, market rates that were previously volatile are now stable and vice versa. This change in volatilities is precisely one of the expected results of the nominalization of monetary policy. Indeed, during the first half of the year, nominal transaction rates showed a high variability, as they moved in line with inflation trends. On the other hand, since August, nominal interest rates have been markedly more stable, a situation that has been verified mainly in short-term deposit rates (30 to 89 days). It is not correct, therefore, to simply compare interest rates observed for any two months, or compare them with the level of the monetary policy rate (MPR). Rather, it is appropriate to consider longer periods and correct for the effect of the variation in UF on the rates being compared. The following exercise compares the average interest rates that prevailed between August and December 2001, a period of stability after the rate cuts, and that observed between February and July 2000, a period that is also one of stability, prior to the cuts. The results are as follows (Table 5): - The MPR, measured as a nominal rate, declined between these two periods by more than 400 basis points, reflecting declines in both inflation and the policy rate. - The average nominal deposit interest rate for 30- to 89-day operations decreased 320 basis points, while the placement rate decreased 270 basis points. - In the case of nominal operations with terms of between 90 and 365 days, the deposit rate decreased by 230 basis points. The placement rate for this same term decreased by 400 basis points. - The MPR, measured as an interest rate on the variation of the UF, decreased 190 basis points. - The collection rate for readjustable operations with terms of between 90 and 365 days decreased by the same amount as the TPM. But the placement rate decreased by only 100 basis points. This shows that the transfer has not been perfect, although it has shown high degrees of efficiency in the cases of nominal rates for loans of 90 days or less, and somewhat less efficiency in the case of operations of more than 90 days. Thespreads between placement and deposit rates have increased in some cases, but this increase is of a clearly smaller magnitude than the rate cuts decreed by the Central Bank. And in some cases the spreads have actually decreased. The aggregate data, however, hide a very dissimilar reality according to the size of the debtors. This, it seems, is the relevant cut to understand the different positions of the public debate. The data shows that for almost 85% of the borrowed funds, the transfer is considerable, we would say almost perfect. But, for the remaining 15% of borrowed funds, representing approximately 90% of the system's customers, the handover has been very imperfect, becoming null, or even harmful, in some cases (Table 6). It should be noted that the very process of nominalization explains why the transfer of rates is greater in the nominal market than in the readjustment, since the inflation risk rewards are manifested in this second market. In fact, in the period analyzed, the spread between placement and deposit rates just increased more in this type of transaction. Over time, the stock of this type of operations will lose importance, a situation that is indeed already happening. The record I have reviewed indicates that the effectiveness of the policy may have suffered by limiting the pass-through of rate cuts to specific segments. However, the evidence is not strong that the importance of this lower relative effectiveness is crucial from a macroeconomic point of view. Recall that interest rates on the vast majority of borrowed funds have fallen considerably. We cannot, however, be complacent about what happens. From the point of view of macroeconomic policy, we are concerned about the issue, since transmission mechanisms could gain efficiency if rate pass-throughs were more widespread. From the point of view of equity, it is clear that there are sectors that face difficult conditions of access to the end of the journey. And from the point of view of efficiency, it is worth asking whether there are profitable projects that are not being carried out due to lack of financing. It is clear then that the problem of access to financing and its conditions must be examined more closely. It is also necessary to go beyond the "complaint stage" and analyze the factors behind the matter. The pro-growth agenda, fortunately, already contains several of these issues, including those related to venture capital, a key ingredient for good projects to receive financing. There are two matters that seem to us to be particularly relevant from the point of view of the transmission of monetary policy: - First, standard regulations and practices should make it easier for customers to switch banks, thereby increasing the system's competition. The reason is simple: as customer mobility is enhanced, changes in monetary policy should be reflected more quickly in the interest rates faced by the public. In this sense, we believe that the authorization for the payment of interest on current accounts is an element that goes precisely in this direction by strengthening banking competition. Among other aspects, the proposal of the pro-growth agenda to establish a guarantee center could be analyzed. And in the immediate term, a system should be implemented to facilitate the expeditious lifting of guarantees in order to allow their timely constitution in favor of the new creditor bank. There are also other issues such as transparency in the disclosure of informationd1the most obvious is the publication of rates on an annual and not monthly basisd1and the restriction that produces that the only possibility of avoiding the stamp tax on renewals exists only in the case of operations with the same bank that initially granted the credit. - Second, considering that one of the most important reasons that explain the restrictions on access to credit is the lack of information, the use and dissemination of information on payment behavior could be improved, developing, for example, a record of positive behavior. The basic premise, in any case, must be more and better information. In any case, the Central Bank's policy takes into account delays in passing on policy rates to banks' customers. A shortening of these timeframes would speed up this pass-through and improve the effectiveness of monetary policy. Conclusions and perspectives Finally, and in conclusion, I would like to briefly review the macroeconomic outlook for this year. Along with that, however, I think it is pertinent to establish, by way of conclusion, that we can be confident that monetary policy has relevant effects on economic activity. It may sometimes be more effective than others, but we are convinced that the action of the Central Bank has great relevance in macroeconomic results. We cannot pretend, however, that monetary policy is the solution to all problems. In this sense, for example, the business climate and its effect on expectations plays a critical role in short-term dynamics. Likewise, the flexibility that exists in the different markets is crucial in determining the characteristics of the adjustment processes of our economy. Indeed, to the extent that prices show greater rigidity, the absorption of the different s/ioc/rs will have greater effects on quantities, including activity and employment. Some may ask, then, if monetary policy is effective, why was it not more expansionary during 2001? The answer is simple: during the second half of last year we faced great turbulence that threatened to persistently divert inflation from the target range of 2 to 4%, affecting the fulfillment of the priority objective of the Central Bank according to the law. This is not the time to review all the events we had to face, but let us remember the seriousness of the financial and contagion problems that South America suffered and the terrorist attacks of September. Fortunately, in recent months the global situation and regional contagion has evolved positively. The prospects for a rapid recovery in the US are increasingly certain, growth projections for most of our trading partners have been revised upwards, and the prices of our most important exports are showing signs of recovery. On the regional front, a very complicated situation remains in Argentina, but the financial markets have responded with great independence, recognizing the strength of our economy. On the domestic side, the various indicators show an evolution of domestic spending clearly below what was anticipated a few months ago, while inflationary pressures have remained limited. In this context, effective inflation has remained at low levels, which in turn has been accompanied by a significant decrease in private sector inflation expectations. All this background has opened the opportunity for monetary policy to take an even more expansionary bias during the last three months, which has been reflected in the rate cuts I mentioned earlier. Otherwise, inflation was risked to persistently decline to the floor and even below the target range over the usual 12- to 24-month policy horizon. With all these elements, the economic outlook is clearly positive. In fact, and despite the sluggish domestic demand, many analysts have begun to revise upwards the growth projections for this year and next, thanks to the clear improvement in the external outlook and the boost in demand that is associated with the decrease in interest rates. In short, it is possible to look to the future with greater optimism, since the conditions are right for the process of reactivation of the economy to accelerate during the coming quarters.
