Title: Inauguration of Banco Conosur
text: INAUGURATION OF BANCO CONOSUR Mr. Carlos Massad President of the Central Bank of Chile 8 January 2003 Banco Conosur, whose official presentation we celebrate today, has a Successful and long tradition as a financier in the national credit market of consumption. These credits are those that reach the sectors with fewer resources and many of these correspond, rather than to consumer credit per se, to Financing of small and micro enterprises that would not be able to access others sources of financial resources. That is why consumer credit has a particular economic and social importance. Today consumer loans represent approximately 10% of the total of bank placements. As of August 2002 they have returned to observe increases of more than 10% per year, which had not been seensince before The Asian crisis. While the level of consumer placements is a small percentage of the Total, in terms of number of debtors, the share of these claims It represents about half of the system's debtors (49%). Indeed, October 2002 the number of total debtors of consumer loans amounted to almost two million people, of whom 1,750,000 have debts less than 200UF. The favourable trend in consumer loans can be explained to a large extent measure, by the lower interest rates that banks apply to this type of operations, due to reductions in the TPM. Another element that has Given the trend inconsumer loans has been the highest Offer of institutions to participate in this market. In recent times, it has seen the entry into the financial system of houses commercials (Falabella and Ripley) that already have a customer base, generally concentratedin the middle and lower middle segments. These houses Commercials know the customer's ability to pay and its characteristics of consumption, which makes it easier for them to assess the risks associated with a credit. 1 In addition, in April 2002 the Superintendency of Securities and Insurance authorized insurance companies to offer loans to businesses and individuals and issue credit cards, in addition to similar authorizations in cooperatives. These innovations stimulate increases in competitiveness in the small debtor segment, by including new agents to the system financial, which leads to a drop in borrowing costs. At present, the number of banks in the national financial system reaches 26 (including Banco Conosur) and is expected for this year the Onboarding new players, some of whom are licensed bank already approved or in the process of approval. The social and economic importance of consumer credit remained manifesto in the public discussion, during the year 2002, about the transmission of the policy rate cut to market rates. The Central Bank Monetary Policy Report for May 2002 noted that the rate cuts agreed by the Bank were not yet reflected fully at market rates, especially in the case of medium and small amounts. The Sixth Annual Conference organized by the Central Bank of Chile, Mid-December, had as its central theme the relationship between the transmission of monetary policy and the banking industry. For such purposes the issuing institute took the initiative, commissioning a study from the IMF so that evaluate this issue, which was added to others carried out within the institution. These studies empirically study the magnitude in which banks They pass on the monetary policy rate to their clients, amajor Relevance when evaluating the effectiveness of monetary policy. Let me highlight some of the results to be drawn from these Research: In terms of international evidence, they are important differences between countries(Cottarelli and Kourelis, 1994). The estimates of the Impact of policy rate changes on van placement rates from 6% to 83%, within a month, and the long-term effects reach a average transfer of 97%. Most comparativestudies between Countries suggest that, in general, less rigidity in interest rates is 2 Associated with the greater development of thefinancial system, greater competitiveness of the banking sector, fewer restrictions on capital flows and less Volatility of the monetary policy rate. In the Chilean case, it is observed that, on average, there is a transfer of both the rates in pesos as in UF, as they follow very closely to the policy rate monetary. Empirically it is found that the effect of changes in the rate of policy on placement rates , both in pesos and in UF for the period 1995-2001, is around 80% in the short term and very close to 100% in the long term (Berstein and Fuentes, 2002). Competitive imperfections or information asymmetries in industry Bancaria, could lead to policy interest rate hikes transmit faster than decreases in this rate. However, According to the results of Espinosa and Rebucci of the IMF, it is not found evidence that this is the case for the banking industry in Chile in general. However, evidence suggests that there are differences in Transmission speed between the different banks of the Chilean industry. These differences would be associated with the size of the bank, the quality of thebank. Loan portfolio and the type of customers of the bank. In this regard, it is argued that that this would be due to differences in the elasticity of demand for credit of customers and information asymmetries. It should be noted that the transfer has been particularly rapidin the case of the rates of operations of high amounts (over UF10,000), while the Evidence that we have indicates that it has been particularly slow in the case of credits of smaller amount. However, even in the case of credits of less than200 UF, although the reductions in rates were delayed, They note significant decreases for the various deadlines. They explain the most rapid increase in these loans, as well as the significant Increase in the number of customers who obtain them, which is estimated at more of 100,000 people in the last 6 months. The accumulated evidence indicates that the process of transmission of rates in Chile It is not substantially different from other countries. Certainly, the national financial system requiresthe highest degree of Possible competition. That is why the entry into operations of new banks, like Banco Conosur, it is very well received. text_original: INAUGURACIN BANCO CONOSUR Seor Carlos Massad Presidente Banco Central de Chile 8 de enero de 2003 El Banco Conosur, cuya presentacin oficial celebramos hoy da, tiene una exitosa y larga tradicin como financiera en el mercado nacional de crditos de consumo. Estos crditos son los que llegan a los sectores de menores recursos y muchos de ellos corresponden, ms que a crditos de consumo propiamente, a financiamiento de pequeas y micro empresas que no podran acceder a otras fuentes de recursos financieros. Por ello el crdito de consumo tiene una particular importancia econmica y social. Hoy los prstamos de consumo representan aproximadamente el 10% del total de colocaciones de la banca. A partir de agosto del 2002 se han vuelto a observar incrementos superiores al 10% anual, que no se vean desde antes de la crisis asitica. Si bien el nivel de las colocaciones de consumo es un pequeo porcentaje del total, en trminos de nmero de deudores, la participacin de estos crditos representa cerca de la mitad de los deudores del sistema (49%). En efecto, a octubre del 2002 el nmero de deudores totales de crditos de consumo ascenda a casi dos millones de personas, de los cuales 1.750.000 tienen deudas inferiores a 200UF. La favorable evolucin de los prstamos de consumo se explica, en gran medida, por las menores tasas de inters que la banca aplica a este tipo de operaciones, en razn de las reducciones de la TPM. Otro elemento que ha determinado la evolucin de los prstamos de consumo ha sido la mayor oferta de instituciones para participar en este mercado. En el ltimo tiempo, se ha visto el ingreso al sistema financiero de casas comerciales (Falabella y Ripley) que ya tienen una base de clientes, generalmente concentrada en los segmentos medio y medio bajo. Estas casas comerciales conocen la capacidad de pago del cliente y sus caractersticas de consumo, lo que les facilita la evaluacin de los riesgos asociados a un crdito. 1 Adems, en abril del 2002 la Superintendencia de Valores y Seguros autoriz a las compaas de seguros a ofrecer prstamos a empresas y personas y a emitir tarjetas de crdito, lo que se suma a autorizaciones similares en las cooperativas. Estas innovaciones estimulan aumentos en la competitividad en el segmento de los pequeos deudores, al incluir nuevos agentes al sistema financiero, lo que conduce a una baja en los costos de los prstamos. En la actualidad, el nmero de bancos en el sistema financiero nacional alcanza a 26 (incluido el Banco Conosur) y se espera para este ao la incorporacin de nuevos actores, algunos de los cuales tienen licencia bancaria ya aprobada o en trmite de aprobacin. La importancia social y econmica del crdito de consumo qued de manifiesto en la discusin pblica, durante el ao 2002, acerca de la transmisin de la rebaja de la tasa de poltica a las tasas de mercado. El Informe de Poltica Monetaria del Banco Central del mes de mayo del 2002 sealaba que las rebajas de tasas acordadas por el Banco an no se reflejaban plenamente en las tasas del mercado, especialmente en el caso de crditos de montos medianos y pequeos. La Sexta Conferencia Anual organizada por el Banco Central de Chile, a mediados de diciembre, tuvo como tema central la relacin entre la transmisin de la poltica monetaria y la industria bancaria. Para tales efectos el instituto emisor tom la iniciativa, encargando un estudio al FMI para que evaluara este tema, el que se sum a otros realizados al interior de la institucin. Estos trabajos estudian empricamente la magnitud en que los bancos traspasan la tasa de poltica monetaria a sus clientes, aspecto de gran relevancia al momento de evaluar la efectividad de la poltica monetaria. Permtanme destacar algunos resultados que se extraen de estas investigaciones: En trminos de la evidencia internacional, se encuentran importantes diferencias entre pases (Cottarelli y Kourelis, 1994). Las estimaciones del impacto de los cambios en la tasa de poltica sobre las tasas de colocacin van de 6% a 83%, en el plazo de un mes, y los efectos de largo plazo alcanzan un traspaso promedio de 97%. La mayora de los estudios comparativos entre pases sugieren que, en general, una menor rigidez en las tasas de inters est 2 asociada al mayor desarrollo del sistema financiero, mayor competitividad del sector bancario, menores restricciones a los flujos de capitales y menor volatilidad de la tasa de poltica monetaria. Para el caso chileno, se observa que, en promedio, existe traspaso tanto de las tasas en pesos como en UF, pues siguen muy de cerca a la tasa de poltica monetaria. Empricamente se encuentra que el efecto de cambios en la tasa de poltica sobre las tasas de colocacin, tanto en pesos como en UF para el perodo 1995-2001, est en torno a 80% en el corto plazo y muy cercano al 100% en el largo plazo (Berstein y Fuentes, 2002). Imperfecciones de la competencia o asimetras de informacin en la industria bancaria, podran llevar a que alzas de la tasa de inters de poltica se transmitan ms rpidamente que disminuciones de esta tasa. Sin embargo, de acuerdo a los resultados de Espinosa y Rebucci del FMI, no se encuentra evidencia de que este sea el caso para la industria bancaria en Chile en general. No obstante, la evidencia seala que existen diferencias en la velocidad de transmisin entre los distintos bancos de la industria chilena. Estas diferencias estaran asociadas al tamao del banco, la calidad de la cartera de crditos y el tipo de clientes del banco. Al respecto se argumenta que esto se debera a diferencias en la elasticidad de demanda por crdito de los clientes y asimetras de informacin. Cabe destacar que el traspaso ha sido especialmente rpido en el caso de las tasas de operaciones de elevados montos (sobre UF10.000), mientras la evidencia de que disponemos indica que ha sido especialmente lento en el caso de los crditos de menor monto. Sin embargo, incluso en el caso de crditos de menos de 200 UF, si bien las rebajas en las tasas demoraron, ya se observan importantes disminuciones para los distintos plazos. Ellas explican el aumento ms acelerado de estos crditos, as como el importante incremento en el nmero de clientes que los obtienen, el que se estima en ms de 100.000 personas en los ltimos 6 meses. La evidencia acumulada indica que el proceso de transmisin de tasas en Chile no es sustancialmente diferente al de otros pases. En general los movimientos de tasas de inters de poltica no son traspasados a las tasas de colocacin de mercado en forma instantnea. Estos resultados no implican que no exista espacio para aumentar la velocidad de traspaso de tasas de inters de poltica monetaria a tasas de inters 3 bancarias. Adems, hay todava mucho trabajo por hacer en el mbito del desarrollo de un sistema financiero ms competitivo, eficiente e integrado internacionalmente. Esto es de gran importancia para ganar eficiencia y productividad en nuestra economa, as como para mejorar la eficiencia de la poltica monetaria. Pero es particularmente importante para buscar frmulas de mercado que permitan reducir mrgenes de intermediacin, lo que favorecer al pas, a los bancos y a deudores como a depositantes. Ciertamente el sistema financiero nacional requiere del mayor grado de competencia posible. Por eso la entrada en operaciones de nuevos bancos, como el Banco Conosur, es muy bien recibida. Pero lo es an ms porque es un banco fuertemente orientado hacia el segmento de prstamos de menor tamao, de gran importancia econmica y social en nuestro pas. Estoy seguro que el Banco Conosur ser un actor destacado, junto a la Asociacin de Bancos y al Banco Central, en la discusin sobre nuevos avances en la modernizacin y desarrollo del sistema financiero nacional. Son grandes los desafos futuros y tenemos que enfrentarlos juntos. Gracias y mucho xito. 4

Title: Monetary Policy Report January 2003
text: January 2003 Monetary Policy Report: Presentation to the Senate Finance Committee PRESENTATION BY CARLOS MASSAD A., PRESIDENT OF THE CENTRAL BANK OF CHILE, AT H. SENATE OF THE REPUBLIC, HELD ON 1 5 JANUARY 2003. Introduction Recent inflation trends in the Chilean economy reveal that cost pressures are lower than anticipated some time ago. These events are the result of a more intense and prolonged process of falling external prices than expected, and of a more limited rate of growth in labor costs. This news, together with a slight expected trend of real exchange rate appreciation and moderate levels of international inflation, will accommodate a gentle decompression of marketing margins, which remain reduced, without generating inflationary pressures of magnitude. Additionally, the oil market scenario incorporates a tendency to decline in the price with respect to its current levels. Thus, although the outlook for slack in the use of installed capacity is not altered compared to what was expected last September, lower inflationary pressures are expected thanks to the more moderate trajectory of costs. With this background, the Central Bank decided to increase the monetary impulse at the beginning of January, cutting the policy rate to 2.75%. For the coming quarters, a lower dynamism is expected in the natural resource export sectors, but the rest of domestic activity has broadly continued the expansion path expected in September 2002, while the composition of this expansion shows incipient signs of change, with greater dynamism in the most persistent components of domestic demand and somewhat less momentum on the part of the export sectors. Thus, the most recent news tend to reaffirm a picture of gradual acceleration for the years 2003 and 2004, supported by the expected improvement in the international scenario and the current expansionary monetary policy. On this last point, it is important to have moved towards the nominalisation of monetary policy. In the previous scheme of indexation to the UF, inflation in December (-0.4%) would have required, in order to avoid generating a negative equivalent nominal rate, policy interest rates of UF4.75%. Such a high rate is clearly inconsistent with the reality we face and would have undermined the achievement of the inflation target in the current circumstances by pushing it below the lower limit of the band at the expense of greater volatility of output and employment. Thus, together with the acceleration of global activity to growth rates above potential growth, inflation will gradually and with swings approach the center of the target range at the end of the projection horizon. In any case, risks associated with the stabilization challenges faced by various economies in the region, especially Brazil, persist; uncertainty about the progress of the international economy, particularly the consequences of the probable war in the Middle East, and the strength of the expansion of domestic spending. Recent developments in activity and prospects With regard to recent developments in activity and its prospects, the most current information shows a pick-up in private consumption. Indicators of habitual consumption d0 which represent about 70% of total consumption d0 show a positive trajectory, both with respect to mid-year and what was projected in the last Report . On the one hand, supermarket sales (Asach), which had been falling since the beginning of 2001, experienced a turning point in mid-2002, after which the trend has remained positive. On the other hand, the National Institute of Statistics (INE) index of supermarket sales, which has grown steadily, has increased its rate of expansion in the most recent period (graph 1). In addition, industrial sales of consumer goods, provided by the INE, recovered from a marginal contraction, although they maintained a rather flat trend throughout 2002. Meanwhile, indicators of durable consumer spending surprised during the fourth quarter of 2002, particularly sales of durable goods from trade and industry and new vehicles. The latter have shown a clear upswing after the sharp declines experienced at the end of 2001, despite turbulence in the region and movements in the exchange rate (Chart 2). This more dynamic trend is supported by the growth of consumer loans, which have shown high annual growth rates since the beginning of 2002 , since the number of clients in the financial system has also shown a clear increase since mid-2002 (figure 3). This has occurred in a context in which reductions in the monetary policy interest rate (MPR) were significantly passed on to the interest rates of the vast majority of various types of credit operations as the year progressed, while long-term interest rates reached historically low levels during 2002. This reflects that expansionary monetary policy is having an effect on current growth and inflation conditions, despite the strong regional financial volatility that has existed since mid-2001; The main domestic financial markets have continued to operate with the necessary flexibility and adequacy, allowing monetary policy momentum to be maintained (Figures 4 and 5). In recent months, new precedents have accumulated regarding the characteristics of the shift from monetary policy to market interest rates. In particular, there are new IMF studies and the Central Bank's own research that empirically study the extent to which banks pass on the policy rate to their clients, comparing it with the experience of other countries. The main conclusion of these is that although in the short term the transfer is not one by one, the evidence for Chile is not far from the practices in this area in more developed countries (Table 1). In general, movements in policy interest rates, both in Chile and in the rest of the world, are not passed, instantaneously, to market placement rates. However, it is noteworthy that the Chilean case is among those economies in which the average transfer is more accelerated. However, there are differences between the various institutions in terms of the type of operation, which is mainly attributed to microeconomic variables. Finally, there is no evidence that in Chile there are asymmetries at the aggregate level in the reaction of the average interest rate between periods of interest rate hikes and falls. Although these results indicate that the case of Chile is not abnormal, this does not imply that there is no room to increase the speed of transfer of interest rates from monetary policy to bank interest rates. This is especially true for smaller loans, where slowness is observed. Unfortunately, there is no comparable information in other countries. Household expectations have also improved in recent months. The latest measurement of the Perception Index Economic (IPEC) shows a significant upturn in the global outlook, attributable to the end of the Free Trade Agreement (FTA) negotiations with the US and an incipient improvement in perceptions about labor market performance (Chart 6). These results are consistent with the fact that the labor participation rate has had increases in recent measurements, after seven moving quarters of decline, while the absolute level of employment presents an acceleration in the margin, according to figures from the INE. This occurs despite the fact that there are no significant breaks in the trajectory of the seasonally adjusted national unemployment rate. In turn, according to the survey of the University of Chile, the unemployment rate of Greater Santiago shows significant decreases in relation to 2001. A set of additional background suggests that job creation, at least in the formal sector of the economy, is taking hold. The indicators of vacancies offered, the occupation reported by the Chilean Security Association (AChS) and the number of contributors in the AFR show sustained increases for several quarters. In any case, for the consolidation of this better working environment it is important that the current trajectory of moderate growth in average wages in the economy be maintained, in line with current levels of unemployment (Graph 7). As forecast a few months ago, investment continues on a path of low growth. In fact, gross fixed capital formation in 2002 is unchanged from 2001. Despite the continued dynamism of the real estate market, which has shown good sales levels since the beginning of 2001, and the low interest rates for mortgage loans, the speed of expansion of sales has slowed in recent months. A similar phenomenon has occurred with mortgage loans, which do not grow at rates as high as they did some time ago (Graphs 8 and 9). Although the stock of homes available for sale has decreased, this has not yet materialized in increases in building permits, which remain at fairly low levels. In any case, for now there are no indications that there is a lag other than the historical one (figure 10). The remaining components of fixed investment (such as machinery and equipment and non-residential investment) do not yet show signs of a change in trend (Chart 11). In any case, the investment rates that are currently appreciated are consistent with economic growth rates above 4%, to the extent that hiring levels normalize and productivity grows according to historical patterns. Thus, as long as the current average profitability of businesses does not recover more vigorously, it is difficult to expect a noticeable increase in the investment rate. However, it is worth noting that the new business opportunities that the Udder Trade Agreement (FTA) with the US will provide, in addition to those of the European Union and Korea, as well as its effect on investor expectations, should favor a recovery in the growth rate of investment (Chart 12). The available background indicates that the process of stock accumulation remains weak, as evidenced by the stagnation of consumer imports, the stability of the relationship between sales and industrial production, and inventories reported by public limited companies that publish Uniform Coded Statistical Sheets (FECU) (Figure 13). This is a positive indication to support the observed uptick in spending. Public expenditure was less dynamic in the second half of 2002, suggesting that private consumption has been the component that has contributed most to the acceleration of domestic demand during this period. In this way, part of the recent fall in stocks may have been surprising, which would motivate a more intense process of accumulation during the first half of this year, to the extent that consumption continues to consolidate. On the fiscal policy side, 2002 would have closed with figures close to those advanced in the recent budget discussion, with an accounting deficit of 0.9% of GDP, consistent with a structural surplus close to 1% of GDP. For 2003, public finances will continue to be framed under the structural surplus rule, which implies expenditure growth with a macroeconomic effect equivalent to 3.4%, and public investment that will increase by about 7% in real terms. With this, a conventional balance equal to -0.7% of GDP is expected for 2003. Importantly, these figures do not significantly deteriorate the Central Government's net or gross debt position. Indeed, the excellent results of the recent placement of a sovereign bond reinforce the idea that the macroeconomic impulse of fiscal policy in recent years and foreseeable over the projection horizon has not compromised the financial stability of the economy as a whole (Chart 14). In addition to the accumulated background on the trend in consumption, the news on the side of global activity comes mainly from the export sector, with a lower growth in exports of goods and services in 2002 than expected a few months ago. Large copper mining has concentrated the greatest developments, due to high inventory levels in 2002 and low prices on international markets (Figure 15). Although a reversal of the sharp drop in output in 2002 is expected, bringing half a point of overall growth to 2003, this magnitude is significantly lower than expected, owing to recent announcements of volume cuts by major companies in the sector (Figure 16). In any case, by their nature, fluctuations in activity in sectors linked to natural resources generally do not directly affect underlying inflation trends or cost pressures. Indeed, when determining the output of these sectors, mainly by conditions of international prices or physical availability of resources, and by demanding a small portion of the labor force, their fluctuations are not associated with changes in domestic spending nor are they associated with changes in labor market conditions. In addition to the mining sector, this is especially the case with the energy and fisheries sectors. In addition, reversing the trend of the previous two years, the value of non-traditional exports to Latin America fell during 2002, which, according to figures for November, reached almost 8%. Within this fall highlighted the lower shipments to Argentina and Brazil that, together, represented 30% of the value of the destinations of 2001, falling to just under 20% in 2002. To these falls is added a significant decrease in the value of shipments to Venezuela (Table 2). These lower exports were not redirected to other markets as relatively quickly as assumed. Indeed, shipments to North America and Asia had modest increases, while only shipments to Europe had a somewhat higher increase, although with a minor incidence in the aggregate. Economic growth in the various geographical trade zones, which was lower than initially expected a year ago, undoubtedly contributed to the fact that the expected redestination of non-traditional exports could not be carried out promptly. For similar reasons, the inflow of tourists during 2002 was also weaker than expected. In any case, a series of factors means that a more promising outlook for exports is expected in the future during the next two years. On the one hand, although the direct impact on trade of the trade agreements negotiated during 2002 is small in that period, there are other channels through which trade liberalization increases welfare, among which are a better allocation of resources and lower prices for producers, reduction in transaction costs, Greater security and certainty when consolidating government policies, better business environment in countries. All this has a positive impact on investment, both in physical and human capital, and on greater technological exchange that means increases in productivity (Table 3). On the other hand, the news in the international environment tends to reaffirm that the world economy, although with ups and downs, is on a growth path, assuming that it will continue smoothly in a trajectory of recovery of trend growth, thanks to the conjunction of expansionary macroeconomic policies in the main economies. In particular, recent interest rate cuts by the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB) should strengthen this picture. This background will support a moderate increase in the terms of trade, between 2.5% and 3% annual average for 2003 and 2004, thanks to a normalization of external prices (Graph 17). Based on forward prices and the expectations of copper market analysts, copper prices are anticipated to increase to an average of USS 0.76 per pound in 2003 and USS 0.82 per pound in 2004 (Table 4). Added to this background is the fact that no substantial deviations are expected from the levels recently reached by the real exchange rate, which together with export prices, generally somewhat higher, should continue to support the returns of various export sectors. The medium-term interest rate structure indicates expectations of a slight appreciation of the real exchange rate in the coming years. The scarcity of capital flows to emerging economies, particularly Latin America and Chile, is seen as quite persistent, which is consistent with this outlook for the exchange rate (Charts 18 and 19). This central scenario does not consider major turbulence in financial markets, but neither does it consider a significant resurgence of capital flows in the region. All this suggests that expansionary monetary policy will continue to contribute to strengthening private spending, in particular consumption and investment. In the longer term, this boost in monetary policy, the better conditions foreseen for the international environment and a gradual recovery in the confidence levels of the various agents will favour an acceleration of growth. It is projected that there will be, in the central scenario, a partial reduction in the capacity gaps that currently exist. In particular, it is estimated that the gap between utilized and available productive capacity, which is the relevant factor in determining inflationary pressures, rather than a particular growth rate, will narrow by approximately 1% of GDP by the end of the projection horizon. It is also assumed that potential annual growth for the next two years will fluctuate in a range of 3.5% to 4%. In this context, the precise evolution of activity in the short term will depend mainly on the changes that, due to supply factors, supply sectors linked to the exploitation of natural resources have, and it is expected that in the central scenario of this Report, growth in 2003 will be between 3% and 4%. Growth in activity in 2004 will be above the economy's potential growth. In any case, as expected, the uncertainty associated with the projection for 2004 is considerably greater than that for 2003. Expenditure, meanwhile, will expand faster than GDP growth in the biennium, supported by an improvement in national income, bringing the current account deficit to about 1 percent of GDP (Tables 5 and 6). These expected growth figures are slightly lower than those of the last Report, which is essentially associated with less dynamic prospects for sectors linked to the exploitation of natural resources. Indeed, there is no very different picture for the rest of the economy, whose evolution is more closely linked to the development of underlying inflationary pressures (Chart 20). However, private analysts' growth expectations have also been reduced. In particular, according to the Central Bank's survey of expectations, the median expected growth has fallen by a few tenths since September 2002, from 3.5% and 4.5% for 2003 and 2004, respectively, to 3.1% and 4.2% for the same years. On the other hand, the average growth projection for 2003 reported in the last issue of ConsensusForecaststue is 3.3%, a figure that compares with 4.1% in the last edition available for the previous Report (Table 7). Outlook for inflation With regard to price developments, it should be noted that total and core inflation rates have remained around 3% and 2%, respectively, with pronounced fluctuations in monthly inflation associated with oil prices and the exchange rate. The rapid depreciation of the peso until last October unraveled with equal speed in November, which, for now, decreases the probability of changing scenarios that could drastically affect the trajectory of future inflation. In this sense, the exchange rate intervention policy announced at the beginning of October has facilitated the better functioning of the market, limiting the risks of extreme scenarios. Fundamental trends have supported this appreciation of the peso in recent weeks, notably the higher price of copper, the relative stability of financial conditions in Brazil, and the successful conclusion of negotiations to achieve a free trade agreement with the US. In turn, the uncertainty of the conflict in the Middle East is still present which, together with the turbulence in other oil-producing countries, has affected the price of oil during the last four weeks. Thus, although both on the exchange side and on the oil price side there are still relevant risks, the current levels and expected trajectories of these two variables are largely aligned with what was projected in the previous Report . With regard to oil in particular, the baseline scenario of this Report expects a substantial reduction in the price of crude oil during the course of this year. This considers that the current difficulties that the Venezuelan oil industry is going through together with the increasingly certain possibility of war in the Middle East are transitory phenomena, to which is added the increase in quotas and the overproduction of the O PER along with the fact that the productive processes of the countries depend less and less on this raw material. Thus, although for the first quarter of this year the price is expected to remain at current levels, and even exceed USS 30 a barrel, it should converge to figures around USS 23 by the end of the year. With this, the price of oil would average USS 25 a barrel during 2003. By 2004 the September estimate remains at USS 23 per barrel. The trajectory considered is similar to that predicted by specialized analysts, such as the Center for Strategic and International Studles (CSIS), for war conflict scenarios, but of limited duration and intensity. Futures are currently somewhat above this central trajectory, reflecting precisely the risks around this baseline scenario, although converging to levels similar to those considered in this scenario (Chart 21). Beyond the impact of this trajectory, which mainly affects CPI inflation, the outlook for inflation over the medium term has been adjusted downwards due to other, more persistent factors, which reduce the cost pressures expected for 2003 and, eventually, for 2004. On the one hand, the compression of marketing margins has been lower than estimated in the course of 2002, thanks to the fact that unit prices in dollars of average imports of consumer goods continued to fall. Thus, this process is already protracted, unexpectedly, for six consecutive years. Indeed, the average dollar import price of consumer goods fell by 5.6 per cent in 2002, after falling by 3.5 per cent in 2001 (figure 22). In part, this reveals that the depreciation of currencies in emerging markets that are Chile's relevant trading partners has been intense, and that it is not limited exclusively to Argentina and Brazil. Additionally, the substitution capacity of suppliers has increased, which has led to a significant change in the composition by origin of the basket of imports of durable consumer goods in recent years, products that also continue to experience improvements in quality and cost decreases thanks to technological development. China, for example, went from accounting for 15% of consumer goods imports in 1997 to 25% in January-November 2002. Unilateral tariff reduction, as well as that associated with the signing of various free trade agreements, also contribute to lower import prices. On the other hand, a slowdown in labor costs is anticipated. In particular, the recently approved public sector adjustment, which is a relevant variable in the trajectory of aggregate wages in the economy, was clearly below the increases of previous years and those observed, on average, in the labour market (Graph 23). In addition, the growth rate of private unit labour costs has remained very limited, thanks to the increase in labour productivity and the moderate increase in nominal wages (Figure 24). Taken together, these lower cost pressures allow for a gradual decompression of marketing margins that would otherwise have materialized through increases in retail prices. The above factors are themselves transitory in annual inflation, to the extent that expected inflation does not deviate persistently from the center of the target range. In particular, as mentioned above, this time it is not estimated that there will be substantial changes compared to what was expected a few months ago in the foreseeable evolution of the capacity and employment gaps that are, in principle, the most persistent elements associated with accelerations or decelerations in inflation. These gaps remain at elevated levels, with a gradual closure expected over the course of this year and next (Chart 25). With all this background, it is possible that the inflation of the Consumer Price Index (CPI) will be temporarily below the floor of the target range towards the second half of this year, to reach 2.1% in December and approach 2.8% at the end of 2004. In this scenario, average inflation will reach 2.5% and 2.4% in 2003 and 2004, respectively. Core inflation (CPI), which excludes fresh fruit and vegetable and fuel prices, is expected to have a qualitatively similar but less pronounced trajectory, remaining around 2% for several quarters before reaching 3.0% by the end of 2004. On average, the CPI is estimated to reach 2.2 per cent in 2003 and 2.8 per cent in 2004 (figure 26 and table 8). Finally, it should be noted that inflation expectations deduced from interest rate differentials have been quite unstable in recent times, going from 3.6% to just over 2% for average inflation over a five-year horizon in just a couple of months. Beyond reflecting the picture of lower inflationary pressures discussed in this Report, these changes could be explained by some degree of overreaction of the financial markets in their inflation expectations induced by movements in monthly inflation and by changes in risk rewards associated with the composition of the desired portfolio. For now, these movements cannot be attributed signs of a misalignment of inflation expectations with respect to 3%. For its part, the median inflation expectations of analysts in the Central Bank survey have not changed in recent months, remaining at 3% by the end of 2003 and 2004, with a reduced dispersion (Graph 27). A final point in relation to inflation projections has to do with the trajectory that money has presented, in particular the double-digit annual growth rate of MI A that has appreciated for several months. Some analysts have pointed out that this could indicate imminent inflationary pressures. On the contrary, the Central Bank's view in this regard, with a set of antecedents recently compiled, is that it can be concluded that the importance of MI A as an inflationary signal in the current situation is very small. First, in a fully credible inflation-targeting monetary policy framework, in which the interest rate is used as an instrument of monetary policy, the quantity of money is completely endogenous, so the money observed in the system matches, by definition, the demand for monetary balances. There is, therefore, no excess supply or demand for money, such as can usually be identified in economies where the Central Bank has an objective for the growth of monetary aggregates. Secondly, this does not prevent that, as in any monetary economy, there is a close relationship between price level and quantity of money. However, the causality of this relationship is such that the supposed inflationary signal that money has is extremely weak if the inflation target is credible. Then, in order to draw policy conclusions based on the evolution of monetary aggregates, given the insufficient stability of the demand for money, it is necessary to analyze the behavior of a set of indicators to assess the validity of the nominal anchor. In particular, medium-term inflation expectations implicit in both financial market operations and surveys are seen at or below 3 percent for all maturities. On the other hand, in 2001 and 2002 the emissiond1as well as the M2A and M7d1have grown less than the MIA. Indeed, the annual nominal growth rates of the M2Ay and M7 issue were between 7% and 10% in December 2002, similar to what happened with the evolution of credit (Table 9). This raises a question mark of relevance to the argument that money growth is a sign of a major inflationary pickup. A priorino there are compelling reasons why this conclusion is more valid with the EIF than with another monetary aggregate. Third, the usefulness of money as an indicator of inflation is a matter that must be determined empirically. Recent research shows that in the period 1986-2002 money does not contribute significantly to explain the evolution of inflation, because the speed of circulation of money is highly volatile. International evidence also indicates that the evolution of money is not particularly useful as an indicator of inflationary pressures when analyzing the case of experiences of countries with low inflation. Moreover, it is not unusual to find episodes in countries of reduced inflation in which money has shown significant increases, without being accompanied by a subsequent increase in the level of inflation. Beyond empirical aspects of projection, it should be noted that the growth rates of MIA money, which have been observed in recent months, are fully compatible with the evolution of the arguments of a correctly specified demand for money, which considers that the semi-elasticity of money in relation to the interest rate is not constant, This seems to be a fairly clear phenomenon for the Chilean case (figure 28). The dynamic (outside the sample) and static (within the sample) projections of money demand follow very closely the behavior of this aggregate in the last year, so it is difficult to argue that a monetary imbalance is incubating and, with it, inflationary pressures (Graphs 29 and 30). Risk scenarios The central trends contained in this Report constitute the scenario that is estimated to be most likely. However, as usual, there are relevant risks that shape alternative scenarios for both inflation and growth. To begin with, the scenario of war in the Middle East can have very varied consequences in the international environment. A protracted and costly war, affecting available crude oil reserves, could mean persistently high oil prices and increased turbulence in financial markets, with adverse consequences for growth and international inflation. In this regard, it is estimated that, if the price of oil remains around USS 30 per barrel for the next eight quarters, CPI inflation would be 1 and 0.5 percentage points higher than the baseline scenario, towards the end of 2003 and 2004, respectively. The global economy has maintained a pace of growth as expected a few months ago. The U.S. economy, after growing moderately in 2002, is expected to grow at similar rates this year, in a context in which industrial activity recovers and the labor market shows no further deterioration in job creation. A return to growth rates closer to potential is expected in 2004 (figure 31). Despite these positive expectations, uncertainty remains as to whether the developed world will indeed return to trend rates in the short term, as does the firmness with which the prices of the country's main exports, particularly copper, will evolve as a result of this recovery. There is, on the other hand, some degree of uncertainty regarding the price that copper will reach in the long term, derived from the significant increases in productivity that the industry has had. Beyond the effect of the global business cycle on commodity prices, this factor limits the accuracy of copper price projections for 2004. In the region, Brazil's new administration faces major challenges to macroeconomic stabilization. Although this is a major risk to regional financial stability, domestic financial markets have been seen to react flexibly to these pockets of uncertainty in recent quarters. Other Latin American countries are also going through moments of instability that could worsen, although their consequences are, for the moment, less relevant than in the case of Brazil. On the domestic economy side, the main focus of uncertainty is on the direction of the recent pickup in consumer spending. The central scenario considers that, at least, part of this upswing is more persistent and responds, with the expected lags, to expansionary monetary policy. If this is not the case, and during the first quarter of 2003 there is a further slowdown due to a further deterioration in household expectations or a reversal of recent trends in the labour market, the dynamism of aggregate expenditure in 2003 will be lower than that considered in the baseline scenario. Recent trends are also likely to assert themselves, which may boost inventory spending and, eventually, gross capital formation, accelerating activity. In the same vein, the real consequences of the important trade agreements signed during 2002 and, more generally, the chances of potential GDP returning to a more dynamic expansion path, remain to be seen. As for inflation, uncertainty remains about the path that its imported component will take, which adds to the direct effects of alternative trajectories of activity and employment. This includes both the possible swings that the price of oil may suffer d0 with more noticeable consequences for CPI inflation d0 and the speed with which the price level of imported goods normalizes. Added to this is the risk that the narrower evolution of labour costs will not be as persistent as assumed in the central scenario. In addition, from the point of view of how the most underlying inflationary pressures are analyzed, there is no complete certainty about the real size of capacity gaps or the level to which marketing margins should return in the long term. With all the above arguments, it is estimated that the balance of risks to growth is to the downside, while that of inflation is skewed to the upside. That is, the Board considers that if alternative scenarios for prices occur, those that result in higher inflation are considered more likely and/or have associated more pronounced deviations from the central scenario. In the case of the projection of CPI inflation in twelve months, the confidence interval at 50% probability ranges from 1.7% to 2.6% by the end of 2003. In the case of the CPI projection at the end of 2004, the confidence interval at 50% probability ranges from 2.0% to 4.3%, reflecting precisely the aforementioned balance of risks, all under the assumption that the monetary policy rate remains constant at 2.75% (Graph 32). The working assumption of the fixed policy rate is essential to correctly interpret these risks around the baseline projection of inflation and growth. Indeed, this distribution reflects the probability of changes in the inflation projection, and not in actual inflation, since the impact of possible monetary policy responses on the latter is ignored. Should the revisions to the projections be significant, monetary policy adjustments would be required to stabilize the path of inflation around the medium-term target. In this sense, the probabilities do not reflect the actual behavior of inflation, but an assessment of the risks that are relevant for the evolution of monetary policy in the future. Conclusion In summary, the Council considers that the current expansionary stance of monetary policy is consistent with keeping inflation within the target range. In the main scenario, CPI inflation is projected to average 2.5 percent over the projection horizon, while economic growth will accelerate to figures that exceed potential GDP growth. It is important to emphasize the conditional nature of these projections. Risk factors remain that may change the future trajectory of inflation, the extent of which is difficult to specify with the information available to date. This means that, at future meetings, the Council will pay particular attention to assessing four main issues: (i) the progress of economic growth in the major economies, the price of major commodities and their impact on the terms of trade; (ii) the development of the regional financial situation and international financial markets; (iii) the evolution of domestic expenditure, in particular the different components of domestic expenditure, as background to assess the pace at which capacity gaps are closing; and (iv) movements in different cost indicators, especially those associated with the labour market and imported costs. As always, the Council will react flexibly to events which, in one direction or another, jeopardize the achievement of the inflation target, which constitutes the fundamental contribution of monetary policy to economic and social progress.

Evolucin reciente de la actividad y perspectivas Con respecto a la evolucin reciente de la actividad y sus perspectivas, en la informacin ms actual se aprecia un repunte del consumo privado. Esto es as especialmente en el caso de los crditos de menor monto, donde se observa lentitud. Lamentablemente, no existe informacin comparable en otros pases. Las expectativas de los hogares tambin han mejorado en los ltimos meses. Estos resultados son coherentes con el hecho de que la tasa de participacin laboral ha tenido incrementos en las ltimas mediciones, luego de siete trimestres mviles de cada, mientras que el nivel absoluto de ocupacin presenta una aceleracin en el margen, de acuerdo con cifras del INE. Esto ocurre a pesar de que no se registran quiebres significativos en la trayectoria de la tasa de desocupacin nacional desestacionalizada. Los indicadores de vacantes ofrecidas, la ocupacin reportada por la Asociacin Chilena de Seguridad (AChS)y el nmero de cotizantes en las AFR muestran incrementos sostenidos desde hace varios trimestres. En todo caso, para la consolidacin de este mejor entorno laboral es importante que se mantenga la actual trayectoria de crecimiento moderado de los salarios promedio de la economa, acorde con los actuales niveles de desocupacin (grfico 7). De esta forma, parte de la reciente cada de las existencias puede haber sido sorpresiva, lo que motivara un proceso ms intenso de acumulacin durante el primer semestre de este ao, en la medida en que el consumo contine afianzndose. Por el lado de la poltica fiscal, el 2002 habra cerrado con cifras cercanas a las adelantadas en la reciente discusin presupuestaria, con un dficit contable de 0,9% del PIB, coherente con un supervit estructural cercano al 1 % del PIB. Para el 2003 las finanzas pblicas continuarn enmarcadas en la regla de supervit estructural, lo que implica un crecimiento del gasto con efecto macroeconmico equivalente a 3,4%, y una inversin pblica que aumentar cerca de 7% en trminos reales. Un punto final con relacin a proyecciones de inflacin tiene que ver con la trayectoria que ha presentado el dinero, en particular la tasa de crecimiento anual de dos dgitos del MI A que se aprecia desde hace varios meses. Escenarios de riesgo Las tendencias centrales contenidas en este Informe constituyen el escenario que se estima como ms probable. En cuanto a la inflacin, subsiste la incertidumbre sobre la trayectoria que tomar su componente importado, lo que se suma a los efectos directos por trayectorias alternativas de la actividad y el empleo. Con todos los argumentos anteriores, se estima que el balance de riesgos para el crecimiento es a la baja, mientras que el de inflacin se encuentra sesgado al alza.
