Title: Informe de Estabilidad Financiera del primer semestre de 2023. Rosanna Costa, Presidenta
text: bench central Chile Presentation of the Stability Report Financial before the Finance Committee of the Honorable Senate of the Republic Rosanna Costa President Central Bank of ChileMay 24, 2023 Introduction Mr. Chairman of the Finance Committee, Senator Ricardo Lagos Weber, Senators who are members of this Commission, Senators. I am grateful for the invitation to present the vision of the Board of the Central Bank of Chile on the recent developments in the financial sector and implications for financial stability that are detailed in the Financial Stability Report (FSR) that we published this morning. This presentation is preceded by the Financial Policy Meeting that we held this Monday and Tuesday, an instance in which the Board of the Central Bank decided to activate, for the first time, the Countercyclical Capital Requirement (CCR) for banks. For this reason, I would like to begin my presentation with a brief summary of what this instrument is and what the Central Bank of Chile has the power to activate it. The Constitutional Organic Law gives the Bank the responsibility of ensuring the normal functioning of internal and external payments. In practice, this translates into a conduct of financial policy that, within the scope of its own competence, contributes to the stability of the financial system. This occurs when the financial system performs its functions normally or without relevant disruptions, even in the face of adverse temporary situations. This is key to the correct transmission of monetary policy and, therefore, to generate an environment conducive to the economy developing its full potential. As economic theory points out, a stable financial system will be able to fulfill its key functions well, such as encouraging savings and transferring them efficiently to investment. Unlike monetary policy, which is more oriented towards stabilizing the economic cycle and thus inflation, financial policy is aimed at preventing the effects that could cause adverse scenarios. Although these may have a lower degree of probability, their consequences for the economy can be very serious. Hence, its task is to ensure that vulnerabilities that lead to these scenarios are not incubated and, at the same time, to adequately prepare the financial system's capacities to face external shocks. To these ends, the Central Bank's financial policy is part of a general scheme in which public entities that exercise the role of regulator and supervisor, such as the Financial Market Commission (CMF), also participate. In particular, the Central Bank issues and administers financial regulation, prepares reports, and issues opinions on the impact of potential legal or regulatory changes on which it is consulted. Added to this is the eventual exercise of the role of lender of last resort for banking companies and other liquidity management tools. Within this framework, the Central Bank plays an important role in the field of macroprudential policies. These are understood as policies that seek to prevent the excessive accumulation of risks, strengthen the resilience of the financial system, and minimize the negative impact of financial crises on the economy in general. Examples of these are the requirement of capital requirements, the establishment of liquidity and provisions policies, the carrying out of stress exercises, and the coordination of regulators in the monitoring of the financial system. In this macroprudential area, the Central Bank monitors the financial situation and the decisions of different actors in the system. It also prepares a comprehensive diagnosis of potential risks to financial stability, vulnerabilities and mitigators. All of this is communicated to the public through the Financial Stability Report and, most recently, in the Payment Systems Report. The Countercyclical Capital Requirement is also one of these macroprudential policies. As the Bank points out in the Document on the Implementation of the Countercyclical Capital Requirement, published in 2021, it is a requirement to the banking system "whose objective is to increase the resilience of said system in the face of severe stress scenarios, as a result of systemic risks, thus contributing to reducing the impact of these events on the flow of credit, financial stability, and the economy in general." For this reason, for the application of the RCC, it follows a preventive strategy that is based on prospectively assessing the vulnerabilities and risks of the financial system 1/. In this way, the use of the CCR seeks to mitigate the procyclical behavior of banks when adverse shocks occur, seeking to ensure that their consequences are not amplified through a decrease in the supply of credit when financing becomes more necessary. It is important to mention that this is a relatively new tool, which was developed internationally after the global financial crisis. Initially, it was proposed that its objective was to influence the supply of credit and affect pronounced cycles of rise or fall in it. However, this vision was modified over time, tending to privilege a precautionary approach, such as the one considered by the Central Bank of Chile. Thus, the RCC should be increased before an episode of financial stress materializes. The release of capital that was accumulated preventively by the activation of the RCC, will allow credit flows to be maintained at a time when the economy is facing an adverse scenario. This will reduce the negative impacts that a negative shock may have on investment, growth and employment. The available evidence shows that banks are reluctant to reduce their capital in times of stress, as it would signal vulnerability and stigma. This results in a procyclical behavior of credit, which can amplify a negative credit cycle triggered by stress scenarios. V More information on the RCC can also be found in the document "Financial Policy of the Central Bank of Chile" and "Countercyclical Capital Requirement (CCR)" both of September 2021. You can also review Box V.l, IEF second semester 2021; Box lll.l, IEF first semester 2022; and the document The Countercyclical Capital Requirement: A Policy Perspective, presented by the Bank's Vice President to the Committee of General Managers of the Association of Banks. The fact that the authority defines its deactivation for the system as a whole contributes to alleviating this effect. For the purposes of defining the Requirement, with the Basel standard in place, between 0 and 2.5% of the risk-weighted assets of each banking institution can be established. In addition, a deadline for its implementation must be defined, the legal minimum of which is six months. In Chile, twice a year, in the context of the preparation of the Financial Stability Report, the Central Bank holds a Financial Policy Meeting. In it, it decides on this Requirement. The first was held in May 20222/, and the most recent one took place precisely this Monday and Tuesday. Like any policy, the decision regarding the CCR considers a broad set of variables to evaluate the potential costs and benefits of adopting the measure. As I mentioned, the main benefit, which is very significant, is that, in the face of the materialization of an adverse scenario, its release prevents the effects of the scenario from being amplified through the banking system. An example of this type of implementation was the release of the RCC in several countries when the global economy was affected by Covid in 2020. On this occasion, and in view of the risks that can be seen on the international stage, and which I will detail below in this presentation, the Council considered that it was a prudent time to activate the CCR. By the way, activating the Requirement can have costs for the banks, which depend on multiple factors, such as the level of capital slack with respect to the legal requirement, market conditions, the amount and term of the activated requirement, among others. The economy could also be affected in the short term, for example, because a change in the RCC could have impacts on the availability of credit. This effect, in any case, depends on the particular situation in which the decision is made and is a relevant element when evaluating its costs. In the current situation, the Board estimates that the activation of the CCR will have limited and transitory effects on the evolution of credit. This, considering that the banks have slack, the amount activated is reasonable and its completion period is long enough. Regarding the international experience in this area, data are available for 49 economies that have this tool. According to them, in the last six months, 22 of these countries have decided to activate it for the first time  as is our case  to maintain a previous activation or to continue with a gradual process of increase. The motivations for these decisions are varied and relate to risk incubation in the real estate sector, credit activity, and risk considerations. Of these countries, which are mostly European, 15 correspond to developed economies and 7 to emerging economies (Graph 1). 2/ The corresponding communiques and minutes can be found in the section on the Financial Policy Meeting on the Bank's website. However, the implementation of this tool is recent and the Central Bank has made and will continue to make an important communication effort so that its use is understood. Later I will refer to the particular conditions that led us to make this decision, which are within the general analysis included in our Financial Stability Report. Situation of the financial system International scenario The rise in inflation at the global level has led many economies to make significant adjustments in their monetary policy. This ended a long period of low interest rates and ample liquidity, in which many global financial market players accepted greater risks in the pursuit of higher returns. The possibility that this change in financial conditions would cause problems in some part of the financial market was a long-standing risk. In fact, as early as 2021, the Financial Stability and Monetary Policy Reports referred to events in which the rise in rates in the developed world caused abrupt changes in global financial conditions. During March of this year, we observed several events of tension in the global financial market that are associated with the effect on the valuation of assets as a result of the change in financial conditions. Particularly relevant was what happened in some regional banks in the United States, which failed and/or had to be absorbed by other institutions. There were also serious problems at a major Swiss bank. The reaction of the authorities has contained the turbulence generated by these episodes. However, doubts persist in the market regarding the evolution of the financial system in developed economies. In particular, because the events of March revealed weaknesses in regulation and supervision, as well as problems in the risk management of the affected entities. This is reflected in high volatility, even tighter credit conditions, and asset prices that have not fully reversed the declines at the beginning of these episodes (Chart 2). As I will detail later, in the future it is not possible to rule out that financial tensions or disruptive events will occur again in global markets, however, this is not the most likely scenario. On the one hand, because these vulnerabilities are still present and, on the other, because the process of inflationary convergence is still developing. Internal scenario The local financial market has not been particularly affected by external turbulence. Since the previous Report  published in November 2022  sovereign interest rates have tended to their historical averages, recording a fall of around 120 and 60 basis points (bps) for bonds in pesos and UF, respectively. Sovereign spreads have also decreased. Corporate and banking risk premiums show a maintenance in the same period, although compared to the beginning of March they increased between 5 and lOpb. As for local political and economic uncertainty, with ups and downs, it has been significantly reduced since the third quarter of 2022. It is currently somewhat above its historical average. On the other hand, the volatility of interest rates had a limited increase (Graph 3). As for the issuance of bank and corporate bonds, greater activity has been observed in recent months. Pension funds have been its main demanders, while mutual funds have increased the liquidity of their portfolios. The lower activity of the real estate sector has not had a significant impact on the performance of insurance companies. However, the Report shows that various indicators of depth of the local capital market have decreased in the last two years, both those that measure liquidity and market size. While liquidity has been reduced in several Latin American economies, the decline has been more intense in the Chilean fixed income and equity market. Market size indicators account for a reduction in some markets that have functioned in the past as buffers against external fluctuations and shocks, such as pension fund assets. These fell from just over 80% of GDP at the end of 2019 to 56% of GDP in the most recent period. The same is true for the total buy and sell positions in the derivatives market of the formal exchange market (Chart 4). Situation of companies As for corporate indebtedness, in the aggregate, it has returned to pre-pandemic levels. At the end of 2022 it reached 117% of GDP, a value similar to those it maintained in recent quarters. This occurred in a context where the growth of local bank credit slowed from the second half of last year. This adjustment in local bank indebtedness is explained by the lower dynamism of credit, together with the repayment of FOGAPE loans (Chart 5). Although companies that are financed with banks have presented a gradual reduction in their indebtedness, the rise in interest rates has raised their debt service. Thus, the debt on sales remains above what was recorded prior to the pandemic. It highlights what happens between smaller companies (SMEs) and in the trade, construction and manufacturing sectors. This reflects the greater use of shorter-term financing among firms, and represents a vulnerability in an environment of higher interest rates (Chart 6). On the other hand, with regard to large companies that report their financial statements to the CMF, at the end of 2022, the exchange rate mismatch remained limited while their financial position, in general, normalized towards 2019 levels. In companies that are financed with banks, operating margins  income from sales minus expenditure on inputs  continued to be below their historical averages. In any case, its most recent evolution showed a recovery, with greater speed in the largest companies (Graph 7). Regarding the non-payment of companies, it has remained on the rise, approaching the pre-pandemic level. The increase continues to be concentrated in companies in the trade and construction sectors; the smaller ones; and those that opted for the rescheduling of FOGAPE debts and credits. Sectorally, the weakness of the construction and real estate sectors continues. As of the first quarter of 2023, the perception of demand for financing, from real estate and construction companies, had deepened its deterioration. In turn, credit approval standards had become more restrictive. On the other hand, operating margins  sales revenue minus input expenses  continued to weaken, especially in smaller construction companies. All of the above places these companies, especially construction companies, in a situation of greater vulnerability that has been reflected in a higher rate of non-payment (Graph 8). The stress exercises for companies show that, for those that are financed with local banks, one of their main vulnerabilities is greater exposure to interest rate risk. In particular, due to the greater use of short-term loans. The impact of a sales shock is growing in importance compared to the previous year. As for the risk of indexation, this is mitigated by the lower holding of debt in UF. By sector, the exercise suggests that risk in a stressed scenario would continue to be concentrated in trade, construction, and real estate (Chart 9). Household situation In the last two years, the financial position of households deteriorated. Thus, a significant reduction in savings has been observed, which in 2022 reached -0.7% of GDP. The economic support measures implemented during the pandemic, both by their nature and magnitude, generated a transitory and unprecedented increase in household liquidity (Chart 10). While these measures boosted aggregate consumption and temporarily reduced people's debt and defaults, the macrofinancial imbalances generated by the abrupt and long-lasting increase in aggregate consumption have been significant. One of them is the high and persistent inflation. This IEF includes a thematic chapter dedicated especially to the situation of households. It describes how these mismatches also significantly reduced their net financial wealth. At the end of 2022, it stood at 120% of GDP, equivalent to that of a decade ago. In addition, pension savings withdrawalswhich totaled 18 percent of GDP and accounted for about two-thirds of the increase in liquiditynot only had an adverse effect on household savings, but also raised the cost of long-term financing and reduced the financial system's ability to cushion shocks (Figure 11). At the aggregate level, credit to individuals continues to show negative annual variations. By component, consumer debt is falling, while mortgage debt is growing at low rates. With respect to consumer loans, there is a greater dynamism in revolving debts, beyond a decrease in the margin (Chart 12). The increased use of revolving credit has made the financial situation of lower-income people narrower. In particular, due to the greater financial burden implied by the intensive use of short-term credit, in a context of higher interest rates. This has given way to a more pronounced increase in its default, which has been concentrated precisely in revolving debts. Higher-income households maintain more liquidity and have increased their mortgage debt. As a result, the increase in its default has been of a smaller magnitude compared to the rest (graph  . Household stress exercises show that this increased exposure to interest rate risk is one of their main household vulnerabilities. Since the previous IEF, debt at effective risk  a product of individual debt and its probability of default  increased from 1 to 1.2% of GDP in line with the higher effective default. Under the stress scenario, this debt would increase to 4% of GDP. By shocks, rate risk is what explains most of the increase. The risk of unemployment is similar to that of the previous year, while that of inflation is somewhat higher due to an increase in exposure to mortgage debt in the highest income quintile. By quintiles, a distribution of risks similar to that of the previous IEF is observed, concentrated in the lowest income groups. Although banks have low exposure to them, this is explained by the fact that they have much higher default rates than those of the rest of the banked population (graph  . Government situation During the last decade, sovereign debt has increased steadily, from 12% to 38% of GDP. In the last year, fiscal policy managed to stabilize this level, and the projections of the latest Public Finance Report foresee it to be around 41% of GDP by the end of 2027 (Chart 15). Despite the recent stabilization of sovereign debt, the space to face new adverse shocks has narrowed. Maintaining fiscal consolidation is critical to mitigating future shocks without exceeding the prudent level of debt. A sustainable debt trajectory improves investors' perception of risk and thereby reduces the cost of financing for the rest of the economy. Banking situation Local banks have high voluntary capital buffers and an adequate level of capitalization, together with appropriate active liquidity management. As I have already mentioned, the annual variation of bank placements has been reduced, associated with credit risk levels with an upward trend. This is especially visible in the consumer and commercial segments, which are at values comparable to the pre-pandemic period. In this context, banks have accumulated provisions to face a possible deepening of this phenomenon. The results of the stress exercises show that the system is in an adequate position to face the materialization of this type of scenario. The initial situation of the year improves with respect to what we observed in the previous IEF. The Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAI) increased from 14.6 to 15.5%, while ROE reached 19.6%, which allowed banks to absorb the risks considered in the exercises. The proportion of banks with negative profitability in the severe stress scenario is somewhat lower than the previous year, reaching 51% of the system's core capital. Finally, the impact of the severe scenario on the difference between initial and final capital would decrease from 3.7 to 2.7 percentage points. In this context, capital slacks in the stressed scenario increase compared to the previous year, in fact returning to pre-pandemic levels (Chart 16). All in all, the banking sector is facing a challenging scenario. Among them, the maturity of financial obligations and the implementation of Basel III for their capitalization, through a process of capital discounts and increase in regulatory limits towards full convergence in 2025. Therefore, like the rest of the agents of the economy, it must continue to strengthen its capacities to face new adverse events. In this regard, it is pertinent to point out that the activation of the RCC does not constitute a judgment by the Bank regarding the level of capitalization of the system at present. As I have already mentioned, the banking system is solvent and maintains slack even when subjected to stressed scenarios. Instead, it is a tool that aims to mitigate the effects on credit in the face of future adverse events. Regulatory Agenda Recent disruptions in international banking highlight the importance of having a properly implemented regulatory and supervisory framework. It highlights that the framework in force in Chile has all the Basel III components fully active, both for liquidity and solvency. In addition, it is applied to the Chilean banking industry as a whole. The implementation of this new scheme began in 2020 and will be completed in 2025. In addition, the CMF and the Central Bank maintain close coordination in carrying out stress tests on the banking system. They also have a broad set of tools and legal attributions to prevent and deal with critical situations. The regulatory agenda incorporates new initiatives aimed at strengthening the Chilean financial system. With regard to the Central Bank's attributions, it considers elements that will enable retained securitization schemes, contributing to expanding the availability of high-quality financial instruments. An update of the regulation for payment card operators or acquirers will also be published, incorporating the possibility of developing new business models. At the same time, the implementation of initiatives already issued, referring to new market infrastructures and exchange rate modernization, continues. In legislative matters, the bill that strengthens the resilience of the financial system  currently in Congress  stands out, which complements the set of tools to face episodes of tension. Likewise, the consolidated debt bill was approved in the first stage, which will improve the credit risk management of financial intermediaries and the monitoring capacity of financial authorities. In addition, the CMF and the Central Bank, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, are refining the bank resolution framework. Finally, it is expected that in the short term the discussion on the adoption of a risk-based supervision scheme for the insurance industry, a sector that plays a key role in the local economy, will be reactivated. Main risks Let me end this part of the discussion with a review of the risks facing the financial system. As I indicated at the beginning, financial policy has a prospective view based on risks. This means that we constantly assess the occurrence of shocks that could have significant effects on the financial system and the economy. Sometimes, these shocks are of a low probability, but they have the characteristic that their realization could be very harmful to the economy. At the global level, the main risk we consider is a worsening of the macrofinancial scenario. A situation like this could generate episodes of high volatility, reduce liquidity and trigger capital outflows from emerging economies, further deteriorating financial conditions. The action of the financial authorities of the developed economies has eased the impact of the turbulence of March. However, uncertainty remains about the magnitude and extent of financial sector vulnerabilities  banking and non-banking  in developed economies. This occurs in a context where risks to inflationary convergence are still present in several economies, which could require monetary policy to maintain a contractionary tone for longer than expected. At the local level, it is essential to continue with the process of adjusting the macroeconomic imbalances accumulated in recent years, rebuilding the capacity to face new shocks. As highlighted in previous reports, it is crucial to rebuild these capacities, since they will allow us to better deal with potential new adverse events. Activation of the Countercyclical Capital Requirement At our Financial Policy Meeting in the first half of 2023, we decided to activate, for the first time, the Countercyclical Capital Requirement (CCR) for the banking system. The RCC will be activated in a magnitude equivalent to 0.5% of the risk-weighted assets of each of the local banks. These institutions will have one year to comply with this requirement. The Council has activated the CCR as a precautionary measure in the face of increased external uncertainty. Although the macroeconomic scenario has evolved in line with expectations, the risk of a severe external shock has increased. Although its probability is low, its negative impact on the economy would be significant. In this circumstance, the release of the previously constituted RCC will help mitigate the impacts on the evolution of credit to households and companies. The effective impact on credit of this measure will depend on the reaction of the banks. However, as I indicated a few moments ago, we estimate that, considering the current level of capitalization, the available slack of the banks, the level of the RCC charge and the period defined to pay it, its activation will have limited and transitory effects on the evolution of credit. The estimates we have show that, considering all the variables just mentioned, two years after learning it, the activation of RCC would reduce annual credit growth, measured in UF, by some half a percentage point. This value is closer to the lower part of the range of projections offered by the literature, taking into account the aforementioned conditions in which the measurement is adopted. However, it is important to emphasize that the implementation of the RCC is framed in a context where it is necessary for all actors in the economy to continue to rebuild their capacities to face possible adverse events. Final Thoughts Dear Senators. We are facing uncertain times. The adjustment of the world economy after the most complex moments caused by the pandemic has been a process that has been extended over time. Other events have been added, such as the war between Ukraine and Russia. In general, a rather unusual scenario in the economic evolution of recent decades. The economic authorities have used all our capacities to mitigate the impacts that the different shocks could have on our economies. In Chile, we implemented important incentives so that credit would flow and companies could survive the sudden closure of their activities. Monetary policy also did its part, giving way to the generation of very expansionary conditions. The development of the pandemic, the adaptation of households and companies and, of course, the measures adopted, made it possible to contain the adverse effects and to observe a rapid recovery of the economy. All this with a limited impact on employment. However, beyond the effort deployed, the effects of the pandemic on the different actors in our economy led to an intensive use of the accumulated slack. In some cases, resorting to a very significant percentage of accumulated savings caused significant macroeconomic imbalances, one of the most important being the high inflation that still affects us. Going forward, in a context of more restrictive global financial conditions and high uncertainty associated with the external scenario, it is impossible to rule out the possibility of events where the economy will once again be subjected to significant stress. This, by the way, does not mean that these scenarios are more or less likely today than in the recent past. Nor that the Chilean or world economy is close to facing new disruptions or a crisis situation. Simply, experience tells us that the probability of extreme events occurring is not zero. Therefore, it is up to us responsibly to prepare ourselves adequately to deal with these episodes and to provide measures to mitigate their impacts. In this sense, this is a good time to strengthen our capacity to react to scenarios of potential adverse future events. This preparation involves the entire economy. It is necessary for all actors to rebuild their capacity to face complex times. This process is already happening, albeit at a rate that differs between the various parties involved. Companies have been reducing their indebtedness from the high levels they reached as a result of the fall in sales and the effects of support programs. The Government has made significant progress in consolidating its obligations, stabilizing fiscal debt and creating space to face new adverse events. However, households are lagging behind, given the significant deterioration of their equity position after successive withdrawals of pension funds. Therefore, it is essential to prioritize initiatives that promote savings. In addition, measures that affect the normal functioning of the financial system, increase uncertainty and the idiosyncratic cost of financing, or reduce its capacity to cushion negative shocks should be avoided. The Central Bank plays an important role in this process. We have made a relevant adjustment of monetary policy to attack the inflationary problem and return inflation to the 3% target. Solving this problem is essential so that the incomes of households and companies are no longer affected by the rise in prices and can rebuild their savings. The challenges for the Bank do not end with a present issue such as inflation. On the contrary, our role in macroprudential policies and financial stability allows us to assess risks and give way to policies that cooperate in the formation of cushions for our economy. The activation of the Countercyclical Capital Requirement goes in this direction. This measure is part of a set of tools that will make our economy more resilient to significant adverse shocks. Senators and Senators, we have faced very complex times in recent years. The slack accumulated in previous years allowed us to face its consequences. But, in some cases, they have been over-occupied. Today it is up to us to begin to recover them and to build buffers and mitigators that allow us to better face the challenges that lie ahead. The Central Bank will continue to work on its most important mission of the present, which is to bring inflation back to the 3% target over the policy horizon. At the same time, we remain concerned about the future, making use of the macroprudential tools at our disposal. We have been strengthening our financial position both through special credit lines and through the progressive dismantling of the forward operations program in consideration of the operating conditions of the foreign exchange market. All this points in the direction of continuing to strengthen the economy's capacity to face external shocks. Moreover, as described in more detail in the Report, there are legislative (and regulatory) initiatives underway that would strengthen the set of tools available. Among them is the Resilience in the Financial System bill, which complements the set of tools to deal with episodes of tension. Also the Consolidated Debt Index, which will improve the credit risk management of financial intermediaries and the monitoring capacity of financial authorities. Both bills were recently approved by the Chamber of Deputies. In addition, the CMF and the Bank, in coordination with the Ministry of Finance, are refining the bank resolution framework. Finally, it is expected that in the short term the discussion on the adoption of a risk-based supervision scheme for the insurance industry, a sector that plays a key role in the local economy, will be reactivated. For our part, the Central Bank's financial regulation agenda continues to focus on various areas that are detailed in the IEF; including initiatives to strengthen the payment system and market infrastructures, among other initiatives that we will also report on in the Payment System Report that we will publish next July. All of the above always bearing in mind our purpose of contributing to the well-being of all the inhabitants of our country. text_original: banco central Chile Presentacin del Informe de Estabilidad Financiera ante la Comisin de Hacienda del Honorable Senado de la Repblica* Rosanna Costa Presidenta Banco Central de Chile 24 de mayo de 2023 *EI Informe de Estabilidad Financiera del primer semestre de 2023 se puede encontrar en http://www.bcentral.cl. Introduccin Seor Presidente de la Comisin de Hacienda, Senador Ricardo Lagos Weber, Senadores miembros de esta Comisin, Senadoras y Senadores. Agradezco la invitacin para presentar la visin del Consejo del Banco Central de Chile sobre los desarrollos recientes del sector financiero e implicancias para la estabilidad financiera que se detallan en el Informe de Estabilidad Financiera (IEF) que publicamos esta maana. Esta presentacin viene precedida de la Reunin de Poltica Financiera que sostuvimos este lunes y martes, instancia en la que el Consejo del Banco Central decidi activar, por primera vez, el Requerimiento de Capital Contracclico RCC para la banca. Por esta razn, quisiera comenzar mi presentacin con un breve resumen respecto de qu es este instrumento y cules son las potestades del Banco Central de Chile respecto de su activacin. La Ley Orgnica Constitucional le otorga al Banco la responsabilidad de velar por el normal funcionamiento de los pagos internos y externos. En la prctica, esto se traduce en una conduccin de la poltica financiera que, desde el mbito propio de su competencia, contribuya a la estabilidad del sistema financiero. sta se da cuando el sistema financiero realiza sus funciones con normalidad o sin disrupciones relevantes, an frente a situaciones temporales adversas. Esto resulta clave para la correcta transmisin de la poltica monetaria y, por ende, para generar un medio ambiente propicio para que la economa desarrolle todo su potencial. Como lo seala la teora econmica, un sistema financiero estable podr cumplir bien sus funciones claves, como fomentar el ahorro y transferirlo de forma eficiente a la inversin. A diferencia de la poltica monetaria, ms orientada a estabilizar el ciclo econmico y con ello la inflacin, la poltica financiera se orienta a prevenir los efectos que podran provocar escenarios adversos. Si bien estos pueden tener un grado de probabilidad menor, sus consecuencias para la economa pueden ser muy graves. De ah que su tarea es cautelar que no se incuben vulnerabilidades que propicien estos escenarios y, al mismo tiempo, preparar adecuadamente las capacidades del sistema financiero para enfrentar shocks externos. Para estos fines, la poltica financiera del Banco Central forma parte de un esquema general en que tambin participan entidades pblicas que ejercen el rol de regulador y supervisor, como la Comisin para el Mercado Financiero CMF. En particular, el Banco Central emite y administra regulacin financiera, elabora informes y emite opiniones sobre el impacto de potenciales cambios legales o regulatorios respecto de los cuales se le consulte. A esto se suma el eventual ejercicio del rol de prestamista de ltima instancia para las empresas bancarias y otras herramientas de gestin de liquidez. Dentro de este marco, el Banco Central cumple un rol relevante en el mbito de las polticas macroprudenciales. Estas se entienden como polticas que buscan prevenir la acumulacin excesiva 1 de riesgos, fortalecer la resiliencia del sistema financiero y minimizar el impacto negativo de las crisis financieras en la economa en general. Ejemplos de estas son la exigencia de requisitos de capital, el establecimiento de polticas de liquidez y provisiones, la realizacin de ejercicios de tensin y la coordinacin de los reguladores en el monitoreo del sistema financiero. En este mbito macroprudencial, el Banco Central monitorea la situacin financiera y las decisiones de distintos actores del sistema. Asimismo, elabora un diagnstico integral sobre los potenciales riesgos para la estabilidad financiera, vulnerabilidades y mitigadores. Todo ello se comunica al pblico a travs del Informe de Estabilidad Financiera y, en lo ms reciente, en el Informe de Sistemas de Pagos. El Requerimiento de Capital Contracclico tambin es una de estas polticas macroprudenciales. Tal como el Banco seala en el Documento sobre Implementacin de Requerimiento de Capital Contracclico, publicado en 2021, es un requerimiento al sistema bancario "cuyo objetivo es aumentar la resiliencia de dicho sistema frente a escenarios de estrs severos, producto de riesgos de carcter sistmico, contribuyendo as a reducir el impacto de estos eventos sobre el flujo de crdito, la estabilidad financiera, y la economa en general". Por lo mismo, para la aplicacin del RCC sigue una estrategia preventiva que se basa en evaluar de forma prospectiva las vulnerabilidades y riesgos del sistema financiero 1/. De este modo, el uso del RCC busca mitigar el comportamiento procclico de la banca cuando se producen shocks adversos, buscando que sus consecuencias no se amplifiquen a travs de una disminucin de la oferta de crdito cuando el financiamiento se hace ms necesario. Es importante mencionar que se trata de una herramienta relativamente nueva, que se desarroll internacionalmente con posterioridad a la crisis financiera global. En un comienzo, se planteaba que su objetivo era incidir en la oferta de crdito y afectar ciclos pronunciados de alza o retroceso de este. No obstante, esta visin fue modificndose con el paso del tiempo, tendiendo a privilegiar un enfoque precautorio, como el que considera el Banco Central de Chile. As, el RCC se debera aumentar antes de que un episodio de estrs financiero se materialice. La liberacin de capital que se acumul preventivamente por la activacin del RCC, permitir mantener los flujos de crdito en un momento en que la economa se enfrente a un escenario adverso. Esto reducir los impactos negativos que un shock negativo pueda tener sobre la inversin, el crecimiento y el empleo. La evidencia disponible muestra que la banca es reacia a reducir su capital en momentos de tensin, puesto que dara seales de vulnerabilidad y estigma. Ello redunda en un comportamiento procclico del crdito, lo que puede amplificar un ciclo negativo de crdito gatillado por escenarios de estrs. En Chile, dos veces al ao, en el contexto de la elaboracin del Informe de Estabilidad Financiera, el Banco Central sostiene una Reunin de Poltica Financiera. En ella decide sobre este Requerimiento. Como toda poltica, la decisin respecto del RCC considera un amplio conjunto de variables para evaluar los potenciales costos y beneficios de adoptar la medida. Como mencion, el principal beneficio, muy significativo, es que, ante la materializacin de un escenario adverso, su liberacin previene que los efectos del escenario se amplifiquen a travs del sistema bancario. Un ejemplo de este tipo de implementacin fue la liberacin del RCC en diversos pases cuando la economa global se vio afectada por el Covid en 2020. Title: Opening Remarks: Joint Forum on Asset and Risk Management - Rosanna Costa
text: banco central Chile Opening Remarks Rosanna Costa, Governor of the Central Bank of Chile Joint Forum on Asset and Risk Management - September 25th, 2023 Good morning, welcome to the Joint Forum on Asset and Risk Management co-organized by the Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum (OMFIF), the World Bank and the Central Bank of Chile. We are pleased to have representatives from several central banks, and from the public and private sector attending this Forum. Introduction As is well known, for many countries international reserves aim to ensure an adequate level of foreign currency liquidity, even in extreme situations where access to traditional sources of foreign currency may be very limited. In this sense, the international reserves act as an insurance against severe events of liquidity tightness, which could compromise financial stability, or the availability of foreign currency needed for economic activity. In the last few years. International Reserves management has been as relevant as ever, but perhaps more challenging given the singularity of the multiple and diverse shocks and its impacts to the economy and hence to central banks. This poses new challenges, making it pertinent to revisit the frameworks and assumptions that we have been using in asset management. On the one hand, the liquidity squeezes seen during the pandemic, where bid-ask spreads almost doubled, raise questions on how liquid the safe assets were at the time of need. On the other hand, as central banks raised their benchmark rates and inflation remained high, fixed income instruments and most financial assets had negative returns in 2022, raising questions about the fulfilment of the capital preservation objective. In fact, in 2022 most assets typically associated with international reserve investments suffered losses. For example, the US Treasury Index reported losses of 12.5%, the Global Sovereign Bond Index lost 17.5% and even inflation-linked instruments suffered losses of 23%. Only the US Treasury bills closed the year with a return near zero. In that period, we saw a spike in correlations across asset classes and losses never seen before in the fixed- income markets. Before 2022, this scenario could only be included in risk analyses by extrapolating some of the key movements seen during the 1970s. But now, after experiencing it first hand, central banks must rethink how this could change their investment approach. In this environment several questions arise, to which we need to figure out the answers: Is there still room for more diversification? Are asset classes available to central banks diversified enough not to compromise the capital preservation objective? Has the institutional risk profile changed? Will we see a rise in short duration dollar portfolios or, with the rise in rates, we are in the verge of a new surge in duration searching? All these are important 1 banco central Chile questions that must be studied in a global and comprehensive way as the investment side of central banks continues to adapt to the new developments in the financial markets. The Central Bank of Chiles experience in reserve management Allow me briefly to share our experience with holding international reserves. The Central Bank of Chile holds foreign reserves to achieve its main objectives, as defined in the Organic Act, of ensuring the stability of the currency and the normal functioning of internal and external payments. In our policy framework of a floating exchange rate regime, these assets also reduce the probability of liquidity disruptions and make it possible to deal with exceptional situations where access to international markets is interrupted, minimizing the likelihood of having balance of payments problems. In this context, the primary objective that the investment policy of international reserves must guarantee is liquidity and capital preservation, so that the monetary authority can dispose, at a reasonable cost, of the resources needed at any time. To achieve that, the Board of the Bank approves an Investment Policy which defines the relevant investment parameters such as currency composition, eligible asset classes, maximum risk tolerance, and the portfolio structure, among other variables. These criteria and limits are defined in the context of a well-established analysis framework, that aims to tackle financial risks in a comprehensive manner. With this in mind, we divide our investment portfolio into two tranches: the liquidity portfolio, and the diversification portfolio. The liquidity portfolio represents 60% and is composed entirely of nominal US Treasury bonds with maturities between one and five years. These instruments are considered highly liquid and safe. The diversification portfolio accounts for the remaining 40% and is composed of nominal and inflation-linked bonds in multiple currencies, with maturities between one and ten years. This sub-portfolio allows us to diversify risks and to achieve higher returns in the long run. In terms of governance, central banks around the world have developed very strong frameworks. The independence between different key units responsible for reserve management is paramount to have sound practices. Importantly, reserve management best practices are well stablished at the Central Bank of Chile as a result of a continuous adaptation process, which is in line with the development of the financial markets, the international regulatory framework and the incorporation of new technologies, among other relevant developments. The governance of reserves has been structured considering the segregation of functions. The Financial Markets Division is responsible for the front- and back-office activities, including the Tactical Asset Allocation, and also advises the Board in defining the Strategic Asset Allocation. The Corporate Risk Division reviews the different risk methodologies applicable to the management of international reserves and performs the compliance function. Furthermore, it also acts as technical counterparty to the Financial Markets Division regarding risk measurement and risk analysis. 2 banco central Chile This scheme allows the Central Bank of Chile to operate with two lines of defense and guarantees the independence between the business and risk assessments allowing for more robust analyses. Furthermore, our internal auditors play a key role as third line of defense, as they place a lot of emphasis in reviewing the processes that support all the investment activities, including aspects related to technology and cybersecurity. All this is complemented with independent auditors and an external advisory committee. Also, on a yearly basis, we review our Investment Policy to assess asset liquidity in the context of the risk/return framework, including all new relevant information that could have shifted the Strategic Asset Allocation. This yearly review allows the Board to act based on facts, as new information, risk scenarios or changes in markets trends can be analyzed. Also, this review is a good opportunity to incorporate changes in liquidity preferences and possible changes into the desired risk/return profile. Moreover, peer review exercises are conducted to check whether our practices are advancing according to international standards. It is worth mentioning that we also have in place an external manager program since 1996. The main objective of the current program is to be an active benchmark for the internal management and to enhance returns. Also, knowledge transfer is expected. The program is evaluated on a yearly basis by the Financial Markets Division and complemented with a risk assessment of the firms performed by the Risk Unit. The evaluation is conducted based on a both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Main challenges A key question that is always present is how to assess the adequate level of reserves needed by a Central Bank. For emerging markets, the most traditional measures include the IMFs ARA, the level of exports or rules like the Guidotti-Greenspan. At the Central Bank of Chile, the Financial Markets Division oversees an integrated framework to determine the required level of reserves. In this exercise, we consider the traditional approaches, but also market analysis, risk measures, economic models developed by our Monetary Policy Division, and banking sector analysis provided by our Financial Policy Division. This integrated approach allows us to have a broader assessment on the potential needs of international liquidity, taking into consideration all relevant and changing variables. It is important to underscore that our monetary policy framework relies upon a floating exchange rate regime. This contributes to mitigating the impact of shocks affecting the economy and facilitates the adjustment of different markets to those shocks. Nevertheless, during 2019 and 2022, several internal and external shocks strained our macroeconomic and financial stability, testing our policy framework. Consequently, the price formation process in the foreign exchange market was jeopardized. We implemented some exceptional measures to restore it, including selling a fraction of our international reserves. We succeeded in normalizing the price formation process in the forex market and now we are restoring our 3 banco central Chile liquidity buffer by increasing the level of our international reserves to reach around 15% of GDP. Now I would like to stress the importance of financial safety nets. Holding reserves is costly for emerging market economies and, in exceptional periods, action needs to be taken to restore and ensure the proper functioning of the foreign exchange market. This represents a challenge for our liquidity buffers. Hence the importance of having complementary sources of liquidity. In that context, we have been fortunate to partner with different institutions which grants us access to international liquidity on a precautionary basis. As an example of that, currently the Central Bank of Chile has access to the IMFs Flexible Credit Line (up to US18,5 billion). This allows us to count on complementary liquidity on a precautionary basis, while we replenish our liquidity buffers. Also, we have access to FLARs liquidity facilities (up to US 1.25 billion), and to the swap line with PBoC (US 8 billion). We also have other sources to guarantee access to foreign currency liquidity such as the New York Federal Reserve's FIMA Repo, a facility that allows us to obtain temporary liquidity in dollars against the delivery of U.S. Treasury securities as collateral. In short, the discussion on the level of reserves must consider many variables. Among them is the level of risk of the economy, given internal and external risks, the strength and depth of the markets to react and adjust, and the existence of other liquidity sources. Another important element is the cost of holding reserves. The Bank is constantly monitoring its level of international reserves to maintain its structural liquidity position in foreign currency, which allows us to have a strong policy framework. Closing remarks If something we surely learned the last couple of years is that financial markets are constantly changing and evolving, shifting the behaviors and preferences of the economic agents. As reserve managers, we must rapidly learn to deal with this new environment and determine how to integrate these changes into our reserve management framework. The Covid-19 pandemic and following years taught us lessons about the relevance of reserve management, and how important it is to have good management frameworks and practices in place to ensure adequate levels of liquidity, capital preservation, and diversification of risks. This balance is very important, because the reserves must be available in real time, at a reasonable cost, whenever needed. But this isnt over. There are many other challenges that we are facing right now and for sure we will encounter new ones in the future. To mention just a few: geopolitical risks apparently are here to stay; extreme climate phenomena and their relation with financial and monetary policy is yet to be studied in more detail. The future evolution of interest rates and their neutral level are also drawing the attention of many market players. And of course, the optimal level of international reserves in a context where shocks appear to be more frequent 4 banco central Chile requires further study, particularly for emerging markets central banks, which must also consider the existence of the global financial safety nets to complete their analysis. In this way, we will be better prepared to deal with future shocks. Thats why this forum is so important, walking together is always the safer way to advance, as these considerations cannot be postponed. Let me finish by thanking you all for taking the time to join us today in this forum. We have two intense days ahead, where most of the questions and challenges I mentioned before will surely arise and I am sure that the discussion will prove fruitful. We have made substantial progress in managing the international reserves, but there is more work to be done. These seminars are a crucial place to share our knowledge and to help each other to better address the issues that most institutions and nations will face in the near future. Thank you. 5

Title: Perspectiva de gnero en el Banco Central de Chile, Rosanna Costa, Presidenta
text: Commemoration of International Women's Day, School of Government Adolfo Ibanez University "Gender Perspective in the Central Bank of Chile" Rosanna Costa, President of the Central Bank of Chile Tuesday, March 8, 2022 Good morning I begin by giving an affectionate greeting to all the women who participate in this activity. For me it is a great honor to participate and, through it, celebrate all women in our country, recognize the contribution they have had throughout history. It is valuable to congratulate ourselves on the road traveled, which has not been easy, and we accompany them in the challenges that we still have to face. At the Central Bank of Chile, we have encouraged the participation of women in areas that are usually more alien to us, such as finance, macroeconomics and even technology, and also in decision-making. In fact, as I will show you in a moment, at the level of positions in the Bank's highest management, we have parity between men and women, and we are working on various measures to encourage greater female participation, at different levels of responsibility and areas of specialization. Personally, I am the second Director of the Central Bank, and I can only greet from this rostrum Maria Elena Ovalle, the first Director of the Central Bank of Chile, and Stephany Griffith Jones, the brand new Counselor, with whom we have a Council with two women and three men. In addition, as the first woman to become President of the Central Bank of Chile, I have the honor and responsibility of opening new doors to spaces, which will surely continue to be occupied by more women in the future. In my presentation today, I will refer to how the Central Bank has addressed the gender perspective in different dimensions, including the role of women in the economy, financial inclusion, their role in decision-making and, of course, what we have done within our organization and also mention some future challenges. Certainly, in a context of great heterogeneity of challenges that women face, this leaves out many faces of millions of women with different needs, some very pressing. I am aware of this, and I do not want to make them invisible by focusing only on some dimensions of the reality of so many women. The role of women in the economy Women are a fundamental pillar in society, working in different professions and activities, with the consequent impact on the economy and business. In recent years, our main economic and financial reports have incorporated a gender perspective into the analysis, thus contributing to disseminating and informing about the role of women in the economy and contributing with empirical background to the design of public policies that support their inclusion and allow them to better deploy their full potential. This has considered dimensions such as participation in the labor market, financial inclusion and contribution to unpaid work, among others. Women in the labour market In 2018, the Bank published a document analyzing the major trends in the Chilean labor market. This document not only pointed out the labor market as a whole, but also looked at some distinctive elements between men and women, from which some interesting antecedents emerge. First, it highlights the dynamics of the labor force, which had been determined by the greater participation of women and a more recent decrease in the participation of young male workers under 24 years of age. Both events were in line with the greater coverage of higher education and the fall in the birth rate (Figure 1). However, despite the growing participation of women in the Chilean labor market, it was still below the average of OECD countries, with a difference that was strongly concentrated among women under 60 years of age (Figure 2). Younger women, in line with greater access to education and the growing relevance of their role in society, showed smaller gaps in terms of participation. As for the type of employment that women access, the data show an importance in the service sectors, in line with the greater development of the country and the relevance that these activities have acquired. In fact, the participation of women in primary and secondary sectors is much lower compared to that of men and has not grown significantly in the last thirty years (Graph 3). Graph 3 Composition of employment by sex and economic sector () (percentage of employed people) 40 A second relevant fact identified by the 2018 study is that women's incomes were lower than men's, something that was replicated internationally. The gap was cross-sectional considering both age, work experience and educational level. Going deeper into this, women had a lower average income growth profile in their main occupation than men, regardless of the years of schooling (Graph 4). In fact, the data show that the average salary profile of women grows only up to 10 to 14 years of work experience, while for men this phase extends to 20 to 24 years of experience (Figure 5). These differences may reflect, in part, the impact of motherhood on women's income growth, the effects of which would be more persistent, although empirical evidence is required to support this. (2) Average between 1990 and 2017 of the difference between the income growth rate for each 5-year bracket of work experience and the income growth of individuals with 0-4 years of experience. Work experience is calculated as the minimum between the number of years since the worker turned 18 or since completing their education. Income is calculated as the ratio between the monthly income of the main occupation in pesos of 2017 and the hours worked in the month in this main occupation. Only male and female workers hired in the private salaried sector on a full-time basis are considered. Sources: Aldunate (2018) and National Institute of Statistics. A third finding is that women's unemployment tends to be higher than men's, which means that they are less likely to find a job and stay employed. The information for 2018 showed that the probability of finding a job for an unemployed woman was 33%, versus 55% for a man. Likewise, once employed, the probability of remaining employed was 81% below the 91% probability for men. Consequently, women's probability of transitioning to inactivity tripled that of men (16 vs. 5%). All the data I have described correspond to the evolution of the labour market prior to the appearance of the pandemic in March 2020, which had a strong impact on the labour market, reducing the participation of both men and women by around 11 percentage points. In the case of the fall in women, two factors stand out: on the one hand, they assume a greater proportion of the care of the family group and, on the other, the service sectors are the most affected by health restrictions, which, as I mentioned, have a proportionally greater impact on women's employment. In recent months, labor participation rates have narrowed their gap from the pre-pandemic level (48% versus 53% for women and 70% versus 74% for men). These lags in participation are a phenomenon that is also observed in several other economies. In turn, the unemployment rate for women reached 7.7% in January, while that of men stood at 6.9% (Graphs 6 and 7). Source: National Institute of Statistics. Measuring Unpaid Work The pandemic has helped to highlight the value of working at home. For cultural reasons, this has been a task that has usually been carried out by women, and that even in times of pandemic had to be covered mostly by them due to the impossibility of contracting care services, either for children or the elderly. I do not want to ignore their greater contribution, but, even so, the figures suggest that the greatest burden is not distributed equally. While in Chile, in 2015, women spent about 2.5 hours more than men on household chores daily, in OECD countries, in recent years, with a similar methodology, they spend about 2 hours more per day than their male peers on unpaid tasks. Aware of its relevance, during 2021, the Central Bank made an effort to estimate the contribution to GDP of unpaid work in the home. It should be noted that, according to the international recommendation, unpaid domestic work (UNRT) is not included in the measurement of GDP, since its monetary valuation represents a challenge since a large part of these activities are not traded in the markets. The results showed that in 2020, in the midst of the pandemic, the performance of these tasks represented 25.6% of the expanded GDP (i.e., traditional nominal GDP plus the valuation of unpaid work), composed of 17.5 percentage points for women and 8.1 for men. Compared to 2015, this fraction increased by almost 5 percentage points (Tables 1 and 2). These numbers indicate that the share of unpaid domestic work in the GDP is higher than that of any other sector of the economy, reaching more than double the contribution of mining or personal services. With this, the share of GDP would also be lower than the maximum of 2020, closer to the values of 2015. Women's Financial Inclusion The growing participation of women in the labor market and with it the generation of their own income, has had a correlation in their inclusion in the financial market. Thus, in the last two decades there has been an increase in women accessing bank accounts and credit. However, this is an area where significant differences remain . On the one hand, on average, women have easier access to demand accounts than men, a pattern that is reversed in current accounts (Graph 8). This could be explained by the additional income requirements that the latter have with respect to the demand account, particularly when compared to the RUT account. The use of the latter instrument has increased significantly in recent quarters, as a result of its use as a means of payment for support policies and the transfer of withdrawals from pension funds. As for the type of loan, it can be seen that the number of debtors in consumer loans is similar between men and women, while, in mortgage debt, on average, for every three men there are two women debtors. And although, in terms of participation, the gaps have narrowed in recent decades, differences persist in the conditions of the loans obtained. In consumer banking contracts, women register on average higher interest rates, shorter terms and lower amounts than men. In mortgage loans, on the other hand, these differences are considerably reduced. The Financial Stability Report (FSR) published by the Bank has highlighted these trends on several occasions. On average, women have shown a default occurrence one percentage point lower in both portfolios in the last decade. The Gender in the Financial System Report carried out by the Financial Market Commission (CMF) in 2021 also suggests that debt is more expensive for women than for men. Women's participation in decision-making We know that diversity enriches discussion and improves decision-making, as it provides a variety of views and broadens the range of information available, among many other benefits. In Chile, even though women have increased their participation in the labor market, they still do not achieve full and equal participation in all sectors and, as progress is made in the organizational hierarchy, their presence decreases. In the financial and corporate sector, female participation is relatively low, especially at the senior executive level. According to the "Gender Handbook" of the Financial Market Commission, during 2020, local financial market entities presented, in general, a low presence of women on their boards, although with differences between entities. For example, in banking the presence reached 7.1%, in insurance companies 17% and in savings and credit cooperatives it reached 28% (Graph 14). Although the comparison is not perfect, in view of the periodic rebalancing of the indices, a slight but sustained increase has been observed in recent years (2019: 10.10%; 2018: 8.90%). When considering the total number of companies listed on the stock exchange, participation is lower (10.4%), and the increase in recent years is also slower (2019: 9.91%; 2018: 9.01%) (Figures 15 and 16). Women's participation in the Central Bank of Chile In this context, the Bank has been busy increasing the participation of women in a transversal way, valuing diversity in its multiple dimensions, in order to meet its institutional objectives. Indeed, for some years now, we have been making a conscious effort to promote diversity, inclusion and non-discrimination. We have incorporated gender equity practices into the recruitment and selection process, and integrated diversity, inclusion, and gender equity issues into the training of all Bank staff, regardless of hierarchy. Two examples: the participation of men and women in personnel selection committees is required, and in the case of high-level hierarchical positions, it is required to have competitive women in the shortlists or finalists. However, as in other institutions, we face the need to support female leadership, to motivate more women to access these issues and these challenges. Internally, we have promoted the participation of women and accompanied their professional development with the mentoring program, taking advantage of the high presence of women leaders in the highest positions of the Bank, who have joined the challenge of being mentors. The lower presence of women in the financial area is a challenge and it is necessary to motivate and summon students to be part of this challenge and participate in this field of work. As a background, in 2018, 53% of higher education enrollments corresponded to women, but only one in four of them enrolled in careers related to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Aware of this, we are generating links with universities and we have a special program of professional internships aimed at women students, which allowed us to increase their participation. This meant that, during the 2021-2022 period, of the 106 students who did their internship with us, 50% were women. It should be noted that a percentage of these trainees were subsequently hired at the Bank, and of these, 58% are women (7 women out of a total of 12 students). In figures, today, 33% of the Bank's staff is made up of women, a percentage that rises to 50% in senior management. But it's not all about aiming for leadership positions. In 2021, the Bank ranked fifth in the ranking of Best Places to Work for Women, among medium-sized institutions, according to the Great Place to Work measurement. However, I want to tell you that we are not calm. This is a path that is just beginning. Future challenges In conclusion, I would like to refer to the challenges we face at the country level. As you know and as we have shown, there are areas for improvement that will help women to continue advancing in different areas. At the economic level, an important one is to recover women's participation in the labor market that was lost as a result of the pandemic. The opening of schools and kindergartens, and the reactivation of service sectors, will undoubtedly help in this challenge. Beyond this, active policies that promote female employment can be evaluated. This is because there is a high proportion of households headed by women and a prolonged departure from the labor force can carry the risk of human capital losses that could be very important for the country. However, even if participation levels were recovered, we would still be below international standards. In terms of financial inclusion, there is also room for better access for women. In particular, good payment behavior should be reflected in better credit conditions. In this sense, the existence of a consolidated debt registry, which is currently being discussed in Congress, would benefit women in particular. Another objective that should be sought is to have a greater number of women leaders in the financial and corporate sector, given their still low presence on boards. Leadership is often associated with male profiles, which can be uninspiring or can even alienate many female students. Showcasing outstanding professionals, many of whom are part of the community of this university, will greatly contribute to more and more students joining these areas. And, at the level of the Central Bank, our commitment is to continue increasing the number of women in the Institution's staff and to assume leadership positions, as well as deepening a culture free of arbitrary and unconscious biases that betray us in our actions more often than we think. As a society, it is very necessary to advance in the participation of women in different areas, to continue breaking glass ceilings and to contribute to their full potential. It is also important to take into account the great heterogeneity that exists. The need of women is diverse and has many faces, as I pointed out at the beginning. Ciertamente, en un contexto de gran heterogeneidad de desafos que enfrentamos las mujeres, esto deja fuera muchos rostros de millones de mujeres con necesidades diferentes, algunas muy apremiantes. Estoy consciente de ello, y no quisiera invisibilizarlas al centrarme solo en algunas dimensiones de la realidad de tantas mujeres. 1 banco central Chile El rol de la mujer en la economa Las mujeres constituyen un pilar fundamental en la sociedad, desempendose en distintas profesiones y actividades, con el consiguiente impacto en la economa y en los negocios. Nuestros principales informes econmicos y financieros han venido incorporado en los ltimos aos una perspectiva de gnero en el anlisis, contribuyendo as a difundir e informar sobre el rol de la mujer en la economa y contribuir con antecedentes empricos al diseo de polticas pblicas que apoyen su inclusin y permitan desplegar de mejor forma todo su potencial. Ello ha considerado dimensiones como la participacin en el mercado laboral, la inclusin financiera y el aporte al trabajo no remunerado, entre otros. Las mujeres en el mercado laboral En 2018, el Banco public un documento donde analizaba las grandes tendencias del mercado laboral chileno1/. Dicho documento no solo seal el mercado laboral en su conjunto, sino que mir algunos elementos distintivos entre hombres y mujeres, desde donde surgen algunos antecedentes interesantes. En primer lugar, destaca la dinmica de la fuerza de trabajo, la que vena siendo determinada por la mayor participacin de las mujeres y una disminucin ms reciente en la participacin de los trabajadores hombres jvenes menores de 24 aos. Ambos hechos estaban en lnea con la mayor cobertura de la educacin superior y la cada de la tasa de natalidad (grfico 1). Con todo, pese a la creciente participacin de las mujeres en el mercado laboral chileno, sta segua por debajo del promedio de los pases de la OCDE, con una diferencia que se concentraba fuertemente en mujeres menores de 60 aos (grfico 2). En cuanto al tipo de empleo al que acceden las mujeres, los datos muestran una importancia en los sectores de servicios, en lnea con el mayor desarrollo del pas y la relevancia que han adquirido estas actividades. Un tercer hallazgo es que el desempleo de las mujeres tiende a ser ms alto que el de los hombres, lo que se traduce en que la probabilidad de encontrar empleo y de mantenerse 4 banco central Chile ocupado sea menor. La informacin al 2018 mostraba que la probabilidad de encontrar empleo de una mujer desempleada era de 33%, versus 55% de un hombre. Asimismo, una vez ocupadas, la probabilidad de permanecer empleadas era 81% por debajo de la probabilidad de 91% para los hombres. Consecuentemente, la probabilidad de las mujeres de transitar hacia la inactividad triplicaba a la de los hombres (16 vs. 5%). Todos los datos que les he descrito corresponden a la evolucin del mercado laboral previo a la aparicin de la pandemia en marzo de 2020, que tuvo un fuerte impacto en el mercado laboral reduciendo la participacin tanto de hombres como de mujeres en torno a 11 puntos porcentuales. En el caso de la cada de las mujeres, destacan dos factores, por un lado, asumen en mayor proporcin el cuidado del grupo familiar y, por otro, los sectores de servicios son los ms afectados por las restricciones sanitarias, que, como mencion, inciden proporcionalmente ms en el empleo de las mujeres. En los ltimos meses, las tasas de participacin laboral han reducido su distancia respecto del nivel previo a la pandemia (48% versus 53% en el caso de las mujeres y 70 versus 74% en los hombres). Estos rezagos en la participacin son un fenmeno que tambin se observa en varias otras economas. A su vez, la tasa de desocupacin de las mujeres alcanza a 7,7% en enero, mientras la de los hombres se sita en 6,9% (grficos 6 y 7). El Banco ha puesto especial nfasis en la relevancia de este abrupto descenso en el empleo femenino durante la pandemia, y sus causas, buscando explorar cuan persistente puede ser. En el IPoM de junio de 2021, se present un estudio especfico que recogi el testimonio de 5 banco central Chile un conjunto de mujeres que abandonaron la fuerza de trabajo, encontrndonos con diferentes expectativas respecto de su retorno futuro, una vez normalizada la situacin sanitaria. Por un lado, estaban aquellas que esperaban retomar al mercado laboral en condiciones similares a las que tenan previo al inicio de la pandemia. Por el otro, aquellas que no volveran y, un tercer grupo, conformado por aquellas que volveran a un trabajo que fuera compatible con las labores del hogar, tales como el cuidado de nios y preparar la comida o la limpieza, entre otros. Transcurrido varios meses del peor momento de la pandemia y en camino hacia una normalizacin de las diversas actividades, es importante que tanto nuestro anlisis como las distintas polticas pblicas den especial nfasis no solo en la recuperacin de la participacin de las mujeres en el mercado laboral, sino tambin en lograr tasas ms cercanas a las de pases desarrollados. Lo contrario sera renunciar como sociedad a beneficiarnos de su potencial y en lo que a ellas respecta, a su mejor desarrollo y bienestar personal. Medicin del trabajo no remunerado La pandemia ha contribuido a poner de relieve el valor del trabajo en el hogar. No quiero desconocer el mayor aporte de ellos, pero, aun as, las cifras sugieren que la mayor carga no se distribuye equitativamente. Mientras en Chile, las mujeres destinaban en el 2015 unas 2,5 horas ms que los hombres a tareas del hogar diariamente, en los pases OCDE, en aos recientes, con metodologa similar, ellas dedican al da unas 2 horas ms que sus pares masculinos a tareas no remuneradas2. Las cifras preliminares de 2021 dan cuenta de menores horas dedicadas al trabajo domstico no remunerado, tanto de hombres como de mujeres, debido a la gradual apertura de los colegios y de la economa. Con ello, la participacin sobre el PIB sera tambin menor al mximo de 2020, acercndose ms a los valores de 2015. Inclusin financiera de las mujeres La creciente participacin de las mujeres en el mercado laboral y con ello la generacin de ingresos propios, ha tenido un correlato en su inclusin en el mercado financiero. As, en las ltimas dos dcadas se ha observado un incremento de las mujeres que acceden a cuentas bancarias y al crdito. No obstante, este es un mbito en el que persisten diferencias 7 banco central Chile importantes. Por un lado, en promedio, las mujeres acceden con mayor facilidad a cuentas vista que los hombres, patrn que se revierte en las cuentas corrientes (grfico 8). Ello podra explicarse por los requisitos adicionales de ingresos que tienen estas ltimas respecto de la cuenta vista, en particular cuando se les compara con la cuenta RUT. El uso de este ltimo instrumento ha tenido un significativo aumento en los ltimos trimestres, producto de su utilizacin como medio de pago de las polticas de apoyo y del traspaso de los retiros de los fondos de pensiones. El acceso de las mujeres al crdito tambin ha aumentado de forma importante, en los ltimos aos, igualando al de los hombres y superndolo en lo ms reciente (grfico 9). En cuanto al tipo de prstamo, se aprecia que el nmero de deudores en crditos de consumo es similar entre hombres y mujeres, mientras que, en la deuda hipotecaria, en promedio, por cada tres hombres hay dos mujeres deudoras. Y si bien, en trminos de participacin, las brechas se han estrechado en las ltimas dcadas, persisten diferencias en las condiciones de los crditos obtenidos. La participacin de las mujeres en la toma de decisiones Sabemos que la diversidad enriquece la discusin y mejora la toma de decisiones, pues aporta una variedad de visiones y ampla la gama de informacin disponible, entre muchos otros beneficios. En efecto, desde hace algunos aos, estamos haciendo un esfuerzo consciente en promover la diversidad, inclusin y no discriminacin. Sin embargo, como en otras instituciones enfrentamos la necesidad de apoyar el liderazgo femenino, para motivar a ms mujeres a acceder a estos temas y a estos desafos.
